# Introduction

“At the same time that we are earnest to explore and learn all things, we require that all things be mysterious and unexplorable, that land and sea be indefinitely wild, unsurveyed and unfathomed by us because unfathomable.” — Henry David Thoreau, Walden

The world of Exalted is full of larger-than-life heroes, whose adventures run the gamut of sword-and-sorcery, courtly intrigue, gritty survival stories, epic romances, and thrilling heists. Circles and Sworn Kinships undertake eerie expeditions into ghost-filled ruins and set sail on swashbuckling adventures. They bargain with worldly kings, fallen gods, and the sinister courts of the Fair Folk. Creation is full of such settings, and more besides — lands scarred by ancient wars between the Exalted and the gods, islands raised by sorcerous means, empires only a few decades old, and cities that have stood for millennia.

## This Book at a Glance

Chapter One: The North describes lands where winter — growing longer and colder toward Creation’s edge — makes famine, disease, raiding, and war commonplace. Refugees of war and conquest brave not only hunger and blizzards as they seek safe haven, but also ghosts and other horrors that haunt the snows. Chapter Two: The Northeast depicts a lightly settled region still recovering from the so-called Second Contagion centuries ago, which ravaged the region’s cities and conquering Realm alike. Its native peoples now struggle against resurgent foreign intrusion into their ancestral lands.

Across the Eight Directions revisits familiar locations from previous editions and expands on new ones introduced in Exalted Third Edition. This volume is the spiritual successor to Scavenger Sons, the premier setting book for Exalted First Edition. It provides a smorgasbord of locations and peoples of interest — both old and new — across the entire Threshold, while in no way presenting its contents as exhaustive. These subjects don’t comprise the entirety of Creation, but instead offer glimpses of a larger whole that Storytellers and players can expand upon at their tables.

Chapter Three: The Scavenger Lands covers this longstanding center of civilization, its many rivers home to countless quarreling principalities under the watchful, greedy eyes of Lookshyan and Guild hegemony, loosely united at best under the auspices of the Confederation of Rivers.

Chapter Four: The Far East offers a glimpse into the deep forests extending out from the Pole of Wood, home to societies largely isolated from the rest of the world and from one another, and to ancient ruins concealed from scavengers’ eyes.

Here, you’ll visit the underground prison-fortress of Fortitude, whose hereditary gangs ride out to ravage the surrounding countryside; the wintry Haslanti League, its scattered city-states united in scavenging the ruins of a fallen empire; Gentian’s shadow houses, where the ghosts of heretical Dragon-Blooded aristocrats overshadow their living descendants; Chiaroscuro of the broken glass towers, that rich, cosmopolitan entrepôt laboring under the Delzahn steppe nomads’ heel; the sacred library-islets of Tomil Teb, where scribes and scholars study ancient texts among the bones of the dead; and many more.

Chapter Five: The Dreaming Sea addresses the mighty supernatural empires and prehuman civilizations that struggle for dominance in the far Southeast, from Ysyr’s sorcerer-princes to the body-swapping relicts of timeless Tzakul. Chapter Six: The South ranges from the warm Inland Sea coast to the deep desert, where command of water, wealth, and trade concentrates urban power in

EX3

Chapter Nine: The Northwest unveils the weird occult powers at work in this chill, isolated region. Everything here is touched by supernatural horror, from the dying ancient beneath the Silverswept Plains to the twisting spiral magic that veils the Lost Isles of Aiun.

### SAFETY RULES

Exalted«s setting often deals with unpleasant — and sometimes problematic — topics, such as slavery, discrimination, prejudice, poverty, and more. Before beginning the chronicle, Storytellers and players should discuss whether any of the setting’s elements or themes might be upsetting or triggering, and how best to avoid distress.

Appendix: The World We Know touches briefly on a variety of topics relevant to Creation as a whole, such as the heavens, timekeeping, languages, and wildlife.

The form this takes will vary from table to table; some players might prefer not to deal with these topics directly in-game, others may ask that scenes involving them fade to black and the plot picks up afterwards. A player might not be aware a setting element is upsetting to them until it comes up in play. It’s also possible that what’s okay for a participant one session might not be the next: current events, a stressful week, and other outside factors can affect one’s capacity or willingness to engage with these topics.

## Suggested Resources

Below are some resources that may help you get a feel for Creation’s themes or supplement your story with real-world historical and cultural information.

### Fiction

The Eyes of the Overworld and Cugel’s Saga, by Jack Vance: These books cover all sorts of weird, scattershot locations with their own distinct issues, often with idiosyncratic ancient magical goings-on that don’t always fit neatly with the reader’s — or, in the case of Exalted, the player’s — understanding of how things work.

At any time, we encourage Storytellers and players to change or ignore setting elements so everyone at the table can feel safe and enjoy the game. Remember to check in with one another from time to time, and encourage each other to speak up if someone needs to pause the action, end a scene, or backtrack and make changes to their characters’ actions.

The Lies of Locke Lamora and Red Seas Under Red Skies, by Scott Lynch: The city of Camorr’s towers, bridges, and other structures were built out of strange materials by a people long-vanished, reminiscent of the First Age wonders scattered throughout Creation. The second book includes a band of pirates who’d be at home harrying the Merchant Fleet in the West.

If your group unanimously agrees to explore these topics, consider employing negotiation techniques like the X-Card, fading to black, and lines and veils to allow everyone at the table the flexibility to engage as much or as little as they prefer. For a more in-depth discussion of safety tools and how to use them at your table, please see Crucible of Legends. the hands of a few, from the psychic twin queens of the fortress-city of Ember to the mysterious, demonic Benefactors of festive Dajaz.

Chapter Seven: The Southwest discusses the faltering kingdoms of a region whose empires have historically unraveled over the centuries, from the cruel squabbling of the Lintha pirate septs to the civil war brewing among the warlike Dayfire clans after their unifying prince Konthoi’s assassination. Chapter Eight: The West showcases the region’s wealthy islands, whose long independence is coming to an end. Some, like Wavecrest, have fallen to the Realm; others find themselves subject to expanding local powers such as Azure’s sea lords or the pekumi warrior-artisans of Randan.

Master and Commander by Patrick O’Brian: O’Brian’s Aubrey-Maturin series gives readers a glimpse of life at sea and an understanding of nautical terminology and customs through the landsman Stephen Maturin’s eyes. The Phoenix Empress, by K. Arsenault Rivera: This series’ protagonists interact with local gods in a way that’s reminiscent of Creation. Storytellers building their own locales or setting up conflict between canonical Exalted polities might take inspiration from Rivera’s depiction of struggles between various cultures and her challenge of imperialism.

### Nonfiction

1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus, by Charles C. Mann: This book presents lots of great historical and cultural inspiration on pre-Columbian societies in the Americas. Many of

EX3

these are particularly appropriate for Northeastern and Far Eastern societies like the Gathering Suns, the Maremé nation, and Land-Under-Robe.

### NATURALISTIC FANTASY

For all of its post-apocalyptic, sword-and-sorcery trappings, Exalted has always been rooted in verisimilitude. This book aims to present peoples and polities whose politics, economics, warfare, religions, and cultures appear plausible, reflecting how real people might act even in the presence of supernatural forces.

Against the Grain, by James C. Scott: An excellent resource, offering details about the intersection of society and food that can show up in actual play. This book addresses topics like the conflict between hunter-gatherer societies and settled ones, how nomadic peoples sculpt their environment, and so forth. Orientalism, by Edward Said: This book takes a critical look at how the West depicts Asian, North African, and Middle Eastern societies. Said’s work is an excellent starting place for Storytellers and players who want to approach portraying other cultures with care and thoughtfulness.

Salt: A World History, by Mark Kurlansky: Accessible and intriguing, this book examines how the demand for salt carved out trade routes, financed wars, and inspired revolutions. Storytellers can gain insight on a particular commodity’s influence over a region, and the ways in which it interconnects humanity. Seeing Like a State, by James C. Scott: This book addresses a broad range of topics on historical societies and governments that’s useful to Exalted play, ranging

from urban planning to state languages to how revolutions happen.

### Television

She-Ra and the Princesses of Power, developed by Noelle Stevenson: Not only are Adora and Mara great examples of Exalted reincarnation, Etheria is a world full of diverse cultures that exists in the ruins of a more advanced society.

### Podcasts

Hardcore History, by Dan Carlin: This well-researched podcast takes a closer look at historical events, and presents them in an engaging, narrative format.

Tsuura hummed a battle song as she swung down from her saddle to examine the body of a fallen defender. She recognized the old man — he’d been a beardless boy the first time she rode out from Fortitude with her war band, and they’d traded blows many times when the Uznikane came reaving. A war cry split the air, full of the overeager note that told her someone was on his way to doing something regrettable. Tsuura was the veteran of hundreds of raids, maybe thousands; she’d stopped counting her victories two decades ago. The sound of trouble whooping from a young warrior’s throat was the same now as when she was young.

As he tore past, she snatched him by his fur-lined hood. It was like scruffing a large kitten, only instead of claws he bore a saber in one hand and a lit torch in the other. He struggled at first, perhaps thinking one of his friends had grabbed him to gain an unfair advantage in their race towards mayhem. Then his brain caught up, and he realized who’d halted his charge. “Gray Tsuura,” he breathed, his eyes flicking from the silver plaits in her hair to the wrinkled hand that held him fast, then back to her weathered and battle-scarred face. She’d been leading raids since his grandmother was in diapers; he was at least smart enough to recognize who’d stopped him and quit his squirming.

“Where are you headed with that torch?” For a moment, she thought he might try to hide it behind his back and deny its existence. And singe his ass in the process.

To his credit, he held it steady. Molten pitch dripped onto his wrist, but the boy didn’t flinch. From the colors he bore, he was a member of the Jagged Thorns. The gang prided themselves on their immunity to pain. “To... to the stables?”

Tsuura resisted the urge to cuff him. The Thorns weren’t known for their cleverness. “The stables that still have horses in them. Tell me, if we kill all the horses now, how far out will you ride to find new mounts? The cattle pens are next to them. If the oxen die in your ill-thought fire, how will the people till the fields come spring?”

He frowned. “That’s for them to figure out.”

She cuffed him after all, pleased at his grunt of pain. These youths, so eager to make names for themselves, they forgot why Fortitude went raiding. “What do we eat if their fields lie fallow? What keeps us clothed and our bellies full if the shepherds are too dead to tend their sheep? Take your torch and find Dergen. Tell him Tsuura said you’re too stupid to be here and help him burn the dead.” The boy ran, smoke from his torch marking his path across the battlefield. He’d learn, eventually, the difference between raids like this one and those where the fight was the entire purpose. Perhaps someday soon he’d test his mettle against garrison soldiers rather than townspeople wielding farming implements. Tsuura cared little about the Realm’s troubles to the south, but she had to admit the turmoil caused by the Scarlet Empress’s disappearance had made Uznikane attacks on nearby towns much easier. The satraps simply didn’t have the resources to protect all the towns in their domains every time riders boiled out of Fortitude. Tsuura missed the challenge.

She turned back to the dead man and pulled the spear from his chest before she headed deeper into the town. No use wasting a perfectly good weapon.

# Chapter One: The North

Chapter One

The North

Most see the North as a land of winter. Indeed, snow and cold weather have at least some hold throughout this Direction. But the Inland Sea’s coast is temperate, its summers warm and its winters cool. Even the White Sea’s long, bitter winters are tempered by hot — albeit short — summers. Farther north lie expanses of cold prairie and taiga, and only beyond that does greenery give way to tundra and glacier.

Still, privation leaves its mark across the North. Shorter growing seasons and fewer viable crops — wheat instead of rice, for instance, or rye instead of wheat — lead to hunger; hunger beckons peasants into banditry and piracy. Predators, likewise hungry, prey on domesticated animals or even attack humans. City dwellers packed indoors through the winter suffer from all manner of pestilence. Icebergs and fog wreck ships. Scarcity fosters war over vital resources. Fatalistic resignation is common, and many cultures emphasize the ancestor cult as an escape from doom-laden life into an afterlife free of hunger and cold.

Northern cultures find their own ways to come to terms with these hardships. They may focus on cooperation and building strong communities, or on fiercely raiding neighbors and rivals. Nomadic peoples focus on herding or hunting, relying on meat to endure lean winters, while settled folk struggle to keep granaries full. Scavenged relics of former ages serve not only as sources of wealth, but as means for survival. Superstition is rife, and pacts with gods, sorcerers, and other supernatural beings can prove the difference between life and death.

## Fortitude

Fortitude’s walls rise stark and gray over the surrounding prairie. The remains of its once-mighty guard towers graze the sky like jagged, rotten teeth. Sections of the foreboding stone walls lie in ruins, but the city is far from dead or abandoned. Within the gates, a perilous market of visiting merchants thrives. But this isn’t Fortitude proper. The true city lies underground, in a vast network of tunnels ruled by gangs and minor warlords. There, only the strongest thrive.

### History

Fortitude was originally a prison-fortress built by the Tsarkuur empire, whose religion asserted that criminals inherited the inclination to commit crime. When capturing thieves, murderers, and political enemies, authorities also rounded up their families to serve life sentences. Smaller cells housed one or two inmates; others — only slightly larger — accommodated entire households.

The prisoners were slave laborers, farming the area’s rocky, impoverished soil and toiling in its mines. The empire also seized skilled artisans, forcing them to weave textiles, forge armor, and distill alcohol. Once, their hard-earned mastery supported their families; now it profited Tsarkuur, attracting merchants until the fortress became a city. Wary that vengeful hungry ghosts might arise, the empire stationed funerists alongside the guards. Captive priests were compelled to perform final rites for fellow prisoners. Tsarkuur fell long ago, but the prison continued operating during its lengthy decline. Its guard force dwindled as opposing factions of the splintering empire called them home to fight. Many simply deserted. Eventually, the prisoners revolted and overthrew their remaining jailers.

Though freedom was theirs, most of Fortitude’s former prisoners didn’t leave. They had nowhere to return to, their lands and homes long since sold off or left in ruins. Others had only ever called the prison’s cells and tunnels home. Together, they claimed the fortress as their domain.

While Fortitude’s residents expanded the city above, they dedicated most of their efforts to the vast network of cells and tunnels underground. Subterranean wards became gang territories ruled by ruthless, charismatic leaders. As the city grew, workers dug new tunnels to accommodate the increasing population and to expand their living quarters beyond their cramped cells.

EX3

Fortitude’s farmers — gang members unfit for battle or in disgrace, reinforced by slaves — continued working the land. But the empire’s stores had always supplemented local crops, and harvests fell short of keeping bellies full. Without an influx of additional food and supplies, the fortress’s inhabitants set their sights — and spears — on nearby territories and their bounties.

### Culture

Fortitude’s people call themselves Uznikane, or “prisoner” in the Tsarkuur language, proudly reclaiming the word from their ancestors’ jailers. Prison society’s harsh, unforgiving rules echo throughout present-day Fortitude; survival depends on making tough decisions in volatile circumstances, and on being stronger than rivals attempting to seize one’s resources, people, or territory. Characterized by outsiders as brutal and selfish, the Uznikane rely on these traits to stay alive. Kill or be killed, seize or starve; they do whatever it takes to live another day.

The Uznikane prize meat above other foods. Gangs send hunting parties into surrounding lands for boar, deer, and waterfowl. Successful hunters earn a place of pride

at banquets. Hunters and warriors eat first, receiving the choicest portions seasoned with spices seized from merchants’ caravans. Lesser gang members content themselves with bland stews of farmed produce — oats, vegetables, and the occasional carp or chicken — and scraps from the warriors’ table. Likewise, warriors and a few skilled brewers drink plundered wine and the best Fortitude beer, while the rest consume the brewer’s dross. Gathering fruit, herbs, berries, roots, and mushrooms is considered children’s work; bands of youngsters stake claims on spots rich in foodstuffs, and bicker or brawl over the day’s take.

Gangs control food distribution within their own territories. Those too weak to find a place in a gang, members of subordinate gangs, and those who fare poorly at hunting are fed at the whim of the territory’s dominant leadership. This can cause instability — whether the unfed underclass rises up or flees, or because gang members resent their leader’s generosity toward people whom they deem undeserving. Most wear a deel or caftan with a leather cloak and boots, often trimmed with fur. Each gang has its own colors and symbols with which members adorn their clothing. Likewise, many gangs maintain distinctive

### Social Structure

While not everyone in Fortitude joins a gang, gangs dominate society; dozens claim sections of the underground city as their turf. Their colors and symbols adorn the walls, declaring to observant passers-by who’s in charge. Lesser gangs vie to control contested areas, leading to frequent skirmishes as territories change hands.

Hierarchy varies between gangs, though most have a single leader. Often, she’s a charismatic person who’s climbed through the ranks herself, racking up a body count of rivals and enemies. Maybe she’s won back a chunk of lost territory or negotiated a truce with a neighboring outfit, or her strength lies in talking circles around her competition and surrounding herself with loyal muscle. Other times, gang leadership stays within a family, passed down from parent to child. Several Uznikane households still bear imprisoned ancestors’ names.

Leadership positions are rarely secure. Leaders must constantly prove their strength or cleverness. Weak rulers don’t stay in power long.

A handful of close associates typically report to gang leaders, keeping them abreast of issues within their territory or challenges brewing with other bands. Captains, enforcers, lieutenants, and street-level soldiers beneath these associates carry out day-to-day operations — collecting payments from merchants under the gang’s protection, guarding shipments through the tunnels, or raiding rival gangs’ caches. Fortitude has no formal legal code. Gang members settle disputes and keep the peace within their territories, abiding by principles their leader dictates. When a conflict can’t be resolved by lower-level members, the gang leader may settle the argument personally. Wise citizens avoid letting it reach that point, lest an exasperated leader punish everyone who can’t reconcile their differences.

Gang hierarchy, like gang leadership, is always in flux. A charismatic leader can transform a ragtag group of nobodies and weaklings into Fortitude’s most brutal and feared gang. Likewise, a powerful organization can grow overconfident and fritter away its strength,

creating an opening for an upstart rival to destroy it. Gangs unravel and new ones form over the course of hours or decades.

Gangs have little use for those whom their leaders deem physically, mentally, or emotionally unfit. Some gangs support members whom age and injury leave unable to contribute; indeed, Fortitude’s artisans specialize in prosthetics and adaptive devices. Other gangs cast such members out. When a gang collapses, it takes time for other gangs to snap up its most able members, and longer still for the rest to find places — if they can at all. Many Uznikane find themselves living in territory controlled by a gang not their own. Some keep their heads down, avoiding rival gang members and not drawing attention. They funnel observations about those rivals to their own leaders. Others provoke fights to prove themselves. Those who belong to no gang quickly learn new leaders’ rules and expectations when territory changes hands.

Though most cells were stripped of their bars centuries ago, the Uznikane still keep prisoners. Many are outsiders captured on raids or caught sneaking into the city. Others are citizens deeply indebted to a gang. A few are disgraced gang members. Inhabiting the coldest, dampest, oldest cells, these slaves are only let out to work. Some harvest medicinal plants and nourishing fungi whose sunless growth comes from Wyld-tainted seeds or from ancient sorceries soaked into the surrounding stone. Others dig precious gems from mines below the city.

### Governance

Several larger organizations currently dominate the Uznikane, most notably the God Killers, the Storm Boys, and the Mother’s Knives. Having once waged sweeping turf wars, they’ve recently forged a tentative truce. Rather than turning Fortitude into a battleground, they’ve brought lesser gangs to heel via bullying and favors. United, they intend to sweep out of the city in a horde to pillage nearby targets. While each gang runs its territory as it sees fit, major gangs keep lesser ones in line on matters affecting Fortitude as a whole. For example, the God Killers currently ensure that caravans pay protection money only once. Gangs who extort more funds or attack visiting caravans find their provisions severely restricted, or their cuts of plunder heavily garnished until they’ve repaid the debt. Repeat offenders meet swift judgment from the God Killers’ blades.

EX3

Not all relationships with outsiders are antagonistic. The Uznikane trade with nearby towns for certain staples, such as foodstuffs and ceramics. Rather than send intimidatingly battle-scarred warriors to treat with local politicians, gang leaders typically choose deft negotiators who know when to compromise and when to threaten. But threats must be subtle; Fortitude’s violent reputation already makes foreign negotiators wary, and its neighbors have joined forces against it before.

### Religion and Philosophy

Ventilation shafts allow some daylight in, and lamps light major tunnels, but the dark always waits. The Uznikane worship it. It surrounds them from birth until death, always poised to embrace them forever. Conversely, winter is their enemy. Every year, cold creeps into the tunnels, ushering in famine. Nearby settlements with plentiful harvests fight to protect their stores from Uznikane raiders when the weather turns. The fiercer the winter, the more meager the spoils. Deep beneath Fortitude, in tunnels far older than the prison-fortress, lies the city’s primal deity, the Buried God. It holds dominion over dying unknown and unremembered in the dark. It cares little for mortal affairs, though its influence can be felt in fatalistic Uznikane beliefs. Sometimes the dark, the cold, or both require a sacrifice. The Uznikane send a chosen victim — this is both a great honor and a doom to be feared — into old, unused tunnels without water, light, or food. There they wander until cold or hunger takes them, or until they suffer a fatal accident in the pitch black. The sacrifice pleases the god, who provides the Uznikane with some meager relief before it ignores them anew, stirring warmer air currents toward the upper tunnels or driving swarms of vermin toward the surface that people might eat.

Outwork-Shrines

Several outworks — outlying fortalices connected to the main fortress by crumbling bridges and moldering tunnels — hold a liminal role in Uznikane religion. They’re seen as part of Uznikane territory but outside the Buried God’s domain. As such, they serve as shrines for lesser spirits with which Fortitude’s people might bargain, such as field gods, deities of violence and murder, and occasional Uznikane ancestors. The Uznikane acknowledge these spirits without revering them, much like praising and making offerings to a gang boss; bargains with them are largely transactional. Priests live in these outwork-shrines, dining on sacrificed animals and other offerings. They typically maintain long-term connections with their original gangs, conveying the spirit’s blessing in exchange for regular sacrifices. But priest-gang affiliations can lead to cutthroat political intrigue — and occasionally to violent ends.

The Uznikane practice sky burials. As Fortitude’s citizens spend most of their lives underground, this final rite exposes them at last to the sky. Funerists transport the deceased to the rooftops of outwork-shrines, where the elements and carrion creatures aid in decomposition.

### Locations

A few of Fortitude’s residents never leave the tunnels. They’ve never seen the wide-open sky, and only feel rain when it drips down through leaky ceilings. Most inhabitants, however, spend at least some time aboveground.

Fortitude’s people believe they’re cursed to bear the weight of great sins from the moment they’re born. Only by performing heroic deeds and dying epic deaths may they atone. Although they retell fallen warriors’ heroic deeds and accept spectral aid when offered, they feel that ghosts should pass on rather than linger; all Uznikane deserve rest after hard lives underground. Many gangs boast champions who embody the gang’s ideals. Heroes rise among the unaffiliated as well — it takes incredible bravery to stand up to the gang captain threatening your family. Savvy gang leaders quickly offer such a champion a place among their ranks or dispatch their own heavies to hasten their epic death. Folk heroes make great stories, but can threaten a gang’s authority.

EX3

### REMNANTS OF TSARKUUR

While the empire is long gone, ruins riddle the landscape, a reminder of what went before. Stave temples — with their distinctive ore-pine posts, palisade walls, and sloping wooden roofs — offer raiders shelter. Built on stone foundations and constructed to withstand harsh winter weather, these structures linger even though the gods once worshiped within moved on centuries ago.

Some Tsarkuur customs persist, passed down among the prisoners’ descendants. “Long songs,” dubbed that for their length and their lyrics’ complex, sustained syllables, depict the mountains and the open sky — things some Uznikane never see. Musicians playing the horsehead fiddle accompany the singers.

Gangs divvy up patrol duties. Merchants meet and bargain with traders who dare enter the city’s gates. Farmers tend meager crops coaxed from rocky soil.

The Old Fortress

After the empire’s fall, the Uznikane allowed the oldest parts of the above-ground fortress to fall to ruins, the symbols of their jailers’ power left to rot. Large portions have collapsed. The Uznikane cleared out those dead wings to salvage materials for housing, smithies, stables, and other structures. Now, those empty spaces serve as staging grounds for raids and training grounds for warriors. Other parts of the old fortress remain overgrown — a labyrinth of tumbled walls, trees, moss, and ivy.

The Upper Market

Inside the southern gate, a year-round bazaar known as the Upper Market operates. Caravans pay protection money for safe passage to Fortitude to trade with gang liaisons. Inns, stables, and other businesses accommodate travelers’ needs. It’s a busy market, but not the sort of boisterous jumble of people hawking wares one finds in other cities. People eye each other warily. Savvy merchants have bodyguards watch their stalls; nonetheless, scuffles break out regularly. Prominent gangs station enforcers here, ensuring caravans and foreign merchants aren’t hassled unduly.

The Tunnels

Few outsiders venture into Fortitude’s lawless stonecarved tunnels. Close to the surface, tunnels are broad enough for carts to traverse and Uznikane vendors to set up shops against the walls. Sconces and braziers provide light and warmth; in some places, ventilation shafts or decay admit shafts of meager daylight. Tunnels grow narrower and more labyrinthine as one goes deeper. Most Uznikane carry candles or oil lamps for when errands take them into ill-lit branches. Many citizens live in alcoves and alleys carved into dead-end branches, scratching out a living while trying to steer clear of gang politics. Cooks dish out soup from community cauldrons, residents refilling it with what scraps they can spare. Children dart about on errands or sit at an artisan’s feet learning skills and performing simple, tedious apprentice tasks. Smaller gangs — sometimes merely semi-organized groups of residents dedicated to mutual aid and defense — often claim tunnel segments, demanding payment from passersby.

The Lower Market

Residents visit the Lower Market, several levels belowground, to purchase or trade services for food,

medicine, imported supplies, and other necessary goods. Bodyguards and hitmen hire themselves out here; information brokers earn a hefty wage knowing other peoples’ business.

The Uznikane have no standard currency. Gangs frequently manage their own systems of credit, granting some control over commerce in their territory. Sufficiently powerful leaders negotiate trade agreements with other gangs, though conflicts and rivalries cause unpredictable fluctuations in exchange rates. Merchants keep their own books, accepting hacksilver for expensive purchases or colorful beetle carapaces for smaller ones.

Violence is prohibited in the Lower Market. Even members of warring gangs abide by the truce while among the stalls. Imported goods and food are too valuable to risk destroying in a brawl, and retribution comes swiftly from all sides to anyone who breaks the brittle peace. Shopkeepers and traders do occasionally overcharge or sell poor-quality goods, but they do well to remember that the no-violence rule only extends to the market’s boundaries. Wronged parties can accost a homeward-bound cheat with little fear of reprisal. Lower Market merchants use a network of broad stairways, sloping tunnels, and shafts with pulley systems to bring goods down from the Upper Market. As these lie outside the Lower Market’s boundaries, merchants must either give a cut of their profits to every gang whose territory they move product through, hire bodyguards to protect their goods, or align themselves with a patron gang that provides an escort.

### Prominent Figures

The proud, ferocious God Killers answer to the cunning warrior Tuyaa the Hammer, who seized power at fifteen. Her hair’s gone gray as she approaches fifty, but her arm’s as strong as ever. Being in Tuyaa’s good graces opens doors for ambitious Uznikane — her memory for other gang leaders’ sins is long and sharp, and she’ll share that information for the right price. Her advisor and childhood friend Esen helped negotiate the current truce between the major gangs. He knows which gang leaders need egos soothed and which need their courage questioned to make them act.

Amar, leader of the jovially cruel Storm Boys, is new to his position. Most believe he’d prefer to pluck his shanz than lead the gang, but his predecessor made that mistake, and it was her last. Amar’s a planner; he waited years to set his coup in motion. He surrounds himself

### Neighbors

### CREATING A GANG

Fortitude is an ever-looming threat for nearby settlements and satrapies. Raids boil out unpredictably, their targets unknown until warriors thunder along the road. Whether the riders trade or pillage depends on which gang rides out and who leads them. Their presence affects trade routes, defenses, harvests, and holy days. Even a tentative trade relationship with the Uznikane can crumble on a whim.

Some questions for Storytellers and players to answer when designing a Fortitude gang include: Who’s in charge, and how do they lead their people? How large or small is the gang? How is its hierarchy structured? What two adjectives best describe the gang’s members and their outlook? What territory have they claimed in the city? Who are their closest rivals and allies? What’s their relationship with non-gang citizens in their territory? What issues does their presence solve or create for their territory’s residents?

with loyal muscle, including the quick-witted, sardonic champion Tiren — the former gang leader’s eldest daughter.

The taciturn, ruthless Mother’s Knives look to dour Naran for leadership. She’s kept bellies full throughout her territory for ten years via strategic raids on neighboring towns, and by striking deals with Lower Market merchants and Upper Market trade princes. Uznikane needing rare items or hard-to-procure imports go through Naran, though it means scratching their mark in the gang leader’s thick debt ledger. At her right hand sits the sorceress Yisa, who left Fortitude as a young woman to seek a tutor for her craft; Uznikane whisper about what hold she might have over Naran. Not affiliated with any gang, Red Lilet is a folk hero of the western ward. This past year, she’s driven out gang influence from her home turf, rallying cowed inhabitants to stand against their oppressors. Several gangs have tried to bring her to heel through violence or bribes, but she’s rebuffed every effort thus far. Rumor has it she escaped from the mines below and intends to rouse the enslaved prisoners there to rebellion. As a boy, Thaach the Herald got lost exploring the deep tunnels. He wandered — hungry, cold, and afraid — feeling his way in the dark when his lamp gave out. He re-emerged weeks later, accompanied by a swarm of rats that kept the Uznikane fed through the winter. Citing a profound encounter with the Buried God, Thaach dedicated himself to the spirit, becoming one of its most prominent priests. Old now, he advises gang leaders on the god’s desires and helps choose sacrifices. Thaach steers the gangs toward creating prosperity for all Uznikane; he doesn’t want his people to grow soft-hearted and lax like the villages they raid, but he’s twice declared egregiously cruel or greedy gang leaders the Buried God’s chosen.

Northwest of Fortitude, the satrapy of Jagged Branch breeds horses and cattle. Its old warrior aristocracy, now merchant landowners, control most land and wealth alongside recently arrived Blessed Isle tycoons; common folk scratch by in farming villages and port towns.

Historically, Jagged Branch had no central governance until the Realm conquered its scattered settlements. Upon the previous prince’s death, satrap Ragara Banoba Merac arranged the election of the current prince, Bagar; she valued his political connections among local elites and his forthright willingness to be bought. With the garrison focused on guarding patricians’ ranches, Bagar works hard to meet Uznikane demands and please their representatives. He occasionally hires gang members to reclaim stolen cattle. He likes the implied threat that he might send the Uznikane after nearby enemies and uses it to his advantage in negotiations. Of late, Jagged Branch suffers attacks from Gray Rokin, a Silver Pact witch who spreads disease among herds and unleashes ravenous pests on crops. Thus far, Bagar has kept Fortitude supplied and the Realm’s tribute flowing despite Lunar depredations, but eventually he’ll be unable to meet everyone’s demands. He wonders how — or whether — he can pit the three against one another and leave Jagged Branch standing. Once a Fajadi colony, the satrapy of Tovar is distinctive for brickwork onion domes on civic architecture, heavily herbed clay-pot recipes, and cataphract-saint folktales that reframe old gods, ancestors, and prophets as Immaculate heroes. Its fertile soil once made it a regional breadbasket, though aggression from Fortitude to the east — greatly increased since the leading gangs united — means many fields along the border lie fallow. Tovar’s once-stable trade relationship with Fortitude collapsed after Queen Ganaay’s advisors insulted Fortitude’s representatives, undervaluing Uznikane work and offering unfavorable terms. Today, raiders sweep in and take food, textiles, building materials,

EX3

and prisoners to work the mines. Many survivors gather their families and flee before their luck runs out; abandoned farms and empty silos bespeak Uznikane rapacity.

Ganaay has exhausted her own considerable wealth fortifying Tovar’s defenses, to little avail, and struggles to wring taxes and troops from her vassals. Satrap Mnemon Pel asked her house for aid months ago, but with civil war brewing, her distant satrapy is a low priority. Scraping together tribute payment grows increasingly difficult, and tax increases breed resentment from nobles and rebellion among artisans and serfs. Tovar’s queen explores other means to repel the Uznikane, including expeditions into Lysand Wood, whose trees whisper secrets. Their roots grow deep and wide, extending far beyond the forest. Tendrils even snake deep into neighboring Fortitude’s lower levels, eavesdropping on gang leaders’ plots and heroes’ hopes. Their words flow back to the forest to be stored in its trees’ heartwood. Centuries of voices intermingle in their sap.

Wisdom-seeking Uznikane venture into Lysand Wood to learn their gang’s history, winnow out enemies’ secrets, and discover their destinies. Mixed with certain herbs harvested beneath Fortitude, the trees’ sap has hallucinogenic properties with which Uznikane priests induce prophetic visions.

Observing Fortitude for centuries has given the forest violent dreams. Its roots draw blood-tinged moisture from soil soaked by gang warfare; the trees have developed a taste for it. Not all who venture into Lysand Wood return. Those who do report seeing eerie likenesses of the lost in whorls of tree bark.

## Whitewall

Nestled amid mountains, taiga, and rolling fields, the city of Whitewall takes its name from its encircling walls of pale stone. Fifteen yards high and blessed by the mysterious divine Syndics, these ancient fortifications ward off the surrounding lands’ nightwalking perils: the monstrous dead and the soul-devouring Fair Folk. Whitewall’s farmlands and mines lie outside the walls, but their workers live within the city proper. Thousands crowd the streets at daybreak waiting for the gates to open. They return at sunset, and soldiers watch to ensure that no one enters or leaves after nightfall. Once the sun sets, horrors emerge; anyone caught outside the walls is fair game.

### Life in Whitewall

Winters are long and harsh. Frigid temperatures and frequent blizzards make travel to and from the city nigh-impossible outside of the short summer months. Residents favor heavy, layered clothing; they especially prize furs. City foresters maintain rows of coppiced groves between the outlying fields, producing a steady flow of firewood they ration out to families and businesses.

Whitewall can barely house or feed its current population of over half a million. Locals live alongside refugees from lands near and far — even a few from the Bull of the North’s distant empire — who’ve fled the chaos burgeoning since the Empress’s disappearance: war, disease, famine, or monsters. These displaced folk huddle in almshouses cared for by priests of many faiths. They weather both personal trauma and locals’ increasing intolerance.

To accommodate more people within the walls, landowners hastily add new floors to tenements, with many reaching as high as seven stories. Snow and rain fall from sloping roofs to cramped cobbled streets below, staining the buildings’ white walls gray. Workers shovel snow into the many roadside grates leading into the sewers; it winds its way out of Whitewall to the Salmon River through a maze of filth and excrement. Thousands of homeless people live amid the sewers’ filth — the almshouses can’t accommodate them all. Lacking housing options, poorer citizens share overcrowded rooms with family and friends; fear of the horrors outside makes them wary of whom they invite into their company. Whitewall has thus become a city of isolated communities, where different languages, faiths, and ideologies dominate each district. Each community tells its own tales about the nightly threats. Some whisper of ghosts and demons possessing children’s toys, inciting misbehavior. Others describe patchwork corpses roaming the surrounding woods. Most common are tales of the Winter Folk, summer-hating fae donning human guises to gain welcome into people’s homes.

Onions, potatoes, parsnips, carrots, skirret, and beets comprise much of Whitewall’s cuisine; roasted whole or boiled and puréed into soups, they warm the bones. Blackberries and blueberries grow wild in summer, providing a sweet filling for hand pies or preserved as jellies and jams for winter. Foragers seek sorrel, rampion, nettle, and wild garlic to flavor dishes. The river’s eponymous salmon are long since extirpated by overfishing

EX3

and pollution; serfs consume occasional cheese, eggs, or small game, but meat is largely for the rich. With disease, famine, and crime rising as ever more people are forced into squalor, many locals grow increasingly xenophobic. As refugees offer themselves up as thralls (p. XX) just to get food and warmth, locals protest the Syndics’ generosity, claiming that jobs are becoming scarce. Groups who want to send the refugees out into the night increase in power and influence.

remains in their hands in violation of Heavenly law. They demonstrate little forbearance for those who protest their edicts, sometimes sending soldiers to their homes to eject them from the city.

### Government

In the city’s center stands the massive Congregation Hall, a government building ringed by three white towers, each a single Syndic’s sanctuary. Congregation Hall constantly bustles with bureaucrats, workers, soldiers, and citizens seeking redress. Archivists and lawmasters keep offices within; some of its luxurious rooms host foreign dignitaries through the winter.

The Syndics

Congregations

A triumvirate of mysterious spirits sculpted from silver and ice rule Whitewall. These are the Syndics: all three look eerily alike, but one appears feminine, one masculine, and the third androgynous. Though people find them alien and disconcerting, their divine blessings protect the city. The Syndics regard Whitewall as a collective, which they value more than any single citizen. Though they allow the collective a show of self-governance in a weekly meeting called a congregation, ultimate authority

Congregations offer the Syndics insight into their people’s hearts. Hundreds attend, filling a large chamber within Congregation Hall. Thousands more crowd the streets outside, waiting for heralds to emerge and announce what’s being discussed, often to cheers and hisses in equal measure. Participants and onlookers alike offer the Syndics a brief, customary prayer before deliberations open.

Deliberations go on for hours; they’re usually rowdy affairs. Dedicated largely to political questions regarding employment, poverty, crime, and immigration, they’re

EX3

thralls, serfs are free persons, but they must remain silent within congregations and can’t defend themselves in court unless backed by a tiun or boyar. Serfs who acquire property become tiuns; tiuns who lose all property become serfs. Most citizens are serfs.

### RELIGION IN WHITEWALL

Religion is largely private. Common folk worship Whitewall’s myriad minor gods at small temples tucked away inside tenements. The Syndics maintain no temples of their own, but they’re privately revered by many. Citizens erect tiny shrines to them in homes or along side streets.

Thralls are property of tiuns or boyars, laboring on their masters’ behalf. They can’t attend congregations or defend themselves in court, but they’re still considered people. Their owners must feed, clothe, and house them, and abusing them could lead to fines or losing the right to own thralls. Many tiuns and boyars persuade refugees to volunteer as thralls with promises of eventual serfdom. Thralls’ children are emancipated as serfs.

Many refugees still worship their own gods, a few of whom accompanied their followers to Whitewall. Priests of local and foreign gods largely get along in trying to tend to everyone’s spiritual needs, though squabbles between gods often mirror conflicts between Whitewall natives and refugees. There’s little ancestor cult to speak of in Whitewall. Ghosts who arise in the city know well that they’re unwelcome; once they leave, the Syndics’ pact keeps them from returning. Of late, a few refugees have invited their ancestors into the city, provoking retaliation when residents find out.

opportunities for organizations or individuals to settle disputes. A Syndic always oversees the proceedings, though they rarely engage. Attendees cast votes to settle disputes or suggest policy changes; the Syndic ratifies or vetoes a decision based on whether they feel it’s in Whitewall’s best interest. Despite the Syndics’ intolerance towards those who question them elsewhere, their people regard congregations as safe opportunities to speak their minds.

The Quaternions

Whitewall’s societal hierarchy consists of four classes, collectively termed the Quaternions.

Boyars have been granted nobility by a Syndic. They’re often major landowners, influential merchants, or high-ranking military officers. Their voices greatly outweigh others in congregations, and they often escape justice through generous bribes or by invoking trial by combat.

Tiuns own property within or around Whitewall. They’re usually artisans, farmers, low-ranking officers, or common soldiers. They may employ serfs or own thralls, and are allowed to speak in congregations. When charged with a crime, they can defend themselves in court, but cannot invoke trial by combat. Serfs are unpropertied laborers, often working for nothing but food, a bed, or the occasional coin. Unlike

Visitors — including refugees who decline thralldom — have no legal rights in Whitewall, but money and influence go a long way. Visitors with great wealth or influence, such as foreign merchants and dignitaries, can get away with many crimes; however, actions that endanger Whitewall as a whole are beyond the pale. Visiting slaveowners without such resources have little recourse if their slaves choose thralldom under a Whitewall master.

### Economy

Despite the countryside’s dangers, a network of fortified farmsteads and mining facilities struggles to support Whitewall. Many of these communities lie in ruins — empty shadows of more prosperous times — but some survive. Refugees and impoverished locals alike look to them to resettle.

While farm produce goes entirely to feed Whitewall’s populace, the city exports valuable ores from its mines. Craftspeople fashion fine weapons, armor, and jewelry. In exchange, merchants bring spices, cloth, pelts, salt, and — most importantly — various preserved foodstuffs. Trading caravans populate the roads during the short summers to make up for time lost to the stagnant, dark winters.

### The Nightwalkers’ Treaty

With shadowlands and bordermarches within a few days’ travel on all sides, hungry ghosts, hobgoblins, and other horrors roam the landscape at night. Some areas are more dangerous than others, and the worst perils — such as Fair Folk hunting parties or mortwight packs — appear only intermittently. Thus, briefly going outside the walls after dark isn’t a guaranteed death sentence. Nonetheless, locals always return home by sundown.

EX3

as possible to ensure that nothing evil slips through despite the treaty; there are always some too slow to return to the city or who fail to reach the road’s sanctuary. As Whitewall’s population grows, more residents suffer this fate.

THE TRAVELER’S ROAD

This ancient highway curves for hundreds of miles through Northern lands, from the Black Shale Road in the north to the Inland Sea in the south. Whitewall lies at its center, and the Syndics and their distant trading partners take its safety very seriously. The road’s fused, glassy stone remains warm and free of ice and snow in all but the worst weather; it’s virtually indestructible thanks to old sorcery and divine blessings.

Despite the dangers, other inhabited settlements endure nearby. Some fields and mines are too distant for workers to return to Whitewall before nightfall, and serfs and thralls must cultivate these farms so the populace can eat. But every night is a struggle for survival. Hired warriors defend these settlements; paid exorcists ward homes with salt and pray to gods for blessings.

For fifty miles in either direction, Whitewall’s mystic treaty protects the road. Eight-foot pillars of white stone carved with occult glyphs stand along the roadside every forty yards, anchoring the treaty’s magic and marking its boundaries.

Monster Hunters

Long ago, the Syndics signed a mystical treaty with the region’s Fair Folk princes and nephwrack lords to protect the city. This takes two forms: one for the Traveler’s Road that passes through Whitewall, and another for Whitewall itself. The pact proclaims that no one on the Traveler’s Road may harm another or work unwelcome magic on them, on pain of death. This rule is supernaturally binding upon the dead and the Fair Folk — including lesser ghosts and fae who wander in from beyond the local horror-princes’ courts. For others, it’s mere mortal law. But Whitewall polices this zealously, fearing that any violation might give the night horrors cause to declare the pact null and void. In accordance with the pact, merchants’ guards and monster hunters lash pactbreakers to the road’s pillars for monsters to feed upon. Off the road, different rules apply. The night horrors may not harm folk within a hundred miles of Whitewall during the day, even in self-defense; they largely withdraw from the area during that time. At night they may freely feed, but Whitewall itself remains inviolate — unless a citizen offers them a direct invitation. This treaty came with a cost. The Syndics must offer two dozen people to these horrors every year, traditionally selected from criminals kept in Whitewall’s underground dungeons. Those unlucky enough to meet this fate are tied to pillars along the Traveler’s Road. What remains when dawn comes depends on what horror claims them.

Syndics and horrors alike have followed the treaty since it was struck, but horrors devour many more than the offerings. Paranoid guards close gates as early

To protect Whitewall, surrounding settlements, and the Traveler’s Road, the Syndics hire hunter-captains, empowering each to assemble and mobilize a corps of monster hunters and rewarding them with rich bounties for monsters they slay. Typically outcastes, mercenary leaders, and mortal heroes, the dozen or so hunter-captains include the occasional sorcerer, Exigent, spirit, or the like.

Some hunter-captains assemble mercenaries into welldrilled tactical units; others rally locals to fight alongside them. Their forces may garrison or patrol specific regions, or move from place to place, hunting down night-creatures in the wilds.

Many aspiring monster hunters have died since this campaign began, but they’ve also had successes. All of Whitewall celebrated when a village boy named Raidan slew the Fair Folk noble Hurtful Jewel in an epic tale of wit and courage. They rejoiced when the outcaste Wood Aspect Serana used sorcery and salt to defeat a howling nephwrack, and when the Boneglaive Militia prevailed against hundreds of hungry ghosts. A successful hunt is a sure way to appease reserved, distrusting locals. Unfortunately, celebrations are often cut short when monster hunters move on to the next village and the threat returns. Retired, washedout, or charlatan monster hunters occasionally take up residence in villages, living off their citizens’ largesse. Villagers elsewhere bribe active hunters to stick around, adding further riches to the already-generous bounties successful hunters receive.

### Campaigns for Resettlement

Deliberations about Whitewall’s booming population dominate nearly every congregation. The Syndics are

EX3

well aware that Whitewall can’t sustain its overpopulation, and they predict riots unless they somehow motivate people to risk living outside the walls. In recent years, they’ve promised land grants to refugees willing to move into abandoned settlements. To convince people the effort is worthwhile, they offer generous bounties to soldiers and heroes to protect them, including a boyar title for strong leaders.

Unfortunately, these offers have only inflamed anti-refugee sentiment, as tiuns and boyars protest that Whitewall already struggles to defend its existing outposts beyond the walls. Likewise, most serfs and refugees reject the Syndics’ offer, preferring the known threats of poverty, disease, and starvation to the night’s unknown horrors.

### Diplomacy

Given its isolation, defenses, and distance from the Blessed Isle, Whitewall has never been a convenient target for Realm expansion. The Scarlet Empress once considered claiming the city for its rich mines but agreed to an alliance instead. The Realm maintains a tiny garrison in the city to aid its defense and support local Wyld Hunts; Whitewall pays nominal tribute but otherwise remains sovereign, without a satrap. Immaculate missionaries accompany the Realm’s diplomatic envoys to Whitewall and have established a few temples. Because of the Syndics’ presence, majesty, and power, the local Immaculate following remains small. Per the terms of the alliance, the missionaries try not to undermine the Syndics’ rule.

The Syndics offered him a boyar title in gratitude for his charitable efforts; his rejection of it further provoked the city’s elite. When Cherak’s Ferem-No-Longer Alen failed to Exalt, his disappointed parents snubbed him, and he grew jealous of the attention and opportunities the house showered upon his Exalted cousins. Certain he had more to offer but embittered at being denied what he deemed his birthright, he renounced his house and emigrated to Whitewall. There, he served for many years as a successful monster hunter.

Having earned a reputation as a fearless champion, Alen finds and recruits warriors to defend outlying communities. He often rides along the Traveler’s Road to spread word of active bounties and check in on vulnerable villages. But he’s troubled both by his advancing age, and by word that he’s inherited his mother’s lands back in Cherak; either way, he’ll need to find a successor, but hates the thought of giving up the authority and reputation he’s earned. The boyar Marlena Faria rules over a petty trade empire from her Alabaster Keep north of Whitewall, managing a dozen different mercantile endeavors. Her soldiers patrol the Traveler’s Road to keep its peace. She’s an adroit businesswoman who navigates Whitewall’s bureaucracies to increase her vast fortune, though dark secrets lurk behind her riches.

Even though Whitewall provides sanctuary against the night horrors, Fair Folk and undead ambassadors enter the city once a year, meeting the Syndics to renew the treaty’s terms. This past year, a deathknight ambassador accompanied the shadowlands’ nemissary envoys. Proud to be the only Anathema openly permitted to visit the city, he visited each Immaculate temple to leave a rose at the monks’ feet.

Faria has bargained with the ghost-tyrants of the Bruised Grove — a small nearby shadowland — to smuggle prohibited Underworld goods into Whitewall, such as beautiful soulpearls and bonewood masks. Savants and monster hunters warn that malevolent ghosts might possess such items to enter the city, the purchase serving as an invitation by the treaty’s terms. Nonetheless, certain wealthy citizens procure them, drawn by the allure of the taboo or believing rumors that such items ward off the fae.

### Prominent Figures

### Neighbors

The Beggar Prince manages many of Whitewall’s almshouses. Rag-clad and barefoot even in winter, this humble young foreigner gives endlessly to the poor. Some believe him a god of humility; others think him a wealthy foreign prince. He’s become a prominent figure in recent years, revered by the poor and bewildering the rich. Some boyars actively oppose him, believing

Miners seldom return to Whitewall at day’s end; serfs work a fortnight between visits home to see family, while thralls stay on site indefinitely. To address this, owners transform mines’ upper levels into underground villages, with reinforced mine entrances kept closed at night. The largest, Irongate, is a full-fledged town of a few thousand souls. Food and trade goods are

found in the Stalagmite Bazaar, a vast cavern emptied of ocher deposits long ago. A pleasure district dominates a deep chamber surrounding a freshwater well containing luminescent blue algae. Iron from the mines discourages the Fair Folk, while owners bring in salt to ward off the hungry dead. But Irongate contends with other dangers, such as cave-ins, bad air, and easily disturbed earth elementals. They feed upon greed and dreams, enthralling those seduced by their honeysweet smiles. ### THE PROSPER CITIES

Prosper West stands on the western span of Skysong Bridge, a colossal First Age construction whose central span collapsed long ago into the Amber River. A high wall at the span’s mouth, where militia archers can quickly assemble for defense, shields the jumble of low buildings crowding the bridge’s pavement. Fishing lines dangle hundreds of feet down into rushing waters below; ropes and pulleys lower and raise lobster traps and fishing coracles. Soldiers guard the entrances to the bridge’s western tower where the city’s ruling priest-lords make their abode. A low ceremonial wall stands before the broken end of the western span. Looking eastward over the river and the thicketed eyot left by the central span’s collapse, one can see the rival town of Prosper East athwart the farther span, its buildings sending up the rich smoke of industry, its tower aglow with geomantic radiance. The two towns feud over the Camberlight, a hearthstone that once protected the entire bridge from wind and weather, heat and cold, mischance and misfortune. But with the Skysong sundered, the stone can only protect one side or the other. Holding the stone for a generation has allowed Prosper East to flourish. Meanwhile, Prosper West suffers. Its people will give anything to one who reclaims the stone for them

fortress-market of Falcon’s Watch. Its ruler, the merchant prince Little Blue Heron, has made a fortune trading in ores, silks, and slaves. Here, merchants trade in information as often as in goods.

Little Blue Heron is currently negotiating with the Syndics, seeking permission to purchase refugees to sell as slaves elsewhere. He couches this as a solution to alleviate Whitewall’s immigration crisis, while eagerly anticipating a hefty cut of the profits.

The Bull of the

North’s Empire

Ten years ago, Yurgen of the Reedplains Elk tribe, an elderly Icewalker reinvigorated by Exaltation as a mighty warlord, emerged from the tundra with the sorceress Samea at his side. Five years later, four other Solars arose and joined his forces.

Known as the Bull of the North for his unstoppable advance, Yurgen carved out an empire through personal charisma, military brilliance, and the strength lent by his Circle, his outcaste lieutenants, and countless leaders and warriors in his train. Together they swept through Malice Bay’s cities like a burning brand; some they conquered through battle and siege, while others willingly opened their gates out of fear or ambition. Then came war with the Realm. The Tepet legions marched through the Bull’s empire, seizing cities while suffering constant asymmetric warfare as his forces refused decisive battle. The house conquered Plenilune (p. XX) and the Saltspire League (p. XX) early in the campaign, garrisoning them heavily as a keystone of their supply lines. But two of Yurgen’s Circlemates, Nalla Bloodaxe and Raneth of Plenilune — who’d faked their deaths while defending the city — remained to assassinate garrison leaders and sow unrest, culminating in a coup that destroyed the garrison and cut supply lines. They also eliminated several officials who’d sold out the Bull to the Tepets. Others received commuted sentences that could be reinstated at any time. The campaign ended at the Battle of Futile Blood, where Yurgen took the field against the legions and won, but at great cost. The wound dealt him by a grandmaster sublime armiger resists Samea’s peerless medical skill and healing sorcery. Two other Solars in his Circle — Nalla and Fear-Eater — apparently perished, as did numerous outcaste champions, allied princes and soldiers, and Icewalker warriors.

EX3

With the empire’s momentum shattered and its numbers depleted, the forces holding it together — wealth from conquest, threat of imperial reprisal, the Bull’s cult of personality, safety from invasion and banditry — diminish daily. More and more, the empire’s residents seek freedom from imperial taxes, military levies, and the oppressive weight of subordination to foreign rule. Decimated Icewalker tribes trickle away into the tundra; subject cities jockey for higher station in the empire or build toward revolt against their foreign conquerors.

Only Plenilune — the Bull’s administrative capital — stands fast, with three of the four surviving Solars and their retinues in permanent residence. Beyond its walls, the empire’s future hangs in the balance, awaiting its ruler’s recovery or death — or whatever else might tip the scales.

### The Bull’s Circle

When Yurgen Exalted as a Dawn, he became the warlord whose name would echo throughout an entire direction — the Bull of the North. A fighter to the core, he’s more at home in the field than at court. Initially he only wintered in Plenilune, strengthening his hold there with displays of power, justice, and largesse. Today he never leaves the city.

Within the city’s manse, sorcerers, gods, and chirurgeons struggle to mend his poisoned, weeping wound; they accomplish little beyond allaying his pain, easing him into deep, dreamless slumbers. He holds court rarely and briefly, arriving armed and armored, his helm masking his pallor. The only ornament he allows himself is a gold brooch bearing a spiral Icewalker glyph symbolizing the sun.

Samea of the Blackwater Mammoth tribe — Yurgen’s Zenith Caste mentor, and a powerful sorceress — developed several rites for Icewalker exorcists to banish and bind the reckless bog-spirits who sometimes possess beggars in Plenilune’s slums, but she has yet to attend to the city’s greater gods. She dedicates all her time and energy to fighting the occult infection plaguing the Bull, leaving her little opportunity to deal with other affairs.

Samea spent years learning from spirits in Icewalker lands and seeking knowledge in ancient ruins. She values sorcerous might over political power, and seeks no titles from her people, who she loves dearly. In this she

finds common cause with Crimson Antler; Samea wishes to protect the Icewalkers, and would call in every favor Yurgen owes her to prevent him from neglecting their interests. However, Samea originally encouraged his dreams of empire, and Plenilune has become her second home; she can’t abandon its people any more than she could the Icewalkers.

Raneth of Plenilune, a Twilight Caste once famed as an artisan, engineer, and scavenger lord, is ill at ease with his current role as the Bull’s viceroy, record keeper, and inquisitor. He serves Yurgen loyally, charged not only with overseeing the city’s growth into the stable center of the new empire’s wealth and power, but with ferreting out those who stand against their Circle’s bid to bring order and prosperity to the region. All too often, this puts him in conflict with the same criminals, petty lords, and powerbrokers who shaped him in his youth as a guttersnipe-turned-spymaster. He grows foul-tempered and isolated as he struggles to dismantle their tangled web of power, privilege, and influence. As the empire trembles, Raneth’s priority is Plenilune’s safety and security; he’ll gladly let the rest go to hell. Should the empire survive, he values it primarily as a vehicle for stabilizing Malice Bay’s cities and making them magnets for wealth and urban culture. The Icewalkers’ welfare holds little importance to him, and he hasn’t much respect for the Bull’s other companions. The Dawn Caste Crimson Antler rarely sets foot in Plenilune, too occupied with the ceaseless work of holding a newborn empire together. A gifted hunter and reindeer rider from the Birchbark Reindeer tribe, she now travels far and wide across the Bull’s territory and beyond, leading raids against the empire’s enemies and performing diplomatic missions to which she’s not ideally suited.

Crimson Antler’s political goals stand in opposition to Raneth’s. Her loyalties beyond Yurgen himself are with the Birchbark tribe, and more broadly with the Icewalkers. Should their interests conflict with those of Plenilune and the empire’s other cities, she’ll gladly subordinate the city-dwellers’ needs to the Icewalkers’, or part ways entirely and return with her people to the plains.

### A Wounded Empire

The Bull’s reach extends across Malice Bay. Its shores and the River of Tears are powerful assets, granting control over trade and travel, but scattered kingdoms
