### LIKELY OUTCOMES

The empire’s future depends largely on Yurgen’s health. If he recovers, he cracks down on deserters, disloyal officials, and breakaway states, then resumes expansion. If he remains sick, the empire continues to unravel down to a rump of Plenilune, the most devoted Icewalkers, and perhaps a few neighboring city-states. And if he dies, the rift between Raneth and Crimson Antler soon escalates until they split the empire between them. Exactly what happens depends largely on the Storytellers’ goals for the chronicle, modified by the player characters’ actions.

and city-states along the coast north of the bay have sworn fealty as well. To the northeast, Icewalkers and other nomadic peoples — spread across over a thousand miles of plains, hills, and woodlands — also acknowledge his authority, although for many it’s only lip service.

The empire has grown faster than governance can accommodate. Terrain and distance are among the greatest challenges facing the Bull, so he makes lavish investments in roads and trade routes through forest and marsh, across mountain and sea. Nevertheless, these long, desolate routes are easily exploited by the empire’s enemies and saboteurs who ensure that trailblazers disappear in the night and ships sink in Malice Bay. Yurgen assigns governors to oversee regions of the empire — gathering taxes and census information, organizing garrisons and their provisions, and enforcing the empire’s laws. These include freedom of religion, harsh penalties for violent crimes, and collective punishment for rebellion. But vassals struggle to retain autonomy, hoarding wealth, troops, and information for their own use rather than putting them at the Bull’s disposal; imperial governance remains fraught with hassles and inconveniences at best.

### Plenilune

Largest and richest of the five Saltspire Cities, Plenilune is like a wire drawn tight. Seized by the Bull of the North to serve as his nascent empire’s capital, then subjected to purges when House Tepet seized it and again when Yurgen’s agents staged a coup to reclaim it, the city hums with discontent from ancestral barons and from purists who scorn the Bull and his Icewalker garrison. The Bull lingers in his palace, still sick with the wasting disease inflicted by a Tepet’s spear. His surviving Solar

compatriots, stretched thin, must delegate his overstrained empire. Plenilune’s current prince, Ayn Celos (p. XX), struggles to become more than Yurgen’s figurehead. Barons, priests, merchants, and insurrectionist leaders all measure the unstable situation warily, sizing one another up for a seemingly inevitable conflict, trying to ascertain who to back. Plenilune’s people watch which way the wind blows, knowing that the city’s soul is at stake in the coming days. Even starry-eyed idealists sense that the future will be writ in blood and iron, rising or falling alongside its newfound emperor’s banner.

The River of Tears

There’d be no Plenilune without the River of Tears. It flows uphill and backwards, spurred on by ancient magic, carrying the White Sea inland from Malice Bay. In ages past, the water ran pure and clean to irrigate fields overflowing with grain. Now, only the dwindling power of the Saltspire Cities’ manses remains to desalinate the river, and even that has nearly failed. But the river hasn’t wholly surrendered to salt. Its banks give way to marshes, fields, and hills. Scrub grass and reeds poke through even its briniest expanses; gulls and other seabirds fly inland along its length, diving for crabs in ponds and streams. Sea fish follow it upstream from the White Sea into fisherfolk’s nets. Small game thrives in the marshlands, including ducks, geese, nutria, foxes, and fat snails treasured for their buttery flavor. The River of Tears’ resilient folk have adapted to their environment. Locals farm crops that thrive in the brackish water — largely barley, canola, beets, asparagus, and orache; tend arbutus orchards; raise bees and salt-tolerant russet sheep; and trade salt with neighboring peoples for other foodstuffs and metal goods. They partner with Guild-backed caravans to send salt farther afield — to Sijan, Rubylak, Whitewall, and beyond.

The Larkbright

The city’s manse — the Plenilune Saltspire, known locally as simply “the Saltspire” — sits atop a river island. This island, the Larkbright, is the city’s seat of power, home to government officials and wealthy magnates. Once a Shogunate garrison, the island retains many monolithic structures from that era, seemingly conjured from the earth, smoothed into great slabs with sharp lines and clean edges. Newer construction favors swooping marble façades or palatial timber lodges. Seen from above, the Larkbright resembles a mandala, with streets and structures arranged to gather the

dragon lines’ subtle energies. To this day, architects follow Shogunate-era design precepts to safeguard the Saltspire’s integrity.

A seawall encircles the Larkbright, its border scalloped into hundreds of pond-sized recesses. A halo of fresh water surrounds the island as the manse’s power crystallizes salt along the seawall, creating a thick white rind. Barons and commercial investors rent these recesses from Plenilune’s prince, sending laborers to harvest salt regularly. Boats only pass close to the seawall when the air is calm; a stiff wind can scour unwary travelers with salt as painfully as a Southern desert’s sandstorms.

At the island’s center stands the Pearlhallow palace complex, an array of baroque towers, walls, gardens, and halls that gird the Saltspire manse. Plenilune’s princes have long dwelled there, forsaking sprawling estates for the dignity and prestige of life within the Saltspire — and the longevity it provides, stretching a prince’s life by decades as the geomancy purifies their blood and body against toxins and infections.

The City Proper

The city has long since spilled from the Larkbright to the riverbanks along huge, ancient Shogunate-era bridges. The urbane west bank is enriched by trade from across the North. At the gates, inns, teahouses, and brothels draw in visitors; deeper in lie the ateliers and boutiques of Rigg’s Way and the walled market of Springloft. The wealthy there build up instead of out, erecting many-storied mansions, townhouses, and towers that ape the Saltspire manse itself. The east bank, though less prosperous, is larger and more populous. Low wood and brick buildings — tenements, workshops, warehouses — stand cheek by jowl, divided by mazes of winding alleys. Artisans, shopkeepers, laborers, fishers, and similar folk scrimp by here. Merchants’ voices echo off Barrow Street’s walls from dawn until dusk. Residents purchase quick, cheap meals from a two-block cluster of restaurants and food carts dubbed Teahouse Row. The district’s wealthy and powerful care little about crime, so folk fend for themselves — staying alert outside their neighborhoods, relying on community leaders for judgment, and exercising mob justice. Most Icewalkers in Plenilune reside along the eastern bank, where the Bull ordered new barracks built to house them. Some among Plenilune’s poor welcome the Icewalkers, who’ve broken up cartels and driven out petty spirits who bedevil their districts. Others chafe

at the imposition of foreign customs and complain as shrines to animal avatars grow ever more common. These conflicts boil over into violence almost daily. Icewalkers travel the city armed by necessity as much as custom, which further provokes the Plenilunars. Sour bargains erupt into marketplace brawls with little provocation. Many of Plenilune’s entrenched powers aim to deepen these divides through policies and proxies, hoping people come to see the Icewalkers and their blood-stained warlord for the invaders they are.

Governance

A tangled mess of walls and gates divide the city into a score of districts overseen by barons. Barons are meant to keep the prince’s laws and levy taxes; most prefer the latter to the former. They extract their due from travelers entering and exiting their district, especially merchants. To trade in the Springloft or on the Larkbright itself, one must pay for the privilege in every intervening district, or risk smuggling goods between districts via Plenilunar syndicates.

The princes, once unquestioned rulers of Plenilune, became ceremonial figureheads generations ago, with the barons forming a regency council. The barons still elect the prince, but Yurgen ended the regency, restoring the prince’s authority — at which the barons still chafe.

Commerce

Though many hated the Bull of the North for conquering proud Plenilune and quartering his Icewalker hordes within her walls, the city’s place of prominence in his nascent empire reinvigorated flagging trade, bringing merchant princes from across Malice Bay and the Saltspire League to curry favor with him and his Circle. Silver flowed into the city faster than it had for decades. But military and political tumult have thrown commerce into disarray. Many traveling merchants avoid the region, lest soldiers seize their goods or changing demands render said goods worthless. Others seek Plenilune despite these dangers, laden with arms, food, and other wartime provisions. Wealthy speculators aim to corner the market on essentials like grain for immediate profit, or depreciated goods like glassware to resell once the market rebounds. Raneth presses the barons to the breaking point, blackmailing or threatening those who levy excessive taxes and fees on travelers. Too entrenched in the city’s system and culture to be pried out like the ticks they are — at least, yet — many barons have begun putting aside ancient rivalries, closing ranks against this new regime.

EX3

Despite all this, war invigorates much of Plenilune’s industry. Smiths beat out swords, spears, and armor as if to a quickening drumbeat; tailors and cobblers churn out steady streams of clothing. Wineshops and gambling dens overflow with local soldiers, Icewalkers, and mercenaries alike. Provisioners and hostlers grossly overcharge refugees. Stablers name their price when selling their few remaining mounts.

Plenilunars enlisting with the Bull are often seen as little better than the Icewalkers they serve beside. For those without a trade, however, it’s the first promise of a better life they’ve had for generations, a chance to rise up — by blood and sacrifice, if necessary. From the opulent Street of Martens to dingy Fallow’s End, Plenilune is vigorously, dangerously alive.

Culture

Plenilunars trace their descent from Shogunate camp followers who settled near the Larkbright and became Plenilune’s custodians after the Contagion, with some intermarriage among merchants, neighboring citystates, and even Icewalkers and other nomads. For all their history as salt-sellers and traders, the Plenilunars retain a kernel of Shogunate philosophy at their core: that there’s a certain rightness to the order of the world, that the Dragons reward righteous dedication and honorable struggle, and that Plenilune’s survival is greater than any single life.

Whatever its virtues, this philosophy is a yoke around the necks of the poor and disenfranchised. While Plenilune’s barons and princes make an outward spectacle of self-sacrifice, eschewing foreign aristocrats’ ostentatious frippery in favor of somber elegance, few have ever made meaningful sacrifices on the city’s behalf.

But the archaic virtues that ordinary Plenilunars aspire to give them a hardiness that’s served them well throughout a history sprinkled with weak princes, Saltspire League treachery, and would-be invaders. They’ve endured famine and siege, stretching already-meager supplies rather than bending to enemies’ demands. Many would rather suffer a thousand indignities from one of their own barons than submit to an outsider’s whim — including the Bull’s. Inveterate culinary borrowers, Plenilunars supplement their limited local fare with White Sea seafood and grain, along with spices and dried fruit imported from southern lands. Common dishes include savory oat noodle soup, fried barley bread with honey and goat

cheese, or smoked fish stewed with greens, all washed down with barley beer. Favored condiments include beetroot kimchi, pickled mustard stems, caraway salt, and sea buckthorn jam.

Religion

Plenilune’s folk revere a pantheon of a dozen-odd greater gods and scores of lesser divinities, giving worship and offerings whenever a god’s purview touches on their lives. Each god has at least one temple, with smaller shrines scattered about the city. Many native Plenilunars — alongside natives of the other Saltspire League cities — follow the syncretic Lerathine creed propounded by the second-century Immaculate monk Diving Kestrel. They believe that the five Elemental Dragons converge within the Lerath: the invisible World Tree upholding all things. Plenilune’s gods emanate from and nurture the tree; they deserve worship and their words carry spiritual weight. Newborn souls fall from the tree like leaves; dead souls nourish its roots. Wicked spirits — whether Anathema, Fair Folk, or the bog-wraiths that haunt rural shores by night — pollute souls and must be thwarted. Temples contain shrines to every god in the pantheon, and welcome non-Lerathine worshipers. Icewalker settlers worship their own gods: animal avatars, nature spirits, and venerated ancestors. Many of these spirits pity Plenilune’s pantheon, seeing them as tainted by long association with urban decadence — stunted, like wolves turned into lapdogs.

Noteworthy Gods

Plenilune’s pantheon is unsure what to make of the newcomers and their warlord-king. Scales-of-Silver, the city’s patron and a goddess of salmon, fertility, and resilience, leads the local river court. Shogunate monks installed her upon overthrowing the ancient, vicious marsh-god Breath Taker by sealing him inside a towering larch. Many offer her songs, stories, and the first cut of meat thrown into a campfire in her honor. Once generous and naïve, Scales-of-Silver has become greedy, giving blessings in coldly calculated exchange for veneration, demanding prayer and incense before worship of other gods.

Other divinities include Iron Thews, god of lands reclaimed from blight; his wife Aeon Singer, ibis-headed goddess of memories preserved in music; and Thunderous Laughter, stout-hearted god of pride in the face of mockery. A coterie of impish bog-spirits and river-nymphs attend all of Plenilune’s gods and play

EX3

trickster with Plenilune’s folk, despite risking Scalesof-Silver’s censure. As popular patrons of music and ribaldry, Thunderous Laughter and Aeon Singer sanctify bards, playwrights, and poets, such that the people hold them separate from the rest of Plenilunar life. The greatest of Thunderous Laughter’s blessings is called the Fool’s Right, whose recipient may publicly mock even the prince without reprisal. Those who accept mockery in good spirit and forgive those who insult them are seen as models of Plenilunar hospitality; only a tyrant leaves no room for humor or farce.

Whatever these gods’ vices and inadequacies, the Icewalkers stir in them the memory of a time when worshipers were eager and wholehearted. Entranced by this new, earnest worship, Plenilune’s gods give cautious approval to the Icewalkers and the Bull of the North, angering many among their oldest cults.

Prominent Figures

Ayn Celos, prince of Plenilune, was formerly the baron of the east bank’s Ironthew Gate district. She earned the throne by convincing Yurgen to take Plenilune as his capital, sparing the citizenry the indignity of outright subjugation. Stories abound as to how she convinced the conqueror — whether besting him thrice in draughts or placing his daiklave at her neck to dare him to strike. She’s since ruled as his figurehead under Raneth’s supervision, albeit with more power over the barons than her recent predecessors. She executed those who’d cooperated most with House Tepet; their successors and the surviving older barons tread warily lest they meet a similar fate.

Celos focuses her efforts on consolidating power away from both the barons and Raneth, neither of whom she believes to have the people’s best interests in mind. She moves more slowly toward integrating Plenilune’s governance into the Bull’s imperial apparatus, hoping to shepherd Plenilune towards choosing a future alongside the Bull — and to avoid being too entangled with the empire should it fall.

Telliro Oskan is the most powerful of the barons, a heavyset bearded man renowned for his vast wealth, phlegmatic temperament, and steely resolve and patience. While publicly indifferent to the Bull and his Icewalkers, Telliro has organized a sizable conspiracy to undermine Yurgen’s rule for his own gain. Members range from fellow barons and merchants to Saltspire League operatives, Guild factors, and priests

of Plenilune’s gods. Wielding a network of informants and thugs, he coordinates raids, fires, burglaries, and more; he aims to foment chaos sufficient to prompt an uprising that his agents can direct against the prince and the Bull. He even courts purple-robed missionaries from the land of the dead, who’ve promised him a champion who might rout Yurgen in battle. Parcalla, Scales-of-Silver’s high priest, openly disdains the changes being wrought upon Plenilune. She preaches that this is false prosperity bought with future strife; that the Bull’s wars make the city a target for his enemies. She’s protected from reprisal by her position and patron, and because the poor love her. A favor-broker among all Plenilune’s classes, she trades secrets and blackmail for silver to feed her faithful. Jega Rekji is among the last of the Swifthoof Reindeer, a tribe shattered in the Bull’s service. Loyal but brokenhearted, Jega trains eager young warriors — including a few Plenilunar street toughs — in combat skills for battles still to come. Fiercely protective of his students, he’s struck down those who’ve harmed them: rival Icewalkers, criminals, and even Plenilune’s own soldiers. Only Yurgen’s personal favor protects Jega from the consequences of his vigilante justice, but even that will run out.

Upon Exalting as a Fire Aspect a decade ago, Brasta of the Bleakwoods Elk tribe began training personally under the Bull of the North, a seemingly godlike figure to whom he pledged unwavering loyalty. Since then, experience, maturity, and the empire’s foundering have shifted Brasta’s views. Though still dedicated to the empire, he’s begun questioning Yurgen’s plans and strategies in council.

A mighty warrior and charismatic leader who commands the loyalty of many of the empire’s Elk-tribe Icewalkers and a handful of fellow outcastes, Brasta views himself as the Bull’s heir, which causes friction within the Circle. This notion was easier to overlook before Yurgen suffered his lingering wound. But today, Brasta’s ambitions make the remaining Solars wary. Barons and wealthy merchants throughout the Saltspire League seek out storied bard Jos Eryll for his poetry and song. Some also court him as an agent, to deride either the Bull or the barons. As a priest of Thunderous Laughter, he may insult, decry, or lampoon any powerful figure without fear of reprisal — and has done so to astonishing success in the past, destroying one greedy baron’s reputation with ten lines and a jaunty tune.

### Other Noteworthy Imperial Holdings

### THE GUILD AND THE REALM

The Guild and Plenilune have profited from one another for centuries, but the Bull’s ascendance makes their partnership’s future uncertain. Guild caravans fill Plenilune’s markets with luxurious treasures: spices, silks, gems, and food from across the region. While Plenilune has pearls, amber, and fur to trade, its greatest asset is salt, which Guild-affiliated businesses buy in bulk and sell for hundreds of miles in every direction. If Yurgen attempts to strongarm the hub city’s Guild council and the major caravans’ merchant princes, the city may lose its most valued customer, devastating its economy.

Before its decline, Ordonel was the League’s financial hub, home to lenders, merchants, artisans, and pedigreed mercenaries. Today’s Ordonels have a cultural disdain for ostentatious displays that eclipses even Plenilune’s. Likewise, its ruling assembly is severe, humorless, inventive, and ruthless. Conspiracies abound to gain wealth and power, cast down rival councilors, beggar Plenilune, or even assassinate Yurgen and his allies or bind them through debt, blackmail, or marriage. The next two Saltspire cities — many-walled Alnome and belligerent Porcellana — stand in open revolt. Porcellana’s people, led by students from its famed law schools, have killed or driven out the Bull’s garrison; fighting continues in Alnome’s streets and gatehouses. The Bull’s other subjects watch to see whether their rebellion endures against the force now mustering in Plenilune to subdue them.

Losing the Tepet legions bloodied the Realm. While many Dynasts remain eager to strike down the Anathema, no Great House is both willing and able to lead the next attempt. The only certainty is that there will be a reckoning.

House Mnemon has long sought a foothold in the Saltspire League, offering manse repairs in exchange for fealty. Their efforts are undermined by local political machinations and by rumors that Realm geomancers destroyed Ordonel’s manse.

### The Saltspire League

To purify the River of Tears, the Shogunate built not one Saltspire manse, but five. Cities arose around each. Only Plenilune’s manse remains fully functional; the resulting wealth and prestige give it preeminence. To the south, the other four cities, whose manses have fallen into disrepair, formed the Saltspire League — an economic partnership and defensive pact against the encroaching Realm, Plenilune’s economic supremacy, and now its new emperor.

Nearest is Ordonel, the least populous Saltspire city. Sixty years ago, its manse exploded amid a botched effort at geomantic repairs, killing its prince and much of the royal family. The city’s merchant houses, fearing that squabbles over the crown could see them lose their wealth — and their lives — to riots or foreign invasion — jointly agreed to seize power as a group, establishing a council to lead the city. They’ve stabilized their reign and alleviated the loss of the salt trade through increased tariffs, shifting alliances with their neighbors, and concessions to the Guild. No few councilors have been assassinated, however, and their well-paid guards have barely weathered revolts by royal pretenders and demagogues. An endless procession of occultists, artificers, and geomancers remains unable to repair the

Porcellana conquered its neighbors centuries ago; it continued squabbling with Alnome long after the Saltspire League established an uneasy peace. Today the two cities define themselves by their longstanding, albeit acrimonious, alliance; they form a league within a league, with each city’s ducal families and merchant houses intermarried with the other’s. They must collude for their manses’ trickle of salt — and other products, such as Alnome’s cheeses and Porcellana’s leather goods — to compete against far richer Plenilune. Farthest south lies crumbling, libertine Astragal, whose manse failed centuries ago. Receiving limited support from their sister cities, the Astragals turned to the Icewalkers, becoming a crossroads for trade. Centuries of intermarriage and cultural exchange have made cousins of nomads and cityfolk; many Astragals seethe at the indignity of pampered Plenilune being chosen as the Bull’s capital. Meanwhile, merchants and artisans — struggling as the ongoing wars disrupt trade — mutter whether it might be better to welcome the Realm, or invite mercenary aid from the Guild.

The people of Tarrack, a city-state near the mouth of Malice Bay, were once renowned as peerless, merciless raiders. Today they’re preeminent sailors, traders, and shipwrights who’ve never lost their pride or reckless courage. While only intermittently at war, Tarrack and

Iruz — a circle of runestones where princes of long-fallen Greater Goryn were once elected. The coalition force currently besieges Zemei, bottling up a sizable imperial force. Bloomfell’s efforts to infiltrate agents to persuade the non-Icewalker imperials to switch sides have yet to bear fruit.

### SCIONS OF FUTILE BLOOD

Many Tepet scions and their soldiers neither died nor returned home after the Battle of Futile Blood. Broadly speaking, these fall into four categories. • Those unwilling to return until the mission is complete conduct guerilla assaults, often suborning local polities toward this end. Talonlord Tepet Vergus Narivan joined Bloomfell’s coalition force; she advises the city’s strategoi on tactics and trains local troops.

The outcaste bandit-captain Paran Death-Eye subdued the agricultural towns of windswept Vanades Yatyj and brought them into the Bull’s service early in his conquest. Though her forces — largely border reiver clans, Medoan outlaws, and dispossessed villagers — have fought for him reliably, Paran is careful to ensure that their loyalty lies with her. She shores up her authority within Vanades Yatyj, laying the groundwork to carve out her own petty empire should the Bull’s fall. While she has yet to break with him lest he recover, Paran reaches out to neighboring princes, offering military protection and brokering trade agreements for use of the region’s barley-grinding panemone windmills.

• Those too defeated to keep fighting but too ashamed to return home in defeat linger in foreign lands. Haunted by failure, the yamabushi Tepet Jatal hires out as a caravan guard for merchants traversing dangerous locales. • Those using the defeat as an excuse to escape unwanted obligations on the Blessed Isle. Rather than return home and accept the bureaucratic post her mother had been preparing her for, quartermaster-champion Tepet Pryll shed her name, sold her armor, and purchased a teahouse in Astragal, where she’s building a small informant network.

Northeast of Plenilune, trees grow gnarled and twisted in the gloom of Mistbound Forest. Here, frost-flowers bloom in the crooks of ancient branches; ever-present mists swallow sound, lending an eerie silence to the landscape. Packs of silverwights and barghests roam the forest, stalking their prey with muffled footsteps. Though the Mistbound is uninhabited by humans, fruits from its ice apple groves fetch a handsome price for those who dare retrieve them.

• Those who began the journey home but got entangled in local affairs along the way. The Immaculate monk Merciful Osprey spent months recuperating in the village of Plume. Helping her hosts confront a demanding elemental seemed a simple repayment before returning to the Isle, but she found herself embroiled in complex spirit court politics

## The Icewalkers

Plenilune have been rivals for centuries. Tarrack’s customs vessels levy hefty taxes on ships entering or leaving the River of Tears; its privateers attack those who haven’t paid. Since Tarrack bent the knee to the Bull, its gentry-senators have been emboldened and empowered to tax trade further, ostensibly to fund fleet construction for their Solar liege.

Three nations composed of dozens of tribes — collectively known to outsiders as “Icewalkers,” and among themselves as “the Sworn” — wander the North in accord with ancient pacts struck with animal avatars. They follow vast, wild herds of caribou, elk, and mammoth across sprawling prairie, lush taiga, and frozen tundra.

The city-state of Bloomfell, not far north of Tarrack, has opened the gates to refugees from nearby imperial holdings — and to escaped troops from the Bull’s conquests. It’s assembling a coalition army that’s marshaling to liberate its neighbors, though some suspect that its jovial, hunting-mad prince intends to substitute her rule for the Bull’s. A dwindling handful of Icewalkers remain trapped in the city, struggling to survive imprisonment, remain hidden, or safely escape.

Today, their societies are in turmoil. Some leave their bands to dwell among settled peoples. Many must fight foreigners’ raids on the sacred herds. And a warlord of their own making, the Bull of the North, has drawn too many Icewalkers into his dreadful war. It remains to be seen whether they, their herds, and their traditions can endure this time of tumult.

Bloomfell’s army has marched on Zemei, an ancient city-state on the road to Gethamane that’s renowned for hilltop castle-temples, hot springs, and the Stones of

These nomadic hunter-gatherers travel for hundreds of miles across the Northern wilderness via skis, sleds,

### Culture

EX3

mounts, and on foot. They spend warm summer nights sleeping under the stars; in winter’s cold, they shelter in collapsible dwellings of wood and hide. Each Icewalker nation follows herds of a patron animal that shapes its culture, religion, and everyday survival. Ancient legend describes how the nations’ founders sought out avatars of elk, mammoth, and reindeer, forming pacts between man and beast that would tie them together for all time. A tribe protects its herd from outside threats and culls the old, sick, and weak. In exchange, the herd provides food to eat, pelts for warmth, and bones for tools and weapons. Its animal avatar protects the tribe against the gravest threats. Each nation’s patron animal holds a central role in its culture. A mammoth tribe warrior adorns herself in ivory while finding fine grasses for the herd; in return, they help her defend her kin. A reindeer tribe shaman sings a grateful prayer before skinning a carcass, knowing that its hide will warm the children at night. An elk tribe artisan crafts warriors’ antler crowns — for each battle won, the warrior caps a tine with a copper ornament. Rings carved into those tines show how many enemies the wearer defeated.

Because of the Icewalkers’ nomadic nature, every object serves a purpose. Wood, bone, and antlers become knives, drums, and cups. Leather, roots, and sinew make clothes, armor, and baskets. Members of different Icewalker nations and tribes easily recognize each other by their clothes and tools; outsiders rarely develop this cultural awareness. This refusal to learn to recognize such differences inflames tensions between settled peoples and Icewalkers.

Icewalker cuisine relies heavily on the nations’ patron animals, using all edible parts of the elk, reindeer, or mammoth in recipes throughout the year. Soups and stews feature tougher cuts of meat made tender as they cook. In colder months, root vegetables such as burdock, dandelion, parsnips, and carrots are added for hearty fare, while in warmer weather, young potherbs are paired with thin-sliced cuts of meat and wild rice for light meals. Icewalkers preserve meat for lean winter months by smoking, salting, or drying, adding chokeberries or currants for flavor. Flatbreads — made with flour, water, and milk and pan-fried or cooked on a hot, flat stone — accompany the dishes. Icewalker art is typically decorative, applied to everyday items — scrimshaw animals carved into ivory knife hilts, or embroidery and leather tooling depicting

significant events worked into cloaks and painted on tents. An oral tradition of songs commemorates notable deeds and people in their history, such as the culture hero Nyokkonen Wild-Hair who wrestled the ice elemental Lirilin for her tribe’s safe passage over Black Duck River.

### Bands and Tribes

Each nation has several tribes divided among numerous bands — kin groups of a few dozen people who camp together. Bands traditionally make decisions by consensus, though they often defer to one or more glory-covered warriors or honored elders. Each band’s members are designated roles based on their skills. The strongest become hunters and warriors; they make shows of force to discourage neighboring tribes and settlements from disturbing their herd. Younger warriors scout surrounding lands, then stay up late sharing exciting stories about what they’ve seen. Warriors sidelined by age or injury spend more time with the band, sharing wisdom with the new generation and playing wargames with figures carved from wood and bone. Pregnant warriors spend the final months before delivery playing these games with the elders, honing tactical prowess while keeping their unborn children safe. When time comes for war, bands rely on these warriors’ battle-cunning. Those too gentle-hearted to kill or hunt, and those whose physical abilities don’t lend themselves to such pursuits, typically become caregivers and artisans. They tend to children and animals, gather herbs and berries, and craft clothes, weapons, and tools. Though lacking the glory of those who bring meat, ward off predators, and battle foes, they’re valued and respected for their numerous contributions.

A war leader, selected from the most decorated and successful warriors, guides the tribe during wartime. Bands follow her strategies when engaging the enemy. A council leads each tribe in peacetime. Composed of distinguished elders and shamans, they monitor the needs of their bands and herds, and cooperate to settle inter-tribal disputes. The war leader defers to and advises the council in peacetime.

### Religion

Icewalkers worship their nation’s animal avatar. They also revere the animals themselves, thanking them

EX3

prosperous times, a tribe’s bands scatter for hundreds of miles. But when winter comes and food grows scarce, tribes compete over grazing land, game, and fishing waters. At such times, people break promises and neighbors become bitter rivals.

### ANIMAL AVATARS

Each of these mighty spirits — originally a mundane beast empowered by Gaia at time’s dawn — oversees all animals of their sort throughout Creation. They rarely act directly, instead sending intelligent, talking animals to speak on their behalf.

after every hunt and burying their skulls at holy sites. Lastly, they venerate culture heroes who forged ancient pacts with their animal avatar. These include the Mammoth Nation’s Wolkanda the Mountain, the Reindeer Nation’s Niklangat Three Miracles, and the Elk Nation’s Thorn-Dancer Senja.

Those who seek to deepen their relationship with their patron animal become shamans. They treat the sick and wounded with herbs, ointments, and medicines — most passed down from their predecessors, some of their own creation. They perform sacrifices and rituals to bless newborn children and animals, freshwater springs, and distinctive land formations that serve as sacred sites and guideposts. Many are evocative storytellers, or can enthrall the tribe as they sing powerful yoiks to their nation’s animal avatar.

Shamans also negotiate with spirits on the tribe’s behalf. This combines diplomatic skill with centuries of oral knowledge; they know the region’s native spirits by name, along with their loves, fears, relationships, and prior bargains. They invoke their animal avatar’s protection against spiritual threats only in extremis; the avatar won’t intervene for petty stakes. Each tribe has a seer who reads the stars and winds to dictate the herd’s movements, or witnesses visions of ancestral ghosts in clouds of smoke. The seer is usually the oldest and wisest shaman, but younger tribesmen may receive the title after showing aptitude for thaumaturgy or receiving a divine blessing.

### Conflict and Trade

Each nation only regards its own members as kin. Their animal avatar guides their approach to life, but may conflict with the other two nations’. When tribes from different nations strive to cooperate towards common goals, simple disagreements sometimes erupt into rancorous feuds. In summer, when foraging yields plenty and few go unfed, tribes often trade or ally with each other. In these

Though often known to local settlements as fearsome raiders, Icewalkers far prefer trading in areas where locals muster meaningful military resistance. However, tribes vary in their approach to trade, with some more eager than others to take what they want by force. With stories of Icewalker raids having spread for generations, few outsiders care to distinguish one tribe from another. They often resort to offering tribute, training militias, hiring mercenaries, or preemptive ambushes. Most Icewalkers prefer trading with the Haslanti to raiding; many tribes hold treaties that forbid Icewalkers from raiding in Haslanti lands while similarly protecting the Icewalkers and their herds. Some Icewalker leaders maintain close relationships with Haslanti merchants, often to their peers’ disapproval. Similarly, the Ryazan people of Tusk (Exalted, p. 85) have a closer relationship with the mammoth tribes, given the Tuskers’ pact with the mammoth avatar.

Those bands whose warriors have left to join the Bull struggle along with their numbers depleted, defended largely by elderly warriors and youths still learning the ways of battle. These bands suffer disproportionately from raids by other Icewalker nations and rival peoples.

### Noteworthy Icewalkers

Inger, war leader of the Rime-in-Spring Mammoth tribe, is living proof that power springs from many different sources. Born with a spinal condition that requires her to recline or adjust her posture while seated to avoid pain, she uses mobility aids to get around — several of which she invented herself. She became a tactical expert by playing wargames with elders, and studied every warrior in the tribe and every mammoth in the herd. After designing a saddle allowing her to ride, she applied her cunning on the battlefield, earning recognition as a war leader for her victories. When not mounted on her mammoth Silma, she uses her love for war games to teach warriors strategy.

The outcaste Kaj of the Blackfur Elk tribe was once one of the Bull’s trusted lieutenants, eager to prove himself in battle. But ever since the Bull retreated to Plenilune, this once-loyal servant has considered Yurgen unfit to lead the tribes. Calling himself the Lord Crowned by Black Antlers, Kaj rides his war-stag to any tribe willing

to host him, using wit and charm to unite people under his rule.

### THE GREATER VOJVADAS

Cosmir: Overseeing lands along the River of Tears — encompassing most tin production and trade — the Cosmir are the richest of the greater families, and will pay any price to remain first among equals. Family members receive no lenience in these matters. For instance, when word arrived that young Cosmir Antisek had snubbed the satrap, the matriarch cut off his funds — no money, servants, or carriage — a swift, firm rebuke meant to secure the satrap’s goodwill.

A strong-thewed warrior and forceful diplomat, Kaj has achieved success with tribes the Bull never reached, such as the ferocious Sky River Elk tribe. Now with a considerable force backing him, rumors say he’s planning to conquer a Haslanti city-state, or forging an alliance with Brasta of the Bleakwoods Elk to split the Bull’s empire between them.

## Clovina

Radju: Controlling much of Clovina’s farmland, the Radju tear into other vojvadas and one another with petty insults and play up their own injured pride. They bristle at being seen as the Cosmirs’ lesser cousins, and at how their rivals portray their land’s slow recovery from war and drought as deliberate neglect. Rumors claim they seek foreign assistance, either to oust the Realm or supplant the Cosmir.

Between the long-fallen Medoan Empire’s northern edge and the River of Tears lies Clovina, a land defined by conquest; rich tin deposits and influence over river trade has seen to that. Stories almost as old as the Contagion describe the Republic of Clovina, when its people last ruled themselves. The devil-warlord Utz Semar conquered it centuries ago, then lost it to the Medoans; now, it’s a Realm satrapy. It’s almost always some invader, rather than Clovina’s people, who’s enjoyed their land’s riches. A generation ago, the Lunar Kanon Tas united the neighboring Utzral hills’ unsettled tribes and swept across Clovina. They torched towns, docks, and tin foundries, destroyed roads, salted fields, and poisoned wells.

The Wyld Hunt slew Kanon Tas, burning the hills’ vast pine forests to deny her escape. But Clovina suffered extensive damage. Its satrapial lease requires House Mnemon to restore Clovina to profitability, even as the house reduces reconstruction funding, withdraws garrison troops, and increases tribute demands.

### Society

Under Medoan rule, many loyal families of land-owning gentry became aristocratic vojvadas. Over time, the Cosmir, Radju, and Stojca families established their power as greater vojvadas — intermediaries between Medo and the lesser vojvadas. They divide Clovina between them, mediating feuds between lesser vojvadas and assembling in the city Tears-of-Beauty to discuss collective concerns. The Realm left this system intact, playing the vojvadas against one another to defuse rebellions before they begin. Since the Empress vanished, House Mnemon offers less and takes more. Satrap Mnemon Beril passes this burden to the vojvadas, who take loans from Guild factors

Stojca: Living in pine forests and foothills along the western border, the Stojca oversee Clovina’s lumber and charcoal production. Deeply stubborn and traditionalist, they cling fiercely to propriety and ritual. They rarely bother with lowland politics, focusing on threats from the hills and in the night, which they address with paranoid ruthlessness

and other lenders to continue rebuilding while meeting tribute demands.

Most Clovinans are land-bound laborers called sclavs. Each serves a vojvada, to whom they forfeit the bulk of their harvest or income. Vojvadas have total legal authority over sclavs; they may relocate them, force them to change vocations, sell them, or kill them. This enslavement purportedly repays the sclavs’ debt to the vojvadas and the Medoan Empire for freeing them from Utz Semar. Sclavs may purchase their freedom, though few can muster the steep sums the vojvadas demand. Some sclavs flee into the hills and become bandits. Others vanish into the anonymous underclass of riverside towns — a combination of refugees, immigrant laborers, and free Clovinans who eke out a bare living outside the vojvadas’ direct control. But most accept their lot with weary resignation and black humor, claiming that things are never so bad that they can’t get worse.

Free Clovinans

Many villages carefully pool their meager wealth so that every few years, families can purchase a lucky child’s

EX3

freedom. Free Clovinans may travel as they wish and comprise the bulk of Clovina’s merchants and skilled artisans. The child of two free Clovinans remains free; if either parent is a sclav, so is the child. In the reconstruction’s early years, Mnemon Beril purchased freedom for hundreds of sclavs — on the condition that they work a few years for her. Their vojvadas were compensated by forgiving debts or deferring tribute payments. Whole villages were uprooted; many sclavs ran away, concealing themselves among masses of the newly freed.

Culture

Along the River of Tears, where Clovinians fish and gather saltworts, the tin and clay trades dominate everyday life. Riverside villages received the bulk of House Mnemon’s reconstruction efforts. Beril used a handful of fixed architectural plans, laying out every building with precise costs. Each reconstructed village supports a specific part of an industry — panning, smelting, digging clay, firing brick or ceramic; all contain docks and storehouses. The new construction starkly contrasts against the old, replacing colorful tiles and wood-andplaster homes with gray brick apartments centered around squat kilns and smelters.

Most riverside sclavs are forced into tin panning. Thousands kneel daily in the icy river, spinning pans of cloudy water, separating grains of pure black tin from mud. Tally masters weigh the results, then send the heavy burlap bags to smelters to purify the ore and make it into ingots.

Away from the river, villages grow sparse, their farms and pastures centering around a vojvada’s manor. Sclavs grow barley, potatoes, and wheat, herd sheep, gather wild greens and fungi, and tend apple, plum, and pear orchards.

Everyday foods include porridge with mutton cracklings, soft cheese and fermented plums spread on flatbread, grilled fish ball skewers, and offal soup; mutton hot pot with eggs and leafy greens, once a common meal, is now a rare treat. Vojvadas traditionally enjoy more extravagant dishes such as black walnut honey bread or whole roasted lamb stuffed with spiced apples and mint. Where vojvadas drink wine, sclavs make do with small beer, water, ayran, or herbal tea. House Mnemon spent little on rebuilding these less profitable villages, focusing instead on bolstering lucrative industries. As if this hadn’t frustrated the country vojvadas enough, Beril then took so many sclavs from

EX3

them to rebuild the tin industry that barely enough farmers remain to tend the land. These aristocrats and their remaining sclavs alike fear they’re one failed harvest away from famine.

### THE MOROI

Clovinans born with cauls intact are called Moroi. Traditionally seen as standing between the living and the dead, they’re trained to act as both mediums and monster-hunters. Since Clovina was made a satrapy, most are taken in by the Order to use their ill-omened gifts for noble ends. Moroi outside the Order aren’t persecuted by the Immaculates so long as they don’t encourage ancestor worship.

Rural sclavs and lesser vojvada sometimes turn to banditry to compensate, stealing reconstruction supplies and giving the local greater vojvada a cut. The greater vojvada, in turn, offers up troublemakers to the satrap as “proof” that they’ve dealt with the bandits. As the Realm garrison dwindles, increased banditry causes supply shortages and reconstruction delays. In the pine-covered foothills, manor-centered villages have higher walls and are home to many pairs of wary eyes. Sclavs harvest wood and burn charcoal for the ever-hungry tin smelters, and scratch out iron from a few surface mines — but only by day. Everyone knows to hang bundles of onion and thyme, tie shutters with green and purple ribbons, and be indoors by dark.

### Worship

Before the Realm, Clovinans worshiped a local pantheon of night-grim gods and their ancestral ghosts. Small roadside shrines commemorating famous individuals’ pyres were common, and most Clovinans carried relics or carved images of their forebears. Every vojvada manor prominently displayed an ancestor shrine. People made small offerings of spilled wine and burnt food at meals alongside prayerful recitations of ancestors’ names. The Clovinans’ worship safeguards the living and dead alike from a dreadful fate. In this land, a forgotten ghost twists into a nameless monster; it may drown those who failed to remember it, steal children, or steal names by devouring hearts and livers. Venerated ancestors both retain their own identities and offer protection against — or even hunt down — their name-lost kin. The Immaculate Order has driven these practices underground. Now, Immaculate exorcists drive out namelost ghosts and once-honored ancestors alike. Heretical worship of deified ancestors becomes common farther from the river, however, and sclavs are reluctant to part with idols that kept them safe for generations. The vojvadas have proven far more stubborn, fighting tooth and nail to retain their traditional ancestor worship. Outwardly they accommodate, accepting enforced prayer calendars and rigidly demarcated

holidays, hosting traveling monks, and even removing ancient paintings and statues — but destroying the ancestor shrine goes too far for most. These they hide in cellars or attics; to compensate for the insult, they now offer their ancestors blood instead of wine. The Immaculate Order finds the situation intolerable. Local monks, led by the stern abbot Crying Truth, pressure the satrap for permission to crack down on these outrages, to ransack every vojvada home for hidden shrines and freely punish heretical sclavs. Beril demurs on the grounds that this would incite rebellion; instead, she uses the threat of violent suppression to bring recalcitrant families in line or to punish aristocrats that she suspects of malfeasance.

### Noteworthy Locales

A sizable city before Kanon Tas sacked and burned it, Tears-of-Beauty remains Clovina’s largest population center, though now it’s scarcely more populous than a large town. Amid burnt-out ruins of rainbow-tiled buildings, sclav and free alike live and work in interchangeable gray-brick structures. Abutting the river on the town’s south side, Mnemon Beril’s manor stands decorated with colorful, abstract mosaics of the finest tile, a symbol to all of their respective stations. Near the city’s heart is Black Sand Market, a tangle of salt-encrusted docks where ships take on cargo. Laborers load ingots of tin and boxes of straw-stuffed ceramics while vojvada agents keep careful watch on comings and goings. The market is the closest thing left to prewar Tears-of-Beauty. Dozens of caffés serve salted teas and bitter beers, cabbage rolls stuffed with cod, plates of fresh bread dipped in savory garum, and honey-sweet baklava. Brightly colored banners flutter from shutters; musicians with five-string fiddles and tin flutes play traditional Clovinan music.

EX3

Many caffés serve as fronts for smuggling operations and illicit services. Their banners’ colors and materials encode advertisements for proscribed wares: untaxed luxuries and weapons, drugs and seditious literature, ancestral relics, and prostitution.

The ruin known as Bitter Leaf was once a powerful manse called Sweet-Leaf Palace. Its valley was Clovina’s breadbasket; its rich orchards produced fine liquors; its barley and maize fields single-handedly fed the surrounding district. Before Kanon Tas, three vaseshaped alabaster towers two hundred feet tall stood open to the sky, their bases surrounded by a fantastic garden of beautiful flowers. Topiaries formed graceful arches, shelters from the elements, and fantastic beasts from across Creation.

in recognition of her service and local knowledge; Mnemon acquiesced despite Beril’s youth. Beril proved an able administrator; her plans raised new settlements with astonishing speed and restored tin production to nearly prewar levels. She ferrets out discrepancies in accounts and reports, harshly punishing anyone who’d cheat her house. Self-conscious of her youth and inexperience, she sometimes overcompensates with vojvadas, making imperious, high-handed demands. Few see the laughing romantic from the Spiral Academy; to Clovina, Beril is a humorless bureaucrat and taskmaster.

Now, only two cracked, smoke-blackened towers remain. The gardens are wild and rotten, the topiaries fallen into disrepair. Campfire tales say the topiaries are alive, that tree-tigers and vine-serpents stalk the shadows.

Beril longs for recognition for her extraordinary efforts, but only receives demands to extract more wealth with less support, and to maintain peace with the vojvadas while allowing the Order to persecute their heresies. She redoubles her efforts, focused on administrative details at the expense of potential threats such as rebels gathering in the Utzral Hills.

The lands around Bitter Leaf lie fallow. Those who sought to resettle found that crops grew impossibly large; apples the size of pumpkins broke the trees, while heads of wheat bore slender stalks to the earth. But the fruits were bitter and mealy, the wheat kernels too stony to mill. Worse, many who work the land sickened, suffering bleeding lesions or malignant tumors.

The Cosmir vojvada oversees the river villages and holds a traditional monopoly on tin production and distribution, making it the wealthiest of the greater families. It’s led by Elena Cosmir, a 50-year-old grandmother. Among the province’s best riders and archers, Elena is an echo of the Medoan empire’s heyday. She dominates her family with an iron fist.

With Clovina becoming profitable again, Mnemon Beril wishes to restore Sweet-Leaf Palace, but the house’s geomancers are too preoccupied with reinforcing Mnemon holdings on the Isle to repair one manse in a distant satrapy. Her early ventures at sending sclavs and soldiers to scavenge the ruins for heirlooms lost during Kanon Tas’ attack have also failed; expedition survivors report mad spirits, hungry ghosts of fallen defenders, and demons bound to protect Tepet secrets.

While Clovina’s other aristocrats looked enviously on the wealth poured into rebuilding the Cosmir tin works, Elena sees the reconstruction as the greatest threat her family has ever faced. In addition to increasing tribute demands, she was forced into accepting large loans at usurious rates, knowing that if they aren’t repaid, her family’s tinworks will be stolen away.

Bitter Leaf ’s inhospitable nature has made it an ideal hiding place for an especially brazen bandit troop. Calling themselves the Bitter Leaf Gang, they openly terrorize nearby towns and villages, daring vojvadas to pursue them into the tainted land.

### Prominent Figures

After the Tepet satrap perished in Kanon Tas’ rampage, one young adviser, Mnemon Beril, coordinated local forces and joined the final drive against the Lunar warlord. Afterwards, the Empress granted House Mnemon the satrapial lease on condition that it funded reconstruction. Beril petitioned to be named satrap

Elena has sacrificed blood, friends, and relatives to ensure that the Cosmirs remain first among equals of the greater vojvadas. The only line she’s refused to cross is breaking faith with her ancestors. After her crimes, she fears what she’ll face after death and believes that only her ancestors can guide her to safety.

The exiled aristocrat Nicol Dumutris was executed by hanging for banditry and murder four years ago; despite this, he’s been reported to be riding again. Calling himself “the Law That Pierces Life,” he reaches out to lesser vojvadas, seeking to forge a new revolution that not only throws out the Realm, but forms the seed of a reborn Medoan Empire. He claims that this requires both the living and the dead; Clovina must reclaim its traditions of ancestor worship, while ancestors must once again guard the living.

claim descent from the culture hero Yskela — a semidivine figure said to have invented song — and, when dealing with outsiders, are noted for their singing’s unearthly beauty.

### OTHER NORTHERN LOCALES

Villagers in Brings-the-Day maintain shrines to household minor fae, offering brightly colored trinkets and cups of sweet summer wine in exchange for aid and protection. People choose their words carefully, lest the fae interpret their desires in ways that range from merely unhelpful to disastrous. At worst, children who’ve moved their parents to the wrong harsh words are stolen away to their fae prince Uaine-o’-the-Cauldron who dwells under Day Hill, replaced by changelings; the parents must undertake some perilous obligation to reclaim them. But Uaine’s fae defend Brings-the-Day against even more wicked spirits, from the hungry dead to silverwights.

For the Utz clans, the wounds of war with Clovina remain fresh. As fire renews the forest, the Realm’s burning of the Utzral hills forced the clans closer together, rallying around the Seer-in-Ochre, a new prophet claiming she’ll finish what Kanon Tas began. On the far side of the Utzral hills lies Rultea. With rich farm and pastureland but little mineral wealth, Rultea is divided between hundreds of petty farmer-lords. Intensely independent, Rulteans idealize self-sufficiency. The Sesus satrap uses this to convince each lord that they must make up for their neighbors’ shortfalls.

Once, fertile soil and riverine shipping kept the satrapial city-state of Koss well-fed and House Tepet’s coffers full. Residents revered Sleek Armosa, goddess of the Stonechat River, for sustaining their prosperity, and filled her temples with prayer and offerings. But a decade ago, Immaculate monks upbraided Armosa for her corruption. Without her aid, the Stonechat silted up; river trade dwindled, while flooding ravaged fields and buildings. The satrap proposed using the Tepet legions to dredge the river, but the Battle of Futile Blood put paid to her plans. Today, Koss stands half-empty, its sodden buildings stained with rot, the prince’s guard too busy keeping the remaining folk from fleeing to adequately maintain the levees, let alone dredge the river.

Historically, invaders from the south who conquered Clovina continued on to invade Rultea; a common expression there says, “Trouble goes east and comes west.” Rulteans remember armies coming from Clovina to claim Rultea; whether these armies were Medoan or Realm means little. This grudge has intensified in recent years as Clovinan vojvadas raid across the border to enslave Rulteans. Such raids are conducted without Beril’s knowledge — and could incite rebellion or light a conflict between Mnemon and Sesus.

In the deep tundra, where whiteness blankets the land and even the brief summers don’t thaw the soil, enormous geoglyphs lie arrayed upon the flat, empty Plain of Pictures. They’re so large that their shapes are only discernable from high above, otherwise appearing as nonsensical trenches and furrows — when they’re visible at all beneath the snow. Legend says they predate humanity, and that meditating at a sigil’s heart can bring enlightenment or awaken sorcerous understanding.

Vojvadas that reject his overtures have been struck by nighttime raids. The populations of farms, even villages, vanish; save for one victim left impaled on a thin lance, inserted so skillfully that they live in agony for hours.

### Neighbors

On Clovina’s western border rise the flinty, pine-covered Utzral hills, home to the seminomadic Utz clans. Led by Moon-Touched survivors of the Wyld Hunt, Utziers supplement hunting and gathering with raids or trading expeditions against settled neighbors. They

Across the River of Tears lurks Sarlistina, a salt marsh with little clear divide between river and land. Tall grasses and blackwood mangroves grow thick where the tide recedes; treacherous roots and shallows in the murky water make piloting even simple rafts dangerous. Small shadowlands dot the area; some mark ancient battles, others where small settlements perished from unexpected flooding, unclean water, or mysterious circumstances. Shoreline communities traditionally execute and bury criminals here, where their hungry ghosts won’t trouble the living. Some Clovinans undertake secret pilgrimages to Sarlistina to seek an ancestor’s wisdom, bid loved ones farewell, or search for blue amaranth — said to be a panacea, and capable of repelling unclean spirits.

## The Haslanti League

Beyond the White Sea’s windswept shores, in a land of brief, dim summers and harsh winters, the rugged townships and cities of the Haslanti League seem unlikely sites for an engineering renaissance. Far from their southern neighbors’ plenty, the League has tamed harsh lands with fortitude, ingenuity, and an inheritance of long-lost wonders.

EX3

Testament to their innovation are their miraculous airboats, able to soar over hundreds of miles of inhospitable terrain, and their iceboats that skate across great frozen lakes. Beneath the earth, savants and engineers work tirelessly to uncover even greater wonders as they painstakingly lay bare the legacy of the sorcerer-prince Bagrash Köl and other ancient civilizations. All the while, the Haslanti oligarchs turn acquisitive eyes southwards to conquests that may yet come.

### The Shattered Tower Convocation

Centuries ago, Bagrash Köl wielded the fabled Eye of Autochthon to conquer a broad swath of the North and Northeast, subjugating the petty kingdoms that arose in the Shogunate’s wake. His empire lasted only thirty years, collapsing in spectacular fashion when the Eye turned upon him.

Though that empire is long gone, its ghost still haunts the North. Bagrash Köl’s flying citadel, an edifice so vast it’s said to have housed gates to allow the sun and moon to pass, staggered across the sky when its creator vanished, disintegrating across the Fang Lakes. Meanwhile, cities in his territory had employed strange

sorceries and relics that went awry after his death; many such cities were abandoned after the fall. The nomadic Haslan clans offered no fealty to the sorcerer-king. Withdrawing from their old country to the empire’s northern border, they supplemented those marginal lands’ slim forage and their cattle herds’ production by raiding border towns and merchants’ caravans. After the empire fell, the Haslan were free to scavenge its wreckage. With much of the sorcerer’s old magic twisted or inaccessible after his death, the Haslan — who’d spent decades puzzling out mundane uses for Köl’s occult devices — were as well positioned as the fallen empire’s own surviving savants to employ its relics.

The Haslan clans feuded with one another and with foreign scavengers over access to these sites. Seeking unity, a convocation of Haslan leaders and shamans gathered upon the ruins of a mighty steel tower fallen from Bagrash Köl’s citadel. The arch-sorcerer had driven their people and gods from their lands; his riches were fair compensation for all Haslan, not a prize to fight over or a bounty for outsiders to ransack. Though they’d remain independent, the clans agreed to tie their

EX3

lots together, presenting a united front against wouldbe invaders and plunderers of their heritage.

### HASLAN VS. HASLANTI

Haslan refers to those descending from the original Haslan clans, while Haslanti refers to League members no matter their ethnicity. Not all League members are Haslan, while not every Haslan belongs to the League.

### Broadening the League

After the Convocation, the newfound Haslanti League established a first wave of seminomadic settlements around key Kölish sites, their herders, hunters, and raiders also scouting for new scavenging sites and engaging in commerce. They traded with neighboring peoples via the White Sea and the River of Tears, exchanging relics, furs, ivory, metals, and gems for food and foreign luxuries.

Over the centuries, the Haslanti colonized new scavenging sites while defending their own against foreigners who’d purloin their treasures. Upon encountering other sites already claimed by potential rivals, Haslanti leaders called a second Convocation. The outcome was to invite foreign city-states to join the League if they were willing to become full partners and share in its ideology. Some rivals accepted these offers; the Haslanti largely drove the others out of the region.

### Haslan Society and Culture

Haslan culture, like the Haslan people itself, predominates throughout the League. City-states of foreign origin retain social structures and customs unique to their people, but even there, centuries of trade relations, intermigration, and intermarriage have influenced their cultures. For example, while the colorful bands on Haslan clothing traditionally indicates the wearer’s clan, family, and marital status, many non-Haslan peoples incorporate the style — if not its meanings — into their textiles.

Most Haslan belong to a clan — an extended family claiming descent from a famous common ancestor. For example, the Damida clan claims descent from the culture hero Damida Bear-Slayer. Villages and other small holdings typically consist of a single clan. City-states mark areas where numerous clans have gathered to take advantage of scavenging sites, strategic trade locales, or otherwise valuable land or resources. Urban architecture retains the central fireplace common to nomadic Haslan tents. Houses often use strawbale and plaster construction; larger buildings typically rely on brick, wood, or stone, with steeply gabled roofs to shed snow and ice. Underground tunnels and roofed, elevated walkways wend throughout cities and towns, facilitating foot traffic during the snowiest winters.

Non-League clans generally continue their traditional seminomadic lifestyle — herding cattle or reindeer, hunting large game, trapping for furs, scavenging, and trading. Each seminomadic Haslan clan consists of many bands, their leaders typically supported by an elder council, a subordinate warleader, and a shaman. Bands themselves divide into several camps, each an extended family. Alliances and antipathies between seminomadic clans and with other local peoples, such as the Icewalkers — many of whom take offense to secular Haslan hunting practices — often shift back and forth over the years.

Haslan clothing — practical, sturdy, and warm — consists primarily of leather, fur, and wool. Jerkins, skirts, trousers, and mittens feature intricate woven patterns. In addition to their brightly colored clothing, the Haslan wear calf leather or reindeer skin ponchos, coats, belts, and boots. Artisans add colorful flourishes and metalwork to leather purses and satchels, making the items both practical and beautiful. Typically, northern Haslan herd reindeer while southern Haslan herd cattle. Both use all parts of the animal, which is reflected in their cuisine. They drink milk, make yogurt and cheese, and use blood in sausage and bread. Meat is smoked and dried to preserve it, or added to everything from slow-cooked turnip stews to rye dumplings. Seasoning relies on salt and fresh herbs. Gatherers supplement animal products with wild greens, mushrooms, and berries. Urban Haslan have far more varied diets; specifics depend on their city-state’s surroundings, the cuisine of neighboring peoples, and the trade routes they stand athwart.

Gift-giving informs Haslan culture. Hunters leave small items as thanks for game they kill, such as tobacco or tea. Trappers build relationships with non-Haslan traders, exchanging gifts at the season’s beginning and end. Haslan families share food, clothing, medicine, and other aid with neighbors in need, asking nothing in return. What good is hoarding, when you have enough and someone else goes hungry?

### Haslan Spirituality and Superstition

Haslan Spirituality

and Superstition

The Haslan are a deeply spiritual, even superstitious, people. This doesn’t conflict with their knowledge or their innovative ethos. Indeed, savants and engineers often attribute malfunctions to spiritual sabotage; many wear lucky ornaments or perform elaborate personal rituals to increase a project’s odds of success. By tradition, each clan acknowledges three divine protectors. Typically, one is a potent spirit revered by many clans, albeit often addressed by wildly differing names and aspects; the other two are lesser spirits or ancestors, including the clan’s heroic ancestor if still active among the dead. This triumvirate rule has loosened within the League along with distinctions between clans; some merged clans revere larger pantheons composed of multiple triads. Prevalent among their protectors are trickster spirits, animal and fertility deities, and gods of fate and dreams.

Haslan gods rarely appear to followers in person. Most communicate through abstruse dream symbolism, omens, and subtle, seemingly coincidental miracles. The Haslan employ no priests; communities maintain oral records of gods’ traditions, worship is conducted individually, and shamans interpret dreams or — when necessary — bargain with gods directly.

Dreams of the future have special significance among the Haslan. A death foretold in a nightmare signals impending disaster. Likewise, dreams of future fortune indicate good luck to be celebrated among friends and family. They consider elderly people’s dreams especially illuminating. Foreigners find odd their propensity to freely describe their dreams in casual conversation and to treat others as unduly secretive when they don’t reciprocate.

### Government

Traditional Haslan clans prioritize communal management and resource sharing, ensuring that everyone’s needs are met. A family’s members seek consensus, relying on elders’ authority, persuasion, debate, and social pressure. Local families belonging to the same clan likewise cooperate and coordinate. Recalcitrant members experience shaming, shunning, and — in the worst cases — banishment from the community.

Haslan-dominated settlements traditionally lack princes or queens. Instead, each clan sends a representative to an urban council, with each clan having one vote. But it’s not uncommon for individual leaders to dominate, whether through personal charisma or belonging to a powerful and prestigious clan. Some settlements dabble with democracy or yield to autocratic rule.

Oligarchs

A parallel power structure has gained traction throughout the League’s expanding cities. To supplement their granaries, workshops, and laboratories, the Haslanti trade with neighboring peoples. This began with offering furs and ivory for grain, but traders tasked with this vital civic duty steadily broadened their interests to include commodities from alchemical medicines to jade. With a stranglehold on trade and its concomitant wealth, they consolidated ever more political authority. Known as oligarchs, these merchants collectively rule the Haslanti cities in all but name, enflaming the ire of many clan leaders, war leaders, and council representatives who oppose local oligarchs’ policies but can’t muster the votes to oppose them. Old grudges flare as Haslan clans with turbulent pasts find themselves yoked into working alongside ancestral rivals at the oligarchs’ dictates.

The Haslanti Convocation

The League’s ambitions have expanded past its clans’ ancestral territories. Some city-states look to secure more sites for archaeologists and savants to investigate; others conquer out of need or greed. Swelling urban populations demand ever more resources, even as oligarchs demand more buffer states against invasion. City-states hash out their conflicting interests in the Haslanti Convocation. This council meets in the capital of Icehome; each city-state sends a representative to determine overarching economic policy and to agree on wars and treaties. Years of ruthless politicking determine if and when an expanding settlement gets a vote. Most council members owe money and favors to various oligarchs; the extent to which this subordinates the council — and thus the League as a whole — to the oligarchs’ interests is a common topic of debate among the Haslanti. Still, the council remains disunited; even the oligarchs disagree on key issues. Selling proprietary inventions to the Guild and engaging in aggressive wars — once largely fringe views — have gained support in recent years.
