### THE GRANDMOTHERS

The League jealously guards proprietary knowledge, methods, tools, and scavenged artifacts. To that end, its regional spy network listens for plots against Haslanti operations, sabotages rivals’ investigations, and reacquires stolen items. These operatives take orders from the Grandmothers. Composed mainly of older, retired Haslanti, most Grandmothers were formerly traders, military leaders, or political strategists. Long years in these occupations give them a keen eye for how people work, think, and relate. Though they often meet in Icehome, Grandmothers operate out of settlements throughout the League.

### Icehome

’s docks bustle with activity. Traders unload goods at all hours. Laborers transport supplies to and from warehouses. Shipbuilders outfit vessels to withstand the White Sea’s icy waters. Airboats dock at Ilovna’s Spire, a hundred-foot stone mooring tower that dominates the city skyline; covered hangars huddle around its base.

### Wonders New and Old

Haslanti excavations and researches have furnished abundant wonders. Scavengers recover a few genuine artifacts, whether speaking chimes that communicate over great distances or mantis-shaped towers that alter the weather. But most finds offer subtle innovations, inspired directly or indirectly by ancient workings. More mundanely, the Haslanti produce high-quality paper, metals, cloth, and alchemical medicines. Their distillation-alchemists produce both high-proof liquor and fuel-grade kerosene. An ingot of Windcreche steel is worth its weight in silver to foreign smiths. Haslanti technical mastery has produced repeating crossbows, airboats, gliders, iceships, and more. The League even melds ancient and modern wonders. For example, the famed airboat Old Redolent floats not on burning whale oil’s hot, cloying smoke, but on fragrant plumes from an everburning red jade censer.

Icehome

On the White Sea’s eastern shore, Icehome has been a meeting ground for the Haslan clans for centuries. Today, it’s the League’s capital, a city uniting its ideals of innovation and tradition. This is one of the few places where nomadic Haslan live alongside their League counterparts, as all respect its ancient role as a meeting ground. However, non-League Haslan rarely visit for long; they return to the plains after concluding their business.

Natural hills surround the city by land. By sea, a high wall wards off the harsh north wind. Icehome’s heart is a chaotic forest of Haslan clanhouses following a

Most business in Icehome takes place in the Old Market District, where banks, shops, and workshops sit side by side with teahouses and dance halls. This adjoins the Convocation Pool, an ornamental lake where the Shattered Tower Convocation once met before the Haslanti mined out the tower’s steel. Civic buildings cluster here, including the League’s Hearth, a conical marble structure where Convocation members gather. The rest of the lakefront consists of wealthy townhouses, high-end shops, and scenic roofed promenades. Forges in the Artisan’s District manufacture armor, iceboat runners, and airboat parts. Occult engineers accept tidy sums to mend scavenged artifacts or integrate them into new inventions. Sculptors and woodworkers produce both traditional and innovative tools and furnishings. Visitors rarely receive permission to watch crafters at work, lest they transmit trade secrets to foreign artificers.

Prominent Figures in Icehome

Jaska White Hare spent much of her youth exploring ruins, learning how to tell useful relics from junk and how to make junk useful with a little tinkering. Now settled in Icehome, she uses her vote and influence in council to fund new expeditions and experiments. She’s spent decades cultivating good relationships with other clan leaders and usually hears of trouble brewing or interesting opportunities before her peers. She’s still a few years from retirement, but the Grandmothers view her as a potential candidate.

White Hare’s prominent criticism of increasing League militancy places her in opposition to many oligarchs and clan leaders. Though some of her opponents have made threatening noises, she’s unwilling to admit the possibility of danger from fellow Haslanti. Tall and scarred, one eye milky from a years-old wound, the outcaste known as the Physician acts as a community leader for refugees in Icehome, having arrived

EX3

with survivors from the Battle of Futile Blood. His intimidating mien draws aid out of those who’d obstruct it, and his medicinal knowledge saves many lives. He speaks gruffly and rarely, as though concerned someone will recognize his voice. Once, he served in the Tepet legions under another name; while some have guessed his past, they respect his privacy. This far from the Blessed Isle, such matters seem of little concern. The Lunar Exalt Gerd Marrow-Eater has lived in caves outside Icehome since before the League formed. Clan chiefs and shamans respect his judgment and often solicit him to mediate intractable disputes. Although younger Lunars sometimes seek him as their shahan-ya, he has little interest in the Silver Pact’s agenda, instead dedicating himself to private scholarly pursuits. The League values him as an ally, especially for his personal familiarity with Bagrash Köl’s works. The elder Lunar doesn’t share knowledge openly, preferring vague hints and riddles that lead fellow scholars to new insights — albeit not always the ones he’d envisioned.

### Windcreche

The small, bustling city of Windcreche is built vertically, repurposing an ancient network of temples carved directly into a south-facing cliff to avoid the worst of the Northern winds. Artisans have carved new stairs over the old, which are too large for human comfort and often too eroded to use. Excavations continue to bring forth more curious finds: strange relics, corroded engines, etched crystalline tablets, and mixed human and inhuman bones.

Academics huddled in the temples study these finds and excitedly pen new treatises on rediscovered methods of engineering and their potential applications in Haslanti artifice. Despite Windcreche’s inhospitable locale, its study of these relics and central location in the League have made it a boom town for savants, sorcerers, and thaumaturges. Farming is poor and hunting is lean on the lonely cliff face overlooking the sea. Fishing supplies some needs, but with a population approaching 10,000 in the caves and amid a growing sprawl of low buildings atop the cliffs, Windcreche increasingly relies on trade supplies from other League settlements, largely shipborne cargoes of life-sustaining grain and dried fish. Windcreche distributes these precious supplies onwards to smaller expedition sites.

### FEATHERSTEEL

This strangely light, easy-to-forge metal weighs but a fraction of steel. The Haslanti value it most for use in airboats, although they also sell ingots abroad for exorbitant profit. But feathersteel is only found in far Northern mountains, often haunted by walking dead or Fair Folk. Compensation is high, but so is mortality.

Windcreche has one great natural resource: the wind. A gale blows steady and strong over the cliffs, day and night. This wind powers the city’s industry. Windmills great and small grind grain and ore and operate pulley systems, moving heavy platforms bearing machinery and goods up and down the city’s face. Wind furnaces and mill-powered bellows smelt steel of a quality rarely produced outside Nexus or the Blessed Isle. But the wind’s greatest gift is flight. Gliders and airboats soar over Windcreche, marvels of the Second Age. A glider is a delicate waxed paper and wicker construct, banded with feathersteel and baleen. An inflated balloon, buoyed by burning whale oil or kerosene and propelled by pedals, holds an airboat’s gondola aloft. Airboats move as swiftly as the prevailing winds, though only specially designed courier vessels can safely travel faster than a trotting horse. The largest airboats carry a dozen passengers or equivalent cargo; in wartime, they can instead deliver glider-borne commandos to the heart of enemy territory. The pride of Haslanti innovation, they’re the cornerstone of League communications network and wartime strategy.

Prominent Figures in Windcreche

At Convocation meetings, oligarch Birna Winter Flame lobbies in favor of Haslanti aggression. She believes in airboats’ military utility, and recommends the League use them while events remain tumultuous — and before neighbors develop reliable countermeasures. Well-connected among fellow oligarchs, she invests heavily in arms manufacture and trade. Her liberal generosity has won her great respect among Windcreche’s people.

Blue Skies Rising is a cloud person (Hundred Devils Night Parade, p. 88) — one of those reclusive air elementals inhabiting migratory sky-cities. Decades ago, she followed a passing airboat to Windcreche, marveling how mortals had mastered the skies. The city’s savants welcomed her, endeared by her meteorological knowledge and infectious enthusiasm. In turn, she

EX3

loves the Haslanti for their boundless curiosity. She makes a modest living offering aerial tours to individuals looking to scout the surrounding lands. Despite her age, the renowned thaumaturgist and artisan Rippling Leaves retains a dedication to work that shames younger colleagues. She has an uncanny talent for discerning newly unearthed relics’ functions. Her workshop overflows with curious devices and chattering mechanisms, its walls decorated with her own paintings — a bewildering array of schematics, portraits, and landscapes recreated from memory or from weathered fragments. For exorbitant fees, she consults on technical, mystical, or artistic matters, occasionally offering tutelage to promising talents.

### Other League Settlements

The Haslanti League encompasses dozens of settlements throughout the eastern North, ranging from citystates to isolated fishing villages, mining camps, and archaeological sites. They spread from the eastern White Sea to the shores of the lakes called Mela’s Fangs. Fair Isle stands off the southern shores of Lake Longtail, dominating the green, hilly island of the same name. Its port, filled with wide streets and low buildings, stands on the ruins of the First Age city of Verodel. A few ancient structures still jut up above the skyline, repurposed as tenements and airboat mooring towers. Massive drydocks dominate the waterside; when the lake freezes each winter, ordinary ships are put into storage and replaced by steel-runnered iceboats that skate across the ice. Despite Fair Isle’s reputation as a city of shopkeepers and scholars, its veteran sailors fight savagely against pirates and foreign raiders. Diamond Hearth, in the Far North, mines the largest feathersteel deposit yet discovered. Decades old, it’s already a small city, sending up smoke from foundries and ringed by earthworks made of mine tailings, visited regularly by supply caravans from coastal settlements. Recently, a supply train reported that the northernmost mining site stands empty and deserted, making many reluctant to venture forth.

Diamond Hearth’s de facto leader, the oligarch Pribizen of Tusk, cuts a dramatic figure with his scarlet cherkeska, shining brass flame pieces and gazyrs, and prosthetic hand of mammoth ivory. He plays the part of a devoted civil servant, but riches are his true loyalty. He presses lavish gifts upon prominent Haslanti merchants and clan leaders to overlook his increasing control over the feathersteel trade — and his occasional illicit sale

of relics and Haslanti prototypes to the Guild-affiliated Unbroken Ice Caravaneers. Through the Caravaneers, he hopes to bargain with the Guild councils of Northern hub cities like Plenilune and Whitewall, or even the Directorate in distant Nexus.

Crystal, a tiny settlement in a high mountain valley even beyond Diamond Hearth, mines platinum, gems, unique icy white-blue glowstones, and even blue jade. Its inaccessibility leaves miners dependent on airboat shipments of food and supplies, but its oligarch investors find the exports well worth the investment. Miners recently discovered a First Age ruin beneath a frozen lake, only its tallest towers poking up from the ice. Early exploration found intriguing, valuable relics. But strange disappearances among scavenging parties prompts caution in Crystal’s council of merchants and leading miners. Rumors of alien beasts in the depths prompt a search for more professional aid.

### Neighbors

The people of the Stragor Principalities, on Lake Longtail’s southwestern shores, have surprisingly little business with the surrounding League. Their religion rejects the First Age and all its works, deeming ancient ruins both physically and spiritually perilous. A few merchants, mostly Guild-affiliated foreigners, are viewed with suspicion for trading lumber and food to the Haslanti for tin and gemstones; trading in relics is banned, though smuggling thrives in the capital city Haspell’s seaport. While High Prince Yemerey of Ban theoretically rules the region, he has little control over the feuding principalities — a state of affairs that the Grandmothers covertly encourage.

Beneath snowdrifts and frozen earth, amid black caverns that have never seen the sun, lie the forgotten ruins of Kertz Derat. The Dawn Caste sorcerer-warlord Derat Khan formed a pact with princes of Hell to survive the Usurpation, and his Demon-Blooded progeny — the Shrouded Ones — dug deep to prepare for war against the usurpers. For centuries, their raiding parties ranged as far as the White Sea coast, burning towns and bringing slaves back to their lair. Growing reckless after the Contagion shattered the Dragon-Blooded Shogunate, the Shrouded Ones raided the empire of Bagrash Köl, whose retaliatory assault slew many and scattered the rest. The escaped Shrouded Ones pledged to return someday to reclaim their ancient home. Until then, these bleak midnight halls shelter only arctic beasts, sorcerous horrors, and the vindictive dead.

## Ascension

local guides reunite with family in the city before rejoining clients on the long return journey southward.

To reach the city of Ascension demands the strength and courage to brave the harsh Wasting Tundra — with its bitter cold, isolation, predators, and strange spirits — to the northernmost mountains of Creation, where ice and clouds lay as one atop a thousand untouched peaks.

The divine pagodas loom over the rest. Within these 20-foot-tall stone towers, monks tend altars to dozens of deities whose blessings support Ascension’s prosperity, favoring spirits of fire, fertility, and the harvest. The monks also study warrior arts, which prove useful when rogues from the wild mining town downslope trouble Ascension’s peace.

Ascension draws a contradictory blend of folk from across the North and beyond. As a timeless sanctuary safeguarded by ancient magic, it attracts artists, hermits, tourists, and mystics. But the lodes of invaluable metals and gems in the mountains beneath it beckon financiers, merchants, adventurers, and rogues. The young, rough mining town of Notch (p. XX) burgeons below the cliffs. Its supply of foreign goods may threaten Ascension’s culture. Its masters’ ambitions might imperil the city’s survival.

### Life in Ascension

Ascension is home to several thousand people. Most live scattered along Horizon Plateau; this stretches for five miles upon the towering Skyrazor Mountains’ southern face, between spirit-haunted Mount Ganshen and the impossibly steep Falconspire.

The city’s boundaries are marked by an ancient shoulder-high ring wall carved with enigmatic glyphs. This anchors sorcery that keeps Ascension warm year-round and draws up freshwater springs from the earth. Outside the wall, the warmth dwindles, but suffices for farms to raise yaks, alpacas, and chickens; harvest stands of juniper; and grow hardy crops, alternating cold-hardy grains like barley and rye with roots and tubers. Farmers build small, sturdy homes and barns to stand firm against avalanches. They stockpile smoked and fermented food in preparation, sometimes living for weeks beneath the snow before life outside their homes can resume.

Within the wall, bees hum lazily amid ancient orchards heavy with apples, pears, plums, sour cherries, butternuts, and hazelnuts. At the orchards’ center stands the city proper, composed largely of low stone houses and shops surrounding a handful of plazas. Some empty structures offer housing for visitors; others slump, overgrown, beneath grape vines and ivy. Wealthy tourists occupy these dwellings, eager to rest after the hard trek along the Graveland Trail (p. XX). Their hired

Built into the plateau is Heartbreeze Mahavihara, a grand monastery-manse where vast corridors and chambers form a maze of underground streets and structures. An ancient, nameless family called the Caretakers overlooks these halls, safeguarding wisdom and traditions in their great monastery and library. They’re celibate, only increasing their numbers through adoption; this doubles as a means of population control. Only Caretakers can become monks (most do); only monks gain access to the library, though they’ve occasionally been persuaded or bribed to copy fragments of text.

In the underground maze’s depths sits a prayer wheel of all colors of jade engraved with starmetal runes. Spirits are drawn to the wheel, fascinated by its spin. The monks offer access to local spirits who promise to enrich the mines and bless the fields, driving a hard bargain to claim the blessings they need to make the city prosper.

Governance

An abbess leads the Caretakers both spiritually and temporally. She arbitrates major disputes, passes judgment on rulebreakers, and sets social and economic policy. She’s advised by a council of Caretakers and common citizens. She rules for life, naming her own successor.

All monks train with bow and spear, as do many volunteer citizens. Led by a Caretaker warden, this militia drives off predators, rogue elementals, and bandits. Historically lax due to Ascension’s isolation, in recent years the militia has expanded its ranks and increased drills in case of attack from Notch.

Culture

Ascension’s lifestyle, arts, and customs trace back a millennium. Artisans weave vividly patterned clothing and rugs; glaze elegant pottery; carve intricate woodwork; and forge copper and iron. Occasional trade with distant lands has gone on for centuries, but it’s greatly increased with Notch’s rise. Today, many artisans focus

EX3

on elaborate crafts for export; others find themselves out of work.

Garments primarily use wool, leather, and furs, although imported cotton, linen, and even silk grow popular. Heavy hats and scarves are removed in summer or within the wall; sleeves are detachable. The mountains’ rich mines allow even ordinary folk to wear elaborate jewelry dripping with semiprecious stones. Upon arriving in Ascension, visitors receive a small jasper stone threaded onto a leather cord to wear during their stay. This necklace symbolizes welcome and respect; losing it or giving it away is a grave insult. The guest returns it to their host upon departure as a sign of thanks and friendship.

Traditional Ascension dishes showcase the city’s staples. Yak meat features in soups, stews, and dumplings. Cooks make barley-flour breads, noodles, dumplings, and honeyed cakes. Yak milk becomes yogurt, cheese, and butter. Butter tea features at social gatherings; a polite guest waits after the first and second sip for her host to refill her cup to the brim before drinking the rest. Pickled vegetables appear as condiments alongside many dishes. Merchants import foreign foodstuffs, from cardamom and cloves to dried apricots and persimmons.

Neighboring Notch’s rapid growth has brought an influx of foreigners to Ascension. While foreign influence inspires Ascension’s artisans and imported goods offer unprecedented prosperity, these things have also brought upheaval into citizens’ lives. Many are seduced by wonders, literature, or travelers’ tales brought by traders from the outside world, and leave with southbound caravans to seek their fortunes. Merchant princes woo local leaders, attempting to seize control of Ascension’s resources from within. Monks faced with strange ideas brought by artists and savants either strive to incorporate them into their teachings or reject them outright.

Prominent Figures

Citizens and foreigners alike petition Abbess Gyawen Parts-the-Clouds, a blind centenarian, for both economic advantage and spiritual counsel. She offers little of the former and much of the latter. Like a wheel’s turning or new growth from an ancient tree, she believes that even Ascension’s traditions must change with circumstances, and that her job is neither to shut out the outside world nor to wholly embrace it, but to find a healthy middle way.

Warden Harzin has overseen Ascension’s defense for twenty years. Barely tolerant of the disruptions a trickle of visitors caused in the past, today he’d cut the city off entirely from the outside world if he could. He’s leery of Notch’s cutthroats and disdainful of the luxuries that commerce brings to Ascension. He deeply distrusts foreign ideas transmitted by the handful of travelers permitted into the city, and intervenes quickly when newcomers step out of line.

### Notch

At the plateau’s base sits Notch, a mining town inhabited by thousands of people as harsh as the midnight cold, eager to invite new arrivals into their alehouses for nights of gambling, brawling, and liquor. A few native miners provide for families in Ascension. Most of their fellows come from distant lands, whether in bondage or desperation. Around them swirl traders, smugglers, swindlers, thieves, and other brave souls seeking wealth and glory.

While a smattering of sturdy stone structures — largely built from ruined Shogunate mining camps’ stones — huddle outdoors, most of Notch lies within the mines themselves, in chambers long since emptied of ore. Residents eke out a living as best they can; many shed their culture’s gender roles, or explore new ones, while seeking work to stave off hunger and frostbite. Despite the symbiotic relationship between Notch and Ascension, the cold, hungry miners resent Ascension’s folk for the warmth and comfort they enjoy. Clothing in Notch emphasizes warmth and durability. Residents wear sturdy hide clothing, fur-lined cloaks and boots, and woven or knitted wool garments. Damaged or worn clothing gets patched and mended; items beyond repair are used to patch others, or made into patchwork quilts and garments. Meals are simple fare, incorporating yak meat, butter, and cheese from Ascension, and cheap flour and dried beans from southern lands. More luxurious goods — fresh fruit, spices, fine wines, and the like — are as welcome an ante at the gambling tables as coin. Miners drink small beer throughout the day; gambling houses serve stronger brews and distilled liquors.

Notch and Ascension are connected by dangerous trails, pulley systems, and elevators lifted by creaking, icy chains. Along this route open hundreds of mineshafts with miles of underground tunnels and limitless opportunities for treasure and danger. The two settlements provide for each other — Notch supplying tools

EX3

and foreign goods, and Ascension food and clothing. Traders and laborers follow these transports, but warily and only when necessary — even the strongest chains can snap with the biting cold.

Abbess Gyawen appoints a governor to oversee Notch. This includes establishing and verifying trade between the two, maintaining order in Notch, and ensuring Ascension’s safety and security. The governor in turn names a sheriff to enforce their decrees. The abbess usually selects a petitioner from Notch; Ascension’s folk largely lack a taste for the work.

The Mines

Mining is Notch’s lifeblood, but the mountains contest miners at every turn. Elementals perch outside mineshafts and carry victims into the clouds. Long-legged, ice-bodied spiders crawl underneath miners’ skin, melting inside their bodies to possess their minds. And then there are the glassfolk — subterranean elementals with translucent, luminescent flesh, who communicate via chiming notes and shifting colors.

Prominent Figures

Elegant Zhanna leads the Prospector League after her predecessor’s recent disappearance. Among Notch’s richest residents, she runs the Rusty Nail wineshop and gambling hall, and owns several valuable mining claims. Manipulative, aggressive, and ruthless, she wields threats and hired bruisers to intimidate or remove local opposition, while outbidding rivals on certain foreign luxuries to resell at a profit. The current governor is Aelum Brassriver, a retired prospector said to have explored deeper into the mountains than anyone else alive today. While he spends most of his time appeasing the abbess in Ascension, Notch is under the heel of his ghost-blooded wife, the gruff but fair-minded Faedun Brassriver; as sheriff, she enacts her husband’s policies and punishes those who break the peace. Generous “donations” from

Decades ago, when Notch was new, the prospector Oviba Woolfinger first encountered the glassfolk after months exploring ancient tunnels. Despite nigh-insurmountable language barriers, she negotiated a peace so long as mortals stayed away from the glassfolk’s crystalline palaces. But as time passed, Oviba’s warnings were forgotten, and now prospectors dare each other into forbidden depths.

Silver and tin appear in surface veins. Deeper levels hold rarer minerals, such as ethereal iron and singing crystals. These esoteric finds are guarded by glassfolk, other elementals, and stranger entities who grow angry when prospectors steal these treasures.

The Prospector League

An organization of prospectors who cooperate to explore the depths, the Prospector League trades in maps, territory, and secrets, and gives aspiring prospectors resources to support hiring mining crews. Taking a cut from members’ finds, the League has money and influence to bribe the Caretakers, contest the governor’s policies, and undermine rival businesses. Some prospectors openly reject the League, deeming it a gathering of charlatans who prey upon others’ accomplishments and share disinformation. Smugglers and traders who believe or seek to benefit from these rumors offer alternative services to would-be prospectors.

EX3

### STOPS ON THE GRAVELAND TRAIL

Just below Notch stands the Qinsu, an ancient wood of low, twisted dwarf juniper. Caretakers traditionally visit this sacred site for meditation, and to negotiate with its artisan-elementals for the pine needle paper used for copying ancient texts. But Notch loggers harvest the Qinsu against the governor’s instructions, angering Caretakers and elementals alike. The low stone, turf, and timber buildings of Luster huddle for warmth around nine hot springs. Here, a few hundred farmers grow cabbage, kale, turnips, and leeks. At dawn, bells ring in shrines overlooking eight of the springs, calling the people to worship Luster’s gods. In the hour before dusk, the last bell sounds on the shore of the ninth spring, summoning them to altogether different rites. A recent battle to drive off conquering merchant-bandits turned one hot spring into a tiny shadowland, its dark waters seething with voices of the dead. The town’s gods and their farmer-priests, who once ruled Luster without question, now grudgingly admit ancestral ghosts to their council.

At the Graveland Trail’s southern terminus sits Cauldron, a city built among the ruins of a Shogunate river port, where the Trail’s traders auction off treasure to southern merchants. Both must bargain with Cauldron’s stew of caravanners, fences, scavengers, smugglers, and crime bosses — groups largely indistinguishable to the outsider. Lording over them all is the infamous outcaste Domra Redsleeve; her old pirate crew and hired swords ruthlessly put down any who’d interfere with trade or with the flow of taxes into her coffers.

Elegant Zhanna convince the Brassrivers to look the other way when it comes to Zhanna’s — and her bruisers’ — actions. Faedun eases her conscience by funneling much of the ill-gotten funds toward feeding Notch’s poorest residents.

The Caretaker Clemsen advises the governor on Ascension’s capabilities and needs. Most think her naïve and unworldly; this is a show to conceal her other job as spy for the abbess, watching for signs that Notch might try to cheat or threaten Ascension. She maintains contacts among prospectors and merchants, gathering information with bribes, charm, and the occasional subtle threat. Her most useful leverage is helping smuggle foreign goods into Ascension past the xenophobic warden.

### Neighbors

Fleeing into the snows with a handful of followers after a failed coup, the prospector Quill Ashmount leads his Burning Wick Syndicate in a war against both Notch and Ascension. Lairing in fortified caves and abandoned mining tunnels, Syndicate agents raid supply

caches, sabotage infrastructure, and infiltrate work teams to recruit young miners to their cause. Some say Ashmount himself bargains for aid with spirits rejected by the Caretakers.

Across the frigid glaciers lies the Ice Queen’s Retreat, a bordermarch whose Fair Folk queen, Jadai of the Silver Nail, weaves snow into fabric and traps dreams in ice. Fields of blood-red poinsettias surround her palace, whose walls are covered in winter ivy. Troops of hobgoblins and ice golems patrol her realm’s borders for intruders. Jadai occasionally offers audiences to individual diplomats or trades gifts with brave merchants, but only if they willingly surrender some dreams to fill her frozen gallery.

Notch sits at the northern end of the Graveland Trail, a long, arduous road where food is scarce and cold winds make even rocks tremble. A thousand years ago, Daimyo Elia Veil-Singer followed the Graveland Trail pursuing a stolen poem. Legend says that travelers can still see her searching within the winter fog, and only reciting the poem will banish the fog and let her spirit rest.

EX3

According to the storytellers, the towers of Dain were once taller than any redwood. The city had been a center of learning, a place of peace and prosperity — although whether for the Linowan’s ancestors or for their ancient oppressors depended on the storyteller. Now its towers were shattered, sunken skeletons dotting a vast marsh. Nobody knew what curses lay sleeping in the muck, but those who approached the ruins felt flashes of an ancient fever. Generations of Linowan had warned off scavengers with harrowing tales and threatening signs.

But there was profit in selling pieces of Linowan history. Tonight, a dozen relic hunters had camped at the marsh’s edge. They planned to steal what they could in the morning and flee before they were discovered. But as daybreak approached, so did two Linowan warriors.

Esado was a young bull of a man, clad in furs and eager to prove himself. He was already better with both spear and hatchet than his peers were, and his shield-arm never buckled. Today’s blood would be his to shed.

Otsi Firebreak stayed a few paces behind the younger warrior, her knives ready. Her blessed ferret-mask, the proof of her battle prowess, enhanced her hearing. If the young man asked for her help, she would step in. But if he defeated the invaders alone, he would earn his own mask of excellence. Esado found a spot in the brush to hide and watch the enemy break camp. When he saw one of the expedition’s armed protectors step out into the woods alone, he flung a hatchet as easily as breathing. The invader fell in near-silence, hatchet embedded in his throat.

His next ambush didn’t go as well: the expedition’s lean guide looked up from her morning meal just as Esado stepped into view. If she had stayed silent or surrendered, he might have spared her, but she cried out in alarm and Esado pierced her gut with his spear. Just as well, he thought. She was as much a thief as the rest of them.

With the alarm sounded, Esado slipped back into the brush and circled the camp, keeping an eye out for archers. But he feared that the scavengers might flee into the marsh, denying him cover and disturbing the haunted ruins, so he didn’t wait long before stepping into the open with his back toward the murky shore. The caravan’s remaining guardians, a swordsman wearing leathers and an axewoman in heavy lacquered armor, dashed to meet him.

Esado thrust his spear and roared to keep the axe-wielder at bay, since he didn’t trust his shield to weather her heavy axe. It deflected his other opponent’s sword well, though, and Esado ran the swordsman through. The spear stuck in the warrior’s body; Esado quickly readied his spare hatchet. As if from nowhere, an arrow grazed Esado’s cheek — of course there was an archer in the camp — and the young warrior reflexively ducked and rolled forward, taking him under the armored woman’s axe swing. He chopped at her calf with his hatchet as he rolled past, sending her to her knees. Back on his feet, Esado grabbed her by the hair. He raised his hatchet... and took a breath. “Drop your axe,” he ordered, breath ragged, “and tell the others to surrender too.” •••

Otsi and Esado bound the survivors and arranged the dead as a warning to other scavengers. “You did defeat them alone,” Otsi acknowledged, “but this was a test of your excellence as a warrior, not a diplomat.”

“An excellent warrior can afford to show mercy,” Esado argued. He didn’t add, And I wasn’t sure how else to deal with that archer.

With her mask on, Otsi had no expression visible to read. “Well, ‘excellent warrior,’ we’re many miles from home and one of your captives can’t walk any longer. What do you wish to do with them?” Esado scowled. His test wasn’t done.

# Chapter Two: The Northeast

Chapter Two

The Northeast

The wild, thinly populated realm of the Northeast begins as a quilt of disparate terrain — prairies, forests, marshes, mountains, rivers, and lakes. Farther from the coast, this gives way to ever-deepening woodland. Penetrating the Direction outside of a few major river valleys proves arduous; most deem it not worth the trouble.

Many also deem the land accursed. Centuries ago, as the Realm invaded the Silver River’s rich Shogunate successor states, a wave of terrible diseases dubbed the Second Contagion swept the region, ravaging cities and Imperial legions alike, leaving fields and fallen cities to be swallowed up by forests and grasslands. In the wake of this and other, lesser plagues that followed, the Empress postponed her plans for the Northeast in favor of other conquests. Even now, much of the lower Silver River remains haunted by hungry ghosts, disease spirits, violently isolationist peoples, and strange beasts seeking refuge in tameless wilderness.

The Northeast’s peoples have thus developed in relative isolation from the rest of Creation. But the Realm, the Guild, and other outside powers remain interested in the wealth they can wring from these peoples and lands, and as memory of the Second Contagion fades, each renews their effort to gain a foothold here. Still, the Northeastern peoples take pride in their independence. They won’t be easily overcome.

## Fray

Flocks of paddleboats, their wheels cranked by slaves sweating below decks, make their stately way up and down the Silver River. These ships drop anchor at the wharves of Fray beneath the catapults of a clifftop fortress. Here, stevedores load shipments of timber, grain, livestock, furs, and slaves to send downriver to the coastal satrapies of the Northeast; others unload ships from the Inland Sea laden with cargoes of wine, metalwork, and other finished goods. Meanwhile, Realm soldiers bearing a crimson tiger insignia patrol docks, markets, roads, and walls. These forces owe no loyalty to any Great House. Instead, they

serve the outcaste dragonlord Hanto Galina, newly crowned Empress of Fray and pretender to the Scarlet Throne.

### History

House Peleps established this satrapy-colony over half a century ago to supply timber for the Realm’s shipbuilding industry. Fray’s economic importance grew with time, demanding constant military presence to ward off Linowan raiders and other local threats. As the commander of a dragon of legionary troops on long-term assignment to the area, Galina earned her troops’ adulation with two decades of victory against Northeastern raiders and plunder from retaliatory strikes against the local peoples. One storied maneuver involved introducing an apparent gap in the legion rotation, luring Lunar forces into an ambush. Several Dragon-Blooded died and the city sustained damage, but the Lunar general Imra Heartwhisper also perished. This led the Shadow Fang Vanguard toward a more hands-off role, giving Fray breathing room. Three years ago, when a new satrap demanded a greater share of the spoils, Galina’s legionnaires mutinied and declared their leader Empress instead of “that debauched rantallion of a Regent.” Seeing no way out but forward, Galina seized the city, put the satrap’s head on a pike, and set about establishing a new Northeastern Empire.

Galina now rules the territories surrounding Fray, replicating the Realm’s court in miniature and conferring patronages and titles of nobility upon loyal officers and allied Northeastern leaders. But with the Realm having reorganized in the wake of the Empress’s disappearance, Fray’s breathing room is at an end. House Peleps’ forces will surely sail upriver to reclaim their rebel colony — if they can.

### Geography

Fray’s upper city stands on a strategic, defensible bluff amid wooded hills, overlooking the Silver River valley

EX3

below. Guarded switchback roads, stairways, and pulley-elevators connect the upper and lower cities.

### FRAY AND THE EYE

Daimyo’s Fort — the mossy Shogunate-era fortress at the cliff ’s edge — once housed legionnaires on local assignment and the satrapial garrison. Now, troops stationed within bear Galina’s colors. An encampment surrounds the fortress as Galina’s legion expands, training trusted auxiliaries and adding them to her ranks. Where neat rows of tents were once pitched now stand new barracks. Workers replace wooden palisades with stone walls and sentry towers, and soldiers drill in the courtyards.

Attached to the fortress is the old satrapial palace-manse, called Green Heron Tower. Administrators crowd its offices as Galina and her staff navigate the new government’s needs. Emissaries from neighboring tribes and Northeastern satrapies bring missives, gifts, and bribes to Fray’s Empress. Representatives for both local merchants and Guild interests seek an audience with her advisors, hoping to negotiate favorable terms. Merchants own lavish estates in the upper city, their homes both beautiful and well-fortified. Bodyguards patrol these properties, discouraging thieves and spies. Galina’s administration watches Realm merchants carefully for sedition.

A shattered First Age bridge once spanned the river from Fray’s bluff, and its wreckage — called the Murle — disrupts river traffic; the Realm left it alone to help maintain control of that traffic. The Small Docks, just upstream of the Murle, unload and disassemble flatboats sent downriver to supply timber, and accommodate other traffic heading upriver toward the Linowan and Halta. Laborers portage these goods to the Large Docks, located just downriver from the Murle. These support galleys that travel downriver to the Inland Sea. The lower city spreads out around the docks. Warehouses line the streets full of goods awaiting ships to carry them upriver or caravans to distribute them overland to cities like Gentian and Tears-of-Beauty. At all hours, the streets bustle with life. Visitors frequent flophouses, inns, and wineshops, and spend their coin in gambling dens. Laborers’ homes crowd in between these establishments — workers learn to live with the constant noise or turn to potent concoctions to help them sleep.

Wealthy Realm and Guild-affiliated merchants have established plantations on cleared land surrounding Fray. These largely provide grain, cattle pasturage, and orchards. Free farmers settle here, establishing homesteads

A deadly circle of All-Seeing Eye agents tasked with fending off Lunar infiltration along the Silver River operates out of Fray, secretly supporting legion and garrison activities. Its handlers once rotated members throughout the region like pieces on a Gateway board. Now, rumor in Fray suggests the Eye may have withdrawn in the face of the Empress’ disappearance, though that doesn’t stop residents from looking over their shoulders. Noteworthy members include the seemingly unkillable sorcerer called Poisonheart, the charming master of disguise dubbed the Alewife, the peerless archer and scout Condor, and the pattern-seeking administrative prodigy Grayfinger.

and villages. Bandits and raiders — whether Northeastern natives or former settlers — often trouble the area; they prefer the profits available from the plantations, but often find free settlements to be easier targets. Fortified logging villages lie scattered around the region. Many stands of old-growth woodland have been deforested and the associated villages abandoned, their stockades dismantled for additional lumber. Some logging villages face intermittent retaliations from Northeasterners resentful of losing hunting grounds and prime gathering spots, or from angry forest spirits; messengers stand ready to ride to Fray for legionary aid. Other villages have made deals with local rulers, elders, and warriors, paying tribute in foreign goods to maintain operations in safety.

### Culture

Fray’s position on the Silver River and its history as a Realm satrapy make it a multicultural locale. Some residents hail from the Blessed Isle, transplanted to Fray to support House Peleps’ logging interests. Guildaffiliated merchants — mostly from the Scavenger Lands and the River of Tears — establish holdings in the city, taking advantage of its favorable position and river trade. Folk from local bands and settlements come here seeking work on the docks, in logging villages, or as soldiers and guards.

Fray is home to such flamboyant characters as the turtlefolk boatman Crozier, undefeated in nineteen duels and veteran of a hundred drunken teahouse brawls; the gambler Nine Teeth, said to have won supernatural stealth from the river god Nanza-Cora in a game of knucklebones; or the shaman Bitter Calf, who commands the city’s underworld through her network of

informants and the favors owed her by local merchants, thugs, godlings, and ghosts. But in bringing order to the frontier, Galina has cracked down on the city’s lawless atmosphere; many of the city’s most colorful residents have departed to avoid conscription, enslavement, or worse for their illicit activities.

A dynamic local cuisine combines Northeastern staples like maize, squash, and river fish with rice, wheat flour, and other foreign foodstuffs and spices from the Inland Sea and beyond. Specialties include thick, aromatic turtle soup; chopped mixed vegetables and shellfish simmered in bacon grease; and roasted waterfowl

EX3

stuffed with cornbread, blood sausage, and cranberries. Galina’s officers and Realm merchants largely favor Blessed Isle dishes prepared by personal chefs. Commerce is key in Fray. To keep supply lines open, commercial negotiators seek out local clans and chieftains on the city’s behalf. They hear leaders’ concerns and are empowered to cut deals with them, within reason. Those leaders are usually willing to talk — better to get some measure of what their people need than have the legion come and take whatever Fray demands.

### Prominent Figures

Hanto Galina, Empress of Fray and General of the Crimson Tiger Legion, is a storied military commander and a decisive, disciplined leader. Though her political ambitions hadn’t originally included a crown, now that she has one, she’s loath to give it up. It’s not a matter of avarice; she simply sees no future in returning to the Isle, and better to live or die an empress than to flee and hide at world’s edge. And while she rules, best to rule firmly, enforcing a stability that today’s Realm lacks while guaranteeing her soldiers’ security. A dozen key legion officers and civil officials comprise Galina’s inner circle. All realize that if House Peleps regains control of Fray, they’ll be tried for treason right alongside her. They include Wheat-Thresher Tanden, Galina’s longtime second-in-command and classmate at the Stair, known for his ruthlessness and candor; Peleps Liana, a former garrison officer and a friend and admirer of Galina’s, who turned coat in the heat of the moment to support the coup; Administrator Cheya, a sybaritic Fray-born financier who knows every local merchant by name and controls the city’s purse strings; and dockmaster Kelet Lor, a taciturn retired Merchant Fleet captain who both oversees river commerce and keeps an ear out for concerns rumbling in the lower city.

The Realm merchant Fennel Danys has been in Fray since its founding, doing brisk business in arms and lumber and helping the city grow and thrive. Today, he’s among Fray’s wealthiest and most powerful merchants, commanding a network of negotiators and a sizable bodyguard. Other local traders respect the old man; his loans and investments kept several businesses afloat in years when Linowan raids were particularly vicious, or bandit gangs plagued boats sailing upriver. This, plus his connections throughout the Northeast, could make him a major local force, but he’s practical. House Peleps put Danys here; he must demonstrate loyalty to Galina

over Peleps, as his family business only survives in Fray at her sufferance while she holds power.

### Neighbors

Half a dozen Realm forts rise within a day’s long march of Fray. Each can accommodate a full dragon of troops, though most currently house a talon to a wing of legionnaires and auxiliaries, with ongoing recruitment and training to bring numbers up. Settlements have grown up around each, most notably First Fort with its bathhouse and Swan Fort with its heavy river defenses. Smaller fortalices stand every five miles or so along the roads between them.

The seminomadic Kiesan people have traded with Fray since before its split from the Realm, providing sturdy horses in exchange for Inland Sea goods. Its leaders accepted Galina’s authority with little fuss; if commerce continued, one foreign governor was little different from another. They hadn’t anticipated the degree to which Galina would treat the Northeast like her own, smaller version of the Blessed Isle. Her demands for soldiers exceed the previous satrap’s, and the clans chafe at providing them.

On the far side of the Kiesans, the Danecho people have largely exhausted the soil in their domains through overfarming and deforestation. They’ve increasingly raided their neighbors for many years, but as their population grows and their resources diminish, more drastic measures are needed; led by their charismatic outcaste warleader Evets Bloodblossom, they eye Kiesan territory as their next home. Danecho warriors let their hair and beards grow from the time they reach adulthood until their first battlefield kill; the victor shears her locks as she stands over her vanquished foe. The Kiesans may not be able to defend themselves if they place too many of their soldiers in Galina’s employ, but they may prove unable to win at all without Galina’s aid.

The nearby Oset people — subjugated decades ago by House Peleps — rebelled once Galina seized power. After a swift victory, she elevated the Oset warleader Erskets — who’d led a sizable pro-Realm faction against his rebel kin — as their new prince. Today, Oset warriors serve loyally in Galina’s army, though discontent simmers among farming villages and market towns over increased tribute demands. Meanwhile, the rebel prince Areilt and his followers, who fled into the Brindled Marshes, turn to banditry, harrying merchants and tribute caravans.

EX3

### OTHER NORTHEASTERN LOCALES

Plague haunts the streets of Sithen. The town sports a fine harbor on the shores of Lake Malagren; the waters teem with fish and the soil is rich and fruitful. But ruins of older settlements litter the shoreline, and each year’s plowing churns up human bones. During the day, mourners in funereal white bury the newly dead beside Shogunate-era gravestones weathered beyond recognition. Come nightfall, folk gather indoors and make hex signs before their doors to ward off age-old forgotten ghosts.

An antediluvian castle-manse looms in the hills above. This is the House of Ancient Victory, which even the inhabitants of ill-starred Sithen call accursed. Every known attempt to loot the House has failed; those few who scaled its high walls or passed its barred gates never emerged. To those with Essence sight, the sign of Saturn burns above the manse like the mark of doom.

The nomadic Ranavet peoples dwell in voluntary isolation amid the sprawling Lushwater Marshes. Here they hunt and fish from canoes; harvest berries, roots, and greens; work scrap metal on portable forges; and worship gods and ancestors, such as Brecha Silverhook and the trickster Imvorathe Fire-Thief, at standing stones and ancient ruins. Having endured centuries of war, plague, and slavery, they spurn outside contact, showering all intruders with arrows from afar. Warbands only leave the marsh on sacred raids, destroying caravans, leaving bodies to rot, and burying plunder for a month before bringing it home. Those who leave under other circumstances are forbidden to return. Merchants traversing the region and scavengers seeking to loot its drowned cities do so at their peril.

Stretching nearly 300 miles, the Baleful Expanse still bears wounds from disastrous battles between Shogunate successor states. While small shadowlands and blasted heaths mark the places where the heaviest losses were incurred, most of the Expanse has regrown with verdant forest and scrubland entangling the ruins of cities, villages, and farms. However, hungry ghosts, virulent poisons, sorcerous corruption, and decaying First Age occult munitions leave the surrounding terrain too dangerous for human habitation. The region’s hazards bar neighboring satrapies from exploiting its resources or expanding deeper into the Northeast; travelers venture there at their own risk. Local guides charge hefty fees to lead people along “safer” paths largely free of ancient weapons and hungry ghosts. But even these routes are perilous; giant wasps, hellboars, quoll lions, and other predators prowl the Expanse, their frightening size attributed to the slow drip of lingering magics.

## The Linowan

Along the lush shores of the Silver River’s upper reaches stretches a vast series of wetlands, bordered by a golden vale cloaked in a gentle spread of deciduous

trees: elm, birch, and sycamore. Beyond them lies the

edge of the great Northeastern forests, where sycamore

groves give way to coniferous woods speckled with tall,

majestic redwoods.

Here dwell the Linowan people — tall and sleek of

build, with warm brown skin and eyes and long, thick

hair. As with many of the Northeast’s peoples, their

hair and eye colors vary from the shades of autumn foliage to golden summer meadows. The Linowan strive for excellence in all things, proving

their skills through everyday work and seasonal contests. Weavers, smiths, warriors, and savants — all their achievements contribute to the glory of their families,

their villages, and the Linowan people. Those at the

pinnacle of their craft compete to receive their people’s

highest honor: a mask depicting a related beast, plant,

spirit, or element, imbued with spiritual blessings.

Facing a Linowan war band is a frightening prospect for

merchants and poorly defended villages. Nonetheless,

their battle prowess and guerilla tactics make them

sought-after mercenaries and potent allies.

### History

Long before the Great Contagion, the Linowan people resisted the rule of daimyos who laid claim to their lands. Rather than submit to invaders, they melted into

the forests and wilds. When sickness came, the stories

say, settled and outlaw Linowan alike banded together

to survive while the daimyos abandoned their subjects.

There they mastered the wilderness and forged pacts

with gods who’d likewise fled Immaculate strictures on

illicit worship.

EX3

The Second Contagion taught them to stay scattered. Though many Linowan still died in the waves of new diseases, their losses weren’t as great as those suffered by the urban polities that had sprouted up in the Great Contagion’s wake. That lesson, along with their gods’ blessings, helped them survive even as deadly fevers swept through the Realm’s newly established Northeastern satrapies.

With the Silver River’s course largely depopulated by the plagues, the Linowan expanded into stretches of wilderness along the great river’s banks, absorbing or driving out surviving locals. To this day, they avoid the ancient ruins (p. XX) dotting the river’s course.

### Settlements

Tributaries branch off from the wide, slow-moving Silver River like roots from a tree; their shallow, grassy banks form an extensive network of wetlands and floodplains. Taking advantage of this wealth of resources, hundreds of Linowan crannog settlements sprawl across this territory.

Wooden piles, their interlocked timbers ensuring structural integrity, elevate these manmade islands above the marshes and river waters. Fresh-cut wooden planks create sturdy platforms upon which the Linowan construct roundhouses of oak logs sealed with dried clay and thatched with river reeds and long grasses. Especially wealthy or resourceful families may construct homes from rare and precious redwood, available only from Halta’s thick, perilous evergreen forests (p. XX).

When a new house is constructed, the entire community makes a festival of the occasion, with every villager young and old pitching in to obtain materials, cut timber, and thatch the high-pointed roof. A Linowan roundhouse can be quite large and often houses multiple families. The largest settlements sprawl out past a village’s normal bounds, forming a cluster of crannogs or spilling out onto the shore. Such towns and small cities attract outland traders, a few of whom intermarry and remain with the Linowan. The sole exception is the holy city of Rubylak (p. XX), which bars all foreign visitors save by the priests’ or the high queen’s decree.

EX3

its way onto wealthy foreigners’ tables as a digestif. Common dishes include slow-roasted backstrap brined with rosemary and honey; fishcakes made with potatoes and spring onions; and fresh berries mixed with tea-steeped corn and sweetened with a dollop of honey.

### A LINOWAN VILLAGE

On the northeastern edge of Linowan territory sits Tindaro village. The village chief Erlaka is a seasoned warrior, earning her fame and boar-mask in raids against the Haltans. She views Tindaro as the first bastion against Haltan aggression. She often finds herself at odds with the merchant Taneir, who left Tindaro at fifteen to apprentice with a Guild dyer. He returned two years ago, laden with gold, silver, and new ideas. Though he’s deferred to Erlaka’s authority thus far, some of his proposals — such as inviting the Guild-backed First Silver River Company to help manage river trade — have gained traction with his peers. While Erlaka intends to compete at the next festival to be declared a royal, she worries that Taneir may throw his wealth behind another challenger.

The Linowan depend on annual migrations. As flocks of birds return to the springtime forests, or spawning salmon crowd the Silver River in late summer, nearly everyone helps catch and preserve meat to last the year. These temporary flurries of activity allow the Linowan to maintain a more leisurely pace in other months. Crafters spend winters weaving, mending, and maintaining the islet-villages. Raiders range far afield in summer. Lorekeepers tell tales by the fire as autumn’s chill descends.

Trappers and hunters seek horns and pelts. Loggers obtain redwood lumber for construction and handicrafts; woodcarvers make fine bowls, utensils, and tools, while furniture makers produce chairs, tables, chests, and more. Gatherers collect herbs for medicines and salves. All of these goods are used at home and sold abroad.

In addition to the mighty river-goddess Yanae (p, XX), households in Tindaro revere the warrior god Khand Spear-Caller, whose jagged glyph they paint on their shields in bright crimson for protection. At winter’s end, the village’s most daring competitors sneak into the cave where the spirit Laughing Bear slumbers. The last person to pluck a tuft of fur without waking him is blessed with a bear’s strength until the next winter.

Small rowboats and rafts swarm around these villages. They’re used both for fishing and to haul raw materials and finished goods up and down the Silver River and its tributaries. When not in use, boats are hauled out of the water and stored in the village for safekeeping.

### Culture

Linowan dress for the climate: temperate, but prone to bitter cold and moderate snowfall in winter. They fashion garments from wool, wood fiber, leather, furs, and occasional imported textiles, embroidered with intricate designs and ornamented with metalwork, ivory, and bone.

Their diet is rich in meat, particularly venison and small game, alongside trout, salmon, and turtles snared from the bounteous rivers. They commonly serve root vegetables, goosefoot, black mustard, celery, nuts, strawberries, bilberries, and blackberries from small personal gardens. Hunters, fishers, and gatherers collaborate to smoke and salt meats for winter. Linowan add wild blackberry wine to stews and medicinal preparations or drink it neat; this sweet, tart libation now finds

Most Linowan adults train with spear, javelin, and shield to protect their villages and to raid rival villages, neighboring peoples, and foreign merchants. Those with a knack for battle may join a chief or chieftain’s personal guard, or sell their services as mercenaries to other nations.

In some Linowan villages, entering the dark undergrowth of the distant redwood forests undetected to retrieve lumber is a rite of passage for young people. Successful youths attain majority and receive a small amulet to mark the occasion, carved from the wood they brought back. These amulets are worn as a sign of pride, particularly for formal gatherings. Marriages can range anywhere from a mutual declaration of devotion witnessed by the village chief to a contracted betrothal. In larger settlements, wedding celebrations involve the couple’s extended families; in small villages, the entire community comes together for a day of feasting, dancing, and well-wishes. The Linowan value etiquette, honesty, and respect. Travelers who show rudeness or who reject gift exchanges and other courtesies may be turned away, as are liars and cheats. Those who violate local customs — or worse, cause direct harm to the Linowan or their lands — suffer branding and exile at the least, and are subject to violent reprisals should they return.

EX3

### Clans and Leadership

LINOWAN MASKS (ARTIFACT ••)

Linowan clans trace their ancestry back centuries, though not everyone claims direct descent from their clan’s ancient founders. Families may be adopted into a clan or take its name as a declaration of loyalty. Clans have risen and fallen over time; some were lost to plague or war, others merged or were subsumed, and new clans split away to follow heroes and firebrands. Anyone wishing to settle in a new village must submit to its leaders’ — and therefore, its clan’s — authority. They remain part of their original clan, but agree to abide by their new village’s laws or customs when those differ from their own. Some clans predominate among multiple settlements in a region, adopting other families as they expand into or annex other villages. The Swift Eagle clan, who once controlled only the village of Alash, have spread out in recent years as their chief, the charismatic warrior Senad, draws families and lesser clans to her banner. Village chiefs ensure that villagers have their needs met. They oversee winter food storage, inspect repairs to structures and defenses, and negotiate with neighboring villages for provisions. If villagers can’t settle a dispute on their own, the chief’s ruling is the final word on the matter. When a clan is spread over a large area, village chiefs serve as advisors to the clan’s chieftain. The clan’s chieftain is both diplomat and war leader, in charge of negotiating with foreigners or leading the battle when talks break down. Clan chieftains are elected from among the clan’s prominent members by vote of the clan’s nobles and the prior chieftain’s immediate family. The chieftain is often a noble, as this brings prestige to the clan, but noble candidates may be passed over due to their poor leadership or to keep the role in the prior chieftain’s family.

Nobles

As a culture, the Linowan prize excellence, and they bestow the rank of noble upon those who demonstrate it. Should one demonstrate absolute mastery of a skill — archery, military strategy, history, music, smithing, or any other talent — she can expect a summons from Rubylak, there to be tested before the high queen’s court. Traditionally, to appear impartial, these challenges are difficult but fair. However, tests for friends of the court may showcase their specialties, while political rivals’ tests often focus on weaknesses in their skill sets.

Each Linowan mask offers its own boon, a benefit based on the feats of the skill that it was created to reward. A mask created for a master javelineer might bless her with an eagle’s eyes, while a distinguished musician’s might strengthen her music’s emotional impact. Mortals can attune to masks, but must pay five Willpower to do so. Others must commit two motes.

While mortals normally can’t create artifacts, Linowan shamans safeguard a two-dot ritual for creating the masks. By propitiating the proper spirits, thaumaturgists can undertake superior projects to craft the masks. The ritual also makes the project easier to complete.

Those who best the challenge set before them become new nobles and receive a unique mask to mark their elevation within Linowan society. Each mask is a work of art. Hewn from redwood and carved into elaborate animal shapes, crafters inlay the masks with precious stones and metals, and shamans imbue them with spirits’ blessings. Some are created especially for their owner. Others are granted by the High Queen from the masks of the honored noble dead.

Linowan society holds nobles responsible for employing their skills on the people’s behalf and passing their skills on to future generations. These obligations come with significant prestige, drawing in apprentices and others eager to serve these bearers of Linowan prowess and tradition. Many parlay this influence over their communities into more concrete authority — particularly warriors, whose martial students and associates can easily dominate a village or region. Not every village boasts a noble, though many do, and some larger settlements are home to several. In smaller communities, apprentices travel to another clan’s holdings to learn skills from a noble. The fields of endeavor in which a person might achieve nobility are athletics, crafting, entertainment, hunting, lorekeeping, and warfare. Each field encompasses several individual skills. For example, crafting includes pottery, smithing, weaving, and building, among others.

Royalty

The greatest living Linowan masters of each skill are acknowledged as royalty. Once per year, each royal must hold a festival in her town at which any other noble may challenge her in her field. Each challenger

EX3

brings a lavish gift, and the contest is judged by all other nobles present. The winner — whether the old royal or a successor — distributes the gifts among her clan. Each royal wears a mantle of office appropriate to her station, often of rare foreign fabrics embroidered with precious metals.

### NOTEWORTHY GODS OF THE LINOWAN

Yanae, the peripatetic goddess of the Silver River, shines like water in sunlight. She grants swift currents to Linowan traders and raiding bands, and advises Linowan shamans when the spawning salmon will be most abundant.

A royal accepts additional responsibilities beyond an ordinary noble’s. She advises both her clan chieftain and the High Queen in matters concerning her area of expertise. She’s also encouraged to train nobles in her field, sharing her secrets so they don’t perish with her — although a royal is often reluctant to share her deepest secrets with potential challengers for her title. Lastly, as the closest Linowan to the ideal of excellence, she serves as a spiritual leader, setting an example for the clans and interceding with spirits too arrogant to treat with shamans.

For much of the past two centuries, one high queen or another has held suzerainty over all Linowan. She’s the final arbiter in disputes among clans. She reigns for life. Upon her death, a grand contest is held in Rubylak to choose her successor from the extant royals, requiring victory in more fields of endeavor than any rival. While any royal may become high queen, most past queens were warriors and strategists, capable of protecting their people when the Linowan went to war. Upon her succession, the queen also enters a sacred marriage as the Silver River goddess’s wife, bringing the people’s petitions to the goddess and speaking in her name at festivals.

### Religion

The Linowan don’t venerate one spirit above all others. Rather, they revere all manner of gods and elementals, ranging from small divinities of earth, water, bird, and beast to mighty heavenly spirits. An individual, household, or settlement may hold one or more spirits in particular reverence, yet still pray to other gods. Linowan shamans, chosen from children with occult talent, serve as both priests and as wonder-workers. In dealing with spirits, they perform tasks and take on geasa in exchange for magical aid, future favors, and mystic lore. All learn the rites to craft magical masks and to seek wisdom in dreams; other, secret rites are passed on from master to apprentice.

Immaculate missionaries have converted a handful of Linowan chieftains, who’ve largely adopted syncretic worship of the Dragons more in keeping with local traditions than the Realm finds acceptable. Some will

Charging Buck occasionally runs alongside Linowan hunting parties. Despite his human form, he sports a rack of antlers and runs on hoofed feet; sighting him through the trees is a sign of good luck. The elemental Kani Ember-Gift, patron deity of the village of Far Islet, appears as a levitating catfish with fiery eyes and barbels. The Linowan claim that it keeps the hearthfire lit in the worst of winter’s cold.
