they thrive in relative isolation, largely sheltered from

Creation’s time of tumult.

### The Fair Folk

Centuries ago, the Haltans’ ancestors — urban folk from

Bagrash Köl’s empire — fled into the great redwood forests, seeking refuge from invading Realm forces and the plagues of the Second Contagion that followed. Led

by the culture heroes Evali Stormbow and All-Friend

Kaja, they settled in territory already claimed by the

Fair Folk. The raksha might have hunted them to the

last if not for a bargain the human leaders proposed:

the forest floor would be the sole province of the fae,

but the trees belonged to the Haltans, who could dwell

there unmolested.

The raksha agreed, with one condition: each year, every

Haltan city must sacrifice three people to the Fair Folk,

sending them to the forest floor to be hunted down in

a feast of fear and pain. Ghastly as the pact was, the

Haltans quickly became accustomed to its grim necessity — and welcomed how the fae presence dissuaded bandits and raiders. Needless to say, the arrangement

does nothing to improve chilly relations with their

nonarboreal neighbors, particularly the river-dwelling Linowan. Many Haltans embrace war with the Linowan, welcoming an enemy who they can demonize

and sacrifice with less internal struggle.

New settlements have a grace period during which they

needn’t offer sacrifices. But eventually, Fair Folk emissaries approach each growing town on the first day of the year, informing residents that their hamlet has been

settled for long enough to pay its share of the tithe. Any

city that fails to pay loses the pact’s protection. It’s been

many years since a city fell to the Fair Folk as a result;

today’s Haltans take special care not to suffer the same

fate, and some cities even sacrifice more than three

people each year to ensure that nothing goes wrong.

In practice, brief brushes with the surface are usually

safe — the Fair Folk aren’t everywhere. But hobgoblins

EX3

and other fae creatures sometimes lurk beneath Haltan settlements, awaiting an opportunity to snatch away a mortal who even momentarily touches the ground. Longer trips are more dangerous; Linowan raiders in particular face great peril should a Fair Folk hunting party catch their trail.

Three mighty princes rule the forest’s Fair Folk: Davanali of the Flickering Table, Marika RushingWaters, and Thousand-Leaves Vajraval. Having taken on conflicting elemental aspects, they politick against one another while playing out a cycle of forest fire, flooding, and regrowth. Each has several lesser Fair Folk nobles in their court, along with innumerable minor fae.

### Daily Life

Haltans typically have high cheekbones, brown skin, and a tall and athletic build. Their hair is nearly always green. Green-haired foreigners find a warmer welcome here than most.

Traditional Haltan clothing is made from durable bark, hemp, and animal skins. Their fashion is pragmatic and

form-fitting to resist snagging on branches and the tug of high winds. Most Haltans eschew shoes or boots, preferring to go barefoot to keep their footing on narrow catwalks and swaying branches or rope bridges. Haltans collect rainwater in barrels and cisterns. In times of drought, water can be hauled up from the rivers, but such work is hard and risks encounters with the fae.

The Haltan diet relies heavily on fruits, berries, and nuts such as hazelnuts, grapes, and rose hips, as well as tender leaves, shoots, and inner bark when in season. Farmers tend to treetop gardens, transporting soil from the surface over the years and replenishing it with composted material. There they grow herbs, vegetables, and flowers for the beekeepers’ hives to pollinate. Mushrooms, harvested from caves in hollows beneath the trees, feature in many dishes.

Animal products, though a luxury, form a significant part of the Haltan diet. Households cage-raise small birds, rabbits, rodents, and lizards for meat, eggs, fur, feathers, and the like. Hunters train hawks to catch small game like squirrels and hares on the ground, or to pluck smaller birds from the air and fish from the

EX3

river. Trappers drop snares from low branches to capture larger animals and work together to haul them up into the trees.

Food is rarely cooked, lest fire spread to the tree. Instead, Haltans eat fresh provender raw, and preserve the excess by salting, sugaring, pickling, or air-drying. Seasoning includes garden herbs, honey, maple syrup, vinegar, and pickled or fermented condiments. Wealthy Haltans import spices; a few cities allow them to build ovens into their homes — carefully overseen by city officials — and to hire cooks to cautiously and safely prepare their dishes. Haltan culture holds that a single person is but one part of the whole community, much as a single branch is part of a whole tree. Many expand this viewpoint to include all of Halta as they grow to adulthood. If every action they take has consequences beyond what they see, they must ensure those actions are necessary for their people’s safety and prosperity. This sometimes leads to friction behind closed doors, as Haltans experience pressure from family, neighbors, and authority figures to pursue life choices — careers, marriages, etc. — that contradict their individual desires and needs. Misfits often leave the cities to pursue wandering careers like trapping or trading, or to join new settlements like Rams (p. XX).

Vegetative metaphors and images appear in many elements of Haltan culture and tradition. A traditional Haltan wedding gift is a pair of seedlings bound tightly together so that as they grow, their trunks and boughs entwine as a symbol of the couple’s love and unity. Children take their mother’s family name. Upon reaching the age of five, a child is considered ready to learn about the world beyond her parents’ home. Young Haltans apprentice under artisans, carry messages across the canopies, and learn to tend the redwood groves.

Wise Beasts

The Haltans have developed a close relationship to fauna as well as flora, having bred animals for generations for cleverness and obedience. Common companion animals include birds, bats, tree frogs, lizards, snakes, wildcats, and monkeys. Some Haltan animal companions are simple pets; others earn their keep as guardians or even servants, performing simple, repetitive tasks such as shelling nuts or accompanying game hunters to retrieve kills.

Most companion animals are no cleverer than a monkey or a very young child, understanding a limited

vocabulary and communicating through gesture and body language. A few go beyond this; originally bred for intelligence from Wyld-touched beasts, they can think and speak as humans do. Quite rare, they’re almost exclusively companions to those Haltans with sufficient wealth and influence to hire or court them. By Haltan law, intelligent animals have significant rights. They cannot be owned like pets, their companionship cannot be offered to another citizen without their express permission, and they must be fairly compensated for their labor. Some enterprising Haltans bring their intelligent animal companions to distant lands, where they entertain the locals with theatrical shows involving all manner of tricks and performances — counting, dancing, legerdemain, comedy, and the like. The most talented often attract the attention and coin of wealthy and influential personages amazed by the skill, grace, and intellect of the performing animals. Nobles with more money than sense sometimes offer great sums to purchase an animal. But most Haltan performers would never willingly sell their companions and will do whatever is necessary to retrieve any animal stolen from them.

Religion and Spirituality

The Fair Folk’s dominance over the forest floor makes other local spirits wary of leaving their sanctums, let alone traveling abroad to seek or command worshipers. This reluctance to intervene in mortal affairs lends the Haltans a wide latitude in determining their own spiritual paths. Most Haltans venerate the forest and the city-trees, but they place the Oracle Tree at the apex of their worship. A few Haltan cultists worship other entities: forest gods and elementals, weather and beast spirits, ancestor ghosts, and even some Fair Folk. Syncretic Immaculate beliefs and other foreign philosophies maintain a rare few adherents in one city or another. Long-ago strife between cults has left Haltans disapproving of proselytization or even of announcing especial devotion to any given spirit.

When lighting fires, Haltans supplement mundane precautions — barrels of water, thick layers of stone shielding the tree from heat, etc. — with prayers to spirits of forge and hearth, such as the fox-faced goddess Ela Lamp-Eyes. Haltan trappers weave weblike snares to catch prey, and burn offerings to the wood spider Kokia-Boga and her seven sisters in thanks for their nets’ sturdiness. Haltans create wreaths to venerate Berchta the Evergreen, a god of pine, fir, and renewal,

EX3

decorating them with carved items representing the blessings they hope to receive in the coming year. The ancestor ghost Grandfather Hauriyan is said to watch over children as they take their first shaky steps along the branches. Haltans try to appease the wind elemental Boughshaker, lest she unleash her fury upon the trees.

Commerce

Each city offers its own specialties for trade, such as Skara’s wholesale foreign imports, Lapai’s fine woodwork and bows, paper and books from Visminthis, or High Jauki’s wines, honey, and berry preserves. Most notably, cities with surplus Linowan war prisoners exchange them for trade concessions, minimizing the number of Haltan citizens tithed to the Fair Folk. Halta trades extensively with other peoples, driven by the need for metals given the impossibility of mining the forest floor and the precautions against fire that restrict Haltan smithwork to a few carefully overseen stone-lined forges. Various foreign luxuries often accompany this trade. Meanwhile, Haltan woodwork and literature have great value in the wider world, alongside exports of rare woods, furs, spices, medicinal plants, and perfumes.

Between strife with the Linowan and the terrors of the Fair Folk, travel to and through Haltan territory can be hazardous. Merchants and other visitors typically hire local escorts to lead them, showing them which branches will bear their weight and guiding them through the maze of catwalks, ladders, and rope bridges zigzagging through the forest canopy — some rotten, others dead-ending in toppled trees or Linowanburned settlements. Among neighboring peoples, several small family-run concerns have traded with Halta for generations, learning the ways of the forest well enough not to need local guides. But commerce with more distant lands generally involves larger ventures, whose high-risk, high-reward nature requires backing from Guild caravans or other powerful enterprises.

Commerce with the Fair Folk is discouraged but not banned. The Ferulae (p. XX) provides, free of charge, negotiators to aid merchants in dealing with the fae; cautious members anticipate that any restrictions on such trade will only lead to illicit dealings, and fear that ill-considered negotiations might open a loophole for the Fair Folk to enter Chanta. As such, gossamer wonders of the Wyld — shimmering garments, silvered faerie blades, strange fruits unknown to Creation, and

the like — can be found in Haltan markets and in rich citizens’ collections.

Fire Control

No amount of vigilance around fire can prevent it entirely. Lightning strikes, Linowan sabotage, and forest fires — sometimes prompted by elementals or by Davanali’s fiery fae court — present a real fire threat to Haltan cities. To stop the spread, Haltans keep water and sand in reserve, and train citizens from a young age to smother flames. Haltan gods with power over fire and rain help limit fires, and sorcerers who can offer magical protection are welcome in Haltan cities. Occasionally, however, a fire moves too quickly for any efforts at keeping it in check; each city maintains evacuation routes into underground tunnels should catastrophe strike. While Haltans import most materials created with forges or kilns — metal tools, glass, ceramics, and the like — a few sites are specifically dedicated to such work. These trees are set in isolated spots, such as on islands in the river, to mitigate accidental fires.

### Haltan Settlements

The Haltans hold trees sacred, treating them with the utmost love and respect. They build their settlements with that reverence in mind.

Far-ranging hunters and gatherers construct nest-huts from tree limbs and small branches. They set these shelters deep into the boughs for maximum coverage and shelter from the elements, and twine them securely together with dried ivy. Outlying villages often begin with similar, albeit larger, structures. The larger and sturdier the tree, the more residents it can support. As villages grow into towns and cities, sometimes spreading out across multiple redwoods, their sophistication increases. Loggers harvest lumber from tree limbs; workers gather stone blocks from forest-floor ruins, taking care never to touch the ground. Carpenters — a prestigious profession — build sophisticated structures from carved and polished wood held together by cunning joinery. Structures follow the shapes of branches and trunks; important or community-oriented buildings, such as schools and meeting halls, stand near the trunk. Certain temples and shrines are made from living branches trained into shape by bough-architects over decades or centuries. Haltan markets are filled with the din of conversation. Shoppers perambulate along boardwalks constructed along major branches or around the tree’s trunk;

EX3

merchants set up shop beneath irregular branch-hung awnings or in the occasional hollow in the trunk. Most Haltans purchase their wares on credit; foreigners and Haltans who’ve proven unreliable at paying their debts must pay up front — in goods or foreign coin, as Halta mints no currency of its own.

### CITIES IN THE LEAVES

Scarcely a decade old, the town of Rams has only a few hundred residents, but it grows as Haltans immigrate to partake in its bounty. Some harvest bark, needles, and cones from stands of rare bluecrown hemlock to produce valuable medicines and dyes. Others hang by ropes above nearby rivulets, panning for gold and gems in the water. Recently, the town was tossed into turmoil after a bloody Linowan raid. Many argue that their individualism — for which most Ramsfolk fled the tight-knit culture of the Haltan cities — must give way to firm military leadership capable of maintaining strict patrols and retaliating against raiders.

Wealthy Haltans, who live among their village’s inner branches, welcome foreign visitors into their homes. The fact that they have extra rooms to comfortably accommodate visitors is both a sign of prestige and a hospitable way to ensure the visitor’s safety while in the trees.

### Government

Known to visiting merchants as the gateway to Halta, Skara — overhanging the Owlet River, one of the Silver River’s major tributaries — is among Halta’s oldest, best-established cities. Skara’s famous Water Stairs, living docks built upon redwood branches shaped to dip down toward the river, allow travelers and cargo to move directly between ship and city without touching the Fair Folk’s haunted ground. Citizens train regularly in bow and javelin to ward off Linowan raiders, and visiting outcastes earn indefinite room and board simply by standing ready to aid in the city’s defense.

The Republic of Halta is a loosely knit alliance of cities. Local governance varies; smaller settlements often invite all citizens to vote in regular meetings, while larger ones typically elect a prince and a small advisory council.

All are ruled jointly from Chanta by a representative council, the Ferulae. Each tree-city’s leadership names one delegate to a five-year term of full-time public service. This ensures that all cities’ concerns and needs are fairly represented whenever any major policy decisions must be made. The Ferulae determine standard weights and measurements; oversee taxes, trade policy, and foreign relations; update fire regulations; and decide when to award delegates to new settlements. Though some delegates serve for decades, re-election doesn’t always measure their popularity or willingness to listen to their electors; some stay in power via bribery or corruption. Smaller tree-cities often feel that their larger counterparts dismiss their concerns — the wind carries fewer of your leaves to Chanta, they say, the farther you are from it.

Any input that the priests of the Oracle Tree see fit to offer is duly and seriously considered, but the Tree doesn’t remark upon every mundane doing of the people in its boughs. While individual priests may be chosen as delegates, the priesthood itself doesn’t hold any formal power over the council.

The Groundwalker Cult worships Thousand-Leaves Vajraval, one of the forest’s ruling Fair Folk triumvirate. Members deem it past time for the Haltans to return to the forest floor; they’ve put forth numerous proposals aimed at renegotiating the longstanding agreement between Halta and the Fair Folk. Though every one of these has been swiftly shouted down, brave cultists venture for brief stints into Vajraval’s domain, seeking

proof that he’ll deal with them honestly. Though other Haltans are wary of the cult’s approach, their underlying message — renegotiating the contract — has generated discussion.

### Chanta

The largest and most revered tree in all of Halta isn’t a redwood. This great and majestic evergreen, overshadowing the surrounding redwoods and eclipsing the sun almost completely with the sprawl of its heavy boughs and enormous foliage, is called the Oracle Tree. Wrapped around this tree like a mother’s embrace is the Haltan capital of Chanta. It’s strong enough to support numerous stone and mortar structures. Paved avenues and low buildings stretch along its branches; great platforms ring the trunk, connected via rope bridges to the forests below.

The Oracle Tree’s true nature isn’t well understood. Haltans believe the tree itself to be a living, sentient being, overflowing with ancient knowledge. It frequently shares its insights with the priests of the city, directing its will through a series of visions that the priests then pass in an advisory capacity to Chanta’s rulers.

EX3

Administratively, Chanta consists of a dozen districts, each comprising a section of trunk and the branches emerging from it. Popular assemblies in each district handle local business; each also chooses a delegate each year for the Canopy Council, which annually elects a prince and serves as her advisors.

Points of Interest

The Ferulae and the Canopy Council both meet at the Everbough. This enormous platform, spread out across multiple branches two-thirds of the way up the Oracle Tree, encompasses over a dozen buildings, pavilions, and open-air meeting spaces, all looking out over the forest below.

Several profoundly holy sites dot the Oracle Tree. These include Vistra’s Eyrie, a shrine-platform in the canopy where priests of sky spirits meet their patrons, and the Pact Scar, a cleft in the trunk where it’s said that the first Haltans bargained with the tree for refuge. But the Oracle Tree’s holiest place is the Heartwood Chamber deep within its trunk, below ground where the roots begin. Here the tree’s priests inhale shimmering vapors that rise from fissures in the wood, granting strange visions from which they seek spiritual insight. The Sky Walk is a park among the branches. Gardeners grow flowers that usually only appear on the ground, creating colorful vistas high above. In places, branches and leaves are trimmed back so the sky shows through, making it a popular place for lovers to go stargazing on summer nights.

prefer ranged weapons requiring little to no metal to create such as javelins, arrows, and slings. A few particularly skilled fighters use the war boomerang — a thrown, bladed weapon that returns to its wielder’s hand. Though the weapon is impractical in dense foliage, its ability to return when thrown amid lighter foliage proves valuable. Some wealthy Haltan warriors have learned to wield the expensive weapon with precision.

Prominent Figures

Just shy of middle age, Aune Ilavarin has served as Chanta’s prince for three years. Her thoughtful advice and cool-headed competence earned her many of the Canopy Council’s votes; she gained the rest through promising new favors and calling in old ones. Several councilors owe their family’s success to Ilavarin’s great-grandmother Vierna, who was prince decades ago — debts Ilavarin leverages when the need arises. While publicly she’s joined the Ferulae in voting down the Groundwalker Cult’s proposals, she’s held private audiences with certain prominent cult members. Though not yet convinced that the time is right to renegotiate the pact, she keeps an open mind. She still grieves the loss of a childhood friend chosen to pay the tithe.

The Haltans’ love for the redwood trees they call home is well-known. To prevent saplings from withering due to overgrowth, they often seed them in fertile soil on the forest’s edge to give them space to grow wide and tall. Encouraged by these attentions, the trees’ root systems quickly overwhelm most other flora as they grow, which can cause deciduous trees such as oak, sycamore, and birch to grow small and stunted, or often not at all.

Boisterous, white-haired Ravenden Arent has represented Skara among the Ferulae for two decades. His garrulous charm and his work as a guide for foreigners in his middle years have yielded him lucrative contacts among visiting merchants, which he put to use after a long illness precluded his return to duty. He takes a hefty cut of profits from metal imports coming in through Skara, and his recommendation or warning can make or break a deal before a trader even makes it past the Water Stairs. A ranger in his youth, he lost three fingers and several beloved comrades in skirmishes with Linowan raiders, and still bears a virulent hatred for Halta’s neighbors downriver. He rails against the Linowan in speeches before the Ferulae, and personally oversees the transfer of war prisoners to the Fair Folk with deep satisfaction.

Whatever its original causes, the centuries-long conflict between Halta and the Linowan plays out today through skirmishing parties led by both sides. Encounters with Linowan tree-poachers aren’t unusual on the outskirts, though poachers who assume that their foes make soft targets soon discover their folly: Haltan rangers know and navigate the canopy as well as the animals that call it home, and they fight with ease from vantage points high above their trespassers’ heads. Naturally, Haltans

Wilander Alrunas, a soft-spoken, erudite priest of the Oracle Tree, serves as one of Chanta’s chief negotiators with the Fair Folk. His early experiences in this role, where he witnessed would-be merchants inadvertently trading away their sight or their zest for life as part of an ill-worded bargain, have left him with a valuable fear of fae trickery. But he’s not immune to the unnatural beauty of gossamer crafts — or of the Fair Folk themselves. Alrunas has found himself bewitched by

### War with the Linowan

EX3

the handsome faerie merchant Silver Silk, meeting him on the forest floor for ecstatic assignations that have come to dominate his waking hours.

### Neighbors

The town of Jackrock bristles on the forest floor near Halta’s edge. Built beside a rich iron mine, the town has its own ways of addressing the Fair Folk menace. Walls, doors, and gates are banded with iron and topped with iron spikes. Every citizen bears an iron dagger at their hip and keeps an iron-tipped spear ready at home. Hobgoblins, silverwights, and other petty fae that venture too close are crucified on iron nails as a warning. These measures serve largely to allay the townsfolk’s fears. Jackrock’s true strength lies in its outcaste autocrat Malin Wail, the warrior-merchant who founded the town and established the mine. In exchange for guarding the town and arranging trade with Guild-affiliated enterprises and with Halta, he claims the lion’s share of its profits, and fills his ever-more-elaborate manor with objets d’art from distant lands.

Burage lies low in the branches, nearly — but never quite — brushing the ground. Its largely Haltan citizens are of two sorts: those on the run from the law, and those who need to get away from the world for a while. It has no ruling council; citizens are expected to handle conflicts on their own or hire someone who can. This ends in violence less often than outsiders might think; no one wants to draw too much attention to themself here.

Wind whistles through empty branches in the town of Uima. The trees here are bare and dead; the only green among them appears in sickly patches of lichen. Old bridges, their ropes and planks dry with age, swing between long-abandoned platforms. Here, it’s said, live the ghosts of those the Haltans sacrifice to the Fair Folk. Uima is a place where parties meet to ensure they’re not overheard. Most take care of their business and leave before sunset.

A few stubborn Haltans keep establishments open here. These include sour, rumor-mongering Fedra’s boarding house, which offers a night’s sleep and not much else, and the rundown Red Leaf teahouse where the cups are chipped but the tea is strong.

## The Gathering Suns

North of Halta, beyond the grip of the Fair Folk, the Silver River’s roiling, twisting tributaries wind through

prairies and wooded hills. This land is home to the seminomadic people called the Gathering Suns. Claiming ancestry from the legendary First Age artificer-queen Helaku, the Gathering Suns travel under the aegis of the Men of Gold: ancient automata that Helaku forged to guard and teach her descendants. But that lineage grows thin in the Golden Men’s eyes, and those few families who still receive the automatons’ blessing — called the Unclouded — now form an aristocracy that rules over the rest of their people.

At the heart of their territory stands Fade, the Hilled City. Behind the city’s gaily painted walls, amid fields of vegetables and maize, rise its eponymous earthen mounds, capped with shamans’ lodges and the ruins of Queen Helaku’s manse. No holier site exists among their people.

Originally the destination of Gathering Sun pilgrimages, a place only shamans and priests called home, Fade attracted farmers, artisans, and merchants over the years. Now their settlements crowd thickly among the city’s twisting streets. While most Gathering Sun clans remain in distant villages or pursue seminomadic lifestyles, their regular pilgrimages pack Fade’s already-crowded roads and plazas on holy days.

### Daily Life

Most Gathering Sun clans emphasize communal bonds, with activities structured around fostering interconnectedness. This has led them to form to a complex social system. An individual may have their own birth family, family by marriage or adoption, sworn siblings, and honorary membership of another clan. This highly social lifestyle also lends itself to a great deal of posturing and comparison. Members of the Gathering Suns tend to have copper-colored skin, aquiline noses, and blond, pale green, or light blue hair. People of all genders commonly wear a wool peplos over a tunic, fastened at the shoulder with a pin or brooch. Garments feature deeply pigmented colors and intricate embroidery. Thick-soled leather shoes protect travelers’ feet in all seasons. The Silver River yields crab and fish, along with berries and wild rice that grow along its banks. River-based irrigation supports larger-scale farming for the settled clans. Herds of cattle roaming the region — followed and hunted by nomadic Gathering Suns — visit rivers and streams daily to drink. Seminomadic clans follow cattle herds during spring and summer, but keep a

EX3

fortified home base they return to every year. Common dishes include herbed wild rice soup with white fish, topped with fried shallots; mildly spicy peppered crab; and spelt biscuits with honey and fennel seeds. Cattle are pit-roasted at lively impromptu feasts for the entire community.

and battle tactics toward inter-clan feuding and fending off foreigners who mistake them for easy targets. Clan leaders exhibit dominance over foreign farmers who settle in Gathering Sun lands, sending soldiers to collect taxes or deploying them when rebellion looms. Some clans are infamous cattle raiders.

The tumultuous rivers are also deeply important to nomadic clans, who use them for travel and for rites of passage. Some participate in waterborne races, tests of skill, and competitions where individuals stand at a boat’s bow taking turns shouting boasts at each other. Although these boasts are greatly exaggerated, outright lies are seen as shameful, and falling into the river while boasting is the quickest way to lose the contest and lose face. While many settled Gathering Suns see these competitions as risky and wasteful, others attend to trade, seek entertainment, or take part themselves in these rites of passage.

Nomadic Gathering Suns believe children should be allowed to simply be children, letting them roam free at an early age. Settled parents typically exert more control over their children, emphasizing the value of disciplined education in a trade; they view nomadic children as uncontrolled and wild.

Many of the Gathering Suns — nomadic and settled alike — train as warriors from a young age. Originally, their martial focus protected the clans from the Shogunate and its successors, but as centuries passed and that threat faded, they turned their fighting skills

Religion

Gods within the Gathering Suns reflect a clan’s values. Many clans worship That Old Wolf as a god of communitarian values; Wolf teaches that one should step away from the pack when one drags it down more than one strengthens it. They also commonly worship artifice gods, such as the canoe goddess Cleaves-the-River. The Unclouded often offer their prayers and sacrifices to Flawless Jainjil, god of purity, to preserve the integrity of their children’s bloodline. Many Gathering Suns gods are wanderers, roaming the prairies to watch over

EX3

the clans that worship them. It’s considered lucky for a god to accompany a clan or reside in a village for a season before moving on.

For settled and seminomadic clans, the shaman’s lodge serves as a gathering point and a place of spiritual guidance. Nomadic clans usually have holy sites such as hills, copses, or lakes that they regard similarly, using them as the center of their temporary homes. In daytime, the lodge is a somber place for spiritual reflection and meditation. At night, these sacred places host large meals, drinking, boisterous conversation, storytelling, and wrestling matches. Drawing a weapon there without proper justification is a serious crime. Foreigners who do so likely face execution or enslavement.

Nomadism

Even among the nomadic Gathering Suns, the degree to which they roam varies. Some clans have no permanent abode. They follow cattle herds throughout the year, hunting and gathering in forests close by the grazing grounds and fishing in rivers where the herds drink. They plant crops along the way — foods such as potatoes that don’t require tending and can be harvested later in the season or the following year, or trees that will offer fruit or nuts in years to come. They set controlled fires to burn away underbrush, making room for fresh vegetation to grow.

Nomadic Gathering Sun clans scorn those who’ve settled and given up travel. Community remains incredibly valuable; owning more than can be easily transported is a sign of greed, and it should be divided and shared amongst the clan for the benefit of all. Thus, nomadic Gathering Suns see settled clans’ homes and belongings as ostentatious and wasteful.

Seminomadic clans maintain a permanent residence that serves as both fortress and holy site. Some people stay here year-round, tending to the infirm and protecting stores and the clan’s Man of Gold. The clan returns to this settlement when invaders attack or when winter brings their wandering to an end. Retired elders, priests, guards, and others who don’t join the clan during the warmer months maintain small farms to supplement their needs and prepare for the winter.

Settlements

Other clans have become entrenched, turning their winter settlements into permanent homes. Their farms are more substantial, with several harvests throughout the year. Many become trading hubs, both for the other clans and for foreign merchants traveling between Halta and Iscomay.

### FOREIGNERS

Most foreigners passing through Gathering Suns lands hew to well-traveled roads and rivers. Their territory lies between Halta and Iscomay; while busy traders rarely wander off-route, some enterprising merchants learn which clans will be close by in a given season and carry goods they value. Others find it profitable to visit settled clans’ villages. Wise merchants employ a Gathering Suns guide to serve as both ambassador and interpreter, lest they turn the locals against them with a faux pas.

Settlements resemble the holy city of Fade in their layout, for purposes that are practical as well as symbolic. A mound in the center emulates the mound upon which the Beacon of Light (p. XX) sits. Atop it, the clan shaman’s lodge — considered a place of peace — sits close by the chief’s lodge. The mound and lodges serve as a defensible place if the clan comes under attack. For settlements built by a river, the mound ensures a dry place when floodwaters rise. The clans’ homes, storage buildings, and livestock shelters ring the mound. Fields of wheat, vegetables, and maize form the outer ring. A wooden palisade encloses the settlement, painted in sunrise hues. Proximity to a mound increases a home’s social and financial value. Most buildings are slightly elevated to minimize flood damage and pest damage, but rise only a single story — less from engineering considerations than to avoid rising above the settlement’s mound. Constructing buildings and canoes symbolizes a pact between clans; one clan appoints a head builder to help another clan with whom they seek to form an alliance. Though rare, helping a clan transition from nomadic to sedentary life requires significant renovation and new construction. Such projects may take the better part of a season to complete. Often people from other clans come from afar to help, reinforcing the Gathering Suns’ sense of community.

### Clans

When dealing with members of one’s own clan, the Gathering Suns have a gift economy, gaining prestige by providing what the other person needs as they need it. Shamans draw up and witness contracts between members of different clans. Trade is for outsiders who don’t share the same values or sense of community. Merchants are typically foreigners, though some clansfolk in Fade have taken up trade, in some cases obtaining unprecedented wealth.

EX3

Gathering Sun warriors take slaves in battle. Skirmishcaptives from other clans — while cruelly punished or even executed for disobedience or attempted escape — are otherwise largely treated decently, with the intent of adopting those willing to adapt to their new clan. Children born to skirmish-captive couples during their servitude are born free. Foreign slaves have fewer opportunities for freedom, short of the occasional ransom or prisoner exchange; their slavery is hereditary. Criminals are often placed in debt, with the severity of their debt determined by the clan’s shaman. They’re expected to labor for the clan until they’ve paid back what they owe, working farms, tending to livestock, and sometimes toiling alongside the clan’s slaves. Those who commit severe crimes, such as murder or attempting to harm a Man of Gold, become outlaws; they’re forbidden from setting foot within shaman lodges, and are tasked with carrying the most cumbersome loads. Outlaws enjoy few legal protections — even killing someone who has been stripped of their caste isn’t a serious crime.

The Unclouded

Although the Gathering Sun peoples all deem themselves Queen Helaku’s descendants, the Men of Gold disagree. By whatever numinous mechanism they recognize Helaku’s bloodline, most Gathering Sun clanfolk no longer qualify, their ancestors having intermarried too often with outsiders. Today, the Men only acknowledge a handful of families. These, called the Unclouded, reign as the clans’ ruling aristocracy.

suffered controversy, having been recently exposed for secretly utilizing witchcraft on other clans’ fallen kin to strengthen their blood. Debates rage in Fade about whether the Odasa should be allowed to remain within the region or banished while the people await a decision from the shamans. Should a clan’s last Unclouded leave or die, the clan’s Men of Gold depart to join other clans. The rest of its members typically follow suit, resulting in the clan’s dissolution.

The Clouded

Those whom the Men of Gold fail to acknowledge as Helaku’s heirs form the preponderance of the Gathering Suns. Called the Clouded, they don’t receive the Men of Gold’s blessings directly. But they gather indirect benefits from Unclouded leadership and teachings and consider themselves one people. The Clouded comprise all manner of folk — farmers, fishers, hunters, artisans, warriors, and the like. Their status varies from clan to clan. Craftsmen often rank highly for religious reasons, due to Queen Helaku’s legacy. Warriors and farmers usually rank just below them, their tasks noble and indispensable. The lowest ranks are almost universally those who handle the least desirable work, such as transporting night soil and disposing of corpses.

A single Unclouded family leads each clan. Intermarriage between different clans’ Unclouded helps strengthen inter-clan ties and keeps Helaku’s bloodline strong. The Gathering Suns celebrate these matches in week-long wedding festivals that bring the newlyweds’ clans together.

Young Unclouded receive special training, both from their Men of Gold and from elder relatives. This includes combat, etiquette, poetry, history, mathematics, medicine, and occult lore. With these skills they lead raids, make trade agreements, and create artworks depicting the Gathering Suns’ feats. Individually and as families, they accumulate glory and wealth beyond other clan members’ reach. The continued thinning of blood troubles the Unclouded. Families employ skilled matchmakers to ensure the best unions, while other fading families secretly seek help from occultists and spirits to ensure their blood remains strong. The Odasa family has

EX3

### FAMILIAL RELATIONS

Though the families do everything within their power to prevent it, some Unclouded parents produce a Clouded child. Such offspring, by their unfortunate nature, are denied the privileges their parents and Unclouded siblings enjoy, such as tutoring and healthcare from the Men of Gold and attending high-level negotiations with other clans or foreign representatives. Some parents send these children to be raised by Clouded cousins; others educate them alongside Unclouded siblings and rely on their skills when they come of age. Though they won’t marry an Unclouded spouse, the Men of Gold may yet declare their children Helaku’s descendants.

Conversely, two Clouded parents may have an Unclouded child. Such rare children are swiftly adopted into the clan’s Unclouded family. Their parents often receive special consideration from the clan leaders, though whether that’s a one-time gift or a permanent position of honor — elevated above their Clouded peers, but not so high as the Unclouded themselves — varies by clan.

Internal Conflict

Although the Gathering Suns consider themselves one people, this doesn’t entirely prevent conflict between them. The Unclouded take pains to avoid open war; Helaku’s bloodline is too precious to spill, and the Men of Gold won’t aid aggressors in such battles. This limits conflict to shows of force and ritual skirmishes, in which the Men of Gold act as witnesses and overseers. These skirmishes, set on rivers or neutral territory rather than within villages, aim to take captives for ransom. Deaths still happen, but tradition demands reparations — typically transfer of people to the harmed clan equal in number to the slain, with transferees filling the dead warriors’ familial and social roles. These restraints don’t apply against foreigners.

### Leadership

Though the way they’re chosen varies from clan to clan, Gathering Suns clan leaders are always Unclouded. Some clans pass the title from parent to child. Others rely on shamans’ auguries to choose a successor. A few clans allow Unclouded members to challenge the leader to ritual combat to take her place — typically only with a shaman’s sponsorship, in hopes that this will limit such challenges to failing leaders, rather than being a tool for ambition. Clan leaders are responsible for their clan’s health and prosperity. They determine which paths to follow in which season, and whether it’s time to encamp for the winter or push on. They lead raids and negotiate with other clan leaders or foreign powers. Some clan leaders make all decisions on their own; others take advice from a council of elders or the clan’s shamans, or they may even listen to every member who wishes to speak. Like clan leaders, shamans come exclusively from the ranks of the Unclouded. As much skilled workers as spiritual leaders, shamans bridge the gap between mortal society and the occult world. They seek omens and auguries in a child’s birth, in movements of birds and clouds, and in smoke rising from funeral pyres. They serve as intermediaries with the Men of Gold, clan ancestors, gods, and other neighboring spirits. And they practice mundane arts dividing life from death — medicine, midwifery, and funereal rites. Shamans aren’t permanently tied to the clan they were raised in. It’s not uncommon for a shaman to leave her clan and join another that’s short on shamans or to serve as shaman to two clans whose paths cross frequently. Fade has its own shaman lodges that are independent of the clans. In theory, clan leaders and

shamans are peers, but there’s often a political tug-ofwar between the two. This can divide a clan’s loyalties between two individuals or groups, and historically has been the most frequent source of a clan splitting into two, often bitter, new clans.

### The Men of Gold

Queen Helaku created the Men of Gold — a troop of over 100 intelligent golden automatons — to serve her and her progeny. When the Dragon-Blooded slew her, these Golden Men led her descendants to safety in the surrounding forests and set themselves to guard her lineage forevermore. These descendants became the Gathering Sun clans, a wandering people, avoiding settled lands for fear the Shogunate would destroy them for their ancestry. This nomadic way of life offered no protection from the Great Contagion, but it helped against the threats that followed — bandits and hungry ghosts, the imperial ambitions of Bagrash Köl and the Scarlet Empress, and the so-called Second Contagion After the Second Contagion passed, the Men of Gold led the Gathering Suns back to their homeland. They still encouraged nomadic existence to guard Helaku’s scions against disease and invasion. Only centuries later did mortal leaders persuade the automatons that permanent settlement was safe. The immortal Men of Gold remain wary, watching carefully for threats to the mortals in their charge.

Several Men of Gold have been destroyed or have gone missing over the centuries, but most remain intact. One or more travel with each clan; should a clan lose its last Man of Gold, another replaces it from a clan with Men to spare. A score now reside in holy Fade alongside its swelling population.

The Men of Gold hold great prestige among the Gathering Suns. They reject formal authority, neither ruling nor being ruled, but their counsel is often taken as command nonetheless. They’re revered as sacred gifts from Queen Helaku, respected for wisdom and prophecy, and admired as heroic warrior-protectors; they occupy a central role in Gathering Sun art, and ballads and epics lionize their deeds. But most importantly, they bless Helaku’s descendants at birth and tutor them in noble arts — warfare, negotiation, medicine, and more. Although their golden bodies emulate human form, each Man of Gold is unique in shape, size, and features. They wear ornate garments offered by their clans — typically in archaic styles passed on as tradition. Though

EX3

capable of human expression, they tend toward calm impassivity; only people with long experience with several or more of them recognize that their personalities are likewise unique.

Gathering Sun warriors live in barracks tucked into the already-crowded sections of the city. They frequently clear the streets for drills, having no dedicated parade grounds within Fade itself.

### Fade, the Hilled City

As Fade attracts merchants from Halta and beyond, the clans who dwell in the city grow wealthy on that trade. They largely circulate these goods as gifts within Fade, lording their fortunes over other clans. In retaliation, other clans have begun to stop merchants on the road — whether through friendly trade offers or raids — depriving their city cousins of wealth. The political strife this has caused seems likely to escalate despite the best efforts of the shamans and Men of Gold.

In a former age, Queen Helaku dwelt in the temple-manse called the Beacon of the Sun. Though smashed in ancient wars and looted by scavengers, the ruined Beacon still looms, its toppled spires glittering here and there with splinters of gold and orichalcum. Fade was built around this holy site. Unclouded guards patrol the grounds, the very task an honor. Few receive permission to enter; no foreigner has set foot within in living memory.

Although its geomantic power has long been broken, the Beacon of the Sun still lives up to its name. From afar, pilgrims spy the sun glinting off shattered spires at the city’s apex; the sight gladdens hearts and quickens steps.

A dozen hillocks ring the manse. Steep ramps lead to the earthen mounds’ tops, where they’re crowned by the Gathering Suns shamans’ lodges. Like other shamans’ lodges, these are not only places of prayer and ritual; they also serve as meeting grounds for the clans’ leaders and places where clan members gather in the evening for socialization and song.

Fade’s streets wind and twist around the bases of the mounds. Outsiders may mix with the clans here —those who’ve been in the city for generations or tend farms that their families owned since Fade’s founding are eventually adopted or marry into Clouded families. Merchants sell their wares in crowded market plazas. Artisans’ houses line the roads, selling wares from porches and entryways: embroidered fabrics, finely woven rugs, and pottery. The smell of meat roasting on spits draws hungry shoppers and pilgrims. On cold winter days, citizens gather by blacksmiths’ shops to warm themselves by the forge as they exchange news. Several clans which have settled permanently in Fade dwell close to the mounds. Their leaders’ grand houses are large enough for several families, allowing them to serve as more informal meeting places than the shaman-lodges. Some clan leaders invite pilgrims to stay with them; such an invite is a privilege mainly reserved for Unclouded visitors. However, a few clan leaders have caused a stir by inviting Clouded houseguests. Houses are round and thatch-roofed; most stand only one story tall.

Fade’s Men of Gold

Whether to differentiate themselves from one another or because they proved ill-suited to rural clan life due to their idiosyncrasies, Fade’s Men of Gold are more motley than the norm, tending toward outsized personalities; they’re far easier to tell apart than their nomadic peers. Their numbers include:

The ruthless Wolf-Eyed Man, who teaches weapon-use, strategy, and tactics. An aggressive, dominant voice in debates among the Men of Gold, he proposes clear, decisive, and irrevocable solutions to problems. He eagerly joins in ritual skirmishes and in raiding foreigners, finding joy in battle. The vain Finch-Voiced Man, who teaches medicine and the arts. He encourages the growth and importance of Fade among the Gathering Suns, increasing trade for novel goods, and welcoming foreign scholars and artisans. A clotheshorse, he disdains traditional garb, instead seeking novel fashions among visiting merchants. The conciliatory Silver-Armed Man, named for their silver right arm replacing one lost in battle, teaches negotiation and trade. They encourage maintaining good relations with other Gathering Sun clans and neighboring peoples. Their occasional willingness to educate Clouded or even foreigners scandalizes the Unclouded.

### Neighbors

After the Great Contagion’s devastation, wilderness has reclaimed much of the region near Fade. Nevertheless, the Gathering Suns don’t exist in isolation. The people of Urudan were once cousins to the Gathering Suns, though most abandoned their nomadic

EX3

lifestyle centuries ago. Where once they traded, raids on either side for resources and slaves have escalated into a bitter rivalry, their antagonism cemented when the Uru retaliated against brutal Gathering Sun raids by destroying a Man of Gold. The slain Man of Gold’s head remains in Urudan’s central plaza, a trophy and sign of superiority over the Gathering Suns.

### MORE NORTHEASTERN LOCALES

A few small fishing villages thrive along the wooded shores of Lake Vostok. Ancient legend describes a secret grotto deep beneath the lake containing a library of mystic lore, gathered by a First Age sorcerer who foresaw that lore’s loss in some great disaster. In addition to whatever protective spells might enchant such a hoard, the lake is home to a behemoth — a huge, swift, immortal aquatic beast intelligent enough to devour scavengers while leaving fisherfolk alone.

The Uru place great emphasis on civil service. Each person performs two years of civil service starting on their fifteenth year. This may take place within the government or the military; women traditionally choose government and men the military, though there’s little stigma against crossing over. This mirrors Uru society’s matrifocal structure, wherein women wield most social power. Often the experiences young Uru build during their service defines their path in life.

The stench of decay hangs heavy upon the Noss Fens. Neighboring peoples give this shadowland a wide berth. Broad and twisted trees, their trunks shrouded in vines and moss, hang low over thorny thickets and expanses of stagnant water. Few animals — mostly boars, raitons, and bottom-dwelling fish — persist among the Fens’ putrid vapors and terrifying shadows. A handful of reclusive villages persist here, their stilt-dwelling inhabitants surviving by hunting and gathering, accepting the land’s perils to remain free of princes and raiders.

The riverine Shogunate city of Darusan, founded to take advantage of a small shadowland’s reserve of bituminous behemoth-marrow, became a seat of learning, philosophy, and the arts. But in the Great Contagion, the shadowland swallowed Darusan. When desperate refugees from the Second Contagion visited the ruins, the city’s ghosts offered their aid.

At the Fens’ heart stands the Mound of Forsaken Seeds, an earthen mass enshrouding a massive step pyramid from an earlier eon. The Mound is home to the Deathlord named the Dowager of the Irreverent Vulgate in Unrent Veils, along with her cultists, undead servants, and nightmarish creations. When the stars are wrong, she ranges out across the Fens as a dreadful apparition — cloven-footed and ram’shorned with dreadful yellow eyes, bearing an enormous soulsteel bow — to hunt beast and man alike.

Today, New Darusan stands at the shadowland’s edge, a tall city of mills and schools at the heart of a semicircle of farming villages and market towns. The shadowland’s ghosts — led by the warrior-savant Five Winds Whisper — work with New Darusan’s people, sharing agricultural and engineering lore, and patrolling their borders at night against raiders and wild beasts. But as raids by neighboring peoples escalate in this time of tumult, Darusan has troubles of its own. Its warrior-ghosts withdraw to the shadowland to fend off neighboring ghost-princes, leaving New Darusan vulnerable.

Recently, far-flung Gathering Sun clans to the north and east have faced new and unexpected conflict. Refugees from the expansionist empire of Iscomay (Lunars, p. XX), aided by other peoples jealous of the Gathering Suns’ Men of Gold, have invaded the region, seizing rich lands and taking prisoners of war as slaves.

## Gapwood

Deep in the Northeastern forest looms the mile-wide hollow stump of a dead tree that must once have scraped the skies. In places, the ragged remnants of the stump tower dozens of yards into the air. Elsewhere, gaps in its perimeter have been filled with marble walls

and gates overgrown with centuries of greenery, reinforced with crude palisades by its latest residents. Within the hollow stands a First Age ruin. Scavengers who once sought solely to profit from its relics now seek to make it a home. Some even raise families there. But they struggle to maintain order in the face of their fellows’ greed, ambitions, and vendettas.

### History

People have dwelt in the hollow since the First Age, when the Lance-of-Sapphire Tree was felled by one of the Chosen. Since then, the site has had many uses and many names. Once the personal estate of the Exalt Meherrin, it later served as campus for the Wind’s Key School of Sorcery; as the fortress Ormidac; and finally, the city of Dehala-in-the-East under the DragonBlooded Shogunate.

EX3

Flensed of inhabitants by the Contagion and again in the plagues thereafter, for centuries its only residents were occasional hermits and outlaws. A generation ago, a group of scavengers deciphered the command codes for the manse, allowing them to ward off wicked spirits and wild beasts and to guarantee clement weather for farming. Together they founded Gapwood, believing that they’d have a better and safer life residing in the ruins than by trying to sell its relics. But residents and traveling merchants alike continued dealing in scavenged Shogunate wares found within the hollow and amid other nearby ruins. As a result of this commerce — and of efforts to clear the roads of obstacles to it — more scavengers, traders, and rogues flocked to Gapwood, all drawn by the prospect of profit.

### Society

Today a crude town council reigns in Gapwood, its representatives a jumble of delegates from older families, mercantile concerns, bandit gangs, and refugee bands. The council elects a mayor each year to chair its meetings. It also names a handful of serjeants as enforcers; these hold their posts until the council votes to remove them. Serjeants are either personally skilled

combatants or have others at their beck and call. Many are strongmen whom the council members dare not eject from the post for fear of a coup. Fault lines run through Gapwood society. Those who seek to make Gapwood a thriving community are at odds with those who’d like to get rich dismantling and selling its infrastructure. Meanwhile, established families feel their property and privileges threatened by newcomers, who in turn are shut out of political authority and from opportunity to lay claim to valuable property. Longtime resentment brews among many residents based on rival claims, old grudges, and the like.

Certain regional mercantile concerns, such as the Guild-affiliated merchant prince Gedeon Tiger-Smile and Iscomay’s fur-trading Aadan merchant family, seek to gain control over Gapwood — ideally through legitimate means, though hiring mercenaries for a military takeover isn’t out of the question. Political maneuvering to make this happen grows ever more intense. They offer council members ever-larger bribes, while those who vocally oppose the sale find themselves threatened, attacked, defamed, or otherwise targeted by efforts to replace them with more tractable successors.

EX3

So far, those favoring independence have played rival merchant factions against one another, but unless the paradigm shifts, that tactic won’t forestall them forever.

exchanges as representatives for the established residents lobby for constraint while burgeoning tycoons argue for expansion.

Lumber is a common building material in Gapwood, and many homes and establishments display their heavy timber framing on the outside, painting the beams and the wood between in contrasting colors to showcase the framework. Some structures have false fronts covering their second stories, using more expensive materials to give an impression of wealth and success while hiding a shabbier construction or rough stone foundation.

Open areas in the city’s interior have served several purposes — gardens, parks, markets, parade grounds, and the like. Today, Gapwood’s folk use such areas for small farms, growing maize, rye, squash, beans, and other vegetables. Ox-drawn plows till the land, often unearthing stones from fallen buildings; residents use these to construct their homes, along with wood and thatch.

Clothing reflects an amalgam of styles, and features long-sleeved shirts, pants with chaps, robes, sashes, sturdy leather boots, and accessories like turbans, hats, and scarves. Gapwood’s cuisine is simple but hearty. Typical dishes include a salad with squash, beans, corn and fresh greens in the summer months, or a hearty, spicy venison stew featuring those staples in colder weather. Moist cornbread accompanies most meals, and teas and cordials alike are sweetened with hawthorn berry syrup.

### Geography

Several gates, constructed during disparate eras, pierce the city’s outer ring. Some remain sealed by ancient magics or mechanisms or have been walled up with wood or stone. The three gates in use today are the western River Gate, its portcullis of imperishable First Age metal standing within a tunnel carved directly through the trunk; the southern Marsh Gate, set in a Shogunate-era wall with new wooden doors replacing a shattered stone portal; and the northeastern Forest Gate, built into a palisade the Gapwooders established where the old walls had crumbled.

A serjeant directs each gate’s defenses. A handful of sentinels keep watch in wooden towers, while gate guards ask travelers their business and stand ready to ward off attackers. The guards turn away known or suspected troublemakers, but many accept bribes — or demand payoffs in the form of sham “gate taxes.” In the bustling districts near the gates, inns, wineshops, and brothels cater to visiting traders, scavengers, and transients. Business owners turn a healthy profit off this new blood; other locals believe that these establishments encourage lawlessness and unrest, which the serjeants allow to continue unchecked. More and more often, serjeants participate in — or even instigate — the disturbances. Council meetings erupt into heated

Several clusters of resident-focused establishments — general stores, assayers, restaurants, shrines, and the like — crop up amid the ruins. These typically stand at the intersection of major avenues or along the periphery of open areas. At the city’s center stands the Skyfire Palace. A sleek marble-and-living-heartwood tower whose broad triangular base sweeps up to a slender peak, this Airaspected manse’s still-gleaming copper spire draws lightning with every storm. Its interior smells of freshcut wood and the tang of ozone. The manse remains in use today, communally owned and overseen by Gapwood’s citizens. The town council meets on an upper floor with a broad, scenic balcony. Several other tower chambers, their walls inlaid with occult glyphs in metal and crystal, direct the manse’s

Essence. Access to these rooms is restricted to a handful of council-approved scavengers and savants.

Religion

Temples and shrines to local gods occupy structures both old and new. Noteworthy gods include the reclusive, hedonistic Glass Butterfly, who oversaw the scholars at the school of sorcery; the battle-god Hennan Ten-Spears, who was sacred to the soldiers when Gapwood was a fortress, and who now blesses serjeants and street-toughs; and the scavenger god Arun-Oros, who’s doing a steady business these days. Gapwood has its ghosts as well, remnants from throughout the tree’s long history, who exchange lost lore for prayer.

### Gapwood’s Serjeants

Hawksight runs the River Gate. A Gapwooder born and bred, she made a name for herself protecting the city on countless patrols and keeping the peace among the newcomers and established residents. Her job gets harder every year. River Gate traffic grows heavier than before, the other serjeants increasingly have their own

EX3

sentries. Sturdy as it is, she says, the palisade at the Forest Gate would be the easiest of the three city gates for attackers to breach; their extra “vigilance” makes up for it.

### STORMSLINGS

Hundreds of handheld Shogunate-era weapons have been unearthed in Gapwood, most of them in a handful of armories. These stormslings — resembling a mundane sling of strange metals, amber, and rubber — throw small, vicious balls of lightning, their power on par with Southern flame pieces. But instead of consuming precious firedust, storm weapons require prayer and offerings upon copper altars to Mela found within the Skyfire Palace’s precincts.

Carver Aigust is tasked with overseeing patrols outside the city. Before coming to Gapwood, she was the right-hand woman for the bandit prince Green Fox, who now sits on Gapwood’s council and arranged for her appointment as a serjeant. She has a deep knowledge of the forests outside the city — including other bandit gangs’ strongholds and smaller settlements her own used to harry. While Carver and her patrols take their duties to Gapwood seriously, they also occasionally raid outlying towns for their own gains.

The town council controls access to stormslings from the Palace’s armory. At any given time, guards on active duty hold a few; the rest can be withdrawn en masse should the town come under attack, or should the council authorize a raid on a troublesome bandit encampment or the like. However, stormslings found elsewhere in or around Gapwood by scavengers remain in private hands, charged at a few functional altars found elsewhere in the ruins or via occult methods puzzled out by shamans and spirits.

agendas and loyalties to entities other than Gapwood, and various parties pressure the council to award the River Gate to another serjeant more amenable to their aims. A frequent customer at the Auspicious Owl gambling hall in her off-hours, Hawksight has accrued significant debts at the dice tables. While many of her losses are to longtime friends and colleagues, a recent spate of bad luck has left her owing half a year’s earnings to one of Seven Ring’s sons. Borjaro the Gerivan, the Marsh Gate’s serjeant, has long been in Gedeon Tiger-Smile’s pocket. A man well past his prime, it’s been years since he was involved in even a minor brawl, though he was a renowned fighter in his younger days. His sentries and gate guards are loyal to him, their devotion a combination of respect for the formidable man Borjaro once was and the steady stream of kickbacks he pays them out of the gate taxes. Gedeon’s caravans enter Gapwood almost exclusively through the Marsh Gate, knowing their wagons will receive only cursory inspections.

Sweet oversees the Forest Gate. The scarred veteran of hundreds of brawls, Gapwood’s council named her to her position after she was instrumental in quelling a riot late last year. She brooks little nonsense, more likely to shut up dissenters with her fists than diplomacy. Her gate guards follow her example — those who argue about entry or taxes find themselves tossed out of the city, bloodied and bruised. When merchants complain to the council about this treatment, Sweet defends her

Other serjeants have few formal areas of responsibility beyond patrolling Gapwood’s districts and protecting its citizens. Some of these appointments are strategic, used by councilors to appease strongmen while keeping them out of critical roles. Others are merely empty honors, intended to keep productive serjeants active after strongmen have usurped their lucrative roles running the gates.

### Other Prominent Figures

The brilliant scavenger-savant Damen Storm-Struck is one of Gapwood’s original founders. Over the years, she’s amassed substantial knowledge about the manse’s workings and sussed out other secrets of Gapwood’s infrastructure. Though she spends much of her time in the Skyfire Palace, Damen hasn’t stopped searching the city for relics. She made her fortune not only by selling them, but also by charging a fee to teach buyers how to use what they’d just purchased. Never content with a solitary pursuit, Damen is also a teacher. Most young Gapwooders spend time in her classroom. She remembers each of their faces and frequently develops personal connections with them, ranging from maternal to acrimonious.

Seven Ring brought her sprawling family to Gapwood in its early days, claiming land with coin and setting her children to protect its borders. Over the years, she’s bought up several neighboring farms via blackmail, shady land deals, and outright force. Though not many in Gapwood like her, its residents begrudgingly respect her, and many have sought her help when the serjeants fail them. Her son Seven Gate sits on the council, but Gapwooders know his decisions are first approved by his mother. The family’s grudge against the neighboring Reed clan is almost as old as Gapwood itself, begun when a relic was found on the border of their two farms

EX3

along a strip of land whose ownership the two families dispute to this day. Their mutual enmity has turned to bloodshed several times. So vicious is the feud, only the bravest (or most foolhardy) serjeants care to step in when a Seven and a Reed fight.

The outlaw leader Rika the Younger spends most of his time outside of Gapwood. The head of a band of

cattle rustlers, he raids outlying Gathering Sun clans and herds the stolen livestock back toward the city. The guards at the Marsh Gate ask no questions as he drives the animals into Gapwood’s safety; they know they’ll receive fat bonuses soon enough. Rika sells the cattle to Guild caravans, whose drovers care little about their provenance.

EX3

One hand over the other, just as you were taught. The light of the full moon cast much of Port Calin into tones of silver, clearly revealing the subtle flaws in the tower’s construction to those who knew how to study the shadows. And Six-Fingered Bu knew how to study the shadows. One hand over the other, he scaled the tower, retaining feeling in his arms by moving rapidly and bracing his legs. The cobblestones were at least a hundred feet below, and the streets of Marin Bay stretched far beyond. If Bu craned his neck to the side of the tower, he could probably make out the rolling hills he’d roamed as a boy beyond the city walls, but he wasn’t climbing for the view.

Bu paused below a lit, open window, watching a shadow play over the curtains within. He’d been born in the rolling hills of Calin in some forgotten shogun’s private fortress, ruined these long years. A child of the Gilan, the thirty-seven exiles who’d fled their ancestral holdings after taking the head of the false Kejihno shogun. Attainted and dishonored by the assassination, House Gilan chose to embrace it within their exile, and worked tirelessly to ruin the family who’d forced them from their homes. The young assassin’s arms ached after only a few moments hanging beneath the window, but he’d trained for this. The shadow finally moved, and Bu silently kicked his legs against the wall, swung outwards, and pressed his arms down to somersault him through the open window. He bounced up and flattened himself against the shadows, as the patrolling guard glanced back at the sudden draft. Kejihno Urigen was the most successful trader the family had seen after two decades’ worth of trade deals gone inexplicably sour and the untimely death of any scion who could reverse their aristocratic fortunes. House Gilan caused most of the death, it was true; but they weren’t House Kejihno’s only enemies, and Urigen’s ledgers would fetch precious jade for Bu’s family coffers. House Tiawara was his patron this evening; the Kejihno merchant had gotten the better of some aged citizen in a trade deal, who killed himself from the shame. A quick death was undeserved for the likes of Kejihno Urigen. Both houses wanted their rivals brought low before they destroyed them. Forty paces down the hall. Wait for the guard to pass. Then forty paces more to Urigen’s office. SixFingered Bu was well-named, for his grip was strong and his digits nimble. The lock yielded to his practiced inquiries. Silently, Bu swung the door open and stepped inside. A light flared in the dark office, the flame on the end of a long taper causing a lantern to roar to life. Kejihno Urigen stood behind his thick wooden desk, clad in armor and brandishing a slashing sword naked in his right hand. The left set the taper aside and raised the lantern aloft, illuminating the man’s gleeful smile.

“Oh, sorry, thought I’d be away tonight?” And Bu allowed for a moment that, yeah, he’d thought that. Urigen didn’t wait for him to answer. “Amazing what happens when you announce your schedule loudly in a teahouse. Nobody suspects you of guile.”

Heavy footfalls heralded the rush of guards, and Bu’s exits from the tower shrank to nothing. He fingered the elegant stiletto hidden in his right gauntlet.

“And now, we’ll hear the name of the other family who’s plagued our rise. Or not; your lifespan’s up to you, but this evening ends the same way. Our hundred years of bad luck ends today,” Kejihno Urigen said.

Six-Fingered Bu wondered how steep the fall from the tower truly was.

# Chapter Three: The Scavenger Lands

Chapter Three

The Scavenger Lands

The vast, fertile Yellow River Basin spreads across much of the East. Civilizations have risen and fallen here over the ages, leaving countless ruins in their wakes. Today, the region is crowded with polities large and small, entangled in a morass of trade, alliance, and petty wars.

Remnants of earlier peoples lie strewn about across the landscape, ranging from overgrown villages and forts abandoned for only a few years to ruins so ancient their origins are lost to history. Untold wealth can be wrung from a successful venture into these ruins, whether it’s coin, jewels, artwork, lost lore, or magical relics. Intrepid scavengers embarking on such enterprises have left indelible marks on the region’s history and culture, down to its very name.

The Scavenger Lands’ coastal territories — known as the River Province — offer a mild and temperate climate, albeit often rainy and disturbed by occasional major storms off the Inland Sea. Farther from the coast the seasons grow more distinct, with hotter summers and colder winters. Storms, floods, and droughts aren’t uncommon.

## Calin

An old, populous nation spread along the cliff-girt coast north of the Yanaze, Calin is a realm of stark contrasts. The land’s Dragon-Blooded rulers care little for anything outside their endless courtly intrigues and byzantine ceremonies. Meanwhile, their people suffer under oppressive taxes and organized crime, and the iniquitous Five Shades families consolidate power in the shadows.

While Calin’s ports remain splendid, the land is in decline, from fallow fields to the wilted splendor of the shogun’s court. Still, hope for change stirs in its coastal cities, nurtured in duelists’ schools and winehouses — hope that the shogun might be toppled and Calin revitalized. However, this perilous path might see Calin end in flame instead of rot.

### History

Calin’s shogunate descends from the Realm. In RY 266, the Empress eliminated the old Shogunate gentes’ remaining privileges and offered them land grants in various satrapies, mostly north of the Inland Sea. Among the largest was Calin, formed in the Realm’s early years from a loose constellation of trading ports, fallen Intou principalities (p. XX), fishing villages, and country estates, establishing a buffer state on the Scavenger Lands’ border and a staging area threatening Lookshy proper. The Shogunate gentes and local Dragon-Blooded families, elevated collectively as cadet house Calin, settled the land and made it their own.

The Realm remained unpopular among the conquered Calinti despite its growing influence on their culture. Meanwhile, Calinti scions rankled at their lack of influence in the Deliberative, and their delegates deemed themselves snubbed by Dynastic senators. Moreover, they grew ever more concerned over saber-rattling by various satraps, garrison commanders, and Lookshy’s General Staff.

In RY 418, at the height of the Realm’s ill-fated trade war with the Guild, Calin seceded, citing oppressive Realm tariffs as a pretext. Declaring an independent nation under the Confederation of Rivers’ auspices, the new shogun ousted the Jurul satrap and her garrison, with neighboring Lookshy apparently poised to come to Calin’s defense.

### Politics: The Great Game

With independence, Calin’s leaders promised that freedom from the Realm would allow their nation to grow into a great power. Instead, the nobility grew indolent over the centuries, fracturing into houses content to exploit and oppress while the once-powerful shogun’s court devolved into leisure and insular political intrigue.

Calin pays little heed to those without the wealth and power to make themselves heard. Its fourteen noble

EX3

houses’ matriarchs maintain palatial estates capable of hosting the shogun’s court. Many nobles trace Exalted lineages to before the Great Contagion, although today’s thin-blooded houses have few Dragon-Blooded members.

### CITIZENS OF WRIT

The shogun’s court chooses to whom it sells writs of citizenship. Most go to valued professionals, such as legal scholars, historians, and physicians. A few go to merchants who’ve earned favors from the court.

The Patronage System

Calin’s military and civil bureaucracies are directly subordinate to the nobility, with the nation itself divided into patronages that the shogun can grant to any noble house other than her own, and which she may revoke and reassign at will. Her house keeps any preexisting patronages, but can’t receive new ones until another house claims the throne.

A patronage is a governmental post that a matriarch can assign to any of her house’s members. These include stewardship of a province or district other than a noble house’s ancestral seat — including such rights and responsibilities as collecting taxes, administering justice to noncitizens, conscripting troops, and providing travelers with military escort for a fee; posts in the shogun’s administration, such as generals, judges, and ministers; and prestigious ceremonial sinecures such as stewardship of Eshira Island, which sank centuries ago, or Keeper of the Rice-Flame Sword, a ceremonial weapon brought forth for a new shogun’s coronation. Favor trading and promises of prestigious patronages dominate interaction between noble houses. They call this “the Great Game.” Nobles have a long memory for exactly who’s favored or slighted their family down the centuries.

In theory, most governmental authority is dispensed through the patronage system, save over the houses’ private ancestral estates. In practice, as the central bureaucracy degrades into infighting and insularity, power increasingly lies in the hands of wealthy merchants, who pay fees to oversee shipping and local industries on behalf of uninterested nobles, and the army, whose officers — increasingly composed of foreign mercenaries — take cuts of the taxes they escort. This bewildering tangle of dysfunction and graft teeters one crisis away from total collapse.

Elections

Citizens elect a shogun who serves for life. Citizenship, however, is a rare commodity. Nobles are hereditary citizens. Others can buy writs of citizenship for great sums from the shogun’s administration or earn them with high office; such citizenship isn’t heritable, perishing with its holder. Writs of citizenship are sharply limited in number to ensure the noble houses collectively

Status is deeply stratified by class, with those who’ve purchased citizenship at the bottom. Even when invited to noble functions, citizens of writ speak last, receive the smallest portions at banquet tables, and are obliged to lose games and contests against their social betters or face disfavor.

Still, such citizens enjoy enormous privileges compared to most Calinti. They’re exempt from punishment for minor crimes and may plead grievances directly to the shogun.

Children of former citizens can rarely purchase their own writs, regardless of their wealth and accomplishments. This is a reminder that hereditary authority lies with the nobility alone.

retain a strong majority over any coalition of would-be reformers.

In addition to voting for the shogun, citizens can ratify a sitting shogun’s proposal to elevate a new noble house by a two-thirds majority. This altogether rarer occurrence has succeeded only three times. Citizens’ rights include holding patronages and directly petitioning the shogun in legal matters. Those who teach a skill may sell licenses to their disciples indicating knowledge in that field. Lastly, noncitizens must bow and speak respectfully to citizens — albeit moreso to nobles, to whom commoner citizens must likewise show respect.

Legally, anyone can be elected shogun. But no one outside a handful of the ruling houses has ever received that honor. Shoguns are usually middle-aged or older when elected, benefiting from a lifetime of accumulated skill and political capital — and allowing for quicker turnover. The ideal shogun embodies the idealized traits of Calin’s noble class: noble of bearing, sensitive in temperament, skilled in poetry, literature, history, and martial arts, and attentive to guests at court. For centuries, only mortals have been elected shogun. No citizen wants to grant power to a rival family’s shogun, and no family wants to forgo new patronages for the lifetime of their own Dragon-Blooded shogun’s
