The Shogun’s Court

The shogun’s personal power revolves around control over patronages. This encourages nobles to vie for her favor, and often wins recipients’ loyalty. With most governmental functions distributed among the noble houses, the shogun’s court itself has become a place for arts and culture. Contests involving poetry,

painting, and various other arts dominate the shogun’s time; nobles contend for recognition and appreciation, while the shogun seeks to strengthen personal ties and evaluate each noble’s fidelity, competence, and moral compass.

Aside from the shogun’s generals, the most powerful officials in the court are those who control access to the shogun. Her grand chamberlain determines who meets with the shogun and in what order, and arranges banquet seating. Her cupbearer passes messages between the shogun and banquet guests, and often serves as an adviser. Lastly, her master of the hunt determines proximity to the shogun on outings and oversees her personal security.

The Shogun’s Army

Mercenary free companies exert a stranglehold over army recruitment. All landowning citizens must raise conscripts — a difficult and unpopular task. Generations of such citizens have deferred the responsibility to free companies; these import foreign troops or recruit locals through questionably legal means, allowing the citizen to foist blame for families being split up or a shortage of field hands onto the companies’ captains.

Shogun is a military title, endowing its holder with power and authority via leadership of the Calinti army. However, other noble houses control most of Calin’s provinces as ancestral lands or through patronages, and those houses dislike submitting their private troops to the shogun’s authority. As a result, the army — once a powerful, centralized force under Calin’s early DragonBlooded shoguns — is today a wildly heterodox force of levies raised and equipped by landowning citizens, heavily supplemented by mercenary companies.

Wealthy noncitizens — including members of the Five Shades (p. XX) — embed mercenaries as agents in

EX3

officer posts to secure their own interests. The previous shogun, Jiong Tanju, fell afoul of this exploit when she attempted to proscribe large swaths of Port Calin’s merchant class and confiscate their funds on behalf of the state. The resulting brief but bloody civil war ended only with Tanju’s assassination; fearing further chaos at the hands of mercenary officers, the Jiong generals stood down the army before news spread. Tanju’s successor regards the army with caution. The Calinti navy is similarly disjointed. Citizens holding relevant patronages in port cities raise and maintain warships. Many wealthy Calinti — citizens or not — illegally retain private militias under the pretense of training marines to guard merchant shipping. This creates friction between the navy and citizen-backed militias, occasionally escalating to skirmishes; a few leaders have been hauled before the shogun for causing too much unrest.

### Noble Culture

The early Realm exerted profound, long-lasting influence on Calin. Aristocrats’ fashions retain elements reminiscent of the Blessed Isle over three centuries

ago. They perform ceremonies for bureaucratic offices long since defunct, and jump to the steps of dances only the very eldest Dynasts remember.

Courtiers wear impractically layered robes of richly embroidered, multicolored silk; their elaborate braided hairstyles and finely cast bronze masks denote their allegiance and rank. While centuries have slowly altered fashions even in conservative Calinti society, visiting Dynasts still mock Calinti nobles as slavishly backward-looking behind closed doors, even by the low standards to which they hold all Threshold cousins. Meals are lavish multi-course affairs, featuring game, fish, red meat, fresh fruit, nuts, eggs — from tiny quail eggs to ostentatiously large ostrich eggs — butter, and honey. Imported spices elevate otherwise common dishes to elite status, and while Calinti are proud of their wines, a host might show off with a rare vintage procured from far-off vineyards. Dishes served include mallow-leaf salad, jellied fish simmered with salsify and ginger, steamed abalone, pheasant in verjuice sauce, and pork marinated in lovage, fennel, and cumin. Delicate soufflés and candied nuts are a frequent dessert.

### THE COURT OF MASKS

The Calinti court mask originates with traditional theater and honor dueling. The decorative abstract masks, colorful clothing, and elaborate musical compositions of native Calinti theater have become a staple of the shogun’s court. Swordplay and martial arts, meanwhile, are valued skills among the nobility, both as a means of artistic expression and for defending one’s honor. Nobles adopted bronze face masks to avoid unsightly scars; this eventually merged into everyday court fashion.

House Jerogal are cousins originally from the satrapy of Northern Ivory, a branch family that split from cadet house Japor when Calin declared independence, seeking its fortunes outside Realm control. Though their wealth is based on patronages overseeing state copperworks and salt manufactories, they’re most famous as patrons of artisan smiths, including the White Mospids, three outcaste sworn sisters reputed as the region’s most accomplished jadesmiths.

Strict codes based on social rank determine the exact shape, construction, and decoration permissible for one’s court mask. It’s bad luck for a commoner to view a noble’s unmasked face. Only Dragon-Blooded of the Fourteen Houses may wear jade masks. Romantic courtly literature abounds with lovers’ betrayals and secret liaisons under false masks. However, impersonating another noble using their court mask or a replica is a crime worthy of the harshest social censure, and a capital crime for non-nobles

House Gabenzi was another house founded after independence, created by narrow court vote from a coalition of wealthy middle-class Calinti. Over a century later, they still chafe under a reputation as vulgar nouveau riche who bought their nobility, and they utterly lack the blood of the Dragons. Of all the houses, they’re the most heavily invested in shipbuilding and imports through Port Calin and have strong ties to the Guild.

### The Noble Houses

Calin’s noble houses are loosely modeled on the Realm’s Great Houses. A matriarch rules each house. They seek advantage through arranged marriages, and vary widely in size, wealth, and political power. Some dominate the Great Game, trading the shogun’s seat between them. Others are so small as to be vestigial, left to self-govern out of tradition and propriety. Nobles enjoy a life of leisure, cushioned from commoners’ needs by attendants, palace walls, and vast country estates. Dragon-Blooded nobles occupy an especially privileged place in the court’s byzantine social rankings; their talents making them the center of attention. Some thrive in courtly life, penning exquisite poetry and engaging in scandalous love affairs. Others find the court stifling and make excuses to travel abroad whenever possible. As central governance decays with the rise of the Great Game, most of today’s nobles perceive themselves as house members first and Calinti second. The families funnel wealth from their patronages to their ancestral estates, which they see as their homelands.

Prominent Houses

The current ruling house, House Kamamoto, dominates its ancestral seat of Port Piaster, particularly

Once preeminent among Calinti houses, House Kenjihno fell on hard times after a spate of bad luck, soured alliances, collapsed investments, and strange accidents. Kenjihno blames its misfortunes on a centuries-old grudge held by a reclusive clan best forgotten, whom they were instrumental in exiling. They control few patronages, but cling to power with the support of a substantial and well-situated ancestral estate outside Port Calin.

### Religion and Ceremony

In keeping with its Realm heritage, Calin promulgates the Immaculate Philosophy as its state religion. Its rarely edited Immaculate calendar still honors gods of far-flung parts of the Realm, some of whom have changed or lost their posts in the Celestial Bureaucracy, or have been driven from their territory by monks for transgressing Immaculate restrictions. A few such gods, denied other opportunities, relocate to Calin to lobby for increased recognition.

The Ministry of Heavenly Peace oversees Calin’s monastic hierarchy and Immaculate ceremonies. Its highest-ranking officials — themselves Immaculate monks, or occasionally lay Dragon-Blooded nobles — treat with gods as guests of the Calinti court.

Other cults quietly flourish in Calin despite its

bearing new heresies that Calin’s Immaculates are neither equipped nor inclined to stamp out.

### The Lot of the People

The Calinti are proud of their heritage and vociferous in their politics. Farmers, fisherfolk, and wealthy city-dwellers alike freely share strong opinions on matters of the day. They take pride in their independence from the Realm and their purported status as the true

heirs to the Dragon-Blooded Shogunate’s culture.

They’re also fractious, a legacy of centuries of competitive trade between different settlements. Inhabitants of neighboring fishing villages often consider one another foreigners, while inhabitants of rival cities ofttimes declare one another barbarians. When pressed, however, they show more solidarity for their fellows than they do for non-Calinti foreigners.

While strong trade links with neighboring polities

and the Realm have made Calin wealthy and its upper

classes enjoy an excellent living by Second Age standards, these advantages are fragile and don’t extend to the common folk. Rural commoners subsist largely on

congee, potherbs, roasted tubers, and rice beer, supplemented with any protein they can scrounge, and seasoned with mustard, pickled vegetables, fish sauce, or miso.

Banditry ravages much of the land. Mercenary forces

fail to adequately patrol the roads, or decide to supplement their income with brigandage. Meanwhile, patronage holders’ excessive demands ruin the soil or

drive overtaxed farmers to flight, and indiscriminate

conscription outright decimates communities.

Even when the military isn’t too mired in graft and

bureaucracy to respond to these threats, it’s primarily interested in defending the holdings of the shogun’s family, letting others decline for political purposes. At worst, the army’s free companies are little better than bandits themselves, as officers loose soldiers on communities to supplement their pay. In swaths of the Calinti heartland, the Five Shades are the only real authority, maintaining brutal justice to keep their businesses unimpeded by uprising. Most Calinti are technically serfs beholden to whomever owns their province’s patronage. But in practice, anyone with sufficient means can afford travel permits

from the patronage holder’s court, and travel restrictions are laxly enforced. Each noble house appoints regional judges to hear

noncitizens’ legal grievances. However, only egregious

crimes have any chance of official redress. Petty criminals and disputes more often face semiofficial militias or simple mob justice.

Scarcely a year goes by without an attempted uprising over punitive taxes or conscription. The shogun’s army has more experience battling revolts than foreign threats. Such unrest is often dubiously blamed on foreign agents’ machinations or priests’ and scholars’

unsound rhetoric, and most houses employ spies and

secret police to crack down on these purported threats. While Calin does have revolutionary intellectuals, usually among the wealthy middle class chafing under the citizenship system’s restrictions, they’re rarely connected to actual uprisings by the rural peasantry, whose grievances are more fundamental.

### Port Calin

Calin’s administrative center, original capital, and largest city, Port Calin overlooks the bay where the Yanaze meets the Inland Sea. Most noble houses maintain estates here and strive to outdo each other with ostentatious public works. The skyline is a baroque jumble of Immaculate temples, amphitheaters, schools, and

noble manors. Lesser structures are no more orderly;

most districts form chaotic mazes of interwoven buildings, capped with a patchwork of wildly clashing painted gables. Day and night, the city bustles with life. Bravos stalk the docks, looking to test their fighting skills. Monks

EX3

Though duelist schools exist in other cities, they’ve become a craze in Port Calin. Dockside training yards instruct bravos and sailors in swordplay; exclusive dojos catering to the nobility draw masters from across Creation by offering exorbitant compensation. Market districts’ barkers swear their school’s masters can endow students with secrets of martial enlightenment, shouting down rivals making similar claims. Some schools act as meeting places for conspirators and secret societies. The Five Shades and affiliated gangs sponsor others to recruit new members.

### THE FIVE SHADES

The noble houses form the most obvious seats of power in Calin, but five other families wield considerable influence over the Shogunate — and seek even more power. Stripped of authority and outlawed after a civil war in which they sought to seize the throne, the Five Shades now lurk in Calin’s shadows, pursuing power through criminal means — and vengeance on their ostensible usurpers.

Denied their birthright, their strength lies in smuggling, assassination, piracy, and banditry. A few especially wealthy members — largely from the Mountain Clan — purchase writs of citizenship, but most prefer to avoid attracting such attention.

Prominent Figures

Port Calin’s steward, Gabenzi Zilva, primarily exerts her authority by selectively punishing financial crimes and vetoing import contracts, destroying merchants who threaten her position while cultivating allies among those who court her favor. Although a noble herself, Zilva acts as de facto leader of the noncitizen merchant coalition, a faction that grows in power each year.

Each of the Five Shades nurses a Dragon Blooded lineage — thin, but stronger than most of the fourteen ruling houses. Their rare Exalted lead the families, wielding supernatural prowess to lend truth to legends whispered about them. The Shades are tied together by blood and marriage; by their mutual treaty, whenever a child Exalts, she’s sent to be trained by the family whose Aspect matches her own.

Kenjihno “the Reader” Kojia, as head of their house, plots to restore their family’s fortunes to its former heights. Knowing the other Calinti houses will withhold aid or outright stymie their efforts, Kojia instead cultivates a relationship with Ragara financiers, and pays a Mountain Clan contact handsomely for information to leverage against rivals. Failure will likely result in their house’s dissolution and Kojia’s own execution, but they’re confident in their ability to conceal their underhanded actions until Kenjihno regains its ascendancy. Their nickname is well-earned; not only does Kojia maintain a vast library of political and philosophical works they frequently consult, they also curate an extensive collection of romances.

The Clan Hidden in the Mist are smugglers and pirates, haunting Calin’s rivers and coasts. They wear gray to match the morning fog and evening mist. The Mountain Clan posture as reputable merchants but garner their wealth through guile and treachery. They’re masters of blackmail, and their elite martial artists are widely feared.

The Midnight Smoke Syndicate favor arson and extortion, and wear flowing midnight-colored robes for when they break stealth and instill terror with soot-blackened blades.

The Guild of the Ever-Shifting Breeze are masterful freelance spies who raise burglary to an art form. No Calinti lord would admit to hiring their agents, but many have.

The Clan Best Forgotten are expert poisoners and elite assassins, infamous for brutality. Traveling merchants and nobles dread their woodland ambushes.

from rival Immaculate denominations and scholars of abstruse philosophies preach to crowds. Artists beg to paint portraits of passing beauties; streets abound with puppet shows, singers, and theater troupes. Market vendors hawk fresh-baked sticks of barley bread, cured meats, pastries, wine, fruits, and more exotic viands.

The Manticore is a ruthless murderer or a daring revolutionary depending on who’s asked. Her monstrous bronze mask depicts a screaming, distorted human face to mock Calinti nobles’ masks. She’s an enigmatic figure, known only through fiery written polemics and a half-dozen gruesome public assassinations over the last three years. She delivers public notices denouncing a noble’s purported crimes, then kills him three days later. Her perfect record was interrupted recently when a Kenjihno Dragon-Blood narrowly saved his mortal cousin’s life. Calin’s Immaculates have declared her Anathema and called for a Wyld Hunt to scour the city for her before she strikes again.

EX3

Port Piaster

Located north of Port Calin at the mouth of the sullen, ochre-clouded River Orpiment, Piaster predates the Realm conquest. As Port Calin grew from insignificant fishing town to one of the greatest ports on the eastern coast of the Inland Sea, Piaster withered, serving largely as a stopping point for travelers bound north, albeit with a quiet serenity about it that its residents deemed virtuous.

All that changed when House Kamamoto traded in long-hoarded favors to make a surprise bid for the shogunate, successfully elevating its daughter Etsuko. Since then, Kamamoto’s estate in the exclusive Promontory District has become the summer residence for the shogun’s court. This alone caused a boom in the quiet city’s economy, as courtiers brought a veritable army of servants and demanded rare entertainments and delicacies that drew coteries of fixers and merchants. Mercenaries in the shogun’s army, too, took up residence, leading to a commensurate rise in petty crime.

Almost overnight, Piaster became a city of cutthroat politics to match Port Calin. In the decades since, the city has seen campaigns of terror and assassination. Vendettas extinguish noble lines, canny rivals force old families out of their homes, and power-hungry citizens raze slums and sell the land they stood upon. Piaster has changed, often for the worse. But it’s richer than ever before, a beast drawing the avaricious and unwary alike into its jaws.

Prominent Figures

Despite her long, successful tenure, the aging shogun Kamamoto Etsuko feels constant pressure to deliver new victories for her house. Though she’s experienced at working around political opposition in court, the current time of tumult’s new challenges threaten to exhaust her. She knows that House Kamamoto can’t acquire new patronages until she dies and a new shogun ascends, and secretly fears that her own family may hasten her demise to reap the benefits. Shengu Idori is among the rare Exalted Calinti aristocrats. This Wood Aspect poet-general has outlived three shoguns; it rankles him that when Etsuko dies, he’ll be passed over again. In the last few years, he’s begun calling in favors cultivated over his long career, spanning citizens, merchants, and mercenaries alike. Convinced he’s the only one capable of pulling Calin out of its decline, he’s prepared to take drastic, devastating measures to force his way into the shogun’s seat.

The fixer Shiranami set up shop in Port Piaster when the court moved north. She collects information about nobles and their scandals the way some people collect books or rare coins, and has a knack for spotting connections between seemingly unrelated events and deploying her findings at opportune moments. Nobles seeking to discredit opponents pay steep sums to employ Shiranami. Others, upon learning she’s targeted them, spend small fortunes to bury their transgressions. Much of her profits goes toward paying bodyguards to protect against kidnappers and assassins.

### Marin Bay

The rainswept port of Marin Bay is Calin’s northernmost city. An exclave separated from the Calinti heartlands by the Chrysocolla riverlands and the satrapy of Pale, its isolation largely shelters it from the authority of the shogun’s court, but correspondingly denies it the protection of the shogun’s army. Instead, it maintains its security through naval power.

Houses Jerogal, Kenjihno, and Shengu all have admiralty patronages tied to Marin Bay. Their squadrons ostensibly guard Calin’s coast from invasion and protect merchant vessels from piracy. In actuality, the navies frequently conspire with pirates or board and confiscate goods from other houses’ vessels. Should attacks become too blatant to ignore, the houses denounce particularly notorious — or ill-connected — naval captains, who find themselves faced with capital charges. They’re then replaced with veteran sailors (often former pirates themselves), repeating the cycle. While justice is elusive in most of Calin, Marin Bay has an especially outlandish reputation for lawlessness. Each of the Five Shades maintains a presence in the city, especially the Mist and Mountain clans, and gangs affiliated with them have a stranglehold over the port. It’s a haven for traders in illicit goods, while underground auctions draw all manner of dubious characters to bid on exotic prodigies.

Prominent Figures

Tiawara Bija, a Water Aspect and former admiral, has held Marin Bay’s patronage for two decades, and held an admiralty patronage there for two decades before that. She’s nurtured the careers of naval officers and pirates alike; almost every captain who regularly docks in the Bay owes her a favor. Never one to hoard resources, Bija calls these favors in regularly, wrangling political advantages for relatives in other provinces, taking the first cut of pirates’ plunder, or gathering information on trade deals, criminal activity, and aristocratic scheming.

EX3

Jira Mikhail is among Calin’s most prominent independent merchants. Hailing from the far North, he’s traveled Creation, and semi-retired to a Marin Bay estate after narrowly escaping death at Lintha pirates’ hands. His reputation and outsider status won him respect from naval and mercenary captains alike. His apparent lack of allegiance to the houses or the Five Shades grants him a neutrality that Marin Bay’s residents appreciate. While he plays Bija’s game of favors in other matters, he takes his current role as a judge seriously, giving sailors hauled before him stern but fair rulings despite outside pressure.

Mantis Hidden-in-the-Mist is one of the Five Shades’ secret Dragon-Blooded masters. Once a down-at-theheels river pirate, he now commands a network of illicit gambling establishments throughout Marin Bay, catering to merchants and pirates alike. Uninterested in fame or glory, he relishes luxuries, the arts, and power over others. Recently, he’s come across a rare prize: a deeply indebted sorcerer, willing to perform miracles in exchange for a clean ledger. Mantis bides his time as he contemplates how best to employ this asset.

### Neighbors

The satrapy of Pale — occupying a chalky expanse of coast between Marin Bay and Port Piaster — was once part of Calin, but House Kenzho remained loyal to the Realm rather than join its fellows in independence. Now Pale’s port towns serve as a staging post for the Imperial Navy’s Wood Fleet and a regular port of call for northeastern trade.

The satrapy occupies a precarious position, perennially threatened with saber-rattling from ambitious Calinti generals. Its Nellens garrison constantly deals with bandit raids and deniable mercenary groups from across Calin’s borders, although it returns the favor on neighboring Calinti settlements. All-Seeing Eye and Intelligence Directorate agents gather information, suborn local merchants and aristocrats, and sabotage each other’s efforts. Historically, both sides feared to escalate further, lest full-scale war flare into a devastating proxy conflict between the Realm and Lookshy. But as the Realm garrison withdraws in the face of civil war, Calin sees a rare opportunity to annex Pale at last. Chrysocolla, a small inland nation south of Marin Bay and east of Pale, recently freed itself from Calinti rule. The uprising went poorly until the rebels indebted themselves to the Roaring Lion Company — a Guildaffiliated enterprise that dominates overland trade between Marin Bay and Sijan — for the money to hire

veteran Nexus mercenaries to drive out the Calinti army. With the war ended, the Roaring Lion Company exploits Chrysocolla’s orchards for their famed golden apples, while pressuring Calin to respect the peace to protect their investment.

The Roaring Lion Company installed a puppet council that manages Chrysocolla’s people, who find themselves little better off than they were under their Calinti overlords. A new revolution brews in the countryside. Some rebels consider seeking aid from nearby Pale, though most remain wary of indebting themselves to yet another foreign power.

The Tempest Fields are a bordermarch that roams east of Calin. A roiling thunderstorm forms an unbroken wall around the Wyld zone; those who attempt to pass through must brave hurricane-strength winds, lashing rain, and unceasing lightning strikes. Once through, the other side of the storm-wall provides little respite. Here, the Fair Folk noble Talakhi of the Open Book carries out a grand romance with the storm goddess Shintra, whom Talakhi lured away from her duties on the Inland Sea. Hobgoblins and huraka form an uneasy court, dealing with petitioners who come to beseech Shintra to return to her waters or beg for the moving storm to spare their village from devastation as it passes by.

## Gentian

On the northern edge of the Scavenger Lands — east of Sijan and north of Great Forks — sits Gentian, heir to the Shogunate, a jewel amid the Avarice River’s red clay. The Exalted dead of ages past gather here, seeking a home in a world that’s passed them by. Centuries ago, Gentian was a provincial capital of the now-defunct Intou Shogunate. That fractious and violent empire — founded on an unlikely syncretism of Immaculate creed and ancestor worship — rose during the Realm’s infancy in a failed attempt to rekindle the fires of the lost Dragon-Blooded Shogunate. After its fall, Gentian languished and faltered. For centuries it was a tired river town, haunted by petal-crowned pagodas and moldering shadow houses of fallen nobility. Today, Gentian is a city on the rise. New Guild-carved roads brought life back where the dead once slept, and an ambitious young daimyo invigorates a new generation of Exalted nobility with grand plans of reconstruction and revanchism. Docks and warehouses eager for goods and shipments

EX3

With Intou’s daring and charisma, backed by the dead shogun’s name and experience, the new shogunate grew apace, drawing in hundreds of outcaste followers and countless mortal princes and heroes with the promise of a new order. At its peak, it spanned from Nathir and the Hundred Kingdoms to the Inland Sea and the foot of the great walls of Medo. Such promise couldn’t last. Intou died to an assassin’s dagger twenty years into his rule, and without his magnetism, drive, and cult of personality, his shogunate never again reached the same heights.

### THE SHADOW HOUSES

The dead hold no official position in Gentian, ceding all titles and offices to their living descendants upon death. Those granted Intou funerals are buried with much of the riches accumulated during their lives. The ghosts of Gentian’s Dragon-Blooded, however, bequeath no material wealth to their successors at all. Their bodies mummified by elite Sijanese funerists and interred in jade-bound caskets, the Exalted dead are entombed not in some grand mausoleum, but in their ancestral estates, surrounded by their worldly possessions. Sometimes the dead Exalt’s living relatives vacate the estate; more often, they withdraw to a remote wing of the mansion and extend it as required to accommodate future generations.

Though the Intou Shogunate fragmented, its splinters lingered as thorns in Lookshy’s side, and its occasional resurgences threatened the balance of power in the Scavenger Lands. However, though Intou’s own ghost adopted later shoguns into the Latter Visar Dynasty to quell years of internecine war, the shogunate never regained its territories. Its heartlands declined over the centuries into a petty backwater of squabbling principalities.

The oldest Intou Dragon-Blooded families — most of whom have had no Exalted scions in generations — inhabit these vast, labyrinthine “shadow houses,” extended successively to accommodate a dozen generations of Exalted dead and their treasures, full of boarded-up windows and ghostly pageantry. The shadow houses’ legendary riches draw many daring thieves to Gentian. Their ghosts now serve the families they sought to rob, working off their living crimes in bonds of slavery.

### The City of Gentian

line the river’s red banks. Shops and teahouses grace the once-remote city’s central square. Laborers find employment expanding the city walls, prising stones from ruined Intou buildings and putting them to new purpose. Rival Immaculate temples line the streets, clerics of different denominations threatening to come to blows over matters of faith. From the now-refurbished shadow houses, the dead watch silently as the living debate their place in the world.

### Fallen Intou

In the Great Contagion’s aftermath, many declared themselves the Shogunate’s inheritors. Most claimed succession by blood. Only one claimed a genuine shogun’s guidance. In those early days, the story goes, the scavenger lord Intou met by chance the spirit of Visar Tan, among the first shoguns of the Dragon-Blooded Shogunate. Tan had died centuries ago, leaving no heirs, but the ghost saw potential in the young outcaste who’d invaded her ancestral tomb. Together, the pair hatched a scheme to return Creation to its rightful rule — theirs. Intou left that tomb as Visar Intou, first of the Latter Visar Dynasty.

Though the Intou Shogunate is gone, its ghosts thrive yet, Gentian among them. The city’s splendor is visible even from afar, set upon a broad riverside road crowded with picturesque wheat fields and orchards. Steeple-roofed halls and elegant pagodas crowd the skyline, carefully rebuilt from moldering foundations with imported timber. Red brick and tile baked from river clay contrast sharply with the city walls’ gray stone, still threaded with scaffolding from ongoing construction. The looming Shogunate fortresses and monolithic shadow houses for which Gentian is famed brood on hilly slopes along the city’s west edge; the eastern city’s riverside bustles with merchants and dockworkers tending teeming barges. Shrines, chaityas, and temples of Immaculate denominations dot the streets, each vying against the others. The abundance of wheat informs much of Gentian’s cuisine. Street food vendors hawk delicate-looking flower buns flavored with scallions and spices. Hearty stew is served in square-shaped bread bowls the locals dub “coffin boards.” Bread accompanies most meals as either soft rolls or crispy pancakes, both suitable for smearing with red bayberry preserves or dipping into sauces. Fishers on the Avarice River catch shad, carp, and paddlefish. While sweet melon pear is a refreshing snack for Gentian commoners, the upper classes deride it as peasant food.

EX3

Gentian grows larger by the year. Immigrants flood in from other former Intou provinces and lands beyond, offering labor to build walls and till farms. Merchants come north on the Guild’s refurbished river-roads, bringing exotic trade goods and delicacies. Most of all, Gentian’s ruins attract priests, savants, and thaumaturgists eager to pore over the city’s rich history and converse with its honored dead. In two generations, Gentian has greatly increased its population, today hosting more than 60,000 souls and growing. Though the Exalted dead — anticipating regaining their lost ancestral territories — largely approve the daimyo’s efforts to renew the Intou Shogunate, many less prestigious ancestor ghosts feel dismay at changes to the sedentary, peaceful Gentian they’ve inhabited for centuries. Though wielding little political power, they maintain some influence over their descendants, and work to sway public opinion against the daimyo and her Guild allies. The dwindling Intou monks lack the strength to quiet this ghostly sedition; the daimyo must look elsewhere for aid.

Those Who Guide the Coils

Established by the new shogun to reconcile his ghostly legacy with Immaculate doctrine, the Intou creed states that an ancestor ghost who remains in Creation out of compassion for her descendants is to be honored and learned from, to better navigate the Coils of Enlightenment. Dragon-Blooded ghosts are especially revered, having purportedly sacrificed a chance at transcendence for the betterment of all. The Intou priesthood affords these spirits more respect than many gods, giving them precedence on the prayer calendar. Intou monks are instantly recognizable by their indigo-dyed robes. Those of higher coils bear the eerie pallor of ghost flower tea usage. Several missionaries of the Realm’s Immaculate Order and Lookshy’s Immaculate Faith reside in Gentian. Often at odds, these monks and sohei find unity in opposition to the Intou heresy. All three creeds’ monks are the primary source of education and literacy in Gentian, and each has direct lines to the peasantry. The Immaculate Order and Faith seek

EX3

Jishin, who once ruled in the now-ruined neighboring city of Aspor; and the Yonshou, descended from early Intou generals, whose honor demands officer roles in Gentian’s small army.

### THE DANCING TEMPLE RIOTS

Most visitors pay little heed to Gentian’s competing Immaculate doctrines. Some see their theological squabbles as comical. For locals, however, the divided faith is deadly serious.

The region’s handful of surviving Intou statelets — from the scenic wooded hills and lakes of Dama to xenophobic, funereal Chrysanth — each claim to be the Intou Shogunate’s successor. None officially view Gentian as the capital or accept its daimyo as their shogun… at least, not yet. Kana has yet to take aggressive action against these neighbors, and indeed has begun making political overtures. Some, alarmed by Gentian’s recent growth and deeming conflict inevitable, align quietly against her. Others, tempted by her offers or swept up by her charisma, grow invested in a revived Intou Shogunate. Knowledgeable observers expect the first of these to swear fealty to Kana before year’s end.

During last year’s harvest season, with the city already crowded with farmers and merchants, word spread that an Immaculate Order missionary had assaulted a ghostly monk at Hesiesh-Dancing-at-Heaven’s-Gate Temple. Civil disorder broke out citywide; mobs of all three sects assaulted rival faiths’ monks and practitioners in the street, and defaced or destroyed homes and shrines. Daimyo Aoki’s forces spent several days enforcing strict curfews and rounding up ringleaders for public punishment.

More recently, Daimyo Kana has expelled several hardline monks from the city and imposed restrictions and taxes on Immaculate temples, making their subordinate position clear. She alternately offers favors or threats to Order and Faith representatives, hoping to play the two creeds against one another. Still, resentment seethes among the city’s faithful, and further disturbances seem likely.

### Prominent Figures

to discourage ancestor worship, while the Intou aim to keep ancestor worship strong. Powerful Gentian ghosts support their temples and the faithful with trinkets, secrets, and blessings. Opposing them is a curious alliance of convenience between Immaculate missionaries on the one hand, and merchants and nobles hoping to see the aristocracy liquidate the treasures entombed in the shadow houses.

### Government and Politics

The Intou shoguns once awarded the role of daimyo, or provincial governor, based on merit and politics. But in the centuries since their shogunate’s collapse, it’s become hereditary within the Sanshin family. Today, Sanshin Kana rules from the Old Palace, a walled compound at Gentian’s heart. There she’s advised by a council composed of both living Gentian nobles and the ghosts of previous daimyos.

Several noble families command the surrounding hinterlands’ towns and villages. These pledge loyalty to the daimyo, send representatives to her council, and maintain shadow houses in Gentian. A few families retain a thin trickle of the Dragons’ blood, producing occasional Exalted scions. These include the Akusha, once famous for their savants, now renowned as scavenger lords; the

Sanshin Kana recently inherited the daimyo’s seat from her mother Aoki. Young, ambitious, vigorous, and intellectual, she’s impressed peers and ancestors with her learning, culture, and martial prowess. Kana grew up among the dead, traveling the deepest recesses of the Sanshin shadow house and begging stories of Intou glory days from her ancestors. She inspires her fellow nobles and Gentian’s populace with fervor for a shogunate renaissance: an empire of order, cultural refinement, and warrior honor, with Gentian at its heart. Kana’s vision of revival has drawn many of Gentian’s living and dead to her cause, even as conservative elders regard her warily. Beyond wooing or conquering neighboring principalities, her priority is to draw outcastes to Gentian and strengthen its failing bloodlines; only a handful of living Exalts remain in the city, and none in the royal line. But first, Gentian itself must be restored, for which she needs trade.

Wood Aspect Jishin Mori harbors no personal ambitions toward power, instead dedicating her skills toward uplifting Gentian itself. An elderly bureaucrat, Mori was a child when her family fled the final sack of Aspor. She works quietly behind the scenes to keep Gentian running amid its current transformation. In meetings with the daimyo, Mori cautions thoughtfulness and restraint, often putting her at odds with Smiling Sky’s grand recommendations.

The elderly Guild factor Smiling Sky is a key instigator of Gentian’s expansion. The price has been high; thousands of laborers, smiths, masons, shipwrights, and
