Prominent Ghosts

### LANGUAGES

As the Intou Shogunate’s founding ancestor, Visar Tan enjoys a special place of honor among its pantheon of saints. She resides in Cloud-Favored Gate — a gloomy manse nestled in the western hills — attended by ghostly servants and jade effigies. Intou monks seeking political guidance visit her regularly, and she graces Gentian annually in a spectacular midnight masquerade party to converse anonymously with residents and dispense guidance to her faithful.

Gentian’s Riverspeak is flavored by the overly formal, slightly archaic dialect typical of former Intou provinces. Gentian’s outcaste families and Intou monks speak Gen-Cha, a courtly Shogunate-descended local tongue taught by the ancient dead. Learning it is a prerequisite to obtaining an audience with the Exalted dead or adoption into a Gentian outcaste line.

more have worked tirelessly to see the old city reborn. He knows which way the winds are blowing among the Intou Shogunate’s ghosts, and he wants in. As financier, he has access to Kana, even without an official spot on her council. Some of Gentian’s older citizens (especially the undead) worry that Kana’s goals are dictated to her by Smiling Sky, rather than trust her to court the Guild on her own terms.

For now, Smiling Sky contents himself with the steady rewards of the Avarice River trade while his rivals laugh up their sleeves at his squandered fortune. Meanwhile, he conducts secret negotiations of adoption with a deceased daimyo who lost her estate as the Intou Shogunate crumbled. When Kana makes her move, he plans to be right there with her. And when Gentian reclaims that ancestral estate, the old Guild master aims to retire in style as a prince among the dead. Kakuichi, a senior Intou monk, is chief priest at Daana’d-of-the-Lotus-Crown Temple. Hardly any Dragon-Blooded have entered the monkhood for generations, leaving such prestigious roles in the hands of mortals like Kakuichi. The monk finds some of the changes Gentian’s revival has wrought beneficial, but worries that it’s happening too fast and at the expense of older traditions. He uses his clout to push back against it in sermons and in private audiences with nobles.

Like all of Gentian’s Intou priests, Kakuichi carries a sacred flute and talismans all carved from the bones of his mentor and predecessor, with which he can call upon his old master’s tamed hungry ghost to aid him against truculent spirits. By tradition, his apprentice Sangmu Blazing-Eye would sculpt his bones into a new instrument upon his death. But Sangmu has abandoned the Intou ways, joining Lookshy’s Immaculate sohei to preach against her old faith. Heartbroken, Kakuichi seeks a new apprentice, but fears that he won’t be able to train one fully before he passes on.

Kana’s predecessor as daimyo, Sanshin Aoki, retains significant influence from her living days among nobles, monks, and commoners alike. Both ghostly and mortal courtiers surround her in her wing of the Sanshin estate; her advisers include several elder Sanshin ghosts who once held her current role but who’ve outlived all their mortal contacts. She’s renowned for personal piety, and remains devoted to her family’s fortunes and Gentian’s traditions. Some also remember her as a great warrior who put down several revolts in the hinterlands.

Aoki advises Kana closely, warning her that Gentian’s expansion may draw retaliation from stronger neighbors. She also meddles in state affairs — promulgating trade regulations, arranging outcomes of judicial trials, negotiating with old friends among neighboring cities’ courtiers and princes, and managing a ghostly spy network throughout the province. Kana fears that her mother’s machinations will undermine her own plans for empire, but such shadow rule is a longstanding Gentian tradition that Aoki herself likewise suffered through.

### Neighbors

The ancient Amaldine Road stretches hundreds of miles from Gentian to Melevhil. A string of inns and teahouses were founded along it during the Intou Shogunate period, providing food and lodging for traders and pilgrims. Though business was steady for centuries, changes in river trade shifted much of the travel away. Many inns shuttered their doors altogether or were taken over by bandits. Today, Shogun Kana and Smiling Sky plan to refurbish the road for trade — and, perhaps, future troop movements. This requires clearing out the bandits. A ruined former Intou city, dubbed the Spall, lies northeast of Gentian. Once a proud citadel guarding the Intou heartlands, now it’s a place of shattered spires and walkways, sundered by First Age weapons and

EX3

Dragon-Blooded puissance in conflicts between rival daimyos. Here the outcaste scavenger lord Jade Tiger rules a raucous society of bandits and warriors with an iron fist. She’s cobbled together this crew from the armies of four warlords she bested in her youth, and from foreign laborers and craftsmen seeking her silver. The Spall’s business is its own slow destruction, as Jade Tiger offers the ruined city’s bounty to the highest bidder. Work crews chisel finely engraved panels and statuary from long-profaned temples; caravans haul stone blocks and metal scrap to buyers in neighboring cities. Jade Tiger also offers blood sport to her guests. Elite gladiators, armed with baroque weapons from the ruins, face off against lions, giant elk, great serpents, and slaves who’ll earn freedom with victory. This makes the Spall a popular destination for magnates whose tastes tend towards the bloody.

A day’s ride downriver from Gentian lies the shadowland of Kelai. Once home to the daimyo Sanshin Idoki’s sprawling summer estate, now the city’s streets lie cracked and broken, and weeds grow where once Idoki’s splendid gardens burgeoned. Yet from the gray soil, ghost flowers bloom. Intou monks visit to tend and pick these blossoms, drying them to produce ghost flower tea.

Kelai’s streets are home to packs of owlwolves. While the animal’s feather-speckled pelt fetches a handsome price in the living world, most hunters seek them for another purpose. The Red Maze Society consists of living and dead Intou astrologers who read fortunes in owlwolves’ entrails.

Distant Melevhil shares Gentian’s pedigree as a former Intou Shogunate territory, though its long-ago tenure had less impact on Melevhil’s history. A busy city of elegant canals and delicate wooden arches, it’s remained largely unchanged since gaining independence, exacting tariffs on river traffic and doing brisk trade in quality timber from the surrounding Goldreach Forest. The Melevhil Council of Electors, a governing body composed of elected officials and wealthy estate holders, isn’t blind to their northern cousin’s expansionist rhetoric. They recognize that Melevhil could eventually be a prize target for a resurgent Gentian seeking to reclaim Intou territory and gain a foothold on the Yellow River — especially as elements of their city’s sizable ancestor cult might serve as a fifth column for Gentian’s efforts.

Officially, the council considers raising levies and mercenaries should conflict with Gentian ever arise. Unofficially, many council members support renewing the city’s devotion to the Intou sect, proactively offering alliance to Gentian in founding a new Shogunate, or both. Either way, Guild-backed enterprises happily offer Melevhil arms and mercenaries; many financiers stand ready to invest deeply in both sides of the potential conflict.

## Nexus

Built where the Yellow River and the Grey River come together to form the Yanaze, Nexus spreads like a banquet across the landscape. The seat of the Guild Directorate and home to a million souls, its reputation is one of longing and loathing in equal measure. Renowned as lawless apart from the inscrutable edicts of the Council of Entities and their masked Emissary, Nexus obeys only the incessant torrent of commerce that passes through its markets and countinghouses. Woe to any would-be agitator who threatens that torrent.

Nexus is a city of extremes. The powerful expend the wealth of nations to gain paltry advantage over one another. Beneath them, the wretched mass of humanity struggles to survive. The sliver of the populace in between claws at itself in bids for security and prestige. Tonight, a mercenary in exquisite livery drags a nervous man from the Cinnabar alley he’s hidden himself in; their mutual employer wants a word. Choking fog rolls down a steep street beneath strings of tawdry paper lanterns. At the docks, an inspector accepts a hefty purse and overlooks certain boxes as they’re offloaded. Welcome to the city of opportunities.

### A Geography of Injustice

Shit flows downhill in Nexus. The Yellow and Gray Rivers flood regularly; this is good news for farmers in the upriver floodplains, but bad news for tenants of lowland urban districts.

Worst off is Firewander, a formerly independent township incorporated 175 years ago. Firewander hugs the Yanaze’s banks; it suffers from both stinking floodwaters laden with industrial runoff and a sewer-bordermarch beneath the streets where grotesque fae lie in wait. Ill health and ill dreams plague the very young and very old alike, and quality of life is poor for even the able-bodied. Impoverished residents exhibit poorly

EX3

concealed animosity toward their employers and financial betters uphill. Riots are common, often spilling eastward toward wealthier districts. Some are spontaneous; others serve as cover for criminal syndicates that pull the neighborhood’s strings. The Council has difficulty enforcing their will here.

### FIVE MARKETS

The Big Market dominates the Nexus District: a massive open-air auction house for bulk goods, where the economic output of small kingdoms changes hands weekly. Libraries of books, tons of grain or salt, and batches of scimitars to arm whole companies are traded here.

On a spit of land directly upriver, the industrial neighborhood of Nighthammer crouches like a sick animal. The glow of molten iron sits sullen at the edge of the sky, day and night. Trip-hammers ring out, chimneys soar, and waterwheels groan. Massive barges unload at even larger docks, many of them remnants of the First Age. Manufactories here produce the choking ash and yellow fogs that plague Nexus’s poor, along with thousands of tons of materials and goods daily. Crowded tenements shudder under the weight of countless migrant families. The common balm to this human misery is cheap alcohol, supplied in quantity by distilleries and served in dingy public houses —owned and operated by Guild-affiliated businesses. Desperation breeds violence; knifepoint robberies are everyday occurrences. Sometimes, forges burn bodies hidden in the coal.

Adjoining and surrounding it sprawls the Little Market, where small business is handled. Stalls here sell everything from astrolabes to street food. Those who know the right codewords can find even more exotic goods and services hidden behind the market’s facades. The brothels of the Harlotry comprise an entire neighborhood in the Nexus District. These range from purely sexual outlets to elaborate dining and musical establishments. Exploitation is common as in other industries, but to many who wear the perfumed veil, working on one’s back is preferable to breaking it. Coffleblock, a grim collection of shacks and cages, specializes in livestock and meat. It also deals in foreign indentured servants — slaves in practice, their names signed by slavers to indenture contracts to evade Nexus’ laws. Here the wailing of people and animals alike never ceases. It reeks of waste and blood, channeled by a bespoke sewer system to the Undercity’s mushroom farms. Coffleblock is lousy with mercenaries; raids and revolts are frequent.

On a broad plaza south of the Yellow River, the Nexus District throbs like a palpitating heart. Here, all streams converge on the grandest commercial district in the world. The Guild’s nine hierarchs meet here, amid webs of proxies and armies of bodyguards, in the Hall of the Directorate — an unassuming two-story building overlooking the Big Market. Across the plaza, the Council Tower soars ten stories into the air. Halfway up, on a cantilevered glass platform, the Emissary itself sometimes watches the business of the day. Cleansed by bracing winds, Bastion stands proud on the northern hills. With wealth rivaling the Imperial City’s, this opulent neighborhood hosts some of the most prestigious residences in Creation. Merchant princes build mansions next to Councilors’ estates; servants scatter lilac sprigs across the pavement to sweeten the air. Children of these worthies attend the School of Philosophy should they prove unsuited to business, learning rhetoric and poetry beneath laurel boughs. The culture district of Cinnabar hugs the hills below Bastion. Libraries, parks, monasteries, schools, and amphitheaters crowd between townhouses of modest luxury. Mercenaries linger on every corner, hired to ensure that the lower classes don’t overstay their welcome. The greatest attraction is the Parko Llana, 200 acres of greenery where religious festivals and secular fairs are held when someone needs to buy the masses’ affections.

Open from two hours after sunset until two hours before sunrise, the Night Market is where Nexus’s residents shop outside of commercial hours. The Council of Entities forbids sale of certain goods after dark: weapons, nightshades, masks. But enforcement of Council decrees is lax. For the right price and a little discretion, the right merchant might bend the rules.

The Undercity sprawls beneath several districts, built on the ruins of cities that preceded it, and out of underground warrens established for other purposes — sewers, cellars, and catacombs. Stairs in Nighthammer and Firewander descend to the Undercity’s labyrinthine streets, where visitors find slums, workshops, mushroom farms, temples, black markets, deep cisterns, and ventilation shafts. Some impoverished or criminal citizens, dubbed “sunless folk,” live their entire lives down here, rarely visiting the surface.

EX3

Laws for the Lawless

The Council of Entities, with ritual solemnity, insists that Nexus has no body of laws and that it’s governed by neither Council nor Directorate.

Nexus has no formal legal system. The city employs no magistrates or peacekeepers. If a woman desires action against one who’s wronged her, she approaches the mercenaries and bounty hunters who offer their services by the docks or upscale caravanserais. The sole exception is the Emissary, who personally levies gruesome, public, supernatural punishments for the highest-profile violations. Here are the laws that govern Nexus:

• None shall obstruct trade

• None shall bring an army into Nexus

• None shall commit wanton violence

• None may falsely claim the Council’s name or sanction

• None shall harbor a fugitive from the Council’s wrath

These six unchanging commandments are collectively known as the Dogma. Additional to these edicts are the Civilities, a corpus of lesser rules declared at will by any Councilor. If Civilities contradict each other, the newest takes precedence. Slavery is against the Civilities (“no person may work for nothing”); merchants sometimes circumvent this for foreign slaves with legal fictions and coerced contracts, but rarely try this in large numbers or against natives for fear of the Emissary’s reprisal.

While the Emissary’s exact nature is left to the Storyteller — it could be anything from a First Age automaton to a long-lived Dragon King sorcerer — by default it’s a unique supernatural entity bound to enforce the Council’s dictates. Its power level should vary based on the chronicle’s needs, but should be at least strong enough to beat an experienced Dragon-Blood oneon-one in a fight.

Knowing when a Councilor intends to change the Civilities can confer massive business advantage, spawning an illicit trade in rumor and stolen correspondence. Similarly, significant energy is devoted to ferreting out those who’ve broken obscure stipulations; dossiers cataloging instances of taking a meal alone in darkness or the barehanded handling of another person’s blood are valuable blackmail material.

### Ungovernable Governance

• None may raise taxes or levies, save the Council

### THE EMISSARY

The Council keeps written copies of the Civilities — each several hundred pages long — in the Council Tower. A staff of scribes, lawyers, and diviners keeps them updated, sometimes multiple times a day if the Councilors are feeling litigious. Collectively, this is the Incunabulum, an understated but vital part of Nexus’s bizarre legal system.

The Council of Entities employs thousands of assayers, tax collectors, purchasers, clerks, archivists, sycophants, informants, and snoops. This network’s activities are coordinated from Bastion estates, but their influence reaches everywhere. Each Councilor has interests to look after; these are personal proclivities, not official duties.

The Council itself elects new members to its number. Potential candidates rise to its attention through a combination of personal prowess, magical ability, connections, unimaginable wealth, and ruthlessness. Various Councilors are motivated by greed or civic duty, reform or repression. Like the city that spawns them, they’re idiosyncratic to a fault. They’re united, however, in preserving their hegemony. Membership is relatively stable. Most Councilors groom a replacement for years; upsets and coups are uncommon.

The Council

The Council of Entities maintains the status quo in Nexus. Depending on how resilient the Storyteller wants that status quo to be, they might be anything from mortals commanding vast mundane resources, to powerful spirits and Exalted more than a match for player characters in the councilors’ specialties. The Emissary, wearing their silver half-mask, serves as an overwhelming enforcer of the Council’s will. Its identity and nature remain a mystery.

Thalevar, Councilor Eclipse — a canny diplomat entering middle age — oversees the docks and ensures that there’s no disruption to trade. He has a reputation for impartiality and a nigh-religious devotion to the Dogma.

EX3

Ephiselle, Queen Midnight, is a recent addition to the Council whose predecessor’s body was never found — except for the blood. She’s rumored to operate spy networks and illicit businesses in Firewander and elsewhere.

Vai Va’a, Evening Master, concerns himself with the promotion of new ideas in the city, recently spearheading a campaign of library-building. Strange rumors dog him, ranging from the mildly scandalous to the outright despicable.

Hayle, Midday Husband, a huge man and patron of the arts, manages Nexus’s sewage and well systems. His diligence has several times prevented toxic runoff from Firewander and Nighthammer from poisoning the other districts’ waters. Pellicia, Dawn Sergeant — Hayle’s adopted sister — liaises with Nexus mercenary companies; she’s a respected and formidable warrior herself. Some fellow Council members grow concerned by her increasing influence. Ibebi, Minister of Ways, eldest on the Council and a sorcerer, is charged with maintaining Nexus’ spiritual

health. He’s often absent for long stretches, negotiating with divinities; even when physically present, he seems vague and distant.

Masakim Lamang, the Doctor, is a short woman, solid as a wall. She speaks for the common people and sees to the populace’s medical needs. In matters of quarantine, she’s ruthlessly pragmatic.

Gwyli Seern, the Astrologer, looks to the stars and reads portents for the city. She maintains the largest entourage, including a contingent of gifted slaves and several thaumaturges.

### Guild Influence

Nexus is the Guild’s city — not in name, but in spirit. Guild founder Brem Marst chose it as the headquarters for his growing syndicate due to its lack of central authority and permissiveness toward his business practices, and the Directorate’s presence has intensified those features in the centuries hence. Artisans labor in Guildaffiliated Cinnabar studios, while administrators slash wages in Guild-affiliated Nighthammer sweatshops.

EX3

It’s from Nexus that overarching Guild policy diffuses across Creation, supplying knowledge and capital, establishing connections, and coordinating economic maneuvers for merchants and business ventures from Wu-Jian to Greyfalls. Nexus is the central hub through which most Scavenger Lands Guild caravans eventually route, while information flows up the Yanaze from the Blessed Isle itself. No other city in Creation has such a high concentration of Guildswomen.

The Guild Directorate and the Council maintain uneasy eye contact from their strongholds across the Big Market. On some level, the hierarchs understand that the status quo is good for business. But when the chance presents itself, only fear of violating the Dogma prevents a hostile takeover of the city; the Emissary has made examples of overreaching hierarchs before. Nevertheless, should a ripe opportunity present itself, the Directorate will be waiting.

Though the hierarchs lack direct political control over Nexus, Guild-affiliated enterprises affect many aspects of life. Its network allows Guild-backed merchants to coordinate prices — raising them to create demand in upscale Cinnabar boutiques, or lowering them to undercut competitors in the Big Market. Anyone can sing on a street corner for coins, but theater companies who pay Guild dues use connections to perform in private theaters or Bastion’s manors.

Notable Guild Enterprises

Though it’s easy to think of the Guild as one massive, overarching organization, it’s composed of thousands

### WHAT CAME BEFORE

Once, Nexus was named Hollow, a First Age metropolis. Remnants of that legacy linger today. The Council Tower is one; so are the cyclopean Nighthammer Docks, crusted by modern piers in a web of scaffolding. A handful of Bastion’s finest residences nestle in the shells of First Age apartment blocks, and beneath the streets lie unknown tracts of collapsed infrastructural systems. Scattered throughout the city are the tombs of six Solar Anathema who lived or died in Hollow. The Council of Entities forbids opening them, though the tombs’ deadly defenses often suffice to discourage even the brave and foolish from such attempts. Residents use the tombs as landmarks and their defenses as tools; sometimes they even bother to warn outsiders not to get too close.

of smaller, diverse businesses and enterprises under one umbrella. Below are examples of Guild-affiliated businesses in Nexus:

With its massive population, Nexus has a lot of mouths to feed. The Council currently pays Ring-Tail Importers to provide grain for the bread dole. This goes to the Golden Sisters Bakery, or any of a dozen other affiliated bakeries throughout the city. Their ovens run day and night, filling the air with the tantalizing scent of baking bread. Many of Nexus’ poorest citizens receive daily rations of bread, olive oil, and salt from these bakeries. Experts at Quillip’s Fine Antiquities, in the Cinnabar district, assay the quality, authenticity, and price of ancient goods and First Age relics brought to them for sale by adventurers and scavenger lords, which they resell at auction. Per the Civilities, they report all transactions to the Council of Entities; the Directorate and several individual magnates pay for copies of these reports. Quillip’s galleries are secured with locks, mercenary guards, and — some say — sorcery. In Nighthammer, the busy Slag-Tomb Forge encompasses an ominous pyramid faced in firebrick. Beneath the brick is the resting place of an ancient Solar Anathema — an edifice of imperishable metal, orange with heat from unknown First Age artifice, that serves as the forge’s furnace. In this time of tumult, owner Lāla Dīkybyra redirects the forge’s output toward weaponry rather than tools. A few other warded tombs are likewise repurposed by ingenious entrepreneurs, though the Civilities forbid opening them lest their curses threaten the city.

Nikos Masonry doubles as a construction outfit and fire brigade. Its workers raise new buildings in Nighthammer, while its bosses attempt to strike deals with the owners of burning structures. If they agree to sell, the Company efficiently puts the fire out. If they refuse, it’s left to burn itself out — or spread.

### Society and Culture

Nexus is a melting pot. Immigrants trickle in from across the Scavenger Lands and beyond, seeking new homes. A few are merchants or wealthy elites seeking opportunity, but most come fleeing war, slavery, taxation, famine, disease, or outlawry. Sometimes individuals and families arrive a few at a time. Other times, disaster or unrest drives people toward the city in waves. Nexus accepts them all.

The Civilities limit how hard the lower classes can be

EX3

worked, out of reformist impulses among the Council and the general desire to avoid revolt. To that end, regularly scheduled festival days offer opportunities for revelry, complete with street food, sports matches, parades, and other spectacles. Even on nonfestival days, entertainment abounds. Nexus’ citizens devour cheap novels and gather to listen to popular musicians busking in market squares. Theaters provide comfortable seating for richer residents and standing room for the less well-off; new dramas open every few weeks. Gambling houses, open at all hours, welcome the wealthy and the desperate. Even if they rub elbows while throwing dice, the class divide is sharp. Lower-class residents maintain close ties with family members and a handful of trusted neighbors, looking out for one another and their homes in the city’s more dangerous districts. Though they don’t have much, they offer small gifts and favors to help a neighbor in need. Material goods are cheap, allowing residents to procure tools even when they’re not sure they can afford to eat, cover rent, or pay a chirurgeon. Clothing for the lower classes is plain and durable, capable of hiding stains from soot or dirt. People wear loose-fitting jackets over trousers or skirts, with hobnailed boots to prolong their footwear’s utility. Middleclass fashions add patterned fabrics in more expensive materials, paired with lace and embroidery at cuffs and hems, signaling that they’re a step removed from the docks or the factory floor.

Chronic hunger and malnutrition are common. Families subsist as best they can in crowded housing units and shantytowns. Many work long hours despite the Civilities, leaving little time for personal pursuits. When workers can wrangle a break, their leisure activities take on a frenetic quality. Nexus’ small middle class mainly serves the upper class. High-end shopkeepers, artisans, overseers, clerks, aides, and the like eke out a modest living catering to the needs and whims of the elite. Though able to afford plenty of material goods, housing remains cramped; many inhabit spaces crammed with well-made furniture and knickknacks, and dream of the day they can afford to rent a larger home.

Good food is nearly as scarce as living space. Many middle-class residents rarely cook at home, buying most of their meals from street food carts. Vendors sell roasted potatoes and meat — primarily cheek, liver, or kidneys — on skewers; choicer cuts are rare luxuries. For those who do cook at home, bread from the daily

ration sops up broth and drippings. A family might use one pot for all their meals, stretching out a stew over weeks or months as they add water to extend the broth and toss in whatever ingredients are at hand. Lacking other seasonings, the broth’s richness comes from the blend of its components.

Families shop for bargains as best they can, purchasing food at the end of its shelf life and seeking clams or mussels with broken shells at the fish market. Cooks purchase pantry staples offered at a discount by shady merchants who add gypsum dust to flour, water down milk and whiten it with chalk, or use lead compounds instead of sugar to sweeten confections. Some vendors decline to disclose the list of ingredients used in meat pies or sausages, on the rare occasions their poorer customers ask. While people go hungry in the lower districts, Bastion’s residents throw luxurious galas for their peers, offering 16-course banquets, opium and other drugs, and escorts’ services. Likewise, they take full advantage of the finest textiles coming into the city, disposing of last year’s garments to purchase today’s new trends. Current fashions include full, wide skirts, heeled boots with buttons, and fitted knee-length waistcoats that button from neck to hem.

The wealthy keep their families’ inner workings opaque, which provides plenty of fodder for the rumor mill and authors of Nexus-based romans à clef. By custom, many are involved in (and gain their fortunes through) mercantile activities. Others swell the ranks of Nexus’ mercenary companies, serving as officers whether or not they have adequate field experience — filling their families’ coffers with hefty fees and battlefield loot.

### Prominent Figures

In Firewander’s densest slum, where the Council’s enforcers don’t go, is a drinking den that locals call the Rooster’s Tail. Its proprietor, Water Opal, hails from a Southwestern nation of seafarers. Enslaved as a child, she fought her way free one night and escaped, taking service on a ship bound for Nexus. Now nearly 50, she runs both her drinking den and a modest crime ring. While the den’s a legitimate business, she fences stolen goods through the back and competes with the Guildsponsored Tranquil Evenings Syndicate for control of the slum’s drug trade. A new arrangement with Queen Midnight will soon sharply expand her operations. Brisegh Osán strides the Nighthammer streets with a

EX3

sneer on his scaly lips and a squad of leg-breakers at his back. Beloved by bosses and hated by workers, Brisegh captains the Nighthammer Iron League, a mercenary company specialized in crowd control and strikebreaking. He himself is an alligator beastman, a great asset when intimidating ironworkers. He has many Guild officials’ support for his zeal in ending production delays, and countless enemies among the city’s tenements and hovels. He fears assassination and never walks alone. If might makes right, then Rom Daoh will make herself mighty. She’s the charismatic leader of the “Liberating Ones,” a group equal parts cult and political lobby. They take the prohibition against slavery seriously. For months, Rom’s followers have mounted a propaganda campaign against slavers. They have popular support in poor neighborhoods, and recently Daoh’s been seen meeting with the Doctor. The Council is divided in their opinions, while hierarchs scramble for blackmail material. Other agitators have died for less, but Rom hasn’t died yet. “We will break every shackle!” she and her followers shout to the streets.

### Neighbors

The Guild Directorate rules the Nexus Marches in all but name. Over the centuries, Guild-affiliated businesses obtained leverage over leaders, purchased land, established way stations, set mercenary patrols, and levied taxes throughout communities within Nexus’s immediate vicinity and along local trade routes, ensuring access to supplies and safe passage for caravans. The Directorate later consolidated much — though not all — of this authority, leaving an amorphous patchwork of governance and economic control that gives political mapmakers fits.

Their wharfs are choked with gambling dens, wineshops, fences, and counterfeiters, for piracy drives Sisphe’s economy. Their sleek outrigger canoes are the bane of shipping and a headache for Guild factors. But the cities are far enough upriver, and the Sisphe crafty enough with diplomacy backed by stolen bullion, to make Guild reprisal prohibitively expensive. Lookshyan river patrols largely ignore them, seeing their crimes as Nexus’s problem until the Directorate purchases Lookshy’s naval services.

As Creation destabilizes, outrigger pirates grow bolder. The cost/benefit analysis that’s protected them may soon change, and not in their favor.

Toward the Inland Sea lies Taigh Phor, ruled by the Tanist of Oaks and her Dragon-Blooded kinfolk. It’s a pretty land of fogs and moors, where the Fern River — a tributary of the Yanaze — broadens into a boggy floodplain. Huge herds of cattle roam the wetlands, guarded from predatory spirits by bondsmaids carrying hazel wands. The Tanist reigns from a ringfort on a hill, iron and gold draped across her chest.

What was once just another petty kingdom, happy to profit off the river trade, has become something dangerous. Two years ago, the Tanist lost her sacred sister-wife to an unknown assassin’s blade. She’s been lost in mourning and paranoia ever since, and her advisors squabble rather than govern. The Guild-backed Clerin Family Trading Company has begun importing large quantities of opium in exchange for incentives from the Directorate, indicative that someone intends a regime change for the region.

## Marita

A few small cities burgeon in the Marches. Some, like Norr, with its many mills, have grown from settlements already under a factor’s thumb. Others, like rundown Lower Send, struggle to remain independent as the Marches slowly engulf them. The hierarchs fiercely debate what policies to take toward each city — and which hierarch will profit most.

Because of its central location, relative independence, and insignificance, Scavenger Lands leaders chose the small town of Marita as the capital of the Confederation of Rivers. Since the Confederation’s founding two centuries ago, Marita has burgeoned from a sleepy town of a few thousand residents into a sprawling metropolis, home to over 100,000 people.

Nykhti and Korakhem — called the Cormorant Cities — are two ticks sucking on the rich vein of Scavenger Lands commerce. Founded by the Sisphe people, they loom above the Gray River, their architecture perpetually crusted with scaffolding as residents build ever higher. This year saw the triumphal completion of a grand bridge spanning the river, finally linking the sister cities.

Today, Marita is a huge, thriving port — a center for trade, diplomacy, and especially intrigue. While it initially grew to support Confederation envoys and their staff, merchants and shipping firms found it an excellent location to buy and sell both legal and illicit goods. Numerous businesses — Guild-affiliated and otherwise — flourish here. So do smugglers, fences, and other criminals who prefer to conduct unlawful business in

EX3

cities large enough to conceal their activities. Today, most residents are in some way associated with the city docks — laborers load and unload ships, clerks and customs agents keep records and collect duties, and myriad others cook, clean, tell fortunes, sing songs, or pour drinks. As the economic heart of Marita, the harbor district also plays an important role in local politics.

### The Docks and the Collective

Besides the Guild and the Confederation of Rivers, the third major power in Marita is the Dockworkers’ Collective. Before the Confederation’s founding, this was an informal group of dock laborers who pooled money to subsidize weddings and funerals for members and families. This benefit society was little different from countless similar organizations across Creation. But as Marita grew, prominent members decided to ensure that their fellows profited equitably from the flood of new commerce.

They began recruiting members of almost every profession associated with the docks, promising that the collective would work to guarantee that all members obtained a fair share of the rapidly expanding port’s profits. Despite its name, the Dockworkers’ Collective now represents nearly every employee associated with the port and shipping: clerks, salespeople, auction house personnel, inn and hostel staff, and — yes — dockworkers.

A century and a half ago, Marita’s newly formalized Guild council — the “Marita Nine” — and their puppet prince tried to force dockworkers to carry more loads of cargo per day without increased pay. The Collective responded by refusing to report to work or set foot on the docks for several days. This strike completely shut down the port, forcing the Nine to reconsider their plans. The Nine would love to break the Collective, but it’s so popular and its membership rolls so long that all attempts thus far have failed.

The Collective remains influential in Marita. But the powerful Jaris family has led it for almost a century; while it still serves the dock community’s interests, it also enriches the Jarises. Any Maritani speaking out against the Collective’s corruption or Jaris excesses is shunned by the dock community. Those who persist are sometimes beaten, or arrested for petty crimes without evidence.

### Local Government

Although Marita hosts the Council of the Concordat that governs the Confederation of Rivers, its local administration operates independently. Before the Confederation’s founding, Marita was small, its prince a puppet of wealthy merchants. Now that it’s larger and far more important, the Chamber of Three governs it. This council has three members: one representing the city’s Guild council, another named by the Council of the Concordat, and the third an elected member of the Dockworker’s Collective. All three members have an equal vote; a simple majority suffices for most decisions. The Chamber’s third seat once represented the wealthier local families, but a series of riots pressured the Chamber into giving it to a representative of the Collective. The Guild and Confederation seats often agree, but this doesn’t leave the third seat powerless. Aside from extracting valuable concessions as a tiebreaker, she can leverage her influence to sway the others, such as by offering to call off a strike or ameliorate a riot — or threatening to start one.

To reduce the Collective’s influence, Chamber bylaws call for popular election of the third seat every five years from among Collective members, and forbid election from the Collective’s leadership. In practice, a combination of demagoguery, vote buying, intimidation, and vote tampering typically throws victory to a Jaris puppet, a Guild stooge, or some charismatic and popular firebrand.

The Serpents

One concession that the Collective’s representative obtained proved quite popular. Marita now employs official bounty hunters who supplement the private bodyguards, thief-takers, and small mercenary bands that the wealthy employ. While their standard pay is low, they earn bounties from the Nine and the Chamber for every proven criminal they apprehend. Known colloquially as “Serpents,” these bounty hunters help ensure that in all but the poorest neighborhoods, the streets are relatively safe day and night. While muggings, assaults, and the occasional daring daylight kidnapping do occur, Marita is among the Scavenger Lands’ safer cities. However, if someone offers a Serpent more than their normal bounty to frame an innocent or let a criminal escape, most happily accept.

EX3

### Cities Old and New

After the Shogunate’s wars, early post-Contagion chaos, and centuries of scavenging, little remains intact from the numerous settlements predating the Confederation of Rivers. The Old City is instead how residents describe the riverside district constructed in the early decades after the Confederation’s founding. Extending along the riverside, the Old City comprises grand public buildings, row houses for visiting officials, docks, and warehouses.

Marita was built on the site of a small Shogunate mining town, whose most intact remnant — a large circular building near the city’s center not far from the river —is called Confederation Hall. Its first floor serves as a market. The Nine and local government divide the second floor between them; the Confederation controls the third floor. At night, the outer walls shed a dim light inside and out, making the interior as bright as late twilight. The top floor supernaturally maintains a comfortable temperature year-round. The so-called New City encompasses districts constructed in later years and wends its way both

inland and outward along the riverbank. Well-built and well-maintained New City buildings are the exception, not the rule, and the Old City’s regular grid of wide boulevards gives way to winding alleys and narrow streets. Both halves of Marita receive fresh water from public fountains and wells, while underground sewers exit Marita far downriver. Buildings in the New City have flat façades, boxy shapes, and whitewashed walls. Old City structures feature round arches and red stucco roofs; their brown bricks are left unpainted. Marita’s well-known alchemical streetlights, originally introduced in the Old City, remain abundant and well-maintained there. In the New City, they’re notably less common and often dwindle to a faint glimmer before a light-tender adds new reagents. Maritan clothing typically features draped, flowing fabrics, with layered colors and prints. Sandals are common footwear. Men often maintain full, neatly trimmed beards. Many hairstyles incorporate headbands, which range from simple woven cloth to elaborate bands with embroidery and beading.

Meals are served communally, on a large platter set in the center of the table. Participants select their

EX3

portions and eat with their fingers, and share drinks from a common cup. Typical dishes include omelets with salty cheese and greens; cardoons stewed with salted meat; baked trout with lemons and olives; flaky pastry mixed with cheese, honey, and bay leaves; and the pine-infused wine called retsina.

merely a proxy for Lookshy’s interests. But even the Confederation’s most ardent detractors can’t entirely ignore it. Its limitations are clear — it’s solely an advisory body with no means to enforce its directives on member states. But it offers Scavenger Lands peoples a place to work out differences peacefully and build alliances.

The Deep Ways

Furthermore, members have developed unofficial methods to work around its lack of official enforcement. The simplest and least problematic are trade agreements predicated on adherence to Confederation policies — an excellent way for large or wealthy polities to pressure smaller, poorer ones into following Confederation mandates. Moreover, some states agree to exchange hostages, ensuring mutual adherence to a policy that both desire but neither trusts the other to uphold.

An abandoned network of mine shafts — the Deep Ways — extends beneath the city. Ancient phosphorescent paint marks some tunnel walls, glowing as bright as a clear moonlit night; other shafts are entirely lightless. Many shafts have collapsed or filled with water. Visitors can pay a small fee for a brief guided tour of the tunnels immediately around an entrance beneath Confederation Hall. There are no public maps of the Ways beyond that area, nor is there a publicly available list of the dozens of entrances. However, many explorers have drafted private maps; all are partial, and most contain inaccuracies. Some individuals sneak away from tours for private assignations, scavenging, or leaving messages or money at a dead drop. The Deep Ways are popular with thieves, blackmailers, kidnappers, and ne’er-do-wells, and are ideal for secret meetings. Some entrances are inside buildings, allowing the well-informed to bypass guards and observers. The Deep Ways also offer undetectable routes into or out of Marita. However, one tunnel looks much like another, and without a reliable map, getting lost is far too easy. Periodically, people vanish into the Deep Ways; stories tell of vengeful ghosts, predatory spirits, and bizarre monsters lurking in the tunnels.

### The Confederation of Rivers

The Council of the Concordat is the Confederation of Rivers’ governing body and Marita’s raison d’être. It consists of one representative from each participating Scavenger Lands state, from powerful polities such as Lookshy, Calin, Sijan, Great Forks, and Nexus to petty Hundred Kingdoms city-states. Each representative has one vote. They meet in a large, open room on the Confederation Hall’s third floor, seating themselves around a huge circular table. While normally only in session in summer, major powers keep a representative here year-round to deal with conflicts arising between the region’s major powers. Nonmembers may also send nonvoting envoys, though few do; notable exceptions include the Realm and Thorns.

Many Scavenger Lands leaders and Guild officials regard the Confederation as useless; some deem it

Other unofficial, unsanctioned methods can force compliance from any Confederation representative — even Lookshy’s. These include blackmail, bribery, extortion, kidnapping hostages, luring targets into addiction or debt, and theft and ransom of precious or powerful heirlooms. Most such espionage occurs in Marita itself. The Serpents offer little protection from these perils; meddling in Confederation business carries heavy risks for bounty hunters, who’re themselves often on the take from major powers’ representatives.

### Prominent Figures

Jaris Morat, a charismatic man in his early forties, leads the powerful Jaris family and the Dockworkers’ Collective. Friends and enemies alike call him brilliant and ruthless. His bodyguard and lover, the hulking god-blooded warrior Patrit, usually accompanies him. While he ostensibly represents the dockworker community, his proposals and decisions almost always increase his family’s wealth and power. His ambitions climb ever higher — he regularly dines with Confederation representatives from Lookshy and Great Forks.

A natural orator, Anera Din’s fiery, rousing speeches have won him clout and popular support among dockworkers. He envisions a Collective free of Jaris influence and speaks of making Marita’s poorest neighborhoods as safe as its richest. Din is a polarizing figure; the Jaris family are among his most vocal detractors, but he has other opposition, most notably Serpents angered by his proposal to abolish the bounty system, and dockworkers concerned by his more radical statements. His death — should enemies arrange it — might tip the city into a violent uprising. Yet even if he lives, his rhetoric already has his supporters sharpening their knives.

nights. Bright blue moss on nearby rocks glows and crackles when the Wyld’s tides rise, warning residents to flee. Tarpis-Kal’s modest wealth comes from unique gemstones that residents periodically find afterward. Maritan gossips claim that the largest, most beautiful gems only appear after travelers vanish near the bordermarch — either swallowed by the Wyld or stolen by the fae.

### THE CHAMBER OF THREE

The industrious Illis-Ton, the Collective’s representative, was Jaris Morat’s protégé. Once, she almost always voted with his interests in mind, with the Collective’s needs a distant second. Now, she attends Anera Din’s rallies and meets with him privately to discuss policy and ideas. Her votes signal this new allegiance to the people and to the Jaris family. While many believe she’s a follower by nature, her intimates suspect her of higher ambitions.

Achus is a rising young power in the southwestern Hundred Kingdoms. Its new Dragon-Blooded queen, Left Hand Chalima (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 220), was a wandering hero before taking the cloak of office from Achus’ prior tyrant-king. The principality’s people and its ghosts are still adjusting to Chalima’s rule, a situation exacerbated by an Anathema sending followers to stir unrest throughout the city. Though not yet a signatory to the Confederation of Rivers, Achus sends an envoy to Marita for the Concordat’s summer session.

Amilar Lodiro represents the Council of the Concordat. A Lookshyan savant teaching at Marita’s Larkspur Academy, their votes attempt to balance the needs of city, Confederation, and the Seventh Legion. Last year, they weathered a minor scandal wherein Illis-Ton accused them of taking bribes, though the Collective representative could offer no proof. Lodiro meets with the occasional crime boss — largely seeking antiquities of interest to their gens — but argues that their job is to represent all Maritani, even those operating outside the law.

The city of Sanazar, standing at a strategic crossroads near Marita, has been the site of many wars over the ages — most recently the War of Bitter Almonds a century ago, which transformed it into a shadowland. Geomantic efforts to diminish the shadowland have broken it into dwindling pockets, but ghosts and ill specters still arise from it at times. With the Mask’s rise, some in Marita fear that a deathly warlord might emerge from Sanazar’s shadowlands to seize their city in the same way.

Lesha Ebun, an elderly factor, represents the Guild. She’s known for keen political instincts and obsession with bureaucratic details. Despite extensive use of anagathic drugs, she’s nearing retirement, and plans on a less active role in Marita’s Guild council once her term ends. She intends to stay in Marita, where she’s built up significance influence over the antiquities trade; this puts her at odds with Lodiro.

Attar of roses billows around Gentle Sigh of Midnight’s Garden, the Mask of Winters’ nemissary envoy. Gifted with wit, grace, and charm, she’s won over many Maritani who initially shunned her. Lavish galas in her rented palazzo have made her many friends among the city’s elite, from the Nine to the Jarises to numerous Council representatives. Many suspect that she plans to suborn the Council to her master’s cause. Of late, she affects a silver mask covering the right side of her face, which rumor suggests conceals wounds from a failed assassination attempt. Though slipping past her zombie bodyguards in their casques of black iron would be an impressive feat, no one dares come forward and claim responsibility.

### Neighbors

Residents of Tarpis-Kal live in the shadow of a bordermarch a few hours’ walk away. This Wyld zone is particularly active at night, its borders brushing the town’s outermost fields on new moons and Calibration

## The Hundred Kingdoms

On the Scavenger Lands’ eastern edge, the Hundred Kingdoms lie scattered like weeds amid cracked pavement. Dozens of principalities, small states, and petty kingdoms sprout amid the wilderness, their numbers ever-changing. A monarch unites a region only for it to fall into civil war upon her death. One kingdom annexes its neighbor but is itself conquered by a larger power later that year. A city-state empties to flee tyranny, disease, or famine. Even the definition of what constitutes a kingdom varies, from a thriving republic with a capital city and standing army to a bandit queen’s fortress and its handful of surrounding villages. Relations between states change with a harvest’s success or failure, or the turn of a season. Many kingdoms trade peacefully with surrounding peoples and meet with one another’s leaders; others raid for their riches. Smaller communities aid each other in hard times, providing food during famines, lending labor during harvests, or banding together when invaders threaten.

EX3

Not all would-be conquerors succeed. Rebellions rise in rural districts and sweep through republics like wildfire. Cities declare independence from distant rulers. Some territories change hands so frequently, villages within their bounds barely pay attention when soldiers ride in bearing their new ruler’s decrees. Wait a few months and someone else will be in charge. Overall, the Hundred Kingdoms are lightly populated, their principalities strewn across a vast region with varied topography. This rugged terrain currently encompasses four mid-sized polities — mountainous Trimrode, Rake’s deep forests, Spandrel’s chain of lakes, the swampy lands of Mire — and myriad statelets nestled in valleys, moors, heaths, and hills. Ruins, too, sprinkle the area — cities, towns, and villages razed or emptied by war, famine, plague, or other disasters. Mountains hide deposits of precious ore; prospectors follow rumors of jade, hoping to strike it rich. Towns dot the riverbanks, trading with cargo-laden boats and demanding taxes for passage.

### History

Five centuries ago, the Laris and Velen Administrative Districts south of Vaneha represented the eastern Scavenger Lands’ most populous and sophisticated remnants of Shogunate civilization. Disputes over water rights erupted into violent conflicts that destroyed Laris, left Velen in ruins, and broke the political alliance — the League of Many Rivers — that held the region together. Refugees flooded into the lands that would become the Hundred Kingdoms. Some sought safety and shelter; others were intent on seizing power and making war. Many hold their ancestors’ grudges and prejudices to this day, such as the endless cattle raiding between Ganoth and Sweetgrass, or how Yerim’s folk treat their Tairis minority as unclean, unmarriageable, and unfit to work with food or livestock.

When refugees from the south arrived in Jasir, priests of the river-god Lycoth incorporated Jasiri tea ceremonies into their rituals. Elsewhere, the Twelve Gods of Noth forged an uneasy peace with the invading Eritine people’s gods, who built new temples on Noth’s holy sites. Over time, worshipers of both pantheons organized festivals around the gods’ similar purviews, albeit with Noth’s gods holding lesser roles. At harvest time, the faithful bake twelve elaborate dishes to honor the pantheons, rich with meat and spices sacred to the Eritrine gods. A city’s architecture reflects its history. Immigrants, refugees, and conquerors erect buildings in their cultures’ distinct styles. Rare remnants of Shogunate architecture still linger, despite much being dismantled or razed. The palace of Worn has twenty wings, each added by a new vanquisher; at its heart stands the council hall of Suka Whitemane, advisor to the daimyo Karal Musari. Temple architecture reflects broad religious movements — though Five Sisters and Yesta-Saycha are hundreds of miles apart, both boast the distinctive fan vaulting of the short-lived Yesta empire. Music travels with the people; many songs have regional variants, with lyrics changed to name local heroes or verses added to match local events. In Rake, “The Ballad of Alix Brightsword” is an upbeat tune, often performed with an underlying military drum cadence. The people of the Red Rye Towns, whose lands were caught between Brightsword and her forays against the warlord Sneering Jenara, sing it as a dirge. While no single culture spans the Kingdoms, each territory has a strong sense of local pride. Residents in newly founded polities celebrate recent victories and the shared history they build with each passing day. Even citizens in relatively authoritarian principalities feel a sense of ownership: it’s their principality, not to be made an imperial possession or claimed by a foreign state. Most folk don’t have to trace too far back in their lineage to find a famed ancestor who was a refugee, runaway, or rebel.

Cuisine

### Many Cultures

Over the centuries, migrating peoples, refugees seeking safety, mercenary companies looking for employment, traveling merchants, and foreign conquerors intent on imperial expansion have all influenced the Hundred Kingdoms’ ethnic and cultural makeup. Even principalities that share borders can be utterly different in terms of history, aesthetics, customs, and political structures. And as states form and dissolve and displaced people resettle, cultures shift along with them.

The southern Hundred Kingdoms rely heavily on rice. Richer ports use ingredients, cooking methods, and spices from across the Scavenger Lands, especially drawing on Great Forks’ complex cuisine. In addition, most Yellow River polities draw inspiration from Vanehan fare (p. XX), having been dominated and colonized during Vanehan imperial periods. Away from the Yellow River, this cuisine gives way to wheat and barley: soups and stews, porridges that stick

EX3

to the ribs, and light cakes that a worker can carry in her pockets. Bakers use spent grain from wheat and barley beers in dense, chewy breads. But each principality has its own foodstuffs. Spandrel’s lakes provide ample carp, perch, and other fish; Rake’s forests are full of deer and wild boar; Trimrode’s steep landscape features goat and mutton. Many dishes still bear the influence of former Shogunate cuisines, such as roast duck in Kallat and shaved ice in Trimrode’s mountaintop towns. After centuries of intermittent war and famine, not to mention many peoples living in marginal land, people make resources last as long as possible. They use every part of herd and game animals, cooking tougher organs long and slow in stews or mincing them as filling for pies or sausages. Blood pudding, head cheese, and hearty broths are common fare. Pickling preserves vegetables, eggs, and fish; meat is dried and salted. Smaller animals, such as rats, squirrels, and grasshoppers, also provide sustenance.

### Politics

The Seventh Legion wields especial power in the region, centered on Nasaru Redoubt at the Kingdoms’ western border. Principalities hire field force troops for their wars, the Lookshy navy sends occasional patrols through the river system, and rangers scout and patrol throughout the countryside. Meanwhile, far-ranging Lookshyan merchants trade here, and Immaculate Faith missionaries spread their gospel.

Even the far-distant Realm has a tenuous presence here. The satrapy of Greyfalls sits spiderlike on the Hundred Kingdoms’ eastern border. An ever-present but historically quiescent military threat, it commands the western terminus of the fabulous Golden Road trade route to Ixcoatli. It also serves as a local mission for Immaculate Order monks, who proselytize in great cities and remote villages alike and organize Wyld Hunts. Merchants — most of the major ones Guild-affiliated — sail river routes, lead caravans, and entreat local factors for capital. The largest principalities send envoys to Marita for the Confederation of Rivers.

### Military

While larger states maintain standing armies, most of the Hundred Kingdoms are too small to host a dedicated military force. Rulers may have a small house guard, but mustering an army means calling farmers from their fields. This makes the region a tempting prize for foreign powers. When armies march, banditry

### LEGITIMACY

While a few modern statelets claim descent from Dragon-Blooded shoguns and daimyos, many assert their right to rule from ancient kings and queens, folk heroes, spirits and ancestors, or a god’s Chosen. A popular champion often finds leadership thrust upon her after overthrowing a petty tyrant, whether she desires a crown or not.

threatens trade, or nightmares boil out of the Wyld, several kingdoms must band together, forming a united front or even electing one ruler as a temporary dictator for the duration.

But all too often, the Hundred Kingdoms fail to unite or to defend their borders. Several times in their history, some power has swept across the land and subjugated its people. Vaneha once annexed the region, and — with Lookshy and the Concordat distracted by other matters — currently prepares to reclaim it. But keeping control of dozens of far-flung statelets has always challenged conquerors. The region’s inhabitants know the terrain better than foreign soldiers and use guerilla tactics to stymie invading troops. The cost of stifling rebellions in remote areas quickly adds up; many a would-be empress has strained her garrisons and drained her coffers bringing the Hundred Kingdoms to heel.

### Home to Heroes

Opportunities abound for brave adventurers traveling the Hundred Kingdoms. Great cats, ox-dragons, cockatrices, flickerfeathers, and other dangerous creatures call these provinces their hunting grounds. Stranger things crawl from shadowlands and bordermarches at civilization’s edge. Villages offer rewards for any hero who can save them from a monster’s hunger — whether perpetual hospitality, rulership, or guidance to perilous ancient ruins where treasure may yet lie. Other monsters are human — whether mortal, GodBlooded, or Exalted. Bandits harry a town, carting off winter stores and leaving residents to starve. Slavers steal entire families from their homes to be sold in faroff lands. Tyrants live in luxury while their subjects suffer, and none dare stand up to them for fear of retribution. Intelligent spirits exhibit such human vices as greed, cruelty, and ambition.

Heroism is subjective, especially among the Exalted. Are the Dragon-Blooded justified in their Wyld Hunt,

EX3

ridding the region of an Anathema threat? Or are they invaders, leaving destruction in their wake as they murder a beloved local hero? Is the Lunar-controlled town a lurking danger for its neighbors, or does the Silver Pact offer protection from outside threats — which brings its own, different kind of trouble? One village’s hero can be another’s monster.

### ADDITIONAL HUNDRED

### KINGDOMS LOCALES

Located beside a bordermarch where ancient menhirs hatch monsters, Hinet’s warriors spend much of their year guarding against Wyld incursions. Its aging queen is determined to perform one last great deed before she abdicates her throne.

### A Sample Principality: Rake

In Belor, a commune of ascetics high in the northern mountains, the senior monk disappeared weeks ago. Some of his brethren believe he’s conferring with their god at an isolated mountaintop shrine. Others suspect foul play.

The tree-girt principality of Rake is among the Hundred Kingdoms’ largest states. Its ruling family claims descent from Alix Brightsword, a hero of the wars against the Realm. The current monarch, Queen Lapis (Adversaries of the Righteous, p. 24), is an energetic, domineering ruler in middle age, with an eye for loyalty and talent. She’s loved for her forthrightness and battlefield leadership, admired for her wit and tenacity, and feared for her volatile temper.

Drowned Ibano’s houses perch on stilts above the flood plain, whose waters keep rising with tears from an elemental’s grief. Farmers unable to tend sunken fields now raid their neighbors and demand exorbitant tariffs on passing boats.

Rake’s eponymous capital sits at a nexus of trade roads, and its settlements — both native and annexed — lie strewn among the surrounding forest. Furnishings and treasure boxes carved from Rake’s ancient oaks are prized beyond the Scavenger Lands.

A clutch of strix harries the village of Coalwood. What should be a simple hunt becomes a much deadlier game when the characters discover the bandit-thaumaturgist who’s learned a trick to control the vicious birds.

The republic of Gait’s rocky hillside vineyards produce wines that induce prophetic dreams. Its vintners attribute this quality to a battle in which a thousand raksha were slain after the Contagion, whose blood they say lingers in the soil.

From the simplest village homes to elaborate temples and palaces, Rake’s architecture takes advantage of the abundant lumber. Flexible frames, projecting roofs, and easily replaceable components allow buildings to survive storms and occasional earthquakes. Builders emphasize their materials’ natural beauty and design structures to complement the surrounding landscape. While the principality is a few hundred years old, the Brightsword family has only held it for about a century. Queen Lapis’s great-grandfather conquered the domain, and power has remained with his line. In that time, through conquest, strategic alliances, marriages, and treachery, the principality has grown — despite some reverses, most notably under Lapis’ uncle Jaspar — into one of the largest in the Hundred Kingdoms. Much of this growth occurred under Queen Lapis’s rule through careful planning and daring assaults. She wishes to increase her own power, wealth, and glory, and counts Rake’s prosperity as part of that success. For now, this works in her subjects’ favor, keeping them fed and increasing foreign trade. Though she intends to pass the throne to her three children, it’s her vassals’ personal loyalty to her — most are her friends and allies, their posts not hereditary — that keeps Rake stable amid rapid expansion. Without her, the burgeoning nation might easily descend into civil war.

The tiny kingdom of Shale was recently usurped by the bandit-queen Inedra and her six rogues. Two of the six are the ghosts of her most loyal companions. Inedra struggles to maintain control over both a rebellious populace and the newfound arrogance of her wild, unruly gang.

Queen Lapis cultivates alliances with Trimrode, Spandrel, and Mire. She’s rightfully wary of land-hungry Vaneha south of the Hundred Kingdoms, and drafts strategy after strategy to turn them back when — not if — they invade. Rake’s neighbors eye the principality warily, watching for signs that they’re Lapis’s next target.

Prominent Figures in Rake

Datei ma Nalat — Lapis’s husband — knows where the bodies are buried, and arranged the interment of many of them himself. A minor Vanehan aristocrat adept in social graces, Nalat’s blackmailed feuding families into strategic marriages to expand Rake’s influence. He quietly sabotages popular figures whose rise threatens

EX3

Lapis’s rule, seeding rumors of disgraceful behavior and planting evidence of treason — even targeting Lapis’s own niece, Kelem. He favors his youngest daughter, Druse, for the throne.

Lapis’s eldest daughter Emeri, a brilliant strategist and a popular general, works tirelessly to protect and expand Rake’s borders. Raised with poems of Alix Brightsword and her own mother ringing in her ears, she intends to not only match her forebears’ valorous achievements, but to surpass them. Emeri knows she has her mother’s favor for the throne; this causes friction with her younger siblings. The middle son, Spar, knows he’s neither of his parents’ favorites — a truth that chafes him. Determined to prove he’s good enough to take the throne, he presents the image of a dutiful son, skillfully performing administrative and diplomatic tasks and attending meetings in Lapis’s name. Talkative and personable, Spar hosts small salons for Rake’s luminaries and visiting dignitaries. He genuinely enjoys socializing, although these events also help him establish relationships and contacts outside of his parents’ influence — some of whom have both the power and the desire to back his ambitions.

Lapis’s youngest child, Druse, charms courtiers and heaps praise upon her siblings. Her philanthropy popularizes her among Rake’s commoners; her poignant poems bring tears to courtiers’ eyes. Many deem her soft-hearted, and thus overlook her potential. This frustrates her, but for now she lets it lie. When not handing out alms or composing sonnets, she studies Rake’s ledgers and meets with its exchequers. Inheriting the throne as she plans will require uncovering which magnates’ debts make them most vulnerable to bribes.

### A Sample Republic: Theris

The republic of Theris follows the slow, lazy turns of the Yellow River. Along the banks, thatch-roofed homes sit on posts above the water. Small fishing boats row alongside traders’ vessels, with citizen-merchants calling up offerings of fresh-caught bream or smoked sturgeon for sale.

Theris’s eponymous capital and its docks line the northern riverbank. Wealthy merchants build elaborate homes on the hills above. Their southern façades feature expansive verandas, giving owners a vantage of vessels sailing up- and downriver, and of the rice fields beyond.

Shrines to river and commerce spirits nestle between teahouses and shops; constructed in a cacophony of styles, their bright-hued awnings attract passersby. Theris’s people add altars for each new ruler’s deities and assimilate them into the city’s festivals and rites, from Vaneha’s militant gods to Henbane’s harvest-ancestors. Legend says that when the conquering mercenary-prince Barent of Nathir sent his priests to destroy the shrines, the Yellow River rose with the spurned spirits’ wrath, drowning the priests while leaving citizens unharmed. Goods passing through Theris include lumber from Rake, furs from Trimrode, and strange wonders that Luz’s hunters bring back from forays into the bordermarches. Crafters’ apprentices keep watch for certain traders’ ships and crowd the docks when they arrive, attempting to get the jump on the choicest materials for their employers.

Theris’s steady commerce makes it a potential jewel in any monarch’s crown. Over the centuries, queens, tyrants, bandit kings and mercenary generals have taken turns ruling it and raking in its wealth. Dockworkers’ rebellions have left the piers slippery with blood, reddening the Yellow River’s muddy waters. The latest revolution formed an independent Theris whose citizens elect officials from among the people. Despite Theris’s bustling trade and local business, its coffers border on empty. Twenty years ago, facing the weakness of the republic’s tiny, ill-trained army, the newly appointed council voted to hire the Nexus-based Sisters of the Turning Wheel to dissuade invasion from neighboring polities. Representatives arrived swiftly amid mercenary escort, offering troops, supplies, and plans to improve Theris’s fortifications. The council — urged on by Councilman Jodaro, a grain merchant deep in the Sisters’ pockets — signed contract after contract. While the deal initially seemed reasonable, the Sisters demand more every year, their agents pointing to obscure clauses supporting their claims. Thus far, Theris’s council has capitulated; if they refuse, the Sisters will withdraw military support and the vultures will swoop in. Today, the council is split between those who’d escape the bargain, renegotiate it, pay it by raising taxes on non-Guild entities, or let things lie because they’re on the take from the Sisters. Councilwoman Asakima, a merchant turned politician, quietly seeks outside aid to untangle the mess without losing Theris in the process. Rising river tolls anger merchants and boat captains alike; they’ve complained to the Concordat Council in

Then address supernatural elements players might encounter. Some are people — whether human, such as the Exalted, sorcerers, and thaumaturges; or inhuman, such as spirits, monsters, and Fair Folk. Supernatural places include manses, demesnes, ancient ruins, shadowlands, or bordermarches. ### SUPPLEMENTAL TOOLS

Feel free to draw upon other roleplaying games for bespoke setting-design tools. Noteworthy examples include Ben Robbins’ Microscope for cooperative location design with your players, fleshing out a principality’s history; Sine Nomine’s Sixteen Sorrows: A Handbook of Calamities for randomizers aimed at detailing specific encounters and scenarios; and Everway, whose Vision Deck system provides visual inspiration for designing locales, characters, and situations.

Consider the local political structure. Has the same family ruled for several generations, or is a newly elected council struggling to undo the mess an ousted prince left behind? Perhaps it’s too small to have a formal government — to whom do people look to manage crises, settle disputes, and offer counsel?

Name some notable figures in and around the locale who player characters might encounter, such as

Creating Hundred

Kingdoms Locales

When creating a locale, consider its location in the Hundred Kingdoms and how the surrounding terrain might influence its advantages, disadvantages, and opportunities. Does it benefit from river trade? Is it halfway up a mountain, making it defensible but hard to supply? Does the terrain favor farming, herding, mining, or fishing? Is it accessible and on a trade route, or remote and elusive? What resources are plentiful? Which scarce commodities cause disputes with neighboring states? Determine your locale’s history. The Hundred Kingdoms are everchanging; few statelets can claim to have been founded before Laris and Velen fell, and with regionwide invasions and unifications, no state’s governance has gone unbroken. When did the polity originally form? From whom do its peoples and cultures primarily descend — autochthonous Contagion survivors; refugees from the Laris-Velen war, Bagrash Köl’s collapsing empire, the Northeast’s Second Contagion, or other disasters; colonists from such invaders as Vaneha or the long-ago Songrider people; or other sources? How have annexation and occupation changed its cultures?

Consider cultural elements that make this locale feel real, including art, architecture, literary traditions, music, and religion. What luxurious dishes appear on noble tables, and what do street food vendors sell? What are some local traditions: religious celebrations, feast days, superstitions? An Exalted location is often inspired by multiple real-world historical eras and settings.

### MORE HUNDRED KINGDOMS LOCALES

The royal palace of Crick was built with bricks salvaged from a First Age ruin, wreaking geomantic havoc only reversible by those brave enough to find the palace’s heart and destroy the misshapen hearthstone forming there. Rooms shift throughout the palace; the walls seep with untamed magic. The sorcerer-queen Lihala cursed the city of Nyskel to eternal silence. Its citizens seek champions to help lift her curse. The more the player characters investigate, the less certain they become that Lihala is the real villain.

The principality of Kinit hosts a tournament in its new prince’s honor. Riches await the victors at week’s end. While the champions compete, player characters uncover a conspiracy to murder the new prince, orchestrated by his predecessor’s loyalists and by merchants suffering under his trade policies. The township of Oldport — impoverished since the Lesser Rock River’s course shifted, leaving its wharves silted and dry — calls out for heroes to deliver them. The Black Arrow bandit gang, granted uncanny powers by their raiton-god patron Zeref, steal what little the people have.

The court sorcerers of the warring kingdoms of Aislar and Argoseen summon demons to attack one another. The people live in terror of the next onslaught, and pleas to their fearful princes to cease hostilities have gone unacknowledged. They entreat the characters for protection.

princes, council members, unhappy officials, dynamic merchants, local champions, meddlesome clan elders, and petty crime lords. What are their roles here, and what agendas are they advancing? How might they view player characters as means to those ends? Determine the short- and long-term goals of the locale’s primary actors. These include both the people’s immediate needs and the rulers’ ambitions. These needn’t be related — while the people want to kill the ox-dragon attacking outlying orchards, their prince concentrates on conquering their northern neighbor. Aims can conflict: a tyrant seeks to secure his reign, while his oppressed people pray a champion will depose him. Define the locale’s most relevant neighbors. Which ones, if any, offer aid in times of need? Are any alliances on shaky ground? What issues might threaten the peace? Which neighbors await signs of weakness that signal an opportunity to attack? What old grudges do each side nurse? Have neighbors raided or annexed one another in the past? How frequently do skirmishes occur today?

## Vaneha

The Yellow and Maruto rivers cradle the nation of Vaneha between them. Its settlements spread throughout the mountainous terrain, built beside upland lakes or thriving in deep valleys’ fertile farmlands. The sacred mountain Ama-ni-Traya rises close by the capital of Jibei, where troops drill beneath blossoming trees. Far to the east, the Great Palisade spans Vaneha’s land border, rebuffing outsiders and discouraging defection. Vaneha’s princes — whether discontent with their borders or obliged to reclaim provinces lost long ago — have long looked outward, sending spies and scouts to learn neighbors’ weaknesses and destabilize their regimes. Some merely sought to reclaim old imperial holdings now lost; others weighed which nearby principalities were ripe to raid or annex. On multiple occasions, the Vanehan army marched upon the Hundred Kingdoms, with the Sword Prince eventually riding victorious through her new domain. Even in times when military defeat, rebellion, civil war, or weak Sword Princes have shrunk Vaneha’s borders back to their lands between the rivers, its rulers have dreamed of empire. Today, Sword Prince Gensuji dreams that same dream.

### Clans

Where migrations and invasions have thrown the Hundred Kingdoms into tumult, the clans that

comprise Vaneha seem much as they were centuries ago. A few have dwindled to a handful of living scions, while political marriages merged others; nevertheless, most trace their lineage back to the princes who ruled before Vaneha’s founding, and maintain libraries filled with illuminated manuscripts describing their ancestors’ heroic deeds. Wars between clans once ravaged the land, but today’s Sword Prince frowns on unnecessary bloodshed. Those who can’t settle disputes via diplomatic means resort to undermining one another politically or economically.

Each clan’s families preside over estates in its ancestral region of Vaneha, its ruling family governing the rest in the Sword Prince’s name. Clans are responsible for their region’s prosperity and enforcing Sword Prince Gensuji’s decrees. Though some chafe at his taxes and corvée demands, concern for family members Gensuji holds as hostage-guests in the capital keeps them compliant. All Vanehans native to a region, no matter their social class, belong to that region’s ruling clan. Those who permanently move to a new region, whether for business or marriage, now belong to that new region’s clan. In practice it takes months or years to feel accepted within their new community.

The clan chief parcels land grants out to favored relatives — usually cousins or members of a cadet branch — for a yearly price, paid in rent or military service. These jitō in turn rent land to tenant farmers and other workers, collecting profits to pay the lease. Most Vanehan commoners are such tenants; they farm, herd, mine, and create textiles and other goods for export. A family’s status as jitō may be inherited for generations, but the clan chief retains the right to recall and redistribute the land grant. It’s not unusual for commoners to trace descent from jitō. Additionally, commoners who marry into larger families or provide exemplary service may someday be named jitō themselves.

Noteworthy Clans

Ancient and respected, Clan Iachi rules the rolling hills of Orm. Its vineyards’ wines are sought after throughout the East. Rumors suggest the clan leader, Tesero, has sent a shipment of his most exquisite vintage to the leaders of the Grass Spiders.

In the city of Noru, where anvils ring day and night, Clan Uema steps up production of weapons and armor for Sword Prince Gensuji’s impending march on the Hundred Kingdoms. The clan’s eldest daughter, the warrior-poet Sen, resides in Jibei as one of the Sword Prince’s “honored guests.”
