Although Clan Datei no longer has holdings in Vaneha, it’s far from extinct. Most other clans employ Datei spies and assassins to further their ambitions, with the notable exception of Clan Iachi. The feud between the two stretches back centuries and is the topic of many Vanehan epics.

### Cities

Stories tell of the breathtaking beauty of Vaneha’s cities. Tiao sits high in the mountains, its hot springs a draw for weary travelers. Clan Atsei’s famed gardens bloom year-round in lakeside Osai. Heavenly voices fill

### CUISINE

Rooted in rice, Vanehan cuisine also leans heavily on rice wine, vinegar, fowl, beans, onions, salt, mustard, and herbs. Common folk make do with soups, stews, baked root vegetables, pickles, and foraged wild greens and nuts. Noble clans and rich merchants feast on honeyed rice breads, red meat, and various imported fruits and spices. River fish is particularly prized, especially eaten raw.

the amphitheater at the cosmopolitan port of Isgari, the choir’s songs echoing off frescoed ceilings. But most say that the most beautiful city in Vaneha, eclipsing all others, is its capital Jibei. The sacred mountain Ama-ni-Traya dominates the horizon; Vanehans consider it the center of the world, and it’s only fitting their capital sits nearby. Streets lined with cherry trees wend uphill toward the Sword Prince’s dragon-backed manse, which overlooks the city. Each clan maintains a manor here, their grounds adorned with tranquil gardens and shrines to the clan’s gods, such as the orchard spirit Jieke Blooms-in-Winter whom Clan Iachi venerates; and Clan Uema’s patron, the forge-god Megemi Ironhilt.

Below these heights, Jibei teems with activity: merchants hawking wares, generals drilling troops, and artisans churning out cloisonné jewelry, armaments, and military provisions. From the clan manors’ balconies, this frenetic enterprise has a beauty to it. Jibei’s artisans built eye-pleasing symmetry into even the city’s poorest parts — which, some say, allows the clan heads and the Sword Prince to ignore what they cannot see.

The small river port of Ramblewater stands beside the Maruto River, on the Vanehan side of the Great Palisade. Here, goods flow in from the Scantling Territories, Nechara, and other upriver sources. Dockmasters thoroughly inspect arriving ships, whose sails are removed until the vessel passes muster. Officials confiscate weapons and other contraband materials. Many of Ramblewater’s residents are themselves beastfolk of various sorts — ill-regarded and discriminated against by some, but Vanehan citizens nonetheless.

Sword Prince Gensuji

The Imperial Daiklave gives Jibei its nickname: the City of the Sword. This ancient artifact confirms Sword Prince Gensuji as Vaneha’s rightful leader and upholds his reign. Though Gensuji isn’t Exalted, he wields the Imperial Daiklave in battle. This, many believe, proves his divine right to rule and lead Vaneha to glory. But most of his power comes from the company he keeps. Each clan sends members of its ruling family to the capital as the Sword Prince’s guests. Though he houses them in lavish mansions and provides for all their needs, they’re still hostages. Should a clan displease him, Gensuji punishes these captive scions. Like many of his predecessors, Sword Prince Gensuji aims to rule the Hundred Kingdoms. He’s summoned warriors and weaponsmiths to Jibei to prepare for the campaign. Courtyards ring with the sounds of soldiers drilling. Forges blaze day and night as blacksmiths craft arrowheads and spearpoints from mountain iron, and aristocrats’ blades from sacred metals mined beneath Agate Lake. Spies dispatched months ago to key Hundred Kingdoms states send reports on enemy defenses and numbers. Saboteurs study roads, rivers, and bridges; assassins sharpen their knives. Gensuji rewards those who help the war effort. Rumor suggests he’s sent several expeditions into the territory once held by Laris and Velen to retrieve weapons

### THE SWORD OR THE MAN?

Can Gensuji wield the Imperial Daiklave because something’s special about him, or does its magic respond to an un-Exalted master? We’ve left the answer — and the daiklave’s potential Evocations — intentionally open for Storytellers to tailor it to their game. Perhaps Gensuji is God-Blooded and the sword acknowledges an echo of that deity in him, or his furious ambition resonates with the blade. How does it aid him on the battlefield? What legendary feats did his ancestors perform with it in their grasp?

or other useful tools that linger in First Age ruins. He craves any advantage that will serve his ambitions of conquest.

The Great Palisade

Hundreds of miles long, this wall of sharpened tree trunks winds along Vaneha’s eastern border. It serves as a deterrent to incursions from foreign peoples who’ve historically raided Vaneha during its weaker periods. It also keeps serfs and slaves from escaping into the forest, offers a nonlethal outlet for punishment, and maintains a labor pool that can be drawn upon for other civic projects. A series of fortified towns spans the Palisade. These serve as watchtowers, gatehouses, and trading posts, allowing Vanehan troops to freely pass and admitting licensed foreign traders on market days. A pair of small port cities — Aravesu on the Yellow River and Ramblewater on the Maruto — anchor the Palisade’s ends. Each maintains a naval squadron and siege engines to guard the river, while admitting brown-water merchant ships.

### Neighbors

A key regional port, the wealthy city-state of Nathir stands where the Maruto River joins the Yellow, bordering Vaneha by land. Its riverbanks are dotted with shrines to the many water elementals who make the confluence their home; augurs study the changing patterns where the waters meet to advise merchants and politicians on forthcoming ventures. Some say the elementals’ presence also enriches the beers for which the city’s breweries are rightly famous, and which fuel revelry at weeks-long seasonal trade fairs. Nathir has sometimes been able to maintain independence via mercenaries, military contracts with Lookshy, alliances with neighbors, Guild support, and a handful of local sorcerers and occultists, the latter largely affiliated with the demonologists’ lodge called the House of Thirty Seals. But Nathir — its people largely ethnically Vanehan — has been subjugated by Vaneha before, and is currently under siege by a Vanehan army. East of the Great Palisade lie the Scantling Territories, held by a mix of beastfolk clans and Vanehan refugees who fled oppression, plague, famine, or labor assignments on the Palisade itself to make a life free of Vanehan rule. These include beastfolk peoples such as the vulture-headed soldiers of Lot and the arboreal Hetaki grass-lizard folk, alongside nonbeastfolk peoples such as the mercenary Bijun princedoms. Settled

agriculturalists and nomadic hunter-gatherers alike

trade with their neighbors for food, arms, tools, and

other goods — or raid for them when opportunity arises. They’d happily set their sights on nearby Vanehan towns if not for the Palisade and the threat of violent

retribution from Vanehan troops.

The Pox Plains, also known as Dead Laris, sprawls

west of the Sandy River. This province suffered the

brunt of the long-ago Laris-Velen War; its enemies unleashed several First Age terror weapons upon it, while

its defenders deployed occult defenses that linger unrevoked. Today, hungry ghosts and corroded war-automata haunt ruined cities; toxic meadows and groves pockmark the grasslands with dull bluish-grays and

ferocious reds; Fair Folk princes and fae beasts emerge

from twisted middlemarches to hunt. Wildlife — including enormous herbivores and terrifying apex predators — has returned to the land, but only a handful of tenacious nomadic bands, small settlements, and scavenger troupes dare the region’s perils.

EX3

Pureq Suway woke with a gasp. The thin mountain air left her mouth dry, and a dull throb had settled behind her eyes. She rolled to her side and stood, favoring her swollen left arm. The sun hadn’t yet risen and it was cold in the pilgrim’s recess, but colder still outside on the winding road. Fog rushed from her breath as she stepped out of the rock-cut shelter to look ahead.

There were only three of them left.

The river was swollen with rain — the ford would hold — just a few more strides and they would be across — shouting in the murk — a wrenching crunch as timbers splintered — a log shot down the waterway like god’s spear — screaming silenced by a liquid rush and then nothing —

Other pilgrims began to trickle from their shelters as she ducked back inside. “Come on, we should get moving.”

“Pureq, look. Mama’s not doing well.”

Cunac was on the brink of tears. He clutched his knees, gesturing to the old woman struggling to breathe on the rocky floor. Mama Chanka was the one who gazed into a volcanic glass mirror and told the future, who could prepare the torch cactus into an ointment that grants visions, and who had insisted that she make the pilgrimage herself this year, despite her great age.

They shouldn’t have stopped in the open, that night a month ago — half their number perished at the river — they should have pressed on into the mountains — rattling bones woke them — a hungry ghost slashed her arm — the poison worked so fast — a friend saved her, pulled her to the safety of a thicket — then the ghosts took her away —

“We’ll wait! We’ll get help!”

Cunac was flagging down pilgrims as they passed, asking desperate questions through his tears. But they were all highlanders, and spoke the tongue of the mountains. They couldn’t understand a crying boy from the distant jungle.

“I don’t have the time,” Mama Chanka said, her voice hollow with pain. “I knew what I was getting into, babú. Who’s the one who sees the future, me or you?” The wise woman smiled and reached up to pat Pureq’s cheek. “Go. The holy city waits. I’ve seen it enough times in my life.”

After the attack it was just the three of them — running scared until, a week later, they reached the safety of the high mountain roads, the comfort of other pilgrims walking with them — now Mama was fading — they would stop early for the night, and it would all be better come morning — “You heard what she said. Let’s go.”

Cunac cried softly, a pitiful little sound over Mama’s last breaths. The two of them walked for hours as the sky brightened. The crush of other pilgrims around them was a comfort to the sorrow in Pureq’s heart. Until, like a dream opening before her, Quiverch rose beyond a final bend in the path. Thunderheads ringed the sky above the highest temple, rushing in from all directions to where it perched like a condor at the city’s heart. Sunlight glistened gold on the lake’s calm waters. Tapestries in red and yellow and green fluttered on the walls, and a great shout rang out, a prayer to the lady of torments who guides the wind. A parade was starting at the gates.

“Is that where we’re going?” Cunac whispered, but his companion did not hear. The storm broke, peals of thunder singing praises to the holy city and its lightning-drenched queen. Pureq fell to her knees as the rain flooded down. It was a sacrament to her, there on the road, as one who once knew sorrow but did no longer.

# Chapter Four: The Far East

Chapter Four

The Far East

East of the Scavenger Lands, open terrain gives way to thousands of miles of forest. Mountain ranges, wooded ridges, steep valleys, lakes, and wetlands all serve to break up this seemingly endless expanse. The entire region throngs with diverse flora and fauna. To this day, the Far East remains among the least penetrable territories of Creation for foreign travelers, merchants, adventurers, and would-be conquerors. Numerous peoples dwell in this seemingly trackless realm, while ancient ruins remain lost and undiscovered by scavenger lords. Primeval spirits and monsters rove alongside all manner of mundane beasts. Even the region’s few petty empires have limited knowledge of and access to the neighbors beyond their borders. The deepest reaches of the Far East contain strange vegetation unknown elsewhere in Creation. Interspersed among conventional forests of oak or pine, travelers encounter woodlands comprised of calamites, lepidodendrons, and other unfamiliar plants. Great herbivorous reptiles like pestletails and siege lizards thrive in these peculiar forests; these are preyed on in turn by tyrant lizards and other monstrous apex predators. Far Eastern weather tends to be mild and temperate year-round, with warm summers and cool winters that rarely bring snow. Occasional storms sweep in from the Fang Lakes, Inland Sea, or Dreaming Sea, depending on the time of year.

## Nechara

A city of monumental palaces, bustling markets, and sprawling slums, Nechara draws its economic lifeblood from shipping along the Maruto River and the interwoven thoroughfares of the Great Southeastern Way. Ruled by its owl-eyed prince, this gateway to the Far East is a metropolis of rival God-Blooded noble houses, matchmakers between gods and aristocrats, competing merchants, foreign missionaries, and fortune-seekers from across Creation.

### History

During the late Dragon-Blooded Shogunate, the riverside town Nan-Char of the Nine Thousand Temples — known for its splendid bridge across the Maruto — attracted gods unhappy with their place in the celestial order and pilgrims seeking divine aid and blessings. Later, amid the Great Contagion, several God-Blooded heroes gathered survivors to Nan-Char, tending the sick and protecting them from fae marauders, hungry dead, and rival survivor bands.

Over the years, these culture heroes — such as Brin the Unscarred, Hipol Talespinner, and the peacemaker Aren Las — intermarried with one another, other GodBlooded, Nan-Char’s gods, and other spirits. Together they founded a new city: Nechara. They divided the surrounding lands into fourteen provinces ruled by as many God-Blooded noble houses, who sought further divine nuptials to strengthen their descendants’ supernatural gifts. Located at the eastern fringe of the Velen Administrative District, Nechara was spared the worst of the LarisVelen war. But while its wealth and strategic location make it a target for raids and invasions, it’s rarely submitted to conquerors and always regained its independence.

Rise of a New Dynasty

Nechara’s rulership has fluctuated over time, ranging from a council of noble house leaders to an unrestrained autocrat. Since the Fair Folk invasion over two centuries ago, the balance has leaned toward a dominant prince, though the houses still push for power at the prince’s expense. Intrigues, coups, and countercoups checker the city’s recent history. Half a century ago, Tirgan, final prince of the Peacock Feathers dynasty, grew deeply unpopular among aristocrats and the populace. Inconstant and vindictive, he changed laws to suit his whims — even granting controversial new rights to Immaculates. Seeing an opportunity, Guren — head of the House of Cerulean Stars and

EX3

leader of Tirgan’s personal guard — toppled his master and former friend in a military uprising, ending the dynasty and stripping its survivors of titles and estates. Then the house heads held an election among their ranks; Guren’s personal charisma, alliances, prestige, and military strength earned him the princedom. Nechara’s neighbors sought to seize the city from its untested new prince. The houses were slow to gift troops to Guren’s army, hoping to force greater concessions from him. But Guren’s house had ties to mighty Ula-Erva, Owl-Queen of the East, who agreed to provide aid in exchange for greater power and prominence in the city. Her owl army helped Guren drive off the foreign powers; her battlefield prowess drew numerous worshipers. She became his spirit-spouse (p. XX), joining her occult power to his lineage. But her sudden rise drew resentment from other Necharan gods and caused friction with houses allied with those gods, causing political troubles for Guren.

Upon Guren’s death, his only surviving heir, Shule, inherited the throne — and with it, the other houses’ enmity. With his mother Ula-Erva vigilant against external threats, Shule turns his attention towards consolidating authority over Nechara, securing his position so that he and his heirs can enjoy their wealth and power.

The prince holds multiple noble titles from ancient lineages, such as Protector of the Maruto River and Lord of the Seven Gates. While he lives, they’re united in his bloodline. Should he die without issue, those titles revert to other houses, potentially splitting the central rule of Nechara among multiple claimants.

### Modern Nechara

Nechara sprawls in all directions. Carefully planned street grids or radial avenues — rebuilt by civic-minded princes after devastating fires or floods — alternate with twisting mazes of unplanned alleys, all thronging with shopkeepers, artisans, service workers, manual laborers, and rogues. Bazaars and caravanserais bustle with merchants from across Creation. The sounds of pack beasts and hawkers never stop; there’s always a bazaar open, day or night.

Enormous ziggurats loom above the city, their heights supporting temples and mansions. Below them, minarets rise above townhouses’ sloped and gabled roofs. Wealthy neighborhoods’ roads are lined with magnificent gardens, redolent with flowers from across Creation. Limestone stelae decorate civic buildings

### SHELTER FROM THE STORMS

Heavy rains occasionally flood the Maruto River, turning Nechara’s streets into rushing tributaries. Across the city, ziggurats keep temples and noble estates above the floodwaters. They also serve as evacuation sites, offering shelter to all Necharans in need until the waters recede. Several noble families have courted gods of rain and river, making extensive flooding rare but not unheard of.

and public plazas, depicting deeds of gods and princes throughout Nechara’s history. The city’s walls stand tall and proud, defying those who’d claim its wealth for themselves.

In poorer neighborhoods, tents and oven-baked brick houses weave along chaotic streets. Foreigners unfamiliar with these labyrinthine layouts easily become lost upon straying from the paved boulevards that run from the gates through the city’s center, looping around the prince’s towering Manzu-Lah Ziggurat.

### Aristocracy

Traditionally, power in Nechara rests with house heads, called timariots. Each timariot negotiates for their own family in commercial matters, maintains a house guard, and holds jurisdiction over the house’s lands. The countryside around Nechara is divided into ancient provinces, called timars, partitioned among the noble houses. The number of timars, and thus the number of noble houses, has remained fixed at 14 for centuries. Should a house fall, the other houses’ timariots elevate another family — typically a cadet branch from another house — to oversee the timar.

In theory, upon the prince’s death, the houses could refuse to ratify a new prince and restore the old capital council — a prospect that simmers beneath the surface of Necharan politics. Many nobles prefer the current system, whether from ambition for their house to seize the princedom, profit from personal association with the prince, or belief in autocracy’s dynamism and efficacy. Others hope for greater autonomy by undermining a prince’s authority or restoring the council. To fund public works projects, increase the army’s size, or pursue other costly undertakings, the prince requests gifts from the houses. Timariots graciously comply when it suits them. Such support may include currency and treasure; raw materials such as masonry,

lumber, iron, and bronze; builders, gardeners, and other laborers; foodstuffs for said laborers; or architects to plan new temples and artists to decorate them. Each house decides how many soldiers to contribute, based on their ambitions or whether they support the current military campaign.

Houses expect concessions in return, whether favorable trade deals, coveted land grants, politically advantageous marriages, or that specific laws be changed or repealed. When a house refuses the prince, he may continue negotiations or turn to a different house. A weak prince finds himself groveling powerless before the houses; a clever prince plays them against one another;

a charismatic prince draws them into her orbit; a strong or ruthless prince makes them fear her personal guard or her blades in the dark.

Like his father, Shule pursues centralized authority at the houses’ expense. He’s introduced reforms broadening his jurisdiction to levy troops and negotiate with foreign powers. Where his father offered the nobles boons to keep their loyalty, Shule woos gods, artisans, and the populace with grand public works. He’s sent diplomats to cities along the Great Southeastern Way, expanding trade partnerships to attract more wealth to Nechara. While many timariots bristle as the prince reduces their traditional roles or undercuts their

EX3

traditional commercial relationships, enough support him and the wealth he brings to prevent a coup like that which Guren led — at least thus far.

Prominent Noble Houses

Nechara’s noble houses employ matchmakers who arrange marriages with gods, spirits, Fair Folk, and other supernatural entities, introducing some of their powers and abilities into their descendants. Some of the more noteworthy houses include:

Prince Shule’s house, the House of Cerulean Stars, is neither the most populous nor the oldest. The Cerulean Stars rose to prominence through feats in battle and were renowned for tactical acumen. Tracing their ancestry to the Eastern forests, they send matchmakers to their ancient, ruined homeland to seek nature gods and elementals. Shule officially serves as timariot, though his great-aunt Junal fulfills most of that role’s practical responsibilities.

The traditionalist House of the Black Shell traces its roots back to the first refugee families. The many princes in their family tree last ruled generations ago. They long ago established ties with local divinities such as Etanu of the Arch, Sevor Shining-Road, and the market-god Thousand-Voiced Siranna. Renowned for administrative and logistical feats, they hold official remit to build and maintain the great limestone roads interconnecting Nechara’s timars.

### MATCHMAKERS AND GENEALOGY

Though matchmakers are loyal to their houses, they all begin their training in the Blossoming Jade Society, where they’re educated in the courtly arts. Seasoned matchmakers teach them secret principles and methods for matching spirits and mortals to produce strong God-Blooded lineages. These genealogical traditions draw on a mixture of trial and error, spirit wisdom, and First Age lore. New genealogical information and procedures earn both money and favor from the houses. Each house’s matchmakers also have their own secret matchmaking techniques they don’t share with the society, though the extent and efficacy of such techniques varies. The noble houses’ genealogical records remain carefully guarded secrets, protected by matchmakers and house elders. Some information resides in elaborately ciphered ledgers; some is only passed down orally.

Originally a minor house, the House of Lilac Petals grew numerous through their ancestors’ willingness to wed myriad spirit-spouses from wildly different bloodlines, and kept that bloodline strong through secret genealogical techniques developed by the legendary matchmaker-savant Graceful Samad. A Lilac Petal’s lineage may contain ghosts, raksha, and elementals, providing her with unique gifts. They grow wealthy through producing saffron.

Renowned for pride, determination, honor, and martial prowess, the House of the Storm Wheel remained loyal to Prince Tirgan to the end. Upon defeat, their timariot surrendered himself to Guren despite longtime antipathy between their houses. Like his father, Shule has appointed several Storm Wheel nobles to his guard, an act that hasn’t gone unnoticed. The House of the Storm Wheel’s genealogy focuses on weather spirits and ancestral ghosts.

### Commoners

Those lacking spiritual bloodlines are deemed commoners. Some hold positions in Nechara’s government as administrators, mediators, tax assessors, and urban planners. Most serve as farmers, fishers, artisans, manual laborers, and the like. But a growing middle class of wealthy commoners has emerged over the centuries, mostly merchants profiting from trade along the Great Southeastern Way.

Disdained by Nechara’s nobles and barred from holding direct political power, these so-called “caravan lords” use wealth and business connections to curry favor with Shule, timariots, and high-ranking bureaucrats and military officers through gifts, bribes, and galas. Shule plays the caravan lords against the houses, shuffling boons and burdens between those who’ve earned or lost his favor.

### Culture

Noble families reside in sprawling palace complexes. Brightly-colored scenes from Nechara’s history decorate exterior walls, embellished with gold leaf and enamel. Inside, the palace resembles a city in miniature, with homes for individual branches of the family, housing for attendants, shrines to the house’s gods, and even private burial grounds. Courtyards provide spaces for socializing and ceremonies.

Public buildings are also elaborately adorned, many featuring bas-reliefs of sacred animals and patron gods. Gateways with round arches connect the city’s districts;

EX3

they’re decorated with tiles glazed a deep, vivid blue. Each gate bears an inscription honoring the prince who commissioned it and explaining why it was built. Urban commoners inhabit brick houses roofed with wood and reeds, their interior walls covered in patterns and images painted by generations of inhabitants. Some houses are multistory, with the ground floor doubling as a workspace, shop, or livestock shelter. Rural houses are often constructed from bundled reeds. Weavers bind bundles of yarn before dyeing it, creating intricate patterns characteristic of their fabrics. Pomegranate-rind, onion-skin, and walnut dyes provide a range of vibrant colors. Lamb is common in Necharan dishes, featured in soups, stews, dumplings, and baked buns. Cooks in every bazaar serve the hearty dish called guveki — made with rice, carrots, raisins, and lamb — from huge cauldrons. Horse meat and fatty sheep’s tail are also prized. For lighter fare, people enjoy tomato, cucumber, and onion salad, or figs with goat cheese, washed down with honey-sweetened sumac tea. Bakers shape bread dough into rings and stamp it with complicated designs before baking. Desserts, served between courses at dinners

and banquets, include rose halva, saffron rice pudding, and mixed fruit compote.

### Military

Each house provides soldiers from its timar to Nechara’s small standing army. Tasked with defending the city from foreign threats, the army also quells uprisings, protects traders travelling the Great Southeastern Way, and deters neighbors that hungrily eye Nechara’s wealth and resources.

Should the prince wish to wield the army’s might beyond this mandate’s bounds, he must plead his case and offer boons to the houses, hoping they’ll gift him the desired levies, armaments, and supplies. Some houses withhold gifts to see what rival houses offer or pressure the prince to sweeten the pot. Houses opposing the prince’s ambitions may deny his requests altogether. When the houses’ contributions fall short, the prince may hire mercenaries or offer incentives directly to commoners to enlist.

God-Blooded nobles dominate the officer corps’ upper echelons, lending any magic and talents afforded

EX3

by their supernatural lineage to their units. Muras of the House of Verdant Leaves, whose ancestry includes the jaguar god Alet-Sul and the wood spider Janu Silverspinner, trains soldiers in stealth maneuvers. Ennesh of the House of Red Birds, granddaughter of the warrior goddess Vengeful Hani, leads lightning raids on Nechara’s enemies.

### CITIES ALONG THE GREAT

### SOUTHEASTERN WAY

The city of Bode is the birthplace of the prophet Andira, who melded the Way of Rain followed in LandUnder-Robe (p. XX) with Pure Way doctrines. Adherents travel here to study her writings, worship at the temples she established, and bathe at holy springs in the grove where she’s said to have found apotheosis with Mela and Daana’d. The city has become a cultural center; artists, musicians, and playwrights take up residence here and perform for wealthy visitors or attempt to secure patrons traveling toward Kamthahar.

At the start of a prince’s reign, each house gifts him with a dozen soldiers, chosen from among their best warriors and strategists to earn the new ruler’s favor. These form the core of the prince’s personal guard, ostensibly transferring their loyalty from their family to his, though some spying on their house’s behalf is expected; the extent of this varies with the prince’s charisma and whatever salary and boons he offers. Beyond that, he may expand his guard as he likes, limited by the availability of trustworthy recruits and what the treasury can afford.

Centuries ago, the far-venturing Ixcoatli prince Xipil conquered the Shogunate city Deneherin. There he founded a state blending Ixcoatli and Velen language, art, and religion. His successors extended their territory as far as the Sandy River, though their empire crumbled long ago. The royal line still bears a thin snakefolk lineage. While most Deneherins use Riverspeak with outsiders, its native language is a creole of Riverspeak and Forest-tongue.

### Divine Patrons

Trained matchmakers in a noble house’s service entice spirits to wed eligible members of that house. Among other potential boons, marriage contracts include a place in Nechara’s prayer calendars. The spirit-spouse joins the city’s vast pantheon, gaining feast days and temple space alongside other Necharan divinities; these start generously, but diminish or terminate after the marriage ends. In exchange, the god begets children with their noble spouse. Nobles may have both a spirit-spouse and a human spouse.

Nechara’s clergy manage these complex prayer calendars, tracking marriages and power-shifts. Noble houses sponsor temples in the city and their timars that prioritize their gods, although each temple must provide ceremonies for all houses’ patrons. Some gods use this opportunity to increase their influence across all Nechara.

Immigrant God-Blooded typically marry into Nechara’s noble houses, while gods accompanying such groups accept spirit-spouse contracts. Recent immigrants often suffer from discrimination — Necharan commoners resent competing with immigrant labor, nobles see new God-Blooded as uncultured, and spirits grumble that worshipers and matchmakers alike pay too much attention to new arrivals. Refugees unaccompanied by spirits or God-Blooded suffer greater disadvantages, as they lack advocates in civic or religious matters.

Four Brides, a haven for merchants, poets, and calligraphers, was recently sacked by the semi-nomadic Ranghay anteaterfolk after a devastating earthquake toppled many buildings and part of the city wall. Many Ranghay have remained behind as conquerors, demanding tribute from caravans passing through the city. Their leader, the astute young general Ta’an, fortifies Four Brides lest rival peoples from the Scantling Territories (p. XX) come to seize the city for their own.

### Necharan Religion

To most Necharans, a spirit’s origins — whether Heaven, Hell, the Underworld, or Creation — doesn’t matter. Benevolent or neutral spirits are divinities; malevolent spirits are devils. Divinities require worship to avert their wrath and to earn their protection against devils. Priests please their divinities with sacrifices, purification rites, music, and exorcism of stray devils. Public rituals assure that Nechara’s divinities remain powerful and well-disposed so they’ll continue guarding the city and maintaining the natural order. Regular civic rites and festivals offer days off from most labor. Priests lead prayers and sacrifices at ziggurat-temples, and parade divinities’ statues and reliquaries through the streets. Pleased divinities manifest to ritually bless Nechara and its people.

EX3

In addition, to emulate the bonds that nobles establish with their spirit-spouses, commoners traditionally seek to establish their own personal relationship with a chosen divinity with whom they feel a strong affinity. A citizen prays to their personal divinity privately, maintaining a shrine at home and wearing an icon symbolizing them, and attempting to emulate their persona and talents. Temples provide introductions to gods and sell the associated paraphernalia.

Necharans believe dreams sometimes contain visions sent by the gods. They seek out dream interpreters for guidance after strange or vivid dreams.

Noteworthy Necharan Gods

Heana Silver-Sandal, Nechara’s frequently absent city god, spends most of his time playing divine politics in the Eastern celestial censor’s court, leaving his subordinates to handle his affairs. Their inability to reach consensus creates opportunities for other gods to push their own agendas. Heana unfailingly returns to Nechara to attend his weeklong Hearthfire Festival every summer, during which he meets with a handful of petitioners; his priests handle his schedule, and appointments fill quickly. God of the mighty Maruto River, sturgeon-headed Undalu-En blesses Nechara’s crops, fisheries, and river trade. He takes personal interest in commerce, often visiting the city’s markets in a merchant’s guise to invest in novel enterprises. He’s also fickle and vindictive, and has been known to indulge in long-running proxy feuds with gods of rain, vegetation, and shipping. Etanu of the Arch has overseen the Grand Nechara Bridge spanning the Maruto since the Shogunate. Traders and travelers seek blessings in her shrine at the bridge’s apex. Many scions of the House of the Black Shell are her descendants. Sometimes she walks disguised among travelers to seek gossip or play tricks, her true nature revealed only by her shimmering shadow. Ula-Erva, Owl Queen of the East, was little known in Nechara before Guren’s reign. Now her Temple of the Violet Evening dominates the city skyline, while her festivals dominate its prayer calendars. Her sharp rise to prominence frustrates other houses’ gods, and she shows little interest in soothing their bruised egos. Restless and aloof, she occasionally takes advantage of Heana’s frequent absences to menace and overawe lesser Necharan spirits, but prefers to take strix shape and hunt in the deep forest.

### Other Faiths

Nechara currently proscribes most Immaculate creeds. Other faiths are welcome — or at least tolerated — if their practitioners respect the city’s rules and traditions. Foreign gods find their influence limited by laws establishing when and where their followers may proselytize, build temples, and hold festivals, and by their lack of access to the prayer calendar. A god whose faithful ignore those laws or otherwise become a nuisance may find herself censured, her offerings heavily taxed, her shrines seized, or her offending followers punished. This leniency is less about placating foreign gods, and more about preventing the poor and oppressed from turning to the Immaculates.

Ancestor worship is widespread through Nechara. Renowned ghost-forebears receive prayers from the living to lend their strength. While uncommon, it’s not unheard of for a deceased ancestor to remarry into the family.

Prince Shule restricts the Immaculate creeds more harshly than many of his predecessors, banning their practices and proselytization entirely. Now, his inquisitors prowl the slums and markets, seeking sects to root out. Native Necharan offenders may be publicly punished for their disobedience, while foreign parties are banished from the city. Those who repeatedly flout the law suffer increasingly direr punishments; several have disappeared altogether. Still, the Prince’s enforcers act cautiously when confronting Lookshyan sohei; the Seventh Legion maintains a redoubt near Nechara, and even Shule prefers not to provoke its wrath. Pure Way monks are more fortunate. As they don’t decry congress between spirits and mortals, they’re less outspoken against Necharan matchmaking traditions, and so they receive grudging tolerance from the prince. Many among the poor flock to them, hoping to fare better in the next life. Followers of other Immaculate creeds resent the Pure Way’s preferred treatment.

### Prominent Figures

Prince Shule of the House of Cerulean Stars rules Nechara as both beloved monarch and feared tyrant. Many lose themselves in Shule’s huge, hypnotic golden eyes, entranced by his inhuman charisma and eloquence. Shule is a man of strong convictions and relentless drive. When he sets his mind toward a project — be it a public improvement, a piece of art, or a romantic

EX3

pursuit — convincing him to abandon it takes significant effort on his closest advisors’ parts. Where recent monarchs were generous with the noble houses, Shule — like the princes of old — is generous with the city, investing in public works with the wealth he’s brought to Nechara. He empowers the caravan lords as a counterbalance to the noble houses, pitting them against one another while he consolidates power. The prince seeks greater control over the city and places members of his personal guard in positions of influence. His inquisitors hunt those who would plot against him.

Shule demands a spirit-spouse stronger than his mother. Thus far, he’s found the matchmakers’ candidates unsatisfactory.

While Shule and his human wife, Lamah of the House of Lilac Petals, have had five children, four died through misfortune or assassination. Many nobles whisper about what happens if their surviving child, the sickly Atur, passes. Grieving for their lost children and fearful for Atur’s life, Lamah has returned to her family’s holdings. There, she entrusts his care to Lilac Petals physicians and bodyguards. Shule considers ending the marriage to take a new human spouse, though this would antagonize the Lilac Petals. Shule’s lover, the architect Kigesh, attempts to intercede with her on the prince’s behalf.

Born to a fine papermaker serving Necharan nobility, the caravan lord Mardan Sin expanded his father’s operations, then sold the entire business to invest in caravans traversing the Great Southeastern Way. Now an old man, he hardly ever leaves Nechara, relying on a network of foreign contacts established during his caravanning years. In his retirement, he seeks to obtain a spirit-spouse despite being a commoner. A matchmaker from the Blossoming Jade Society has responded to his inquiries, though they keep such meetings deeply secret.

### Neighbors

The seminomadic peoples of the Broken Horn confederation traverse forests and marshes east and south of Nechara, raiding caravans along the Great Southeastern Way. Broken Horn villages nestle in hard-to-reach promontories, gullies, and deep clearings, well-defended from raids. Many descend from renegade Necharans who fled oppression, famine, disease, or war over the centuries; they know the city’s ways and weaknesses well. Others descend from Lunar warlords and savants

who’ve dwelt among them. Nechara’s princes and caravan lords view Broken Horn raids on villages, tax collectors, and merchants as the most immediate threat to the city’s prosperity. Prince Guren battled them more than once; Shule has yet to do so.

Belem Spearbreaker, the mercurial Moon-Touched chieftain of the Rodiri people, has led the Broken Horn for twenty years. Many warriors see him as a father. Belem encourages this; he drinks and fights alongside them, leading by example.

Quick both to anger and to celebrate, the Rodiri stand at the forefront of Broken Horn raids, driven by eagerness for glory and fury over prior losses. The confederation’s Lunar patrons, most notably Naven Earth-Render and the sorcerer Ibarith, contact him on occasion, offering various boons in exchange for information on the Necharan houses’ genealogical records and their matchmakers’ secret lore.

The steep rocky cliffs called the Dragons’ Crags jut from the forest floor like dragon talons. Most merchants traveling the Great Southeastern Way take the long way around rather than risk traversing them and encountering the bellicose air elementals that make their homes on the heights. Those who approach the cliffs speak of strange events: seeing the night sky ablaze with multicolored fire, or hearing a haunting song sung in a forgotten language.

Parashi’s Retreat stands a day’s ride south of Nechara, en route to the Dreaming Sea. Parashi of the House of Red Birds built this hilltop mansion as a place to meet secretly with his spirit spouse, the music goddess Lerias-Ai. His descendant Nihali hosts galas there for nobles to relax and meet with spirits. Matchmakers frequent the retreat, interviewing potential spouses for their clients or arranging meetings to test their compatibility. It’s an open secret that the retreat’s also a place for dalliances one’s house disapproves of, not to mention other clandestine meetings. Visitors are expected to forget other guests they see while partaking of its luxuries, especially those wearing masks. Still, spying and blackmail aren’t unheard-of here; participants in perilous liaisons are wise to remain cautious.

## Wolf’s Paw

The city of Wolf’s Paw occupies an isolated valley north of the Golden Road that links Greyfalls and distant Ixcoatli. Once a proud city-state, today many of its buildings are abandoned and overgrown. For the talking wolves of the Uskwood have seized power,

EX3

### OTHER FAR EASTERN LOCALES

The nearly abandoned city of Mara’s Kick — called Immuraya during the Dragon-Blooded Shogunate — looks out over cascading waterfalls from the slopes of the Glowrand Mountains, near the Meander River’s source. It once stood on the shore of an upland lake formed by an ancient dam whose locks raised and lowered riverine vessels hundreds of feet to enable commerce between highlands and lowlands. But the dam collapsed centuries ago, leaving great stone docks arching out over empty air.

A flock of jabiru birdfolk have made the docks their aerie — a vantage point for raiding likely targets on the river below. Their families inhabit the dockside ruins, maintaining weirs just above the waterfalls. Many lack the wing strength for flight; these take switchback paths and rickety stairs to the valley that was once the bottom of the dam’s lake.

The birdfolk rarely go deeper into the old city, as it’s home to Whispering Rain, a sorcerer renowned for peering into the shadows of the past. They say the streets around his manse are haunted by phantoms of earlier eras, his magic having stretched the veil so thin that travelers unwittingly bring forth shades of their own histories, for good or ill.

A shimmering green haze hangs over the First Age ruin of Pomander. Wood Essence, once channeled from a central manse through spirals of standing stones, now seethes and churns throughout the city. Vegetation overruns every floor of every building, inside and out. Ivy and kudzu sheathe sky-scraping towers in rippling curtains of greenery; flowering trees burst up through otherwise impervious First Age pavements. Pomander’s people don’t live in the ruins, lest swiftly growing roots and vines strangle them in their sleep. Instead, they travel every day from neighboring villages to farm grain and vegetables on rooftops and balconies, herd pigs up stairways swollen with mushrooms, gather fruit and nuts from tree-choked avenues, and harvest grapes from vine-wrapped porticoes.

Villagers stick to Pomander’s outskirts; elementals swarming the city’s heart make deeper exploration dangerous. Scavenger lords report swarms of gnarled wood-spiders, aggressive clouds of razor-edged leaves, and other menaces.

ruling over its human populace from the manors and

palaces they once built.

The eldest wolves lounge upon silken divans and gilded thrones, red tongues lolling as servants feed them sweetbreads on silver plates and brush their fur with

ivory combs. Meanwhile, their pups run wild in the

streets or raid flocks and herds in nearby lands. The remaining mortal residents live in fear of their masters’ fangs and wild appetites.

### History

Fleeing a terrible plague to the north, a handful of survivors founded the town of Quill on the Elleret River’s shores. Though far from other settlements, abundant

fishing and copper in the nearby hills provided food,

tools, and trade. By the time refugees from a now-forgotten war conquered it two centuries later, Quill had grown from small town to prosperous city.

Even as Quill expanded, its citizens recalled their ancestors’ uncertain early days. Sentries and healers

staffed the gates, keeping out anybody bearing signs

of illness. When word arrived of sickness spreading

nearby, they closed its gates until the outbreak passed.

Open-air markets and temporary inns appeared outside

the walls; many became permanent fixtures.

Out of the Uskwood

The ancient Uskwood stands a day’s walk upriver from

Wolf’s Paw. This tangle of old-growth broadleaf and coniferous forest occupies a bordermarch; its Wyld taint grants the capacity for speech to animals born there. Moreover,

the intelligence of Uskwood-born beasts is bound up in

their flesh, such that native predators grow smarter each

time they consume another Uskwood-born beast’s flesh.

Uskwood herbivores have scarcely more intellect than

ordinary animals of their sort. They may chatter on

about various woodland topics or plead for their lives

when threatened, but otherwise behave little differently from beasts elsewhere. But Uskwood predators and carrion-eaters soon grow well-spoken and sagacious,

capable of introspection, planning, and even philosophical musing.

EX3

But intellect isn’t instinct. Uskwood animals feel the same appetites and inclinations as any other animal of their ilk. Even the wisest predator is only as prone to overcoming its instincts as humans are to overcoming theirs — that is, not as often as one might expect or wish.

Rise of the Wolves

Over the centuries, Uskwood’s wolves developed their own society and culture. Packs that once kept to their own territories first fought for dominance, then formed alliances to control the forest. They drove other dangerous beasts — bears, boars, and great cats, as well as hobgoblins and other fae — to the wood’s fringes and killed those who wouldn’t submit to their authority. Carrion birds did the same in the forest canopy. Wolf and bird squabbled over carcasses but otherwise maintained an uneasy peace. As growing wolf populations ranged beyond the forest to feed, they crossed paths with the Northeast’s resurgent human populace. Despite curiosity on both sides, hostility won out; humans hunted wolves to protect themselves and their flocks, while wolves attacked loggers who threatened the Uskwood’s borders. Watching mortals compel one another to labor with threats of violence, the wolves realized they could do the same. First, they extorted food from farmers and shepherds. Then, when Quill’s soldiers came to battle them, they defeated the human army, hunted and killed all but a few stragglers, and then swarmed into the city to claim its throne.

### Human Society

The surviving humans became servants to the wolves, who renamed the city Wolf’s Paw and proclaimed themselves its rulers. Wolves moved into slain nobles’ homes, donned their jewelry, and laid down laws. After some internal wars and squabbles, the strongest and most cunning wolves established themselves as aristocrats.

Human farmers tend fields and flocks. They shear sheep for wool, make cheeses from cow, goat, and sheep milk, and gather chicken and duck eggs. Artisans make leather, parchment, and tallow candles and soap. Meat, however, is for wolves’ consumption, with few exceptions. Wealthy humans pay large fees to wolf magnates for meat; faithful servants and distinguished soldiers occasionally receive meat dishes as a reward. But most human households only eat scraps gleaned from bones boiled for broth — if the wolves haven’t picked them

clean. Common dishes include eggs fried with spinach and cheese, herbed peppers-and-onion stew, baked mushroom-and-barley loaf, and cold apricot soup. Over the generations, humans in Wolf’s Paw adapted to life in service to wolves. Experience taught residents how to appease them and what actions will likely get someone killed. Still, talking wolves aren’t human, and humans can’t always anticipate what instinct might drive them to do. Parents pass wisdom down to children, spinning lessons into bedtime stories and nursery rhymes. Everyone knows The Tale of Snapping Jaws and can recite the rhyme about The Boy Who Ran from Wolves.

In many ways, Wolf ’s Paw runs like a normal city. Residents include blacksmiths, stonemasons, miners, and woodcutters. A human council named by the ruling wolves hears and handles human citizens’ concerns, addressing issues beneath the wolves’ interests. Experienced diplomats ensure that visiting traders and dignitaries know to address to wolves correctly and relatively safely. Humans serve in the militia; the most trusted run alongside wolves when raiding neighboring settlements, their opposable thumbs useful for chopping down doors and carrying plunder.

### Wolf Society

Four or five generations of wolves pass during a human lifespan. Those who die of old age live for 10 to 15 years and come disproportionately from aristocratic wolf families. Aristocrats send commoner wolves on dangerous raids against foreign settlements and caravans, winnowing the wolves’ numbers so their population doesn’t grow too fast.

Wolves have adopted some human adornments, such as earrings, anklets, and jeweled collars. A few don close-fitting, restrictive coats in the winter that make rival wolves pause. It’s a signal that the wearer can win in a fight despite her accoutrements, or that she bears such authority in the pack that no one would dare challenge her. Commoner wolves range outside the city to hunt; they’re also allotted farmed livestock, often elderly animals no longer useful for milk, eggs, or wool. Aristocratic wolves favor meals prepared and served by human cooks; they sometimes hunt wild game brought from faraway lands by foreign merchants. Hunting is a social event for commoner and aristocrat alike, especially under the full moon.

EX3

The Brezala Market once lay outside the city walls, only to be encompassed during one of Quill’s expansions. Before the wolves’ conquest, its stalls remained widely spaced, a custom from the days when pestilence raged and people kept distance between them to curtail disease’s spread. Today, animal merchants pay little heed to human cautions and set up shop right next to their neighbors. In one stall, human blacksmiths sell tools; in the next, junk-dealing magpies have trinkets on display. A vendor roasts meat and vegetables on skewers, doing business with wolves and humans alike.

### WOLVES IN THE WYLD

The wolves of Wolf’s Paw return to the Uskwood on occasion to hunt, to recruit other wolves, and to reproduce. Because only those animals born within the bordermarch gain intelligence and the power of speech, new wolves must be whelped within its bounds, lest they be no different than their mundane cousins. (Such mundane offspring are killed or abandoned.) Likewise, to improve their intellect, wolves must hunt other animals born in the Uskwood. Thus, the wolves of Wolf’s Paw maintain small, tightly supervised farms within the bordermarch for breeding prey animals. Stock is then sent to farms closer to Wolf’s Paw, for convenience.

The Riverwatch — temple to Dandraya, city god of Wolf ’s Paw — sits on the Elleret’s banks. The temple is as old as the city itself, built by Quill’s original settlers. Today, wolves and humans leave offerings and pray side by side. Most priests are human, though a few devout wolves wear Dandraya’s copper medallion and lead their fellows in worship.

Hunting in the Uskwood is a privilege reserved for nobles, though especially gifted commoner wolves may receive dispensation by proving themselves worthy. Limiting hunting privileges keeps commoner wolves from growing too intelligent.

The Old Hall, a three-story municipal building, dominates the city square in the center of Wolf ’s Paw. A marketplace occupies the ground floor, the city council meets on the second floor, and the topmost floor holds offices and archives. Human bureaucrats scurry through the halls like mice, trying to balance doing the wolves’ bidding with keeping the human population safe. Even in winter, the windows are thrown wide to admit crow messengers.

Aristocratic urban wolves maintain political ties with Uskwood wolves, ensuring that their strictures are enforced and that a steady supply of Uskwood-born food animals reaches Wolf’s Paw. In exchange, Uskwood’s wolves receive gifts of livestock and avoid costly war with the urban wolves.

### The City

Crows fill the air over Wolf’s Paw, carrying news from the Uskwood and beyond. Package-laden humans hurry along behind richly clad wolves down bustling cobblestone streets. Humans live and work in homes and shops with whitewashed walls and sloping thatched roofs. Aristocratic wolves inhabit grand manor houses dotting the city’s hills, formerly belonging to Quill’s nobles. The manors’ exteriors remain largely unchanged; inside, human spaces have been modified for wolves’ comfort. Commoner wolves typically dwell on the grounds of their lords’ estates, though the most valued and trusted may be rewarded with indoor quarters. Empty, overgrown houses dominate some districts. Cobblestones lie cracked and uneven; debris from crumbling structures spills into the streets. Wolves run in these lonely places, sharpening hunting skills by chasing prey through abandoned structures. Not all humans who lived here are dead or fled; amidst the wolves’ brutality, there’s safety in numbers, so most humans cluster together in more populous districts.

Upland, well apart from the river, rise the granite walls of the Quill Arena, the city’s coliseum. This oval amphitheater first served old Quill as a fortress and later as a venue for festivals, sporting events, and dramas. Today, its stands fill with wolves and blood soaks the arena floor. Young wolves test their prowess here, pitted against lawbreaking wolves, nonspeaking wild beasts, human criminals, and prisoners of war. Occasionally, bloodlust stirs the audience, and wolves leap from the stands into the arena; whoever’s left standing wins. Wolf aristocrats prioritize new construction around the coliseum, allowing workers and aficionados to live nearby.

Farms dominate the city’s outskirts. Field workers raise staple crops like wheat, corn, potatoes, and barley. Animals born here are ordinary livestock, meat raised to fill wolves’ bellies. Seasonally, young talking animals arrive from farms inside the Uskwood. Raised alongside their mute cousins, they’re ultimately destined for aristocrats’ plates.

EX3

### Governance and Politics

A dozen aristocratic wolf clans jockey for power in Wolf ’s Paw. They’ve carved up the city and surrounding lands into a handful of territories, each held by a single clan. Each desires to claim the best territory — which changes over time as the city grows — while fending off challengers, including packs of young wolves seeking to overthrow and supplant a noble clan. The struggle is largely sublimated into political posturing, financial games, and the like, but sometimes devolves into physical challenges between leaders or their champions, or occasionally broader battles and free-for-alls. Aristocratic wolves care little for human affairs but recognize the need to address day-to-day concerns. To that end, they appoint trusted humans to a city council and leave them to manage problems that farmers and peasants bring to their attention. Each noble clan names one human to serve at their pleasure on the council, mainly from the city’s wealthiest human families. Each such family holds client status beneath a noble wolf clan. The council operates largely autonomously, bringing only the most pressing issues to the wolves. It makes

every effort to solve problems without wolf involvement, since there’s no guarantee the wolves won’t settle matters with fangs and claws. Councilors throw lavish parties for foreign envoys, minimizing interaction with temperamental wolf aristocrats.

While noble wolves have the final say over goings-on in Wolf ’s Paw, a few other factions have a voice in city affairs. Wealthy human merchants, with their social networks and commercial experience outside Wolf’s Paw, set policies regarding foreign trade. Crows and other talking birds, able to travel swiftly to neighboring cities and the Uskwood, act as spies and informants for the wolves; the cleverest earn places as advisors.

### Religion

Wolves and humans share many gods, though their relationships with them differ. Some gods’ purviews align more closely with wolves than humans, or vice versa. The streets of Wolf’s Paw swell once a week with worshipers — both wolves and humans — heading to the Riverwatch for services to Dandraya. Though wolves tend to leave after the major rituals are completed, humans stay for several hours, socializing and gossiping in a wolf-free area while the priest sermonizes.

EX3

Noteworthy Local Gods

Nine-Handed Dandraya, the sapphire-clad city god of Wolf ’s Paw, was formerly a river god charged with overseeing the Elleret. As Quill grew, she parlayed increasing river traffic into a Heavenly promotion. Now, thanks to the wolves’ presence in the city, she’s setting her sights on another — if Than Thir’s not fulfilling her heavenly duties, Dandraya would do so happily. The forest walker Than Thir, chief god of the Uskwood, has long cared little for Heaven’s dictates; she casually sends false reports rather than properly survey her domain. Though she has nothing to do with the Uskwood’s gift of speech, she’s fond of beasts who use that gift well — in clever speeches, witty turns of phrase, or stirring poems — and offers them her blessing.

Wolves ask Clawgrim, Hound of the Endless Hunt, to run alongside them as they seek their quarry; humans make offerings asking him to turn predators away from their flocks. Crows bring trinkets to the nest of the bird-god Sokeli the Wise, hoping she’ll bless them with quick wit and favorable winds.

The harvest spirit Wind-in-the-Rows mainly receives petitions from human worshipers asking for good soil, gentle rains, and abundant crops. Wolves who pray to her ask for much the same — after all, a fruitful harvest in the fall yields fat quarry in the spring. Not all human residents of Wolf’s Paw are content to remain the wolves’ servants and victims. A secret cult to the poison god Auled Evening-Beauty seeks to leverage his knowledge and blessing against their lupine oppressors.

The Immaculate Philosophy

Immaculate missionaries occasionally visit Wolf ’s Paw in hopes of converting the locals and restoring the natural order. Their sermons aim to persuade the wolves to return to the Uskwood, though few have been so swayed. But syncretic beliefs have emerged from this proselytization.

Though the Uskwood’s wolves aren’t beastfolk, an obscure Immaculate scripture says beastfolk are human because they’re flesh and blood with four limbs, speech, and intellect. Wolf savants have decreed that, as this applies to the Uskwood’s wolves, they’re human as well — and as apex predators, they’re also entitled to mastery over non-wolf human prey. Although monks know many contradictory passages, these wolves fervently adhere to their interpretation.

Meanwhile, orthodox human converts — who view the wolves as lower down in the Perfected Hierarchy — talk among themselves about what that means for Wolf ’s Paw. Their ancestors weren’t always under the predators’ control. Perhaps the time is coming to return things to their rightful order.

### Prominent Figures

Elizar’s muzzle has grown white with age. Nearly 17 years old, he likely won’t live to see next spring, and his pack of children and grandchildren are eager to claim his place. He’s not dead yet, though. In the last year, he’s grown fascinated by the Immaculate Philosophy. Though he’s not a convert, he’s survived all these years by not hedging his bets. He seeks insight into human experiences on the off chance that he does get reincarnated as one. To that end, he invites a selection of cityfolk to dine with him on occasion. Conversation at these dinners has grown heated, making tensions — and hackles — rise.

The young wolf Nathian has survived bloody raids, deadly hunts, and several coliseum brawls. Each victory expands her following among her peers. Nathian and a small pack of followers have claimed an abandoned neighborhood for their own, separate from the aristocratic clans. She’s joined hunts in the Uskwood when invited, noting what an honor it is, though as her intelligence grows, so does her resentment towards the nobles. As her adherents’ numbers grow, so do her ambitions. Nathian might yet carve out a greater stake in the city without the aristocrats’ help. The human Mátyás instructs newcomers on proper etiquette around wolves, and often accompanies them during interactions with the aristocracy to ensure everyone keeps the peace. His position allows him to sit in on negotiations between wolves and foreign envoys, Guild merchant princes, or other powerful entities, making him privy to sensitive information. Mátyás has turned this into a lucrative side business as an information broker for the human council and other parties. The human Belah has served in Elizar’s household for nearly twenty years, managing the wolf ’s mother’s and grandmother’s affairs before him. She’s unobtrusive, quiet, and competent. Most days, the wolves hardly know she’s there, so efficiently does she carry out her duties. That’s to her benefit: a cultist of Auled, she’s in a perfect place to carry out her grim duties, should the cult target a wolf in her household.

EX3

Neighbors

Rogue wolves stalk the alleys in the city of Thresh. Packs claim neighborhoods as their territory, driving out human street gangs or forcing them to join together — with the wolves in charge, of course. These young rogues fled Wolf’s Paw, whether to avoid dying in their lords’ wars or because they chafed at their duties. In Thresh, wolves experiment with living as humans do, sometimes even alongside them. Most settlements around the Uskwood kill wolves on sight, lest they become another Wolf’s Paw. However, Thresh’s government has done its citizens few favors, letting corruption and hunger run rampant. The human underclass — though still wary — embraces the presence of the occasional talking wolf as a sort of rebellion. Beyond Thresh, on the Golden Road, lies the city-state of Evor. Seized centuries ago by the Realm as a foothold for eastern expansion, it proved more trouble than it was worth; losses to bandits, raiders, rebels, and Lunar intrigue outweighed trade profit and tribute. Officially part of the Eastern Realm Administrative District, it’s effectively independent today, overseen by a council of merchant-oligarchs.

The Realm merchant Rosewood Dohera doubles as an agent for Greyfalls satrap Cynis Verheen. In addition to observing trade and local politics, she monitors the Uskwood for threats to the Golden Road. Human citizens of Wolf’s Paw have made private entreaties to Dohera for help in driving out the wolves, but she’s expressed no interest in doing so unless their raids reach Evor itself.

## Land-Under-Robe

Over the centuries, the legendary Storm Wall has slowly spread to encircle a vast swath of Far Eastern forests and mountains. Within this miles-deep ring, the weather remains forever in turmoil — thunderstorms, gale winds, hail, flash floods, droughts, and even tornadoes strike without warning, one form of foul weather sometimes lasting weeks or months before another takes its place.

Those who struggle past this boundary emerge into a balmy, clement land of calm breezes and gentle rains. This is Land-Under-Robe, the domain of the Storm Queen — a formidable weather goddess — and her court. Dozens of villages and towns do her homage, making offerings in her name.

At the center of these lands stands Quiverch, heart of the Storm Queen’s divine hegemony. Here, by a shining mountain lake, the people of this realm gather among temples and granaries, shrines and storehouses. Here they labor endlessly, building and rebuilding these holy structures to draw in pilgrims from across the Far East.

### History

Centuries ago, the villages of the Pachapunu Mountains suffered terribly from droughts, storms, and floods. After years of suffering, a band of villagers attempted the dizzying, perilous climb to the Atanyuka, palace of the Storm Queen, on a promontory rising from near-mythical Lake Amaru. The goddess found favor in the survivors’ petitions — and in the blood of those who died in the climb. So long as the people prayed, sacrificed, and came to her in supplication, she said, she’d shelter them under her robe, sending neither drought nor tempest, only bountiful weather for good harvests. The bargain was struck. And over time, more and more neighboring peoples joined the pact, abasing themselves before the Storm Queen to receive her grace. Each sent priests and oblates to serve her in the Atanyuka, while their gods prostrated themselves and took places in her nascent spirit court. Countless pilgrims followed to witness the Storm Queen’s majesty for themselves and to thank her for her generosity. Today, the Storm Queen’s influence extends across hundreds of miles, a thearchy driven more by worship and weather than soldiers and swords. Storms, droughts, and floods no longer trouble peoples under her sway; such ills only afflict ungodly foreigners in other lands, past the eternal chaotic weather marking Land-UnderRobe’s borders. Her people flock to holy Quiverch, reveling in its ever-changing temples and endless festivals, offering praise and blood in exchange for yet another rich harvest.

### Economics

Money has little meaning for most in Land-UnderRobe. The Storm Queen’s treasurers manage the flow of resources, dictating what each settlement will produce and providing the supplies needed to fulfill that production. Officials collect anywhere from half to three-quarters of various raw materials and finished goods; families retain the rest for their own use and for barter.

EX3

Neighbors often provided needed items as gifts rather than bartering, or accept a deferred trade or a favor in return. When dealing with strangers, a range of small, portable items — being easily carried by travelers — are commonly welcomed in trade. These include nuggets of gold or other metals, semiprecious stones, and colorful feathers. Necessities like food, clothing, and tools are kept in storehouses that are open to the public. A person needs merely present herself and express her need to the clerks, and her need is met. Most such items aren’t lavish. Clothing is functional rather than fashionable. But residents receive items suitable to their station, whether an artisan’s specialized tools or an ecclesiarch’s (p. XX) extravagant robe and gem-studded jewelry. For most, meals — though fresh and nourishing — are simple fare, such as ulluco soup, unleavened almondand mayfly-flour pancakes, guinea pig and aji tamales, roasted leafcutter ants, maize and beans stewed with chili peppers and onions, or baked potatoes in salted clay sauce. Meanwhile, ecclesiarchs dine on such gourmet comestibles as wild game, river fish, young roasted llama, passionfruit, foxtail amaranth with honey, and fresh lizard ceviche.

### Culture

Artists throughout Land-Under-Robe receive patronage from high-ranking priests and ecclesiarchs. Brilliant murals decorate temple walls. Monumental roadside sculptures — stone arches, monoliths, and likenesses of the gods — tower over passing pilgrims. Ceramists and potters depict gods on delicate vases. Writers pen religious works recording scripture and history, while poets capture the Storm Queen’s glory and pilgrim’s plights in verse.

Clothing involves brightly woven cotton and alpaca fleece. Feathers are reserved for weddings and funerals, except for priests, who wear feathers year-round. Villagers on pilgrimage paint their faces with colors and patterns to indicate their home villages. Villagers revere the elderly for their wisdom and long years of service to the community. Wrinkles and gray hair are signs of status. God-Blooded who show little sign of aging may shave their heads and wear clay masks to conceal their youthfulness.

EX3

### Quiverch: A City as Everchanging as the Clouds

Tassels are a common feature in Land-Under-Robe. They adorn shawls, bridal hats, and necklaces. Pilgrims, winners of festival competitions, militia sent against bandits, and even the bandits themselves wear them to mark their accomplishments — the most accomplished display them in layers. Llama herders tag animals’ ears with tassels; the colors indicate who the flock belongs to, and help shepherds identify specific animals from afar.

Musicians in Land-Under-Robe take inspiration from day-to-day life, telling stories of harvests, pilgrims passing through, and renowned elders’ youthful adventures. At weddings and feasts, guests join in on dances that feature intricate footwork and hand movements. Visitors are encouraged to participate; children pull shy observers into the dance and teach them simplified versions of the steps.

### Religion

Land-Under-Robe’s religion, the Way of Rain, teaches that the divine and the mundane are separate, but that each depends on the other to thrive. It acknowledges the disparity in power between gods and mortals. But while gods rule the world, people are its caretakers, and the Quiverchi treat their duties very seriously. Way of Rain morality emphasizes praise and devotion toward the gods, and supporting one’s neighbors through charity and good works. But it also stresses self-improvement. Some seek this through scholarly and artistic pursuits. Others aim for physical perfection, or eschew worldly comforts to pursue divine wisdom.

Tradition states that those who live exemplary lives, caring for others as well as themselves, receive an afterlife in sun-filled lands with gentle rains. People who show disregard for others, such as liars, layabouts, murderers, and thieves, suffer endless punishment at the heart of a terrible lightless storm. Lingering as a ghost is a gift of from the Storm Queen — a second chance not to be wasted or abused.

Actual spiritual practices involve music, dance, and theatrics. Priests sing their scriptures and sermons, with congregants joining on the refrains. Impromptu religious dances are held during rainstorms. Festivals feature morality plays wherein actors play gods, personified concepts, and archetypal everywomen.

Quiverch: A City as

Everchanging as the Clouds

As pilgrims climb past roaring waterfalls and up steep mountain roads to the high plateau at Land-UnderRobe’s heart, the echoes of thunder greet them before the holy city Quiverch comes into view. Bright banners catch the chill wind descending from the mountain peaks. More waterfalls cascade into Lake Amaru from the mountains above; mists from these falls drift out across the lake to veil the shining Atanyuka and the causeway connecting it to the city.

Entry to the city proper requires blood sacrifice to the Storm Queen. Pilgrims prick their earlobes with thorns and use the blood to stain their lips red. Quiverch’s skyline is a riot of structures. Inns and hostelries encircle the unwalled city, their keepers loudly competing for custom. Temples to the Storm Queen and her court, their straight-edged façades of precisely fitted stones plastered and painted with brilliant pictograms, rise above shrines to lesser gods. Sacred banners flutter in the breeze amid streamers of fragrant incense-smoke. Fresh animal sacrifices litter the ground around the shrines; priests remove these offerings at end of day. Buildings dedicated to mundane matters are no less impressive — even humble administrators attend to their ledgers surrounded by grandeur. Of the city’s grand structures, only the blessed Atanyuka is deemed permanent; no other is ever complete. This is deliberate; the city is a constant hive of activity, with brigades of laborers building new temples and palaces to overawe visitors and flaunt Quiverch’s wealth and power, dismantling older structures for materials. Corvées drawn from settlements in Quiverch’s orbit provide menial labor. Other workers haul up water, food, textiles, pottery, and other goods from surrounding settlements, storing them in clan and government warehouses for distribution.

A Transient Populace

Temple priests and ecclesiarchs are the city’s most permanent residents. Ecclesiarchs — the Storm Queen’s long-lived priestly advisors — dwell in opulence within the Atanyuka itself. Temple priests occupy quarters in the temples in which they serve. The city’s road priests stay at austere monasteries when in Quiverch; those meager accommodations are sumptuous compared to their lodgings on the road, where they often sleep on rocky ground. Corvée laborers live in barracks until they return home.

EX3

Most other Quiverch residents — merchants, administrators, warehouse workers, etc. — reside in settlements further down the mountain. They walk to the city early every morning and return home when the workday ends. But Quiverch has far fewer permanent residents than most cities; most occupants at any given time are pilgrims and hostelry staff.

### THE ATANYUKA

### The Storm Queen

dwells in opulent luxury amid her priests and divine allies in her step pyramid palace-temple, the Atanyuka. Built of glistening white granite veined with gold and quartz, the Atanyuka reflects sunlight and moonlight beneath clear skies, and reflects lightning when the Storm Queen invokes a thunderstorm to awe her worshipers. The palace stands on a high promontory amid Lake Amaru; a single bridge, lined by ceremonial guards, links it to the city.

Temples and Ceremonies

With the exception of the Storm Queen, gods must compete for pilgrims’ prayers. Each year, their priesthoods oversee construction of more extravagant wonders to entice pilgrims, drawing on an allotted share of the city’s stockpiles and corvées. Lesser gods’ priests often bargain for materials from richer temples to build new wonders. So dramatic are the changes, pilgrims must buy maps each year to navigate Quiverch. Temples jockey for spots on the parade calendar to increase worship. Priests wear elaborate costumes and throw candy and jewelry to pilgrims. In the offering market, sacrificial animals squawk and vendors hawk trinkets pilgrims can bring home, with every transaction accompanied by a prayer to Land-Under-Robe’s barter gods.

Petty godlings maintain shrines in the market, often little more than booths with an attendant priest. Needy pilgrims, their petitions unanswered by greater spirits, often try their luck here. A few of these godlings pass themselves off to confused pilgrims as more famous and powerful divinities, although this is risky business; woe betide an impostor should the impersonated god find out — or worse, should it come to the Storm Queen’s attention.

Each god has their own preferred offerings, whether a beautiful piece of pottery, a perfectly ripe cherimoya, or a shell from the distant sea. Larger favors often require animal sacrifice, though the Way of Rain forbids sacrifices larger than the worshiper’s fist. Children offer iridescent beetles to save a sick mother’s life; bridegrooms argue that a bird-of-paradise’s tail feathers don’t count towards its size. Some gods skirt the rule by asking for a palmful of blood from larger, still-living animals. The mountain’s water is sacred. Pilgrims participate in ritual baths beneath waterfalls, on ghats along Lake Amaru’s shores, and in sacred pools and temple cisterns. Others gather water from the mountain to bring back to their home villages as an offering to the shrines there. Vendors on every corner barter away vials and bottles for this purpose, ranging from plain and unadorned to exquisitely shaped or etched.

On its penultimate level, a dozen priests chant and dance in rotation, performing a perpetual ritual to maintain the Storm Wall. Temple guards stand watch over them; acolytes tend to their needs. Disrupting the ritual would throw Land-Under-Robe’s weather into chaos for months, until the weather gods could wrestle it under control once more.

At all hours, monks lead celebratory processions through the streets, waving colorful banners and playing lively music as pilgrims watch or join in the parade. Others recite the Storm Queen’s scriptures to attentive audiences in temple courtyards or act out her triumphs while pilgrims feast in her honor. These events change from year to year and season to season, guaranteeing that no matter how many pilgrimages someone undertakes, they never have the same experience twice.

The Storm Queen

Ancient and powerful, the Storm Queen has dwelt here since time immemorial. She’s the highest authority amid the region’s weather spirits, reporting directly to Heaven. She maintains good relationships with her celestial superiors and the spirit censor of the East via artful (and often incomplete or false) correspondence, gifts, and bribes that include prayer, sacrifices, artwork, slaves, and occasional salvaged First Age relics. The tall, heavyset goddess’ skin gleams with the multicolored mud of a thousand floods. Her hair crackles with lightning. Despite her taste for blood sacrifice, she bears her worshipers little malice. She views them like prize cattle — to be nurtured and protected by her servants, but ultimately there to nourish her. She likewise sees rebellion as a disease that threatens the herd and must be culled.

While the Storm Queen participates in ceremonies and rituals, she holds herself at a distance, only interacting
