### NOTABLE GODS OF THE COURT

Quelan-Quel, god of Lake Amaru, is among the Storm Queen’s oldest allies and one of the court’s highest-ranking members. A beloved figure in Quiverch, pilgrims look for her pleasure barge out on the lake; many of the court’s gods congregate there to socialize, gamble, and connive, away from the Atanyuka’s pressures. She holds an annual race against the ashen barge of the drought-god Old Chakuzu; folklore claims the race’s outcome determines whether crops will thrive or falter that year.

The twin-faced goddess Soona oversees ripening of the region’s crops. In the bounteous guise of a fleshy woman walking alongside a well-laden llama, she sings in a warm, echoing voice, bringing a rich harvest. As the specter of famine, she’s a gaunt woman with oversized eyes and skeletal hands, withering crops and farmers alike with her hopeless glare, then disappearing in a gust of hot, foul wind.

Though she prefers to wander Land-Under-Robe’s villages, Soona now lingers in Quiverch. Her beloved high priest, Nanat, fell to his death from a temple balcony; she believes this was murder — perhaps by an ambitious subordinate, a jealous lover, or a rival high priest or god. She seeks answers, both to avenge Nanat and from fear of losing her status amid divine intrigues.

Once a celestial god of fleeting pleasures, Sacriete was exiled from Heaven for reasons he won’t disclose, then found worshipers among peoples that later fell under the Storm Queen’s sway. He bristles at owing fealty to an earthly goddess — especially one who disdains him — yet will do anything to claw his way to the top of her court. Sacriete is popular among pilgrims, flitting around Quiverch as a flock of birds-of-paradise that gather into a man wearing a brightly feathered cloak. His temple overflows with worshipers indulging in intoxication and assorted entertainments. He replaces his high priest often, dissatisfied with their inability to expand his cult to the extent he desires.

Atl oversees yellow fever in the Glassfrog River valley, a stretch of which has only recently arrived within the Storm Wall. Reborn with each flooding of the Glassfrog as a small slip of a girl in muddy clothes, she frolics among the floodwaters, bringing disease in her wake. In the decade since the last flood, she’s aged to an awkward and clumsy adolescent.

Angry with the Storm Queen’s breaking of the flood cycle, Atl schemes from her small shrine in the offering market to cause chaos in Land-Under-Robe, making her mistress’ reign more difficult. In her own guise or that of a strange child or elderly toyseller, she spreads rumors, reveals secrets, and sells cursed toys that bring illness or misfortune.

the spirit court surrounding the Storm Queen. As the

Outside of Quiverch, they serve as emissaries to their people, guiding their communities to best serve the Storm Queen’s aims. Weather gods and their subordinates manipulate the weather throughout her holdings, fanning out into the countryside to bring gentle or cruel weather

The Storm Queen’s Priesthood

God-Blooded children are raised by their mortal parent’s families. From the time they take their first steps, such children train to become priests of the Storm Queen. Education is a family affair: aunts and uncles teach them songs and scriptures, grandparents bring them to Quiverch to visit the temples. A few rebel and flee into the countryside; the rest enter the Storm Queen’s service at age 13. The most loyal are trusted as missionaries, while the rest serve in the Atanyuka or in Quiverch’s temples. But most of the Storm Queen’s priests are mortal, drawn from youths brought by hopeful villagers for training. Initiates spend years learning ritual dances; memorizing songs, prayers, and ceremonies; studying mathematics, medicine, and anatomy; engaging in martial training; and serving as attendants to senior priests. Some — unable to endure the rigors of training — give up or wash out, either returning home or becoming priests to vassal gods in city or countryside temples. The rest are eventually ritually ordained by a senior priest, who draws their blood as a sacrifice to the Storm Queen.

Newly ordained priests are inducted by their superiors into one of the priesthood’s two orders. Temple priests participate in holy rites, organize the city’s bureaucracy, direct labor overseers, and serve senior priests as personal aides. Road priests assist troubled pilgrims en route to Quiverch, lead armed patrols of village levies against bandits, act as urban guides and peacekeepers in the ever-changing holy city, or venture beyond the Storm Queen’s lands as missionaries.

The highest-ranking priests, called ecclesiarchs, handle administration for the Storm Queen’s priesthood, discuss religious matters, and serve as intermediaries between the priesthood and the Tempest Court. The ecclesiarchs extend their lives through an annual rite wherein a pilgrim volunteers to ceremonially marry the Storm Queen, live the high life for a year, and then become a blood sacrifice to the goddess; anointing themselves in that blood staves off the ecclesiarchs’ aging. Volunteers usually offer themselves up to end severe chronic pain, age-related disabilities, or the like; they’re admired for their holiness.

Other priests bristle at the nigh-undying ecclesiarchs’ hold on power, yet maneuver to claim the occasional opening when an ecclesiarch dies or gets ousted. Schemes to remove an ecclesiarch percolate among the priesthood’s middle tiers. This rarely involves assassination; more often, an ecclesiarch who earns the Storm

Queen’s disfavor merely loses access to the life-extending ritual. After that, time quickly catches up, staved-off decades returning in a matter of weeks or days.

### Beyond Quiverch

Pilgrimage roads extend from Quiverch through the surrounding mountains, even beyond the Storm Wall. Shrines to the Storm Queen and her court’s gods speckle these roads, ensuring that pilgrims’ devotion begins long before reaching the holy city. A handful of holy sites to major Tempest Court figures have become minor pilgrimage sites in themselves, but none — as yet — compare or compete with Quiverch.

Though road priests patrol the pilgrimage roads, bandits and swindlers nonetheless prey on tired pilgrims. Despite these trials, many make multiple journeys to Quiverch across their lifetimes. Elders often die trying to see Quiverch one last time. Pilgrims fear that the Storm Queen’s wrath will destroy their crops and hope that the priesthood accepts their children; they carry scarlet coin in their veins to pay for both. Villages and towns lie scattered across the surrounding mountains, hills, and valleys. Fields and terraces of maize, greens, cotton, and fruit orchards occupy valleys and lower slopes, while higher-altitude villages grow potatoes and quinoa. The villagers live a blessed life thanks to the Storm Queen. Their children grow up healthy and hale. Each harvest brings in a rich bounty. However, this idyllic life comes at a cost. Over the centuries, many local traditions have been lost as settlements integrate into the empire. Ruined cities lie empty and overgrown, their populations scattered by the Tempest Court to disperse rebels and quell their cultures. Changing weather patterns lead to the loss of unique crops, and shepherds must lead their flocks farther afield to graze. Villages close to pilgrimage roads must accommodate the influx of travelers at the cost of adequately feeding and sheltering themselves.

In the Mountain’s Shadow

Land-Under-Robe’s endless halcyon weather has another price. The Storm Queen and her weather-god lieutenants push foul weather to the realm’s borders, inflicting it on lands beyond. Thunderstorms and floods alternate with drought, causing terrible death and suffering.

Settlements can avoid these misfortunes by petitioning the Storm Queen to extend the Storm Wall past their lands. But this means submitting to her rule and

EX3

accepting Land-Under-Robe’s hegemony. Missionaries give settlements new names, often after an animal endemic to the area; residents append the settlement’s new name to their own names. Local gods become the Storm Queen’s vassals.

Perhaps most importantly, the settlement must provide constant, tangible support toward maintaining Quiverch. This includes sizable taxes in grain and other goods, laborers for endless urban renovation, and — of course — pilgrims to pray and make offerings to their divine sovereign and her court.

Settlements don’t always abide by the Storm Queen’s rule. Those that fail to pay taxes promptly, shelter bandits and heretics, or the like suffer a season of foul weather — storms, drought, flood — to cow them into submission. Should a village prove intransigent, the Storm Queen ruins it utterly, drowning it with floods or baking it beneath endless sun.

Still, this doesn’t entirely prevent banditry and rebellion. Outlaws lair in forests, hills, and caves, often with unhappy spirits’ aid. Not only do they raid villages, rob travelers, and attack tax caravans laden with foodstuffs, they burn roadside shrines to spite the Storm Queen and her court.

Whatever geographical limit there may be to the Storm Queen’s climatic influence, she hasn’t reached it. But the farther her sway extends, the fiercer the foul weather along the border becomes. And every new settlement brought within the Storm Wall pushes the border outward, afflicting new lands.

### Prominent Figures

The ecclesiarch Queya Phuyu is an old, old woman, though her face remains unlined and her hair holds only a few twists of white. In her sumptuous quarters in the Atanyuka, she meets with Quiverchi planners and architects, overseeing the everchanging temples and guiding each new development’s aesthetics. She leads a faction of ecclesiarchs pushing for military authority to raise and lead troops against some of Land-UnderRobe’s more egregious bandits; these would come from labor corvées, delaying Quiverch’s renovations. Other factions see this as a power grab. Rival ecclesiarch Oqolo Tuayna, a prominent traditionalist, denounces Phuyu as overly ambitious and questions her faith in the Storm Queen.

Born in an outlying village, Rapaqallu led a rebellion against the Storm Queen’s forces in his youth. Though

it was quickly quashed, the detachment of road priests who put down the rebellion saw potential in Rapaqallu and brought him on as an acolyte. Decades later, he’s now a road priest himself, patrolling the farthest-flung villages. Though his sermons evince a fierce pride in the Storm Queen’s rule, he’s dogged by rumors that he passively aids rebels by deliberately failing to report unrest along his route.

The elderly Kaltan runs a tea shop on Quiverch’s outskirts. He also tends a shrine to his father, the minor tea god Golden Li. Kaltan chronicles Land-Under-Robe’s history and legends; he collects stories from priest and pilgrim alike, sketches temples before they’re dismantled, and has his finger on the city’s pulse. Ever the storyteller, he’s a font of useful information and nigh-forgotten trivia regarding the land’s history. When his father cautions him to watch his words, he protests that telling stories never hurt anyone. But recent misfortunes — falling from a ladder, a kitchen fire, illness among his patrons — leave both worried that some divinity wishes to discredit or silence him.

### Neighbors

The nation of Vira perches arrogantly amid the mountains east of Land-Under-Robe. Its handful of tall, labyrinthine cities throng with skilled artisans, engineers, artists, and intellectuals. Surrounding villages grow potatoes and maize in terraces irrigated by mountain snowmelt. Soldiers extract tribute from valleys below, bringing up foodstuffs and lumber for their cities and laborers for their mines, roads, and other public works. Priests emerge from temples marked with suns, storms, and serpents to bestow divine blessings upon princes, farms, and soldiers.

But what once was a thriving, expanding civilization struggles against famine, landslides, and other disasters born of the expanding Storm Wall. Empress Suquya has moved the capital to Atoc-Uyu, the northernmost Viran city, as the Storm Wall slowly creeps across the nation’s south. The tempest-wracked cities of Xohul and Travertine, all but abandoned by residents, now serve as boltholes for Land-Under-Robe bandits and rebels. Meanwhile, Vira sends raiders through the Storm Wall to pillage food and goods from the closest Land-UnderRobe villages. Legend says the Blackblood Clans once dwelt amid fertile lowlands, worshiping the earth and all that lived within it. But centuries ago, when their weather god Amira Shattersky abandoned them to seek the Tempest Court, the rains began and never stopped, turning

EX3

fields to the lakes and marsh of the Turuqitan wetland. Today they worship Bend-in-the-Gale, god of reeds; they dwell in reed houses on artificial floating islands built from reeds. Healers use reed-based poultices and feed their patients reed-flower tea. Hunters and fishers go out in reed boats; weavers make reed mats for trade.

tribal leaders — serve as representatives; they discuss and resolve issues of mutual importance, from conflicts between tribes to external threats. But these weighty matters take place amid festivities and celebrations, where other attendees participate in feasting, contests of strength, and dancing circles.

The clans’ ancient animus toward Land-Under-Robe only grows as the Storm Wall slowly creeps across the Turuqitan wetland. Blackblood folk spit on hearing the Storm Queen’s name; they turn away pilgrims with threats and spears. Their hunters raid Land-UnderRobe folk who attempt to settle on the wetland’s shores, burning new villages to the ground.

One drum is particularly important, both to the Maremé as a whole and to the Wanikuya. The Heart of the Maremé is inlaid with rondels of white jade carved with pictograms depicting ancient stories; its drum skin once belonged to an ancient behemoth. According to the Maremé, they’ve always had this drum. It’s fiercely guarded; most Maremé would lay down their lives to protect it from harm or theft. They play it only in times of great need, whether to calm a mighty spirit or call the tribes to war.

## The Maremé Nation

The Maremé nation constitutes a loose confederation of several tribes, each ranging in size from a few hundred to several thousand souls, scattered in and around the eastern forests between the Hundred Kingdoms and Mahalanka. Many tribes are seminomadic, traveling within their favored environments — whether riverlands, marshes, or the tree canopy itself. Each tribe specializes in tools and skills suitable to its favored environment, such as scythes and reed cutting for the marshland Ra’amdo tribe, or training birds for the arboreal Wodadé tribe. Marriages, contracts, and trade between the tribes distribute those tools and skills widely. For outsiders, this fuels confusion about just who the Maremé are; some assume all Maremé tribes resemble the one they know, while others believe the Maremé share no common traits.

### Wanikuya: Drums in the Forests

Music, particularly drumming, connects the Maremé tribes. Each tribe owns a large ceremonial drum with stories of Maremé heroes written around the base. Individuals carry small drums worn at the waist, family heirlooms passed down through generations and decorated with ancestors’ names. Drums communicate messages across long distances in the forests, using a specialized Maremé drum language capable of communicating simple ideas. Drumming is also central to the Wanikuya ceremony that unites the tribes, with teams of drummers playing without stopping for the entire event. Four times a year, at the changing of the seasons, anywhere from a dozen to a hundred members of every tribe travel to a location decided at the previous Wanikuya. Five councilors from each tribe — chosen by and including

During the Winter Wanikuya, each tribe’s champions compete for the great honor of carrying the Heart. For several days, they pit their strength, wit, wisdom, and endurance against one another, submitting to judgment from the tribes’ elders to determine who’s most worthy. While foreigners may compete in the games, the tribes deem their entry merely a gesture of good sportsmanship. Should an outsider win, they receive gifts and favorable contracts from the Maremé, but never the Heart itself.

### Di’in’mé: Protection Contracts

Neighboring peoples know the Maremé best for the protection contracts, or di’in’mé, that some tribes enter with local villages. So long as the village makes regular payments and takes no hostile action against the tribe, the tribe refrains from raiding the village, and will come to the village’s defense when needed — whether against foreign slavers, neighboring villages, or even other Maremé. This occasionally brings tribes into conflict, as the Maremé have no qualms with raiding villages protected by other tribes. The di’in’mé epitomizes the Maremé view of contracts, which govern marriages, tribal alliances, trade, and other important affairs. Maremé nobles can be called upon as mediators between members of their tribe if one feels a contract was violated. (Violations between members of different tribes are addressed at the Wanikuya.) Contracts can be permanent or temporary, and may contain any number of escape clauses. Failing to honor a contract is a source of indelible shame. Tribes and individuals who do so are exiled, no longer considered Maremé people. Foreigners who

EX3

abuse one tribe’s trust find that other tribes turn on them as word spreads, especially at Wanikuya. While the Maremé claim to reject the institution of slavery, they keep indentured servants. This involves a contract to provide domestic labor for one’s master for a set term — typically ten years — while the master provides for the servant’s basic needs. However, contracts may be agreed to under duress, such as offering a captive the choice between indentured servitude or death, and one master can trade the contract to another at will. Mistreating an indentured servant theoretically brings the same shame as any other contract violation. But in practice, Maremé often look the other way when presented with a prestigious or vindictive master’s cruelties.

### Social Divisions

As nomadic and seminomadic people, acquiring food is a daily priority. This engenders a sense of egalitarianism and cooperation within the tribe. Someone who’s well off today may be brought low by bad luck tomorrow. So the only official social ranking within the Maremé is the division between noble and vassal.

In theory, within those divisions, no individual outranks another, and claiming higher rank than another within the same division can easily provoke a fight. In practice, charismatic leaders, powerful warlords, coteries of elders, and the like often subvert this egalitarianism. Savvy Maremé privately acknowledge them as rulers in all but name.

Nobility derives from deeds: victories in battle, successful negotiation of important contracts, lifesaving ingenuity in managing limited resources, and curing the sick can all elevate a Maremé to this status. Each tribe’s noble representatives elevate new nobles at Wanikuya. Likewise, they may strip away nobility for severe misdeeds: losing battles through cowardice, betraying the tribe’s trust, failing to honor contracts, and so forth. Leaders often cement their power by elevating their cronies while refusing elevation to or stripping nobility from rivals. This can backfire; done to excess, it prompts mockery and disdain at Wanikuya. Other tribes may offer membership and nobility to heroic Maremé seen as unfairly passed over.

Upon coming of age during puberty — the rites vary from tribe to tribe — every nonnoble Maremé

EX3

establishes a contract with a noble, becoming their vassal. Those stripped of nobility must do the same. In a traditional contract, vassals follow their lieges’ orders in battle or other emergencies, but they aren’t servants and have no additional obligations to their lieges. They have no obligations at all to other nobles, but those who ignore a noble’s expertise and wisdom may lose face. Traditionally, the noble-vassal relationship is of mutual respect, as vassalage contracts contain escape clauses allowing nobles to divest themselves of undesirable vassals and mistreated vassals to seek new lieges. But prestigious nobles and skilled vassals have significant leeway in setting terms. Meanwhile, weak or disreputable nonnoble youths and nobles alike have little recourse but to contract with those few Maremé who’ll take them, and they may find themselves taken advantage of. This can involve abusive contract terms — which the Maremé deem dishonorable to demand — but more often entails threats of invoking an escape clause to leave the other partner in the lurch. A noble’s parents, siblings, and children share her rank in most respects. But they cannot hold vassals, and their rank depends on the one they’ve gained it from; if she’s stripped of nobility, so are they.

### Daily Life

How individuals are expected to contribute to the tribe’s survival is largely determined by gender. Maremé hold that only an individual can assign gender — or lack thereof — to themself. Naturally, it follows that, to the Maremé, gender cannot be assigned at birth; one must allow children and adolescents to try on different genders and tell others what their gender might be. By their coming of age, a Maremé young adult typically has developed a nuanced understanding of their gender and the gender roles that suit them. Maremé encourage adults who need more time or whose understanding of their gender develops as they age to embrace their curiosity about themselves and to embody their understanding of their gender as it evolves over the course of their lifetimes.

Adult women maintain and defend the camp, negotiate contracts, and raise children. Likewise, women own and inherit all property beyond personal items. Their control of tribal and familial resources and their influence over the next generation grants them easy access to political power. Adult men occupy themselves with procuring food and military action outside the camp. Those who feel no connection to gender, whose gender cannot be described as masculine or feminine, or

whose gender encompasses masculine, feminine, and more ways of being occupy a special position. Maremé legend holds that such people have been touched by forest gods; they’re raised to be diplomats and shamans. Marriage contracts cover not only what material goods each spouse brings to the union, but also covers their duties and responsibilities within the home. The contracts last from one to seven years; when they expire, spouses may renew their terms, renegotiate them, or dissolve the contract and end the marriage. Many Maremé marry other members of the tribe in which they’re raised, though romance also commonly blooms when people meet at the Wanikuya. In fact, several dances and competitions there are specifically geared towards young people impressing one another. Young children assist with chores, and learn to cook, weave, ride, and fight from the camp’s women. As they grow older, they accompany men on foraging and hunting trips. They sit quietly or serve refreshments while negotiations take place, learning what makes a good contract or favorable trade. Much of this is a community affair: a child learns from everyone in the camp. Parents have ultimate say in more complicated matters, though they often listen to others who work closely with the child.

The Maremé live in tents that are quick to assemble or break down. Animal hides and bark are the primary coverings, depending on what’s most available locally. Sizes vary, from single-person tents to pavilions accommodating three generations of a family. Some tribes build permanent meetinghouses, shrines, and similar structures in locations they return to seasonally. These stand unused when the tribe is elsewhere. Small family groups share meals together, seated on the ground around a large tray of food. Those too sick or injured to join their kin have food brought to them first. Next, those able to join but too infirm to feed themselves are served. Lastly, those in the circle serve themselves. By tradition, food preparation and meals are silent.

Most Maremé meals consist of nuts, fruits, berries, and vegetables. Occasionally, families supplement meals with meat from small game, which they cook over a spit or wrap in leaves to roast among a fire’s embers. Fish forms much of the diet of those who live by the water. Most Maremé clothing is functional rather than decorative, made from cotton and linen. Flowers, plants, and other locally available materials dictate what dyes

## Saploth, the Crimson Lily Citadel

a tribe uses. The Tileli tribe’s earthy reds come from red onion skins gathered in summer. Hunters of the Hu’wi tribe dye their clothing green using nettles, the better to stalk prey unseen.

NOTABLE MAREMÉ TRIBES

The Dagui’on inhabit the forest’s edge. Among the most aggressive and prideful Maremé, they often raid nearby villages, and train war animals to supplement their fighting forces. The tribe’s shamans offer blessings in the form of painted, lacquered walnut shells that successful warriors string into necklaces to adorn themselves or their favored familiars.

Many tribes frequently engage in combat, so armor and shields are common. These include ornate leather or wooden helmets, hide-covered wooden shields, and lamellar sewn with wooden plates. The A’kutu tribe instead favors sewing on holed Ixcoatli coins obtained from traders.

The Ra’amdo navigate the wildlife-rich Caiman Marshes on wide, flat boats pushed with poles. They mostly roam near the wetland village of Bentorva, maintaining a closer relationship with them than most do with the subjects of their protection contracts. Intermarriage between the Ra’amdo and Bentorva’s folk grows common, such that some other Maremé feel the Ra’amdo are forgetting who they are.

### Religion

Maremé religion centers around contracts between humans and gods. These are rarely personal; most were forged long ago, by either a tribe or the entire Maremé people.

The jaguar goddess Sadunel-Ata’s contract with the Maremé people guides many of their actions. She’s a jealous goddess, demanding most of the Maremé’s worship; this causes friction with other gods who therefore feel slighted. As part of her contract with the Maremé, their nobles may petition for her favor. She gifts those who please her — usually by completing some task, such as offering animal sacrifices or preventing a jaguar hunt — with a feline familiar. Because of this, some Maremé are skilled at raising war cats. Reaching-Fingers, the chief forest god of the Maremé lands, also receives regular worship. They have little interest in mortal affairs other than warfare. Forestdwelling Maremé tribes’ guerilla tactics fascinate Reaching-Fingers; they occasionally appear to warriors on the eve of battle to discuss tactics and strategy. If local tribes go too long without skirmishing, ReachingFingers may demand they go to war to keep the god entertained.

Maremé lands shelter trickster spirits who, by ancient contract, may steal food if someone speaks. These spirits — the flame-headed lemur elementals called ataren-temsé, the wood spiders serving Reaching-Fingers, and a few others — are in turn sworn to harass intruders who invade the Maremé woods, though this contract’s specifics are among the Maremé shamans’ secrets.

They’re among the most isolationist Maremé, eschewing di’in’mé contracts and rarely interacting with other tribes outside of the Wanikuya.

The elder Sa’mané is a respected thaumaturge of the river tribes who has no gender. Sa’mané spent a year as Reaching-Fingers’s apprentice, learning to read futures in the veined undersides of leaves. Sa’mané’s advice warned the Ra’amdo tribe that a neighbor signed a contract in bad faith, and set the famed warrior Ba’teqal on the path to winning the Heart of the Maremé — a victory whose tale the tribes still tell. Elderly now, Sa’mané permanently resides in a hut alongside the Blue Vine River. Sa’mané hopes to find a worthy apprentice from any tribe to pass their gifts onto before they pass.

Saploth, the

Crimson Lily Citadel

In the days before the Exalted, when nonhuman peoples walked the world, the saurian race now called Dragon Kings held a high place in Creation. They built wonders across the eight directions, and from their great cities oversaw a prehistoric golden age that’s all but forgotten today.

EX3

The Dragon Kings built the city of Saploth at the apex of their society as a testament to the great heights they’d reached. Its people crafted mighty relics; its theaters performed plays whose stories still echo today. Its neighborhoods encompassed high towers, sprawling manors, grand plazas, and verdant gardens. The Harpand-Drum Palace stood proudly at Saploth’s heart, encircled by the grand amphitheater of the Unfurling Petal Arena. There, Saploth’s priest-queen oversaw the bloody rites by which her people venerated the Unconquered Sun.

As visitors walk between the beast’s jaws, a gleaming boulevard beckons them into the city. A thousand ribs from the same behemoth line this Avenue of Approaching the Sun; eternal lanterns set into the bones still shine at night, casting an eerie glow. Statues of Dragon King princes and scholars once lined Saploth’s streets; most now lie scattered in pieces. At the avenue’s far end, the Harp-and-Drum Palace looms above an encircling arena of sand and brown dust. Bridges extend from the palace’s golden spires in great sweeping arcs, linking it to towers near and far throughout the city.

Amid all its grand beauty and innovation lurked strange occurrences. Residents spoke of haunted places, of ominous echoes drifting down fog-shrouded alleys. They avoided places the undead were said to wander — skeletal Dragon Kings who refused to relinquish their rule. A coterie of their unquiet remains may yet lurk among the city’s abandoned parlors.

The inhuman lords once gathered along these bridges to watch the bloodshed in the Unfurling Petal Arena below. In Saploth’s early days, priests offered living sacrifices of their own kind to the Unconquered Sun in solemn rites. In later eras, Dragon Kings cheered as slaves slaughtered one another or struggled against wild beasts and exotic monsters, staining the fine sand with their blood.

While humankind reached its own heights in the First Age, Dragon King society faltered. Saploth reflected this decline: its forges churned out poorer quality metal and crystal until, ultimately, their fires went out. Great artists fell into obscurity; the city fell into disrepair. With the advent of the Shogunate, the city raised fortifications against humankind’s advance. Saploth, once a center of ingenuity and learning, became a haven for riot and blood sport. The gore that splashed upon its amphitheater’s stones like so many red flowers gave the city its sobriquet: the Crimson Lily Citadel. The city lies quiet now. Within its workshops rest elegant, unused tools; its storerooms overflow with goods from a bygone age. Beasts and the dead haunt its streets as the buildings crumble around them. The broken dragon lines leading to the Harp-and-Drum Palace flare with wild Essence with no one to maintain them. Saploth slumbers in forgotten decay.

### The Ruins of Saploth

The Horned Gate greets those who approach Saploth on the long-overgrown main road. Carved from a titanic behemoth’s skull, its twisting, spiraling horns unnerved those who meant to storm the city. Watchtowers carved from its cyclopean bones still dot the outer fortifications. The forest, once kept at a respectful distance, now laps at the walls. Vines grow over stones and bone; boughs overhang the lofty parapets. Walls that stood impregnable for thousands of years now buckle as tree roots gnaw at their foundations.

### Descendants of a Forgotten Age

The so-called jungle stalkers — feral descendants of the Dragon Kings, reincarnated with only bestial instincts and no one to guide them to spiritual refinement — run riot across Saploth. Packs stake out territory, each ruled by their strongest member until someone stronger takes their place. The bravest (and those with nothing to lose) claim territory closer to the haunted arena. One such alpha has prowled the northern city for close to a century. Explorers who’ve evaded her pack and escaped Saploth have named her the Sapphire Stalker for her brilliant blue scales. Larger and more intelligent than most, she commands her pack. Thanks to her well-earned longevity, Sapphire sits on the cusp of enlightenment. When she sleeps, she sees flashes of a past life in which she resided in the golden Harp-andDrum Palace, ruling as queen. At times, she’s drawn across the bridges to the Palace, where she stares in frustrated longing at her people’s ancient script, seeking understanding. Though fiercely territorial, as Sapphire grows closer to her past glory, she finds herself becoming curious about outsiders. As she doesn’t yet grasp spoken language and remains driven by saurian instincts, audiences with her tend to be short; her patience wears thin, and none have escaped her claws unscarred.

Nenemaak walks the ruins in search of others like the Sapphire Stalker. This winged Dragon King didn’t hail from Saploth in this or any incarnation. Originally from

EX3

revenants — using threats, malevolent charisma, and necromancy. Garbed in the tattered robes of ancient Dragon King priests, the Celebrant performs ghastly rites to the Neverborn before every battle on the sands. It walks hunched over, its cowl half-concealing its flayed face. A pack of obedient mortwights follows, snarling, at its heels. Its other servants prowl the city, seeking stalkers or scavengers to trap and return to their master for its games.

### TOWER OF THE SCALED HERMIT

This ancient tower, its sandstone walls carved to resemble scales, has largely withstood the ravages of time. Dragon King savants used the city’s sorcerous engines to ignite a pillar of fire so bright it could be seen for miles. When lit, the fire served as a warning beacon to other Dragon King cities, its color alerting them to the type of danger: a hostile army’s approach, an impending natural disaster, a wrathful spirit’s rampage. Long has the tower lain quiet; its decayed engines failed entirely after Nenemaak’s geomantic adjustments triggered the beacon, make it impossible to light again until they’re repaired.

the southern mountains, he was similarly troubled with flashes of insight that drove him from his clutch. After many trials and with guidance from beings older than he, Nenemaak remembered what he truly was. He’s taken it upon himself to restore the Dragon Kings to their enlightened state.

Nenemaak’s journeys took him to the Eastern forests, where he sought the legendary Dragon King metropolis of Rathess, only to flee from the horrors he found there. Turning to Saploth, Nenemaak has taken up residence at the top of the Tower of the Scaled Hermit, where most of his primal kin cannot reach. When he’s not attempting to elevate the stalkers — an effort that’s thus far borne little fruit — he seeks to repair the tower’s damaged geomancy. This has recently caused the tower’s beacon to flare above the trees in a colorful display, stirring rumors of a powerful occult weapon hidden in the region. Largely safe in his tower eyrie, Nenemaak nonetheless watches the city cautiously for potential threats. None seem greater than the arena’s fell inhabitants and their dreadful master.

### The Arena of Shadows

In the arena, specters from the past lurch and shamble across ashlike sand. Once dedicated to the sun, the site has become a shadowland nestled at Saploth’s heart. For centuries, the jungle stalkers avoided the arena, lest they be forced to fight in cruel mockery of the games in which their people once rejoiced.

The Celebrant of Shedding Skin, a dreadful nephwrack, now rules the Arena. It’s bound most of Saploth’s undead to its will — from foolhardy scavengers’ hungry ghosts to the jungle stalkers’ horrid

The Celebrant pits captives against the undead remnants of dead gladiators and monstrous beasts. Its prized pet is the spectral echo of the massive behemoth from whose skeleton the Horned Gate is built. This ghostly monster — so large that it scarcely fits in the sprawling arena — stalks the Underworld near the shadowland’s edge, awaiting its master’s call. Its long, spindly legs carry its immense bulk; numerous horns grow from its skull-like face. The nephwrack has fed it well since it bound it, throwing many rivals to the beast’s maw.

When not watching its slaves fight, the Celebrant commands them all — be they stalker, undead, or mortal — to build a temple to its dark masters beneath the Harpand-Drum Palace. With enough worship, the Celebrant hopes to poison the manse and attune it to the deathly energies it prefers. It pursues this goal with as much zeal as it does the fights in the arena.

### Neighbors

Descended from the Dragon Kings’ human servants, the nomadic Ah-Ciliz have dwelt in the surrounding forest for centuries. They’ve passed down stories of the mystical dragons who ruled them and worship their memory as gods. Though the dead and the jungle stalkers make Saploth too dangerous to approach, they consider it a holy site, and its relics — from etched shards of blue-green metal to Dragon King bones — sacred things that empower their people. They believe the stalkers to be emissaries of their gods, not realizing they’re one and the same.

Their current leader, the hunter Votan, has braved Saploth six times to retrieve its relics. During one such trip, Votan encountered the Sapphire Stalker and felt, from their brief interaction, that she sought to deliver him a message from the gods. Now his clan’s shamans give him offerings and advice, sending him back to the city every few months to attempt to establish contact with her. She leads him to relics that he brings back to the Ah-Ciliz. Foreign merchants from the Soaring Ibis Company who’ve gotten wind of this send stealthy

EX3

agents to track Votan through Saploth. They intend to acquire relics for themselves, or even better, to capture the Sapphire Stalker.

A tributary of the Blithe River flows through the Jewelbank, an area about four miles long and a mile wide. Where once ancient traders used it to shorten the journey between now-fallen Karatul and Almios, now its waters are all but devoid of travelers. Branches dripping with moss and unnatural crystals overhang the water, and the fish that swim in its currents boast mouthfuls of sharp adamantine teeth. Beyond the riverbanks, the forest is overgrown with flora seen nowhere else in Creation. These plants and trees — and the animals that hunt nearby — descend from Dragon King experiments. Left unchecked in their creators’ absence, the Jewelbank’s inhabitants survived and mutated further.

### ELYTRUM

Dense forest, rich with fruit trees, grows within a hundred-mile ring of jagged hills north of Rathess. Once, numerous villages and city-states rose here, each with its own songs, crafts, and customs. Today, most stand abandoned, crusted with masses of strange violet fungus and surrounded by mass graves. The last survivors cluster in the tumbledown city of Elytrum, their final sanctuary amid the fungal plague. The survivors subsist on farming, gathering, and fishing; no land animals beyond insects and arthropods remain. They wear colorful, long-beaked masks, packed with medicinal herbs meant to thwart the fungus’ unseen spores. After generations of sickness, they’re largely immune; nonetheless, new infections outnumber births. Hooded caretakers tend the sick, and attempt to quarantine rare visitors lest they bring the plague to the outside world.

Infected creatures go through the motions of life, growing slow, stolid and silent over several days, like a zombie. When a victim dies, a spindly purple fungus-manikin tears itself from the corpse. The ruins and forest throng with the child-sized creatures, whose fruiting bodies spread the plague; the survivors destroy them on sight. In the forest’s demesnes, manikins build elaborate structures of stone, wood, bone, and fungus. Coronas of colored light crackle across these twisted edifices beneath the new moon. Elytrum’s people shun these sites; the caretakers whisper of some great and awful power drawing ever closer to those places as it moves beneath the skin of the world.

The Jewelbank’s treasures occasionally tempt traders and adventurers, though few who enter the area leave unscathed. Animals here hold little fear toward human hunters. The fruit, though sweet-smelling, is poisonous. A wrong step can unleash a cloud of spores that settle in the lungs and cause all manner of illnesses.

## Amaryllis

Along the Golden Road between Greyfalls and Ixcoatli, there rises a quartet of huge silver pyramids, the forest’s colors dancing off their reflective surfaces like petals on a pond. These change with the seasons: blues and grays in winter, golds and greens for high summer. These pyramids stand at the heart of the city of Amaryllis, which lies at the fringes of a woodland bordermarch. Ruled by four Fair Folk — the Sovereigns Eternal — and their fae lieutenants, Amaryllis is unusual for its social order, wherein mortals bend the knee to the Fair Folk. It wasn’t always thus. When the Contagion hit, it plunged the mortal city of Amaryllis into civil war, further winnowing its already decimated population. When the Fair Folk invaded, Amaryllis might as well have just thrown open its gates for them. Some sources suggest this was actually what happened — raksha rulers were a better option than everyone dying. The Sovereigns Eternal don’t seem to mind this rumor, but then again, they don’t mind any rumor that divides the populace.

### A Wyld-Touched City

Wyld energies radiate from a nearby promontory across miles of forest, river, and cultivated fields, encompassing the entire city and much of its farmland. Creatures exposed to this bordermarch sometimes acquire traits from pollinating insects and flowers; these might include antennae, flower-petal hair, vestigial butterfly wings, a rose’s prickles, or a bee’s long tongue; they might exude a sweet scent or scatter pollen in their wake. Humans acquire these traits less frequently, but a few citizens find themselves thus marked nonetheless. Even inanimate objects manifest these qualities; older buildings’ walls and windows naturally form bas-reliefs of flowers, wasps, or honeycomb. Amaryllis’ mortal residents retain their souls. While criminals meet their fate at the soul-hungry mouths of their Fair Folk rulers, the Sovereigns Eternal decided long ago that overall, the best method of feeding is skimming the emotions off the top of the boiling pot of this city’s people, along with those of visiting merchants and other travelers. The Sovereigns encourage

EX3

all manner of exciting activities — from trade, theater, and celebrations to cutthroat crafts-guild politics, banditry, and even rebellion — to stir up passions for them to devour. They even appoint bureaucrats, artisan’s guild leaders, and military officers as much for eccentricity and vanity as for competence. As a result, Amaryllis is full of colorful markets, back-alley deals, festivals, and funerals.

Meals — rarely dull in Amaryllis — offer a feast for both the eyes and the belly. Fresh fruits add a pop of bright color to a dish, and a sweet or tangy element to its flavor. Hot peppers enhance the taste of even mundane offerings, and sweet desserts round out each repast. Local specialties include baked cheese stuffed with meat, olives, capers, and tomatoes; spicy goat meat stew with papaya; and deep-fried dumplings rolled in sugar. Amaryllis fashion features brightly colored hand-painted or wax print fabrics, used in skirts, coats, and headwraps. Ruffles on sleeves, necklines, cuffs, and hems add extra interest. Long, curly or wavy hair is currently in fashion, adorned with ribbons, beads, or other trinkets.

The Sovereigns Eternal have redesigned and rebuilt the city to overwhelm the grandeur of its First Age days. The four pyramids form the centerpiece to a beautiful, shimmering city. Proud sycamores line avenues running through Amaryllis’ center, lovely as any Blessed Isle boulevard. Smaller lanes branch off in all directions, flanked with tidy brick and cedar buildings. Some are plain, with only a painted door as an ornament. Others are trimmed with frothy wooden lace, stylized stone visages, and shards of glass and colorful stones. Wealthier townhouses sport airy porches, and even in less fortunate areas, paper lanterns of every color burn night and day. These float in basins of water or hang from strands of rope and ribbon, mimicking the Sovereigns’ glistening pyramids. The streets throng even at night, and music rings through the air. All this activity and beauty draws trade from across the East, despite the prominent fae presence. The Sovereigns Eternal welcome the influx of foreign dreams and desires; they impose no restrictions or tariffs, the better to attract travelers. Merchants from distant lands flow into the Buttercup District’s markets to buy and sell. The city’s handicrafts — some marked by the Wyld, others displaying a fae-blooded artisan’s

EX3

THE SOVEREIGNS’ PACT

### The Sovereigns Eternal

only devour souls by unanimous consent among the four. While nothing directly prevents one from doing otherwise, they’ve sworn a binding oath that if caught, the transgressor must submit to a humiliating forfeit agreed upon by the other three. As creatures of passion, they occasionally lose self-control; each watches the others for an opportunity to reveal such a slip.

Myara of the Seven Keys stands all of four feet tall. A train of servants carrying stacks of books taller than she is usually follows in her wake. She wears a ring of seven keys around her neck, each of different materials. One is rumored to be iron, to “keep her sharp.”

touch — bring high prices elsewhere. Especially popular are breastplates that gleam like a beetle’s wing, moth-shaped masks so realistic that they seem to move, and honey that brings deep, peculiar dreams. Staying in Amaryllis has its consequences. The bordermarch occasionally warps visitors, while a traveler might catch a Fair Folk’s eye. Loreleis invite potential paramours into flower-draped parlors, while a Sovereign’s hobgoblin guard watches for anyone who might offend their master. These dangers don’t always dissuade immigrants. The food is wonderful, the courtesans welcoming, the pyramids shine with the lights of the forest and the sky — why would anyone want to leave?

The Sovereigns Eternal

It’s said that Lhanz Lun was the first to breach Amaryllis’ walls with his raw strength and power. He commands the city’s military and leaves the rest of the politicking to the other three Sovereigns Eternal. A ten-foot-tall nightmarish cross between a wasp and an ogre, Lun has few interests beyond warfare. He often wears nothing but his orichalcum-striped breastplate, his daiklaive, and enemy combatants’ blood. But despite his appearance, he’s no unthinking berserker; skilled in strategy and tactics, he’s also a competent military administrator.

Fairy tales throughout Creation warn of evil sorceresses hiding behind rich robes and kind countenances. Skein-of-Eyes likes to say that they’re talking about her. No one’s certain what she looks like beneath her cloak of midnight purple, concealed as she is with one of her many masks constructed from sumptuous fabrics, precious materials, and priceless gems. It’s said that canny, sweet-voiced Skein-of-Eyes was the first to breach Amaryllis’ walls through disguise,

Myara is the most likely Sovereign Eternal to be out among the people. She holds great influence over Amaryllis’ healers, occultists, teachers, and scholars — she trained many herself, and knows all their secrets — and appoints leaders for most of the city’s artisan guilds. It’s said she was the first to breach Amaryllis’ walls with the tempting lie that she possessed a cure for the afflicted populace.

No one ignores Lord Seven-Dooms when he enters a room. Setting aside his seven-foot stature, he’s uncannily lovely, with silk-soft skin, cheekbones that could cut a heart in two, and full lips ripe for kissing. His dark eyes weep blood at emotional moments, and he always smells of cedar wood and rich red wine. While not the most physically puissant of the Sovereigns Eternal, some consider Lord Seven-Dooms the most dangerous. He has nigh-complete control in every social situation; many a mortal has fallen into his arms and, sometimes, borne his fae-blooded infants in a childbed of blood and death.

It’s said that Lord Seven-Dooms was the first to breach Amaryllis’ walls by weeping outside the gates and preying on its soldiers’ sympathies. He oversees nothing directly but the city’s courtesan guild; neverthetheless, his influence is everywhere.

### Prominent Figures

Itaru Emet efficiently and effectively administrates the Sachet, Amaryllis’ tax bureau. Word of his competence spread, however, and the Sovereigns Eternal learned that if you want something done, Emet is the person to ask. Now he spends his days tangled in their political schemes, trying to please their strange whims and avoid their ire. His daughter Tamur takes after him; Emet worries she’ll end up ensnared in the Sovereigns’ schemes as well. He listens for opportunities that might suit her outside Amaryllis, but keeps his inquiries discreet lest the Sovereigns take notice or offense.

EX3

The bordermarch’s Wyld influence gave Endara IronTongue her iridescent eyes, but the Sovereigns themselves planted the seeds of revolution in her heart. She envisions an Amaryllis free of Fair Folk rule, where mortals can thrive without fear. Once one of Skeinof-Eyes’ intelligence agents, now she stays one step ahead of her former colleagues as she meets with other like-minded mortals to foment rebellion. Yeral the Wise gathers his faithful before the pyramids once a week, delivering sermons dedicated to the Sovereigns’ might and splendor. His cult has grown rapidly over the last year, buoyed by the occasional Sovereign’s personal appearance. In truth, the Fair Folk care little for the cultists, but their fervor tastes sweet on the air. Yeral and Endara haven’t yet clashed directly, but his sermons and her speeches each allude to the other’s misguided ways. Skirmishes have broken out between their followers, threatening to boil over into a larger conflict.

The merchant prince Jadesh Banatharya brought his trade to Amaryllis a decade ago and has grown his influence since. Though throngs of traders pass along the Golden Road, many of their routes stop short of Amaryllis itself for fear of its strangeness. Banatharya seeks to lure in more business for his new patron Myara of the Seven Keys, offering tempting but unsavory deals on the city’s wondrous craftwork.

### Neighbors

The small trading town of Calathea sprang up on Amaryllis’s doorstep two generations ago. Since it lies outside the bordermarch’s reach, some Golden Road

traders now bypass Amaryllis and do business in this safer boomtown instead. Headquartered there is the Winter Boughs Company. For a price, this Guild subsidiary provides Calathea with mercenaries to protect it from the bandits that the Sovereigns Eternal encourage — and against Amaryllis should the city move against them. Also on the Winter Boughs’ payroll are the sorcerer Cerien, whose demon scouts are almost as terrifying as the Fair Folk, and the outcaste champion Posan Stormfist. Posan’s ambitions are no secret: he challenges Amaryllis now, but intends to rule it someday. Beyond Amaryllis’ farmland stands Wildrose Wood. From this Wyld-touched forest’s overgrown thickets, human and fae bandits alike harry traders and travelers headed to the city, sabotage supply caravans, and steal treasures destined for the Sovereigns’ parlors. Their puissant Fair Folk leader, the swaggering, grayeyed duelist Bregne of the Quicksilver Blade, nurses a grudge as old as the Sovereigns Eternal: she ought to have breached the city’s walls beside her four peers, but one or more of them betrayed her.

The trade city of Eke Ya’axa, Amaryllis’ eastern neighbor on the Golden Road, has recently been conquered by the Thousand Fangs Army, bringing it into the Lunar elder Raksi’s Total Control Zone. The city’s fortified palace-temples lie scattered among villages and fields, connected by a series of sacred roads and market plazas. Amaryllis has long been friendly to Raksi, treating Lunar visitors as honored guests; Raksi herself occasionally corresponds with Myara and Skein to discuss arcane fae lore. Newfound anxiety among Amaryllis’ people that they’re Raksi’s next conquest only feeds the Sovereigns’ hunger.

EX3

Nystia slumped against the cavern’s smooth stone walls, exhausted. Her tools lay neatly around her: an ancient text, sigils drawn with powdered pearls, a bowl of pure, clear water. Her talisman’s glittering ruby eye stared at her from within its silver setting, its glow fading as the ring of her spell’s words died down.

Her peers in Ysyr would smirk to see her so disheveled, might whisper behind their hands at the toll her spell had taken if they saw her so weakened. But she was alive. Better, she was triumphant. In the center of her circle sat the most exquisite creature she’d ever seen. A finely wrought collar encircled his neck, its spellwork etchings still glowing molten-yellow. To look at him now, her captive was serenity incarnate, but ten minutes ago, he’d been a snarling blur of rage and teeth and fury when he realized Nystia had trapped him in place. Had she flinched, had she slipped at any step, she’d be dead — or worse.

She smoothed her sleeves and rose to her feet. The Fair Folk artisan’s eyes tracked her, their blue as bright as any wyrdlight illuminating the streets of Ysyr. He might have been a statue brought to life, a moonsilver idol set to motion. Sorcerers in Ysyr shaped themselves into their own perfected images, acquiring an uncanny beauty; Nystia wondered how much of what her captive showed her now was influenced by her own features. In those last moments before her spell took hold, he’d shown her what kinds of things he could make out of her. She’d nearly been drawn in by it, that temptation to let him mold her beyond mere beauty into perfection.

It was precisely why she’d chosen him. Items he crafted appealed to their owner’s vanity, made them see not only how wonderful they could be, but how splendid they already were. Mirrors reflected flawless images of those who peered into them, swords sliced the air in graceful arcs, flutes piped notes clear and true when touched by a musician’s lips.

Nystia stood to make a fortune.

She approached her captive, careful not to disturb the powdered-pearl sigils. Even now, she sensed his power. Once more, the image of what he could make out of her tugged at her desires and ambitions. She pushed them away with great effort.

The collar’s sigils, cooling now, cast a red-hot sheen on the skin of his neck. When they were the same dark gray as the rest of the ornament, the binding would be complete and she’d lead him to her home high above the city. “We’ll be the envies of Ysyr,” she told him. “The princes will stand in awe of my might, and you’ll shape their dreams into baubles... for the right price.” She imagined how word would spread as they ascended to her crystalline quarters. In the months to come, what guests she’d entertain! Perhaps she’d allow those who were willing to pay a chance to watch him work. Even his process was beautiful to behold.

Her Fair Folk companion didn’t respond. Nystia drew closer, though she knew she shouldn’t. His intoxicating offer thrilled her still, made her breath catch with its terrible concept. She’d be perfect beyond anything her sorcery could achieve. Eternal. She could reach into the circle and loosen the collar, and...

Nystia snatched her hand back and scuttled backwards in horror. Her captive’s laughter echoed off the walls, surrounding her with his otherworldly mirth. How close she’d come to letting him go! Her composure ebbed back slowly. By the time it returned, her captive had gone quiet again. His eyes still glowed that wyrdlight blue, but now she saw past their shine and could read the murder in his gaze.

One more time, she checked her working to make sure the bond had held. He was hers for a year and a day.

# Chapter Five: The Dreaming Sea

## Champoor, the Nighted City

Chapter Five

The Dreaming Sea

A realm of wonder and terror, the Dreaming Sea touches upon the Wyld and brings strange prodigies back into Creation. Here, far beyond the Realm’s reach, mighty supernatural powers move openly upon the world, their empires rising and falling across the centuries. The Fair Folk of the Orchid Court rove these strange waters in glass ships, raiding coastal settlements. Prehuman peoples dwell in isolation upon lost islands and forgotten coves. The Dragon-Blooded lords of Prasad carve out a mighty nation upon its western coast; the sorcerer-princes of Ysyr extend their reach across its southern shores. Today these empires clash, as others in the region have clashed before, leaving weird and haunted ruins scattered in their wake. A tropical region, the Dreaming Sea’s coast remains warm year-round, with a dry season at midyear. The rainy season occupies the rest, occasionally bringing with it Wyld-spawned weather phenomena like rains of fish, frogs, or flowers. Farther inland, such as on the great steppes south of Prasad, the climate grows drier overall, with more temperature variation — hotter in the dry season, cooler in the wet.

Champoor,

the Nighted City

Once, Champoor was the capital of Simharajala, a vast empire. Its armies and fleets subdued neighboring peoples and swept away bandits and pirates. Its merchants went forth bearing silks and spices, teas and medicaments, delicate porcelain tableware and hardy soapstone worship vessels. They returned with jade, silver, and foreign wonders. Its guardian gods watched over its cities and fleets, warding off hostile spirits, sorcery, and the Fair Folk.

Simharajala grew rich and fat on trade and tribute, blessed with a harbor on the Dreaming Sea. Its defenses were both natural and manmade. Fortresses and warrior clans held its borders. For a time, it seemed the empire would abide forever.

To the west rose haughty Prasad, beloved of the Dragons. To the southeast, Ysyr crawled from its Contagion grave with magic beyond anything Simharajala could command. Pirates and Fair Folk clawed at Simharajala’s commerce; rebellions wracked the outer provinces; pretenders raised armies against the throne. The guardian gods quarreled and scattered, some defeated by Pure Way monks, others suborned by the Dragon Clans’ blandishments. As Simharajala teetered on the brink of disaster, the darkness yielded up its salvation: the Court of Secrets.

A ship rose from the depths inside the harbor itself, a junk lashed together from the bones of fallen leviathans, its sails the luminescent membranes of creatures that stalk the lightless depths. As the city’s weary defenders watched in awe and fear, it came to rest at Champoor’s docks, mooring itself with ropes braided from drowned sailors’ hair. From its decks emerged the dragon Tenepeshu of the Tenebrous Depths, goddess of deep waters where sunlight never reaches. In her train followed gods and spirits driven from their holdings by the relentless expansion of Prasad and its Pure Way. Ushered swiftly into the imperial palace, the dragon-goddess and her retinue made a shocking offer: for the sake of thwarting Prasad and punishing its proud impiety, they’d drive off the invading armies. In return, they asked that the city open its doors to gods and spirits from the Dreaming Sea’s deeps, offering them refuge from the Fair Folk and worship from Champoor’s people. With the sound of siege machinery battering at their city’s trembling walls, the emperor and his counselors agonized only a short time before accepting this divine offer unconditionally.

It was a decision nearly all of them would come to regret.

Tenepeshu told the city’s rulers to issue an edict: none but soldiers tasked with the city’s defense should venture forth for three days and three nights. Messengers exhorted residents to gather what supplies they required, to lock their doors and shutter their windows, and not to emerge no matter what they might hear.

EX3

The next morning, the sun didn’t rise over Champoor. The perfect darkness of the oceanic depths prevailed, blotting out the moon and stars. From beyond the city walls rose a great cacophony: the clash of arms, magic’s shivering echoes, shrieks of agony and despair. A great crashing, as of ships’ hulls clashing and breaking, echoed across the harbor. The waters rose in a great blood-tinged froth. By the end of the third day, all was silent.

On the fourth morning, dawn rose pale and tenebrous. Every Champoori dawn since has been no brighter, the city abiding in shadows the inky blue of Tenepeshu’s coils. On the plains lay the shattered remnants of a Prasadi army. Exultant, Champoor embraced the Court of Secrets as saviors and benefactors, and praised the Court’s spirits above even their own city’s indwelling god-mother, Camaya, and the patrons of their clans and people. Those gods had, after all, failed them in the face of Prasad’s wrath, unable or unwilling to save them from conquest and slaughter.

Champoor was once a great empire’s capital. Perhaps it will be again. For now, its people reside in darkness and decadence, as the city’s powers that be scheme, plot, and plan for a future whose course is not yet decided.

### Champoori Castes

The Champoori peoples are ethnically and culturally related to the Prasadi. They’re likewise divided into castes with privileges and rights dictating what professions they may follow and how they interact with one another socially, politically, and spiritually. Each caste has a ward in the city where its members reside and congregate. There are no casteless Champoori. Resident foreigners are treated as members of the caste mostly closely matching their personal professions. In order of rank, the castes are:

• Sanjhar, who oversee society’s workings. They include rulers, bureaucrats, diplomats, priests, savants, generals, admirals, staff officers, and so forth. Sanjhar clans tend toward insularity, especially those with divine blood.

• Kadhar, who deal in life and death. They include life-bringing farmers, fishers, midwives, and physicians, and death-touched butchers, executioners, and funerists. Military personnel — whether officers, soldiers, or sailors — are Kadhar; most farm or fish when not in active service. All Exalted are Kadhar, whatever their profession or prior caste.

• Silhar, the makers and shapers. They comprise all manner of artisans, artists, and skilled tradesfolk. Un-Exalted sorcerers, who shape reality, are always deemed Silhar.

• Vashar, who trade in intangibles. They comprise merchants, entertainers, tutors, thaumaturges, and the like. In practice, wealthy Vashar merchants tend to marry into higher castes nowadays, elevating their status while maintaining their business empires.

• Rorhar, who perform manual labor and unskilled trades. They hold ill repute among higher castes, exacerbated by the prevalence of Rorhar criminals seeking to escape their lowly state. Their interactions with other castes are minimal and formalized. Every caste is further divided into clans largely claiming descent from ancient dynasties, deities, or culture heroes, each with their own social and political responsibilities. Often, vast disparities in power, wealth, and influence cause friction among them.

At Simharajala’s height, this structure provided a solid social framework for territories and citizens. While most citizens lived and died within their birth caste, laws governing intermarriage, adoption, and fosterage into other castes — exceedingly strict under early militant dynasties — grew gradually more liberal. As the empire waxed vast and prosperous, a merchant caste family could find routes for an intellectually inclined son to join the Sanjhar, while a martial artist daughter could take up arms with the Kadhar.

The Kadhar Collapse

Prasad’s relentless expansionism and subsequent border wars devastated the Kadhar, whose forces couldn’t overcome armies commanded by Princes of the Earth. Previously the largest caste, their native-born warrior clans swollen with formally adopted foreign mercenaries, their numbers diminished greatly. For decades, the warrior caste struggled to secure roads and sea lanes against bandits, pirates, and Prasadi reprisals. Trade dropped off sharply — a severe blow to merchants and artisans alike. To counter this, the guard cohort that maintains order in the streets was reassigned to military duties, leaving swaths of the city all but lawless. Foreign mercenaries policed warehouses, manors, temples, and other key areas, leaving citizens in poorer wards to fend for themselves. With many Kadhar farmers dead or under arms, food grew scarce. Poverty increased. Some high-caste

### Champoor’s Old Religion

Under the old empire, each caste and city claimed ancestry and protection from a pantheon of patron deities, each of which established its own distinct mystery rites. Many gods served both in Champoor’s pantheons and some other spirit court. During the long war with Prasad, some gods fled Champoor; those who remained often found themselves at odds, jostling over roles in

Today, Champoor’s gods and their Sanjhar priesthoods struggle to find a new equilibrium. Chief gods once worshiped throughout Simharajala find themselves at odds with the city’s local pantheon over their purviews, worshipers, and temples. Old Gods of Champoor

The Sanjhar pantheon includes gods of rulership, diplomacy, and insight. City gods throughout Simharajala served as local guardian gods, though most parted

ways when their cities left the empire. The foremost Sanjhar god is Vishwa Sacred-Fire, god of Simharajala. However, Champoor’s city god, Camaya of the Fertile Plains, challenged his position after the empire’s collapse; her fierce personal ambition is entangled with her passionate dalliance with Tenepeshu. Sanjhar temples soar in towers high above the city. Many of their rituals involve meditation — the long climb up the towers’ winding stairs is often called the First Contemplation.

EX3

The Kadhar pantheon’s leadership was once shared by the cosmopolitan fertility god Ferajja Greenflame and the dignified war god Marta-Keiya. But after Prasadi Dragon-Blooded slew Marta-Keiya in battle several years ago, she’s been slow to recover, and other gods and their priesthoods squabble for dominance. Meanwhile, the enigmatic sea god Horizon-Lord Nevaru — patron of fisherfolk and longtime member of the Court of Secrets — has risen in importance in the pantheon and among the faithful. Kadhar rites typically involve blood, whether sacrificing a domesticated animal or nicking oneself with one’s blade.

Most Silhar gods are artisans and creators, many of them taking credit for natural wonders throughout Simharajala lands and inspiring the empire’s greatest makers. Sungadha the Shaper is said to have carved out the Champoori coastline. Bhuvul of the Black Hand, a lugubrious god of smiths, whispered the design for the sacred mace Kaupiri to the legendary blacksmith Septapriya in a dream. Rites honoring Silhar gods involve making small handcrafts, typically from folded paper or braided cord. Petitioners create hundreds of items over time, seeking intercession on a specific matter.

Of all the city’s pantheons, the Vashar gods adjusted most easily to the Court of Secrets’s presence. Many of them — sea gods who blessed merchants with favorable winds and swift currents, gods of hidden knowledge whom savants implored for wisdom, and the like — already belonged to that spirit court. Others, like Golden Thrush, god of morning songs, have watched their colleagues’ power rise while their own influence wanes. Worshipers perform rhythmic chants and sing paeans to the Vashar gods. These range from simple psalms to hymns layered with complex harmonies.

Traditional Rorhar gods include Savrithi of the Unbroken Back, a patron of oxen and endurance; the curious and surprisingly meticulous luck-god Jarani Knucklebones; and the generous rain god Gurdra, who clears filth from the air. But while the Sanjhar priesthood strictly limits ceremonies to the established pantheon, unofficial cults welcome any petty godling willing to aid the downtrodden. Rorhar rites typically involve arrhythmic music and wild, ecstatic dance.

The Game of Secrets

### The Court of Secrets

The Court of Secrets once held a legitimate role in the Celestial Bureaucracy. Gods of mysteries, conspiracies, shadows, and all manner of skullduggery watched over their purviews, reporting important discoveries to Heaven and ensuring events in Creation followed destiny’s demands. But the court’s links to Heaven grew tenuous over the millennia as corruption, the Usurpation, the Great Contagion, and other disruptions left the Celestial Bureaucracy in disarray. Tenepeshu, once a celestial censor assigned to root out wrongdoing among Southeastern spirits, found herself without oversight. Seizing an opportunity, she engineered a coup of the unruly Court of Secrets, suborning or driving out rivals, and keeping the rest too preoccupied with scheming against one another to challenge her.

Since then, Tenepeshu has expanded the Court of Secrets to grow her own power. She’s absorbed the former Dreaming Waters Court entirely, with its gods and elementals of Southeastern rivers, seas, tides, aquatic creatures, sailors, drowning, and suchlike. She’s also welcomed numerous spirits fleeing from lands conquered by Prasad. Under Tenepeshu’s rule, the Court of Secrets offers upward mobility unusual to a spirit court. To keep subordinates from collaborating against her, she motivates them to conspire against each other through games and contests; winners advance within the court’s hierarchy at rivals’ expense.

Champoor’s New Gods

Tenepeshu and her court assumed responsibility for protecting Champoor, supplanting guardian gods who’d perished or fled in the face of Prasadi aggression. In practice, although the Court’s presence deters invasion, its spirits leave citizens’ day-to-day concerns to priests and underlings, whose wealth grows even as poverty spreads.

Prasad’s campaign against Simharajala offered Tenepeshu a convenient opportunity. Her courtiers — craving worship, secrets, and opportunities for advancement — eagerly followed her to the surface. They choose their priests from lawbreakers and conspirators, and bless those who engage in malfeasance and clandestine behavior. Aristocratic families scheme against one another. Criminal enterprises thrive.

Since arriving in Champoor, the gods of Tenepeshu’s court have played at what they call the game of secrets, an entertainment that entangles them with mortal lives and feeds them delicious prayer. It is, in truth, two games. The lesser, played in the city’s lower wards, involves unearthing mortals’ secrets in order to blackmail them into joining one’s cult. “Bystanders” — folk without dangerous secrets — should be left alone, although mortal cult leaders often ignore this stricture, drawing in cultists through other means. Tenepeshu elevates the most successful gods to the greater game, played in the upper wards’ temples, where each god of the Court attempts to bring her rivals’ cults low by bringing their most scandalous secrets to light. Should a god’s cult suffer such calumny that the emperor banishes it from the upper wards, the most successful god in the lesser game takes its place.

### Geography

Champoor stands at the tip of a broad peninsula that juts into the westernmost end of the Dreaming Sea. The rolling, hilly plains surrounding it, though fertile, offer little in the way of defense. For that, Champoor relies on its high, thick city walls, pierced by gates that open every morning at sunrise and close at full dark. A webwork of roads, once kept immaculate by Champoori civil engineering teams, are now only maintained along the last few leagues.

The roads near the city were once lined with businesses serving overland merchant travelers: caravanserai with warehouses for storage; bathhouses to wash away road dust; restaurants, teahouses, and pleasure dens; and shrines to foreign gods. Those establishments that survived the war became the nucleus of gradually expanding shantytowns occupied by impoverished former residents. Profiteering merchants own nearly every inch of these slums, throwing up ramshackle new construction, gutting and repurposing warehouses, and charging increasingly extortionate rates to rent even the smallest room.

These inequities prevail within the walls as well. Champoor itself is divided into wards, each devoted to the caste for which it is named.

The Diadem

The Sanjhar ward, called the Diadem, centers around the sprawling imperial palace complex. Over the centuries, artisans and architects erected a dozen edifices

EX3

of wildly disparate architectural styles, joining them with walkways, domes, water features, gardens, and the palace’s own boundary wall. Once deemed the jewel of the empire, much of the estate lies in functional abandonment, the imperial family having declined dramatically in size over the centuries. Today, only the complex’s most central buildings regularly house residents. The royal gardens have become all but impenetrable, overgrown with bracken and haunted by wild animals. Residences and galleries stand locked and empty; tempting targets for thieves intrepid enough to dare the palace’s diminished but vigilant guard forces and tutelary spirits.

Around the palace stand manors and mansions of non-royal Sanjhar clans, many of whom exist in a state of genteel poverty. In fact, much of the Diadem is deeply in debt, mortgaged to the hilt by residents struggling to maintain anything resembling the honorable lifestyle of their forebears, but denied by the straitjacket of social expectation the opportunity to seek other, more gainful employment. Every year, a few Sanjhar diplomats find excuses to extend their foreign missions, summoning their entire families to join them. Temples in the Diadem remain well-kept even as surrounding estates fall into disrepair. Tribute from crime lords and hush money from the game of secrets’ targets keeps their coffers full. Simultaneously places of prayer and locations for clandestine meetings, the Diadem’s temples stay open day and night.

Sanjhar children receive private tutoring until they’re old enough to take on apprenticeships. With the families’ resources dwindling, however, less prestigious tutors replace Champoor’s great minds in the schoolroom. Rather than devoting attention solely to their employer’s children, teachers educate a passel of cousins and the occasional family friend for little pay. With few other options, they accept the jobs. Impoverished aristocratic families make pacts with the Court of Secrets. The gods offer wealth dredged from wrecks on the Dreaming Sea’s floor in exchange for participation in dreadful rites. The gods reap the benefits twice over: the rites supply them with prayer, and the families’ maneuvers to hide their involvement makes them pawns in the game of secrets. Government officials trudge through Champoor’s midday twilight to work in once-majestic buildings. The bones of their offices remain sound, but their façades reflect the city’s economic and moral decline. Faded paint goes untouched, cracked stonework unrepaired. Their

clients are aristocrats and crime bosses alike, pushing bribes across their desks alongside their agendas.

The Harrows

Before they were the Kadhar, the earliest Champoori soldiers were farmer-militia, working the fields when they weren’t needed to defend the empire. Even now, soldiers sow and reap between tours of duty. Likewise, its navy began as fisherfolk — sailors on leave from the fleet trawl the coastal waters for striped mullet and garfish.

The Kadhar ward, called the Harrows, stands west of the Diadem. Military clan dwellings ring the ward’s barracks. The war with Prasad and the ensuing troubles left many homes empty, only for mercenary companies who married into Champoori nobility to claim them. Now, former mercenaries function as new clans, vying for supremacy over the old while remaining wary of newer companies who clamor to share their privileges. Meanwhile, two generations of peace have allowed the older families to regroup; they set their sights on a return to glory, and scheme to recapture what was lost. By the barracks stands the Red Hall: the complex that once headquartered the city police battalions, and contained several war gods’ temples and the arsenal. Many of its structures are now property of private mercenary concerns and used primarily for their needs. The mostly empty arsenal building is assiduously attended by its protectors, the Priyana clan, who tenaciously cling to duty in the face of their rulers’ apathy. By the ward’s city gate, a farmers’ market sprawls. Its stalls don’t display the abundance of old, and buyers complain over the high cost of food. Much of this is due to still-lingering cascade effects from the war; the warrior caste’s heavy losses also left the workforce severely diminished, forcing the remaining farmers to leave many fields fallow. Meanwhile, taxes paid in grain have dwindled, largely due to banditry and tax evasion, increasing the city’s food demands. Mercenaries-turnedKadhar rarely join their Champoori colleagues in farming; any increase in fieldworkers the last few decades comes from older Kadhar families, additional Rorhar laborers, or the established farming clans turning to the gods for help.

Fish remain abundant, but fewer fisherfolk take to the sea to catch them. Here, the Court of Secrets stepped in. Maritime spirits herd schools of fish into waiting nets and gather great masses of seaweed for dockworkers to haul in.

EX3
