### CHAMPOORI CUISINE

Simharajalan culture favors indulging in the pleasures of food and drink. The sanjhar traditionally threw great feasts for the people, while the markets brimmed with street food and all manner of foreign staples and spices. Though poverty has grown widespread, folk still eat and drink as well as their lot allows, and hospitality demands offering rice to guests.

The waterfront district prospers most. Its docks bustle at all hours, crowds surging and ebbing as merchant ships arrive and depart. Traders offload goods and barter for treasures dredged from offshore wrecks. Lantern-sellers — many of them Rorhar children — earn a meager income selling paper lanterns and candles to new arrivals amid Champoor’s ever-present shade.

Seafood, millet, and black chickpea predominate, often accompanied by coconut, lime, and pomegranate. Cattle provide plentiful butter, buttermilk, yogurt, and cheese. Most meat, however, is chicken, mutton, goat, or rat, typically grilled on skewers or fried in ghee. Milky-white rice beer is flavored with ginger or yarrow.

In the Rorhar ward, poverty and resentment simmer among the dispossessed. Laborers, travelers, vagabonds, and criminals live packed into dark, dangerous slums. One day, perhaps soon, that resentment will boil into full-blown revolution. Champoor’s enemies watch, wait, and feed that growing anger, the better to scoop up the spoils.

Traditional dishes include crab and ridged gourd curry, smoked mashed eggplant, greens and bitter melon dry-fried with coconut, and shrimp with hyacinth beans in tamarind gravy. Wealthier families enjoy such delicacies as black pepper quail, banana blossom curry, and beef braised with pomegranates, accompanied by red wine or mead. Sweets include mango yogurt rice and banana cardamom dosa; jaggery also sweetens herbed lime water or spiced cottonseed milk.

### Crime and Cults

The Lower Wards

The lower castes largely live and work in proximity to one another. Certain neighborhoods were once allotted to each caste, but the lines have long since blurred. The Lower Wards form the bulk of the city’s urban sprawl. The Diamond Fountain, a still-magnificent university complex, attracts scholars from across the Dreaming Sea to the Vashar ward. Most foreign and domestic students reside in this area, within easy walking distance of its specialist academies and three major libraries.

To access nightlife and recreation in Vashar neighborhoods, residents walk brisky along well-maintained footpaths and roads alongside palanquins and rickshaws. The ward sees a regular influx of visitors; foreigners and criminals alike spend coin freely in gambling houses and drinking establishments. The entertainment district’s atmosphere is both seductive and violent, suiting its clientele’s search for catharsis in myriad forms.

In the neighboring ward, Silhar artisan clans reside near their businesses, many of which stand idle. Those

The Nighted City’s cults are deeply entwined with its criminal element. Gang bosses, swindlers, madams, corrupt officials, and greedy sea captains lead Champoor’s desperate and depraved in dark rituals to please the Court of Secrets. Sorcerers and thaumaturges support their cults’ goals by occult means, aiding in smuggling goods, sinking enemy ships, spying on rivals, and seducing politically vulnerable opponents. The result is a dark, rising tide that lifts all participants’ ships; as cult leaders’ business prospects and coffers swell, gods receive sacrifices of wine, scrolls, and lives. Cultists form alliances and rivalries as they become entangled in the game of secrets. Sussing out opponents’ misdeeds and wielding them for blackmail or selling them to the highest bidder is a top priority. In addition to extorting their targets to join the cult, leaders often pull in people their patrons deem “bystanders.” Those mostly innocent Champoori might lack valuable secrets, but they control desirable assets or can provide leverage to reach an otherwise untouchable family member.

Noteworthy Cults

The Silver Wheel, led by notorious fence DiamondArse Ashdi, is a street-level cult. Its deacons are thieves and smugglers who recruit nimble-fingered Rorhar pickpockets and unscrupulous merchants. The cult’s patron, the greed-spirit Shining Eyes, passes information about vulnerable trade routes, poorly guarded

EX3

riches, and officials susceptible to bribery on to Ashdi. Though Shining Eyes mostly plays the lesser game, sometimes her cultists uncover bigger, more tantalizing secrets that she trades for favors from gods of the upper wards.

The ancient, exclusive Garden of Twilight’s Pearls offers banquets of seasonal delicacies, theatrical performances, bathing and massage facilities, and the attentions of exquisitely trained courtesans. Its overseer, the former-courtesan-turned-clan-head Soumitra Vashar Hasari, also serves as high priest to the nightgod Rachlys-Aetri. Keenly insightful and compassionate, Hasari uses influence with his numerous past and current clients to better the lot of the city’s poor and dispossessed. But his avuncular demeanor conceals a ruthless streak; he’s occasionally arranged and led secret blood sacrifices of slumlords and slavers — something that can’t remain hidden forever, and which will demand a reckoning.

The Thorn Cutters have recruited nearly all the members of the aristocratic Kurachitra clan and its retainers. Their patron god, Ishali Reads-the-Wind, promises them riches and power in exchange for the secrets they command. These they have in abundance — many of their ancestors were former advisors and spymasters to Champoori emperors.

### Prominent Figures

The emperor, Champara Sanjhar Ishao, presents himself gracefully during the day, charming guests with wit and lavish style. He drowns his nights in self-indulgence — drug-sotted parties, orgies, affairs with aristocrats’ spouses — that his court struggles to conceal, to the delight of the Court of Secrets. He despises his wife, the quiet intellectual Ravarti Sanjhar Aminda, disinviting her to royal functions and refusing to share her bed; they have no children. His image as a weak, selfish monarch grows daily.

Mehra Kadhar Sarala heads the Mehra, among the strongest old-guard Kadhar military clans. In her late sixties, she’s a grizzled veteran of numerous border clashes and bandit-hunting expeditions, and equally adept at negotiating provisions from Sanjhar bureaucrats and surrender from rebel leaders. She serves as the emperor’s chief military advisor, though he — having little concern for affairs of state — largely leaves matters in her hands. Conspirators have begun subtly feeling out whether she’d back a coup; she’s currently unwilling, but the seed’s been sown.

### Neighbors

Champoor’s largest nearby concern remains the expansionist empire of Prasad. Deflected from conquest decades ago by divine providence, few of the city’s politicians, soldiers, or diplomats believe this permanently dissuaded Prasadi ambitions.

Consequently, Sanjhar diplomats keep a sharp eye on the inland city of Peresthan. Once belonging to Simharajala, Peresthan fell to Prasad shortly before the siege of Champoor. Today it’s a growing urban center dotted with parks whose forests and lakes give visitors an escape from the city’s bustle.

Prasad has sharply curtailed trade between Champoor and Peresthan. This deprives Champoor not only of livestock, but also makko. Made from evergreen shrubs found in Peresthani forests, resinous makko powder forms the base of most incense used in Champoori rituals. Only Prasadi merchants may sell it, at exorbitant costs. Smugglers grow rich off makko, but risk death from Peresthan’s garrison. Today, Prasad is reinforcing said garrison; this threatens makko smuggling, but may also presage a new invasion of Champoor. Centuries ago, Simharajala conquered Tanjipal, the great island southeast of Champoor that the agrarian Sayamitri people call home. With the empire splintered, a few city-states, most notably Baljavir with its busy port, remain Champoor’s tributaries in hope of protection from pirates and rising naval powers. But most, such as theocratic Tivaroor and stormy, martial Varsha, rebelled. Now Mehra Kadhar Sarala hopes to begin reclaiming Simharajala’s empire here. Arms, provisions, and ships amass in Champoor’s harbor district in preparation for an expedition.

On the Dreaming Sea, a new threat menaces the Nighted City’s ships. The Brimstone Fleet, a coalition of pirates descended from Simharajala’s rebels and exiles, takes a special interest in vessels flying Champoor’s flag. The Champoori merchant clans have begun building and arming heavier ships, pressganging the poor into rough crews and sending them out to face the reavers and gather intelligence from their encounters. Many of the Rorhar thus employed have learned the ropes quickly, but several ships have vanished with all hands — perhaps destroyed, or perhaps joining the pirates against the state that’s oppressed and abused them.

## Madara, City of a Thousand Wings

Madara, City of a

Thousand Wings

### MADARAN IDEOLOGIES

The people of the port city of Madara hold a centuries-old spiritual connection to the element of Air, which many citizens express through bird familiars. But the city had its wings clipped long ago, surviving the centuries only by bowing to one empire after another. Most recently, since Simharajala’s collapse, it’s submitted to Prasad — not yet as an annexed territory, but as a reluctant, semi-independent protectorate. Today, Madara struggles to assert political and economic sovereignty against Prasadi hegemony and the great powers of the Dreaming Sea.

### Survivor of Empires

Madara lacks organized political parties, but a few ideologies are common and recognizable in the city during the Time of Tumult.

Revivalists advocate for a return to traditional caste systems, with royal clans and a strong central leader. Autonomists emphasize Madara’s independence and the importance of economic and military power. Collegiates lobby for safety through diplomatic connections, trade, and connection to the spirits.

though Madarans believe they’ve simply risen above the royalist corruption previously in their midst.

### Battleground of Ideas

Madara dates to the Great Contagion’s aftermath, when Wyld storms reshaped the Dreaming Sea’s coasts. Mortal refugees found a defensible home upon a newly formed delta where the Six Bounties River met the sea. Through sacrifice and clever negotiations with the peripatetic air elementals of the Skirling Court, the first Madarans’ culture-hero founders secured favorable weather for staple crops and for river and sea trade. As their relationship with the spirits flourished, so did the young city.

But the Dreaming Sea holds many dangers, from mighty mortal empires to remnants of the ancient Fair Folk horde. Ambitious neighbors have burned Madara, inflicted devastating raids, and conquered it a dozen times since its founding. Through this disaster and upheaval, Madarans have cultivated a reputation for resilience and startling opportunism. Madara’s feuding royal clans often contended for princehood — even making deals with foreign empires for support — until recently, when Madara overthrew its ancient nobility. Sixty years ago, as Simharajala focused on defending against Prasadi aggression, Madara’s growing middle class staged a coup, supported by the Guild-affiliated Copper Stave Company, various other mercenaries, and elements of the Simharajala garrison. Driven by local intellectuals inspired by Volivat and Guild thinkers, these usurpers purged both Simharajala’s administrators and wealthy members of Madara’s long-feuding royal clans — two groups with significant overlap — and instituted a parliamentary government led by a Protector General and a Trademaster General. Madara gained a reputation for brazenness and impropriety among neighboring caste-oriented cultures as a result,

Madara has always been cosmopolitan, and it’s only become more so since breaking from Simharajala. The city actively courts craftspeople, merchants, soldiers, and laborers for dock and farm work. Any person or organization that can prove a significant financial stake in Madara can purchase a seat in parliament and help direct the city’s fiscal policy. As a result, the city’s political decisions are eclectic, inconsistent, and susceptible to graft. Modern Madaran culture encourages active engagement in political discussion and lobbying, which results in near-constant ideological conflict among the citizenry.

The Madaran parliament controversially accepted Prasadi suzerainty a decade ago, following several brutal Fair Folk attacks that cost the city much of its defenses. Prasad’s Dragon-Blooded rulers offered generous terms to gain a protectorate offering reliable, defensible access to the Dreaming Sea, but popular response to their presence was worse than the Madaran parliament expected. Madaran revivalists champion “lost scions” of the old royal clans to return to power and negotiate better terms with Prasad, while autonomists see Prasadi sabotage behind every bout of civil unrest and every Ysyri privateer raid. Some military veterans and Pure Way devotees advocate for proactive entry into the empire, seeing Prasad’s might as both tempting and inevitable.

### Politics

The Madarans officially dissolved their caste system upon breaking from Simharajala. Key political figures such as the idealistic royal heir Orazeri Ersul, religious

EX3

leader Mara Cloudshaker, and low-caste revolutionary leader Usaad Shahar cooperated in forming the new government, aiming to smooth the transition to a more equitable society. In practice, there’s still significant discrimination against members of the former lower castes. However, outbreaks of mob violence and laws against inquiring as to others’ former castes have blunted the most overt demonstrations of these conservative impulses.

In the decades following the dissolution of the caste system, people grew accustomed to new power structures and social mores. Laborers who were once members of the lowest caste now had a say in the laws the Madaran parliament passed; in theory, their voices and votes count just as much as the former royals’. In practice, wealthy and well-connected families control the city, commanding others’ votes through bribes, influence, intimidation, and — when all else fails — deploying gangs of legbreakers. Though clans still wield much of the financial power in Madara, parliament has elevated its hundred-odd voices to prominence above and beyond their family ties. Public association and advocacy provide obvious avenues to political influence; an informal relationship with any member of parliament is a powerful resource.

Parliament: Powers and Lobbyists

Madara’s lawmakers meet in Parliamentary Hall, with its two octagonal tiers, 16 elegant turrets, pointed arches, and tall domed roof. According to the Interim Parliamentary Powers and Prerogatives Contract written six decades ago, Madara’s parliament may set, assess, collect, and allocate taxes through the Trademaster General, and draft and direct military forces through the Protector General. The parliament quickly negotiated the addition of legislative and judicial powers so that high-profile civil and criminal cases would go directly to a brief parliamentary decision. Legislators wield their powers by majority vote, so most successful lobbyists are some combination of attorney, fiduciary, and rhetorician. Lobbyists earn significant profit by helping wealthy clans secure favorable tariffs, but some lobby for less profitable goals, whether advocating for public works, safety measures in high-risk trades, or fair outcomes in criminal cases. Even within the three main ideologies, political factions vie for power. Revivalists rally around different proposed leaders. Military clans push their own agendas. The Interlocutors, an amalgam of Autonomists and Collegiates, derail sessions with impassioned

speeches. The tiny Laborer faction agitates in favor of poorer workers, warning of riots if demands aren’t met. Politicians who favor yielding completely to Prasad whisper in all their ears; others urge alliance with Ysyr to defend against the encroaching empire.

Clans

Madara’s clans — each claiming affiliation with a different ancestral bird-spirit — remained largely intact, though their fortunes and statuses within the city’s society have changed over the last few generations. Clan Arakha, formerly a royal clan, retained much wealth and power by preserving shipping and trade interests throughout the Dreaming Sea. Most older members are staunch Revivalists, but the clan’s newest generation envisions a thriving, independent Madara. Among their more prominent members is the outspoken autonomist Arakha Shanaz. Artisans and builders comprise the Dayyad clan. Its elderly matriarch Dayyad Atmaja is renowned for designing the breathtaking, many-towered Parliamentary Hall, which visitors to Madara marvel over to this day. Over the years, its members have largely married into and absorbed the smaller Mianda warrior clan. Stereotyped as poor and hard-working, the formerly low-caste Udhazar clan specializes in tanning — traditionally deemed an unclean occupation — along with metalwork and other crafts. After the coup, enterprising Udhazar artisans bargained directly with foreign merchants; some families became quite wealthy, moving up in society to hobnob with former social betters. Their matriarch, Udhazar Ghosha, is famed for philanthropy toward poorer clan members.

### Culture

Tall columns and high domes dominate Madara’s airy buildings. Inside, stunning tile work decorates the walls and ceilings, with gilded accents outlining geometric structural details. In addition to complex and colorful abstract designs, many mosaics depict birds in flight — a motif repeated throughout the city. Stone birds spread wings atop the domes; statues depicting Madara’s heroes display carved avian companions perched on their wrists and shoulders.

Traditional Madaran clothing favors flowing fabrics in rich colors, with intricate embroidery and designs. Designers often work a clan’s traditional familiar into their garments: tunics with ibises along the cuffs and

EX3

hems, silk slippers adorned with sunbirds, tiny hummingbird figurines woven into elaborately dreadlocked hair. Foreign artists drawn to the city by its stunning visual style incorporate foreign techniques that clan clothiers adapt into more conservative outfits. Street vendors hawk spicy meats on skewers; flatbreads; and fruits such as mangoes, grapes, and apricots. At aristocrats’ tables, saffron flavors thick stews and chefs coat slices of meat in thin sheets of beaten silver. Only the especially religious eschew all bird meat; most consider such a prohibition impractical. Profit increasingly becomes a national virtue in Madara. Former low-caste clans familiar with poverty seek opportunities — whether risky, immoral, or illegal — to care for elders and give descendants better lives. Snobbery between former high-caste clans and the nouveau riche causes friction in Parliament, political and economic intrigues, and occasional bloody feuds. Citizens may not keep slaves. Visiting foreigners may, but most Madarans deem this disrespectful to the wind-spirits and encourage owners to free their slaves or leave the city.

### Religion

Madaran culture-myth posits that each living thing has a perfect fate, decided by an immanent judge with 125 names. Most Madarans believe that while all spirits are connected with this judge of destiny, entities connected to the sky and the element of Air are its natural voices and interpreters. Even malevolent gods and demons serve this purpose by challenging mortal souls to find their true fate and accomplish their life’s purpose. Priests serve as spiritual counselors, and occasional mediate with spirits. They also oversee Madaran funeral rites. Corpses are cleansed by fire; ashes are spread on the wind and bones given to the water. Clan members’ veneration of their clans’ ancestral bird-spirits is largely a private matter. But while many of these spirits are dead, departed, or entirely mythical, some clans do perform rites requesting blessings from some birdgod or ghost who acts as the clan’s ancestral patron.

Blessings of the Air

The Skirling Court requires regular rites to appease them. These range from week-long festivals celebrating the

EX3

exchange for worship and offerings. To this day, citizens affirm this spiritual connection by bonding with a familiar from a bird species traditionally associated with their clan — or a gull, if the citizen claims no clan.

### PURE WAY SYNCRETISM

A significant minority of Madarans followed the Pure Way even before their city became a Prasadi protectorate. The Madaran concept of an unseen judge speaking through many voices parallels Pure doctrine about guidance from an invisible pantheon. But Prasadi traditionalists may take exception to the idea that mortals can interpret omens from their familiars.

seasonal winds, to burning a tenth of the season’s sweetgrass harvest, to dedicating games like the Skirmish (p. XX) in the spirits’ honor. Every day, Madaran matriarchs burn sweet incense whose smoke curls into the sky, and children hang bright streamers out their windows to flutter in the wind. In the stormy season, Madarans offer sacrifices so the winds and rain won’t destroy their houses, fields, and ships. In the dry months, their rites appease the spirits to prevent drought.

Elementals of the Skirling Court include the gruff storm-bull Isman Vir, whose great heaving sighs are said to turn windmills’ blades; the playful twin spirits of updrafts and warm breezes together named Those Who Soar Above; and Swift Kadmani with her iridescent wings, a spirit of morning mists who has a fondness for unruly children. The spirits grant gifts in return. Herds of wind-horses and schools of cloud-fish provide enough rain to prevent droughts, but not so much the rivers flood their banks. Mighty stormbirds turn aside tempests, guide winds into becalmed sails, and beset hostile foreign navies with thick fog, hail, and lightning. Local superstitions concern how best to please the spirits. When greeting a lover, it’s customary to also kiss the air, sharing the affection with nearby invisible elementals. Likewise, Madarans say it’s unwise to speak ill of enemies on blustery days, lest a mischievous spirit carry your words to their ears. Some superstitions are simply good sense, such as being kind to mortal horses lest the wind-horses see you mistreating their brethren, or honoring psychopomps so they bring dead loved ones to the blessed cloud-paradise Ayavindra and don’t accidentally carry off living souls.

### Familiars and Citizenship

To outsiders, Madara is the City of a Thousand Wings. The city’s founders struck a sacred accord with local air spirits, gaining favorable winds and weather in

In Madara’s spiritual traditions, birds symbolize their accord as creatures of flesh and spirit, land and air. A bird familiar is a personal spiritual guide; Madarans routinely consult familiars for omens and include them in daily noontime prayer. A familiar’s loss constitutes tragic spiritual damage; popular myth encourages those who lose their familiars to petition the spirits for a new familiar or to seek the lost familiar in the Underworld. After someone with a bird familiar dies, it’s not uncommon for the familiar to die within three days; the two are buried together. Wind-priests grant natal residents the ceremony of spiritual contract and citizenship at age 10. Roughly one in twenty participants gains a familiar as a sign of the spirits’ blessing. Foreigners may undergo the rite of citizenship by paying the wind-priest a fee and convincingly arguing their love for Madara; the spirits occasionally bless these new citizens with familiars as well. Foreigners’ slaves may undergo the rite of citizenship if they have the funds and can escape their masters; this has occasionally caused diplomatic incidents. A citizen receives preferential hiring over non-citizens, and has the right to protection from violence, theft, and enslavement. Though bird-blessed citizens don’t claim special rights, they enjoy more positive public regard and trust, and often gain positions of authority. Folklore speaks of youths journeying to petition the spirits and returning with a bird familiar signifying their newfound wisdom.

Foreigners with bird familiars may be mistaken for members of an appropriate clan, although Madarans tend to be understanding if the foreigner is forthcoming about the confusion. Indeed, residents see a visitor with a bird familiar as more spiritually advanced than other foreigners, and may encourage her to undergo the rite of citizenship. Certain birds, such as grosbeaks, are deemed inauspicious; conservative Madarans shun a traveler who’s bonded with such a bird. Knowingly killing a familiar is a crime of sacrilege. The bird-blessed are encouraged to mark their familiars in some way, such as a ribbon tied around one leg, to avoid hunting accidents, and hunting birds within city limits is forbidden. On rare occasions, a familiar goes unmarked — say, for use as a spy or thief — though the person spied on may then claim ignorance that the bird they killed was a familiar.

EX3

### A Madaran Living

### THE SKIRMISH: SPORT IN MADARA

Madara’s abundant water and silt suit a variety of crops and crafts. Currently, the city-state focuses on growing cash crops like tea, cotton, and sugarcane, both for trade and for tribute to Prasad. Wealthy clans viciously protect monopolies in fermentation-related trades like leather-tanning and rum-brewing. Madaran companies jealously guard methods to create fermented tea — colloquially called dark tea — which pleases mortals and spirits alike. Since these crafts are often pungent, Madara has a distinctive odor from miles away.

Team sports are an important outlet for wealthy and poor Madarans alike. Manual workers enjoy the (relatively safe) opportunity to vent aggression and earn extra money, while upper-class Madarans appreciate the visceral distraction from heady financial and political matters. Longstanding team rivalries provide everyone a good excuse to argue and to bond with fellow team supporters. Though some sports remain associated with traditional castes, many sporting events have become meeting grounds for people of differing classes and backgrounds, not to mention opportunities to rendezvous in the relative anonymity of a passionate crowd.

Madara has always profited from the shipbuilding trade, especially in the last decade. Prasad’s Dragon Caste pays exorbitant sums to develop its own blue-water navy, and the empire’s fledgling admiralty board is willing to experiment to find their ideal navy composition. Prasad plans to adapt Blessed Isle naval traditions to face challenges characteristic to the Dreaming Sea, such as Ysyri sorcerers and Fair Folk reavers. Construction is time-consuming and resource-intensive, however; Prasadi ships and work crews overcrowd Madaran docks and lumberyards for days or weeks at a time, interfering with local business and raising tensions.

Clever bird familiars serve helpful roles in nearly every aspect of Madaran society, but they’re particularly useful in hunting, fishing, and controlling pest populations. Fishermen tie cords around trained cormorants’ throats and send them diving into the river to catch fish. The birds, unable to swallow larger specimens, return to their owners. Owners then remove the large fish from their throats and reward them with smaller ones. Birds also gather intelligence. It’s illegal and risky to use a familiar to spy on other citizens, but practically speaking, Madarans assume that someone is probably watching whenever they’re outdoors. Bird-blessed Madaran mercenaries are famously useful scouts and archers who charge heavily for the risk posed to their familiars. Likewise, thanks to their familiars, Madaran guards are notoriously difficult to evade — although they’re likewise easily bribed.

### In Prasad’s Grasp

The Empire of Prasad expects protectorates to facilitate free passage for Prasadi envoys, merchants, soldiers, and missionaries. Madara, as both a high-value strategic and economic investment and one of the empire’s few access points to the Dreaming Sea, has a

Madara’s oldest signature sport has many names and variations, but most call it the Skirmish. It’s a complex full-contact sport with ten-person teams, wherein players race for and wrestle over a brightly colored cotton ribbon to take it back to their goal. While horseback and aquatic variations exist, the most prestigious Skirmish format requires bird-blessed players with familiars trained to snatch smaller ribbons from different parts of the field. Since each clan has its own associated bird familiar species, this “Blessed Skirmish” encourages diverse teams whose familiars bring different strengths to the team.

particularly heavy flow of Prasadi visitors throughout the year.

The Anishka Geha — an ancient fortress outside the city — hosts a sizable Prasadi garrison, which makes a show of respecting Madaran sovereignty by limiting its presence within the city to a hundred Prasadi soldiers. Nonetheless, Prasadi marines patrol the city’s shipyards, and its growing blue-water navy regularly practices maneuvers a stone’s throw away — both to warn off potential raiders and encourage respectful behavior in visitors. Madara’s military aggressively recruits foreign warriors and outcastes with promises of citizenship and high pay, but has little hope of warding off Prasad should the empire choose to annex the city.

Prasad, having overreached in its rush to expand into the Dreaming Sea, acts as suzerain instead of conqueror in Madara. The empire sees this arrangement as temporary and puts only a token effort into pretending otherwise. Even with Madara’s semi-independence, Prasad’s constant military presence and demands for tribute put a strain on the city’s resources.

EX3

Prasadi visitors view Madara’s wealthy elites — mostly merchants, guildsfolk, and military captains — as up-jumped members of castes ill-suited to rulership. Madara’s captains of industry stand to lose their wealth and influence in a Prasadi regime change, so they work the lower classes ruthlessly in the name of protecting the city’s freedom.

Prasad’s direct influence over Madaran society is recent but obvious. High-caste Prasadi travel parties have strict expectations for spiritually suitable food and accommodations, and will pay exorbitantly for so-called “civilized” hospitality. Madaran clans hire genealogists to prove their relations to influential Prasadi clans and jatis, while Pure Way converts discriminate against leather tanners and other workers whom they deem unclean. Poets, historians, mapmakers, and other educated professionals receive both significant Prasadi patronage and threats from autonomists afraid of growing Prasadi hegemony.

The Prasadi Future

Madara is currently a good investment for Prasad, but if the city falls short of its promised tribute, shows significant civil unrest, or suffers major damage to its docks and shipyards, the empire may annex the city to recoup its losses. In this scenario, Prasad will “re-establish order” by occupying the city, appointing a Dragon Caste governor to command the parliament, and installing a permanent military garrison. They will then begin the slow process of restructuring the city and its population (The Realm, p. 166). Madara’s resistance to a determined invasion will suffer thanks to citizens sympathetic to — or outright spying for — Prasad, but legislators will fight viciously to hold onto political power if they have any forewarning. They’ll call in economic favors from neighboring cities, beg aid from the Skirling Court, seek new and risky alliances — most notably with Champoor or distant Ysyr — and incite religious fervor among the lower classes. The poor have little but their faith and their familiars, after all, and many will fight to the death if both are threatened. Of course, the more Madarans use their faith as a rallying cry, the more monks of the Pure Way will see Madaran faith as heretical.

### Prominent Figures

Gale Kayang, current Trademaster General, loves the sounds of a shipyard in full swing, the taste of victory over a worthy opponent, and the rush of cocaine, not always in that order. Gale styles themself an entrepreneur who rose from poverty to wealth, though their success

stems heavily from a knack for sabotage and a lack of scruples. They successfully lobbied for promotion to their current position in the aftermath of the disastrous Fair Folk raids a decade ago, and retain a positive public reputation despite numerous personal scandals. Ba Myan is the only Protector General Madara has ever had. This God-Blood was middle-aged when she led the Simharajala deserters who supported the coup. Though her mind has only sharpened since, age and illness have ravaged her semidivine health. She clings to life and office with the same single-minded dedication she relied on to purge her royalist predecessors. Though mostly bedridden, Ba personally manages the city’s municipal and coast guards and uses them to spy on Prasadi visitors. Her subordinates lack her brilliance and fire; many fear that Prasad merely awaits her death to annex the city.

Ophris Herouth Chaarahi is Prasad’s ambassador to Madara. By the terms of Prasad’s suzerainty, the Wood Aspect wields five votes in parliament over matters affecting Prasadi interests, but she primarily uses her voting power to court potential allies. A dangerous combination of charming and ambitious, Chaarahi intends to become governor of Madara when the empire inevitably annexes it; she sows the city with favors like seeds that she can later harvest to smooth the coming transition.

Hawagarim “the Unyielding” Umid is one of several “lost scions” claiming descent from one of Madara’s decimated royal clans. Unlike most, his claim happens to be true, though he doesn’t realize it. A poet, actor, and community leader, he’s indoctrinated several hundred lower-class citizens into his eccentric Pure Way cult. Hawagarim’s goal in life is to live comfortably, which has put him on the wrong side of several predatory lenders. He seeks a wealthy patron to leech money from, and it’s only a matter of time before a foreign or domestic investor turns him into a political catspaw.

### Neighbors

As a centuries-old port, Madara has many trading partners and rivals. A few nations qualify as both. Of all the Fair Folk — Madara’s oldest enemies, the nightmares that drove the city’s founders from their ancient homeland — the Fleet of Motley Dunes are Madara’s most persistent tormenters. Part of the Pearlescent Fleet (p. XX), these scrimshaw-armored reavers know that the wind and waves may turn against their ships anytime they approach Madara, but they

EX3

stage erratic raids from their inhospitable island hideout because they savor the unique soul-taste of familiars. They’ll even offer naval aid to Madara in times of great need if they fear the loss of their favorite delicacy.

### THE OFFSHORE RETREAT

A small, rocky isle near Madara holds a publicly owned prison, euphemistically called the Offshore Retreat or the Guesthouse. The Madaran prince Sacha Deusiem built the Retreat centuries ago to house political opponents that she wanted kept alive — for practical or sentimental reasons — starting with her older brother. Since then, the prison has held new political prisoners after each change of Madaran leadership.

The Garajnay Tribes share ethnic and cultural similarities with Madara, but they’ve struck an accord with the dead. The Garajnay live in a coastal shadowland wrought from the demise of an ancient, broken city a few dozen miles from Madara. There they raise evil-tempered, carnivorous horses and grow potent medicinal fungi. The living Garajnay share their homes with dead ancestors, welcome dead warriors into their bodies in wartime, and train their horses to hunt invaders, thieves, and rustlers. Within their shadowland the Garajnay are formidable, but when distant neighbors offend them, they hire Madaran mercenaries to express their displeasure. Madarans who seek their deceased bird familiars’ shades in the Underworld occasionally pass through Garajnay, purchasing supplies and information from the locals to aid their quests. Northeast of Madara, the isle of Shimmering Thread lives in perpetual gentle rain. An eternal waterspout rises from the manse atop the island’s central mountain, sapping the wrath of any storm that approaches. Shimmering Thread’s sorcerer-tyrant summons storms to rout hostile navies, but she provides a safe harbor for any ship willing to pay upfront in jade. Shimmering Thread shelters occasional far-flung Ysyri privateers, and its sorcerer-tyrant is said to be of Ysyri descent. Sailors whisper a dozen rumors about how and why she left Ysyr, and whether she still serves the empire.

## Volivat

Towers climb out of the waves several miles off the Doorstone Peninsula’s coast, rising above the dam encircling the city of Volivat. Cargo-laden ships from across the Dreaming Sea dock at piers jutting out onto the waters. Their workers unload goods, but they haven’t yet reached their final destinations: Volivat lies not on the sea but below it, a hundred fathoms deep. Sharp-angled buildings capped with graceful domes line Volivat’s streets. Colorful mosaics decorate every inch of open plazas, often depicting heroic scenes. Marble façades gleam softly in the city’s extended dawns and twilights — Volivat’s depth means there’s less direct sunlight than at the surface. Inside the buildings, frescoes adorn the walls, and diffused light shines down through thin layers of alabaster. Though Volivat’s climate is normally pleasantly balmy, direct

Over time, parts of the prison have been put to other uses: a barracks for visiting dignitaries’ honor guards, the workshop where the sorcerer-engineer Karuka Drajal made his thousand mechanical birds, a temple to the goddess Tiei of the Cranes. Many of these sections are sealed off, though rumors suggest their former occupants may have left valuable things behind.

Currently, Madara’s parliament rents cells by the season to foreign clans who want hostages, problematic relatives, and useful opponents kept somewhere comfortable, safe, and boring. Most of the Offshore Retreat’s prisoners are mortal, though the parliament accepts spirit or Exalted prisoners if paid enough to profit after hiring outcaste guards.

midday sunlight can send the temperature soaring. Citizens spend the hottest part of the day inside or stroll languidly in the shade provided by retractable linen awnings.

As beautiful as much of the city is, some quarters hint at the devastation Volivat has suffered through the ages: market squares reduced to rubble from an invading force’s assault, buildings whose water-stained façades crumble at a touch, and shattered statues swept into heaps amidst broken mosaic tiles. Volivat’s citizens work to restore damage from recent crises, but they must also perform unending maintenance against water damage, mold, and the like. Artisans and scholars spend years sifting through the rubble, seeking treasures to rescue and refurbish. Volivat’s citadel sits in the Alamieri Plaza at the city’s center, looming over surrounding structures. While architectural flourishes and ancient art bedecks other buildings, the citadel remains austere. Its ancient designers favored function over form, though its symmetry echoes that of the ornate buildings surrounding it, a concession to the exquisite exteriors nearby. The elected Antecessor (p. XX) dwells within its protective walls,

EX3

and engineers and scholars come and go, tending to surviving First Age mechanisms in the citadel’s vaults. In courtyards lined by lemon trees, professors and philosophers deliver lectures to tight knots of students. Volivat is a center of learning, home to schools and colleges for lawyers, mathematicians, and engineers. Libraries abound, from the Antecessor’s public collection in the city’s center to smaller athenaeums maintained by private citizens, browsable by invitation only. Some of these repositories house First Age texts that archivists study and attempt to restore. Elite soldiers patrol Volivat’s squares and drill in the citadel’s training grounds, displaying strength, deftness, and grace that might fool outsiders into thinking they watch a troop of Dragon-Blooded at practice. These warriors are no Exalts, however. They are the Yennin (p. XX) — “Children of Ten Fathers” in Volivat’s tongue. They number in the thousands, a small but mighty percentage of the city’s population. From well before they’re born, the Yennin carry the heavy duty of being Volivat’s champions.

Provisioning the City

Botanical alchemists work high above the city in sunbathed spires, coaxing crops from tubs of fertile soil. Flowering vines snake out of windows and down towers’ sides, verdant evidence of their masters’ agricultural prowess. Over the centuries, alchemists have bred many plant cultivars to thrive in the city below, requiring less light or different climes but blooming just as brightly.

These harvests, while astounding feats of alchemy and agriculture, only supplement Volivat’s food supply. Most provisions must be fished from the seas and imported from neighboring shores. To ensure a secure, uninterrupted line of supply, the city owns or allies with several settlements along the mainland coast. Volivat sends a contingent of its own workers to tend the land alongside local farmers. Alchemists inspect the fields, applying concoctions to soil and crops to fend off pests and increase yields. In some places, Volivati helots — often Doorstone Peninsula natives pressed into Volivat’s service — protect their coastal allies’ borders. Some rulers interpret their presence as more veiled threat than friendly gesture.

### Origins

During the First Age, the Exalted Host sculpted a city out of the sea. They sank massive dams that climbed

from the ocean floor to several fathoms above the waves and created great mechanisms to pump the water out. Volivat was a marvel of sorcery and engineering, a jewel of a city, and a center of maritime trade. When the Great Contagion raged across Creation, in a desperate and draconian attempt at quarantine, Volivat’s leaders deactivated the pumps and let the ocean waters rush in, flooding the city and condemning the sick to a mass watery grave. Still-healthy citizens retreated to the highest towers and turned away any ships that came calling. Still the Contagion reached them; those who didn’t succumb to it died out in the years after it ended. A century later, seafaring nomads explored the spires rising out of the sea and rediscovered the city beneath. They reactivated the pumps, and as the waters drained, Volivat’s domes and grand structures reemerged. Some First Age texts and relics had survived their long submersion, whether made of waterproof materials, protected by occult means, sealed in watertight rooms, or carried up to the towers before the city flooded. The new settlers absorbed the information, and as they swept seawater from mosaic-covered courtyards and inhabited their predecessors’ halls, they integrated elements of Old Volivat’s culture with their own. They restored the libraries, planted gardens, and slowly reclaimed Volivat’s place as a maritime power and an essential trading port. Though their sorceries pale in comparison to the wonders of the First Age, Volivat’s willworkers attempted to recreate that previous city’s miracles, with varying degrees of success.

### Culture

Folk in Volivat go by a single name for most purposes. Only in official circumstances or to distinguish themselves from another of the same name do they append the name of a noteworthy parent, the number of their deme (p. XX) of origin, or some relevant sobriquet. The Volivati follow no one specific faith. Shrines to many gods appear throughout the city, and citizens are free to worship as they please. Ocean elementals, gods of learning, harvest spirits, and gods of swift currents alike welcome those who come with questions or seeking debate, and accept offerings of wine, fruit, bread, and incense at their altars.

Many Volivati turn their religious impulses toward philosophy rather than spirits. Scholars, caisson technicians, and manual laborers alike welcome metaphysical

EX3

debate during midday rest or over lemon liqueur after dinner; many gather into informal schools to study various doctrines. Noteworthy traditions include those of Piassi, who proposed that the material world merely manifests the harmonies of the music of stars; Glora the Elder, for whom all things arise from the ebb and flow of elemental Essence; and Nerian of Fourth Deme, who theorized the existence of seven immutable higher principles that define all things by their presence or absence.

Volivati meals feature fresh seasonal ingredients, such as garden peas, broad beans, figs, and chestnuts. Staples like olive oil, onions, garlic, fish sauce, lemon juice, and vinegar lend flavor, in addition to spices imported from throughout the Dreaming Sea. Preparations are often simple but tasty, such as fish grilled with oil and lemon, small plates of cheese and olives marinated in olive oil and spices, or lentil soup with garlicky chard and dumplings.

Other traditional dishes include octopus and potatoes simmered in wine and vinegar; oysters roasted in lemon leaves; gnocchi with clams and mussels; and figs and herbed goat cheese on toasted bread. Many Volivati enjoy the honeyed wine called mulsum before the meal,

and sip lemon liqueur while enjoying honey cakes and all manner of fresh fruit for dessert.

Clothing tends toward a simple linen chiton in the warmth of day, with mantles or cloaks thrown on during the coolness of early morning or late afternoon. Wealthier Volivati set themselves apart with foreign textiles, vivid dyes, intricate embroidery, and lavish jewelry. Hair is typically grown long and either held back by a headband or piled up into an elaborate coiffure. Vivid alchemical hair dyes are coming into fashion among modish younger citizens, sometimes with multiple bands or stripes of brilliant color.

### The Yennin

Among the First Age wonders Volivat’s new settlers discovered was the formula for creating offspring with up to ten parents, called Yennin. The city’s ruling council selects parents from among Volivat’s strongest, wisest, and most gifted citizens: warriors, sages, musicians, and artists. These pass the best of themselves on to their children, who are born with exceptional talents and physical abilities.

EX3

Most Yennin are brought to term in First Age natal caissons. Few modern-day savants understand the caissons’ arcane workings beyond their basic operation; this becomes a problem when the ancient chambers threaten to fail. Volivat sorcerer-engineers work desperately to understand them and enact makeshift repairs. The materials the caissons’ original creators used are rare or of unknown origin, and many of the spells that shaped them were lost when the city flooded.

### CHILDREN OF TEN MORTALS

Yennin themselves don’t serve as parents to the next generation of their kind. The process of engendering a Yennin involves a carefully regulated Essence pattern, and their own puissant energies throw that pattern out of balance. The same applies to Exalted, God-Blooded, and other supernatural entities. It’s not impossible, but low odds of success — alongside risks to both child and natal caisson — make attempts rare, barring occasional ill-fated experiments.

The wisest Yennin set their formidable minds to finding other workarounds. Some summon neomah to assist them. Others seek skilled crafters to build replacement caissons, importing rare materials from distant lands and experimenting with substitutes as they pore over fragments of the original designs.

Yennin familial relationships are complex, as individual parents often contribute to the creation of several offspring over the course of a lifetime. Citizens have an entire vocabulary to describe how Yennin who share some parents are related to one another. Every parent bears some degree of responsibility for their child’s upbringing, depending on their specific relation: a parentof-the-third-kind has distinctly different obligations than a parent-of-the-seventh-kind. Unlike the occult elements of a Yennin’s gestation, this arrangement is purely social, with parents negotiating roles before the child’s birth. One may oversee certain aspects of her child’s schooling, while another dictates which parents the child lives with, when, and for how long. From the moment they first draw breath, the Yennin count themselves among the city’s elite, and train to be its protectors. They’re stronger, faster, and more dexterous than other humans. Those who count military leaders and savants among their parents often have keen strategic minds. Children of great orators and poets might make the city weep with impassioned speeches. The Yennin are multitalented, placed in advanced classes and given rigorous study regimens as soon as they’re old enough to learn. Though a Yennin’s life offers every comfort Volivat can provide, it’s also defined by service. They’re created to lead, fight, increase Volivat’s wealth, or solve its problems. Only a small fraction of Yennin grasp the sleight of sorcery, though their odds are better than the average citizen’s. The city’s alchemists carefully guide most of their initiations, though enlightenment sometimes comes by other means — often through study of the city’s First Age tomes and relics. Volivati sorcerers strive to recreate spells their First Age predecessors wielded, or to unlock the soil’s secrets to help feed the citizenry.

As such, Volivat doesn’t look solely to the Yennin for its heroes. Each Yennin esteems ten mortals as her parents; the city’s savants sift through Volivat’s mortal champions — often themselves children of Yennin — to determine who’s best suited to pass their gifts on to new Yennin. Political power passes less often through direct succession, although Yennin may groom their grandchildren as their inheritors instead

While sorcerers are expected to direct all their efforts toward rekindling the glory of past ages, the council often solicits their expertise regarding infrastructure and maintenance of the city’s ancient workings, which grants them significant access to those in power. Sorcerers don’t rule the city, but many have the ears of those who do.

### Politics

Volivat is a republic, governed by an elected council — the Convocation of Ten — and an Antecessor to whom the council answers. Councilors oversee trade, make laws regarding civil order, set and implement collection of taxes, and advise the Antecessor in military matters. The Antecessor prioritizes which topics the Convocation will debate, sets military policy, and negotiates with foreign leaders. She may, when the council is slow to act or the need is urgent, make laws without their input, though this power is best used sparingly; council factions have sometimes removed dictatorial Antecessors by force.

Elections are held every three years for councilors, and every five for the Antecessor. Interim elections are held if a member dies, steps down, or is otherwise unable to carry out their duties. All free adult Volivati citizens may vote, provided they come to the city to cast their ballots. In theory, this means even farmers in Volivatowned mainland villages may participate; in practice, few set sail to do so.

EX3

Officially, any citizen may be elected, but the Convocation of Ten consists predominantly of the city’s wealthiest members. Yennin and mortal sorcerers are collectively limited to two seats each — granting them a voice in Volivat’s governance without risking them taking over the council (not that the Yennin always agree with one another anyway). Particularly influential rivals carry grudges into the council chambers from time to time, splitting votes and throwing leadership into disarray.

For local matters, the city is divided into 24 demes — an inner ring of eight districts, and an outer ring of 16. Issues of zoning, criminal trials, lawsuits, and the like are addressed democratically at weekly deme assemblies by vote of attending heads of household.

Foreign Policy

Accessible only by sea, Volivat maintains maritime trade relationships with coastal nations and merchant princes. However, it’s outright owned a swath of nearby farmland for centuries, and in recent years has annexed a few nearby city-states and principalities, such as Trizzi with its thousand vineyards and silver-rich Pelisse. The current Antecessor and her council, being expansion-minded, have their eyes on a handful of a few other locales, most notably Port Donia and its shipyards and Lasca, whose hills are full of marble. While Volivat’s neighbors prefer independence, some weigh this against the benefits of Volivat’s might standing between themselves and Prasad as the empire’s reach extends deeper into the Dreaming Sea. Better, perhaps, to serve the devil they know.

The hundreds of Yennin resident in Volivat give prospective invaders pause. Though not Exalted, their skills are well-honed on land and at sea. Any siege — even initiated by powers as mighty as Ysyr or Prasad — would likely be long and bloody, the cost in material resources and soldiers’ lives perhaps too great to commit. Still, Volivat’s merchants must guard against pirates and privateers; seaborne raids to seize wealth and secrets from the city’s vaults and spires aren’t unheard of.

Volivat and Ysyr

A century ago, the empire of Ysyr acknowledged Volivat as a potential competitor for dominance in the Dreaming Sea. The sight of Ysyri ships on the horizon became fraught with uncertainty: their sails might herald a trade offer or a naval assault. Ysyr briefly managed a successful invasion, holding the city for a matter of months before Volivati rebels drove the attackers out. Though the Ysyri forces took several priceless relics and First Age manuscripts with them as they retreated,

they left behind Volivat’s greatest prize, the natal caissons.

From that point on, Volivati strategists and sorcerers expended considerable effort defending against Ysyr’s ambitions. Yennin captains studied Ys naval maneuvers. Volivat’s archivists sifted through musty vaults for artifacts, spells, mechanisms, and stratagems that might help rebuff their enemy; diplomats sought information on sorcerer-princes’ desires, predilections, rivalries, and fears. The two powers vied for control of shipping routes and sea-lanes, and Volivat dockmasters maintained constant vigilance against Ys spies and saboteurs.

Relations between Volivat and Ysyr have drastically improved over the last couple of decades Nonetheless, tensions remain. Scholars from each city visit the other to examine certain First Age mechanisms essential to their infrastructure. While some view this as dangerous — what if Ysyr finds a way to sabotage the pumps that keep the sea from drowning Volivat? What if the Volivati still the engines that churn beneath the Chalcedon Mountains? — others see an opportunity to glean First Age knowledge previously barred to them. With Prasad establishing a Dreaming Sea fleet, Volivat’s and Ysyr’s leaders have concluded that their cities lie in its inexorable path. Individually, their fleets still vastly outnumber Prasad’s blue-water navy, but it won’t be long before the empire swells its numbers and adapts its familiar river-based tactics to the open sea. It’s less a question of whether it will happen but when, and whose ships will be the first to skirmish with Prasad’s.

### Prominent Figures

Iron-haired, square-jawed Antecessor Cariola belongs to an ancient Volivati family with many Yennin in its ancestry. She’s served Volivat since she was a young woman: first on the council, then as Antecessor for the last twenty years. She’s both a popular leader and a master of favor-trading on the council; recently, she’s turned her hard-earned skills and clout toward bargaining with Ysyr. She has two grown children with her husband, and has in recent years become a parent to three Yennin. Her elder offspring understand what an honor it is, but resent what they perceive as their diminished places within the family.

Admiral Drigo, a Yennin in his middle years, leads Volivat’s navy. He attributes his height and skill with the blade to his parent-of-the-first-kind, Sword-Captain Reynad, and both oratory skills and quick temper to his

EX3

parent-of-the-fourth-kind, the councilwoman Dona. He harbors lofty ambitions for his post-military career, but after a pair of assassination attempts, suspects someone is threatened by his rise. He makes careful inquiries to identify the culprits and their agendas. In the meantime, he encourages Dona to push for Volivat’s expansion in council, intending to be at the forefront of those missions to prove his worth.

Erena spends more time within the dams ringing Volivat than she does in the city itself. She’s among the few dozen technicians who maintain the mundane workings of the city’s First Age pumps, replacing wornout parts and inspecting mechanisms for corrosion and wear. She knows where maintenance shafts open out into locations all over the city. For a price, she leads those who desire secrecy — councilors, lovers, smugglers, rebellious children — through the labyrinthine tunnels. Such access is illegal to nontechnicians. She pours money earned from this illicit side-job into procuring parts for a First Age schematic she discovered while working.

Tuli is a clerk in the Venerable Society of Procurers, an import/export company with one office in a spire atop the dam and two in the city proper below. The Procurers act as trade brokers for Volivat’s artisans, negotiating for materials with foreign merchants and managing crafted wares leaving Volivat. Mildmannered and unassuming toward her superiors, Tuli is actually a smuggler, using her position in the Society to find and connect clients. She does a brisk trade in stolen goods and sensitive information throughout the northern Dreaming Sea.

### Neighbors

Along the Dreaming Sea’s northern coast, in Mount Iraya’s foothills, rests the city of Nysina. The relationship between Nysina and Volivat has lasted for centuries; stories describe refugees from Old Volivat sailing into Nysina’s port after the Great Contagion subsided. The city bears scars from a Fair Folk invasion wherein Hornet-Prince Tinok’s raksha army built papery nests around Nysina’s existing buildings. The raksha are long gone, but some of their structures still stand; modern citizens live and work within their concentric chambers, mending wear and tear with wood, cloth, and plaster.

Nysina supplies Volivat with grain and shipbuilding timber. In return, its merchants occupy permanent slips at Volivat’s docks, trading with ships from western locales that only venture halfway along the coast before

turning south toward Y’danna, Palanquin, and Ysyr. Nysina permits Yennin-led battalions to pass through their lands en route to other conquests, neither offering resistance nor demanding payment for crops trampled by soldiers’ boots.

The verdant kingdom of Tern sits west of Volivat. Its capital, with its boxy, utilitarian architecture, is hardly more than a large town. Tern’s tranquil beauty lies in vast farmlands and grassy plains where livestock graze. During the month of Resplendent Fire, starshowers fall upon its abundant fields. Wondrous crops grow, nourished by heavenly rain and fertilized by stardust. Maize harvested from such plantings reveals golden silk beneath its husk; nectar from Tern’s melons aids seers with their visions.

Once under Simharajala’s thumb, Tern has been free for decades from foreign soldiers and enervating tribute demands. But so too does it stand unprotected by Simharajala’s fleets, and its people must now fight to survive. Over the last few months, Tern’s militia-guards have seen unusual numbers of heavily armed Volivati merchant vessels scarcely concealing their efforts to scout a potential conquest. Tern’s residents whisper about what annexation might entail; they know they’re no match for the Yennin, but have nonetheless begun planning their defense.

### Yennin Traits

Yennin Quick Characters have higher dice pools compared to other characters; most have multiple pools of 10-14 dice and at least one static value at 5-6. They also have increased health levels: up to (Essence) −0 levels, (Essence + 2) −1 levels, (Essence + 2) −2 levels, and (Essence + 4) −4 levels.

Yennin have a pool of (Essence x10) personal motes. Experienced Yennin typically have Essence 2-3; only the eldest and most exceptional of them reach higher. Their Charms are expressions of their superhuman Attributes. Select from the following Charms to create Yennin Quick Characters:

Inhuman Precision Focus (3m; Supplemental; Instant; Uniform): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) dice on an attack roll, plus an additional die for each point of penalty to her target’s Defense, up to twice the base amount.

Tenfold Might Exertion (5m, 1wp; Reflexive; One scene; Withering-only): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) on Strength-based rolls and adds this

EX3

amount to her effective Strength to determine what feats she can attempt. Withering attacks add (higher of Essence or 3) raw damage.

Foe-Breaking Champion (3m; Supplemental; Instant; Decisive-only): The Yennin adds up to (Essence + attack roll 10s) extra successes as dice of damage on a decisive attack. While using Tenfold Might Exertion, she also doubles 10s on the damage roll.

Flashing Blade Swiftness (2m, 1wp; Reflexive; Instant; Dual): The Yennin reflexively makes a withering or decisive attack. Once per scene.

Every-Direction Guard (3m, 1i; Reflexive; Instant; Perilous, Uniform): The Yennin adds +2 Defense against an attack and ignores up to (Essence) points of penalties. This doesn’t affect surprise attack penalties. If she successfully defends, she doesn’t suffer an onslaught penalty from that attack. Unassailable Champion Aegis (5m; Reflexive; One scene; Dual): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) soak and gains Hardness 4. If she’s unarmored, she instead adds (Essence + 5) soak and gains Hardness (Essence + 5).

Enduring Vigor Concentration (2m; Supplemental; Instant): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) successes on a Stamina-based roll. Alternatively, she can ignore up to (Essence) points of wound penalties, crippling penalties, or penalties from poison, fatigue, or deprivation.

Mile-Conquering Stride (3m; Supplemental; Instant): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) dice on a rush or disengage, or that many successes if she’s unarmored. Success grants her Initiative equal to her extra successes (the lowest such value, if rolling against multiple opponents), maximum (Essence). Battle-Ready Vigilance (3m; Supplemental; Instant): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) dice on a Join Battle roll. She gains a special pool of motes equal to her 10s, which are lost if not spent by the first round’s end. If she wins Join Battle, 9s grant motes as well. Unrivaled Sensory Focus (4m; Reflexive; One scene): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) dice on Perception-based rolls. Their senses are also enhanced — they can make out minute visual details out to one hundred yards away, hear sounds beyond the range of human hearing, and identify others by scent alone.

Ten-Voiced Utterance (3m; Supplemental; Instant): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) dice on an influence roll. If it’s against a single target and leverages a Major or Defining Intimacy, these dice are converted to successes.

Enthralling Visage Perfection (6m; Reflexive; One scene): The Yennin gains a bonus dot of Appearance, which can raise it above 5. Dice added by her Appearance are converted to successes. Unbending Will Meditation (4m; Reflexive; Instant): The Yennin gains +2 Guile or Resolve and ignores up to (Essence) points of penalties. This doesn’t affect penalties from her Intimacies. Tenfold Prodigy Brilliance (5m, 1wp; Simple; Indefinite): The Yennin adds (higher of Essence or 3) successes on Intelligence rolls, except those involving artifice and sorcery. If she leads a undertakes a project (Exalted, p. 226) or other bureaucratic task, the time necessary is halved. This applies only to planning, authorization, allocating resources, and the like, not physical labor. It can’t affect tasks that take a year or more to complete.

In addition to native Charms, Yennin can learn Martial Arts Charms, attune artifacts and awaken their Evocations, and potentially learn sorcery. Their Martial Arts are restricted by the Terrestrial keyword (Exalted, p. 427) and they’re dissonant with all artifacts (Arms of the Chosen, p. 16). A rare handful of Essence 4+ Yennin surpass these limitations; some even attain Mastery with Martial Arts or resonance with one magical material. As with mortals, most Yennin can’t initiate into sorcery; even the most powerful can’t reach beyond Terrestrial Circle sorcery.

## Ysyr

Amid the Chalcedon Mountains on the vast island of Gralon rises the cyclopean city-state of Ysyr. Gleaming columns of basalt and crystal encircle the city; soaring towers climb higher than any mortal art could achieve. Pleasure-gardens and orchards cascade down the flanks of terraced plazas; wide avenues lead into the mountain’s heart, revealing vaulted chambers with jewel-dusted domes.

And the city breathes. Deep below, ancient engines from the First Age still turn, though their architects are long dead and their purpose has faded into obscurity. Their steady hum vibrates throughout Ysyr, low and ever-present.

EX3

Atop this ancient machinery stands a city shaped by its sorcerer-princes’ caprice. By their art, they’ve made Ysyr a city of rampant magic. Baked-mud automata haul heavy goods to market and raise up stone houses; airy constructs of rainbow glass deliver messages. Ever-burning braziers of turquoise flame line the halls hollowed into the mountain; underground gardens of jasmine and lily bloom without ever seeing the sun. Life in Ysyr — however bitter it may be — always shines with wonder.

This opulent city of excess is among Creation’s greatest concentrations of sorcerous power, albeit built on a dangerous and delicate foundation; the engines below fail by the century. Within, an underclass of slaves dreams of broken chains. Beyond its walls, it spreads its forces thin in its hunger for conquest. Pulled in all directions by its sorcerer-princes’ contradictory fancies, Ysyr must strengthen its grip on the Dreaming Sea or fall into ruin.

### Culture

Sorcerer-princes and their households feast on banquets unmatched throughout Creation, with

exotic dishes prepared by demon chefs from ingredients grown by magic or gathered by elementals. Presentations emphasize art and spectacle as much as nourishment: roasted peacocks surrounded by a court of smaller birds; towers of pale crustaceans fished from the Underworld’s Sea of Shadows; edible Wyldgrown flowers whose consumption sparks strange visions. Overseers, clerks, and sorcerer-princes’ servants, though rarely invited to such feasts, receive bonuses in the form of rare ingredients, and may dine on leftovers once the sorcerer-princes have had their fill. Ordinary Ys live on a dole of bread supplemented by other prepared foods. Common staples include wheaten bread, dried fruit, hard cheese, smoked mutton, and salted fish, along with assorted vegetables, beans, lentils, red wines, poppy-seed oil, and fish sauce. Most meals take the form of porridges, soups, and stews. Due to the sorcerer-princes’ dominance over spirits, the Ysyri have little in the way of religion. Some cults devote themselves to various sorcerer-princes both living and dead — a practice officially frowned upon, though a few quietly encourage such behavior. Other underground religions include thirdhand Pure Way offshoots, ancestor cults, and cults to secretive, dead,

EX3

engine-inflicted mutations and remake her flesh into her own ideal of beauty and perfection.

### LANGUAGES AND TERMINOLOGY

Ysyri natives speak an offshoot of the ancient Ys tongue. Gralon’s other peoples have their own languages. Sorcerer-princes, Ysyri administrators, Gralon nobles, and the empire’s merchants also typically know Firetongue, Forest-tongue, or both.

For Ysyr’s common folk — if any can be called common, given their many and myriad forms — life is far different. Some are handpicked by a sorcerer-prince to join her retinue and enterprises; they work and live at that prince’s sufferance, who has all but complete control of every aspect of their life. Many princes select and clothe their slaves to match their own aesthetic, accessories to their glory. Some even inflict or remove certain mutations on their retainers, as much for fashion as function.

Ysyr is pronounced “ih-SEAR.” “Ys” refers to the people of Ysyr; it’s pronounced like “east” without the “t.” “Ysyri” refers to things produced or owned by Ysyr and the Ys; it’s pronounced “ih-SEAR-ee.”

or long-departed gods. Many of the sorcerer-princes themselves indulge in abstruse occult philosophies invented whole cloth by local thinkers.

### Society

Miasmatic Essence billowing from the engines transfigures the Ys. Most children don’t change until they reach critical saturation in early adolescence. These changes are unpredictable: some might find themselves with too many hands at the end of their wrists, or rippling silver skin, or many-colored spit that sizzles with acid. These traits aren’t hereditary; Ys children don’t inherit their parents’ transformations.

The suffusion of Essence has another effect, one that elevated the Ys from a seafaring tribe into one of the greatest powers on the Dreaming Sea: within some, it quickens the ineffable spark required to initiate into sorcery. Few actually become sorcerers — initiation still requires prodigious effort, talent, and more than a little luck. Still, the potential exists. However, Ysyr is a city not only of sorcerers, but of slaves. When the Ys founders first found the ruins and devoted themselves to its engines, they laid down the Rule of Chains: that all Ys were slaves to the city itself. This sentiment, yoking highborn and lowborn alike to the common good, is a vaunted ideal, the foundation of Ys rhetoric, and a convenient fiction.

Well over a hundred sorcerer-princes rule over Ysyr, each claiming a considerable allowance from the city’s coffers. Personal entourages of servants, retainers, and apprentices attend their towers. While ostensibly they’re slaves to Ysyr just as their own attendants are slaves to them, the magocracy’s princes serve themselves above all others, eagerly indulging in luxury, theatrics, politics, and pleasure. It’s a rite of passage for each newly risen prince to strip away her

All other slaves are held in common by Ysyr itself, assigned work, goods, and quarters by the city bureaucracy according to the city’s needs. This insulates them from both the generosity and caprice of the sorcerer-princes, guaranteeing them a relatively stable life. Those who display keen minds or special talents receive the opportunity to learn various skills and trades; while this rarely leads to any material improvement in their circumstances, it gives many a precious opportunity to exercise what little agency they can. Children live with their parents until the city’s engines change them. During their youth, children are afforded considerable freedom, with the state providing resources and education. The moment of transformation is the best opportunity for the sorcerer-princes and their functionaries to measure a child’s potential for eventual initiation, and so the young of Ysyr are prepared one and all for the possibility of ascending into the magocracy. Every child — even one born to the sorcerous elite — lives in anticipation and fear, knowing that the odds of awakening to sorcerous power are razor-thin. But the rewards are incalculable.

### The Magocracy

At the top of Ysyr, both politically and literally, the sorcerer-princes rule from their towers of agate, marble, and quartz. By right of sorcerous enlightenment, they lead Ysyr and its fledgling empire into an age of power and prominence. At least, that’s the tale they tell. The reality is less glamorous, but no less grand. Collectively, the princes form the magocracy — a belligerent and mercurial government drawn in all directions by its fiercely independent members’ obsessions. They would have destroyed Ysyr centuries ago if left to their infighting and galling shows of one-upmanship; that they’ve not only survived but also managed to present an illusion of cooperation to the outside world (aside

EX3

they’re granted other prestigious and useful positions: named sorcerer-admirals or governors, but never prince. Loyal service grants them ongoing opportunity to refine their arts and secure their authority, but they’ll never join the Ysyri inner circle.

### THE GATHERING OF PRINCES

Held beneath the luminous gold-and-carnelian domes of the Pavilion of Power Perfected, the magocracy’s annual meeting outshines the empire’s lesser galas. It’s preceded by grand entertainments — displays of spellcraft and artifice, many-limbed musicians and dancers, and more — and followed by a sumptuous feast of cuisines and delicacies from across the Dreaming Sea. While many sorcerer-princes participate in the flesh, others attend remotely via occult means such as simulacra or magic mirrors. For some, business at the edges of the empire prevents personal attendance. But for most, this is merely caution; the gathering has seen violent disruptions before, from magical accidents to assassinations to coup attempts.

### By Stone and Spell

Magic and enchantment pervade Ysyr, the product of centuries of savants imposing their philosophies and aesthetics. Perhaps the most visible sign of sorcery is the city’s dependence on bound spirits: demons and elementals are everywhere, from the poison-eating sesseljae who hive and throng in Ys infirmaries to the flame-wisps who attend the ever-burning braziers of the Shadow Quarter.

from a few dramatic civil wars) is an achievement to match even the most masterful spellcraft. The main instrument of this cooperation is a bureaucracy of slaves, the Clerks of Working Order. The magocracy typically meets once a year, with little on its agenda beyond boasting, scheming, and reauthorizing the clerks to continue governing the city. Each prince selects three slaves from her own retinue; these comprise half of the Clerks’ governing council. The remaining seats are filled by lottery from among the city’s commonly held slaves. Together, the Clerks of Working Order maintain the city’s literal and metaphorical mechanisms, assigning work, negotiating trade, and enforcing laws.

These laws don’t extend to the sorcerer-princes. When using their own resources, each prince is free to trade, war, and treat with whoever they wish. Abuse of this prerogative is one of the few issues that’s reliably rallied the magocracy to collective action, censuring those who endanger the fragile political ecosystem they all enjoy. It takes time for Ys sorcerers to rise to the level of sorcerer-prince. New willworkers spend years as apprentices to those at the top, demonstrating their dedication to their craft and their lack of sedition, and reshaping themselves until they achieve physical perfection. All spend a stint on the front lines of the empire’s wars, honing their spellcraft in battle.

Ys sorcerers treat non-Ys sorcerers with respect and even encourage them to apprentice themselves to the sorcerer-princes, though no foreign spellworker has been elevated to their ranks for centuries. Instead,

The Ys also count raksha among their slaves, captured during daring raids into the territories of the nearby courts. While relatively uncommon compared to bound spirits, the Ys value these raksha slaves for their unique skills and captivating features.

Beyond servitors, the city is resplendent with strange enchantments — floating towers left to crumble by their forgotten architects, gardens where fruit from distant realms ripens daily, fountains whose waters wash away unwanted memories. The greatest concentration of such wonders is found in the Thousand-Year Archive, a stair-lined shaft bored through the heart of the Chalcedon Mountains. Inside, a veritable army of archivists and occultists study, catalog, and store the collected treasures of generations of sorcerer-princes, preserving their notes and experiments against the ravages of time.

### Visitors from Afar

One of the few laws binding even the sorcerer-princes forbids mortal foreigners from setting foot in the city proper. To do so would expose them to the ancient engines’ transformative Essence, a blessing and a sacrament meant for the Ys alone. Instead, foreign dignitaries, merchants, and petitioners dwell at the foot of the Chalcedon Mountains. This is Humility, the closest any foreigner comes to the City of Sorcerers — a sprawling, manicured outpost protected by wards and weapons alike.

Humility is a closely curated experience overseen by the Clerks of Working Order. Markets are flush with such Ysyri products as precious ores from the mountain’s heart; delicate and puissant herbs; and minor

EX3

talismans, both legitimate and otherwise. The Ys slaves working the teahouses and markets — their mutations concealed behind aesthetically pleasing masks, robes, and gloves — are the very picture of hospitality, presenting an immaculate image of bliss while collecting whatever information they can glean from foreigners that may be of worth to their handlers. When a sorcerer-prince deigns to descend to Humility, they do so like a hurricane, upending the town’s carefully regimented life. In a fit of pique, an errant prince may bend the outpost around her own celebrity, entertaining foreign dignitaries with lavish displays of wealth and extravagant games of chance. These visits are mercifully brief and infrequent, but often require considerable repairs.

### Slavery: Dreams of Broken Chains

The slaves of Ysyr — which is to say, all the Ys except their rulers — enjoy comforts and opportunities unusual in Creation, but they’re slaves nonetheless. Most live and die without ever leaving the city, and while they can better themselves to pursue more satisfying work, their lives are ultimately subject to the clerks’ judgments and the sorcerer-princes’ whims. City-slaves are allotted berths near their places of work, as well as clothing, food, medicine, and other essentials. Overseers award skillful or efficient work with gifts of excess goods, forming the basis of a barter economy that measures itself in food, cloth, tools, and palimpsest. Slaves enjoy freedom of movement within the city so long as they execute their responsibilities faithfully; many take advantage of this and the city’s sorcerous wonders, spending an evening entranced by demon-harpists’ music or roaming the glowblossom gardens before readying themselves for the next morning’s drudgery. Slave rebellions, though infrequent, seem an inevitable part of Ys life.
