The clerks operate networks of informants and seek to break up incipient plots by appeasing rebels or reassigning them to difficult, faraway duties — often sending them and their families elsewhere in Gralon, where their mutations isolate them. The greatest, most terrible threat a rebellion might pose is to damage the sorcerous engines turning below the city; indeed, several sub-engines have been ruined during major uprisings across the centuries. Those who endanger the engines or conspire to do so endure the cruelest punishments devised by the sorcerer-princes, such as being granted immortality only to be cast in molten gold to ponder one’s crimes for centuries.

Many Ys seek to rise within the system rather than overthrow it. A sorcerer-prince’s entourage, though more directly exposed to their master’s whims, also enjoys her personal favor. The princes largely disdain foreign servants, who are forbidden to enter Ysyr and know nothing of Ysyri culture. They perforce bring their slaves abroad when traveling, relying on them as intermediaries with the foreigners they walk among. The sorcerer-princes also emancipate reliable Ys to place them in positions of authority elsewhere in the empire. Distrusted and feared by the peoples they oversee, most such Ys feel that serving the magocracy remains a better option than fleeing to go it alone.

### Ruling the Dreaming Sea

Before they were conquerors, before they were sorcerers, the Ys were mariners, and they haven’t forgotten their love of the sea. At any time, a hundred ships flying the Ysyri flag’s bronze flame lie anchored in the harbor-city of Kyn. The city-slaves operate a vast fleet of fishing vessels, and the day’s catch can be found on the plates of slaves and princes alike, sped up the mountain on carts of never-melting ice.

The Ys navy is well-supplied with the labor and resources it requires to project power to Palanquin and beyond. Its command structure resembles other sea powers, with ranks ranging from ordinary mariners to admirals; in fact, the admiralty is among the most powerful ranks a city-slave can aspire to, standing parallel to the Clerks of Working Order. While assignment to a battle-ready frigate is dangerous, it’s nonetheless a coveted position for the sense of freedom it affords. Many sorcerer-princes revel in the opportunity to lead a trade expedition or naval campaign because it affords them a chance to ply their spellcraft under real-world circumstances. They sail aboard flagships designed to their exacting aesthetics, stocked with alchemically preserved supplies and the finest crews. Apprentice sorcerers are often attached to missions to season them; it’s rare for any significant military action to be taken without at least one sorcerer’s personal support. And their support is truly invaluable. Those who sail against the Ys find that forked lightning cleaves their masts in twain; obsidian butterflies shred their sails; and spirits of water, air, and flame harry their crews. When the Ys lay siege, sorcerer-princes shatter walls with thundering blasts and unleash demon raiders, not settling for anything less than unconditional surrender. Whatever else they may be, the princes of Ysyr are rarely subtle.

EX3

### Territories: Gralon and Beyond

especially for the more capricious and temperamental princes.

Attacking Ysyr is a fool’s errand. Girded by mountains and warded by sorcery, the city is all but impregnable. This safety emboldens the Ys to pursue aggressive expansion, bringing the Dreaming Sea to heel by sail and spell alike. When Palanquin finally bowed a century ago, Ysyr became suzerain of the southern sea. Now its sorcerer-princes set their sights on the rest, putting them in contention with other mighty states like Volivat, Y’danna, and Prasad.

Still, the island isn’t wholly subjugated. Defeated peoples retreated long ago into Gralon’s mountains, hills, swamps, and forests. There they eke out a living and raid settled lands, their old gods and ancestors battling demons and elementals that the sorcerer-princes send against them.

Ysyr and the magocracy have precious little interest in the affairs of backwater vassals, demanding tribute in exchange for relative autonomy. This tribute is paid in goods and services alike, especially in contributing ships and sailors to the Ysyri navy. In return, Ysyr provides protection and access to its markets and specialists, dispatching skilled slaves and clerks as consultants, problem-solvers, or tutors.

The magocracy has no leader, but it has Oxemnes of the Subtle Fire — and the difference is mostly semantics. A virile, barrel-chested man, Oxemnes has deep brown skin, silky black hair in elaborate jeweled braids, and a smile that could thaw the North. He’s the current driving force behind Ysyr’s imperial project, always ready to badger, bribe, convince, or swindle fellow princes to support his vision of a Dreaming Sea under Ysyr’s thrall.

One prerogative the sorcerer-princes hold absolute over their vassals is the right to purchase any child who shows sorcerous potential. While used primarily to recruit promising apprentices, it also helps to keep vassals dependent on Ysyr for sorcerous power and serves as a convenient pretext for hostage-taking. The errant Spear-Queen of Johhadim discovered this to her deep misfortune — six of her seven children were taken, although only one shows even the barest glimmer of sorcerous potential. While their primary concern is for the coastal powers of the Dreaming Sea, Ysyr also exercises dominion over Gralon’s other peoples, most notably the walled city of Nysh, silk-draped Quru, and the forested sister-kingdoms of Osamunde and Osamitir. All four — and a handful of other minor powers besides — have pledged themselves to Ysyr. While some rulers consider the relationship a uniquely warm one, others fume over tribute demands, wartime losses in military service to the empire, and reckless sorcerer-princes’ abuses. They’re cousins to the Ys, sharing the same fair skin, ice-colored eyes, and love of the sea. Osa timber feeds Gralon’s shipyards; sailors from Nysh and Quru trade far and wide, flying Ysyr’s flag above their own. In addition to residences in Ysyr, most sorcerer-princes also raise palaces elsewhere in Gralon — on dizzying peaks, amid shadowy forests, and especially overlooking the sea. Settlements quickly spring up nearby to supply them and their retinues — though not too near,

### Prominent Figures

Behind Oxemnes’s avuncular façade is a calculating politician whose skilled application of spells like Peacock Shadow Eyes and Corrupted Words ensnares victims in a web of mind-shaping magic, and whose willingness to cultivate relationships with important slave families gives him the upper hand against his peers. Still, his power remains implicit. The eldest sorcerer-princes still recall the mad reign of Cyrex Serpent-Eyes as Ysyr’s sorcerer-tyrant; Oxemnes must tread softly lest they tear him down for reaching too high.

If there’s such a thing as a typical sorcerer-prince, it’s Cynerean the Blue. Ambitious, vain, and preternaturally handsome, with a predilection for azure silks and sapphire jewelry, he votes in the magocracy with a single goal in mind: to increase his own power. His fierce, charismatic advocacy of individual sorcerer-princes’ sovereignty makes him an opposition leader against Oxemnes, but his true passion lies in sorcery rather than politics. He’s a peerless expert on the sorcerous properties of stone, ore, and crystal; his personal holdings throughout Gralon include many mines where his ever-increasing quotas burden his slaves to the point of collapse. Blind to any concern but his own research, his plans to excavate ruins beneath the sorcerous engines — in secret, as it violates council edict — could put all Ysyr at risk.

Ydan Wei and Ydan Aoh are sisters. After her own ascension, Wei lavished all her younger siblings with

EX3

tutelage, elixirs, and any other advantage she could find, but only sickly little Aoh ever rose to the challenge of sorcery. They’re skilled diabolists, each commanding an honor guard of demonic servitors to protect them, their possessions, and their immediate kin — pampered, yet still technically slaves — from occasional assaults by other princes. They seek now to overstep the bounds of their own power through a year-long ritual to conjure and compel a demon of the Second Circle. Already, their work has cast a certain infernal influence over their adjacent estates, calling out to unbound devils like a beacon in the night. Kavatra is a young sorcerer-prince, slender and sharp-featured, their golden body as limber as a reed. Still new to the intrigues of the magocracy, Kavatra is obsessed with the question of sorcerous initiation. Why are some Ys butterflies and others mere caterpillars? Indeed, they wonder, might the inequities of city’s caste system be ameliorated should sorcery become more widespread?

With theoretical research providing no answers, they’ve begun performing increasingly gruesome experiments on the worst of the city’s criminals, exposing subjects to concentrated Essence from the city’s engines in lieu of execution. But Kavatra has achieved little beyond creating misshapen horrors fit to guard the catacombs beneath their manse. They now seek new sources of research subjects, and their scruples diminish under the weight of their cruelties.

The many-armed Janosz Ryl is one of Ysyr’s chief clerks, a position of considerable power and influence. Like all Ys, he dreamed of the day he’d awaken to sorcerous glory, and although he’s never shown any occult talent, he conducts himself with a sorcerer-prince’s imperious bearing. The real power of Ysyr, he says, comes from the orderly function of the city-state; when a society crumbles into anarchy, no spell can repair it — only work. To this end, he’s perhaps the city’s most relentless taskmaster, pressing anyone in his service to the very edge of their abilities. He punishes those who fail to meet his standards to instruct them in the virtues of dutiful obedience.

### Neighbors

The Oro Confederacy — a cluster of seafaring peoples blessed by Dreaming Sea gods and led by a visionary shaman-king — remain independent despite their islands now lying within Ysyr’s sphere of influence. Decades ago, the sorcerer-prince Alaguen Smoldermane destroyed several Oro ships when he conjured a tempest

for his guests’ entertainment. The Oro demanded an apology and compensation; Alaguen refused, suggesting the Oro captains should have moved when they saw his sails. Ever since, the Oro watch vigilantly for Alaguen’s banner as he suggested, raiding his ships without warning and evading all but the most dogged pursuit. Alaguen’s fellow sorcerer-princes, amused by the situation he brought upon himself, refuse to help, making the Oro his responsibility alone. Today, the Ys navy is spread thin. Emboldened by easy victories, the sorcerer-princes have fragmented their forces in favor of personal crusades and passion projects. This aggressive posture has drawn attention from other nations, including Dorce, an expansionist island kingdom west of Palanquin. Dorce’s tamed ship-capturing krakens have claimed three Ys frigates that entered the kingdom’s waters; these now sail under the Dorcean banner, an open provocation that the magocracy must answer. But thus far, a handful of sorcerer-princes posture in council over who’ll lead an expedition, gridlocking any real action against Dorce.

### Secrets of Ys Sorcery

Many residents of Ysyr hold the spark of sorcerous potential — a blessing from the ancient engines of Pinnacle. That power thrums in their bones and their blood, waiting to be quickened into understanding. Their sorcerous initiations reflect their sacred engines, the mutagenic Essence they absorb from birth, and their philosophy towards summoning and abjuration. • Sacred Core Concentration: The sorcerer condenses her Essence into a core — a supernatural organ that cycles power throughout her spirit, usually taking the form of a glowing mandala or gem over a major chakra. When she stunts her shape sorcery actions to highlight her core, she gains (stunt rating + 1) sorcerous motes. Foes can attack the core as a difficulty 4 gambit with (Wits + an appropriate combat ability); if they succeed, the sorcerer loses access to this ritual for the rest of the scene.

• Twisting Form Trance: Harnessing dangerous mutagenic power, the sorcerer may add (Appearance + Integrity) non-Charm dice to a shape sorcery

action. In return, she suffers a gruesome but cosmetic transformation of the ST’s choice, inflicting

a −3 penalty on social influence and disguise rolls. She can’t use this shaping ritual again until after a night spent meditating, during which the sorcerer renews her body-perfecting workings to remove the transformation.

EX3

disappears, reappearing in the nearest place of safety at some point in the next three days. Sorcerers who know Binding of Encircling Iron as their control spell can cause their Wyld servants to dematerialize into their own bindings. Sorcerer-princes in Ysyr use these as a way of counting coup, ornamenting themselves with ogre-torques and lorelei-bangles. In this state, the target has only a dim awareness of the outside world, but can still be influenced by the sorcerer, reducing his Resolve by 2. With a thought, the sorcerer may force a raksha to materialize from within the binding, which reappears on the servant’s form. Distortion (Goal Number: 9): A rival sorcerer may loosen the binding, reducing the target’s Tie towards the sorcerer to Minor for (Essence) minutes.

### ON BINDING THE WYLD

The Storyteller can allow a binding to happen offscreen, requiring several hours or days of work, depending on the local prevalence of Wyld creatures. Targets with high Essence, bodyguards, or other forms of protection always require on-screen capture. Powerful creatures (Essence 4+) cannot be bound unless the characters undertake a suitably arduous quest to discover some hither-to unknown weakness or some other suitably difficult task at the Storyteller’s discretion.

• Soul-Slaking Transference: Tugging on the sorcerous tether that connects her to a bound demon, elemental, or raksha, the sorcerer gorges herself on her servant’s Essence. Once per scene, she may drain up to (her Willpower x 5) motes from a bound character who’s both materialized and at up to short range; she gains one sorcerous mote per five motes drained. The target is left enervated for the rest of the day, suffering a −2 exhaustion penalty and recovering Essence at half the normal rate.

Devised fifty years ago by a rare coalition of Ys sorcerers, this spell has allowed Ysyr’s princes to add Fair Folk slaves to the demons and elementals who toil in their city. The air vibrates with the song of hammer on anvil as blazing Essence condenses around the target. With a forceful gesture, the sorcerer wills the Essence to condense, becoming molten iron. This spell can be cast on a raksha or other creature of the Wyld at up to medium range, rolling (Wits + Occult) against (the higher of the target’s Resolve or Essence). The bindings are completely indestructible to the captured creature, but others may damage them as if they were artifacts.

## The Orchid Court

Glass-bottomed barques crowd the harbor on the isle of Moste. Their sails, furled now, ripple with woven dreams as their dead-eyed crews row them toward land. Ashore, a retinue awaits the honored peers of the Orchid Court. Slaves draped in silk and silence stand ready, their gazes downcast.

See! Reef-Sovereign Ralen, with his narwhal-horn scepter and his escort of seven drowned men. A giant’s shin bone stands as his ship’s mast. The expressions on the figurehead’s face changes with every glance, but the terror in her eyes remains fixed.

See! Lyala of the Ebb, stepping distrustfully on solid land. Sea urchins cling to her nacreous hair, their spines venomous to any who dare to touch. See! The shadow passing beneath the waves heralding Salt-Rimed Umir’s arrival. He eschews ships altogether, pulled from his city’s deep-sea trench by a school of razor-toothed barracuda.

See, too, how Tide-Princess Suljin observes their procession along the docks from her jewel-encrusted palanquin, borne aloft by lamprey-faced hobgoblins. Her gull-feather cloak ruffles in the salt breeze. The Orchid Court has assembled. The ripples from their meetings may well turn into tidal waves that crash along the Dreaming Sea’s shores.

### The Wyld-Dark Sea

Across the Dreaming Sea, vast swaths of water churn with a pandemonium that even the bravest human crews fear to navigate. In some places, such as the

EX3

waters around the island of Chalbor north of Y’danna, the Wyld permeates each of the sea’s layers; the creatures that swim in these depths are as peculiar as any found in land-locked bordermarches. In other places, chaos rides atop the waves like an oil slick, its position everchanging as tides and currents carry it near and far. Fae rule these waters, laying claim to islets that speckle the surface. Fair Folk reavers capture unlucky Creationborn crews blown off-course into their domain. Some preside over undersea cities full of drowned seafarers and marine beastfolk. One freehold roams the tides on the back of a giant, overturned, claw-footed bathtub. Though the Orchid Court has granted some Creationbased merchants permission to sail their Wyld-touched shipping lanes, not all raksha captains honor the treaties. Mortal captains share tales of spotting colleagues’ flags from afar, only to be greeted by a crew of deadeyed sailors when they pass by. While some human rulers would prefer not to deal with the raksha at all, they’re the foremost source of gossamer-spun wonders and other Wyld-touched goods: music captured in stoppered crystal vials, cloaks woven from a village’s sorrows, candied joy. Rare is the community that cuts off all trade with Fair Folk merchants; they have only to witness the once-thriving port town of Reum, whose triumvirate barred raksha cargo ships from docking. Weeks later, the Barnacled Countess’s fleet came raiding to take what they’d previously been willing to trade for. Now Reum lies empty; its soul-eaten citizens serve in the Countess’s coral palace. Other Fair Folk have no desire to bargain with humans, viewing them only as chattel. Woe betide Dreaming Sea folk when the raksha go a-reaving. They capture victims for provender, but also as slaves and retainers. Thralls row the crystalline oars on raksha galleys or comb the tangles from a noble’s seagrass hair in his palace beneath the waves.

### The Orchid’s Petals

The Fair Folk nobles of the Dreaming Sea convene to form the Orchid Court. Though the region’s raksha act independently of one another, territorial disputes, pacts made with human settlements, and the growing problem of Ysyr require deliberation. The Court gathers formally twice a year; for the past century, they’ve done so on Tide-Princess Suljin’s islet. When pressing matters arise between summits, the Tide-Princess sends hobgoblins made of pin bones and kelp to summon the other nobles to her shores. Hosting the Court

grants Suljin a measure of prestige among her fellow raksha, but she holds no formal sovereignty over them. Though several captains clamor to war openly against human settlements on the coast, and the raksha of Mien-Beneath-the-Waves blow battle-hymns on conch shells, the Court thus far hasn’t made an official declaration of war. Such wars have cost the Court dearly in past centuries, and most have become accustomed to biding their time. But the chaos of the Time of Tumult seems propitious for invasion, offering new support to the militants.

The Fair Folk of the Orchid Court fall into three main factions: the land-dwellers of the Roving Isles, the seafaring fae of the Pearlescent Fleet, and the raksha who live deep below in the Brittle Star Principalities.

The Roving Isles

Scattered across the Dreaming Sea’s Wyld zones, the motile Roving Isles range from tiny, rocky outcroppings inhabited by lone fae to significant land masses where several nobles and their entourages reside. Cities full of glories and nightmares decorate the islands, no two of them alike.

Shipwrecks litter the coast of tiny Inel-Tem, where the lorelei Lyala of the Ebb has struck a bargain with a storm god. The trees of Inel-Tem’s forests are lightning bolts, branching brightly into the sky. Broken-off branches make powerful blades; Ysyri sorcerer-princes covet them, and forges in the Nighted City blaze like the near-forgotten daylight when their smiths work the metal. Lyala takes a grim view of branch-breakers; those caught in such grave acts of theft must answer to her.

Starry-Eyed Muuth presides over Ashtai-on-the-Waves and its otterfolk citizens, who bring him gossip they’ve gleaned while scavenging. Ashtai rests atop the water, swelling and shrinking with the tides, though inside its coral-walled palace, the halls are always vast. Visitors get lost in the palace’s twisting passageways without Muuth’s minions to guide them. When found, they tell of meeting strange sirens in the nooks and alcoves who sang the wanderer’s secrets like a dirge. Ilsha and Netha were once a single island until their ruling raksha siblings — the cantankerous Litheri Poisonjaw and impulsive Dirge-Sovereign Omerrin — began a bitter feud that literally tore the land apart. The sea between them churns, its currents in conflict over which brother holds their loyalty.

EX3

Tide-Princess Suljin claimed the isle of Skade for her own, enslaving its human population and commanding them to raise her sea-foam palace. It’s within these airy halls she hosts the Orchid Court. While most of her human slaves are soul-eaten, Suljin declares the most beautiful and talented off-limits for feeding and keeps them as pampered attendants. Some serve food at her banquets; others sing or perform at her command. Her hobgoblin servants spy on guests and bring her word of their machinations. Captured enemies become food for Suljin’s lamprey-faced thralls, as do courtiers who displease her. Thus far, none of the Roving Isles’ other princes have successfully challenged her rule. Rumors of dissatisfied nobles swirl throughout the Isles, but their islands have, curiously, drifted far off-course.

The Pearlescent Fleet

The term “fleet” is a misnomer, as each ship of the Pearlescent Fleet is a polity unto itself. Captains rule as they see fit, ordering crews to sail their glass-bottomed boats wherever adventure, treasure, or battle lie. No hierarchy or military structure exists — though many style themselves captain, or admiral, or commodore, they’re epithets only.

Naval skirmishes occur between Fair Folk ships nearly as often as hostilities with human vessels. Raksha crews may set their sights on the same quarry and exchange ballista fire and tsunamis while in pursuit. Commodore-siren Dailin orders her defeated rivals’ flags to be sewn into her Thistletail’s sails. She currently has her sights set on The Amaranth’s fiery crow, and considers anything caught in between — ships, sea creatures, or even entire islands — collateral damage. Meanwhile, the Fishbelly’s ragtag crew of hobgoblins delight in training siaka on their targets’ ships and diving for treasure amidst the ensuing wreckage. The Pearlescent Fleet names no representative to the Orchid Court. Whichever captain’s ship reaches Skade first when it convenes speaks for them all; the others may gossip or heckle, but their words carry no weight. While some captains seek to ensure that they can further their own political interests — or that they can suppress their rivals’ pursuits — most only wish to test their crew’s skill and their vessel’s agility as they race for the harbor, relishing the excuse to skirmish with old foes. Flotsam and debris litter the waters around Skade for weeks after the court’s business concludes. For the past few years, Reef-Sovereign Ralen has ensured his cutter, Crimson Starfish, has business near Skade when Tide-Princess Suljin opens her halls. He

has yet to lose a race or a battle and seems to have advance knowledge of when Suljin will call a meet. Among the nobles, he’s one of the most strident advocates for war against Volivat — for surely, the dreams of the Yennin would provide an unparalleled feast.

The Brittle Star Principalities

Deep below the waves, the Fair Folk of the Brittle Star Principalities dwell in vast graveyards of sunken wrecks. Their rulers entertain subjects in halls built beneath leviathans’ bones, lounge on thrones made of calcified starfish, and claim their territory along the narrow miles of a coral reef. Many raksha who live on the sea floor have exchanged humanlike aspects for features mimicking aquatic life: they develop gills, trade legs for tails, and form sleek fins that cut the water. Some no longer venture to the surface at all, instead sending their fish-faced children to speak for them in the Orchid Court. In the wreck of the galleon called The Azurine, many-armed Pertasi drills her army of the drowned, anticipating the day they’ll surge ashore and subjugate Champoor. She holds a centuries-old grudge against the water dragon Tenepeshu, who shunned her before the Court of Secrets.

Morillen lures mortals with her siren songs into airfilled caverns warmed by hydrothermal vents. Her guests recline on giant clamshell chaises. Her music makes them remember the bittersweet pains of lost loves and old regrets. Her hobgoblins collect their tears with thin porcelain spoons, mix in dried sargassum, and brew them into a cordial.

Salt-Rimed Umir rules the Brittle Star Principalities from his barnacle-covered palace. His spies whisper to him of Tide-Princess Suljin’s weaknesses — mortal servants of whom she’s overly fond, which courtiers she’s snubbed, a crystalline dagger whose bite she fears — all information he intends to use to seize control of the Orchid Court. He’s repeatedly warned his peers about the Wyldborn monsters called hannya, whose might even the raksha fear. Umir worries most about Karanthis, the Living Maelstrom, whose churning vortex threatens to swallow up Fair Folk holdings as it roams the Dreaming Sea, though thus far Suljin and the captains have failed to act — it hasn’t come close to their domains, after all.

Foreign Relations

The Orchid Court’s Fair Folk trade with mortal Dreaming Sea peoples, whose governments monitor such transactions carefully — though greed for fae-crafted wonders often wins out over caution. The

EX3

Fair Folk rarely accept payment in silver, and mortal foods offer them no sustenance. Instead they barter for mortal slaves to feed upon, commission works in order to devour the creator’s inspiration, or demand other, more esoteric costs. Some even honor offers of treasured heirlooms and artifacts.

### OTHER DREAMING SEA LOCALES

By the power of ancient sorceries tangled in the city’s First Age foundations, anyone in Realgar who knows the proper incantations can command flames. Ordinary folk know only simple incantations to light lamps, cook food, and warm homes; artisans of the wealthy Bronze Lodge produce exceptional metalwork using unnatural heat. But knowledge of the most potent and destructive incantations is restricted to a hereditary ruling class of incantators. Their powers have historically rendered Realgar all but impregnable to assault, allowing the city to escape the grasp of Dreaming Sea empires. Its problems have traditionally come from within, and disputes between incantator families may yet provoke another civil conflict that razes much of the city.

A few decades ago, the Orchid Court learned that Ysyr’s sorcerer-princes had discovered a method of binding and enslaving Fair Folk, luring them into ritual sites or set traps for those who come to trade. Some bold sorcerer-princes have even chartered ships to hunt in Wyld-touched waters. What fragile relations once existed between the city and the Orchid Court have broken down, since the princes have made it clear that they regard the raksha as little more than commodities. Hostilities have increased on both sides of late as demand for raksha-crafted wonders increases among Ysyr’s merchants. Several captains entertain the idea of uniting the Pearlescent Fleet and have made exploratory strikes. The recent capture of Suljin’s favorite advisor, the gossamer-architect Aletur, may be what finally drives the Tide-Princess to act.

Relations between the Fair Folk and the Dreaming Sea’s spirits range from neutral to outright hostile. Gods and elementals residing amid the sea and its islands influence all aspects of life; their winds fill the Pearlescent Fleet’s sails, and undersea spirits can feed or starve the Bitter Star Principalities. Some spirits prefer to hide, avoiding being drawn in to Orchid Court intrigues or becoming their targets. Others actively oppose the raksha, protecting worshipers from Fair Folk depredations or defending their own purviews from fae meddling. Positive relationships are rare, generally involving hedonistic spirits insensitive to the damage the Fair Folk do. Opportunistic gods use the fae to increase their own influence, sending them after a rival god’s worshipers, or bargaining with them in a protection scheme against their own.

## Dis

From afar, the cyclopean city of Dis looms like a basalt mountain, casting a long shadow on the waters. Nearing the far-flung island of giants, one can make out the city’s spiraling chambered towers, the ancient petroglyphs etched upon its walls, the strange geometries of its temples and monuments. It’s peopled by the gigantes, a prehuman race whose empire once spanned the Dreaming Sea. All that remains is their capital, seat

The trees in the Akarian Wood grow in precise geometric patterns, their trunks and branches aligned no matter which angle an observer views them from. The forest’s grid system is maintained by flocks of leafwing cranes — a species of wood elementals who’ve been its stewards since the Time Before. Mathematicians, geomancers, and seers come to study the patterns’ complexities and perform sorcerous workings. Poachers and hunters however, are unwelcome; the elementals often bury such trespassers among the roots to nourish the trees.

of their primeval civilization. But Dis is still feared across the Southeast, a name spoken in tales to frighten children and in hushed whispers among the lords of Prasad, Ysyr, and Volivat. Gigante raiders prey on the Dreaming Sea’s peoples, taking slaves and plunder back to their eerie city.

### The Gigantes

The gigantes are titanic beings, from twenty to sixty feet tall. They’re roughly humanoid in figure, but not of human features or proportions. Their overlarge heads accommodate massive wide-toothed jaws, bowing slightly under the skull’s weight. Their eyes have an anthracitic sheen; heavy muscles sheathe their elongated limbs; their hairless, rough skins range from alabaster white to obsidian black to slate gray.

What the Southeast’s peoples know of the gigantes mostly comes from their dreaded raiding parties. Warbands of up to a dozen gigantes leave Dis to seize as many slaves as they can bring back, attacking ships and coastal villages. No ordinary vessel could bear such

EX3

a crew’s weight; they travel on whales, siaka, and other sea-beasts enthralled through their prehuman magics, or traverse the skies by sorcery. They raid infrequently — only when Dis’ slave population needs replenishment — though some periods have seen numerous, aggressive attacks. The once-flourishing culture of the gigantes’ empire still thrives in Dis. Within its walls, poets recite antediluvian epics, savants debate philosophy and pen great treatises, and rakes dally with their paramours. It’s ruled by a prince, heir of a royal lineage that falsely claims descent from the makers of the world. At the great Fluxstone Table, twelve magisters advise the prince in matters of policy and receive her edicts to deliver unto the city’s populace. Its arts and culture are all but incomprehensible to human audiences — baroque compositions that seem to repeat endlessly, any variations too subtle for outsiders to grasp.

### Slaves and Soulgems

Many gigantes are sorcerers, invoking spells through sigils of impossible geometry, ritualized reenactments of archetypal events, and lengthy, sustained chants. Dis is also home to the strange, ancient magic of soul-binding. By implanting an eerie jewel — a soulgem — in a human’s or animal’s brow, a gigante can chain their soul to her own, suborning them to her will. The soul-bound

### SOUL-BINDING

Soul-bound characters suffer a Psyche effect that imposes a Defining Tie of loyalty to their gigante master that can’t be eroded and renders them incapable of action unless commanded by that gigante. A gigante can share her soul-bound thralls’ senses and can issue orders to them from afar. The binding entangles the gigante and her thralls; emotions, memories, and Intimacies may spill over from one to another as dramatically appropriate. A soul-bound character may spend one Willpower to shake off this control for a scene if doing so aligns with a Major or Defining Intimacy. He can voluntarily weaken his Tie to the gigante during this time, but must pay an additional Willpower each time he does so.

A character with Occult 3+ or an applicable Lore, Medicine, or Occult specialty can attempt to remove an embedded soulgem with a difficulty 5 (Intelligence + Medicine) roll. This takes at least an hour and inflicts an unavoidable level of lethal damage.

remain conscious and aware but lose control over their own bodies; when not ordered to action by their cruel masters, they seem listless and hollow, screaming in silence. There are other uses such stones might be put to, but the gigantes know them not.

Dis’ store of soulgems is limited. In murky prehistory, gigante artificers allegedly cut them from a primordial being’s crystalline heart, but whatever their source, it no longer remains. The surest sign of a gigante’s status is how many soulgems she holds; the vast majority belong to the prince and the royal family, while the destitute have none. The gigantes deem humanity their inferiors, latecomers to Creation possessed of incomplete souls. Nonetheless, human culture, scholarship, and crafts intrigue them, a fascination tracing back to their first conquests of mortal Dreaming Sea kingdoms. Watching slaves at work is a common pastime. Gigantes place wagers on slaves’ activities; those who prove distinctive often receive nicknames, briefly becoming prominent figures in Dis’ culture. Many gigantes have favorite slaves; some remove such slaves’ soul-bindings to keep them as counselors, confidantes, or companions. Dis’ philosophers often debate the ethics of slavery, giving rise to abolitionist movements throughout its history; these have been violently suppressed by those whose interests they threaten. The gigantes toil only in raiding and in lofty mental pursuits; the work of maintaining a city is done by soulbound human slaves. The gigantes need eat only rarely to sustain themselves, but delight in feasting and other sensual pleasures. Elephants, giraffes, river dragons, and other great beasts are raised as livestock; arable land beyond the city’s walls supports fruit trees, marijuana, betel nut, and a prehistoric flower that grows nowhere else. The city’s infrastructure is likewise constructed and maintained by slave labor.

### Commerce

While Dis’s neighbors fear it, some still trade with it. Dis exports strange stones and precious metals quarried from its depths, prehistoric prodigies, drugs, culture, and works of both gigante and slave artisans. In turn, it imports spices, jade, and art from Prasad; gemstones, silk, and sorcerous wonders from Ysyr; lemons, alchemical concoctions, and copied First Age texts from Volivat; glassware, cloisonné enamels, and brocade from Y’danna; coca, sugar, and tobacco from Southeastern Guild companies; gossamer relics and exotic Wyld-warped sealife from the Orchid Court; and slaves from any trading partner who’ll supply them.

EX3

Visiting merchants find themselves discomfited and wary upon first reaching Dis, knowing the gigantes only from their raids across the Dreaming Sea. While few ever grow accustomed to a city that dwarfs them as their own homes dwarf an ant, experienced traders know there’s little to fear from the gigantes in their home, so long as they come with business to transact. Lack of a common language is the foremost barrier to relations, though some Dragon-Blooded, Yennin, and sorcerer-prince savants learn the gigantes’ ancient, difficult tongue.

Legendary Size: Gigantes don’t suffer onslaught penalties from smaller enemies’ attacks unless inflicted by magic. ## Tzakul

Deep in the predator-haunted Crow Marshes, the vast ruins of the prehuman city of Tzakul lurk on the coast of the Dreaming Sea. Polished glass and colored stone spires loom over the streets, forming city blocks shaped like equilateral triangles; many towers have collapsed or toppled, creating a labyrinth of weathered rubble and debris. Scarcely a sixth of the ruins are on land; the rest lie in shallows close to shore.

Despite its great age and ruined state, Tzakul is far from abandoned. More than a thousand entities known as relicts, constructs of glass and obsidian, still dwell amidst these ruins. Each relict’s appearance is unique, but all have the same eight-limbed body structure. The relicts are the city’s original prehuman inhabitants. Millennia ago, they transferred their souls into the artificial bodies they occupy to this day. Amphibious, needing neither food nor air, most spend their days in Tzakul’s submerged regions. Some perform a wide range of seemingly inexplicable actions, such as arranging hundreds of small objects in complex patterns. Others work to repair the city. Tzakul was once more ruined than today; the relicts have successfully restored many broken spires to near-pristine condition, complete with furnishings unsuited for human use. However, most relicts spend time in less comprehensible group activities, resembling both worship and sorcery.

Relicts understand and speak various ancient and modern languages, but most see no reason to respond to or even acknowledge outsiders. When they speak, their answers are typically terse and enigmatic. While they express an ambition to restore Tzakul to its former grandeur, they never explain why they haven’t completed this task millennia ago. When asked their rituals’ purpose, they respond with such cryptic declarations as “We seek to fully become” or “We wish to return to flesh and glory.”

These two answers represent two competing agendas ― some form of transcendence versus regaining their lost fleshy bodies and renewing their diminished numbers. These two goals are antithetical, and some relicts undo or alter their fellows’ rebuilding efforts. Despite this

### CRYPTIC UTTERANCES FROM THE RELICTS

“Our voices are echoes, and we have forgotten the song. Can bells sing? We do not know.”

Participants find themselves immersed in an empty mindscape, devoid of even their own bodies. By force of will, they impose illusory forms first upon themselves, then upon the surrounding emptiness. In doing so, they craft narratives and challenges with which to ensnare competitors, breaking an opponent’s will and — ultimately — robbing him of his very flesh, awakening from the game wearing his body.

“The world has changed. The shadows have drained with the tide; the towers cannot pull the sea.” “Blood turned to fire; bone turned to glass. Can glass become fire? Can fire become glass?”

“Flesh is as rain. We cannot say if we are cloud or sea.”

long, slow struggle for their future, no outsider has ever observed physical violence between relicts. But they’re all quick to attack any outsider who assaults any relict or attempts to vandalize or loot Tzakul. Exploring Tzakul reveals tantalizing fragments about the relicts’ current civilization and the long-ago era when they possessed living bodies. The city also contains objects designed by and for Dragon Kings, humans, spirits, and other beings, some useful, others intriguing: a sundial dividing the day into uneven hours; statues of forgotten gods with unknown symbols carved into their bases; a series of locks in a dry, elevated canal. Scavengers have unearthed a few artifact weapons in ruined areas, though most are unsuitable to humanoid forms. Other artifacts are far stranger, such as a ring of ten-foot-tall obsidian pillars that shows a different sky from its center, or the statue of some extinct avian whose gimlet-eyed stare grants its observer uncanny visions. However, the prize most Exalts and scavengers seek is the secret of storing and transferring souls. Relicts never share information regarding the mechanisms behind this process. Should an outsider steal tools or devices relevant to these mechanisms, the relicts make every effort to recover them, by force if necessary.

### The Soul Game

For many outsiders, Tzakul’s primary attraction is the infamous soul game. In an amphitheater-vault beneath the city, relicts immerse themselves in a malleable mindscape pitting their soul against their rivals, potentially seizing another player’s body to wear instead of their own.

Although dozens of relicts — and the occasional curious visitor — gather around the vault’s perimeter to observe the games, there’s little to see. Up to nine participants

These games have attracted attention among the Dreaming Sea’s desperate and daring, because outsiders can also play. Old or dying mortals seeking renewed vigor offer to pay young, healthy individuals to exchange bodies. Others compete for the thrill of the game, the opportunity to experiment with a wildly different shape, or to unearth a rival’s secrets in his mindscape.

Relicts never deliberately switch their mind into an outsider’s body. Most who lose to mortals play again until they regain a relict body, but a few eventually leave Tzakul. These individuals often become vagabonds, artists, or scavengers. The Exalted and other beings of immense supernatural puissance cannot swap bodies via the soul game; their Essence overwhelms its spiritual conduit. As such, we haven’t included soul game mechanics, leaving it to Storyteller narration. If it’s necessary to play out a soul game, we recommend treating it as social influence, with “surrender your body” a life-changing persuade action or an appropriate bargain or threaten action. Storyteller characters who change bodies have their physical dice pools, static values, soak, and other traits based on physical Attributes adjusted to reflect their new physique and gain the new body’s health levels, mutations, and any other distinctive physical features. They retain all other traits.

The Soul Vaults

The current relicts aren’t Tzakul’s only potential inhabitants. At the heart of a towering, intact spire, a series of guarded and warded vaults holds thousands of polished obsidian spheres, each containing a relict’s dormant mind. A soul-sphere is approximately six inches in diameter, marked with distinctive swirls of sheen and color. Relicts never reveal this vault to outsiders; they attack anyone who tries to damage, steal, or even touch these spheres.

One-Who-Strives takes it upon itself to follow visitors around and divert them from its brethren. It spies on outsiders, noting their conversations and studying their activities. ### AN EXAMPLE OF THE SOUL GAME

Her old bones aching, Meersha crouched in the misshapen, uncomfortable obsidian chair alongside five relicts and three other humans, including her rival Arat. The relict in the center of the ring of chairs raised one obsidian limb in a cryptic gesture. At first, nothing happened. Then waves of strange sounds and smells blotted out Meersha’s vision, while a cacophony of vibrant colors deafened her. Consciousness slipped momentarily from her grasp.

The elderly Nathiri scholar Kalin Bei came to Tzakul decades ago and won a soul game, inhabiting a relict body. At the time, she exulted in the opportunity — what better way to study relicts than to become one? Yet she’s learned that wearing one relict’s form doesn’t make the others trust her with their secrets. She’s learned much and has theories on what their endless projects seek to achieve. Now she yearns to play the soul game again, to regain a human body and return home to publish her findings.

With no memory of moving, she stood in a vast chamber with a mist-covered floor. Arat stood before her, growing in size; normally well-muscled, here he was nothing short of hulking. He was once a Guild mercenary; Meersha knew his chosen arena would be battle, aiming to crush her will through helplessness, pain, and defeat.

### Relict

Meersha, for her part, was once an information broker. She knew Arat’s past.

Relicts are intelligent, free-willed constructs of obsidian and transparent glass. They stand seven feet tall and have eight limbs: four legs, two arms, and two modular limbs that can function as either. They can walk and run on four legs or run considerably faster on six legs. Each relict was once a living member of an extinct prehuman species who transferred their souls into their current bodies. Most have no interest in interacting with mortals or Exalts, but some answer questions and trade for useful objects. The following traits are for an average relict; many vary from this baseline.

The chamber became a noisy, crowded wineshop in the throes of a brawl. A dagger appeared in Arat’s hand without his willing it; as it pierced Meersha’s throat, her form writhed into that of Arat’s brother, dead three years ago at his hand in this very brawl. “Kinslayer,” she whispered in his brother’s voice. Arat’s eyes went wide with shock. Internally, Meersha smiled. She’d break his spirit, and his younger body — and mercantile empire — would be hers.

An outsider is most likely to glimpse a soul-sphere in the soul game. Spheres are compatible with the game, and relicts occasionally bring forth a sphere so that its occupant may participate. Woe to the outsider trapped in such a sphere!

It seeks to return to flesh and glory, and while it rarely answers questions directly — and sometimes does not at all — it regularly asks questions about visitors and where they’re from, and responds with tantalizing recollections about Tzakul’s past. Meht-sehket knelt, eyes downcast, arms raised in supplication. She placed her offering upon the altar before the enthroned aeon. The sun’s pale light offered no warmth amid the timeworn stone monuments of the Twilight Grove, nor did the hungry gaze of the sphinx-soul seated by its master’s side. “Today, Ledaal Rehu took my father’s head for a crime he did not commit. A leader to our people, he took no part in my brother’s rebellion,” Meht-sehket said venomously, her shoulders shaking. “You seek vengeance.”

She’d never heard the aeon speak before. His voice was deep, his words echoing as if they were sealed within a tomb. “Yes. My father was a good man, killed by a Dragon’s whim. I seek blood.” The aeon said nothing, but his sphinx-soul rose from its haunches and prowled towards her, slow and menacing. She risked a glance and immediately regretted it. Onyx eyes met hers, capturing her with an unyielding gaze as it stalked closer still. Another shiver ran down her spine. “You shake in fear, little bird,” the sphinx growled. Meht-sehket drew her eyes down once more. She could feel the sphinx-soul’s stare as it circled her.

“It’s not fear,” she lied. “The Grove is cold for the living.”

“A vengeful soul would burn hot, not shiver like a rain-drenched mouse,” the sphinx said. Its paws moved into her vision. “Does not your fiery heart warm your limbs?”

From his throne, the aeon watched. “Must you draw this out?”

“Patience, master,” the sphinx replied. With one thick, padded paw, it raised Meht-sehket’s head to look into its coal-black eyes. “She comes seeking your power? Let us test her soul. For one such as her to make a request from one such as you, it is only fitting.”

“A… test?” asked Meht-sehket.

“Indeed. You claim you seek blood, torn from the veins of your enemy? How fortunate that you shall ascend in your father’s place after my master removes the Dragon from your path. Is vengeance all you seek, little mouse, or does ambition cloud your heart? Let us see.”

The sphinx lifted its massive paw and ran its claw along her stomach, speaking words in a tongue Mehtsehket didn’t know. She could feel the breath begin to leave her lungs, her heart racing as she struggled to suck in air. Like a string wrapped around a finger, the sphinx pulled her soul out bit by bit, leaving the scarcest end tethered to her body. She could only watch, gasping, as its chthonic claws stretched her soul across the altar. Its tail wrapped around an amphora, a grave offering left to the aeon. “A vengeful soul, without ambition or deceit, will burn as hot as a white flame, hot enough to boil the water within the wine,” The sphinx said, its black eyes watching as her hands wrapped around her own throat. She couldn’t speak.

The sphinx placed her donation bowl upon her soul, pouring the wine from the amphora into it with its tail. “A soul cooled with lies, however…”

It smiled and tucked its paws beneath itself, staring into Meht-sehket with ravenous eyes. “A soul cooled by lies will make a good feast for one ever so hungry. I am sure the master will not contest.” Meht-sehket gasped, her brown eyes moving down to stare at the bowl. She could feel the sphinx’s teeth gnawing at her soul, ready to snap it free of its tether. She squeezed her own throat, as if that could pull the soul back before the ritual was done.

The three watched, as the first bubbles began to rise in the wine bowl.

# Chapter Six: The South

Chapter Six

The South

In a Direction renowned for desert heat, the South is ruled by water. Great cities cluster along the coast and spatter the courses of inland rivers. Some nomadic peoples gather amid wetlands; others rove savanna and steppe, watering at streams, wells, wadis, and oases. Control of water grants power. City-states here often exert firmer rule than elsewhere, as those who’d rebel or flee find themselves hemmed in by the desert. Nomads fight to control water sources, or else treat them as sacrosanct. Wealth from many sources — cash crops, mining, incense, and more — is funneled through oasis roads and river cities to coastal ports, enriching rulers and merchants alike.

Along the Inland Sea coast, the Southern climate offers hot, dry summers and cool, rainy winters. It grows hotter and drier in the adjacent steppes, with precipitation diminishing as one travels farther inland. Amid the rocky earth, barren stones, and rolling sands of the deep desert, temperatures remain high during the day year-round, while growing cold during the night.

## Ember

From the Summer Mountains’ western slopes rises the fortress-city of Ember, the final fastness of the Nywera. The Nywera came to this ancient Shogunate citadel a century ago, following their twin seers’ prophecies. Their civilization’s leaders gather here, gazing over the Summer Mountains toward the homeland they fled. In the Twin Queens’ court, they debate how best to honor what was lost and defend what they’ve built.

### Flight from Prasad

A century past, Nywera seers foresaw that doom that would befall Ekyo, the First Hearth — their ancestral home east of the Summer Mountains. The Empire of Prasad, resurgent and powerful, would rise like a storm on the savannah, seizing the Summer Mountains and the trade routes beyond. The Nywera would be defeated and consumed. They could only save their people by leaving Ekyo behind.

Following the same visions that foretold their doom, the Twin Queens led their people on an exodus to a promised land of valleys in a great, impregnable fortress’s shadow. There, within and around that abandoned Shogunate stronghold, the Nywera founded the city of Ember and rebuilt their civilization. For a century, they’ve watched Prasad expand. Now they prepare their city’s defenses, unwilling to be driven from their home again.

### Among Sacred Groves

On Ember’s outskirts, around steaming mineral springs, the Nywera’s most precious resource grows: torchpine groves, needles glimmering red even in the night. Replanted along the region’s fiery dragon lines, these precious trees burn hot enough to feed excellent forges; their sap forms high-quality incense; their flowers, perfume. The pollen can be used as firedust. None of these uses compare to the remarkable discovery that’s made the torch-pine sacred to the Nywera. When inhaled, torch-pine pollen inspires visions so powerful that they shatter the mind. Only twins can weather the visions; they share the burden together, and — if they survive the experience with minds intact — glean oracular abilities from the experience. Nyweran savants once cultivated torch-pines in great numbers in Ekyo, only to destroy them to deny the Prasadi during their exodus. Using cuttings and seedlings, the Nywera grew Ember’s groves over the last century with sufficient yield to establish a stockpile. Despite this, Nyweran elders warn that aggressive harvesting to amass a war chest is unsustainable. This is a daily topic of debate among the Nyweran elite who claim stewardship of each grove.

Groves and Estates

Grove stewards cultivate Ember’s torch-pine groves. Originally a duty entrusted to savants to ensure the trees would grow in these foreign soils, the role of steward has fallen into the hands of a wealthy, powerful hereditary elite. Merchant princes, high priests, and

EX3

chieftains’ favorites — many descended from the original savants, who gained status and riches from their role — oveersee the trees, setting prices on harvested pollen and controlling who has access to it.

### Twins

’ gifts differ from one another. One might read memories from objects while his twin receives visions of future events; one may read thoughts while her twin senses emotions.

Each steward’s estate contains a torch-pine grove ringed with low walls, with sentinel towers watching for intrusion day and night. The steward, her family, and her servants inhabit a manor house on the grounds; grove laborers reside elsewhere, traveling to and from the estate daily.

Such power has a price. Should one twin die, she may take both twins’ magic with her into death. If not, the survivor burns out, overwhelmed by the power that together the pair could hold at bay; the result may involve seizures, stroke, coma, or death.

Twins

Gifted twins — those who’ve survived the torch-pine pollen ordeal — form Nywera’s ruling class. Nywera deem all twins to be wise, natural leaders, and gifted twins fill some of the most elite positions in society: high priests, merchant princes, generals, and seers. Families expect great things from twins, holding them to high standards and harshly punishing those who don’t meet expectations. One twin’s success elevates both; one twin’s failure shames both.

All Nywera aspire to raise twins. During the week-long spring festival of Budding Leaves, hopeful parents offer nine ritual dishes to the blue-blooded fertility goddess Njemakati in their household shrines. Wealthy Nywera can afford to burn the offerings most pleasing to Njemakati — including red wine, silver trinkets, and embroidered silks — and receive her blessing with greater frequency; as a result, the wealthy often have at least one pair of twins in their family. Twins are rarer among lowborn Nywera, but it’s not uncommon for parents to adopt two orphans of the same age and call them twins. ### Governance

Nyweran territory is divided into districts, three of which form Ember proper. Half a dozen more encompass the villages and grove-estates of the surrounding Iron Valleys. Each village or urban neighborhood is overseen by a reeve, who takes charge of the people’s day-to-day needs. Reeves report to their district’s highreeve, supplying them with surplus goods for redistribution and keeping them informed on local matters. The high-reeves themselves report to the Twin Queens’ court in a similar manner.

When a reeve dies, resigns, or is dismissed for criminal or shameful acts, their district’s high-reeve names a replacement — traditionally the former reeve’s child or sibling, forming aristocratic lineages in all but name. Similarly, the Twin Queens select replacements for high-reeves.

A high-reeve is often a twin. Such high-reeves frequently appoint their twins as advisors or emissaries, tasked with representing the district — and their family’s interests — in the duumvir’s court.

The Twin Queens

Traditionally, the Twin Queens — chosen from among Ember’s gifted twins — act as duumvirs. They serve until one twin dies or old age forces both to step down. When the current duumvirs can no longer serve, a council composed of district high-reeves, generals, Nywera seers, and respected elders assembles to interview twins who’ve proven their wisdom and bravery. Council members weigh candidates’ deeds and discuss their plans for Nywera’s future. Seers share pollen-granted insights and debate what triumphs and troubles depend on the council’s choice. Babirye and Nakato, legendary heroes famed for foresight and bravery, are the current Twin Queens. They came to prominence as young heroes during the exodus from Ekyo and the rekindling of Nyweran civilization

### Dancing Societies

Masked dancers dominate Nywera religious ritual, donning costumes in emulation of gods and honored ancestors. Their societies are part social group and part mystery cult, dedicated to the reverence of heroes and spirits. Joining a dancing society is a vital rite of

passage for all Nywerans. These masked societies exist throughout Nywera holdings, from large societies in Ember to smaller ones in outlying villages. They form a network of friendship and community for Nywerans travelling throughout the Summer Mountains. Warriors favor the scorched mask of Flame-Touched Ochen, who first trained Nyweran soldiers to wield firewands; these dancers perform for select crowds supplemented by displays of colored fireworks. Entrepreneurs and savants prefer the elephantine mask of Thrice-Brilliant Nayaka, whose dancing society teaches the three treasures of success in exchange for lavish offerings and elaborately choreographed performances. Farmers, herders, and the like commonly join the Moon-and-Shadow society; they don skull masks, each marked with a vivid angular symbol whose color, shape, and position signifies a specific honored ancestor.

Nywera tremble in terror during the dancing march that honors Seluwin Mkango, a prince among those

Dragon-Blooded are rare but not unheard-of among the Nyweran elite. The great hero-twins Hulana and Ishoka are said to have both been Dragon-Blooded, though every Dragon-Blood born since among the Nywera has had a mortal twin. These are regarded as sacred protectors and tragic figures who often outlive their sibling. Queen Babirye herself is Dragon-Blooded; she’s determined to overcome tragedy and rule Ember with her sister Nakato at her side for centuries to come.

Most Nyweran households — from cow herders to courtiers — possess an ukali board. The game, focused on protecting one’s stones while capturing the opponent’s rods, is educational, teaching young shepherds how to guard flocks or warriors ways to outmaneuver enemies. More advanced configurations, using multicolored pieces and alternate rules, entertain philosophers and politicians. Worshipers of Kimitani the Sagacious set up ukali boards in their household shrines, seeking wisdom in the layout.

### Culture

The Nywera brought their religion with them across the Summer Mountains. Gods of wisdom, fertility, art, and prophecy traveled alongside their followers. They left much behind in their temples in Ekyo, but people carried idols and altar cloths from household shrines to Ember. So, too, did they bring stories and knowledge of honored ancestors.

Nyweran architects work skillfully with stone and wood to integrate traditional temples with ancient Ember’s monolithic structures. With precision and care, they fashion many-spired temple complexes in mandala patterns from local stone. Sculptors carve reliefs into temple walls to retell Nyweran epics, such as when the great hero twins Hulana and Ishoka slew thunder-shrieking Zamna-Vudu, and when they buried the cruel elemental Three Hundred Diamond Eyes in an ocean beneath the Summer Mountains. Typical Nyweran dishes feature chicken, goat, beef, river fish; root vegetables such as yams, carrots, and turnips; and groundnuts, sesame, or cowpeas. Foods are often roasted whole or simmered in tomato-based broths, and accompanied by spicy sauces. In the market, vendors sell fried bread filled with savory ground beef and herbs, or sweet versions stuffed with fruit. At home, nsima — maize or sorghum flour boiled into a thick paste — is served with various side dishes; etiquette demands

Dancing is important to Nyweran culture, even outside its dancing societies. Secular celebrations feature traditional group dances; teahouses clear the floor later in the evening for music and dancing. Society members attempt to recruit the most skilled and graceful dancers.

### The Final City

The sprawling fortress-city of Ember is built upon and around an older foundation. A great citadel of the Shogunate, Henmagan was carved into the side of the largest of the Iron Valleys, over a hundred feet above the valley floor. Hundreds of buildings stand on ledges cut into the escarpment. Sloping ventilation shafts convey air and a little light to habitable caverns and chambers deeper in the cliffside, as well as water to numerous cisterns. Nyweran masons repaired the city’s buildings and infrastructure, while warriors reclaimed dozens of vaults and chambers beneath, purging them of wild beasts, hungry ghosts, and other dangers that kept out scavengers and other would-be settlers for centuries. Other areas remain abandoned, still haunted by those same perils and more — whether bad air, cave-ins, forgotten spirits, or unraveling sorceries.

Each of Ember’s five gates is accessible by both a switchback stair and a hoist-and-windlass cargo elevator controlled from above. Several small guard towers manned with archers overlook each stair. The gates open onto Ember’s lowest tier, the Repository, which contains granaries, storehouses, and industrial districts. Smiths add torch-pine logs to furnaces, the intense heat allowing them to craft finer, stronger products. Artisans create incense and perfumes both from torch-pine sap and from other trees and flora native to the Iron Valleys.

EX3

Further stairways and elevators climb to Ember’s middle tier, where feathers tied to poles signal the entrance into the Ahru-Takuna Markets. It’s named for a god of trade and hornbills who followed the Nywera from their homeland; she watches merchants for dishonest dealings. Nyweran market stalls sell high-quality ironworks, colorfully patterned sarongs, and wooden figurines of deities. Many Nywera live on this tier. Multistory apartment complexes — their facades painted with vivid scenes of Ekyo landscapes and culture heroes — are built atop the carved ledges, each floor occupied by a single family.

### THE IRON VALLEYS

The Nywera fled across the Summer Mountains and journeyed northward to resettle among the Iron Valleys — a series of valleys surrounded by high peaks and forested plateaus, connected by artificial terraces, stairways, switchback roads, and tunnels cut by ancient hands. The region is rich in iron, salt, and diamonds that supply Nyweran markets and trade caravans.

Shogunate-era ruins pepper the land, some built into the mountainsides. A handful of automatons patrolled their halls, following orders given them as the Contagion raged until Nyweran seers divined the command codes to shut them down. The few that remain intact are kept in reserve deep within Ember, as the Nywera cannot effectively maintain them.

The Paramount looms upon a plateau above the rest of Ember. Stairs winding in and out of the rock face convey people to this acropolis, whose ancient structures have found new residents and new functions. Bureaucratic offices are repurposed as meeting places for Nyweran leaders and as temples to mountain gods. Rebuilt townhouses with arcades and courtyards serve as wealthy Nywerans’ homes.

Ancient obelisks carved with vivid lion-dragon imagery stand around the valleys’ periphery on Shogunate-era roads, bridges, and mountain passes. These possessed limited intelligence and mechanisms for assaulting intruders, such as fiery eye-beams or command of local wildlife. Some are broken; others have lost some functions, but still obey command codes that Nyweran seers successfully intuited. As a ruse, the Nywera present these to outsiders as gods, passing off the command codes as secret prayers.

Near the plateau’s edge, a rocky pinnacle rises an additional hundred feet. At its summit stands the Bastion of Unbroken Thought, an ancient manse that shows its master mass movements — whether landslides, herds, caravans, or armies — in the surrounding region. Repaired by Nyweran savants, it’s become the Twin Queens’ palace.

### Prominent Figures

A famed warrior, politician, and builder, Babirye is widely regarded as one of Nywera’s greatest heroes since the time of Hulana and Isoka. When facing an opponent, she glimpses his lifetime of experiences in an instant, deducing his motivations and desires. In battle, she combines this with Dragon-Blooded power to devastating effect, winning duels and countering generals’ stratagems with unparalleled grace.

She Exalted as she and her twin Nakato took the torchpine pollen, tempering their bond in a tempest of emotions. She grew famous as a warrior — driving back Prasadi outriders from the temple-city of White Heart in Ekyo, slaying restless dead plaguing Henmagan’s ruins, and leading Nyweran warbands against the golden-helmed warriors of Kitangaala during Ember’s early days.

Babirye now balances concern for her sister’s failing health against her people’s needs. Where Nakato accepts her fate, Babirye rejects it. She splits her time between councils with Warmaster Mishoka and audiences

with sorcerers and savants who might prolong Nakato’s life. The latest visitor — a pale, regal woman with raven hair — claims immortality can be procured in the legendary afterlife called Cold House. Skeptical, Babirye nonetheless quietly gathers resources for the journey. The generals and high-reeves grow impatient with Babirye, expecting her to lead from the front as Prasad annexes territory west of the Summer Mountains. Begrudgingly, she solicits mercenaries to join her in scouting the Prasadi legions’ movements, though Nakato is never far from her mind.

Nakato earned her legend as a peerless seer, spiritual leader, and peacemaker. She didn’t Exalt as her sister did, but her foresight is enormously potent, divining the destinies of people and empires in the dance of flickering flames. Nakato was among the seers who guided the Nywera to Ember, and her foresight helped navigate complex conflicts with neighboring peoples in those early days. After over a century of life extended by rare herbs and tinctures, rumors abound of her physical decline. She coughs up blood and wastes away; no medicines soothe her pain.

EX3

Nakato concerns herself not with her failing health, but with building Ember’s future. Although her demeanor is serene and sagacious, Nakato is a ferocious political animal, using oracular insight to drive hard bargains to get what she needs. Willing to recruit outsiders to her plans, she possesses a network of friends and spies in the region — such as Zefod Farseer, advisor to the Potentate of nearby Seraph; Ghadira, a priest of the Kitangaala; and Szonia Draska, an emissary from the far-ranging Szonia clan of the Eskari peoples — who provide context to her visions. She always welcomes more such allies.

The sorcerer Za-Tephra is one of the humanlike fire elementals called ifrit. Impressed by Nywera prowess and resourcefulness during their exodus through the Summer Mountains, he swore loyalty to Ember upon their arrival. Za-Tephra assists the Twin Queens in negotiations with local spirits, liaising with fire

### WHAT THE NYWERA LEFT BEHIND

Just east of the Summer Mountains, amid grasslands made fertile by volcanic soil, lies Ekyo, the First Hearth, Land of Honey and Flame — the ancestral Nywera homeland. Its ancient cities — Sweet Cinder with its crimson-roofed palaces, White Heart of the thousand temples, garden-mantled Dancing Cranes — live on in Nyweran legend and song.

Nyweran temples emulated Ekyo’s holy mountains, where their gods were said to dwell. Among the holiest mountains is Mount Akhu, where torch-pines first grew. Few Nywera ever ventured here, fearing the gods and the volatile firebird elementals that call the mountain home. Local Guild enterprises, such as the Mango Blossom Company’s artisans or the Raymarch Sisters’ caravans, investigate Mount Akhu for traces of the torch-pines they cannot procure through Ember.

In the years before Prasad conquered Ekyo, the Nywera disguised their exodus as flight from taxation, famine, plague, and war. But a few thousand remained, to support the lie of military defeat and from unwillingness to abandon their home. The victorious Prasadi outlawed dancing societies and resettled many survivors, replacing them with loyal jatis. A few Nywera resist their new rulers, striking out as bandits from abandoned villages and hinterlands where torch-pine groves once grew. Admired and hated by the jatis, the rebels receive aid only from distant Ember’s agents. But most Nywera in Prasad — even many rebels — now follow the Pure Way.

Though he rarely speaks of it, Za-Tephra remembers fallen Henmagan. Enlisting lesser elementals’ aid, he searches for the ghost of a lover slain centuries past. Warmaster Mishoka commands Ember’s warriors and, through subordinate generals, all warrior Nywera. Since her twin brother’s exile from Ember by Babirye for illegal slave raids against a neighboring valley’s people, she’s become more combative in council meetings. She doesn’t hang on the Twin Queens’ every word; some make her out to be villainous as a result. Mishoka believes the flight to Ember was a mistake. She wishes to set eyes on lost Ekyo and to visit the temple her father helped build in their fallen capital of Beacon. Mishoka and an alliance of high-reeves are responsible for smuggling weapons and food to dissident Nywerans who remained behind, subjects of Prasad beyond the Summer Mountains.

### Beyond Ember

Ancient outposts of Henmagan litter the Iron Valleys. Such structures often form the hub for Nyweran villages, where families live together in blocky sandstone townhouses or large thatched huts. Here they herd goats, cows, fowl, and other livestock, and cultivate root vegetables, winter wheat, and hardy savanna rice. Where the Nywera once lived in Southeastern grasslands, they’ve adapted to their new home. Around the Iron Valleys spreads chaparral, savannah, miombo woodlands, sagebrush steppes, and plains of cacti. The region is rich in animal life, including antelope, rhinoceros, great cats, and claw striders. Some distance southwest of Ember unfurls the Jade Road, a trade route linking Prasad to the Varang CityStates and the Realm. There, Nywera merchants exchange crafted goods, mineral wealth, and rare torchpine materials for foreign wares.

### Neighbors

Many Nywera dwell in Saddle, the nearest trade city along the Jade Road. Once a small town, it’s grown significantly off Nyweran trade, resulting in major rivalry and occasional wars with its neighbor, the ancient

EX3

trade city Djabu. Farms and pastures spread out beyond Saddle’s high walls; within, farmers and artisans rub elbows with merchants, mercenaries, and nomads.

### THE FALLEN-STAR LAKES

Said to have been formed by a fusillade of falling stars, this sprawling series of lakes — also called the Witchwaters or the Behemoth’s Footsteps — lies between the Scavenger Lands and the near South. Many of the smaller lakes are seasonal, their waters subsiding to form marshes or draining away entirely in the dry season, then refilling in the wet season. In addition, all manner of supernatural phenomena haunt the upland lakes; prodigies from these regions sometimes wend downstream to trouble more settled areas, or scatter into the miombo woodlands to the south.

There’s tension between Ember’s rulers and elders, who want to conceal their new homeland’s wealth from ever-expanding Prasad, and Nyweran merchants, who seek attention to better market their wares. By and large, Nywerans in Saddle pass off valuable Emberite products as coming from other, distant lands. Built along the Tsoron Valley’s walls, the Ishenga villages traditionally traded with other mountain communities, offering baskets, ropes and other goods fashioned from their valley’s abundant hemp. In recent decades, Ishenga farmers found it profitable to grow cannabis as a cash crop for foreign trade. The resulting prosperity drew the attention of Nyweran slavers.

Seminomadic clans and urban merchant-venturers alike comb the upland lakes both for mundane goods — furs, honey, gems, tin — and for unearthly treasures. They especially bargain with the peculiar spirit courts of Lake Yafeya, investigate Lake Firemoth’s moonlight-spun ruins, and coppice the enchanted groves of Lake Grayglass.

The Ishenga faith imposes numerous restrictions to maintain believers’ purity: Outsiders cannot touch the Ishenga, sleep in their villages, or bathe in their water. Nywera raiders have violated all of these commandments. Pure Way monks offer the desperate Ishenga and their gods a place in Prasad’s empire if they submit, an offer many find appealing.

The Twin Queens send diplomats to the city-state of Seraph — carved into the slopes of Mount Taeras high in the Summer Mountains — to court allies against Prasad. A despotic savant called the Potentate rules Seraph and its surrounding meadow-villages, ensuring her hegemony through the Taeran Guard: elite winged warriors inhabiting cliffside monasteries, all but inaccessible to others save for lifts meant to carry supplies. The Potentate controls the Guard through alchemical treatments they require to remain strong, healthy, and flying.

The Potentate promises to support the Twin Queens against future Prasadi aggression, but only if Nywera’s warriors provide aid against Seraph’s rivals and enemies near Ember’s borders. These include the warriors of Kitangaala, blessed by their god with inexhaustible stamina, and the city-state of Cadence, whose curse-drummers have collected tribute from neighboring peoples for centuries under threat of calamity. The Shellrider nomads wander the region’s rivers and oases to harvest medicinal herbs and nutritious plants — such as horned melon, gemsbok cucumber, marula, amaranth, and okra — hunt small game, and gather precious water. Their giant tortoises, which grow large and strong enough to carry a full-grown adult, can walk

The lowland lakes’ city-states once grew rich on this commerce, but the Realm conquered them one by one. Now a Cynis satrap oversees this Satrapy of Lakes from the port city of Kurun Gebata, where Lake Kurun flows into the Inland Sea.

Shellrider culture values verbal arts. Teachers and storytellers pass down history and moral lessons through the nomads’ rich folklore. Speakers impress elders with cleverly delivered verses, and children puzzle out riddles to keep their minds sharp. Traders barter with foreign merchants, offering aromatic resins and semiprecious stones for fine metalwork and other finished goods.

Most Shellrider nomads call the Katiim home. Passage through this ancient cactus forest is perilous without a guide. Its roads are nearly impossible to discern, having been sculpted by the nomads over generations; caravans have become lost in the shadows of stories-high cacti, wandering through labyrinthine thickets of the spiny succulents. The nomads harvest cactus spines for blowgun needles, and gather cactus flowers for salves and poisons. Nomads and giant tortoises alike subsist upon cactus flesh and juice, as well as their flowers, fruits, and seeds in season.
