## The Varang City-States

the Pillar, while a comet might mark someone in any sphere as potential royalty.

Located along fertile river valleys west of the Naharai Mountains and the Fallen-Star Lakes, the Varang citystates are jewels of the South. Ruled by astrologically selected princes, they have — by and large — traditionally embraced respect for detailed and clear-cut order. Clocks, the movement of the stars, and a system of social spheres all rule their citizens’ lives. Now, as the fixed order of the Empress’s reign fractures, so too does their society face the prospects of disorder and turmoil.

However, most birth horoscopes lack noteworthy celestial phenomena to emphasize a specific future path. As such, their recipients are tied instead to the earth. This social sphere encompasses low-status manual laborers: farmers, ditch-diggers, miners, and the like. Earth-sphere social roles tend to be rural, while celestial-sphere roles focus more on urban life. To balance this, rural families often foster or adopt the earthsphere children of urban parents, while urban families do the same for rural celestial-sphere children. A few scattered orphanages take in unwanted children born as pariahs.

### Social Spheres

The city-states’ highly stratified society expects its members to follow the path the stars have laid out for them, whether that be bricklayer or prince. Each citizen belongs to a social sphere: a rank and role dependent on complex natal horoscopes and her parents’ spheres.

A citizen’s garments divulge her sphere via colors of fabrics and embroidery, symbols stitched on sleeves and cuffs, jewelry, and other adornments. Varangians instantly know the station of any fellow citizen they meet. Details vary between cities — some, like bellicose Kesil (p. XX), use tattoos to indicate sphere affiliation — but Varangian travelers quickly absorb these distinctions.

One’s social sphere depends on the planet or planets dominant in one’s horoscope. People in the sphere of Mercury pursue vocations involving travel and movement, such as merchants, sailors, porters, or messengers. The sphere of Venus includes roles involving pleasure, relationships, and reproduction, such as chefs, artists, diplomats, and doulas. Mars encompasses military roles, as well as others involving violence such as hunters, slavers, and butchers. Jupiter covers knowledge-oriented roles such as savants, skilled artisans, astrologers, and bureaucrats. Saturn addresses death, endings, and liminal roles, including physicians, funerists, historians, and priests.

Ostensibly, every single Varangian’s horoscope determines their life path. In practice, class often gets in the way. Magistrates, merchants, and other high-ranking or wealthy citizens bribe astrologers to change their children’s charts so they won’t have family members laying brick or digging foundations. Astrologers who reject bribes may suffer reprisals, such as physical threats or having a corrupt bureaucrat revoke their license.

Pariahs and Foreigners

Those rare Varangians with no defined sphere are called pariahs. They encompass citizens whose exact time of birth cannot be determined, those who failed utterly at their designated role’s training or duties, and those who so utterly loathed their sphere they chose a

Horoscopes provide more specific information based on other auspicious and inauspicious factors surrounding a person’s birth. These include the hour, day, and month of the year; the phase of the moon; where the planets stand in Creation’s 25 constellations (p. XX); conjunctions between planets; and even the appearance of meteors and comets. ### IS VARANGIAN ASTROLOGY REAL?

Modern Varangian astrology combines several astrological systems employed centuries ago by local thaumaturges and sorcerers. These worked in gifted occultists’ hands for the small-scale, limited purposes they’d originally been intended to address. But over time they were codified into forms more agreeable to wealthy and powerful families, further stratifying society and concentrating power in those families’ hands. Meanwhile, expanding populations pressed the work into the hands of savants lacking the occult talents to draw useful conclusions. Today, astrology is largely a well-meaning sham. A handful of gifted astrologers sometimes make valid predictions, but they’re hard to distinguish from the deluge of meaningless ones issued hourly by gifted and ungifted astrologers alike. Even were sufficient thaumaturges available, no astrological system can sort everyone’s future path into neat categories this way.

pariah’s life over the one an astrologer dictated. They wear gray, denoting their status to other Varangians. Members of all spheres regard pariahs with suspicion and pity. To support themselves, many perform menial tasks or distasteful jobs beneath a sphered citizen’s dignity. Others turn to criminal activity — whether scraping by as pickpockets and thieves, or accepting powerful citizens’ patronage as leg breakers, thugs, or even killers.

Varangians sometimes regard foreigners — who lack the benefit of precise astrological guidance — with pity, too. Foreigners must find their own paths through the world, guessing at what they might be good at, or even reaching above their stations. However, many gamblers view foreigners as lucky, and invite them as companions at gambling tables. Having no horoscope makes foreigners chaotic, free of fate’s bounds in a way the gambler hopes might rub off on the dice.

### Culture

Though fabric and styling differ by sphere, most Varangians wear a short-sleeved, knee- or ankle-length

tunic beneath a long, draped shawl of wool or linen. These multicolored shawls may be embroidered or embellished with woven belts and sashes, and most feature fringe or tassels — sometimes in multiple layers. Draping is both fashionable and functional. For example, soldiers arrange their shawls to keep their sword arm free.

Music fills Varang cities’ streets and salons. Composers produce music for flute, lute, and harp, which are used in dramas and festivals alike. Dancers time their steps to cymbal clashes and drumbeats during parades. Weddings are multiday affairs. Both families celebrate the couple, from small gatherings in their homes to large feasts that include extended family and notable members of the community.

Varangian brewers make beer from barley, a libation whose popularity outstrips wine. Lentils and chickpeas feature heavily in soups, stews, and hearty dishes seasoned with garlic, leeks, and peppergrass. Figs, dates, pears, and pomegranates offer lighter fare; people enjoy them eaten fresh or as fillings for lavish desserts.

EX3

Varang culture obsesses over timekeeping. Clocks are ever-present, ensuring that no parent is ever uncertain of their child’s time of birth, and otherwise shaping society in ways unfamiliar to other peoples. Their culture prizes punctuality; the streets pulse with activity around every hour. Lateness conveys disrespect. Busy Varangians keep appointment books to be certain they’re keeping to their schedules. Meetings disperse as soon as they end so that attendees can get to their next engagement promptly.

### Governance

While Varangian astrology narrows down the number of citizens born to lead, far more horoscopes show potential for leadership than there are positions of authority to fill. Thus, high offices — chief administrators, generals, etc. — are assigned by sortition. Magistrates oversee annual lotteries, followed by public examinations to certify their horoscopes’ integrity. The lottery’s specifics vary between cities, from drawing clay tablets from an urn to elaborate grids of tokens and dice. Potential princes demand more thorough winnowing. From birth, those whom the stars mark for royalty are watched intently by family members, royal astrologers, and other Varang princes. They seek portents and omens during the child’s infancy and early years; uneventful childhoods suggest unworthiness. Other milestones throughout a candidate’s youth and early adulthood mark their readiness for rulership. Upon a prince’s death, a council of the city’s astrologers and officials elect one of the remaining candidates — almost always from an aristocratic family.

In principle, leaders don’t come from specific families; birth horoscopes determine everyone’s role. In practice, princely families keep key roles within their bloodlines by various means — secretly laying lavish offerings before Urim’s star-gods; using specific foods, drugs, and midwives’ tricks to speed or delay birth for an auspicious day and hour; and arranging for astrologers to alter charts, typically through reciprocal bargains with astrologers belonging to other princely families. Families jealously guard offspring whom fate — and family connections and wealth — determine will hold high station.

With the Realm’s garrison protecting them against larger outside threats, Varangian soldiers — aside from janissaries — have limited experience with real war. Varangian military conflicts historically take the form of ritual skirmishes between cities. Generals from opposing sides agree on a time and place for their forces

to meet, and engage in mutually agreed-upon contests to determine a victor. Such encounters include formal exchanges of arrow fire, bouts involving small groups of fighters, challenges by champions, and the like. Exalted and other supernatural combatants, who can warp these formalities around them, are traditionally banned from participating.

### Religion

Varangians traditionally revere gods of the heavens, from mighty constellation spirits to lesser star-gods. But many of their gods are also earthly spirits who they associate with celestial phenomena. For instance, Tasal, city god of Urim, portrays himself in myth as an avatar of the constellation of the Peacock, while Hafzah Catches-the-Sun, god of the Shiphrah River, claims also to be goddess of the Great Celestial Waterfall (p. XX). But such worship cannot happen freely; the Immaculate Philosophy has been the official Varang religion since the Realm conquest centuries ago. Still, the astral gods dominate local prayer calendars, and Varangians are quick to praise them when no monks are nearby. The wealthy and powerful maintain covert shrines in palace towers close to the sky. Other folk attend secret temples located underground, where followers paint the night sky on stone ceilings or hang canopies of indigo fabric dotted with glass-bead stars.

As Immaculates, the Varangians believe that by living humbly and serving faithfully, they’ll be reborn into a higher sphere in their next life. Local folklore associates the Immaculate Dragons with the five astrological houses, as reflected in religious art. Daana’d pilots a golden barque; Hesiesh stands atop an amethystine bier; Mela bears arms and armor of crimson jade; Pasiap shelters beneath an ivy-covered doorway; and Sextes Jylis strums a sapphire lute.

Counting-Temples

Mercantile organizations originally funded, overseen, and blessed by powerful star-god priesthoods, counting-temples have a long history in the Varang CityStates. Today these trading companies profess themselves secular organizations, carefully avoiding obvious religious impropriety in their urban compounds, but they conduct secret rites while on the road. Their grip on Varang commerce limits Guild penetration into the region.

Some counting-temples’ wealth and reach make them established names even outside the Varang City-States. These include the counting-temples of the Gull and the

### Yane

### VARANGIAN NAMES

Varangian names largely draw inspiration from Arabic, Persian, and Hindi. Members of well-to-do families use surnames, while pariahs and members of poorer families only have a single name.

North Star, who dominate trade across the Inland Sea, and the Gauntlet counting-temple’s ruthless slavers. Other, less influential businesses include the Autumn Stars counting-temple’s bankers and the Butterfly Star counting-temple’s funerist cartel.

### Varang Cities

Each Varangian city’s streets and plazas spread out in geometric patterns, ostensibly based on the stars at the hour its first foundation-stone was laid down. Astrologers’ and star-gods’ towers rise high over the city, dominating its skylines. Most tower spires contain massive clocks, their mechanisms calibrated to ring every hour from dawn to dusk. The streets swarm with people, especially just before and after the hour chimes. Some run to and from jobs; others stroll to enjoy the city’s beauty, or ride swaying palanquins carried by servants. All wear brightly colored clothing denoting their sphere. While especially important buildings have stone facades, most Varangian architecture uses sun-dried mudbrick that deteriorates over a matter of decades, leaving structures unsound. Moreover, city blocks or entire districts may be rezoned to suit new purposes, or ruined by war, flooding, earthquake, or other disasters. Laborers smear on new layers of mud to maintain their strength.

Engineers raze decaying buildings and build anew atop the rubble, typically without filling in basements and cellars. Citizens reinforce and connect these buried rooms, then use the resulting network of labyrinthine vaults for storage, traffic, secret worship, and illicit business. The deepest chambers also house ghosts, artifacts, and other, stranger things. Aboveground, Varangian artisans cover new structures with intricate mosaics using fragments scavenged from the razed buildings’ debris.

Administrative capital of the Varang city-states, Yane is first among equals — a peer, not a ruler. Representatives from the other city-states gather in this so-called City of the North Star to discuss pressing matters, make laws, and oversee trade. Its costal location makes it a haven for Varang sailors and draws merchants from across the Inland Sea. Many Dynasts pass through as well; it’s the satrap’s seat, the central port of call for Varang trade with the Blessed Isle, and a common entry point for secondary school graduates touring the satrapies. The docks spread across a swath of the city, incorporating stone and wood where mud brick would give way to the sea, with stairs and sloping streets winding up the flanks of the city’s tel. Powerful merchant clans likewise reside in manors of wood and stone in the city; these often stand in sunken areas where surrounding structures have been rebuilt on rubble. Cult worship of wind and sea gods persists in buried places and outlying sea caves despite Immaculate efforts to root it out. The satrap’s residence, dubbed Ifrit House, stands on a low, rocky hill outside the city. Fluted columns frame the front steps; fountains water gardens of brilliant flowers. The interior is currently furnished mostly in Varangian style, and linen curtains billow in the sea breeze.

Yane boasts several Immaculate temples where intrigued Dynastic tourists worship alongside devout Varangians. The largest, Mela-Marshals-the-FourWinds Temple, stands on a high platform at the city’s center. This square edifice’s corners point to the cardinal directions. Carved reliefs cover its walls both inside and out, depicting the Five Elemental Dragons amid their associated astrological houses. Representatives from all city-states intermittently gather here to discuss matters that affect the entire satrapy. An observatory occupying the top floor allows lawmakers’ astrologer-aides to consult the stars during decision-making. Of all the Varang city-states, Yane is the most cosmopolitan. While the stars determine citizens’ roles — aristocratic families still govern, and most Yanite merchants were born into Mercury’s sphere — there’s less stratification here than in the rest of the Confederacy. To many in Yane, whether a person was born to the celestial or earth sphere, or no sphere at all, is less important than what they contribute to the community.

### Other Noteworthy Varang City-States

For this reason, pariahs gravitate toward Yane, attracted by the opportunity to find employment with foreigners unconcerned by their social status. Many become sailors, shipwrights, artisans, and traders, apprenticing under and working for people who see their gray garments as little more than sartorial choice. Much of Yane’s presatrapial history and culture was lost when the Realm conquered and razed the old city centuries ago. All that remains is what’s been passed down by the Yanites and what lingers in the buried parts of the city. This presents an opportunity. Scholars and scavengers excavate the tunnels beneath; the former clandestinely share their findings, while the latter sell them. This is part of the local counterculture, though Yanite authorities tend to conduct regular raids to try stamping it out.

Prominent Figures

Kinzeri Elat, Prince of Yane, has few civic duties; disinterested in politics, she’s quietly ceded policy decisions to an unofficial council of merchant house elders and the satrap’s staff. Instead, she spends her time entertaining aristocratic visitors, studying Varangian astrological sciences, and writing lengthy letters to distant cousins on the Blessed Isle. Though she’s happy with her studies and the pleasant quiet of her palace, she fears that quiet time is ending. With much of the garrison withdrawn and neighboring polities rattling sabers, she must personally negotiate with foreign dignitaries, seeking alliances and considering marriage offers that might help preserve Yane’s security. Satrap Ledaal Nemaya is a visionary bureaucrat and mathematician who saw the Varang City-States’ sphere system as an ideal laboratory to experiment with synoptic economic models that might squeeze more tribute out of a satrapy without fomenting revolt. But her weak political skills leave her at a loss as crisis looms post-Empress. She finds herself leaning more and more on her advisors, especially the ambitious social climber Nellens Soderin and the obsessive antiquarian Wave Ukiyo, neither of whom she can fully trust. Mahazi Maala, a well-respected astrologer, is a close friend of the satrap. She’s also deeply corrupt, having spent decades taking bribes to provide doctored horoscopes. But she’s recently been blackmailed to do the opposite, and the prestigious Harsi family now seeks revenge for giving their heir a manual laborer’s horoscope. Instead of opting for a palanquin and a squad of soldiers, Maala dresses unassumingly, takes well-lit routes, and keeps friends in high places. She has been quietly preparing for an untimely death, but — unsure

which of her clients might be responsible — has written a posthumous confession to take everyone down when she goes, potentially sending Yane spiraling in chaos. Assenath Iscah has been Yane’s commander of the guard for much of his life. An unassuming man in his fifties, he knows where all his troops are at all times, and has a brilliant mind hidden under quiet, pale eyes. He resents the satrap, and while he keeps a cool front in her presence, he’s quietly been looking for ways to get rid of her while the Realm is in upheaval. He surreptitiously seeks aid from cultists of the sea god Mu-Mat Tidespinner, whose intercession he hopes will help him control the docks in a crisis.

Proud and tenacious, Nilima the Blessed climbed from poverty to become Yane’s most storied courtesan. She only takes clients during the new moon; her waiting lists last for months. Self-educated, she’s famous for conversation and erudition, sometimes accompanying clients on delegations to neighboring city-states as an advisor. She regularly visits Prince Elat as a mistress rather than a courtesan; as the prince finally grows interested in governance, Nilima is becoming her most trusted advisor, encouraging independence from the Realm and reliance on the old gods.

Other Noteworthy

Varang City-States

Kesil — the high-walled, many-towered City of the Banner — has a long and storied history of warriors and god-kings; its legendary founder, Prince Ajan, reportedly once ruled all Varangia and beyond, though his empire collapsed after his death. To many, Kesil’s best days are in the past. Its warrior tradition offers less profit than other Varang city-states’ mercantile focus, seeing use mostly in mercenary work and service as Realm auxiliaries. But Kesil may experience a resurgence in this time of tumult. As the Realm withdraws its garrisons, Kesil’s experienced military may allow it to dominate its neighbors through intimidation or conquest.

Dueling is legal in Kesil. Complainants settle disputes by fighting to incapacitation, while warriors cross blades until first blood to win accolades and keep skills sharp. Sick or elderly Kesilians unwilling to die abed consult astrologers on auspicious days to seek reincarnation, for which they’ll schedule duels to the death; their juniors see accepting such a duel as an honor. Some claim that Sapir, City of the Key, is the oldest Varang city, origin of spheres and astrological sciences.

### THE BLUE SEERESS

Hailed in song and story as the greatest of all Varangian prophets, the Blue Seeress lies entombed beneath a clocktower in the city of Urim (Exalted, p. 96), her body incorruptibly preserved. Attendants wreath her bier in flowers and collect tithes from visitors; scribe-celebrants keep her fires burning and record her prophecies in thick codices.

A pall of flickering orange smoke hovers eternally over the vales of Fallen Krothera. Centuries ago, the Realm sent in several legions to smite the Lunar elder Lightless-Wings’s heavily fortified dominion. LightlessWings and his newfound Solar mate Maurea Tidesong were slain and their people scattered, but the legions suffered terribly and the land suffered worse; sorcery, First Age weapons, and mighty Exalted powers rent the world asunder. Today the Fair Folk prince Samandra Six-Rings rules the smoldering middlemarch-palace of Cindercatch and its fiery elemental legions, while bloodthirsty smoke-ghosts stalk the borders of blackened shadowlands.

So great was the Seeress’s power that even her corpse issues prophecies in times of chaos and strife. Since the Realm conquest, she largely lay quiet in her crystal coffin, smiling faintly. But recently she began speaking once more — first in whispers, then in reverberant proclamations — of fire and bronze, blood in Urim’s streets, chaos in Heaven, and deaths of stars.

Its scholars are said to be without peer; its libraries brim with treatises both ancient and new. The sick, the aged, and wealthy gourmands across the Varang citystates seek out its astrologer-chefs, who prescribe diets balancing ascending, resplendent, or descending ingredients — those deemed to intensify, harmonize, or denature the body’s Essence — and ban consumption of ingredients at odds with the patient’s horoscope. The city’s reputation spans the South and beyond. But Sapir is in decline. Famines drove merchants and peasants from the city. Crackdowns to keep them (and their taxes) from escaping led to riots, revolts, and fires until the satrap stepped in. Some wag dubbed it the City of the Rising Smoke after the latest conflagration; the ill-omened name has stuck.

Today, while parts of the city — markets, Immaculate temples, the university — bustle with new construction, other districts lie abandoned, home to indigents, vagabonds, and criminal gangs. The newly elevated prince, Jaasau Ibranum, struggles to rebuild despite long-term debts to other cities’ aristocratic houses and to various counting-temples, all thrust on the bookish youngster with her office.

### Neighbors

Several Varang city-states claim sections of the Itungu Steppe as their territory, but they control little beyond the Wezun River’s bog-iron towns and ancient fortalices. The Itungu’s nomadic residents, such as the mercantile, camel-herding Kej-No and the aggressive Erez horse-archers, simply ride away from Varang tax

## Chiaroscuro

Shattered glass towers glint over the horizon; wet stone battlements adorned with brazen steam-powered cannons face the sea. Though fallen far from the First Age, Chiaroscuro now shines as the jewel of the Delzahn people. It remains a pivotal port and trade hub in the South, its teeming populace a mélange from every corner of Creation.

### Geography

Roads of dark red glass run through the city, some wide enough for men to walk twenty abreast, others barely wide enough for a donkey cart. These cinnabar roads form a perimeter around Chiaroscuro, broken only by the sprawling Foreigners’ Quarter. Thick veins of glass reach towards the docks and out into the surrounding countryside; narrower avenues stretch into the city. Despite their frictionless, diaphanous appearance, travelers find the roads easy. Dust and liquids drain via grates into a tangle of underground sewers that empty into the ocean. The roads also ameliorate the weather; rain falls on them more gently, heat feels less fierce, and a comfortable breeze perpetually soothes the weary traveler. At night, the cinnabar roads glow softly, radiating gentle warmth. Curving blue-green sea walls of imperishable crystal guard the harbor, calming the storms that lash the coast in the rainy season while maintaining a cool breeze and steady currents nearby. At night, they shine a luminous silver-blue, guiding ships towards the city.

EX3

Outsiders, travelers, and the desperately poor survive in the lawless Foreigners’ Quarter. Encompassing a swath of the city particularly hard-hit by Shogunateera wars and post-Contagion strife, today it’s a morass of rubble and roofless ruins. Streets wind aimlessly between walls of ancient debris; ragged plazas encompass mud-brick buildings, semipermanent hide tents, alehouses, hostels, stables, and slaughterhouses. Residents and scavengers alike move with caution for fear of sinkholes, volatile ancient weapons, and hungry ghosts.

But even the Foreigners’ Quarter is safer at night than the Whispering Circles. Chiaroscuro contains several small shadowlands, each no larger than a few city blocks. Salt wardens, who claim descent from the city’s original inhabitants, carefully maintain wards formed by grooves in the pavement that they keep filled with caked salt to cage the shadowlands’ hungry ghosts and spectral creatures. This effort requires constant vigilance. As a result, wardens are largely exempt from law; interfering with or disturbing their work is taboo. So effectively do they labor that few hungry ghosts breach the city in any year. When they do, wardens prove themselves competent hunters and exorcists, although they sometimes hire outsiders to help with the dirty work. During the day, hundreds risk stepping past the wards into the Circles to collect scraps of imperishable glass and search for lost wonders. Centuries of scavenging have scoured away easily secured treasures, so scavengers now scale half-shattered towers, rummage beneath monumental rubble, or delve into forgotten tunnels.

Scavengers sell glass scraps to the Faience and Glasswork Association. This confederation of glaziers, knappers, grinders, and glassblowers has an economic stranglehold on trading and working the steel-hard First Age glass, as well as more common varieties of glass and crystal. The Association maintains strict secrecy and control over its techniques. Trading in glass — normal or Chiaroscuran — without the Association’s blessing earns threats and economic reprisal, and only Association members may legally buy or sell Chiaroscuran glass.

### Life in Chiaroscuro

Towers of imperishable glass rise hundreds of feet skyward, but only a handful remain habitable. Apartments in glass towers are reserved for Delzhan nobility; others may petition the reigning tri-khatun (p, XX) for residency, and pay exorbitant rents for the privilege.

GRANDMOTHER BRIGHT’S PLAZA

Tucked away in a corner of the city, one plaza seems at perfect peace. At any given time, the six surrounding First Age tenements accommodate 1,001 living residents — no more, no less. Overseeing these residents is the spirit named Grandmother Bright, who chooses who’s permitted to enter her home. Those who press the issue, or violate the Plaza’s peace with theft or bloodshed, find themselves facing an ancient and powerful spirit’s ire.

At night, the streets throng with ghostly figures, going about their business as though alive, and vanishing with the dawn. 1,001 dead residents linger here, sharing Grandmother Bright’s protection. As with the living, no new ghost can reside here unless another ghost departs.

Criminals sometimes take refuge in the Plaza, protected by Grandmother Bright’s whims. Wise hunters don’t enter but post guards at entrances and exits, ordering them to take the troublemaker when they attempt escape.

All manner of relics scavenged from the ruins provide these apartments with miraculous amenities, such as staves of black glass that cool the air and weep clean water into gem-encrusted marble basins. Merchants hawk supposed black-glass water as a panacea, claiming efficaciousness for everything from headaches and impotence to pox and plague.

Most Chiaroscuro natives rent small dwellings from aristocratic landlords. Artisans’ and merchants’ tenements nestle in the shadow of ruined, uninhabited towers; built of sandstone and lime with colorful glass windows, they’re often piled three or four stories high. Each apartment houses an extended family, with communal spaces for eating — though most lack cooking facilities, so residents must purchase prepared food from vendors to bring home. Thick woolen rugs dyed in rainbow hues offer bedding and seating; hanging stainedglass sculptures decorate the walls. Dining tables are short, narrow rectangles, typically stacked against a wall except for meals. The ground floor, by tradition, can stable at least two horses; families without horses use this space to keep a few chickens, as well as any slaves.

From morning’s chill into the night’s road-red glow, the city’s markets sell food and drink: sweet and savory wheat breads; dates and figs; grilled sturgeon skewers drenched in pomegranate sauce; small plates of fluffy

EX3

rice topped with nuts, onions, and saffron; as well as mugs of bitter black coffee; bowls of honey-sweetened pomelo juice; sour fruit wines; and dark barley beers. Rich merchants and Delzhan nobles sample horse, cow, and goat, the meat slowly roasted over low heat and fragrant smoke, and enjoy cold yogurt soup or tart iced sherbets after a long day in the heat.

Common dress includes loose trousers and a kneelength tunic with a round hem, cinched with a wide belt. Some tunics have long, flowing sleeves; others are sleeveless.

The use of scraps and scavenged remnants of the old city bleeds into Chiaroscuro’s arts; nothing is finished, nor so broken it cannot be used. Artisans repair broken ceramics with glass or gold-infused lacquers, making the seams a unique expression of the vessel’s life. Likewise, ordinary folk hang kaleidoscopic stainedglass panes on their walls in place of paintings. The best of these artworks are shadow-poems: windows designed such that, when sunlight passes through them at a specific angle, the dividers between the panes align to cast shadows of Delzahn script on the floor or an opposite wall.

Trade

Workers load and unload cargo from docked ships and caravans at all hours. Captains may also pay the city extraordinary premiums to use the Hand of Argou, a surviving First Age relic. This disc of white and yellow glass, wide enough to encircle a yeddim, glides through the air at jogging pace as directed from the harbormaster’s glass tower, supporting up to a ton of people and goods.

Once unloaded, merchants and their assistants parcel goods into warehouses and sell them at bazaars and market plazas throughout Chiaroscuro. Best known is the Salt Market: a large plaza of green and yellow glass alongside the Foreigners’ Quarter, where half a dozen cinnabar roads converge. Two trades dominate half the market — salt and natron mined outside of Chiaroscuro, and slaves purchased largely by those same mines. The Salt Market is not only Chiaroscuro’s primary slave market, but also a threat and a promise. Slaves forced into the mines usually live only months before they die gasping and delirious. The market sells other goods; for a small fee, anyone may spread a blanket and hawk their wares, so long as they don’t impede traffic.

EX3

Two tall stone aqueducts reach into Chiaroscuro from the green southern hills, carrying precious water into the city’s countless cisterns and fountains. A third aqueduct is broken, shattered by a freshly Exalted Solar during a Wyld Hunt just weeks ago. Neighborhoods surrounding the breach still bear signs of damage from the flooding that ensued before engineers diverted its flow. Rebuilding efforts are underway, with heavy wooden scaffolding and blocks of hard-wearing granite brought in at tremendous expense; although the cost is potentially ruinous, the tri-khatun deems it less so than the water riots that will ensue if drought strikes the city.

### The Delzhan

To many Southerners, Chiaroscuro is synonymous with the Delzhan, but that wasn’t always so. For centuries, the Delzhan — an extended family of herdsmen, traders, and raiders — were only one of several desert-dwelling nomadic clans surviving along the Southern coast and interior scrub. They had little to do with the native Chiaroscurans who even today form the vast majority of the city’s populace.

When a wave of Lunar-backed insurgencies swept the South four centuries ago, Chiaroscuro’s then-rulers took the opportunity to rebel, expelling the diminished Realm garrison in a days-long battle that damaged much of the city and its surrounding farmland. The Delzhan seized this opportunity; sweeping inland, they seized and sacked an unprepared Chiaroscuro, then presented the heads of the rebellion’s leaders as their first tribute to the satrap. Some savants claim that the satrap invited the Delzhan to attack the city, offering control of Chiaroscuro in exchange for a more loyal tributary.

Delzahn Culture

Clan is of vital importance to the Delzahn. Formal adoption into a clan is a common rite of passage; similar rituals mark changing one’s clan upon marriage or ending a vendetta. Clan membership is matrilineal. While the clans share the same overall culture, their reputations, inclinations, and traditions vary; it’s common for a specific clan to lionize certain virtues or vocations, with parents pressuring children accordingly. Within Chiaroscuro, however, the clans have intermixed to the point that choice of clan is often a matter of politics and lineage; changing one’s clan as a show of support is increasingly common.

Urban Delzahn favor long tunics and sleeveless cloaks of thin cotton or linen in stylish cuts and dyed in a variety of brilliant colors. Men wear elaborately patterned veils. Silk is an expensive status symbol that aristocrats favor, particularly during festivals or formal occasions. Color choices are often intensely political; clans each have favored colors, and proper dress can signal allegiance, sympathy, and enmity.

Gender Among the Delzahn

The Delzhan practice strict and complex roles driven by their gender. They acknowledge only two genders, though each Delzahn determines for themselves which gender suits them.

A man’s honor is quick and hot, like fire; it lives in his glorious deeds and in stories told of him. For many, this drives a warrior spirit, inspiring frequent honor-duels and impressive feats of athletics, horsemanship, and endurance. Men proudly display their scars, and Delzahn deem an unscarred man little better than a boy. For others, manly honor inspires art, craftsmanship, and handiwork; weaving and needlework are held in high esteem as profoundly masculine crafts. Honorable men weave cloaks embroidered with their forefathers’ names and deeds. Distinctive maker’s marks are ubiquitous among Delzahn craftsmen’s products.

A woman’s honor is clear and endlessly resilient, like imperishable Chiaroscuran glass; it resides not in a moment’s passing deeds, but in herself. Women who understand this to mean their faces and beauty become practiced with oil and powder cosmetics, and favor elaborate coiffures and clinging silks. But most focus on studying and diligent effort, learning at the feet of older women who teach intellectual arts — mathematics and medicine, storytelling and poetry, law and sophistry, astronomy and astrology, management and logistics. Women oversee most of Chiaroscuro’s businesses and bureaucracies.

These roles also define courtship and marriage. Marriage is reserved for opposite-gender couples, preferably of similar social standing. Women woo lovers with epic poetry or provide detailed arguments indicating why their proposed match is ideal; men court partners with feats of bravado or works of art. Women manage the household and finances after marriage. Kinship is matrilineal.

Any wife may end her marriage with a public declaration, bequeathing her former spouse whatever portion of their shared wealth she sees fit. Stories are replete with women leaving husbands destitute, both justly

EX3

Dereth

### OUTSIDE THE GENDER BINARY

Within the confines of Delzahn gender roles, some are unable or unwilling to fulfill their assigned role, identifying more closely with another gender or its prescribed expectations — ranging from body image to vocation to permitted romantic partners. The Delzhan recognize these individuals as dereth. Folk stereotypes attribute them with distinctive personalities and good fortune in romance.

Those who actively rebel against gender norms face stigmatization or ostracism. But as a cosmopolitan trade port, Chiaroscuro offers many opportunities for nonconforming Delzahn to join welcoming non-Delzahn subcultures — or to take ship for more accepting lands.

Long ago, nonbinary or genderfluid Delzahn were regarded as gani zaeth — individuals balanced between mundane Creation and the spirit world — and trained as shamans. With conversion to the Immaculate Philosophy, shamanism is rarely practiced, but the role still persists to some extent in isolated clans. Many urban Delzahn lack familiarity with the gani zaeth; thus, opinions on the practice vary widely.

Dereth dress to present themselves as their intended gender just as non-dereth do. Most bear a gray garment or accessory clearly visible upon their person; this distinguishes their garb from non-dereth crossdressing, which is a minor social taboo.

Failing to acknowledge a dereth’s gender isn’t illegal; it doesn’t have to be. Doing so is profoundly taboo and a monumental insult to the dereth’s honor, family, and clan, instigating impressive vendettas.

While the Delzahn believe in a rigid, oppressive gender binary, remember that in reality — and even throughout Creation! — there are many genders, and many ways people experience or express their gender, including not having one at all. If the Delzahn’s take on gender upsets or triggers anyone at your table, whether player or Storyteller, we ask that you change or discard it as a setting element.

### Governance

and unjustly. In practice, most provide enough to help an ex-husband establish himself elsewhere, to avoid censure or reprisal from his or her family and friends. A husband seeking an end to his marriage does so through private channels, usually aided by his mother, sister, or a close female friend.

Some Delzahn remain unmarried, through personal preference or disinterest in romantic relationships. They often establish households with other friends who are unmarried, and welcome in those nieces and nephews they’ve grown close to.

Foreigners, who often act and dress in ways that conflict with Delzahn mores, aren’t expected to conform. Their hosts consider them backwards, but promptly smooth over any faux pas a visitor makes. The Delzahn view gender as an ideal to strive toward, and divergence from it as spiritually unhealthy. Everyone — Dereth and non-Dereth alike — struggles from time to time. Most quietly assume that nonconforming Delzahn are confused or wrestling with who they want to be, or that time spent with foreigners has influenced their thinking. Commenting in this regard is rude; Delzahn tend to avoid the topic of gender altogether.

The Delzhan and native Chiaroscurans alike are ruled by the tri-khatun and the tri-khan. The tri-khatun is the eldest matrilineal descendent of the previous tri-khatun. The tri-khan is her husband; if she’s unmarried, she chooses another male relative to temporarily hold the role.

The tri-khatun arbitrates disputes between common and aristocratic clans and families, and holds ultimate civil and legal authority over the Delzhan people. As such, she also oversees the bureaucracies that administrate the city. The current tri-khatun encourages marriages between aristocrats in her court and Realm patricians on the current satrap’s staff, aiming to influence satrapial administrative policy in favor of the Delzahn court.

The tri-khan oversees the military, holding final approval over troop deployment and promotions. He also acts as chief diplomat and ceremonial head of state, speaking on the city’s behalf during civil and religious festivals. Most importantly, he presents the Realm’s tribute.

Beneath them are a tangle of aristocratic families, descendants of Chiaroscuro’s original conquerors. Each claims titles and privileges, and collects rents within the city and from holdings along the coast and into the scrub. A savvy tri-khatun learns what tensions exist between families and uses that insight to her advantage. Some feuds must be settled quickly lest duels

EX3

make Chiaroscuro’s streets run even redder. Others, the tri-khatun can turn to the city’s advantage: suggesting one family brought more coin into the coffers than another redirects the rivals’ energies from bloodshed toward productivity.

The Realm

Chiaroscuro enjoys privileged status amongst Realm holdings, due to as-yet-unrevoked concessions offered by the Empress centuries ago. House Sesus demands heavy tribute, but the city’s merchants are wealthy enough to shoulder the resultant taxes without undue suffering. The Empress never allowed any Great House to hold the lease for an extended period, dangling the satrapy’s wealth as a prize to incite fierce competition within the Dynasty.

The Realm maintains a legal monopoly on Chiaroscuro’s silk trade. The beautiful, lightweight fabric is in high demand among Delzahn nobles, whose pursuit of changing court fashion ensures a constant demand. Chiaroscuro ships much of its glassware to the Blessed Isle, alongside fine horses and roasted coffee. Occasionally, a lucky resident unearths an artifact within the ruins; the satrap seizes such finds as well — or accepts them as part of the tribute if the tri-khatun obtains them first.

Annually, the tri-khan presents the satrap with token gifts. Since the Realm conquered Chiaroscuro, this has always included ritually renewing the gift of Blessed Spring, a nearby Wood manse where the satrap traditionally resides.

The Immaculate Order

Long ago, the Order established itself as the only legitimate religious authority within Chiaroscuro. Monks have vast latitude for investigating and punishing potential heresies, coming down especially hard on foreign idolaters. Dozens of Immaculate temples rise throughout the city; the tri-khatun pays for their construction and maintenance. Judges administer formal justice in Immaculate temples; proceedings open with a prayer and are overseen by priests.

In the city proper, hints of older pre-Delzahn faiths still linger. For instance, dozens of minor superstitions, from the proper way to fill a lamp to the order of adding ingredients to a stew, are termed “Iosis’s way.” Few in Chiaroscuro consider this deeply; to most, “Iosis” simply means “the greatest good” — a colloquial phrase for the right way to act. Few recall the old belief in Iosis as a transcendent being of pure light — but these few have formed the nucleus for the local branch of the Cult of

the Illuminated, claiming that the Solar Exalted are Shining Ones sent by Iosis to purify the world.

### Prominent Figures

Nasrin Dana Delzhan became tri-khatun two years ago when her mother, Roshan, passed unexpectedly. Young and unmarried, she must balance leading her family, handling affairs of state, and fending off a veritable army of suitors. She’s assisted by the acting tri-khan — her father, Pedram, who’s experienced in the role — and her aunt Omid. Dana’s mother was a prudent ruler who perpetually played the clans against each other, as well as the Realm against the Guild, thanks to her extensive network of clandestine agents. Unfortunately, Roshan died before passing along the keys to her codes or her agents’ identities. Dana has a rosewood box filled with unreadable dispatches; she spends long hours trying to decipher them. Dana’s dereth younger brother, Nasrin Sharif Delzhan, always disdained court intrigues in favor of the secrets of glass. Apprenticed to a renowned glassworker, he seemed destined to be the Association’s next leader until his own inquisitive nature led him astray. Sharif found ways of grinding and reforging imperishable glass outside of the Association’s approved methods, relying on carefully measured sand timers. Worse, his philosophical writings question the Perfected Hierarchy, positing that Creation is one substance always being broken and reformed, with no piece superior to another. If he weren’t the tri-khatun’s brother, Sharif would likely have perished in a duel by now. His telescopes and crystal blades are without compare, but openly purchasing his goods is a swift way onto the Association’s blacklist. Worse, the Immaculate Order takes a dim view of his writings. Sharif has carefully remained strictly speculative to avoid outright heresy, but few monks view this as anything more than pretense. Satrap Sesus Alon Paras has held her post for over twenty years. An older, heavyset woman, Paras was a bureaucrat of little note in the Thousand Scales, and her appointment was unexpected — save to the few aware of her status in the All-Seeing Eye. Since her appointment, Paras has carefully cultivated agents in Chiaroscuro, guiding them with the care of a woman handling a venomous serpent. She maintains three distinct networks of spies that serve the All-Seeing Eye, House Sesus, and herself, embedding them from the highest tower to the dregs of the Foreigners’ Quarter. Her greatest prize is Jahan Sayf, a journeyman in the

EX3

lapis, and ivory that promise cursed fates — such as fatal illness, death by misadventure, or haunting by murderous spirits — to would-be robbers. Indeed, scavengers’ unmarked graves lie scattered about the tombs. Curses occasionally spill over onto Rana’s people, such that visitors who express interest in the tombs face shunning or even violence.

### NOMADIC DELZAHN

Rural cousins oversee herds of goats, camels, horses, and cows, and guard large slave-run farmsteads that grow crops and fodder. Desert-dwelling clansmen have a curious place in Chiaroscuro. Seen only a few times a year when driving in the herds for sale and slaughter, city-dwellers view them as romantic figures, paragons of hospitality and honesty who — in the name of practicality and justice — frequently step outside the strict roles that civilization demands. But they also believe that they’re ill-mannered, ignorant, simple, and provincial.

The scavenger lord Osco claims to have circumvented the curses, recently obtaining and selling the blue diamond called the Eye of Venus. Since then, charlatans, scavenger lords, and ambitious merchants have moved in, seeking ways to follow in Osco’s footsteps to secure Rani’s riches. Strife has sprung up between locals seeking to drive the scavengers out and others hoping to profit from the outsiders’ efforts.

Desert riders favor thin, undyed cotton and linen clothing. They drape cloaks and veils across their bodies and faces to keep dust from blinding and choking them and to keep off the sun’s glare while still letting the wind carry away sweat.

## Zephyr

The tri-khan and tri-khatun may claim to rule the nomadic Delzahn, but they have no actual authority beyond personal influence, social connections, and controlling access to Chiaroscuro. Nomadic Delzahn accept gifts from urban Delzahn and harry their rivals in exchange, but often do more harrying than Chiaroscuro’s rulers desire.

Glassworker Association, from whom she hopes to discover the secrets of Chiaroscuran glass; when the former tri-khatun discovered the plot, Paras felt compelled to assassinate Roshan personally.

### Neighbors

Legend says Many-Splendored Zarin was rich and powerful, an oasis of lush beauty, until the desert swallowed it. It vanished into myth as a morality tale, a city so wicked that Heaven blotted it from Creation. Recently the outcaste treasure-hunter Grandori discovered the city, sunken onto an island amid an underground freshwater lake. A town has arisen both above and below ground, where scavengers jostle with settlers drawing water for farming and herding. Meanwhile, envoys of neighboring polities come seeking a piece of the action, merchant princes look to set up shop, and local petty warlords maneuver to seize a potentially rich new city. Eastward along the coast, travelers pass the great monuments of Rana. Its people, guided by priest-kings and -queens of ancient lineage, scratch out a living in dusty fields where wells and irrigation ditches are too often dry. Despite the land’s poverty, they’re surrounded by gleaming marble and limestone statues chased in gold,

For as long as Creation’s historians can recall, civilization has followed the river Elidad. In ages past, the first Zephyrite Sky Princes raised a thousand sorcerous obelisks marking the borders between the rich black earth of the riverbanks and the deserts beyond. Since that time, the Elidad has provided seemingly inexhaustible bounty to Zephyr. Where the obelisks still stand, the mighty river irrigates the fields punctually, and the soil’s fertility replenishes seemingly without limit. Zephyr — formerly the last of the great Southern powers to resist the Realm — is today divided into two satrapies. The Alluvion encompasses the broad expanse of the river delta and the modern capital of Azarhamon, as well as a network of oases that allow the Realm access to the rich copper mines of the western desert. Thousand Pillars, administered from the ancient, sprawling city of Perch, runs south through a thousand miles of fertile riverbanks and past a dazzling array of ancient temples, palaces, and manses.

The Realm’s control of the Elidad terminates at Hyacinth, where the river arcs west toward its mysterious underground source amid the desert. A few months ago, the city fell to the Lunar priestess Ketzepah Narrow-Ways and her inhuman allies. This alarmed the Realm satraps and local princes, but Zephyr’s common people remain largely unperturbed, seeing only the newest conqueror attempting to claim the riverlands.

### The Sky Prince

Legend holds that Zephyr’s first rulers held court in a crystal barque that sailed the sky above the river, from which they could gaze down upon their domain.

EX3

Though this wondrous vessel has long since been lost, if it existed at all, rulers since have taken the title of Sky Prince. During the First Age, some foreign conquerors retained their own titles or instituted reforms of Zephyr’s absolute monarchy, but the title of Sky Prince has always returned.

Zephyrite records name dozens of Sky Princes, though a few, including the earliest dynasties, have been expunged. During the First Age, it’s said Zephyr was ruled by Anathema until the Dragon-Blooded overthrew them. Since then, most Sky Princes have been DragonBlooded, though some were mortals, ifrits, and — during one particularly tumultuous period — a demon.

### People of Zephyr

The river valley’s inhabitants are ethnically diverse but culturally homogeneous. Zephyr has absorbed so many foreign invaders, immigrants, and refugees that there’s no longer an identifiable majority population. Neighbors quickly come to regard newcomers who follow Zephyrite customs as fully Zephyrite. Zephyrites typically dress in light wool garments. Both men and women crop their hair short, but almost always cover the head. Peasants wear domed reed hats to protect themselves from the blazing sun; others don wigs of horse or human hair. The richest of these are spectacular affairs of layered, bejeweled tresses upon wooden frames, held in place with long pins. Society is largely divided between the working class of farmers and laborers and a middle class of artisans, scribes, and bureaucrats. An upper class of rich landowners originally formed around high-ranking officials’ families, but since becoming a satrapy of the Realm, this aristocracy grows increasingly divorced from direct government, except for families that retain hereditary rights to collect taxes on the ministries’ behalf. These ancient houses’ estates dot quiet expanses of the riverbanks. The ministries largely leave them to self-govern their fiefdoms, provided they deliver the expected taxes.

Religion

Zephyrites traditionally worshiped an overarching pantheon of regional deities. These included Enatiri of the Ninth Way, the melancholy poet-god of the Elidad; the mercurial weather god Ahm-Asek, whose mood might usher in a lovely day or a sudden storm; and the many-eyed hearth god Wereth Soot-Stone, who has a soft spot for the unlucky. In addition, each city and region venerated its own local divinities.

People asked for their ancestors’ blessings as often as the gods’, while funereal rites petitioned a place alongside the honored dead in the blessed afterworld of Aaruat. Folk still inter the ashes of the dead in the necropoli dotting the Elidad’s west bank. The Realm attempts to enforce Immaculate doctrine within the Zephyrite satrapies. But even after centuries, the Order struggles with Zephyr’s entrenched religious beliefs and practices. Healers invoke divinities by rote while setting broken limbs, farmers scatter a few seeds on the river in planting season to appease the old gods, and every year, the river casts up potsherds and stones carved with religious iconography. Even after banning the old pictographic Zephyrite script, sending children to Immaculate-run schools, and purging heretical sects, Zephyrite folk traditions persist. Aggressive efforts have spawned religious revolts.

Government

Scions of House Imerah, Zephyr’s ruling cadet house, proudly trace their lineage back over a thousand years. Centuries ago, during a fierce but losing war against the Realm, they yielded in exchange for various privileges; these included maintaining governmental traditions that border on heresy — a matter that irks the Immaculate Order still.

Before the Realm, all religious and secular authority derived from the Sky Prince as supreme ruler, with the Zephyrite priesthoods doubling as ministries. Priestministers of Hamath the Sower tallied the harvest and organized winter granaries, Azadun Breakwater’s river-monks constructed and maintained the royal barge fleet, and so on. These priesthoods were officially dissolved after the Realm takeover. But while their shrines were converted to Immaculate temples as per Order doctrine, they retained their bureaucratic offices. Today, a shrine-minister heads each ministry, liaising with gods whose purviews overlap with the ministry’s. In principle, both House Imerah and Zephyr’s Immaculates share oversight of these liaisons, watching for heresy. In practice, Imerah turns a blind eye; the house values its relationship with Zephyr’s gods and takes pride in the old ways.

Secret cults run by shrine-ministers are widespread, though subject to severe punishments if discovered. Most Exalted Imerahs hold the rank of shrine-minister personally; as Dragon-Blooded, they’re authorized to worship as they wish, though the Immaculates watch them lest they lead mortals into heresy.

EX3

The gods’ entanglement with the ministries grants them unusual influence over affairs of state. The ministries’ day-to-day policy is largely shaped by counsel, bribery, and threats from the spirits — many of whom deeply resent the Immaculate Order — who appoint shrine-ministers, and from the aristocrats whom shrine-ministers report to. It’s a precarious system that frequently breaks down due to graft and corruption, and shrine-ministers suffer a high turnover rate. Immaculate abbots pressure House Imerah to instate monks as shrine-ministers, with limited success. The satraps have traditionally opposed this; strife in the ministries can reduce productivity or even trigger revolts, diminishing the amount of tribute they can wring from the satrapy. More often, Immaulate monks take on stints in mid-ranking administrative posts, watching for heresy while overseeing cargoes and managing accounts,.

### The Alluvion

A sea traveler’s first sight of Zephyr is its greenery and the scattered, blocky white buildings of the Elidad delta’s many coastal towns. A chain of lighthouses marks

the delta’s mouth to guide ships by night. Engineers have painstakingly dredged three of the river’s eight great branches to admit the passage of blue-water ships downriver as far as Azarhamon, a hundred miles south of the coast. Locals congregate on the banks to witness especially splendid vessels’ passage; local fishermen pull up alongside to touch the hull for luck. The Elidad delta is Zephyr’s most populous and geographically diverse region. Fishing communities give way to fields — some still dedicated to subsistence farming, others now hosting tobacco plantations, flower orchards, and other cash crops. Here and there stand small towns dedicated to boatbuilding and cultivating small groves of gold-flowering acacia. Salt-marsh villages keep goats and tortoises as food animals; shorthaired yeddim pull plows or carry goods as beasts of burden.

All roads and river branches converge on Azarhamon, the great cosmopolitan metropolis that straddles the Elidad. It’s Zephyr’s face to the outer world, where foreigners from throughout the South congregate to trade and where most of Zephyr’s merchants, scribes, artisans, and bureaucrats make their homes.

EX3

ironically altered to better suit Dynastic tastes. While even wealthy locals might consider honeyed dates, roast duck, or a stew of kid goat to be fine dining, visiting Dynasts have an insatiable taste for the exotic that’s driven an industry of extravagant delicacies. Importers bring giraffes hundreds of miles from the savannahs around the Lap for professional chefs to roast them whole with ghee as a popular party centerpiece. These brokers also procure austrech eggs, swan’s tongues for soup, fruits, and wines from distant locales to grace visiting Dynasts’ tables. Gourmands prepare these delicacies in constantly mutating styles that bear little resemblance to traditional Zephyrite cuisines, but which satisfies the inquisitive Dynastic palate.

### THE CYNOSURE COAST

The Alluvion lies on the Cynosure Coast, a stretch of coastline dotted with Dynasts’ vacation estates and aristocrats’ grand homes. Azarhamon is one jewel of a city among many.

In Qeset, a parade has been winding through the streets for a decade. New participants join in when others drop off, playing music, carrying flower-bedecked palanquins, and throwing small trinkets to passers-by. Most merchants sell from street carts, the better to claim prime spaces on the ever-changing route. In Basam, master-weavers spend their lives creating the tapestry of a single client’s life, recording her deeds from birth until death. Lives of the city’s heroes hang on display in its library. The greatest of these span several floors; visitors climb ladders to examine their storied deeds.

This is emblematic of Azarhamon as a whole. Everywhere one looks — whether architecture that works dragon iconography into a superficially Zephyrite style, or purportedly “rediscovered” ceremonies that laud Dragon-Blooded supremacy — everything is exaggerated to present tourists with the façade of a land that the Realm rules justly.

The eponymous Cynosure remains famous for its picturesque beauty. A wave of Dynasts and wealthy patrician merchants retired there centuries ago, erecting fabulous towers and manors overlooking the sea. But Cynosure’s wealth and prestige have diminished, and all too many ancient, ivy-wreathed estates lie tumbledown and abandoned.

Prominent Figures in Azarhamon

Azarhamon

Azarhamon is among Zephyr’s younger cities. During the Realm’s initial conquest of the Threshold, the Empress promised a return to the Zephyr of old, establishing her rule with the construction of Azarhamon — intended to be the kingdom’s new capital — on the ruins of the previous capital of Azar. The Empress saw Zephyr’s subjugation as an important stepping-stone to establishing her legitimacy, a jewel in her diadem as it had been for monarchs across the ages. Designed as a bastion of Dragon-Blooded hegemony, it’s unsurprising that Azarhamon is a popular destination for recently graduated Dynasts touring the Threshold. Even at a distance, such tourists witness the gleaming steps and broad, sweeping eaves of the Twinned Serpents Ziggurat, a palatial manse complex that serves as the seat of government, the royal family’s residence, an Immaculate temple, and the satrap’s office. Not a week goes by that the city’s Dynastic residents and esteemed visitors aren’t invited to some party, gala, ceremony or diplomatic function at the Ziggurat. The Realm sees Azarhamon as a resort for sampling an ancient civilization’s culture — one that’s

The current Sky Prince, Imerah Eladdan II, is a gregarious socialite and skilled administrator. She hosts her guests with grace and style sufficient to dazzle even jaded Dynastic scions, and has built an enormous network of contacts from the many young Dynasts who visit her palace each year. She’s found a niche in Dynastic politics as an unorthodox matchmaker, intermediary, and confidante. Most importantly, she knows how to leverage political favors to the hilt in negotiating tribute and treaties. Twice widowed and nearing fifty, Eladdan contemplates retirement. She has high hopes for her youngest daughter, Peninah. Now in her early teens, Peninah dreams of sailing the Elidad and exploring its ancient manses, though she knows her mother has different plans for her. The child’s pale green eyes closely resemble those of a young Cynis diplomat who visited Azarhamon years ago.

Cynis Vaunek, whose jaded cynicism is matched only by his charm, has been the Alluvion’s satrap for decades. He’s maintained his Dynastic lifestyle of extravagant galas — and upheld heavy tribute demands — through gifts and trade concessions from his galas’ guests, whether obtained via blandishments and cajolery or blackmail and extortion. But the younger generation has grown wary of his tricks, forcing him to seek other sources of income. Over the past few years, he’s begun embarking on riskier ventures — most notably, secretly backing efforts to

EX3

rob ancient Zephyrite tombs. If discovered, the resulting scandal would stymie Vaunek politically and financially, and would likely instigate religious riots — and, in the worst case, unleash furious hungry ghosts.

### THE TWILIGHT GROVE AND AARUAT

Across the river from Perch, amidst a shadowland on the western shore, stands Zephyr’s most ancient and prestigious necropolis, the Twilight Grove. This second city of ziggurats and mastabas reflects Perch as through a dark mirror. Since the First Age, all but the most devout Immaculates among the aristocracy have come here for burial.

### Thousand Pillars

South of Azarhamon, the delta converges into the Elidad River proper, almost three miles across at its widest point and one at its narrowest. The north wind suffices to sail against the current, while the current propels sailless vessels downriver. Vessels of all sizes ride the water day and night, mostly small fishing boats of bundled reeds. Dignitaries and bureaucrats sail between cities in swift, bright-painted barques; wealthy nobles and tourists outdo one another with ever-larger and more ostentatiously decorated pleasure barges.

Mourners gather in Perch to conduct funerary rites. At sundown, attendants bear the honey-embalmed body to the shore; servants carry the deceased’s favored possessions. There a stately barque of white wood awaits, crewed by ghostly slaves. Those so honored are borne across the river, where attendants extract the corpse’s embalmed heart and seal it in a porcelain jar. If and when the deceased arises as a ghost, she carries the weight of her heart onwards into the dark, through ten-foot-high fields of white wheat.

This satrapy, reaching a thousand miles into the desert but clinging tightly to the Elidad’s length, is Thousand Pillars. Most stretches of the riverbank hold only miles of fertile wheat fields that support the cities. Farmers are bound to their land; most families have worked the same soil for a dozen generations or more. Serfs rarely escape Thousand Pillars: the surrounding desert is difficult to traverse for even properly outfitted traders, and nearly impossible for poor farmers equipped with only what they can carry.

In the Plaza of Hieratic Wings, ringed by temples to gods and ancestors, a delegation of aeons — dead worthies from dynasties past — hold court over a banquet of honeyed pomegranate and blood-dark wine. Monstrous soul-sphinxes and lamassu stand in attendance, eyes glittering with malice. There the aeons interview the deceased for days, even as her body is laid to rest, debating her life’s merits. Should they deem her worthy, they teach her arts to conjure, tame, and shape the hungry ghost sealed within her embalmed heart into a mighty sphinx. If she succeeds — however many decades it takes — she joins the aeons’ ranks as a prince among the dead.

The Elidad’s mystical obelisks, supposedly erected by the first Sky Prince, irregularly dot the boundary between fertile fields and desert sands. Some of the black stone pillars have lost their power, whether because vandals defaced them or because time outright toppled them. Thus, while much of the river experiences regular and beneficial flooding, some stretches suffer erosion and unpredictable flash flooding. Their design and function remain a subject of perennial fascination among visiting sorcerers. Centuries ago, Heptagram scholars removed two obelisks for study. The Thousand Pillars city of Newuz suffered a disastrous flood later that year; the obelisks were returned on the Empress’s orders.

The Twilight Grove’s shadowland links Zephyr with Aaruat, one of the Underworld’s great empires. Much of Zephyr’s past has ultimately settled here, with innumerable dead cultures, peoples, palaces, temples, and monarchs overlapping and merging in a chaotic symphony of ages. Above the aeons stand Aaruat’s rulers, the archaeons: seven wise, puissant ghosts, each a celebrated Sky Prince from the First Age. The satrap visits Aaruat to barter power and lore from these mighty spirits. They treat with her as an equal for now, but express displeasure that Zephyrite offerings to the ancestor cult have lapsed.

Perch

In Thousand Pillars’s southern reaches, Perch lies resplendent on the Elidad’s east bank, a stately city of elaborately plotted symmetries and grand colonnades. Famed as a seat of culture and craft, Perch boasts many of Zephyr’s finest metalworkers, sculptors, and poets. During the late First Age, the capital of Old Perch was a grand and thriving metropolis. The Shogunate’s wars devastated its structures and deeply reduced its population. The capital moved to another city, and many of Old

Perch’s best and brightest followed. For centuries, Perch sank into genteel decline, until the Realm’s division of Zephyr into two satrapies returned it to prominence as Zephyr’s southern capital.

Perch experienced a revival as architects, engineers, and city planners flocked there to repair buildings long neglected and pursue the prince’s vision of a modernized

EX3

city layout. Today, Perch’s artists look forward, focusing on innovation and eclecticism. Patrons commission great works from promising young creators, hoping to reap the rewards of their generosity in years to come. Portraitists capture Zephyr’s elite in stunning detail; street artists make a living sketching candid moments and selling them to their subjects. Poets and musicians captivate audiences in teahouses and concert halls. Political unrest threatens to tarnish Perch’s artistic golden age. Many citizens rankle at the Realm’s financial and religious demands. Poets subtly condemn Dynastic greed in verse, while some artists’ depictions of the satrap and her ilk present their subjects in stark, unfavorable lights. Visitors and citizens stroll through the Plaza of Seven Trees in the city center. Its water calendar is a draw for tourists and scholars alike, the former to describe in letters home and the latter to study its elegant, precise workings. At its opposite end, in the shadow of the tallest of the fig trees for which it’s named, politicians deliver impassioned speeches, shrine-ministers sermonize, and writers give readings to the gathered crowds. The Princes’ Library, with its cool granite walls, is among the few First Age structures only lightly damaged during ancient wars. Its collection didn’t survive intact; when the capital moved, scholars and savants smuggled most of its books and scrolls along with them. The curators labor to rebuild the collection, replacing lost tomes and paying dearly for those that remain in other libraries’ possessions.

At any hour, diners in the Faded Peony Teahouse might witness a poetry duel. It’s among Perch’s most popular tourist spots, not only for its excellent cooks, but also for the many creatives who frequent it. Participants often prearrange the exchanges of barbed words that play out on this meager stage, having been guaranteed a healthy gratuity from their audience. But sometimes battles of wits and words turn into actual fights, a practice the proprietor, Second Son, outwardly frowns upon but quietly profits from.

Prominent Figures in Perch

Thousand Pillars’s current satrap, the sorceress Ledaal Yasmet Imara, oversees the satrapy with a light touch. Underground smuggling rings, heretical cults, and political unrest plague Perch, but despite her inclinations to the contrary, she can ill afford to crack down with an understaffed garrison and the looming prospect of infiltration or invasion from Hyacinth. She spends her time accompanied by demon servants and bodyguards,

poring over the old city’s stone libraries or conversing with ghosts and gods venerated by the city’s secretive cults.

The most visible face of Realm ambitions in Perch is Imara’s elderly uncle, Ledaal Saruald. An eccentric retiree, Saruald has earned respect as one of the Realm’s foremost savants of Zephyrite history. He dresses as an ancient Zephyrite noble: flowing white robes, elaborate oiled wig, and heavy jade and gold jewelry. While this habit was initially met with veiled amusement, Saruald’s infectious enthusiasm for local ceremony and history won him friends among Perch’s scholars and nobles, while his increasingly profane displays of obeisance before Zephyr’s gods earned devout Immaculates’ ire. Some dismiss his behavior as senility; others speculate that he’s deliberately undermining the Order’s authority, or even that he harbors ambitions to usurp the satrapy as a new Sky Prince.

Descended from a long line of Thousand Pillars nobles, Iset Hamor holds the title of River Prince, awarded him by the previous Sky Prince and ratified by Eladdan II upon her accession. Witty and gregarious, he works amicably with the satrap, although he harbors ambitions not only for Perch, but Thousand Pillars as a whole. He envisions an independent Southern Zephyr free of the Realm’s influence, with himself ruling as the southern Sky Prince. To that end, he consults in secret with the shrine-ministers and travels to nearby Aaruat to consult with, and seek the blessings of, its archaeons.

Hyacinth

At first glance, Hyacinth gleams like kintsugi in reverse. Where ancient wars smashed through its fantasia of golden First Age turrets and flying buttresses, Old Zephyr’s Dragon-Blooded engineers mended its wounds with quartzite and granite, restoring its broken symmetries. And while much of the city forms a labyrinth of alleys, markets, slums, and condemned buildings, ancient boulevards still radiate outward from the city center’s palaces and temples.

Hyacinth’s residents are largely merchants and artisans; far greater numbers of tenants, laborers, and slaves work the fields outside. All take pride in their city of wonders, even reduced and broken as it’s become. First Age engineers widened the Elidad where it feeds into Cephel Lake, allowing them to control the river’s floods, direct its flow to irrigate the surrounding land, and store water in preparation for the dry season. Sandskiffs dock here, offloading passengers and goods from settled oases across the Burning Sands.

EX3

warriors and Hyacinth collaborators, is both widely loathed and riven by internal divisions. And gathering sufficient forces to hold off a concerted Realm attack — let alone to pursue further conquest — will take time that she doesn’t necessarily have.

### SANDSKIFFS

These small, flat-bottomed boats sail the sand seas that occupy broad swaths of the Far South. Their construction involves unusual materials — rare woods, plant waxes, and wild silks — some found only in the Summer Mountains, others only in the Firepeaks, none amenable to cultivation. A few rare families pass down the occult techniques used to prepare such materials and construct these vessels, often growing rich in doing so.

Great quarries ship stone blocks downstream, supplying most of Zephyr’s granite and sandstone. Pottery workshops turn out polychrome ware decorated with geometric patterns. Intricate abstract murals painted on houses’ plaster walls conceal minuscule animal images, both to praise various beast-gods and to spite the Immaculates. Crocodiles sun themselves on the riverbanks, sacred to Belet-ar, god of fertility and protector of travelers on the Elidad. His shrine-minister, responsible for Hyacinth’s granaries, also oversees a menagerie by the riverside; there dwell bulls, lions, monitor lizards, and hippopotami. Officially a zoo, aristocrats claim its beasts as sacrifices for their burial rites. Much has changed since Ketzepah Narrow-Ways conquered Hyacinth. The Realm garrison and Immaculate monks are dead or fled. Her troops — nomadic warriors of the desert-dwelling Harban people, longtime enemies of Zephyr — have executed nobles and officials who she deemed complicit with the satrap. Scaffolding encrusts ugly new fortifications rising outside the city’s mended gates. And Ketzepah herself stalks the city in many shapes, weeding out sedition.

Religion marks the most dramatic change to Hyacinth. In former Immaculate temples, dragon iconography has been stripped away, replaced by images of the Unconquered Sun, Hyacinth’s old gods, and Harban divinities. A trickle of Zephyrite pilgrims filter out of Perch in secret to visit these temples, eager to rekindle the old faith. And Ketzepah performs imaginative, brutal public sacrifices to the Unconquered Sun of any who don’t repudiate Immaculate beliefs.

But Ketzepah’s victory isn’t absolute. Citizens shelter secret Immaculate gatherings, while lay followers observe monks’ dietary rules as private acts of rebellion. Ketzepah’s puppet council, composed of Harban

Most of Ketzepah’s support comes from those who benefited most from her conquest: cultists of Zephyr’s old gods, merchants and nobles whose taxes no longer go toward Realm tribute, and slaves she’s freed. She knows that the monetary and human costs of battles to come will erode her support quickly. For now she holds fast, training local auxiliaries, cultivating allies among desert peoples, and sending agents to foment paranoia and unrest in neighboring Perch.

The Dragon Kings

Most assume Ketzepah’s half-dozen reptilian allies to be some coterie of lizardfolk sorcerers who she met in the desert. Few recognize them as the intelligent, prehuman saurians called Dragon Kings. Unlike the savage stalkers of Saploth (p. XX), the Dragon Kings of old awakened their memories of successive reincarnations through now-forgotten arts. Only they and Ketzepah know in what ancient fastness they lay before she awoke them from enchanted slumber, but in a land defined by history, these Dragon Kings rival the eldest gods as witnesses to the passage of millennia.

As devotees of the Unconquered Sun and the South’s old gods, Ketzepah’s crusade against the Immaculate Order suits these Dragon Kings well. Their physical and supernatural gifts make them formidable allies. Ketzepah’s predilection for combining human sacrifice with political execution disconcerts them, however; they feel that only aged Dragon Kings or worthy opponents defeated in combat should receive such an honor. They eagerly await their next battle; until then, they spend their time in contemplation or preaching the Sun’s prehuman gospel to perplexed Zephyrites.

Prominent Figures in Hyacinth

When Ketzepah Narrow-Ways was a child, her people’s gods and ancestors fled from Immaculate monks. When she was a young woman, Immaculate collaborators among her people welcomed the Realm in. Today she despises spirits and hates the Realm, but her true loathing is reserved for the Immaculates. She tolerates divine allies but cannot trust them, and has even less faith in her fellow Chosen. Even Luna is too fickle for her tastes. The only god she worships is the Unconquered Sun, whose scriptures she learned from the Dragon Kings; a god who never acts on the world cannot disappoint her.
