## Origin, the City of Talking Lions

The mid-ranking palace bureaucrat Iron Rose found opportunity in Hyacinth’s fall. Selling out colleagues for sedition earned her a place on Ketzepah’s council; initiative in hunting down secret Immaculate practitioners earned Ketzepah’s favor. Cunning and vicious, Iron Rose happily undercuts other councilors to maintain dominance. Her only concern for how much her peers and Zephyr’s people loathe her is the expense of bodyguards. She does love her three children, though perhaps not so much as her ambitions.

The Dragon King warrior Nefkirit entered enchanted slumber millennia ago beneath the citadel of Citrine Lotus, awaiting a day when his people needed his martial skills. When Ketzepah awakened him and his peers, Citrine Lotus lay in ruins and his people were long gone. Accustomed to command, he took charge of the others

### THE TWELVERIVER SEA

Running along the eastern border of the Firepeaks, the Twelveriver Sea is a narrow freshwater inland sea — an island of greenery amid the brown desert scrublands. The Diamond Road connecting the Lap to Gem runs along its eastern shore, leading to the rise of several small trading cities and towns in the vicinity, such as oft-invaded Ontre with its fisheries, the incense-perfumed marketplace of Red Ivory, and the former Realm capital of Viodun with its famed amphitheater and baths. Despite the sea’s propitious location, it lacks grand metropoli and expansive nations. The area has suffered from Realm invasion, landslide-induced tsunamis, and a long history of foreign raiders. Nomadic peoples frequently come pillaging, from Sabaki warbands to the fearsome Neekhoe scorpionfolk, while Threshold slavers sometimes mount expeditions here. Though the raiders aren’t united, the Lunar Golden-Leaf Liseli (Lunars, p. 37) keeps a close eye on the region and manipulates events there. Despite occasionally sending waspfolk raiders to swoop in on Realm expeditions, Liseli prefer a softer approach, using stolen faces to manipulate rulers and merchants with bribes, extortion, and appeals to greed or ambition.

The Twelveriver Sea is currently Realm territory in name only. Liseli and her allies allowed the Realm to claim it only long enough to stoke the region’s hatred, then repeatedly bled every Realm effort to control it until it no longer seemed worth the expense. Officially, the region was folded into the Lap’s satrapy; however, it’s independent in practice.

and swore service to Ketzepah, grateful for being awakened and given a purpose. But he grows uncertain of Ketzepah’s bloody-handed crusade, and discusses with his fellow Dragon Kings — none of them contemporaries — whether to part ways and seek their kin.

### Neighbors

The nomadic desert folk who call themselves the Fruit of the Cacti roam the desert wilderness west of the Elidad, beyond the Lake of Plums — a dying oasis usually considered the edge of habitable land. Though its plums are long extinct, the nomads visit under full moons to trade with passing merchants. Only their sandships let them freely roam the hostile deserts beyond. Matriarchal and led by their eldest wise women, they worship such desert spirits as the Red Sigh, a god of wind and sand who guides their ships in exchange for prayers and offerings of precious desert fruits, and the Guiding Star, who directs those in need to water sources as a shining light. The sandstorm known as the Devourer howls unending across the desert. Terrible flying beasts and great steel insects ride its winds, appearing suddenly to assault those caught up in the gale. Amid the storm’s eye hovers the floating tower of a potent sorcerer-spirit, the Smokeless Flame. The Eleo beetlefolk brave the storm bearing slaves to trade with the Smokeless Flame when it passes close to their territory, their carapaces protecting them from the scouring sands. They emerge with weapons crafted from the steel insects’ fangs and the sturdy, hollow bones of flying beasts to trade.

Origin, the City

of Talking Lions

Blessed by Masinghala the Lion God, Origin in its prime expanded at spearpoint across the central Firepeaks and as far as the Dying Sea. But protracted warfare saw the city’s empire falter, paving the way for Gem’s rise to power. Now subject to Gem’s suzerainty, Origin’s people have been humiliated by their ancient rival, but this has lit the fire of their pride. They bide their time, prowling for the right opportunity to free themselves so that their star will rise again.

### History

Origin was the first of the Tsavo Cities — settlements founded or conquered by the ancient Galana peoples as they fled westward from their former homes in the Burning Sands. At its zenith nearly four hundred years

EX3

ago, it claimed all the Tsavo Cities under its dominion. But the mountain empire of Grand Apkoro, aided by crimson-bannered ghosts with leering devil-faces, decimated Origin’s armies. The other Tsavo Cities seized the opportunity to rebel against Origin’s sovereignty. Intermittent warfare between the Tsavo Cities has characterized the centuries since. Only recently have they united again under Rankar VII, Despot of Gem. Betrayed and usurped as a youth by Gem’s House Arajana, he escaped into the desert. There, after many adventures, he united the nomadic Sabaki tribes under his banner. Claiming Gem’s throne, he went on to conquer the other Tsavo Cities through military force, economic might, diplomacy, and guile. Origin was the last Tsavo City to submit, bowing peacefully to Gem rule in RY 758 to avoid a devastating siege. But while Rankar turns his gaze outward to further expand his empire, Origin awaits an opportunity to break free of Gem’s control and reclaim its sovereignty.

### The City of Origin

Origin nestles in the fertile Amma River basin, amid low hills just north of the river. Avenues radiate outward from the city’s central Sacred Precinct, shaded by fragrant khaya trees. Mud-and-timber temples dedicated to Masinghala and other local gods dominate the district, their whitewashed exteriors adorned with lions, rivers, trees, and other natural imagery. A main arterial road, the Grand Prowl, runs from Origin’s southernmost gate to Masinghala Hill at the district’s center — a sprawling walled compound encompassing the Lion God’s temple-gardens. Around the sacred precinct stands the Market Quarter, where the townhouses and compounds of wealthy nobles and freeborn merchants cluster around market squares. Here, traders from Tsavo tribes and clans mingle with local artisans and outland merchants. A member of Gem’s House Arbani might sell firewands right next to a Zhao merchant prince offering samples of silks. Teahouses and hostelries offer services for differing clienteles, ranging from hole-in-the wall refuges for thrifty visitors to sprawling compounds serving wealthy patrons’ every whim. Origin’s outermost district — known as the Tall Grass — largely abandons straight avenues for a tangle of alleys winding past square, squat mudbrick dwellings. Clustered amidst these streets are unclean businesses such as butchers, tanners, and dyers, whose dye pits contain the indigo for which Origin is renowned. Only the Grand Prowl and other gate roads cut through the maze; they’re lined

here by carvanserai catering to foreign travelers. Most of Origin’s peasants and slaves live in the Tall Grass. It’s a pastime of young nobles to carouse here and cause trouble. Residents enjoy the Amma basin’s bounty, from fish and game to fresh vegetables, amaranth, millet, and rice. Common dishes include tiny noodles called katta simmered with tomatoes and beef; chili-spiced tilapia served with fried bananas and rice; prince’s-feather greens braised with onion, peppers, and mint; stewed lamb covered in a dark, rich sauce made from jute leaves; and coconut and egg jam spread on toasted bread. Ginger mixed with lemon juice and mint cleanses the palate and cuts through the rich flavors.

### Religion

A former Southern God of War and grandchild of the Unconquered Sun, Masinghala gave up his position long ago to become a god of the hunt and relax in the paradise that was the Amma Basin. It’s said that when the Galana came westward to the Basin, Masinghala’s talking lions greeted them and brought them to his holy place. He appeared before them as an enormous lion with a mane of white fire and a halo of spears. They pled their case, and he allowed them to remain so long as they agreed to be stewards of his paradise.

Origin’s people revere Masinghala as a god of generosity, virtue, and nobility. A great hunter, he’s also a leader who cares for his pride, magnanimously sharing his land with the Galana and their subjects as well as his blessed children, the talking lions. In recent years, Masinghala has become more withdrawn. His priests say that when Origin yielded to Gem’s rule, the Lion God lost faith in the Galana.

The Lion God’s priesthood is open to all except slaves, but most priests belong to freeborn and noble families that have served him for generations. Priests offer guidance, supervise sacrifices, perform devotions to the Lion God, and care for the talking lions. They also act as a bank for the Galana, loaning money and other resources they’ve collected from offerings and donations. Other gods are revered in Origin; many have temples and shrines across the Tsavo Cities. These include Ahlat, Southern god of cattle and warfare; the city mother Omenala, who helped craft the city’s laws and who punishes evil with sacred pythons; Xeya the Lightning Spider, who commands the rains; Adamant Sulrakh, prince of dinars and arbiter of honorable trade; and the sightless river goddess Amma-Inawi, who holds the floods at bay in exchange for offerings of fish and finery.

EX3

Talking Lions

### OTHER WATERS EAST OF THE FIREPEAKS

While Origin’s people see lions as sacred animals not to be harmed unless in self-defense, Masinghala’s talking lions are divinely blessed. They’re fêted and celebrated by the people, with most dwelling in the temple-gardens at Origin’s heart. Many talking lions enjoy humans’ reverence, but when they grow restless, they leave the city to hunt in preserves in the Amma Basin, closer to their wild kin.

Dozens of oases speckle the Southern desert, but few match Shevas Jamaw. This deep blue, greenery-ringed lake gleams in a rocky hollow beside a broad plateau, where stony desert meets a sea of sand. The tiny city that’s grown here is a key hub for deep Southern trade; caravans and sandskiffs stop for water, provisions, incense, and the opalized wood found at the plateau’s edge. By an ancient bargain with earth elementals, only material exposed by nature may be collected. But no elementals have appeared within living memory. Locals and foreign merchants now debate mining for opaline wealth.

By tradition, one may earn a talking lion as a boon companion by performing a great service for Origin or offering a sufficiently pleasing sacrifice to the Lion God. The priesthood petitions Masinghala to ceremonially bless the hero, after which a lion chooses her and the two bond for life.

The Grand Chott, a sprawling salt pan, briefly becomes a shallow brackish lake during each rainy season, then dries out again in weeks. But every few years, torrential rains fill it entirely until the next summer; lush greenery envelops its shores, while insects, fish, amphibians, and reptiles emerge from estivation to spawn. Desert nomads gather here to drink, hunt, swim, and trade, while sandskiff pilots schedule visits for when the lake fills. Few dare violate its sanctuary, but raids on the paths leading there aren’t rare.

A bonded talking lion is a significant status symbol in Origin, and their fame extends far enough that even foreigners desire them. Earning one was once the province of heroes who’d performed mighty deeds: slaying the fae Sirocco Princes of the Dying Sea, standing against the red-bannered ghosts of Grand Apkoro, soothing Mountain-Eater Domo with a song, or the like. But in the last century, it’s become more commonplace to offer a significant donation to the priesthood to receive a talking lion companion. Rankar VII gained his talking lion in this way, making one of the grandest donations to the temple ever using Gem’s wealth.

Rivers from the Firepeaks feed the Dying Sea. Its saline waters support little life beyond brine shrimp and insects, but all manner of vegetation and desert wildlife prospers along its shores. Settlements and seminomadic peoples thrive among the sea’s many deltas, mummifying their dead within the lake’s salts. Flamingoes and other migrating birds flock here every few years to breed upon the innumerable islets and mud flats deep within the basin.

### Social Class

Origin’s sprawling royal clans descend from ancient Galana aristocrats. Royals are traditionally appointed to the most powerful government positions, and they prefer to remain within the city proper to curry favor with their elders and the gods. Local nobility — lesser branches of the royal clans — rule much of the Amma Basin; all aspire to join the urban elite, either through marriage into a royal clan or by earning the prince’s favor. They wear gandoras and caftans dyed a vivid indigo to distinguish themselves from lower classes. Sewists decorate these flowing gowns with elaborate embroidery around chest and neck — designs popular among aristocrats throughout the Tsavo Cities.

Near to Dajaz, the Boiling Lakes steam constantly, heated by magma beneath the earth. Rocky islets rise from the seething waters, their shapes veiled by white vapor. Their remote and inhospitable location makes them a home for elementals, sorcerers, Fair Folk, and other entities seeking refuge from the outside world. Beneath the largest of them, simply called the Great Boiling Lake, lies a submerged Solar tomb from the Usurpation.

Villages and towns in the Tsavo Cities often have shrines for local gods and elementals, usually tended to by a single priest who trains their successor. Temples to ghosts of local heroes stand alongside them, but most ancestor worship is a matter for individual families. In the Firepeaks’ foothills, some clans raise shrines to famous ancestors and visit them in cavernous shadowlands.

The freeborn are farmers, artisans, and traders from tribes and clans that have come under Galana control. Professions such as ironworker, woodcarver, and weaver are hereditary, practiced by particular clans over generations. Clans that share professions organize into lodges that set standards for the profession and advocate before the city’s assembly for favorable policies. Freeborn people proudly wear mud

EX3

cloth gandoras decorated with intricate patterns depicting their profession and clan affiliations.

problems with slave revolts originating among successful enslaved populations that wish to be freed.

Gesere, a special caste distinct from the freeborn, are skilled masters of oratory, music, and storytelling. Liminal figures standing between the mundane world and the legends they share, they memorize countless local histories and stories, and play instruments such as the balafon, goje, and kora. The Galana believe gesere to be gifted with great wisdom, and call upon them to mediate disputes between mundane parties and for troubles with spirits. At least one can be found in most villages around the Tsavo Cities, while noble families often retain them as advisors and teachers. Some live nomadically, travelling between villages to offer their services.

### Government and Military

At the bottom are slaves captured in wars, acquired in trade, or born into slavery. Slaves comprise a significant portion of Origin’s population, though their conditions and status vary widely. A warrior captured in battle is highly valued and may even rise to high rank in Origin’s army, while a farmer enslaved in his clan’s defeat might remain in his home village, paying his master an annual fee of goods and services. Families that have been enslaved for generations are sometimes indistinguishable from freeborn families; Origin has had numerous

Origin’s prince is both the Lion God’s sacred consort and lord of the Ayrema, an assembly of more than 600 nobles and clan elders whose main duty is meeting regularly to administer Origin and the Amma Basin. The Ayrema oversees public works, taxation, and the appointment of officials. As Masinghala’s representative, the prince may override the Ayrema’s decisions, though exercising this power without restraint is unpopular. A prince rules for life, and her chosen heir succeeds her.

While chieftains may petition Origin for assistance, the Ayrema leaves daily governance to their discretion so long as taxes are paid. Thus, subordinate clans at the edges of Origin’s territory retain a great deal of autonomy. Some settlements’ leaders have found new backers in Gem’s noble houses; they now refuse to pay tribute, challenging Origin’s rule over them. The prince has sent skilled diplomats to settle the matter peacefully and bring the clans back into compliance. Should those efforts fail, her generals stand ready to quell the brewing rebellions.

EX3

The Ayrema typically appoints generals from clans famed for skill in warfare. While once Origin’s army boasted great numbers, conflicts over the last century have reduced those numbers severely: ceded territories cost Origin in both troop levies and the financial resources to support its army. Increasingly, Origin has adopted Gem’s military strategy, relying on hired mercenaries rather than incur the expenses to train and equip its own army. But many fear that mercenaries’ loyalty may be bought by Gemfolk, Guildsmen, or other enemies.

### MANY CULTURES OF THE TSAVO CITIES

The Tsavo Cities encompass dozens of cultures that live alongside one another. Among them are the taciturn Seraw fisherfolk; the Ghola cattle-herders whose sacrificial bulls, it’s said, are favorites of Ahlat; Tebyan nomads who read portents in the desert wind; hard-bargaining Kanuri gold-traders; and many more. In Origin, these diverse clans often live in their own neighborhoods managed by community elders.

### Prominent Figures

Prince Zakhaira inherited her seat unexpectedly just three years past when her husband, the previous prince, died in suspicious circumstances on a hunt. Famed as a consummate hunter and restless intellectual in her youth, and then as a rising star in the Lion God’s priesthood before her marriage, she’s taken to her latest role eagerly and proficiently. Having brought key townships back into line through bribery and threats, she publicly condemns Origin’s submission to Gem and sends envoys to Rankar demanding that he reduce the tribute her city owes. More cautious members of the Ayrema fear that her boldness will result in Gem tightening its grip on Origin instead.

Zakhaira utilizes her close relationship with the priesthood to win the Lion God’s support. She seeks to rekindle Masinghala’s faith in her people so that he’ll aid them against the Despot. She believes that only with the Lion God’s backing can she ensure Origin’s future and that of her young son, Airan.

Zakhaira’s granduncle Sakoura is an elder statesman who doesn’t wish to see Origin falter further due to short-sightedness. He loves Zakhaira as he does all the royals, but he opposes her in debate before the Ayrema to illustrate the flaws in her ambitious thinking. While he wishes to see Origin freed from the Despot’s influence, he believes the process cannot be rushed, or else Origin will be doomed to tragedy. Sakoura’s family has intermarried with Gem’s noble houses of Sahlak and Arbani, and he fears what will become of his sons should Gem and Origin go to war.

Sakoura’s talking lion Diara is famed for her frankness and impatience. The two work together to influence Origin’s nobility.

Few in Origin are as fearsome in battle and jubilant in celebration as Lokras the Mygdon, the famed DragonBlooded mercenary general who’s pledged himself to Origin’s future. A significant land grant cemented

Lokras’s loyalty to his adopted homeland, and now he fights for the future of his family there. Lokras finds Zakhaira a kindred spirit. But he’s a pragmatist; he doubts that Origin will triumph if it comes to war. He’s made it clear to her that if she cannot convince him that she’ll win, his mercenaries may abandon Origin… or join Gem against her.

The gesere known as the Vulture of Pearls fervently believes that revolution should come to all the Tsavo Cities. Careful to conceal her identity with a black litham and caftan lest Origin’s aristocrats try to silence her, she retells legends of heroic rebellion to stir the hearts of slaves and impoverished freeborn alike to cast off the rule of the nobility, whom she claims have lost the Lion God’s favor.

### The Amma Basin

Comprising the region surrounding the Amma River and its tributaries, the Amma Basin extends across a swath of the Firepeaks’ foothills and into a wetland delta near the Diamond Road, encompassing Origin and its possessions. Elephants, caracal, buffalos, lechwe, and many more gather around watering holes throughout the Basin. The river delta — which dries up at its terminus rather than draining into a lake or sea — contains hundreds of small islands covered in greenery and salt patches. The Isle of Faama, largest of these islands, is the sacred preserve of the Lion God and of Origin’s prince. During the Basin’s seasonal floods, countless species of animals shelter there; it’s most famous for its enormous prides of lions that prey on the abundant wildlife. Legend says that these wild prides guard the Galana, but most prefer not to test their luck by antagonizing them. Origin derives its wealth from the Basin’s abundance of natural resources: gold from mines in the foothills and salt from the delta, not to mention leather, pottery, woven goods, and ivory. Farms in the grasslands grow millet, sorghum, and rice to feed the Tsavo Cities,

EX3

supplemented by game meat and fishing. Farther east, riverine villages of rondavel huts dot the delta, where fisherfolk on mekoro punt along, searching for tigerfish, tilapia, and catfish. The basin’s kola nuts — savored for their energizing, bitter flavor — are often chewed during business meetings and social gatherings. Its papyrus is vital to the scribes of Kandara’s Great Library (p. XX).

### The Tsavo Cities

After founding Origin, Galana caravanners established Gem in ancient tunnels honeycombing the dead volcano Cinere, rediscovered Kandara and its the Great Library among the shining salt pans of the Glister Sands, and conquered the ancient city of Scathe. While the Tsavo Cities culturally resemble their progenitor, they’ve diverged over the centuries.

Scathe

Carved from the Vermillion Peaks west of Gem, demon-haunted Scathe (known as Skarth in foreign lands) is an ancient city built on chains. The city’s enslaved population — regularly replenished by raiding nearby mountain peoples — outstrips that of any other Tsavo city. Most labor to mine silver, gold, and copper in the Vermillion Peaks, enriching Scathe’s ruling Galana elite. Scathe’s native Athi people stand between the two. Many serve as overseers; others are skilled architects and stoneworkers, like their ancestors. They’ve always raided and enslaved laborers to carve Scathe from the mountains; only now they do so on behalf of their Galana overlords. Set upon a rocky, windswept plateau, much of the city is underground. Rock-cut architecture defines its civic buildings; palaces, tombs, and temples to grim gods lie beneath ground level, hewn whole from the surrounding stone. They’re encircled by stepped plazas leading up to the plateau. Aboveground, common folk inhabit dark houses and tenements built from the quarried basalt, their windows granting sweeping views of the mountains. The unceasing sound of stoneworkers’ chisels echoes off these rough-hewn facades, the cacophony only drowned indoors by raucous coffeeshops’ flutes and drums, or outdoors by the desert wind.

Class in Scathe is a matter of income. Most residents scrape by as miners, desperate to find raw gems that their employers will purchase from them and resell to Diamond Road merchants. Only those with the richest, most productive mines and estates may claim the rank of Resplendent Master. The city’s governing council consists entirely of Resplendent Masters or their proxies — often junior family members expected to inherit their riches. Certain rights are reserved exclusively to

Resplendent Masters, such as elaborate jeweled robes or owning demon-callers as slaves.

The Snarling Leopard demon-caller clans descend from demon-blooded Dajazeen exiles. They practice ancient, half-understood rites to call up unbound demons, involving chanting, incense, and dancing amid elaborately drawn patterns of colored sand. The clans revere these demons as their families’ guardians, and occasionally take one as a sacred lover.

Centuries ago, the first Resplendent Masters promised the Snarling Leopards’ nomadic ancestors wealth and power in exchange for calling demons to fight for Scathe. But the Resplendent Masters broke their word and enslaved them. Now demon-callers are kept separate from their kin, brought together only to beckon demons on their owners’ behalf.

The Leopards have waged bloody uprisings against the Resplendent Masters over the centuries. Even today, unbound demons still lurk amid Scathe and the surrounding lands, while infernal curses weigh heavily upon buildings and bloodlines alike. Some portions of the city are all but abandoned as a result.

Kandara

Galana merchants travelling across the Glister Sands first uncovered the ancient, sand-swept ruins that would become Kandara of the Great Library. Fallen statues, cracked fountains, and sprawling foundations suggested a once-bustling civilization. Since then, settlers, traders, scavengers, and savants have transformed the First Age ruins into a desert oasis, allowing Kandara to become one of the great centers of learning in the Age of Sorrows. Savants from across the region traverse the Glister Sands to partake of Kandara’s great knowledge. Inside its towering sandstone walls with their colorful murals of heroes and gods, townhouses and universities populate the city’s outer ring. There, wealthy foreign savants receive tutelage from the Keepers — the Great Library’s rulers and caretakers — in philosophy, mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and numerous other disciplines. But the Keepers require that any who study here must offer new knowledge in exchange, which is transcribed into papyrus scrolls to add to their stores. The palatial structure of the Great Library extends deep into the ground. Multiple floors of wings extend in each cardinal direction; these contain endless racks of crumbling texts and many decaying First Age mechanisms of little-understood purpose. Mortal Keepers maintain the library, following instructions that its bizarre tutelary spirits pass along to them. Over centuries, the Keepers

EX3

gambling dens and public banks. The houses struggle ruthlessly for money and power, knowing a wrong move could cast them down.

### THE SABAKI TRIBES

The Sabaki Tribes share heritage with the Galana but remained nomadic after the fall of their homeland. They’ve long been famed as skilled hunters and cheerfully reckless warriors. Starting in childhood, all Sabaki train in ritual dances that ostensibly heal the sick and call the rain, although few unequivocally demonstrate supernatural gifts. But their reputation has evolved; today they’re also known as Gem’s warriors, enforcers for its despot, Rankar VII. Rankar joined the Sabaki during his youthful exile from Gem; after years of brilliantly planned raids, personal daring, and charismatic embrace of Sabaki ways, they acclaimed him their war chief. Today he pays the tribes handsomely — including firewands and firedust — and commands both their warriors and their loyalty. He’ll keep it while he remains generous and victorious.

Since Rankar VII returned from exile to claim the throne, Gem has risen to new heights of power and prosperity. Despite this success, the noble houses can’t enjoy their victory as fully as they’d like. Many stood by when the former House Arajana ousted the Despot. While he claims to have forgiven those who didn’t aid him, should his goodwill sour, the houses fear losing their monopolies and their lives. All appear eager to prove their loyalty, sharing their spies’ reports with the Despot and offering him gifts and flattery, while seeking to discredit their rivals in his eyes.

have managed to translate a fraction of the ancient texts that the Great Library contains. These run the gamut from ledgers and cookbooks to maps of First Age cities and manuals of sorcery.

The Despot of Gem saw Kandara as a gleaming jewel for his budding empire. When Kandara refused to submit peacefully, the Despot sent Sabaki warbands and mercenary companies to besiege the city. Through bribery, the Despot turned many of Kandara’s own mercenaries against the Keepers, then slaughtered a quarter of the rest to take the city. Kandara has recovered in the decades since, but the Keepers are slow to forgive the Despot’s conquest, as well as the lack of aid from Origin, their former ally.

Gem

Food-laden caravans wend their way south through the Desert of Glass, betwixt dunes half-melted by terrible forces in a former age, where sheets of cloudy, pitted glass meet stretches of shard-strewn sand. Their destination: the dead volcano Cinere, whose looming caldera and the winding tunnels beneath contain the fabled city of Gem.

Gem’s social classes are like Origin’s, but the Despot has absolute power. He appoints magistrates from among the nobility, who jockey for his favor. Each of the dozen noble houses holds a monopoly on one or more goods or services, requiring vast sums to acquire and annual payments to the throne to maintain. These include House Iblan’s silver and gold mines, House Sablak’s dream parlors and brothels, and House Trasti’s

Before Rankar dissolved House Arajana for treason, it held monopolies on constructing buildings and excavating volcanic tubes and First Age vaults. It’s said that many Arajanas fled into tunnels that only they have the maps to, having destroyed the records before their rivals seized their assets. Rumors speak of terrible, ancient secrets House Arajana unearthed deep below Gem — secrets holding wondrous, dangerous power. In the city proper, Arajana’s agents pursue opportunities to unseat Rankar, while the Despot seeks allies to help root out the traitor house and its influence among the other houses.

Occasionally, miners unearth a rare form of green opal, called dreamstone or dream opal, from Gem’s mines. Placed beside a sleeping person, the stone captures and records their dreams. When touched to another’s forehead, that person will experience the recorded dream the next time she sleeps. Dream merchants hire those who dream vividly, paying them handsomely for what they see when their eyes are closed. In sumptuously furnished dream parlors, customers can request specific types of dreams: flying and adventuring, ruling a city, exploring the Wyld — whatever they wish.

### Beyond the Tsavo Cities

On the shores of Lake Tohma in the Firepeaks, the shadowland of fallen Grand Apkoro rests. Once, the Apkoro empire conquered the Tsavo Cities with the help of its mysterious army of red-bannered ghosts. But when that army withdrew to the Underworld, abandoning Grand Apkoro, instability and infighting caused the empire’s collapse not long after. What remains are scattered, feuding principalities whose rulers all claim dominion over the old empire. The leaders of Ain Gorga, Apkorrum, Kor Khemish, and Shurrap rail against one another and side with Underworld warlords to conquer their peers.

EX3

Should one successfully unite — or subjugate — them all, Origin may become an eager new empress’s next target.

### Jewel of the Burning Road

Beyond the Glister Sands, the dragon lines of the Porphyry Wastes churn, shifting the dark-hued sands like waves on a great sea. Ruins lie scattered across the Wastes: manses destroyed by unstable Essence, abandoned fortresses, cracked towers of emerald-green stone. The Kurkoyyu people who live in leeward towns, where the monk Petrel spent many years proselytizing and doing good works, have largely converted to the Immaculate Philosophy. Sabaki bands visit the Wastes to practice certain of their healing dances, which they believe to be most efficacious here.

## Dajaz

is one of the southernmost points in Creation, more than a thousand miles beyond Gem. The Burning Road that connects Dajaz to Gem and then to Creation at large is long and difficult, but centuries of trade have given rise to numerous settlements and caravanserai. At these sites, cisterns catch and hold water during the year’s few precious rainfalls, and spirits loyal to the Benefactors watch over travelers — at least, so long as those travelers provide them with strange favors and blasphemous worship.

South of Gem, the Glister Sands give way to the dazzling brilliance of the Saltblaze Plateau. The Burning Road to Dajaz crosses the plateau, connecting Athi townships and caravanserais in a chain. Traders and pilgrims alike traverse its routes. In major towns on the Plateau’s borders, the Blue Dune Company offers their services as guards to protect travelers from bandits, manticores, and basiliscs on the long stretches of empty road. Sandskiff pilots seek the shifting web of dragon lines called the Sidewinder Tributaries. These strong, swift quicksand currents allow for faster travel across the desert, though their fluctuations mean merchants and travelers can’t rely on them when estimating a journey’s

duration. Inexperienced pilots often find that the currents pull them far beyond the point where they wish to

return to calmer sands, depositing them in some distant part of the desert where the tributary runs out.

Dajaz

At the world’s edge, the towers of Dajaz rise to survey mountain and sand. Water spills from deep springs and spiral-pumped wells to slake the city’s thirst and make Dajaz a stain of green upon an otherwise sun-baked, sun-bleached expanse. It’s a riot of silken pavilions and shanties, pleasure-houses and back-alley brothels, a place where the flotsam and jetsam of Creation walk alongside princes at play.

The city was founded atop an aquifer by one of the nomadic tribes who travel the Firepeaks and the surrounding deserts, but it flourished by the grace of the Benefactors — white-veiled spirits who forged a pact with the Dajazeen as the Contagion’s ravages died down. Together, mortal and Benefactor have built Dajaz into the so-called City of Blissful Sighs, where any pleasure known to humanity (and some known only to Hell) can be had for a handful of silver.

In exchange for much-needed foodstuffs from northern trading partners, Dajaz sends caravans heavy with iron and lapis lazuli, liquor distilled from scorpion venom, luminous fire-poppies, and obsidian blades taken from great vents of molten glass dotting the farthest South. These treasures make Dajaz extremely attractive to merchant-princes. Many make the long journey to fill their carts with Dajazeen wares, only to spend a small fortune indulging in the many and varied delights the city provides. Dreamy tales from bliss-rattled merchants have given Dajaz an undeniable reputation — one that attracts wealthy nobles, sorcerers, and errant Chosen from the South and beyond.

### Sinners, Saints, and Slaves

Once nomads, now pleasure-mongers — above all else, the Dajazeen see themselves as celebrants, acolytes in some great mystery cult devoted to themselves, to the Benefactors, and most of all to ecstasy. This is most apparent in the wealthy aristocrats, merchants, and landowners at the top of Dajazeen society, but their fêtes and celebrations spill out to even the meanest streets. The divide between rich and poor becomes porous mid-festival; everyone expects foremen and overseers to purchase their laborers’ first cup of wine or mouthful of qat. The well-to-do marry only amongst one another, but they eagerly take lovers of any station. This isn’t altruism. While the nightly revels are an ancient tradition, they keep the lower classes content. The ancient masters of the Dajazeen deem a sated people plied with food, wine, and music more pliant than the hungry and desperate. Paeans to the Benefactors are woven throughout every feast, game, and dance, whether subtle or overt; in this way, the revels also slake the Benefactors’ fathomless thirst for worship and gratitude. The same doesn’t extend to slaves, who live and labor as chattel for their masters’ profit. Most are taken from Firepeaks nomads; although they’re ancient kin to the Dajazeen, neither has any love for the other. To Dajaz, nomads are uncivilized barbarians; to many nomads, the

EX3

Dajazeen are swaggering fools made soft by luxury — and devil-worshiping sycophants to boot. The nomads raid the city’s outermost holdings and waylay travelers on the Burning Road; in exchange, parties of ilis enkti — Dajazeen holy warriors sworn to asceticism outside of certain key festivals — slaughter and enslave nomads wherever they find them. Occasionally, foreigners pay to join these war parties and claim a share of plunder.

celebrate with music, drink, sport, and dances in honor of the Benefactors. Workers typically dine on burgoo and bread. Meanwhile, wealthy guests partake of such dishes as fermented sand-ray sashimi (an acquired taste), live honeypot ants, roasted dormouse stuffed with pine nuts and honey, or flamingo stewed with dates in spiced wine.

Most civil authority resides in a forum of landowners known as the Raucous, where spectacle and threat are the foremost tools of statecraft. When they gather, the loudest and most ardent voices dominate, with every landowner entitled to entreat, argue, harangue, or insult the body and their individual peers — so long as they can get a word in. A line of shaman-kings rules alongside the Raucous, holding a limited veto as a check to the chaos of democracy. A shaman-king may make trade agreements with merchants from outside of Dajaz, direct the ilis enkit toward specific targets, or mete out punishments for members of the Raucous who grow lax in their worship or bargain with spirits other than the Benefactors. The Benefactors raise these rulers from childhood, and ensure that they have every inch of their skin tattooed with the terms of the pact that founded Dajaz.

Dajaz wouldn’t exist without the Benefactors. Oh, there’d be a city, but it wouldn’t be the City of Blissful Sighs. It would be a mean and meager place, they say, where mortals fought amongst each other for control of well and water, the ground stained red by blood. The Benefactors don’t rule the city, but they give it life: they who tapped the Sea Beneath the Rock; they who bless miners with strength and merchants with wiles; they who instruct the Dajazeen in the alchemy of pleasure — they who protect Dajaz still from nomad zealots and the ambitions of outsiders.

### Life in Dajaz

Daily life begins before the sun rises. Most wake when Wyld-light auroras blaze across the night sky and the air is cool. The city stirs with a growing riot of smells and sounds: warm bread pulled from ovens and street-merchants calling for customers. Laborers begin work in that long, red twilight, whether in mines, workshops, or the bazaar that greets visitors and traders. A scattering of farm laborers give precious arable land over to hot-weather crops like beans, okra, and sweet potato, while ranchers rear giant sand-rays, shrews, and many-colored lizards.

### The Benefactors

That they’re demons is of little concern. Though they wear impenetrable white veils and call themselves spirits, anyone with occult knowledge can guess the truth. Most are demons of the First Circle, but a few greater demons count themselves among the Benefactors’ numbers: FireWidow Hazeca, Elzire Who-Mourns-a-Distant-Sea, or Alphonsine of the Labyrinth Unending. Within Dajaz’s walls, no one can summon or bind them, but neither can they leave. This place is both prison and reward for some long-forgotten service, a kinder cage than Hell. They dwell among the Dajazeen people, choosing palaces or hovels based on their inscrutable fancies. To refuse hospitality to a Benefactor is unthinkable. Indeed, a demonic patron blesses her chosen house with many well-intentioned wonders: prophetic nightmares, children born from stolen flesh, and gory entrails of enemies left by the hearth.

Work halts in late morning, and Dajaz grows silent as the midday sun waxes to its full heat. Most spend these smoldering hours underground in caves and cellars. Those of means retire to water gardens where cold water is pumped up from deep below the city. Wealthy or not, the Dajazeen divide this time between meals, games, and especially trysts; they consider it the height of romance to hide one’s love from the sun. Midday treats range from humble lizard-and-hot-pepper skewers to chilled fruit sherbets and candied scorpions. Work resumes in mid-afternoon. By twilight, when the air quickly cools, most gather in public forums and squares. There they share communal meals and

EX3

### NEW THAUMATURGICAL RITUAL:

BLOOD FROM THE STONE (•)

Ray-hunters, merchants, and others who brave the sands treasure this ritual, which was first taught by the Benefactors. The thaumaturgist marks a stone with her blood, spends a point of temporary Willpower, and pierces the stone with a pick. A trickle of fresh water flows from the stone for several minutes, enough to slake her thirst for an entire day — although the water is unusually warm and tastes of iron.

The Benefactors also defend the city from attack. Centuries of guerilla warfare have taught nomad raiders and Fair Folk war parties to attack Dajaz quickly or not at all, escaping before the city’s devils can muster a response.

### THE ROLL OF IGNOMINIOUS DEVILS

While most Benefactors are demons of the First Circle, they include an unspecified number of greater demons. This is left ambiguous for Storytellers to adjust according to their needs — in a high-XP game, the city may require a Third Circle patron to challenge the players, while fledgling Exalts might be better matched against demons of the Second Circle, or even First Circle demons who have grown craftier and more powerful than most of their kind.

For all the contact that occurs between mortals and demons, there are precious few Demon-Blooded in Dajaz. While many Benefactors take lovers and playthings, some magic inherent in the city or their bondage forbids them from conceiving children. Only rarely does a demon or Demon-Blooded traveler visit Dajaz from elsewhere; these are not caged as the Benefactors are, and may find themselves targets of their hosts’ jealousy.

### Beyond the City Gates

Given its remote location, Dajaz has little presence in Creation’s politics. Its closest tie is to Gem and the other Tsavo Cities, linked as they are by the Burning Road and a mutually profitable flow of trade. Beyond this, its primary influence is on visiting pleasure-seeking potentates. Locally, Dajaz deals primarily with settlements along the Burning Road, providing them with food and support to grease the wheels of trade. Dajazeen soldiers also defend those settlements from raiding parties of Firepeaks nomads, wild spirits, and scorpion-tailed Fair Folk. Dajaz’s masters sometimes trade with the fae, offering slaves in exchange for crystallized dreams and Wyld-wine.

### Prominent Figures

Ujada Born-from-Fire was a whisper away from greatness. Charismatic, brilliant, handsome, proud — he was a Nexus street-tough who rose through the ranks of the Guild and built his fortune by spinning a delicate web of half-truths among his many backers only to be betrayed, beaten, and branded by his lieutenant and lover. Slippng into obscurity, he emerged six months later at Dajaz’s gates, newly baptized as an Infernal Exalt. Dubbing himself Dajaz’s “High Celebrant,” Ujada now inflicts new festivals and rites of his own design upon the city. He rewards those who join willingly with dreams as pleasant as opium haze; those who refuse, he ensnares with his devilish power, forcing them to dance until their feet bleed or their hearts give out. These festivals grow increasingly blasphemous, not merely venerating the Benefactors but imbuing Ujada’s acolytes with hellish power.

Dajaz’s shaman-king, Zaffre the Bold, is a wide-eyed ascetic ill-suited to governance and easily cowed by the Raucous. His fitful, drug-induced trances offer prophetic glimpses of the past and future but wrack the poor man with agony. Nonetheless, they’ve led him to uncover secret caches throughout the Firepeaks, including an immense sarcophagus of Malfean porcelain bound by chains of silver, electrum, and iron. He dotes over this treasure despite his many failed attempts to pry it open. The merchant-prince Nazareya is also known as the Blue Asp. Although her family’s wealth comes primarily from lapis lazuli mines, she has a fondness for (and skill with) demonology, brokering trade between visitors and Benefactors. Nazareya got her start trading favors for minor blessings, but as she took on more prestigious clients, she discovered her talent for contracting demonic assassins. The bloody work has recently put Nazareya and her family in danger, but she cannot extract herself without powerful allies.

The ancient blood ape Skullcrusher is matriarch of all erymanthoi residing in Dajaz. Withered and aged despite her immortality, she still delights in the crisp thrill of violence. She dwells among the poor, infirm, and elderly, especially those abandoned by their own children. Those who strike down faithless sons and daughters may earn her favor, and with it, the goodwill of a score of blood ape thugs.

Mizra Mehu was once poor, and she hasn’t forgotten. Made wealthy by a long lifetime as a smuggler and secret-broker, she’s clawed her way into the Dajazeen upper classes. She now sits atop a vast network of agents positioned throughout the polities tied to the Burning Road. Caravan workers, beggars, orphans, and bastards deliver intelligence and contraband goods into and out of Dajaz at her bidding — but she desperately seeks a successor who’ll keep them safe after her death.

The morning sun’s light fractured across the battle-churned sea, spilling gold between two ships locked in mortal combat. The defender was a large, proud Nandao armed merchanter, its crew largely Baihu, though a few sailors displayed the purple hair and Wyld-touched markings of deep Westerners. Everyone aboard wore expressions of grim determination, naked fear, and — on one particularly bellicose sailor — a serene smile. The ship crawled with Lintha marauders who slunk out of the ocean’s surface and clambered up the side with fearsome hooked chopping blades called auhzian. The defender’s huge, elegant dragon’s wing sails were aflame in three places, victims of an opening salvo of flaming arrows; the ash and smoke they shed lent the scene a hellish aspect.

The Baihu ship was one of seven, her sister vessels trailing behind in a convoy that stretched for miles. They were three days out of Nandao, which made the raid an incredibly daring act. The aggressor ships, equal in number, were of irregular make and manufacture. Each was of a different style with its own strengths and weaknesses, but all swarmed with Lintha pirates, themselves marked with the signs of a hundred bloodlines and the cold, cruel countenance of demon-worshipers. As members of the crew individually cast quick glances away from the battle at hand to the rest of the sea, they glimpsed the other ships of the merchant fleet aflame.

The attacking vessel had also been a blue-water merchant vessel once, albeit of Tengese manufacture — but the years hadn’t been kind to it, nor had its captors. Fearsome iron plates reinforced the hull; flies buzzed around jutting spikes from which human remains dangled, scraps of sunbaked flesh still clinging to the bones.

The sea foamed beyond the attacker’s bow, belching forth thick, acrid, yellow-white demon smoke that mixed with the black smoke of the burning sails. Some hideous demon more suited to the seas of Kimbery than those of the Southwest thrashed there, straining against rusted chains sunk deep into the ship’s hull. This demon lent the Lintha ship its unholy speed, allowing the buccaneers to descend upon their target before its crew had time to rouse from their bunks. The attacker’s own sails were furled, largely protected from the Baihu ship’s ranged counterattack.

The captain of the doomed merchant vessel looked over his crew as the invaders made chum of the deck’s defenders with vicious sword thrusts and well-placed arrows. The thick smoke had by now obscured the sun’s light, casting the ships into eerie twilight. He locked eyes with the Lintha commander, an older man about his age. Even from a ship’s length away, the Baihu captain spied the rows of serrated teeth in the demon-blood’s jaw when he cracked a smile. The Lintha grasped one arm with a gloved hand, then ripped out the linked fetishes embedded into his flesh with a single, swift jerk. As bright blood sprayed over the deck, a chill wind whipped up from the surface of the water, not blowing the smoke away but darkening it instead.

Spectral figures oozed out of the bloodied fetishes. With his final breaths, the Baihu captain prayed for a miracle — an errant water elemental, perhaps, or for one of the teenaged crew members to display the sudden signs of a Dragon’s favor — that never came.

# Chapter Seven: The Southwest

Chapter Seven

The Southwest

Once a realm of mighty empires and wealthy republics, the Southwest’s great powers have decayed over the centuries. The Realm holds An-Teng supine beneath its boot and broke both Greater Zhao and the Baihu leagues. Beyond the Realm’s grip, splintered remnants of other powers — the mercantile Fourport League, the Forty-Fourth Immortal’s elemental hegemony, the nascent warrior empire of Raolai Damay — lie scattered about, fallen to internal strife, war, natural disasters, or supernatural threats.

Today, the Southwest is a realm of shattered and dying states. Fractured societies, civil wars, and governments tottering under their own corruption are endemic here. The Southwest maintains a tropical climate. The weather tends toward warmth year-round, though it grows hot — especially away from the coast — in the summer, during the cycle of Water. The rainy season, comprising the cycles of Wood and Fire, brings rain, storms, and flooding. Lastly, winter occupies much of the cycles of Earth and Air, and offers cooler, drier weather.

## An-Teng

The satrapy of An-Teng is renowned across Creation as a gentle, peaceful country. Dynasts come to see their every whim tended to amid this land’s splendid architecture and natural beauty. Its three provinces’ royal families brutally punish behavior that detracts from the land’s image, whether that be provincial rebellions or speaking out of turn. As such, the Tengese raise their children to hide their true feelings in public, disguising the seething hostility that many feel toward arrogant Dynastic tourists and their own native aristocracy. Amid An-Teng’s cities, people disgusted by high taxes or Dynastic outrages join secret societies and criminal gangs, or smuggle family members out of the country in search of better lives. Country folk join outlaw bands to prey on tax collectors and merchants, quietly supported by the villagers to whom they funnel their ill-gotten gains. The Tengese have their own lives and concerns from which the Realm is an unwelcome distraction.

For centuries, An-Teng has simmered with discontent beneath its serene surface. Today, with the Empress gone and the Realm garrison largely withdrawn, that discontent may finally erupt into countrywide rebellion.

### History

Conquest and subjugation scar An-Teng’s long history. In the First Age, An-Teng was famous for its luxuries. Heroes, princes, and the Exalted visited its cities to partake in its riches, sit for its artists and sculptors, and debate with its savants. Others struggled heroically to liberate the slaves its founders had procured to support their affluent lifestyle, eventually succeeding against its Exalted rulers’ opposition.

When the Dragon-Blooded rose up, they mercilessly slaughtered An-Teng’s Solar princes and the royal families descending from them, installing former petty nobles in their places. The Tengese put up the greatest resistance in An-Teng’s former capital, the City of Flowers. There, the Dragon-Blooded slaughtered the defenders in the streets, blasting them with sorcery that blighted the land such that nothing grows there even today.

During the Shogunate, successive daimyos made AnTeng their battleground. Armies marched on its cities; navies clogged the River of Queens. Out of self-preservation, the Tengese princes bowed to one DragonBlooded ruler after another, extracting ruinous taxes from their people in tribute. Breaks from this system were rare — most notably the peasant revolt and ensuing decade-long reign by the culture heroes Kanviti Mountain-Song and Sowathi Mei, who some Tengese secretly worship as gods even today.

Centuries later, after the Contagion, the Zhao and Baihu peoples — fleeing the destruction of the Seven Tigers — arrived on An-Teng’s shores and conquered much of its territory. They fled again after a generation, sailing south to escape the rising tide of the Realm’s power.

EX3

When the Scarlet Empress’s envoys arrived in the City of the Steel Lotus, the Three Princes — deeming conquest inevitable in the face of her legions and Exalted champions — preemptively offered fealty, and courted her favor with lavish gifts of jewels, silk, rare animals, and fine wines. The Empress graciously accepted, upholding their authority so long as their gifts continued. Today, An-Teng’s people offer lavish tribute to their conquerors. Dynasts travel the entire country for free, living off Tengese hospitality. This includes inns as opulent as the Blessed Isle’s finest, and restaurants and theatres too expensive for natives to afford. The Tengese pretend to ignore how foreigners exploit their country, hiding their hatred of the Dynasty lest visiting Exalted or local officials punish them and their neighbors for their outbursts. They steer those who can’t conceal their feelings away from interacting with Dynasts, often ensuring that they find work in slums or remote towns where foreigners won’t encounter them. Rebellious elements hiding in the mountains or forests plan to take back their homeland, training in guerilla warfare while awaiting their chance to strike. Historically, they’ve fought as bandits and raiders, knowing that an army of Tengese peasants had no chance in open battle against the Realm’s legions. With the Blessed Isle in chaos and the legions withdrawn, leaving only the Three Princes’ troops and a dwindling garrison, the time to act may even be upon them now.

### A Land of Beauty

An-Teng’s breathtaking views and sweeping vistas have inspired painters and poets since ancient times. It’s traditionally divided into three domains. The Shore Lands have sandy beaches, clear oceans, quaint fishing towns, and cities as grand as any in Creation. Farther east, the Forest of Compassion dominates the Middle Lands, full of plants and animals unlike those found anywhere else. The High Lands encompass a swath of the mountain range known as the Firepeaks, where incredible vistas overlook the rest of An-Teng. The mighty River of Queens flows through the countryside from the High Lands to the sea. The Tengese drink from its waters and travel up and down its length on ten thousand boats, harvesting fish and transporting goods among towns and cities. It connects all three of An-Teng’s provinces, joining together their diverse peoples.

### Culture

An-Teng has strict social classes: visiting Dynasts, the three royal families, various lesser nobles, Immaculate monks, the common folk, and slaves. Tengese speak with and work alongside others of their social class, but none would speak to someone above their station without reason. To those above them, especially the DragonBlooded, Tengese bow their heads and speak as little and as politely as possible; offending one’s social superiors often results in a thrashing at the very least. Tengese officials impose especially brutal punishments on those who displease the Three Princes or Dynastic tourists. (Complaining about one’s social superiors in private is another matter; indeed, it’s something of a pastime.) The Blue An people — predominant in the Shore Lands and Middle Lands — tend to be short and slight with light brown skin and dark hair. The Red An, descended from both Blue An and Blessed Isle folk, resemble them but are taller and paler; these include both commoners descended from settled garrison troops and aristocrats who’ve long intermarried with Realm patricians. The Gold An, who predominate in the High Lands, tend to be darker than the Blue An, often with blond or red hair. Various other ethnic groups appear in smaller numbers throughout An-Teng, especially amid the Shore Lands. Some descend from immigrants or conquerors — such as the tall, sallow Baihu and burly, dark-skinned Zhao who ruled briefly after the Contagion. Others are children of visiting merchants, Realm janissaries, or even spirits.

Tengese cuisine reflects the cultures and peoples who make up its history. Roasted or boiled silkworm pupae — leftovers from the silk industry — are a popular snack. Dishes containing jambú buds numb the lips and tongue and change how other food tastes for a time, making it a favorite for adventurous eaters. Other common fare includes under-ripe ambarella fruit with black shrimp paste; broken ear-root salad with vinegar, chilis, coriander, and fish sauce; and mashed plantains with pork fat and fried sausage. Bite-sized truffles made from cocoa powder, condensed milk, and butter are rolled in sugar, coconut flakes, or other sweets for a luxurious dessert.

Almost everyone speaks Tengese, a Flametongue dialect. The royal families also speak High Realm, while many Red An speak a Tengese–Low Realm creole. Several of the more isolated ethnic groups have their own local tongues.

Tengese dress tends toward bright colors, with nobles wearing dyed silks and the lower classes cotton. Shore Lands folk wear robes and trousers and don colorful conical hats to ward off the sun. Middle Lands farmers work shirtless in hot summer months; High Lands residents add woolen quilted layers to combat the mountain cold. Commoners crop their hair short; sumptuary laws reserve long hair for the upper classes, who style it elaborately using pins and combs.

siblings, and children, but also many degrees of extended relatives. Parents raise children communally, with all blood relatives sharing responsibility for care, teaching, and discipline. Grandparents tell stories of long-dead ancestors over meals; grandchildren chant these tales during planting and harvest. Tengese families traditionally prefer to discuss problems and reach consensus, but ultimately defer to the matriarch — the eldest living woman in the family.

Every social class favors ivory adornments — peasants wear smaller pieces strung on hempen cords or embedded in lacquered wood, while the wealthy set it into silver and gold filigree. Only the royal family may wear jade. Almost everyone in the High Lands, with its rich mines, owns at least a little silver jewelry. The poor wear simple bands at neck or wrist; the rich wear ornate pieces embellished with expensive gemstones.

Intricate formalities traditionally guide social interactions. Such lessons begin early, with children observing parents’ proper behaviors and practicing them at home. Matriarchs maneuver exemplary family members into desirable jobs and arrange favorable marriages for them. Government officials prioritize the needs of upstanding citizens who adhere flawlessly to Tengese norms, while harshly punishing dissenters who voice their views outside of rare, private, sanctioned venues.

### Religion

Publicly, An-Teng is devoutly Immaculate. People pray and make offerings according to the prayer calendar. Cities and villages alike throng with festivalgoers during Realm holidays, and even the poorest farmer expresses delight at the opportunity to host an Immaculate monk. In private, the Tengese and their gods often maintain secret cults in defiance of Immaculate principles — typically in the hinterlands, away from nosy government officials and meddling monks.

His ill-starred counterpart, the Pale Mistress, orchestrates chaos, disaster, plague, famine, and death; but much as winter presages spring, so too does she end stagnation and bring necessary change. She has no formal priesthood; the Tengese leave offerings to her at desolate shrines under cover of darkness, begging her to overlook their homes and ignore their families, or to protect them from other malevolent spirits. The price of her aid is the ill fortune she oversees, which manifests thereafter in the region. A few unwholesome cults seek her favor through awful deeds. In death, many such cultists become kaleyi, or “hungry dancers”; when she wanders the land in sickly or monstrous form, their twisted ghosts follow in her wake.

Foremost in Tengese prayers are two gods so powerful that even the Three Princes never call them by name. The beloved Golden Lord oversees law, stability, social order, virtuous conduct, righteous action, and the land’s fertility. Tall and shining, clad in golden robes and bearing a diamond scepter, he dwells with his court in the luminous Pinnacle of Mercy in the High

### TENGESE NAMES

A traditional Tengese given name combines an adjective and a noun directly from Firetongue, such as “Onyx Blade” or “Dawnlit Snow.” Family names follow the same structure.

Given names aren’t appended directly to family names. Depending on circumstances, one might be addressed as “Gentle Tea of the Noble Peony family,” “Gentle Tea,” or “Noble Peony,” but not “Noble Peony Gentle Tea.” Family businesses usually share the family name — e.g., “Noble Peony Shipping.” Upon taking the throne, each prince assumes a oneword regnal name drawn from ancient Tengese genealogies. Commoners often supplement that with a nickname; this is never used in formal address. The prince’s original name is only used in private, by family members or especially close friends. While it’s proper to address social equals or inferiors by name, one must address social superiors by title. This often includes elder family members, and always includes the Three Princes and the gods.

### Governance

An-Teng’s Three Princes — Liashan the Lax-Handed, Kiotaran of Upward View, and Josei of Notable Genius — rule the Shore Lands, Middle Lands, and High Lands respectively. Descended from rulers installed by the Realm, their families have held power for centuries. Each oversees their domain, appointing officials, initiating and guiding public works projects, and ensuring taxes and tributes are collected. For the most part, each operates autonomously from his counterparts, though they consult with one another when concerns span their domains.

High-ranking government positions go to members of noble families. Though Tengese royal lines rarely die out, noble families are technically in line for the princedom. Thus their scions receive the best education and, while they don’t own territory, they enjoy other privileges such as the right to maintain household guards.

EX3

### HER ABSENT MAJESTY

Traditionally, the princes were men reporting to a sovereign High Queen of all An-Teng. When princes’ needs clashed and talks broke down, they looked to her to settle disputes. The Scarlet Empress claimed the High Queen title when the Realm conquered AnTeng. Since her disappearance, the question of who should succeed her remains unanswered.

Noble status comes in nine merit-based ranks. A person who earns a government posting, secures a military victory, or serves An-Teng in another significant capacity may rise in rank. Each succeeding generation’s rank diminishes by one step, encouraging heirs to strive for or surpass their parents’ status.

Each principality has its own government, albeit with similar structures. Many offices — such as tax assessor, archivist, courier, and judge — hold the same responsibilities throughout. Others are specific to their principality. For instance, dockmasters oversee the Shore Lands’ ports; granary-ministers ensure that food grown in the Middle Lands is properly distributed; fortress construction in the High Lands falls under public works rather than the military.

Appointed magistrates oversee criminal cases, though few enter their courts; common folk try to resolve matters among themselves or seek mediation from Immaculate monks, while the wealthy and powerful often settle things privately using political influence or threats from household guards. However, garrison troops act with impunity, for which even the aristocracy has little recourse. And Dynasts stand above the law; no one has the authority to punish them, barring deeds sufficient to warrant retaliation from the garrison commander or satrap.

Growing Unrest

The Three Princes collect heavy taxes to send tribute to the Realm yearly, provide lavish gifts to Dynastic visitors, and maintain themselves in luxury, leaving most citizens in poverty. In addition, Tengese officials, visiting Realm grandees, and garrison troops alike may verbally or physical abuse the common folk; being above the law; few ever see justice. Some who can no longer abide these conditions flee the country, hoping for a new start in foreign lands. Others seek out and join rebel groups.

Most operate on a local level, with little coordination or long-term planning. In cities, rebel organizations divide members into smaller cells. Leaders cooperate, but street-level members know little of larger undertakings, protecting other cells’ anonymity if captured and interrogated. In some places, Tengese magistrates overlook their activities — either in solidarity or for hefty bribes. Hinterlands groups are less secretive, recruiting members by protecting smaller villages, or by seizing funds from tax collectors and redistributing them — whether to directly aid their own families, from general sympathy for the common folk, or simply so that grateful villagers will mislead Realm scouts as to the bandits’ whereabouts.

Officially, any who harm the Princes or the Realm are traitors and sentenced to death. Major rebellions and direct assaults on Dynasts reap brutal, bloody retribution; Middle Lands folk recall Singing Storm’s Revolt a generation ago, which ended with thousands of rebel bodies piled high on the River of Queens’ banks. But less ambitious bandits and insurgents rarely see capture, especially in hinterlands far from garrison postings. While the satrap suspects complicity from the Three Princes, rebels remain elusive, tipped off by sympathetic — and often well-bribed — Tengese commoners.

Noteworthy Rebel Groups

Operating primarily out of the Middle Lands’ forests, the Ghost Leopards use guerilla tactics to harry garrison troops and Realm merchants. They protect villages and redistribute wealth, earning devotion from rural Tengese; this depends largely on their charismatic leaders Bright Crest and Graceful Heart, who struggle to keep more violent and self-centered Leopards in line. The Golden Lord’s Kingdom, originally based in the High Lands, has spawned offshoots in the cities of Sapphire, Dragon’s Jaws, and Salt-Founded Glory. They combine rebellion with religion, worshiping the Golden Lord as a creator god and reviling all non-Southern peoples as unholy. Smuggling funds their operations; many of their smugglers believe more in silver than in the Golden Lord.

Founded a year ago, the City of the Steel Lotus’s budding Firedust Regiment seeks to inflame An-Teng’s tensions to the breaking point. To that end, members — largely intellectuals, merchants, and petty criminals — spread rumors of atrocities, burn Realm traders’ warehouses, and kill garrison members they catch alone. They await a violent Realm response that’ll rouse the countryside to insurrection.

### THE SEVEN-STRANDED VINE

The Shogunate failed to destroy the old royal family completely. Two scions escaped, forsaking their names to hide as simple laborers. Nursing their resentment, they swore themselves to the Yozis for a chance to regain their lost throne. Today, a handful of distant descendants maintain their unholy pact.

Tengese inclined toward rebellion or violence often find themselves forced out of mainstream society, joining street gangs or revolutionary groups, or becoming bandits or pirates. Mainstream Tengese blame these outsiders’ behavior on foreign influences or bad blood. It’s said that Zhao blood causes violent tempers, while Baihu blood carries treachery and greed.

Their secretive demon cult, the Seven-Stranded Vine, worships She Who Lives in Her Name. They don’t engage in open revolt nor work with mainstream rebel groups, instead wielding rumor, sabotage, blackmail, and assassination to sow dissension between the common folk, the Three Princes, and the Dynasty. Their aim is an independent An-Teng, rooted in Tengese traditions of familial and political stratification — with themselves at the top.

Elite Troops of the Three Lands

The Prince of the Shore Lands employs hereditary sorcerer-assassins known as the Shadow Puppeteers. The Puppeteers perform grim occult dramas, casting the shadows of marionettes resembling An-Teng’s enemies on a screen. Within hours, the target dies, strangled by her own shadow.

The Vine’s high priest, Night Butterfly, claims direct descent from the old royal family. This silver-haired, one-eyed dancer maintains contacts across An-Teng, using his troupe’s travels as cover for his movements. He shares power with Silent Smile, head of the Fallen Magnolia family; he oversees cult matters while she directs their finances. But rumors suggest they harbor a deep enmity for one another.

Those who don gold-embroidered white silk ancestor sashes from the Middle Prince’s armory take on the power and aspect of ancient Tengese princes and heroes. Called the Elephant-Riding Ghost Generals, they lead the region’s armies in battle, sitting astride the strongest elephants.

### Military

An-Teng lacks a standing army. The Realm permits only the aristocracy’s house guards to bear arms. Each royal family commands a few hundred soldiers; lesser nobles typically maintain a few dozen at most. Should need arise, the princes can assemble their vassals’ house guards into an army, but such disparate, uncoordinated contingents can’t withstand properly trained forces in battle. For the moment, the Realm garrison fills the need for regular troops.

Instead, Tengese military tradition leans toward irregular warfare. Mobile skirmishers lead guerilla wars through forest and mountain to break supply lines, poison wells, or lure enemies within reach of deadly beasts and angry spirits. Farmers practice in secret with farm implements, training as a militia.

Realm soldiers see Tengese levies as incompetent. By tradition, the Tengese don’t teach their children martial skills, lest they be tempted to take up arms and draw the garrison’s retribution. (As a result, the Realm rarely calls up Tengese auxiliaries.) Of course, the Tengese aren’t innately pacifist. When trained to fight, they’re

The High Prince protects the Masks That Command the Animals. Each mask’s wearer can summon and command one of An-Teng’s native species. While Prince Josei reserves the Mask of the Tiger for himself, he contemplates who among his personal guard might be best suited for those of elephant, ape, and hawk.

### The Shore Lands

Wealthy foreigners flock to the Shore Lands, drawn to balmy resorts and thronging port cities overlooking the warm Southwestern waters.

The soil and climate here poorly suit most crops. Waves and winds buffet the coasts, and the summer’s dry season extends long into autumn. Even the brief rainy season, with its fierce storms, offers little respite for would-be farmers. Inland, noble families oversee fields of sugar cane and orchards of blood oranges, mangoes, starfruits, persimmons, and golden plums. But rather than provide sustenance for the Tengese, laborers preserve the orchards’ fruits — whether dried, sugared, pickled, or made into wine — for landowners to export. Some landowners import provisions from the Middle Lands; others leave their peasants struggling to feed themselves from poor, leftover strips of land good for little more than buckwheat.

EX3

With a bustling harbor open all hours of the night and an entertainment district where lights never dim, many visitors to An-Teng never explore further than the City of the Steel Lotus. Courtesans pamper wealthy visitors, offering every pleasure they can imagine. Wealthy patrons attract poets, artists, artisans, and scholars from across An-Teng and nearby lands, establishing a cosmopolitan ferment of styles and ideas. The Three Princes meet here when regional matters demand collaboration — or when the satrap summons them. Most Dynasts begin their visits to An-Teng here, where they can find a taste of home alongside native delicacies. The luxury housing available in the Royal and Market Districts is but a short, pleasant stroll to anywhere worth visiting, and pleasure barges float along the canals at all hours. The satrap, Ragara Soras Jor, resides in the Dragon’s Brightness Residence; he spends much of his time visiting prominent Dynasts, merchants, and officials. The port of Dragon’s Jaws, with its utilitarian gray stone walls and breakwaters, sits in the City of the Steel Lotus’s shadow. Where the country’s capital revels in luxury and culture, Dragon’s Jaws handles mundane necessities — trade in bulk goods, fishery warehousing, manufacturing, garrison barracks and transport, and the like — and serves as the Realm garrison’s home barracks. Outcasts wishing to leave An-Teng and foreign immigrants alike come through here seeking a better life. Both typically find themselves disappointed — trapped in menial labor, entangled in criminal enterprises, or snatched up by press gangs and slavers. Several ships docked in Dragon’s Jaws fly plain sails and nondescript flags. These are Lintha vessels, covertly allied with An-Teng. Lintha ships dock at Shore Lands ports to trade, repair, and hand over captured smugglers. In return, they harry Realm merchants at sea and offer the Tengese a share of the spoils. The Sea-Greeting River flows through Salt-Founded Glory, capital of the Shore Lands, where it meets the River of Queens. Canals spread from it through the city; common folk traverse these with rowboats, moving aside for merchant ships and the occasional aristocrat’s yacht. Wooden pilings raise the city’s buildings above the rainy season’s floodwaters.

A consortium of four merchant families hold enormous practical power through dominance over local markets, command of organized crime syndicates, and bribery of government officials, hemming in the authority of the Shore Lands’ ruler — Prince Liashan of the Lax Hand — and officials. The most powerful family,

Fallen Magnolia, guides the others’ activities through fiscal manipulation and blackmail, and uses a copy of Prince Liashan’s seal to smuggle rare goods out of AnTeng. Noble Peony dominates the shipping industry; Righteous Urn owns numerous fruit plantations and wineries; and Virtuous Camellia owns An-Teng’s only cinnabar mine.

Prominent Figures

A Realm apologist and sycophant, Liashan the LaxHanded — often known by the derisive nickname “Laxhander” — idolizes the Blessed Isle’s culture and its Dragon-Blooded Dynasty. He spends his time courting the satrap and visiting Dynasts in the City of the Steel Lotus, leaving actual governance to family members — especially his eldest son and heir, Uplifting Snow — and rich merchants in Salt-Founded Glory. The youngest of An-Teng’s Three Princes, Liashan envisions a glorious future for his family, including Exalted children of his own. To this end, he entertains Great House scions, hoping to arrange a fruitful marriage and secure prosperous alliances. Uplifting Snow chafes at the prospect of an Exalted scion displacing him and his family; he keeps tabs on his father and aims to undermine marriage negotiations, all while struggling to counter the Shore Lands’ rebel groups. Ragara Soras Jor, An-Teng’s Earth Aspect satrap, dresses finely and speaks with calm eloquence. His skill at tricking rivals into embarrassing themselves recently earned him the opportunity to manage this profitable satrapy. He’s since ingratiated himself with Prince Liashan and the Fallen Magnolias, gained leverage over regional officials, and kept careful tabs on the garrison commander’s own political activities.

Jor channels his personal profits toward repaying personal obligations to Ragara Banoba, and intends on securing further advancement within the house through success in An-Teng. He views people and circumstances alike as tools toward this end. Most useful of these is his oldest friend and former lover Rose Sevasar, a mortal patrician classmate from the Spiral Academy. Sevasar has served for decades as Jor’s majordomo and spymaster, his loyalty guaranteed by Ragara support for his children’s and grandchildren’s advancement. Ledaal Shuri was an excessively arrogant youth even by Dynastic standards, until her family bought her a commission in the Vermilion Legion to teach her humility. This succeeded admirably, but her career ended when she lost her arm in battle. Afterwards, House Ledaal gifted her a prosthetic jade arm and pulled
