### The Middle Lands

### THE CITY OF DEAD FLOWERS

Humbler than the Shore Lands, the Middle Lands supply An-Teng’s agricultural needs. In the north, river valleys and canals water fertile fields, rice paddies, cacao orchards, and mulberry groves producing raw silk for export. In the south, the Forest of Compassion grows medicinal plants, as well as narcotics and stimulants. Throughout the land, merchant caravans travel on roads stamped flat by passing elephant herds. Only through the land’s great fecundity do countless small hamlets remain adequately fed despite the Middle Prince’s heavy taxes.

Once An-Teng’s capital, the City of Dead Flowers now occupies a shadowland, its tumbled streets haunted by hungry ghosts. West of Prosperous Garden, a valley that once hosted the River of Queens now cages a stagnant oxbow lake, its surface cloaked in perpetual fog. Human bones choke the brackish dregs of its canals, gnawed by night creatures that lurk in the mud. Dark flowers hang from broken walls and ruined eaves, thirsty for spilt blood.

At the city’s center, the overgrown Palace of the Lotus harbors all manner of ancient ghosts. Nameless local cults gather here to worship the shades of An-Teng’s First Age monarchs or to seek tutelage from more dreadful spirits. More recently, reports indicate that a deathknight has taken up residence in the palace. This gossip has spread all the way to the City of the Steel Lotus, where visiting Dynasts discuss the prospect of a Wyld Hunt.

The capital, Prosperous Garden, grows rich on shipping foodstuffs downriver to hungry Shore Lands cities. Much of the city’s civil architecture is ancient, but the growing middle class prefers a modern style that’s common in newer districts. The prince’s disregard for politics and his wife’s efforts to strengthen local mercantile interests has nurtured newfound political power amid the city’s bourgeoisie.

Poverty drives impoverished peasants from the surrounding area to take refuge at the city’s fringes. They eke out a living as best they can, scavenging for First Age relics or working the land’s tainted soil. Some secretly propitiate the Pale Maiden (p. XX), begging her to spare their harvests; others welcome traveling players, hoping entertainment will soothe the dead. And a few have slain travelers as offerings to the city’s specters.

Merchants do brisk business on the city’s canals in barges and sampans that customers access via floating bridges or rowboats. Many homes boast small vegetable gardens; citizens take pride in serving food they grew to their guests.

Shuri has proven a skilled administrator, though her prioritization of merit over connections makes her politically suspect. In her off time, she indulges in vice, carouses with local merchants to gather information, and sponsors investigations into the City of Dead Flowers’s shadowland. She maintains regular contact with Ragara garrison subcommanders in the Middle and High Lands.

Emerald Cliff runs a smuggling empire out of Dragon’s Jaws. Her associates carry silver and fine foreign silks up the River of Queens into the Middle Lands. Along the way, her goods pass through Salt-Founded Glory, where the Fallen Magnolia family takes its cut. Hoping that An-Teng will someday be free of the Realm, Emerald Cliff funnels a sizable chunk of her profits to Tengese rebels hiding in the mountains.

In the Forest of Compassion, south of Prosperous Garden, the River of Queens winds through dense groves of bamboo, teak, and banyan. Without a guide, travelers get lost if they stray from the river or from elephant trails. Away from these safer paths, Solar tombs and manses hidden deep within the forest draw their share of adventurers.

Adorned with Wisdom as a Sapphire is a place of learning where scions of government officials, wealthy families, and the Three Princes’ most loyal servants receive tutelage. Scholastic guilds employ teachers to lecture and guide students in law, philosophy, art, and the like. While some buildings are dedicated specifically to study, classes may occur wherever students and teachers gather in the city: parks, nobles’ homes, or teahouses.

Sapphire’s libraries secretly preserve heretical books, and host underground philosophical debates where no topic is prohibited. Many use this forum to bring attention to Realm crimes and argue for a free, equal AnTeng. However, protests that grow too openly critical of Realm policy have brought harsh crackdowns from

the Middle Prince’s troops, the Realm garrison, and Immaculate monks.

Prominent Figures

A scholar, Prince Kiotaran of Upward View is more interested in astrology and harmony than politics or rebellion. Though he wishes for a free An-Teng, he’s unwilling to countenance the suffering that rebellion would inflict upon the people. He shows polite deference to visiting Dynasts, speaking subtly of alliance instead of occupation; beyond that, he tends to what administrative needs he must before retreating to his observatory at nightfall.

A formidable and pragmatic politician, Kiotaran’s wife Golden Slipper directs much of her husband’s administration. In recent years, she’s overseen the expansion of Prosperous Garden and the Middle Lands’ merchant class, deftly securing lucrative trade deals and allies, while funding talented nonnoble youths’ tutelage with the scholastic guilds.

The renowned savant Rising Owl of the Diamond Stream family, teaches history and etiquette to wealthy nobles and merchants. Privately, she despises the prince and the Realm; hoping to see revolution in her lifetime, she directs potential dissidents to underground salons and directs them with contacts in rebel groups. The head Immaculate abbot Sandstorm Scours the Desert keeps a ledger of those she suspects of heresy and sedition. At her direction, monks observe public speeches and teachers’ lessons for signs of dissent. While she’s passed her concerns about the most egregious actors to Kiotaran and Golden Slipper, allowing the royals the opportunity to deal with the problematic elements first, she considers their responses lackluster.

### The High Lands

Isolated and strong in their mountain homes, the High Lands’ people are less polite and soft-spoken than their lowland cousins. The mountains hide strange and wonderful creatures: colorful birds that can imitate speech, monkeys with prehensile tails, or huge banga flies whose venom aids in surgery and whose wings are used in astrology. Many High Lands villagers make their living hunting and trapping, and send their children to trade their wares down the River of Queens. Small villages, rather than cities, predominate the High Lands’s rugged, picturesque landscapes. Few Dynastic tourists visit, satisfied to partake of Shore Lands luxuries. Even the Immaculate Order’s reach is limited; the

sparse population offers few opportunities for wandering monks, and makes it hard to justify the expense of more than a few scattered temples.

Villagers dress in layers to account for cooler mountain temperatures. In addition to warm silk garments, many wear woolen jackets whose sleeves are decorated with thin multihued stripes and intricate colorwork. Dishes unique to the High Lands include river moss soaked in fish paste with lotus seeds and fresh herbs, then grilled in banana leaves; strips of buffalo or pork marinated in lemongrass and tirphal and dried for a year; and colorful sticky rice made with turmeric, jackfruit, and ginger leaves. Popular drinks include rose-apple cider and a hot beverage made with glutinous rice and sweetened with cinnamon, sugar, and hibiscus.

The ancient Tengese built Jade Plum Citadel, capital of the High Lands, to defend against invasion from south or east. Today it’s a trade hub controlling entry to An-Teng via the Firepeaks’ passes. Though it’s less populous and less extravagant than the other capitals, its palaces remain opulent and its markets throng with foreign riches — jewels from Gem, incense from the Dying Sea, and more.

The Realm garrison maintains a small force in Jade Plum Citadel to protect tribute headed for the Blessed Isle. Although patrols seek out rebels, they’re spread too thin to engage all insurgent threats. Halfway up the Firepeaks’ slopes sits Thousand Dragons Lake. Temples to the Immaculate Dragons, the Golden Lord, and the Pale Mistress spread out along its shores. Local legends speak of a sunken manse on the lake’s floor, guarded by freshwater sharks. Higher still, above the snowline, stands the Pinnacle of Mercy. Few dare the steep mountain trail, haunted by wild beasts and fierce elementals, to brave its shining ivory gates and petition the Golden Lord directly. No petitioner entirely recalls their visit — and a few perish in the Pinnacle’s halls.

Prominent Figures

Josei of Notable Genius takes his duties as High Prince seriously. He spends most of his time strengthening ties with independent-minded lesser nobles, addressing disputes, overseeing tax accounting, and sending less-favored subordinates to hunt rebels and bandits. With few Dynastic guests and little support from the garrison, he finds the Realm’s tribute demands vexatious. With the Empress gone, he schemes toward independence, tacitly supporting monarchist rebels while

directing garrison expeditions against revolutionaries who’d see him overthrown alongside the satrap. The priest Ivory Gate serves the Golden Lord at the Pinnacle of Mercy. It’s her job to liaise with the Immaculates, which she’s done with grace and efficiency for many years. Temperamental Tengese whose families worry that they might cause trouble with the Dragon-Blooded come to serve under her. The gentlest of these become her acolytes, learning virtuous conduct in the court of the Golden Lord. She finds opportunities to send the rest into the mountains to conduct long-term projects on her behalf. There, they can begin anew, often in a rebel enclave.

The bandit prince Silver Mane’s raiders harry caravans traveling the Smoketail Pass through the Firepeaks. Silver Mane was born to banditry; her parents were smugglers and raiders. In the last few years, she’s united four raiding bands under her banner, allowing them to strike bigger, better-defended targets. Already famous among An-Teng’s outlaws, she’s attracted less welcome attention with a recent series of high-profile raids; Ledaal Shuri and several wealthy Tengese merchants are stepping up their troop presence in the area. Tensions with the Golden Lord’s Kingdom escalate as the rebels chafe at the increased scrutiny. Duke Anedys leads a court of earthy Fair Folk — reminiscent of the Blessed Isle’s Mountain Folk — beneath Jade Plum Citadel. As full Tengese citizens, his people enjoy mingling with their neighbors but avoid contact with Dynasts. They rarely leave their underground homes and mines, but secretly provide the Golden Lord’s Kingdom with weapons and training, desiring independence as much as any human Tengese.

### Neighbors

Steam rises amid the rugged, overgrown Sagebrush Hills north of the Shore Lands. Here, the ifrit Tenjin oversees the Simmerwander Hot Springs. Many of the region’s spirits come here to relax, dine, or debate while enjoying Tenjin’s storied hospitality. The waters are too hot for most mortals to survive, but Exalts, sorcerers, and beastfolk whose abilities or physiology allow them to withstand the scalding pools are welcomed as honored guests.

The so-called Theocracy of the Jade-Souled occupies the mountain valleys northeast of the High Lands. Half a century ago, the Heavenly Pillar Oath — a Sworn Kinship of Tengese outcastes — established themselves here to ward off bandits and raiders dispatched by the

Lunar elder Golden-Leaf Liseli. Many villagers worship the Heavenly Pillars, who politely deny their divinity but take no direct action against their cult. Moreover, Tengese dissenters, rebels, and heretics have trickled in over the years, seeking safe haven. Aware of the potential for rebellion brewing on the satrapy’s doorstep, the Immaculate Order would like to see them firmly quashed. But while the Theocracy makes itself useful fending off Silver Pact aggressors, the abbots bide their time.

The region immediately south of An-Teng, previously under close Realm control, lies in chaos after decades of Lunar assault, piracy, famine, rebellion, and other troubles. Only one satrapy, the wealthy maritime republic of Low Yethrai, remains strongly defended; it seethes with refugees and expatriate nobility. Neighboring satrapies include storied Duneport, riven by civil war between rival princelings; once-forested Eleven Songs, now a smoldering wasteland haunted by bandits and wild beasts; and the lake country of Vetiver, its cities now barracking a Lunar conqueror’s troops.

## The Lintha

When lookouts on the Western Ocean spot black and silver Lintha banners on the horizon, even the most battle-scarred captains’ guts roil. They urge their slaves to row faster and beseech gods of the wind to fill their sails, all the while tallying what’s in their holds and estimating how quickly they can have their goods hauled on deck should the pirates overtake them. Sailors from An-Teng to the Cinder Isles fear the Lintha, whose farthest-ranging enclaves trouble Western shipping as distant as the Coral Archipelago.

Claiming descent from the demon prince Kimbery, the Lintha people ruled a vast Western realm before the Divine Revolution. But with the enemies of the gods slain and their Great Mother imprisoned in Hell, the Lintha rapidly fell from power. A handful escaped, re-establishing their population and culture through intermarriage with other peoples.

The survivors’ descendants call the city of Bluehaven their home. It has no fixed location, drifting at the center of a gyre within a cerulean sargasso sea. The wind dies and treacherous currents pull the unwary into deadly reefs or trap them until heat and thirst drive their crews mad. There the Lintha survive as pirates and attempt to restore their self-proclaimed “true blood” through careful matchmaking, sacred cannibalism, and counterproductive eugenics.

### THE UTZ SEMIVIR

The poet and historian Kan Pol the Younger studied the curse, writing about it and the Lintha’s origins extensively in a book called the Utz Semivir. Most Lintha have memorized long passages from its pages, especially those declaring the Lintha divine, speaking of their inevitable rule, praising cannibalism, or condemning coupling with non-Lintha. The book is full of strange leaps and logical fallacies, which matters little to a Lintha using it to support her argument.

In the following centuries, the Cult cemented its power and influence, largely suppressing or driving out rival ideologies in favor of Kimbery worship and Kan Pol’s sterile philosophy. Now more than ever, Lintha culture is steeped in bigotry, cruelty, and nihilism.

### Family

### History

The Lintha scattered with their empire’s fall. Untold years later, a shipful of descendants set out to revive their nation and reclaim the West. But after many adventures they were captured by a Western prince, and sentenced to death by being stripped of provisions and set adrift without sails or oars, to perish of exposure and thirst. As more and more Lintha died and siaka began circling, the starving Lintha partook of the only sustenance available: the bodies of their dead. When the situation was at its most hopeless, an island rose from the waves. Naming herself Lintha Ng Oroo, their island-sister, she carried the survivors to a ruined citadel rising from the sea: the Lintha capital T’floor Na, the Place of the Stonehearted, which the Lintha knew as the Blue City. The citadel’s ghostly warder wept to learn of the survivors’ blood drinking and consumption of kinflesh. Declaring the Lintha cursed, he exiled them from the city, and ordered Ng Oroo to return to the sea. They settled upon their island-sister in the sargasso sea’s isolation, sustained by her clean waters and abundant wildlife, building ships from her never-depleting trees. They put to sea once more, raiding villages and reselling plunder. Within a generation, they controlled many Western sea-lanes, and menaced many more. Three centuries ago, the Dragon-blooded prodigy Lintha Ng Hut Dukantha — brilliant, studious, ambitious, and cruel — grew obsessed with ancient lore regarding Kimbery, tormented by dreams of her calling. He vanished into Ng Oroo’s depths during Calibration on his sixteenth birthday. A year later, his voice thundered across Bluehaven announcing his return from Hell and summoning the faithful. He proclaimed himself Chosen of the Great Mother, speaking with her voice and will. He initiated priests and taught them sorcery. He returned to Hell at Calibration’s end, leaving

The Lintha see themselves as all one family. Their obsession with “blood purity” complicates this. Only truebloods — those born to two Lintha parents — inherently belong. Those with only one Lintha parent are halfbloods, and are no more Lintha than any foreigner. Lintha address one another with titles derived from terms for familial relationships. They largely use such terms only as titles, disregarding their standard usage. • A cousin is a foreigner or halfblood initiated into the Lintha family. Some eagerly petition for membership, starstruck by stories of Lintha conquest and easy plunder; others awaken with a sore head chained in a rowing galley. Lintha regard adopted foreigners with disdain, using them for scut work and for jobs that require expendable bodies. • A sister or brother is a full member of the family. Native Lintha are born to this title. The most exceptional cousins occasionally earn it through years of faithful and successful service.

• An aunt or uncle oversees activities outside of Lintha territory, such as spy networks or slave-worked farm holdings. Most are foreign-born, allowing them to better conceal their affiliation.

• A mother or father has begotten at least two legitimate Lintha children. Their prerogatives and responsibilities include captaining ships, overseeing business interests both overseas and at home, organizing community services, and meting out punishments the sept’s members incur. • A grandmother or grandfather serves as the matriarch or patriarch of an extended family within a sept. The larger septs have several grandparents in Bluehaven. The eldest sept member at an exclave typically claims the title as well.

• An elder grandmother or elder grandfather commands an entire sept.

### LINTHA NAMES

Lintha Ancestry

Lintha names often take inspiration from Vietnamese, Indonesian, and Gaelic. They use the following pattern: “Lintha” + sept name + title + given name, such as “Lintha Haquen Mother Labhra-Mor.” Interlocutors vary what elements of a name they use with the conversation’s level of formality.

• The Lei Kiangi — the eldest of all elder grandparents — stands at the peak of Lintha society. She meets twice each month with a council of the other elder grandparents — called the Septian Covenant — for their proposals and counsel. In theory, she holds absolute power, empowered to seize anything from any sept and issue any reward or punishment. In practice, she avoids overreach lest she spark a revolt or meet an assassin’s blade. She serves for life; upon her death, the Septian Covenant selects her successor.

• The Great Mother is the demon prince Kimbery, who reigns in Hell. The Lintha worship her as a goddess.

Occasionally, a greatsept’s elder grandparent allows a young foreign or halfblood child to be ritually adopted as a sister or brother. Such foundlings are rarely treated better than cousins, and require the Lei Kiangi’s permission to rise higher among the Lintha.

Sex, Marriage, and Castration

Lintha practice matrilineal polygamy; adults have multiple spouses, their unions arranged for political favor and for maximizing the chances of favored physical traits. They also aren’t especially faithful when out at sea.

Half-bloods born of liaisons with non-Lintha — adoptees are forever non-Lintha for this purpose — are considered shameful, diluting already-thin Lintha blood. Past moralizers called for widespread castration, sterilization, and other unsavory mutilations for all Lintha, to curb the flesh’s weakness to temptation; such procedures remain common punishments for producing half-blooded offspring, preventing future mistakes. Consequently, Lintha typically claim half-blooded children as the result of pure unions at sea. The truth is usually obvious, but only religious zealots benefit from pointing it out.

Fanatics sometimes self-castrate after producing two or three pure-blooded children. Such sacrifices, while

Stories depict the Lintha of old as six to seven feet tall, their skin a glistening green, their frost-white hair gleaming like oil on water. But few modern Lintha resemble this ideal. Today, they tend to be long and lean. After generations of intermarriage with aquatic beastfolk, many have protruding joints, bulging eyes, or rows of gills on their cheeks and necks. Others appear more human — or occasionally less, the result of liaisons with stranger entities.

Despite their own myths about their origins, the Lintha people have always been human. Their ancestors obtained magical powers and distinct features through demonic progenitors; this is fundamentally no different from how modern “thin-blooded” Lintha bear the marks of other lineages. The Cult of Dukantha’s dreams of pureblooded strength are nonsensical and fundamentally unattainable.

### Septs

The Lintha are divided into a handful of expansive kinship groups called septs, driven by political rivalry and claims to the purest expression of Lintha blood. They range between a few hundred and a few thousand members, divided into several extended families. Mutations common within a sept are touted by kin as signs of the Great Mother’s favor, and by rival septs as signs of miscegenation. A Lintha who Exalts as DragonBlooded is celebrated for proximity to the demon prince Kimbery’s bloodline, disregarding that Exaltation descends through their human ancestry. Septs centered around distant enclaves exist, albeit unrecognized by the Septian Covenant. Their origins include banished Bluehaven septs, ideological renegades, or ambitious cousins. Some claim descent from the Lintha of the First Age, though little evidence supports them. Their relationships with Bluehaven vary: most are welcome to trade with other Lintha. Bluehavenbased captains let their ships pass unchallenged, and may even take shelter in these distant ports if the winds blow them that way.

The largest, richest septs — those that hold outsized influence in Bluehaven — are called greatsepts. Today’s greatsepts are Gajui, Haquen, and Ng Hut, but fortunes can change quickly.

EX3

Preeminent among even the greatsepts, the Gajui possess enormous wealth, sizable fleets, and a scattering of enclaves across the Southwest and the West. In Bluehaven itself, they share a water-gathering and water-selling duopoly with the Haquen sept; their long struggle for the upper hand in that duopoly and in overall wealth and prestige has bred an intense rivalry between them. They’re cosmopolitan in their tastes and unusually tolerant of foreigners; they sponsor pirates and smugglers, bargain with merchants and factors, and maintain hidden pleasure palaces on distant shores. Sharklike features, such as rough skin, gills, or solid black eyes, aren’t uncommon among them. The Haquen hold a clear second place when it comes to wealth and influence, which they flaunt constantly. They maintain relationships with foreign courts, from whom they adopt new foods and fashions — often with their own gaudy spin. This gives them a reputation as trendsetters in Lintha society; they’ve spawned the current fad of vivid veils and flowing scarves common to many captains. They pride themselves on individual excellence and mastery of ancient martial arts, their members dominate the Sword Princes (p. XX). They often evince youthful — even childlike — features and nictitating membranes.

Once a minor sept, the Ng Hut leapt to their current position when Lintha Ng Hut Dukantha (p. XX) returned Exalted from Hell. Dukantha’s cult is popular and powerful, and the Ng Hut dominate its upper ranks; the other septs take care not to offend the Ng Hut, lest the cult wield its influence against them or deny membership to their kin. The Ng Hut encourage others to take great risks on their behalf for uncertain rewards, acting as stewards, financial backers, and loan sharks within Bluehaven and abroad. It’s said that their gifts are as dangerous as their smiles.

The traditionalist, perfectionist Angsana never hesitate to point out others’ failings or lapses in decorum. The sept’s obsession with custom leads many to become record keepers and historians; as such, their perspective dominates Bluehaven’s official histories. Other septs may take offense at unfavorable portrayals of their deeds, but acknowledge the Angsanas’ renowned fairness in both this and other matters. Their swordmasters often oversee duels and contests; their reavers and merchants alike uphold bargains even with foreigners. The Dara-Seid — derided by their peers as half-bloods, mongrels, and bastards — largely lack the inhuman features associated with ancient Lintha and modern septs

This comes from piracy and from cultivating trading interests around the Realm’s southwestern satrapies — in some cases through betraying foreign business partners, to shortterm benefit that will hurt the Lintha in the long-term.

### NONCONFORMIST LINTHA

Lintha who object to their culture’s unpleasant aspects — racism, sexism, brutality, slavery, the quest for “purity” — wrestle with those issues in several ways. Some keep their heads down and try to change the Lintha from within, acting like traditionalists and climbing the social ladder, hoping to gain sufficient authority to quietly improve things. They may be openly nonconformist, keeping their actions just enough within the rules to avoid major consequences, hoping to attract other like-minded Lintha. Still others leave Bluehaven entirely, founding heterodox enclaves on distant shores or getting banished (whether intentionally or not). Others meet unfortunate ends at fellow Lintha hands.

### Culture

Lintha appropriate their fashion from the cultures they raid, but each wearer puts her own personal spin on their outfit, adding silken scarves, elaborate jewelry, or bird-of-paradise feathers to complete the look — these accessories themselves spoils from successful raids. Long-haired Lintha often put their hair up in twisted knots or rope braids.

alike. Indeed, they’re often indistinguishable from foreigners; many claim their blood too thin to call them Lintha at all. For their part, they deride the Utz Semivir, claiming that Lintha truth is found in bloodshed, not dead philosophers’ arguments for inbreeding. They’re among the most ferocious, warlike, and cruel septs, with no few dogged by rumors of cannibalism. They eagerly welcome foreign cousins, but few have a taste for their vicious revels.

Despite the self-proclaimed purity of lineage evinced by their lean, green-skinned frames, the dwindling Dewantara have sunk near the bottom of the Lintha pecking order. They rarely have children, yet proudly refuse to initiate foreigners or intermarry with Lintha they deem thin-blooded. They’ve no truly exceptional captains, swordmasters, or merchants, their most talented youths dying of mischance before achieving their potential. Many believe them cursed; few expect the sept to survive much longer.

Once a greatsept, the Ixora have fallen far. Three decades ago, their elders sought to betray the Haquen and seize their most valuable mercantile interests. The Haquen slaughtered Lintha Ixora Elder Grandfather Borog-na and many other Ixora; the Lei Kiangi stripped the sept’s assets, burned their ships, and forbade them from owning ships. Most survive by begging positions on other septs’ fleets, taking menial roles normally assigned to cousins, or commanding vessels in far-flung enclaves isolated from Bluehaven’s politics. The ambitious, hot-tempered Sennong rarely linger in Bluehaven for long, remaining at sea most of the year. That, combined with an insolent and secretive attitude

Many Lintha sport piercings, ranging from delicate gold hoops to sizable earlobe and lip plugs. Tattoos are also common; these often chronicle milestones and victories at sea — a dragonfish signifies their first voyage, while a dagger celebrates sinking an enemy ship. Others are meant to ward off bad luck; a shark’s tooth tattoo to repel predators should the sailor fall overboard, or an albatross to guide them home to Bluehaven. Aboard ship, Lintha eat preserved foods that travel well: hardtack, salted cod, beef brined in barrels, and sour beer. They acquire fresh fruits, vegetables, and meat from communities they raid or trade with, occasionally supplemented with fresh-caught fish during longer voyages. If cooked, food is generally boiled; stew is common. Dishes in Bluehaven and land-based Lintha enclaves feature fresh meat and liberal seasonings looted from spice cargoes. At sea, crewmembers sing shanties to keep time as they perform shipboard activities such as raising sails or rowing. Songs typically tell of famous raids, or are hymns to Kimbery.

Polydactyl cats are considered good luck — sailors believe their actions can predict the weather, or even protect the ship from storms. More practically, their extra toes give them an extra advantage in catching vermin and in keeping their balance in rough seas. Lintha take things rather than make them. If they need it, a neighboring village or passing ship surely has it, whether that’s fabrics and finery, weapons, building supplies, or the builders and crafters themselves. Jobs aside from sailing, trading, and killing are for lesser peoples.

EX3

Though they have no qualms about dealing in slaves for profit, the Lintha consider keeping them nearby uncouth. Slaves may farm cash crops for Lintha on outlying islands, but cousins and members of fallen septs do scut work on ships and perform servants’ roles in Bluehaven.

Law and Order

Each sept polices its own members. Grandparents hand down judgments in family disputes; mothers and fathers enact punishments. Elder grandparents handle conflicts between septs; when they can’t reach a satisfactory settlement, the Lei Kiangi acts as final arbiter. Outsiders have no rights unless a Lintha takes them as guests, typically in exchange for payment or favors. Guests are considered their hosts’ property. Any transgressions they commit while in Bluehaven reflect on the sept that’s taken them in, and thus hosts often assign a cousin to accompany the visitor wherever she goes.

### The Cult of Dukantha

The Lintha depend on the Cult of Dukantha. Its sorcerers bind, build, breed, or tame the supernatural beasts pulling sailless Lintha ships. Dukantha himself offers blessings and enchanted gifts each Calibration. In turn, the cult treats all Lintha as members, barring those who’ve been excommunicated for opposing it. Priests act as councilors and spiritual advisers, fulfilling their responsibility to keep a family of cutthroat pirates unified in the Great Mother’s name. They intercede between Lintha and spirits, and prepare sacred, cannibalistic feasts that honor dead Lintha and keep their strength within the family. They enforce Dukantha’s will, and through him, the Great Mother’s. Only fathers and mothers may become priests. Their initiation requires a physical sacrifice to prove one’s dedication, often taking the form of repenting a past sin. A man who’s sired a half-blood child might castrate himself; a woman who fled combat may slice her leg’s tendons. Initiates cast blood and flesh from these mutilations into the Altar of the Great Mother, a brass cauldron of acid sacred to Kimbery, binding the initiate to her.

Desiring outcastes’ and sorcerers’ power, the cult inducts them as priests upon Exaltation or sorcerous initiation. Those who accept receive adulation and training; most embrace the cult’s lifestyle soon enough. Those who refuse earn the cult’s hostility. The Feast of Dukantha, celebrating the anniversary of his return from Hell, has become the highest of holy days. Septs compete to outdo one another’s gifts to Dukantha, measured in human sacrifices, jade, and sadistic artifice. He favors them with private conversations, dispensing blessings and judgments.

Other Gods and Heresies

The Great Mother isn’t the only deity the Lintha worship. Cultists beg and sacrifice to sea gods — whether Siakal of Bloody Slaughter, Zhuziao of the Black Deeps, Storm Mothers, or Still Fathers — to spare Lintha seafarers’ ships and lives. Only a fool disrespects the ocean’s puissant spirits, and the Lintha raise no fools. The Cult of Dukantha and the Lei Kiangi harshly punish those whom they discover are adherents to either of two notable heresies; such heretics must maintain their beliefs in secret. Semivirists claim that no pure-blooded Lintha could Exalt as Dragon-Blooded, and therefore Kimbery — who rejects impure blood — cannot have Chosen Dukantha. The apocalyptic Oroites believes that Kimbery can be freed from her prison by destroying the Lintha people.

### The Sword Princes

Originally founded by the Haquen, this martial society draws expert Lintha swordfighters from across the septs. Members challenge one another to duels, both to settle personal disputes and prove their skill. Through these challenges, a Sword Prince advances in ranks, called kur. Dozens of fifth-kur Sword Princes serve aboard ships while they hone their skills. Only one Sword Prince can attain the rank of first kur at a time, achieving the position through single combat. The current first kur, Lintha Haquen Father Tow-Ang, Saint of the Blade, has held the honor for a decade. Some

The cult’s high priest is always an Ng Hut grandparent chosen by Dukantha. They must ostensibly be of pure Lintha blood, so no outcaste ever holds the role. Other grandparents of various septs serve as senior priests; the high priest and Dukantha choose them jointly.

The Sword Princes’ signature weapon is the auzhian — a sword whose tip curves backward into a wide, serrated hook. Pointed blades jut from its hilt, pommel, and hand guard. The Princes hire foreign smiths to craft these weapons, paying them handsomely for their efforts. Many practice the Devil-Prince Sword, a martial art emphasizing agility, flamboyance, and humiliating or maiming enemies.

Ng Oroo once rose high above the waves, a proud living island where the Lintha prospered. Ancient wars, the Contagion, and the Wyld have pocked and scarred her. Every year she sinks lower; the Lintha dread the day she’ll vanish forever beneath the waves.

### The City of Bluehaven

Bluehaven builds atop itself, piling ships on one another. The oldest rest on Lintha Ng Oroo’s submerged shores, anchoring the floating city. Lintha lash new ships to neighboring ones, or strip them for materials to build atop what’s already there. Thousands of Lintha reside in this puzzle of ships for most of the year. The number of Lintha present at any given time rises and ebbs like the tide, depending on the time of year, activities in the Western Ocean, and how many ships in the fleet are out on raids or home in port. The population swells around Calibration as family members return home for the Feast of Dukantha, straining the city’s available quarters, fresh water, and other supplies. The gyre’s slow but inevitable turn pulls everything, causing each district to twist over time, grinding against one another like teeth of monstrous wooden gears.

Approaching the City

Reaching Bluehaven isn’t easy. Heavy-drafted ships dash themselves against islets and reefs or become trapped on submerged sandbars. Sargassum tangles oars, making rowing slow and excruciating. Navigating by the subtle tug of currents requires an experienced hand at the wheel. Artillerists train ballistas on approaching vessels while patrolling Lintha ships board and escort those vessels to the docks. Foreigners can — and occasionally do — visit Bluehaven, but only by bribing or otherwise persuading a captain to bring them. Such visitors find themselves restricted to the Floating Market unless a Lintha escorts them elsewhere. Leaving the city presents its own difficulties; captains won’t go out of their way to deliver passengers to specific destinations, and those believed to be spies never leave.

Ng Oroo

An island sags at the sargasso sea’s center, small enough to walk across in half a day. Its few runty trees grow

Fresh water that flows without source or end fills two channels that cross the island, meeting near its center. A long-ago Lei Kiangi assigned the Gajui and Haquen to collect the water and distribute it throughout Bluehaven, a right they guard jealously. At irregular intervals, pus from Ng Oroo’s poisoned wounds seeps into the canals; this pale, greasy effluent fills the air with a sickening stench and poisons anyone fool enough to drink it. Only during these times do the Gajui and Haquen charge other septs for water from stores they maintain. They set prices carefully: too steep, and other septs might decide it’s easier to simply take what they need, risking civil war. Even so, both have grown rich from other septs’ spoils. A small hillock rises at Ng Oroo’s center. Along its side gapes the Throat of Hell, a small cave leading down a sharp, slick incline into a foul oubliette of rank water. Gusts issue forth periodically; this, the Lintha say, is Ng Oroo’s breath, which gives voice to her pain-maddened groans. Stories persist of a secret path to Kimbery within, but only Dukantha has found anything but seawater, disappointment, and death.

The Floating Market

The Floating Market fits most outsiders’ vision of Bluehaven: ships lashed together in a mad spiderweb of rigging, draped in an anarchy of colored silks and foreign navies’ captured colors serving as rugs and doors. Children hawk trinkets from trophy vessels, while every sept does vigorous business reselling plunder to Lintha merchants who represent its original owners. Restaurants and public houses open and close at owners’ whims, preparing dishes from plundered food and drink alongside such traditional Lintha specialties as jellied eel and shark-fin soup. Everything is heavily seasoned, salted, smoked, pickled, or fermented; spices are common plunder and fresh food keeps poorly in oppressive heat and humidity.

Below decks is a humid, stinking warren. During the day, scant light leaks in; at night, it’s pitch black. Fire is prohibited; violators have their eyes burnt out. Thousands of cousins and siblings live here in cramped

of Riches. Here the wealthiest Lintha live in luxury, commanding pirate fleets and enjoying the finest plunder. In each junk resides an extended family and their favored servants. Small by shore-bound aristocrats’ standards, such apartments are spacious and private compared to the Floating Market’s warrens.

### LINTHA COLONIES

Although Bluehaven is the heart of Lintha culture, a few Lintha enclaves lie scattered across the Great Western Ocean, inaccessible save by secret routes. These communities operate independently of Bluehaven, supporting their residents and fleets with plunder. While most welcome other Lintha vessels, their Bluehaven brethren sneer at their backwater ways and refuse to acknowledge non-Bluehaven septs.

The District’s families busy themselves in games of status, wealth, and glory. Bluehaven’s elite meet over drinks, dances, and lurid performances to boast of their successes and ferret out one another’s weaknesses.

Asura hides amidst heavy fogs and sharp outcroppings, raiding convoys venturing to the Caul. It’s home to Lintha Haquen Fia-Shaw Flowers Unbending in the Storm, a Changing Moon Lunar with a siaka spirit shape who serves as Sha’a Oka’s envoy to the local Lintha.

Lintha residing outside the District only enter by invitation. Residents may name any punishment for trespassers short of maiming or death; denizens enjoy flaunting their creativity for torture as entertainment. A wise thief slits her own throat before being taken alive.

An ox-walrus behemoth pulls the iceberg-enclave Tethi across the Northwest. The Najek sept directs it into shipping lanes to raid or wreck merchant vessels. Especially hardy survivors of these raids may be adopted into the family; the rest feed the behemoth.

The Golden Tower

Looming above the District of Riches stands a tower encased in gilded wood and plaster, topped by a sculpted dolphin frozen mid-leap. Its ten-yard-wide base rests on an artificial atoll of broken ships.

In Wu-Jian, the Lintha Grandmother Fang and Grandfather Maw run an extensive crime racket, offering protection to merchants and business-owners, auctioning off pirated goods, and smuggling contraband out of the city.

Gullet of the Beast

At the Market’s outskirts rests an upside-down warship, twice as wide and three times as long as a typical galley. A dozen enormous holes pierce its hull of strange, imperishable First Age material, shreds and tatters of bulkhead furled around them like flower petals; they’re roughly patched with wood. A massive iron door looms amid one such patch. This is the Gullet of the Beast, the warehouse that feeds Bluehaven. It’s crammed with dried meat, flour, salt, honey, spices, wine, and rum. The Gullet isn’t Bluehaven’s only warehouse-ship; several mundane vessels are permanently moored about the city. The Lintha have raised these above the waterline and bulked their exteriors to keep water out. Sorcery keeps their holds cold enough to minimize spoilage.

The District of Riches

Away from the Floating Market’s frenzy, three dozen palatial junks are bound together, forming the District

This is Bluehaven’s treasure vault. Its lower floors hold chests of coin, ingots, arms, and other imperishable goods; the Lei Kiangi draws on this to fund extensive fleet repairs or other major undertakings. The upper floors showcase gems, sculpture, books, and other treasures for loan to Lintha magnates or sale to foreign collectors. The Tower also holds artifacts reserved as gifts for worthy Lintha.

The Lei Kiangi’s apartment occupies the tower’s peak. Her guards patrol the tower, securing both person and treasure. Bound spirits, sorcerous wards, and mechanical traps keep unauthorized visitors out, alert the guards to those who slip past, and ensnare thieves. Two massive green jade gorilla-lions prowl the halls, their keen noses alerting them to non-Lintha intruders.

Plaza of the Humbled Supplicant

A warship rides low in the water offshore, bound by bronze anchors, reachable only by sea. A broken steel automaton faces the prow, kneeling prostrate towards a 12-foot granite statue depicting Lintha Ng Hut Dukantha, Chosen of the Sea that Marched Against the Flame. This is the Plaza of the Humbled Supplicant, Bluehaven’s predominant temple.

Parents bring pure-blooded Lintha newborns here to be anointed with blood and seawater. Rivals settle disputes in ritual combat using hiltless blades. Doubtridden faithful come seeking answers and solace.

EX3

Priests execute condemned criminals’ sentences. The cult views both Kimbery and Dukantha as jealous deities; no other spirits receive worship here. Priests and supplicants inhabit the ship’s berths, sleeping in tiers of hammocks once used by long-dead sailors. The Altar of the Great Mother lies in the ship’s aftercastle. Priests lead small groups of cultists in worship, lost in ecstatic prayers fueled by the acrid fumes released by dissolving offerings. During holy days, fights breaks out to gain entrance and hundreds of souls cram inside.

### Prominent Individuals

Sharp-eyed, cautious, and traditional, Lintha Gajui Lei Kiangi Wari Fan has been a steady hand guiding the Lintha in tumultuous times. But her refusal to act on the Realm’s instability leads rivals — chief among them Lintha Haquen Elder Grandmother Sarangkai — to whisper that cowardice stays her hand, and that the Lintha need a younger, more dynamic Lei Kiangi to lead them.

Lintha Ng Hut Dukantha embodies his people’s brilliant cruelty and burning ambition. His studies of ancient Lintha history and occult practices inspire his followers in his absence; those who gain an audience with him might impress him with new findings. In his youth, he believed Lintha fleets should sweep across the world, capturing the Blessed Isle and beyond. After emerging from Oroo Cave, his views changed. The Lintha dominated the West; dying for conquest they couldn’t win was wasteful. With the Scarlet Empress’ disappearance, however, he entertains counterarguments. Dukantha only returns to Creation during Calibration for the Feast. But he’s promised that if Bluehaven should ever face destruction, he’ll come when called, crushing those who threaten his family.

eaten by malaria and yellow fever, burnt down, and torn apart in battle over the decades — only to be rebuilt. Founded on a small island hidden amidst the archipelago north of Bluehaven, Pixt Thawn shelters smugglers, pirates, terrorists, rebels, and washouts from across Creation. This includes a handful of semiretired Lintha too old or injured for piracy. For the right price and a hostage, they’ll ferry outsiders to Bluehaven; for higher fees and more precious collateral, they’ll pilot a foreign ship there.

Currents pull unfortunate ships into what the Lintha call the Coffin Vurjawna — a becalmed shadowland cul-de-sac where hundreds of rotting hulks jostle one another. The ghosts of countless dehydrated sailors haunt the place, allowing safe passage only to those who offer sacrifice and to the fearsome Lintha funereal parties who come hear to lay their dead to rest. The Lintha claim their honored dead dwell in the magnificent Underworld island-city of Swirkshafa, sailing lost ships to dominate the Underworld’s seas as their descendants dominate Creation’s, and trading with Kimbery’s other children in Hell. Dukantha’s high priest, Lintha Ng Hut Grandfather Yrjow Han, plunged his face into the Altar’s acid for his initiation, badly scarring and half-blinding himself. A master of divinatory sorcery, he obsesses over dreams and omens. Seeing signs of a great slaughter, he warns Bluehaven’s elite of incipient danger and the need to abandon past slights. Most listen politely, then continue as they were, leaving Yrjow Han gnashing his teeth and contemplating more extreme options.
