### OTHER SOUTHWESTERN LOCALES

The mainland closest to Bluehaven is the eerie wilderness called the Violet Coast. In the evening, the dark red sands glow an intense purple that can be seen for miles around. The hungry ghosts of spurned lovers walk these sands, and aquatic Fair Folk sing seductive songs offshore, luring travelers to their deaths beneath the waves.

North and east of the Violet Coast spreads the jungle called the Silent Crescent, home to the elusive Lunar Ten Stripes and his jaguar beastfolk. Though the villages in this area give thanks — and gifts of food — to Ten Stripes for protecting them, very few have ever laid eyes upon him.

Inland from the Violet Coast and south of the Silent Crescent lies the ancient, dreadful marshland called Calan’s Loss. Legends and fragments of First Age epics say that the Solar warrior-hero Calan’s tears of grief over her lover Tomun’s death reshaped the thriving forest into the swamp that survives today. Marsh dragons roam through its rivers and mud, and its trees — dubbed Calan’s Tears — weep brackish water from their bark. The spirits here are the same that showed Calan and Tomun no mercy millennia ago. Calan’s eternal curse wracks them with pain, and the fens reverberate with their anguished wails.

representatives occasionally attend the Feast of Dukantha, piloting a vessel of bone, hair, and nails. The Cult honors the dead with monthly offerings of blood and sunken treasure, in exchange for granting living Lintha free passage through the Coffin.

## Nandao Danh Nhân

Encompassing the sizable island Nandao and a scattering of nearby islets, Nandao Danh Nhân — shortened by most to “Nandao” — owes its history to the ambition of the Seven Tigers, those Dragon-Blooded warlords who united several peoples in an ill-fated attempt to invade the nascent Realm. When the Empress slew the Tigers and shattered their armies, the Baihu people fled into the Southwest. They eventually settled at the Meiyu Sea’s mouth in the archipelago that now bears their name, along with the adjoining peninsula called the Talon and the tip of a larger peninsula, the Spine; meanwhile, their Zhao compatriots departed inland on a path of conquest.

Baihu shipbuilding is so esteemed that foreign princes will pay a small fortune to own a Baihu galley, and more for Baihu sailors to crew it.

Finances aside, Nandao and its fellow Baihu satrapies enjoy outsized social influence. Educated Baihu travel throughout the Southwest, bringing with them such distinctively Baihu literature and philosophy as epic poems about sailors and oceanic spirits, innuendo-laden tragedies, and treatises on mathematics, natural philosophy, ontology, and theogony. Staples in Nandao include nutty red rice, sweet potato, chili peppers, fish, and poultry, and spices such as cardamom, ginger, garlic, turmeric, and candlenut. Traditional specialties include a stew featuring several varieties of chili peppers and yak cheese; a cone-shaped rice tower surrounded by spicy beef, fried prawn, sweet potato fritters, and steamed vegetables, served as a festival meal; and roasted chicken served with peanut and tomato chili.

The Baihu fought bloody wars to dominate the archipelago. Victories over the raksha prince Seven Doors Unopened and against Lintha marauders are among the few they share as a whole. Their cities grew apart; no leaders proved capable of unifying their independent-minded folk. To this day, Baihu city-states nurse grudges against old rivals and seek to outmaneuver allies while uttering meaningless platitudes about fidelity. The Realm exploited these divisions, conquering the Baihu in three successive wars, annexing a chunk of territory as a satrapy each time.

Nandao’s military has long been rooted in a robust citizen army, supplemented by heterodox mercenary forces. All youths of age are drilled in crewing a war galley and the use of crossbow, sling, and sword. V’neef Lin has offered retired legionnaires to train the Nandao people with Realm martial expertise. Nandao’s prominent families are torn on this, reluctant to allow Realm interference in their traditions, even as they respect the offer’s value. Some have accepted these trainers already, others demand assurances from the house, and some refuse outright out of tradition and self-reliance.

As with nearby Zhaojūn (The Realm, p. 169), the Empress chose not to unite the three fractious Baihu satrapies, leaving each to a different Great House’s oversight. This arbitrary division did little to quell rivalries between city-states, and satraps have historically struggled to curb Baihu infighting.

As a coming-of-age ritual, Baihu youths take a small boat on a solo voyage or venture into the wilderness alone. Their time at sea or in the wilds tests their self-reliance, proving to them and their families that they can endure hardship.

Nandao has traditionally maintained close ties with House Tepet, whose intermarriage with the city Nai Lei’s royal line formed cadet house Yueh. However, Tepet’s diminishment has soured their relationship; they’re no longer the reliable allies Nandao needs. Today, House Yueh warily accepts House V’neef ’s attentions and aid, even as they’re aware of Peleps’ interests in the neighboring Baihu satrapy of Huang Hei.

### Society and Culture

Taken as a whole, the satrapy produces valuable goods sought elsewhere: rustic but well-favored wines, elegant black porcelain, olive oil, furniture, and silks.

### Politics

House V’neef exerts great influence over Nandao’s city-states. The satrap accomplishes much through simple favoritism. City-states that remain obedient and offer favorable trade deals with the house receive preferential treatment in tribute demands and the archipelago’s internal squabbles; recalcitrant city-states encounter political roadblocks and find the Merchant Fleet’s anti-piracy squadrons mysteriously withdrawn. The house’s efforts to expand its naval presence have accelerated since the Empress’s disappearance, in hopes of maintaining its influence here against Peleps opposition.

EX3

Nandao’s vessels battle pirates and occasionally sabotage merchants from rival Baihu satrapies Huang Hei and Hsiang Tam. They trade with various Southwestern peoples, from An-Teng to the Cinder Isles, and sometimes beyond. Their most consistent clients are the Zhao, who acknowledge the Baihu as one of their Three Righteous Peoples, and the native Meiyu folk. Nandao’s people traditionally disdain both — the otherwise proud and martial Zhao as poor sailors, and the Meiyu as fractious and clannish.

As one approaches the famed Sunset Harbor in the River Nai estuary, the source of the city’s sobriquet becomes clear — a titanic breakwater of violet porphyry capable of sheltering hundreds of ships against the occasional fierce Western typhoon. The stone is unique to Nai Lei: dense and quartz-flecked, hewn from the southwestern face of the Kyhuong Mountains. Though challenging to carve, its durability shames even marble. Architects frequently compose great structures in Nai Lei from it.

### Noteworthy City-States

The city’s twin fortress-manses, called the Watchful Eyes for their shape and position when viewed from the sea, were constructed from violet porphyry by some unknown architect long before the Baihu arrived. They now serve as storage and housing for active military. Residents often paint less ostentatious dwellings’ clay bricks to match the famous material.

A dozen city-states speckle Nandao’s coastline and heartland. These range from tiny provincial settlements to a few wealthy metropoli.

Nai Lei

The Amethyst City of Nai Lei came to prominence centuries ago as a prosperous commercial center and a regional capital for the Five Winds League — a Baihu confederation against early Zhao aggression. Today, the cosmopolitan city-state shines as brightly as its namesake stone: a city of riches, ancient culture, musicians, playwrights, merchants, and travelers.

Outside the city, tenants and serfs work fields of sweet potato and rice. Round-hulled basket boats comb rivers and sea for fish, shrimp, and squid, their sailors’ bodies tattooed with abstract patterns suggestive of sea life. In the foothills of the Kyhuong Mountains, hunters pursue wild pigs, muntjacs, and hog badgers.

EX3

The Amethyst City’s native aristocracy has withered in the last few centuries, ceding power to the Lamenting Stone Assembly, a powerful cabal of merchant oligarchs who chart Nai Lei’s financial course. House Yueh (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 20), a locally powerful cadet house descended from House Tepet, dominates the assembly, but rivals increasingly snap at its heels for a chance to partake in Nai Lei’s splendors.

### GODS OF KAIDAPURA

Kaidapura’s pantheon has dwindled since the Realm conquest. Some gods, fearing Immaculate retribution, abandoned the old ways, making no further demands on — and offering no more favors to — priests and worshipers. Others left Nandao to seek veneration in lands beyond the Realm’s grasp.

House V’neef has proven an indispensable partner to the city in trade and credit. But by establishing a Merchant Fleet depot in Sunset Harbor, it’s put the city at odds with House Peleps — and with House KúiDien, the Peleps cadet house ruling the rival satrapy of Huang Hei.

Yonga, god of nighttime storms, leads Nandao’s sky and mountain gods. He inherited the position from his twin brother Kaida, god of daytime storms, whom Immaculate monks imprisoned for encouraging uprisings against the Order. Yonga now holds melancholy vigil over the Palace of Twin Thunders, scheming for Kaida’s release. He consoles himself with his Immaculate-approved annual festival, a carnal undertaking of godly proportions.

Royal Trandao

Rising from the river Nai’s shore up the Kyhuong mountains’ slopes, terminating in a network of divine palaces perched atop great Mount Kaidapura like a crown, the holy city of Royal Trandao is a breathtaking sight. For all its magnificence, though, no Baihu city has suffered more under Realm dominion. Excessive taxes have impoverished its people; the Realm seized its wealthiest dwellings under flimsy pretexts and gifted them to its own officials. Mount Kaidapura houses the gods’ palaces, and Royal Trandao their favored priests. The years have been unkind to all.

Today, Royal Trandao is a half-empty city. In summer, Nai Lei’s merchant princes and Realm grandees move to their summer residences here to escape the heat. There’s little work for locals beyond serving Realm tourists and supporting the Immaculate presence. The government discourages practice of local customs to accommodate their foreign overlords’ comfort. No longer do bells ring when the goddess Tich-An enters the market, for they drew the poor seeking alms and blessings from her attendant priests and thus disrupted Dynasts’ outings.

The religious songs of Royal Trandao’s heritage fade from common memory; books containing such lyrics vanish into Immaculate storage, even as Immaculate monks sing mangled versions better suiting the Philosophy. Monks discourage ancestral dances as inappropriate revelry. As older practitioners die out, some citizens fight to preserve their traditions, teaching songs, dances, and stories to younger adherents in private.

Under the Realm, Trandao has deteriorated to a skeleton of its former glory. The Palace Immortal’s marble

Ze Yan, goddess of outcasts and exiles, once oversaw home and hearth. During the invasion, Realm monks extinguished her temple’s sacred fire; now only its ashes remain. She still waits by the great hearth — her magic keeping its lingering heat from seeping away — to offer warmth and comfort to those with no place to call their own. She wears tattered finery and offers silver coins to those in greatest need. Lately, she’s begun looking for ways to rekindle not only the sacred flame, but also worship of the pantheon, even though doing so may draw Immaculate attention. Ze Yan’s brother Ran Ze lives alone in a cottage he built in a crater on a rocky islet offshore. Once a god of righteous warfare, he challenged a Dragon-Blooded commander to an honor duel, only to be thrown bodily from Royal Trandao’s heights. Though the injury healed long ago, he still walks with a limp symbolizing his defeat; he believes himself unworthy to see his home, and lives a quiet, contemplative existence.

towers stand scarred and worn. Streets once adorned with semiprecious stones and elegant brass gilding lie cracked and barren, their bounties stolen by opportunists and scavengers. Temples that once held Baihu priesthoods have been scoured of blasphemous imagery and repurposed as Immaculate monasteries, their watchful monks striving to stamp out heretical rites. Only their ancient, splendid water-clocks still function, sustained by the waterfall from the mountain’s crest. Today, the pantheon’s priests anoint their successors in secret, while the faithful pass down religious lore to their children in the dead of night.

EX3

### Prominent Figures

Nandao’s satrap, the patrician-born V’neef Rose Lin, is a masterful politician and socialite. Easily reading the room and always ready with a smile and soothing word, she skillfully defuses tensions and devises compromises. Her uncanny ability to turn others’ conflicts into personal successes has ironically earned her enemies; she’s a thorn in the side of House Kúi-Dien and its Peleps allies. She keeps in touch with many retired Nandao dignitaries, coaxing them out of retirement or seeking their aid in influencing their successors. Admiral Lam Dai is a long-respected figure in Baihu politics. Victories in his youth against the pirate fleets that once plagued the archipelago in his youth, and his later clashes with Huang Hei’s navy, have become the subject of folktales. In retirement, he supports his homeland by mentoring promising young officers and captains, occasionally using his substantial political influence to break deadlocks in the Lamenting Stone Assembly. Recently, V’neef Lin persuaded him to reenter the admiralty in preparation for possible attack by Peleps and House Kúi-Dien, although he fears being pulled into bitter Dynastic politics might undermine his service to Nai Lei or sully his legacy of competence and loyalty.

Young and plain-featured, Empty Lotus has the unobtrusive, submissive posture of a house servant. These traits support her secret role as a priestess of Ze Yan. She’s cultivated a network of fellow believers masquerading as servants, who enjoy the small revenge of stealing trinkets their masters won’t miss and redistributing them to the poor. A shrewd judge of character, she watches for those whom her goddess might aid or who might aid her goddess. As her network grows, she ponders what such a well-positioned group of conspirators might achieve, and the responsibility of leading them.

### Neighbors

Huang Hei — renowned for its sailors’ skill and its marines’ ferocity — has clashed with Nai Lei for centuries, even after both submitted to the Realm. Today, House Kúi-Dien, a Peleps cadet branch, dominates the upper echelons of Huang Hei’s military hierarchy and formidable navy. Though Huang Hei is a Ledaal satrapy, the satrap and diminished garrison lack the strength or inclination to oppose Peleps’s ambitions. Peleps seeks to use its catspaw to harry House V’neef’s assets and harm its interests in the region, for which Huang Hei’s privateers are ideally suited.

Cynis oversees Hsiang Tam, the Baihu satrapy occupying the peninsula called the Talon. Its seafaring tradition leans toward commerce; its militia and hunters guard against strange beasts and occasional fae marauders from farther inland. Trade relations with the wealthy Zhao city-state of Zhujen have enriched its city-states greatly, though increasing piracy and diminishing aid from the Realm navies imperil that prosperity. Its leaders, the hero-princes Tui-Phan the Summoner and Gia-En the Blue Nightmare, squabble over where to find support in this time of tumult — most likely with either Peleps or V’neef. The island of Bromeliad in the northern Meiyu Sea takes its name from the fields of flowers that the legendary sorceress Ghostly Crane planted there in her twilight years. Strange, ethereal folk now dwell there in simple agrarian communes, meeting and celebrating in annual festivals. Their overlong limbs and large, luminous eyes hint at inhuman heritage, perhaps from Ghostly Crane’s servants or allies.

The islanders’ unusual appearance and pacifistic nature makes them popular targets for slavers, but they’ve recently found protection from an unlikely source. Upon claiming Hsiang Tam’s satrapial lease, House Cynis’ merchants sought Bromeliad’s bounty of perfumes and dyes. Satrap Cynis Hamai especially covets the midnight bromeliad, a poisonous blossom of peerless lethality. It’s supposedly harvested from the crevice at the isle’s heart, where only the island folk can venture. The tiny isle of Dozhun’s Folly, significant only for rich seams of black jade in its jagged rocks, hosts a mining complex infamous for its bounty and lethality. It suffers frequent flooding despite engineers’ best efforts, and the criminals sentenced to labor there consider it a death sentence from drowning, cave-ins, or their predecessors’ hungry ghosts. Every year the mine deepens, conditions worsen, and jade grows sparser. Brutal repression of revolts worsens matters. The day is coming when House V’neef must commit scions to deal with the island’s crises, or abandon it to the dead. Several former Baihu colonies — such as Tuyet, whose folk train otters to herd fish into nets, and stormy Urn — cluster on the rugged, thinly settled northern coast of the Spine (The Realm, p. 171). Over the centuries, they’ve intermingled with the native Meiyu folk, whose princes claim descent from the long-fallen Chanak dynasty. Baihu rebels flee there, often joining local pirate bands. While the Empress never deemed the area worth annexing, ongoing Peleps, V’neef, and cadet house raids have razed pirate coves and looted city-states; as Realm

EX3

control grows unstable, many here grow eager to return the favor.

## The Dayfires

Among the crownlike peaks of the Omanij Mountains, overlooking hill and forest, stands Raolai Damay, fortress city of the Dayfire people. Here these daring raiders and fierce warriors gather, laugh, and trade, but of late their laughter grows forced. Since its founding three decades ago, the city has never been taken by an enemy force. But it may soon fall to threats from without or within. An assassin slew Konthoi — the warrior-prince who united the Dayfire chiefdoms and founded Raolai Damay — just as his endeavors promised them new strength. Tenth Born, the sorcerer who bolstered their armies, has retreated into her mountaintop manse. Brother fights brother for the privilege of looting the spoils of empire. The Realm marches from distant Zhaojūn to exact long-awaited vengeance. The new prince, Jalai, is old and canny, but lacks the fallen hero’s brilliance and charisma. Without powerful new allies or a new hero to rally behind, Raolai Damay’s decline seems likely to outpace its ascent.

### The Rise and Fall of Konthoi

Descended from princely warriors, Konthoi of the High Rock clan was blessed from birth with the secret of tiger-shape normally only gifted to the goddess Queen Storm-Tiger’s greatest devotees. As a child, he was swift enough to pluck a tailfeather from the Eastern Wind, who gifted him with a magnificent warscythe; he led his first cattle raid at age thirteen. Through bold sorties, rousing speeches, and devotion to comrades and gods alike, he won the loyalty and companionship of a retinue of warrior-priests and mystics, including the Zephyrite sorceress Tenth Born. As his legend grew, Dayfire leaders flocked to his banner, uniting under a single ruler for the first time in generations. Previously fractious and disparate, the Dayfire raised tulwar and warscythe in coordinated attacks, subjugating neighboring peoples and conducting raids along the distant Meiyu Coast. Hard labor, sorcerous might, and stolen coin raised up Raolai Damay and a ring of lesser fortresses around it, securely positioned in the mountains to shelter the Dayfires from retaliation. From her manse within the new capital, Tenth Born wove protective spells into the city’s encircling walls and towers.

Upon learning of the Scarlet Empress’s disappearance, Konthoi saw opportunity for his people. He led armies to annex a handful of independent city-states on the Meiyu Sea’s southern coast, and conducted daring hit-and-run raids as far as Zhaojūn, never allowing its Realm garrison opportunity to bring its full might to bear. He even entertained alliance with House Peleps via Kúi-Dien Isala, an emissary from distant Huang Hei.

Konthoi sought to centralize his authority over his vast new territory. This earned the ire of Dayfire chieftains who felt he threatened their power, including the proud, irascible warrior-prince Marei and the ruthlessly ambitious raider Liao. Konthoi’s new ideas and receptiveness to foreign advisors’ counsel frustrated Dayfire traditionalists, while others envisioned themselves on Konthoi’s throne. A year ago, an assassin slew Konthoi in his sleep, leaving his nascent empire rudderless. While his uncle Jalai — the new High Rock clan head — now rules in Raolai Damay, most of the Dayfire chiefdoms have splintered away into would-be successor kingdoms under rival princes. Many of the city’s warriors have followed, each leaving the city behind to serve one of the squabbling lesser kingdoms into which Konthoi’s empire has fractured. They leave Prince Jalai with too few people to defend Raolai Damay against his erstwhile allies, enraged former victims, and the Realm. The gods argue amongst themselves, and Tenth Born has retreated to her manse, her magical aid withdrawn.

### Society

Centuries ago, when warring Meiyu dynasties displaced the Rao culture from their ancestral homelands, many Rao sought refuge in the Omanij Mountains and the surrounding lands. They grew strong by raiding neighbors for food, weapons, trinkets, and slaves to sell to foreign merchants. These Rao became the Dayfire peoples: masters of hit-and-run strikes and daring night raids. Today, people throughout and beyond the Meiyu Coast fear their prowess, all the more for their warlike pantheon’s divine blessings.

Dozens of Dayfire chiefdoms spread throughout the lands south of the Meiyu Coast. In each chiefdom, power is held by members of several clans — noble families claiming descent from legendary founders or deities, forming a warrior aristocracy. Clan leaders elect the chiefdom’s prince, though this is often a formality to name the previous prince’s chosen heir. Below the clanfolk stand free commoners who herd, farm, craft,

EX3

and serve as soldiers; those who excel at war may be adopted or marry into a clan.

Clans train for war and spend much of the year raiding; successful raiders often enjoy privileges in old age as members of the prince’s war council or as priests. Everyone else is a commoner, expected to provide for the community as farmers, shepherds, metalworkers, weavers, brewers, farriers, and storytellers. Children learn their parents’ professions along with other common skills —how to spin wool into yarn, milk cows and goats, work the forge’s bellows, and wield sword or scythe. Adults apprentice them in professions they show talent for.

Dayfires aren’t obligated to remain in a specific profession; many change careers based on community needs or emergent talents. A shepherd who showed no aptitude for working clay as a child might still become a potter in adulthood. Most Dayfires join a war party once or twice in their lives, as a rite of passage or to commemorate an occasion; a few discover they’re suited to it after all. Most Dayfires live in communities of a few hundred, where raiders traditionally share spoils among their fellows and their multigenerational families. But for those in Raolai Damay with its teeming thousands, it grows harder to keep everyone fed. Though the Dayfire chiefdoms are more prosperous today than at any other point since their exodus, a growing destitute underclass lacks both the means to support themselves and family connections to potential benefactors. While farmers, herders, and artisans have always sufficed for subsistence, since Konthoi’s rise the Dayfires — especially their leaders — have grown accustomed to abundance supplied by plunder. With major raids stalled since Konthoi’s death, unrest brews. Raolai Damay’s current culture seems unsustainable without renewed rapacity to support its conquests.

### Culture

Dayfire warriors drink a mix of blood and milk for breakfast — from cows to gain strength, or from goats for agility. While raiding, they forage or eat plundered provender when they can, and otherwise subsist on hard bread and smoked ginger-rubbed meat. At home, they dine on the first and largest share of beef, pork, goat, and wild game. Other Dayfires lean more heavily on grain, legumes, vegetables, fruit, and dairy. Traditional dishes include barley and millet porridge with milk and berries, garlic sausages in parsley sauce,

and mushroom soup with cheese, celery, lovage, and thyme. Many drink wine to excess; birch sap is another well-loved beverage, either fresh or lightly fermented. Tunics and trousers are common everyday wear among Dayfires. In colder weather, they sport cloaks whose elaborate embroidered patterns vary from chiefdom to chiefdom and clan to clan. Aristocrats wear fur caps, while commoners don knitted wool hats. Dayfire folk favor gold, silver, and bronze jewelry, adorning themselves with heavy bracelets and numerous stud piercings. They grow their hair long, sweeping it back or tying it in a bun on one side of the head; beards are neatly trimmed.

Geometric henna patterns on face and hands, regularly applied by kin or servants, indicate social class, noteworthy deeds, and marital status. Other colorful dyes mark specific professions, making them apparent at a glance. On feast days, priests ceremonially revise or enhance these patterns to signify life changes, deeds, and feats of skill — an apprentice finishing her first blade, or a raider bringing back a notable prize. Nobles and skilled professionals amass an elaborate patchwork of designs over their lives, but most Dayfire folk have relatively few — markers of first achievements, marriage, or major journeys.

During harvest festivals, Dayfire youths from neighboring villages participate in stick-fighting contests to win the respect of their peers and of clan leaders. Participants arrive wearing bright sashes, necklaces, or henna patterns that mark them as fierce opponents; some are gifts from other youths, showing support or romantic interest. The gathered crowd sings songs and chants to encourage their favorites. Contestants duel using thin, six-foot-long sticks; winners continue to the next round until a final victor emerges.

### Raolai Damay

Constructed of limestone blocks quarried from the surrounding cliffs, Raolai Damay sits upon a broad plateau among the Omanij peaks. A single road climbs eastward toward the city through a maze of walls, cliffs, deadfalls, and defiles. Local guides escort merchants and friends safely, but approaching armies find themselves in a nightmare of choke points, endlessly harassed by Dayfire warriors accustomed to such terrain. Much of the city remains lightly populated, characterized by low buildings, open yards, natural rock formations, and overgrown lots. Nonetheless, many newer buildings climb vertically to maximize use of

EX3

occupy multiroomed wicker dwellings on stone foundations; wealthier folk can afford larger wooden towers. Once bustling, the district has grown quieter with so many Dayfires leaving the city. Children explore abandoned homes and shops, sometimes encountering thieves scavenging for valuables.

### MORE SOUTHWESTERN LOCALES

Countless hot springs — a legacy of geomantic workings from the Forty-Fourth Immortal’s longago elemental empire — pockmark the landscape surrounding Pearlmask. But smoke from the once-beautiful city now mingles with the springs’ steam in a pall of smog. After losing years of harvests to crop blights and flooding, the weakened city-state has been sacked repeatedly by neighboring peoples, leaving much of its populace dead, fled, or taken away in chains.

The Mercantile District, to the south, forms a maze of plazas and winding streets lined with hawkers, shops, and workplaces. The largest plaza holds the Grand Sundial, forged of gilded bronze, around which traders sell spices and jewelers evaluate gems. Many foreign merchants live here, some since the city’s founding. Public houses offer refreshments and lodging to affluent travelers; the wealthiest provide extortionately priced accommodations second only to nobles’ manors.

The Empire of the Three Devil Princes stands at the farthest corner of Creation. A land of wonder and mystery, it’s known for its trade with the Fair Folk, with fortunes in silver and brass coin changing hands for all manner of gossamer marvels. But today, the empire sinks into turmoil as its ancient supernatural princes quarrel with one another. It’s said that unnatural armies of beastfolk, demons, and fae gather in the empire’s great cities, though rumors differ as to whether they’ll turn on one another or march outward on a mission of conquest.

The Temple District rests at the plateau’s heart. Here, in a natural bowl-like depression, massive temples encircle a grand arena. In times of famine, plague, and war, the populace gathers to sing dirges. In happier times, riders race horses around the arena, an exercise that’s equal parts religious ceremony and entertainment. Gambling on the races’ outcome is likewise sacred; even children and the destitute place mock bets with one another.

The turbid, crocodile-haunted waters of the sprawling Fenakulla Swamp conceal countless sinkholes that open onto a web of flooded caves and conduits. Settlements of blind olmfolk dwell in the lightless deeper reaches of the cave system, emerging to gather and hunt, and to trade with neighboring peoples for food and goods. But after decades of peaceful coexistence, the olmfolk warleader Violet-Wreath and his hotblooded followers have begun terrifying night raids against neighboring peoples.

the plateau’s limited space, with an eye toward the city’s future growth. With the city’s population having diminished in the past year, vacant homes and shops highlight those empty spaces.

Walls separate the city’s five districts: The city gates open on the Barracks District. Any invader must pass through a gauntlet of labyrinthine streets and fortified homes, hounded by archers on the inner and outer walls who buy time for residents to retreat. During peacetime, warriors descend the mountain to hunt; small detachments remain behind to drill and patrol. Their families live in barracks housing, though some have spread into homes abandoned by peers who returned home to other kingdoms. The Residential District is the largest district, encompassing the plateau’s northern half. Most families

The temple complex itself consists of monumental stone buildings linked by brilliantly painted peristyles and arcades. Here, Unachsi’s physician-priests prepare herbal pastes and tonics to prevent infection, promote healing, and cure illnesses. Adherents of Shentra of the Bloody Vineyard offer petitioners red wine so they may ask the god’s blessing with crimson-stained lips. The complex’s fortified vaults contain supplies and space to shelter civilians should the residential district fall. The Royal District forms a crescent along the plateau’s eastern edge. Here, gardens and young groves surround long, low manor houses inhabited by princes, clan heads, successful war leaders, priests, god-blessed warriors, and their families. The most prestigious sites overlook the cliffs, providing breathtaking views of hills and valleys below. Two structures dominate the district — the tall, twisted manse called the Tower of Faded Mercy, where Tenth Born performs her sorceries; and the Palace of the Prince, a massive fortress-manor that Konthoi designed as the ideal place for a final stand.

### Dayfire Religion

The Dayfire gods seem as bellicose as their worshipers; even the most benign offer blessings in battle. Road gods hurry raiders toward their targets or away from

EX3

pursuit; hearth gods bless those warriors setting out to defend the home. Harvest gods welcome raiders’ spoils as offerings alongside their fields’ produce.

as the empire crumbles. She’s recently withdrawn into the wilderness, where Raolai Damay’s concerns don’t reach her.

Traditionally, each settlement worships one patron god above and alongside others, with that god’s high priest co-reigning with the chieftain. Konthoi rejected this custom when founding his new city; many priests still feel slighted at this. Jalai currently negotiates with several major priesthoods, but he can’t play them against each other much longer.

Belligerent Kyset Serpent-Slayer spurred the Dayfires on their greatest raids and conquests, earning him Queen Storm-Tiger’s esteem in the process. He earned the people’s love by exterminating a plague of snakes conjured by the vengeful Circle of Nine. He cares deeply for them in return, and schemes to bring them prosperity through war. His priests brew battle-potions from holy serpents’ venom to inspire berserker rages in faithful warriors.

Several Dayfire gods took up residence in Raolai Damay as Konthoi rose to power, abandoning their sacred places elsewhere in the region. Some leave the city to visit those ancient shrines a few times a year. Others entirely yield their roles in those locales, whether to divine protégés and attendants or to rivals and interlopers. For instance, the forest-god Emakel Behind-the-Trees left her temple in the dryad Kinereth’s hands. This has created a new dynamic in some places, where the caretaker spirit solicits worship in their patron’s name — or their own.

With many Dayfires and foreign merchants leaving Raolai Damay after Konthoi’s death, some gods have likewise returned to their homelands, abandoning lavish temples in the mountain city. This leaves many priests performing rites in near-empty chambers. Offerings dwindle; once-overflowing coffers run low. While outlying Dayfire chiefdoms enthusiastically welcome leaders and warriors home, not all gods share such happy reception, especially those who neglected worshipers for decades. For example, the hearth-god Tarin of the Ruby Chalice left her village in her spouse Sulir Smokeleaf’s capable hands. During her absence, the village prospered, and Sulir earned the people’s adoration. Though Sulir welcomed her counterpart home, the villagers are markedly less excited, and worry that Tarin isn’t up to the task.

Noteworthy Gods

The warrior-exemplar Queen Storm-Tiger commands awe and fear. Her devotees hunt and feast in her honor; initiation into her inner mysteries demands facing tigers, bears, or other great beasts in single combat in the wild. Defeat means death as the beast’s meal; a victory that catches the goddess’ eye earns the right to wear her lightning-swift tiger shape. Storm-Tiger loves only the Dayfires’ devotion and warrior traditions; otherwise, Raolai Damay’s losses and troubles don’t concern her. She’s contemptuous of the growing civilian class, and while she admired Konthoi’s march of conquest, she relishes renewed strife between rival chiefdoms

Unachsi Sings-For-The-Dead and her spirit attendants oversee death in battle. It’s said that her tears are the rains that wash blood from battlefields, and her dirges guide lost spirits toward rest. Her devotees are as much healers as morticians. Unachsi believes that only when people are struggling to survive — especially on the battlefield — are they truly alive. Would-be priests imbibe a concoction that induces a vision-filled coma; not all awaken from it.

### Prominent Figures

Prince Jalai, a wizened old warrior-scholar, has only ruled for a few months. Uncle to Konthoi and a respected war leader in his forces, the two had a tempestuous relationship, as often political enemies as allies. Upon Konthoi’s death, Jalai was named High Rock clan head, and consolidated support among Raolai Damay’s warriors and priests to maintain control of the city. He’s sufficiently respected that several Dayfire princes acknowledged him as sovereign, but much of that support has cooled, and a few have since withdrawn their acknowledgement. Jalai considers alliance with either House Peleps or the Lunar warlord Orzusha (p. XX), knowing that either choice demands both submission to a mighty power and confederation with peoples bitterly resentful from centuries of Rao raids. It seems that he has no good options, and he prays to the gods for intervention. An iron-eyed woman just past middle-age, Kúi-Dien Isala was among Konthoi’s closest advisors by the end of his reign. As another foreign advisor, her closeness to the Prince worried Dayfire leadership. Jalai keeps her close, recognizing her diplomatic acumen and knowledge of Meiyu politics — and her offer of Peleps aid — even at the cost of her detractors’ support. Isala has been the biggest proponent of Dayfire submission to the Realm: Konthoi’s wars were a failed

EX3

gambit that’s brought his people misery. Believing that Tenth Born has secluded herself to grieve for Konthoi, she seeks to draw the sorceress back to the court while it’s still possible to avert disaster through alliance with House Peleps. She seeks a messenger who can brave the defenses of Tenth Born’s manse, but hasn’t found anyone yet.

### NOTEWORTHY DAYFIRE CHIEFDOMS

Anipsa Fel stands north of Raolai Damay, among war-torn valleys where Rao chiefdoms traditionally raid each other and Meiyu Sea settlements alike. Prince Liao holds the loyalty of both the Ahtam clan chiefs and neighboring princes through personal leadership in winning plunder by raiding Meiyu settlements, generous gifts to fellow leaders and warriors, and sudden, shocking violence toward those who’d challenge his authority.

Young, dynamic, and gifted with Queen Storm-Tiger’s blessing, Claws-Dripping-Crimson is the most popular of Raolai Damay’s remaining war leaders. He knows that ruling Raolai Damay is beyond him; his impetuosity and rage dull his effectiveness as a strategist and sovereign. He harbors terrible guilt at being one of the conspirators behind Konthoi’s death. At the time he feared Konthoi’s ambition would invite Zhaojūn’s military attention, which Claws-Dripping-Crimson’s kin would bear the brunt of.

Kebren Fel sprawls to the southeast, overlooking forests haunted by wild beasts, fae creatures, and the hungry ghosts of Shogunate battlegrounds. Prince Marei, a longstanding traditionalist and critic of Konthoi, rules by the vote of several other chieftains. The high priestess Rutia rules at his side, conveying the gods’ will and providing guidance through haruspicy and her own cynical insight into human nature. Both aim to keep Kebren unentangled with Realm and Lunar involvement.

Now realizing that the united Dayfires might have been able to repel such an attack, his shame and anger drive him to lash out against princes who’ve abandoned Raolai Damay in its hour of need. Claws-DrippingCrimson respects Jalai’s rule but ferociously opposes Kúi-Dien Isala talk of submission to the Realm.

The shepherds and goatherds of hilly Melandi Fel, to the south, are renowned as masterful slingers and javelineers; their vintners produce potent purple wines praised in every chiefdom. The young prince Odrysa has ruled here since her mother’s death two years ago. Raised in Raolai Damay, she loved Konthoi like a father, and still loves Jalai like an uncle. But when most of the Melandi clan leaders demanded independence, she didn’t feel secure enough in her position to resist.

Propitious auguries drew the sorcerer Tenth Born to Dayfire lands, where she met the young warrior Konthoi. She saw in him the potential to create a lasting empire, with Tenth Born herself as the power behind the throne. Over time, she came to regard Konthoi as kin. Grief-stricken and shocked by his death, she vanished into her manse and sealed it against those who might climb its sheer walls; bound elementals block approach from the air.

Tenfold, once a mighty river port of the Caracal dynasty, fell to the Theleta Fel chiefdom centuries ago. Later, the petty empire of the Acanthus people — renowned for their archer-princes and fragrance-priests — seized it, subjugating Rao and Caracalli alike until Konthoi set them free. Today, Prince Erdones struggles to remain independent of Raolai Damay and the Acanthus alike. But this grows more complicates as faerie raiders serving Spear-Empress Bhadri (Lunars, p. 92) filter into the region.

Within, she consults auguries to determine who among the Dayfires might best continue the work she and Konthoi began. Her grief has abated, but her fury hasn’t. Raolai Damay’s residents say they’ve recently seen Tenth Born’s shadow fly over the streets, heralding her forthcoming reemergence — and, perhaps, her vengeance.

### Neighbors

City-states along the southern Meiyu Coast include Glum, decrepit capital of the long-ago Sainam dynasty; Sang, where the Empty Path sect’s poet-mystic Awlan Veils-the Stars found enlightenment; and once-rich Laden, now in the thrall of lawless mercenaries originally hired to defend it. Centuries of feuding make it difficult for these city-states to ally, whether against Zhao invasion or Rao raids. Nonetheless, Meiyu princes

and merchants struggle to form a stable defensive pact. Meanwhile, envoys from Zhaojūn, local satraps, cadet house matriarchs, and other powers seek to sway this city or that into foreign orbits.

The city of Advent clusters around the forested flood plains of the Azudi river, its blocky brick structures painted in striking yellow and white. Winding streets contain markets for spices, pottery, and slaves. With Konthoi’s death, Advent’s citizens rebelled and drove the Dayfire out of the city. They’re negotiating

EX3

submission to House Ragara in exchange for sufficient provisions to increase their army and hold off any Dayfire forces that might attempt to reclaim the city. When war finally comes to Raolai Damay, it may be in the form of a vengeful Ciori army bearing Realm steel. The mountain fortress Kyset’s Feast, which Konthoi’s forces seized from the Ciori in a bloody battle twenty years ago after a disease-riddled siege, has become a shadowland. Its stone walls and squat towers are scorched black and haphazardly patched with stone and timber; crimson ivy crawls up its façade to entangle its crumbling parapets. War-ghosts puppeteering armor of rusty iron and rotten leather haunt its battlements; they patrol the surrounding lands, and use Dayfire warriors’ chained, leashed hungry ghosts as hounds. Iron Fang, the fortress’s final captain, rules here as a ghost-warlord, animating a metallic juggernaut composed of hundreds of fused blades and breastplates. He and his warriors offer their services as mercenaries to the Dayfires’ enemies. South of the Omanji Mountains, amid tropical savannah and forest, stands the once-nomadic Osaze Nation. They skillfully practice bronzework and animal husbandry, and their temple-laden city-states — built

atop ruins of the Shogunate-era Seriza Adminstrative District’s libraries and monastic retreats — teem with life and vibrant artistry. They suffered from Dayfire aggression until they found protection under Orzusha, a Lunar claiming to be an aspect of their moon-goddess Ikuseghan Unyielding. Appearing as an elephant — an Osaze symbol of strength and wisdom — she trains a chosen few in magic and blesses favored warriors with bladeproof hide and stone-shattering strength. Today she entertains emissaries from Prince Jalai with skepticism. She’d value the Dayfires as allies against the Realm, but the antipathy between their peoples may be irreconcilable.

## Decanthus

Dread grips the hearts of the mortals of Janrai Isle. Not long ago, they cast nets and herded peccaries in relative peace. Now the lost city of Decanthus looms weirdly amid the reeds, its organic, alien structures crawling with monstrous shapes. In ancient times, an Anathema’s sorcery flung the entire city into Hell. Now it’s somehow returned, and the twisted descendants of its people have arrived with it.

EX3

Only fragments remain of the original city, as nothing came back from Hell that wasn’t rooted in Creation. A few ancient stones anchor the foundations of houses grown from throbbing demon-flesh or manors of infernal brass and basalt. In other places, where demons once razed entire swaths of old Decanthus and erected wholly hellish structures, those structures vanished when the city returned to Creation, leaving vacant lots. In those lots, new buildings constructed of local wood, brick, and bamboo now rise. Even from a distance, they’re clearly of infernal design, rambling and cyclopean, shaped for demonic rather than mortal use. Likewise, the city’s demon residents remained in Hell, from the city’s Second Circle master — feline, ligneous Nicanor, the Tamer of Thralls — to the lowest of the low. Only Demon-Blooded descendants of the old city’s mortal inhabitants emerged with Decanthus. Those with only the thinnest traces of human or animal blood threading their monstrous veins skulk in cellars and sewers to avoid the sunlight. Others struggle to maintain some form of civilization.

### Noteworthy Locales

The Brinesong Docks spread out along the water’s edge. Here, aquatic Demon-Blooded of a hundred heterogeneous strains clamber in and out of the water, harvesting Creation’s sea life or sunning themselves on wharves of petrified wood and calcified flesh. A handful of endlessly rebuilt First Age fishing junks creak at anchor; they’re now more demon than boat, their hulls living bone rather than dead timber, eyes blinking like fireflies on their membranous sails. Several noteworthy

Demon-Blooded — quick-witted Nethun of the Eels, the deadly tracker Mistdance Liaster, honey-voiced Zair the Lender — squabble for supremacy here, but all unite against outside threats.

Over the centuries in Hell, demon wasps transformed Decanthus’ granaries into the Obsidian Larder: a mass of bulging hives of black brick and glass, thrusting upward like an inverted bunch of grapes. Here dwell the Pellucid, a swarm of freakishly beautiful amalgams of crystal wasp and mortal flesh, ruled by the enormous, grim Thanchavil Diamond-Queen. They’ve amassed enormous influence by doling out their food reserves — infernal comestibles unavailable in Creation, craved by Demon-Blooded residents and potentially valuable to enterprising foreign merchants. They supplement these foodstuffs with fresh meat from outside Decanthus, seizing domesticated beasts and herdsmen with equal relish.

Nicanor once dwelt in the Palace of Lost Yearning, a meandering sprawl of brass, glass, marble, and basalt. Its wings and colonnades enfold its garden: a labyrinth of metal trees and shrubs bursting with sulfur-yellow blossoms, infested with bizarre demon-animal hybrids. With their master gone, the palace’s residents intrigue against one another to claim his brass-brambled throne. Dominant figures in this game include the perceptive Ever-Desirable Calinei, most cherished of Nicanor’s concubines; the ruthless vizier Athir-Meneth; and the clever, unpredictable guard-captain Rasping Fen. Whoever takes unquestioned command of the palace guards and Nicanor’s treasury — laden with jewels and eldritch artifacts — will likely gain mastery over the city, then the rest of Janrai Isle.

“Hail! Hail the conquering hero!” Dozens took up the chant, following the procession up and down the city streets.

The bright, peppery sounds of brass horns cut through the crowd’s roar. Rose petals fell from the cloudy blue sky, flung in huge clumps from the high rooftops of Azure’s temples. The procession strode along the huge Sea Lord’s Road, which gradually ascended from the military anchorages and the private anchorage for pleasure boats to the palatial hanok in the deep city. Thousands of citizens thronged the temples, joining their thousands of fellows lining the streets under the austere stone statues of Sea Lords past and present. Others cheered from where they stood before elaborately painted frescos and stones.

The heavy gama, a freshly lacquered wooden litter crafted from the shattered hulks of shipwrecks, lifted Sea Lord Ryu Jinsu, victorious admiral of the Fifth Fleet, high above the adoring crowd. Enemies in chains, slaves taken from the Neck, shuffled behind him; servants carried huge chests of treasures from the Cowries and strutting naval officers paraded under the humid heat of Azure’s midday sun. Three days past, Ryu Jinsu had been due to sail for the Auspice Isles and peacekeeping duties, but he had let those winds blow off in favor of attending his triumph. Pockets of dour, silent spectators stood among the cheering crowds; Jinsu’s missives to the home isle, though popular with the common people, had elegantly obfuscated the hideous loss of life resulting from the admiral’s mediocre tactics. Many of the city’s prominent families lost their most promising scions to Siakal’s children. Sea Lord Dang Tae waited at the end of the procession, along with the other standing Sea Lords currently in the city. His cousin and nephew sailed with Ryu Jinsu’s fleet, only to be eaten by sharks when their ship broke apart, attempting to ram an enemy vessel whose hull was rendered hard as stone by the earth elemental fused within. Dang Tae cursed Siakal, and he cursed Ryu Jinsu. Nevertheless, Ryu Jinsu had returned victorious, destroying the rest of the enemy fleet that wasn’t comprised of invincible ships. And so Dang Tae, like many of his fellows, gathered here at the end of the triumphal procession, fearing that another such glorious victory would destroy the Fifth Fleet and leave Azure endangered. The plan was already in motion; Dang Tae looked at the front of the dais, where the dignitaries from foreign navies gathered to bear witness to Coral’s might. A Realm admiral under flag of truce stood with her officer corps alongside a master marine from Okhiro in the Neck, clad in armor that dated back to the Shogunate.

Dang Tae’s eye caught those of a pale man in a salt-stained leather jacket and fine white cloak. Across his back was slung a massive soulsteel-and-stone goremaul, the mark of the Drowner of Saints, an admiral of Skullstone. Two nights ago, Dang Tae had paid an intermediary with stolen silver; the night before, he’d met the taciturn deathknight under cover of a new moon. Once Ryu Jinsu returned to the Neck, he’d meet his end at the Abyssal’s goremaul.

All it cost Azure was its claim to Tern, one of the minor Protectorate islands, which Dang Tae could easily arrange once he’d risen to power in Ryu Jinsu’s place. The Sea Lord clapped his hands and joined in the cry as his fellow passed unaware on the raised dais that hosted the lords of Azure. “Hail!” He clapped the victorious admiral on the back, then offered him a cup of Juche’s sweet wine from a daring raid upon a Realm merchant ship.

Hail indeed, and farewell.

# Chapter Eight: The West

Chapter Eight

The West

A vast mega-archipelago dominates the Great Western Ocean’s waters. Its islands range from tiny skerries to mainlands large enough that whole inland civilizations never see the coast.

After the Contagion, these islands developed largely in isolation from the rest of Creation, sheltered by distance, complex winds and currents, hostile aquatic spirits, ancient sorceries, and monsters. But the Direction’s wealth — in spices, pearls, dyes, slaves, and other riches — drew foreign powers’ attention. Merchants found their way across the ocean, initially via Fajad and Faxai-on-the Caul, and later through WuJian. Then, the Realm’s military stepped in. Today, much of the West suffers under military occupation, whether garrisoned as Realm satrapies or as protectorates of local imperial powers such as Azure, Makelo, and Randan. Merchant ships, their bellies full of treasure, watch keenly for pirates and privateers. For the West, this is an age of turmoil, one that elevates some and tramples others underfoot.

The Great Western Ocean moderates the West’s climate. Temperatures are generally warm to hot yearround, divided into a clear, sunny dry season occupying the year’s first half and a stormy wet season in the second half. Farther north, the Coral and Skullstone Archipelagoes tend to be cooler, occasionally seeing rare, wet snowfalls at year’s end.

## The Wavecrest Archipelago

To its neighbors, the republic of Wavecrest seems an enviable, peaceful place, defined by bountiful harvests and obedience to Dynastic masters. But this massive island chain’s cultures forged a shared identity through centuries of internal strife and mutual protection against threats both natural and unnatural. In today’s time of tumult, House Peleps tightens its grip upon Wavecrest, and social and religious tensions build toward an eruption of bloodshed.

### Breadbasket of the West

Wavecrest’s fruitful volcanic soil is legendary; over two centuries of protection by the Realm’s Water Fleet, its trade economy has grown to match its natural bounty. Historically dependent on short-range island-to-island trade routes, the satrapy now also uses deep-bottomed ships to trade breadfruit, bananas, maize, pork, and chicken to distant islands that otherwise depend on fish for sustenance. These neighbors also depend on Wavecrest’s tools and metalwork, which have advanced substantially in recent centuries due to the archipelago’s relations with the Realm. Some neighbors offer valuables such as spices, coral, or pearls; others trade services and handiwork for the satrapy’s bounty. Other common ingredients in Wavecrest cuisine include seaweed, sweet onions, salted candlenut paste, and mashed fermented taro, alongside imported ingredients such as chickpeas, bulgur, cinnamon, saffron, and rose water. Many recipes begin with a sofrito of garlic, onions, and peppers. Traditional dishes include poached eggs simmered in tomato sauce; crispy fried dartfish with seaweed salad; steamed pork wrapped in taro leaves; overripe breadfruit with coconut milk; and candied cinnamon eggplant.

While Wavecrest is best known by its Western neighbors for farming and trade, its people practice both traditional and modern occupations. Centuries of Realm occupation have created thriving industries in shipbuilding, mining, metalwork, and hospitality. The satrapy’s famous professional dancers perform traditional dances that express the republic’s histories and myths. Though Wavecrest depends on Imperial garrisons for military and naval protection, each community retains its own warrior-athletes, trained in wrestling and traditional weaponry such as slings, spears, and shark tooth-studded wooden axes.

The Realm invested heavily in Wavecrest’s protection and production, and has recouped those investments many times over through extracted tribute and trade. The archipelago’s rarest treasures, however, spring

EX3

from bordermarches and middlemarches, many of which cloak the slopes of the republic’s sacred volcanoes. Wyld prospectors sift the bordermarches for unusual treasure.

### GODS AND STRANGER THINGS

Small cults dot the archipelago’s many islands, and many of Wavecrest’s most legendary island-kings and priestesses had supernatural ancestry or the blessings of Exaltation. Volcano-priestesses clash with Fair Folk cults that spring up near Wyld-tainted volcanic slopes; elementals form long-term symbiotic relationships with small islands and their people. Fertility gods serve as subordinates in volcano-gods’ courts. Some sea monsters enjoy veneration and sacrifices and may spare vulnerable mortal communities or shipping lines while worship continues. Tsunami gods and wind elementals sometimes rage across the islands, leaving destruction in their wake. Wavecrest is too large and varied for any simple description of its religious history to suffice.

### The Shadow of Hamoji

The volcano Hamoji sits at the center of Abalone — Wavecrest’s largest island by far — and looms in every approaching ship’s view. The volcano is strange and fickle; its shape and climbable routes shift from month to month, for it sits in the archipelago’s broadest middlemarch. Though at times it belches ash and smoke like any other volcano, it’s also expelled poisonous flowers, snow, and jets of lurid violet magma. Wyld-altered hybrid creatures sometimes descend from Hamoji’s slopes, individually or in seasonal waves. These oddities often have practical or occult value and can make brave, fortunate prospectors extremely wealthy. Other strange prodigies threaten Abalone’s people, requiring heroes to brave Hamoji’s slopes to hunt the monsters down. Several of Wavecrest’s islands have their own volcanoes, whose gods have their own personalities and relationships with local peoples, spirits, and fae. The archipelago’s inhabitants view their volcanoes and volcano-gods as synonymous, and prioritize understanding the volcano-gods’ moods. The bulk of this important work falls upon several orders of hero-priestesses, who collaborate to interpret volcano-gods’ histories, personalities, and desires. Hamoji’s priestesses are the most numerous but must often coordinate (or conflict) with their sister orders, given the volcano-gods’ propensity for long-running feuds. As Abalone is Wavecrest’s largest, most populous island, so is Hamoji the largest, most renowned volcano. Hamoji’s temper can be felt and heard across Abalone, and when no prayer or ritual appeasement suffices to calm the god, his priestesses brave his Wyld-enveloped slopes to throw a sacrifice into the volcano. Centuries of experience have shown that live human sacrifices appease Hamoji best, often with immediate effect. Hamoji’s weaker siblings sometimes follow his example, so Wavecrest’s cultures have settled on a shared legal and executive system to please their volcano-gods.

### A Hierarchy of Sacrifice

The Wavecrest archipelago’s people once raided and warred against each other regularly. Tribal cultures fought for dominance over their own islands, and for each island’s dominance over the others. Victory brought spiritual power and wisdom, embodied in each

island’s ruling princes or priestesses. In time, this conflict brought about Wavecrest’s prince of princes, the Feathered One, who would be of every island in the archipelago, and of none. The Feathered One is now a president elected by the royal families of each island, appointed for life, and typically selected from among the royal families — though the electors sometimes choose particularly popular commoners or charismatic holy persons. Upon their election, the Feathered One dons their cape of office. Woven of feathers from seven species of tropical birds, it’s said to bestow the wisdom, honesty, and forethought of all prior Feathered Ones upon its bearer. As the embodiment of Wavecrest’s united spiritual power, the Feathered One’s own strength and good health is crucial to performing their many responsibilities. Their most sacred duty is to serve as a final sacrifice to Hamoji should no other sacrifice please the volcano-god.

Where Wavecrest’s island-princes once raided each other for sacrifices, the archipelago now draws sacrificial offerings from its prisons. Under Wavecrest law, any crime more severe than rudeness is punished through a specific prison sentence, ranging from a day to a mortal lifetime. When a volcano hungers, any prisoner may be sacrificed. Recently, the prison population has grown particularly thin, for Hamoji and his siblings are unusually restless in this time of tumult. The current Feathered One has ordered soldiers to crack down on minor crimes — including the crime of failing to report someone else’s crime — to keep the prisons well-stocked.
