### Outside Influence

Wavecrest is the Realm’s largest and most productive Western foothold, and a cornerstone of House Peleps’ power. Thus, it’s garnered enemies even beyond the raids and natural disasters the archipelago has always weathered. Deep-water trade has exposed it to cultures across the West and beyond. As contact with influential outsiders grows, the satrapy struggles to hold onto its own culture and values.

Wavecrest’s modern importance as a trade hub has resulted in an urban boom over the last century. Young people migrate in increasing numbers from farming and fishing communities to a handful of large, diverse coastal cities. Tensions rise between fast-paced, individualistic urban culture and these smaller communities, which value tight-knit family, community pride, central leadership, and traditional modes of worship. Hamoji’s priestesses draw a clear line from the youngest generation’s exposure to foreign faiths to Hamoji’s recent irritability, though most avoid criticizing the Immaculate Philosophy publicly.

City-dwellers have a reputation for criminality, and so find themselves quickly accused when they stray too far or linger too long in insular, traditional communities. Even local youths who travel abroad seeking opportunities for their families find themselves alienated upon returning home. Left rudderless and abandoned, many become disaffected sailors and merchants, devoting themselves to profit and exploration instead of traditional values.

Among the many threats to Wavecrest’s way of life, the Immaculate Philosophy has the greatest foothold. Though the Immaculate Order lacks the power to enforce its perfected hierarchy across the republic — its monks are few, and receive limited support from the satrap, garrison commander, and Feathered One — it’s aggressive and persistent, particularly in cities with a heavy Realm presence. Immaculate missions here focus on public works and avoid controversial statements about the worship of gods — particularly volcano-gods, who might devastate Wavecrest if displeased. The missionary’s greatest weapon has been education. People, especially in backwater areas, eagerly accept opportunities to study literacy, modern crafts, and languages that allow them to participate in profitable trade.

EX3

sun-beaten farmers and broad-bellied merchants, the archipelago was founded on a shared conviction that through courage and ritual conflict, its people might grow closer to the divine. All children here learn that they descend from heroes, and that their refinement will continue for as long as they hold to their faith.

### AWAY FROM THE COAST

Jungles cover much of the Wavecrest Archipelago’s inland regions. Towns, villages, and seminomadic bands trade with — or fight — one another more often than they do with coastal cities. In fact, many do no business with places like Seahaven or Gateway at all. Residents hunt wild boar and feral cattle, grow citrus, cassava, and cashews, or cultivate mulberry trees to make cloth from their soft inner bark. The vigilant Okele follow the banteng herds, fending off foreign poachers whose depredations could drive the animals into extinction. Villagers in Kupaula dwell in the shadow of an ancient, vine-wreathed ruin, harvesting beeswax in its towers’ shadow and edible bird’s nests from the caves beneath.

Today, Immaculate circumspection grows strained. A religious reactionary group whose ancient tribal name translates roughly to Ochre Heart Witnesses stages public demonstrations and private attacks against Immaculate followers across the republic. The Witnesses rarely attack monks directly, preferring to goad Immaculate lay followers into violence — aiming to radicalize the citizenry and allow the Witnesses to lead a popular revolt.

### Kneeling With Straight Backs

Over a century before Wu-Jian opened up the Great Western Ocean to mortal sailors, ambitious Sesus Dynasts sailed from the Caul and made landfall in the Wavecrest archipelago. It became the Realm’s first significant conquest in the West soon after, with minimal violence. Though Sesus retains sizable business interests there, House Peleps has held the republic’s satrapial lease for most of the two subsequent centuries and owes much of its current might to its measured exploitation of Wavecrest.

As a satrapy, Wavecrest has weathered island-shaking storms, Anathema saboteurs, and several instances of Hamoji’s displeasure, but it’s been too large and too well-defended by the Realm’s Water Fleet for any other naval power to meaningfully threaten until recently. The republic’s feuding royal families largely put their old strife behind them for the opportunities presented by Realm control. In Creation’s eyes, Wavecrest has been tamed.

But Wavecrest folk say that people raised and fed upon the islands’ rich black soil carry volcanic embers in their heart. Though outsiders mock Wavecrest as a nation of

Though House Peleps is among the proudest of Dynastic houses, it’s also practical. Given Wavecrest’s isolation from the center of Realm power and the potential for a volcano-god to object if the Realm grew too grasping, Peleps’ Rightly Guided Admiralty Board historically wielded its own power judiciously while limiting the Immaculate Order’s activity in the satrapy. As tensions rise and Peleps’ needs grow, however, Wavecrest pride grows intolerable to the Great House. The Admiralty Board agrees that, to subdue the satrapy after centuries of a light touch they must break the people’s will, which requires breaking Hamoji and his siblings.

### The Dragons’ Tightening Grasp

Desperate either to secure the Scarlet Throne or to carve out a new Western empire far from any rivals, House Peleps pushes Wavecrest’s plantations, logging crews, and shipyards past capacity. The republic never struggled to meet its quota for tribute before, but now finds familiar tax collectors replaced by cruel foreigners willing to make harsh public displays of residents who won’t meet their increasing demands. Citizens now fear banditry and raids from their own fellows, and rumor spreads that entire communities may soon be arrested for complicity in such crimes. All the while, the Water Fleet sails further abroad, preparing for wars on the Blessed Isle and across the West, leaving Wavecrest less defended than it’s been in over a century. The current Feathered One stands caught between the satrap’s increasing tribute demands and the growing desire for independence among the royal families that elected him. Accustomed to depending on the Imperial Navy for protection, Wavecrest— despite having built or retrofitted hundreds of Imperial ships over the years — can muster only small, short-range craft historically used for raiding and patrols. With taxes and pirate raids increasing, and with no immediate hope of breaking the Realm’s hold on the archipelago’s ports, the republic’s royals push the Feathered One to conceal from the satrap their efforts to convert trade ships to warships and to start raiding the archipelago’s neighbors.

Prominent Cities of Abalone

The island’s capital, Seahaven, welcomes sailors traveling from points east. As Abalone’s largest and oldest

EX3

port, it hosts the Feathered One’s Sea Spray Palace; the satrapial palace; Wavecrest’s naval headquarters; and the Obsidian Stockade, one of the biggest prisons on the archipelago.

To the northeast, the cosmopolitan merchant town of Gateway accommodates the headquarters of the Western Trade Alliance shipping cartel (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 246). Most trade to and from other Western ports passes through here; investors grow rich buying and reselling entire cargoes of cotton, salt fish, hardwood, sugar, or spices in Gateway’s markets. Tall lookout towers rise over Gullwing’s port. Abalone’s westernmost city provides a jumping-off point for expeditions into the Wyld and forms the first defense against Fair Folk raids from Creation’s edge. Though it’s been long years since such an attack, Gullwing’s guards remain ever vigilant, especially with the Imperial Navy’s presence diminishing.

### Noteworthy Lesser Isles

With the archipelago’s largest land area and over twothirds of its population, Abalone is synonymous with Wavecrest in most outsiders’ eyes. But Wavecrest contains many smaller isles, each contributing to a shared way of life.

Aoheku, just north of Abalone and second-largest island in the archipelago, is dominated by the volcano of the same name. Bordermarches spread across most of the isle, so its people have adapted to strangeness. Aoheku natives follow byzantine social taboos laid down by ancestral mediator-heroes and do mostly peaceful business with the onyx-fleshed hobgoblin servitors of the enigmatic Black Lizard Court. The court’s Fair Folk princes claim Aoheku’s western slope, shore, and any living creatures that stand thereupon. The isle’s mortal folk avoid Wyld mutation by obeying the proper taboos, and have a history of culture heroes who adhered strictly to these rules while outwitting the Fair Folk.

Beyond their shores, Aoheku’s people are known for canny negotiation tactics, stiff manners, and trading in drugs (medicinal and recreational) found nowhere else in Wavecrest. Traditionally trained Aoheku warriors favor stealth and poison more than their neighbors do. Even untrained residents often have blowguns and darts close to hand, for life on the Wyld’s edge can shift at any moment.

The volcano god Aoheku herself presided over the ancient pact between mortals and the Black Lizard Court, and her priestesses traditionally anoint only FaeBlooded princes. Local Immaculates have attempted purges against the court, but the Fair Folk have oathbound allies scattered throughout the archipelago, and Aoheku always has more resources than those apparent to outsiders.

The southeastern isle of Kumul was first in the Wavecrest archipelago to have peaceful contact with the Realm. It served as a key port-of-call on the Wavecrest–Blessed Isle route until Wu-Jian superseded the Southwestern trade routes a century ago. Kumul’s royal family adores Dynastic culture and seeks to set an example of “civilized behavior” for the neighboring isles. Though a much smaller island than Abalone whose trade presence has dwindled this last century, Kumul’s shipyards remain among the West’s busiest. These shipyards have largely devoured Kumul’s once-bountiful forests; the island now imports lumber to preserve its remaining scenic wilderness and hunting grounds, which Dynastic tourists favor.

Today, Peleps retirees invest heavily in Kumul’s development, hoping to recreate Blessed Isle culture there as a stepping-stone to independence from the Realm. They’ve founded a secondary school there, and aggressively court renowned professors and tutors to raise Kumul’s educational system to their standards. The island’s royal family welcomes Immaculate guidance and clears old elemental cults’ sacred groves for the construction of new monasteries. Modern maps disagree, but the people of Vaaisami have always considered their island the westernmost land in Creation; when they look out over the Great Western Ocean, they see the past and future written in its weather. The Vaaisami people fiercely protect deep stores of occult knowledge and thaumaturgic traditions from outsiders. Their insights connect them to an ocean they see as greater than any god, defining the veil between material and immaterial worlds. Through initiatory rites and shared oaths with oceanic spirit courts, Vaaisami traditions have endured across centuries, even as time and resistance washed away foreign invaders. Today, the island occupies a place of spiritual honor; its neighbors consult the Vaaisami on occult matters outside the volcano-priestesses’ purview. As a result, Immaculate missionaries make

EX3

persistent, invasive conversion attempts throughout Vaaisami; the Order wishes to use the island’s reputation to bolster the Immaculate Philosophy across the archipelago. The Vaaisami have escalated from harsh words, to threats, to nonlethal force against these intruders, but new missionaries keep coming.

Prominent Figures

Bangga Anggurma, the current Feathered One, is a charismatic middle-aged man with an experienced salesman’s confidence. Formerly a respected village elder, he won his current role by campaigning tirelessly and publicly running rhetorical circles around his opponents. In private, he’s a deeply anxious man who regularly consults the stars and Hamoji’s rumbling omens. A peacetime leader lacking past Feathered Ones’ athletic prowess, he’s terrified by royal electors’ demands for a return to raiding and sacred warfare, but fears that showing weakness will enrage Hamoji and risk thousands of lives. Indeed, he suspects that the volcano’s recent activity reflects the trepidation in his own heart. The legendary hero-priestess Kamach Achi, self-proclaimed Chosen of Hamoji, has spawned countless household tales and morality plays through decades of valiant exploits. Though her body has aged, her spirit only grows fierier. Now, she sermonizes against the people’s waning observance of traditional faith. Achi is the most vocal and popular opponent of the Immaculate Philosophy in Wavecrest, and though she claims no affiliation with the Ochre Heart Witnesses, she doesn’t publicly denounce them either. Achi seeks duels with prominent Immaculate monks to either prove through her prowess that the Order doesn’t belong in Wavecrest, or to earn a good, public death through sacred combat. Wavecrest’s satrap, Peleps Senit, spent nearly a century at sea, working her way up through the Imperial Navy’s ranks. Her reputation for delivering decisive victories landed her the honor of overseeing one of House Peleps’ most prosperous Western holdings. While her house prepares for possible civil war in the Realm, Enit struggles on several fronts. Some of Wavecrest’s royal families push the Feathered One and their people toward rebellion, a fire also stoked by Kamach Achi. Meanwhile, sabotage of Imperial Fleet vessels suggests V’neef or Lunar operatives at work on the Archipelago. And the Admiralty Board presses her to ready Wavecrest as a potential beachhead for conquering the West — expanding shipyards; identifying potential rebels; and gaining the upper hand over the garrison commander, Immaculate leaders, and other possible Realm rivals.

Nellens Lanasa Koiko has been archimandrite of Wavecrest’s central Immaculate mission — the West’s largest — and director of the Order’s strategy in Wavecrest for over twenty years. The Fire Aspect child of a Wavecrest outcaste adopted into House Nellens at its founding, she’s dreamed her whole life of spreading the Immaculate Philosophy across her father’s backward homeland, and then the islands beyond. Lanasa views her work as a war on many fronts, with House Peleps vacillating between ally and interloper. Lacking the resources to confront the volcano cults directly, she sends aggressive missionary groups to islands she deems vulnerable. She views the resultant outbreaks of anti-missionary sentiment as evidence of the Immaculate Philosophy’s necessity. Lanasa would push the satrapy’s religious tensions into open conflict if she thought the Order could decisively win. With Peleps’ growing frustration at Wavecrest’s civil disobedience, Lanasa believes her opportunity is near.

Neighboring Isles

The otterfolk of Minat wage eternal war against pirates and raiders along the archipelago’s northwestern edge, driven by a collective oath sworn long ago. As their cliff-girt isle can only be approached by air or through mazy underwater grottoes, few outsiders have visited their complex rope-and-stonework villages. The otterfolk enjoy trading for novelties and exploring above or below water, but they react to insults quickly and forgive slowly, if at all. Minat’s boarding parties strike offenders with spears and nets at lightning speed. Reefs and unpredictable tides surround barren, desolate Aseios. Recently, Western Trade Alliance investor Yuharon Kinis sent hired prospectors to the uninhabited island, where they discovered a vein of beautiful bonelike mineral they dubbed marble-ivory. Months after Kinis staked a claim on the island and his agent, the merchant-adventurer Ehlen Eventide began full mining operations, three of Wavecrest’s royal families announced “ancient claims” on Aseios. The royals blockade the isle while they jockey and bluster to determine which family will take it. Slave miners and overseers on Aseios starve while Kinis offers rich rewards for blockade runners who can salvage her investment. The people of Grallat once warred against cruel wood spider elementals at their island’s heart, then struck a bargain with their foes with an Exalted mediator’s aid. The elementals still delight in tormenting and confusing mortals, but they’ve grown accustomed to worship and sacrifice. In return, they lend the populace their natural wood-spinning art.

EX3

Grallat natives inhabit villages and towns of woven timber and sail seamless wooden ships that equal the finest mortal-made vessels. They profit well from trading exotic wooden craftwork and from delivering messages and passengers across the Western archipelago. A handful of radical Grallat captains conduct opportunistic raids on islands and weaker neighbors’ ships for human sacrifices, carefully leaving no witnesses.

## Randan

The seawalls of Randan glisten like mother-of-pearl, but up close, every brick is glazed with images of monsters, heroes, and gods in a hundred colors. Rich scents of black pepper, cinnamon, and clove overlay the markets’ stink of fish and foundry smoke. Even common folk wear linen ablaze with madder, saffron, and indigo; their betters don rainbow silks flashing with jeweled embroidery. As soldiers parade around the aristocracy’s craft-lodges, their leaders stand resplendent in brocade armor resilient as bronze or coats of ceramic plates as hard as steel, their masked helmets shining with silver, gold, and gems.

A gateway to the Far West’s bounties, Randan holds suzerainty over a scattering of tributaries and recent colonies, extracting beneficial trade terms and ceremonial tribute by dint of deep coffers and sharp spears. Led by its pekumi warrior-artisans and their queen, the Randani have known prosperity and abundance for generations. Now the island is torn between hunger for expansion and the allure of stability, beset from without by competitors and pirates and from within by agitators and the ancient feuds of their own gods.

### Of Wares and Wonders

The island of Randan has limited natural resources — while thickly forested, its mines offer little useful metal. Nonetheless, the Randani have built a mercantile empire on cunning, skill, patience, courage, and a heritage of ancient thaumaturgical secrets. Once a loose confederacy of warring clans and citystates, war unified Randan, while a lineage of conquerors and uniters tempered it into its modern state. Now largely at peace with one another, its artisan-aristocrats turn their blade-sharp minds outward. Their ships trade at every port for hundreds of miles, dealing in silk, ivory, amber, steel, spice, and more. This bounty flows through Randan’s ports, their markets teeming with merchants from colonies and client-states. Like a beating heart, Randan sends fleets throughout the

### RANDANI NAMES

Randani names draw inspiration from Japanese, Indonesian, and Portuguese names. Most heimin have only a personal name, while pechin have a clan name followed by the particle “u” and a personal name. Epithets are common. Each new queen takes a regnal name upon ascending the throne.

region, maintaining a steady rhythm of trade while putting rebellious vassals and pirates to the sword. Randan’s port capital, Ohdanu, rises along a gentle slope from docks and coastal slums to the luxurious districts of merchants and master artisans. On the highest hill, the palatial estates of the craft-lodges encircle the queen’s temple-manse, the House of Tranquil Tides — itself a delicate confection of swooping pale green arches and aquamarine towers. The city’s merchants boast that if you cannot find it for sale in Ohdanu, it’s not for sale anywhere in Creation. Hawkers bilk the naïve with counterfeit treasures, but those with sufficient wits, connections, or coin can procure enchanted wares produced by thaumaturgical prodigies: ever-burning candles, swords that sing when swung, or gowns whose colors change to match the sky. The island has a handful of smaller cities and large towns, although none match Ohdanu’s splendor and bustle: forest-ringed Ekkadim feeding Randan’s need for timber, industrious Kumeina and its busy shipyards, steadfast Hannepa with its unconquerable walls. Farmlands and villages dot inland roads and the coast, as do fortresses in varying states of use and decay — silent memorials to when the Randani warred amongst themselves, with nothing to show for it except blood, stone, and history. Quieted by decades of peace, these ancient rivalries still find expression, infrequently erupting into bouts of civic pride, competition, or enmity.

### Class and Caste

Three factors predicate one’s social standing in Randani society: class, lineage, and skill. Any one of these suffices to secure influence and wealth, but true power lies at the intersection of all three.

During the island’s wars of unification, tribal classes and castes experienced their own upheaval; new ones formed, old ones became obsolete, and others blended together or splintered. Today only two true castes

EX3

remain: pechin and heimin. Pechin are Randan’s aristocracy, trained as warrior-artisans with power, prestige, and authority; heimin are everyone else, from wealthy merchants to base beggars. To be pechin is to be born pechin. Only adoption or queenly decree can change that.

Pechin families claim descent from ancient thaumaturges, their secret rituals passed down for centuries. These rituals are jealously guarded; some can only be performed in Randan itself, their workings tied to ancient sorceries on the island. Not all members of a family possess the inborn talent necessary to command this power — often, lineages pass their thaumaturgical secrets to only one or two gifted scions. Pechin families even adopt heimin children who demonstrate the gift, paying birth parents a hefty fee. While the Randani take a dim view of chattel slavery, they grudgingly deal with slavers to purchase and adopt foreign children with thaumaturgical talent.

Skill, then, is the only avenue open to anyone regardless of birth. Originally founded by pechin and still dominated by them, the craft-lodges are the most hallowed Randani institutions, equal parts guild and temple. The pechin have always used craft and artistry to honor

their gods, lands, and selves, practicing their chosen vocation as devotion and meditation. Master artisans, whether pechin or heimin, often rise to great prominence as artists, scholars, and saints. The island’s mythology honors grandmasters like gods; children are weaned on stories of figures like the Three ArtisanQueens, the Red-Anvil Sage, or Danurme of the Holy Loom.

The highest social class, the pekumi, consists of pechin who’ve mastered all three noble arts of warfare, crafting, and thaumaturgy. By law and tradition, only pekumi may hold the highest offices in the craft-lodges and Randan’s government. Even pechin of the most refined lineages must acknowledge the authority of pekumi of lesser origins.

### The Craft-Lodges

All but the most hopeless pechin belong to a craft-lodge as a matter of tradition and dignity. The beating heart of Randani tradition, each lodge is devoted to the pursuit and perfection of a single craft. Typically, lodges define their crafts broadly; for instance, the Smiths’ Lodge includes all metalworkers, while the Weavers’

EX3

Lodge encompasses threadmakers, tailors, and the like. While talented heimin can rise high within the lodges, only pekumi may claim a seat on the lodge’s guiding council and a voice in its governance.

### A RANDANI FABLE: THE DEMON QUEENS

Legend tells of an age when three demons — Lanthild, Shaper of the Mind’s Clay; Berengiere, the Weaver of Voices; and Alveua, Keeper of the Forge of Night — held the village of Randan in thrall. The people were helpless before the demon-queens’ whims until three women stepped forward to confront them. “You claim we’re yours to toy with because we’re not your equals,” the women said. “But we say we can match your gifts and your strengths.” So they challenged the demons to a contest, with Randan itself as the prize.

Young pechin and those few heimin admitted by talent, fee, or charity receive a rigorous education in rhetoric, history, mathematics, philosophy, and law, as well as the many logistical and artistic skills required for that lodge’s craft. Their adolescence is punctuated with tests and trials, and when they come of age they stand before three of the lodge’s councilors in one of its secret sanctums to negotiate their future. Elders take great interest in talented young artisans’ paths, laying out detailed designs for their futures. Those of lesser promise receive appointments as bureaucrats, traders, or functionaries.

The demons laughed. What mortal could put dreams in a jar, weave voices into fabric, or bind a soul into a blade? They accepted, seeing no harm in the jest. A week passed before the first woman, a potter, brought a jug to Lanthild. “This is my best work,” she said, “for as I threw it and turned it and fired it, I knew that all I love depended on my success. All my dreams are in this jug; if it should fail, all my hopes fail with it.” And Lanthild cursed, for she knew she’d lost.

Each craft-lodge offers patronage for Randani merchants, tradesfolk, and laborers involved with the lodge’s craft. For example, the Weavers’ Lodge licenses and oversees production of cotton, hemp, and silk throughout Randan’s territories, and employs thousands of laborers as rag-pickers, dyers, and assistants. Tradesfolk pass their trade from generation to generation, becoming unofficial vassals to a lodge. Loyal or distinguished families earn recognition from their patron craft-lodge; exceptional service is often rewarded with better pay and prestige.

Another week passed before the second woman, a weaver, brought a tapestry to Berengiere. She couldn’t speak, so she drew her message in the sand. This is my best work, she wrote, for as I spun and wove and embroidered it, I sang my people’s songs until my throat was raw, and then sang until my throat was a mass of scars. I’ve given my voice to the tapestry, for I can never speak again. And Berengiere cursed, for she knew she’d lost.

Some lodges establish sprawling complexes where shippers deliver raw materials for laborers to prepare. For instance, Smiths’ Lodge foundries receive coal, iron, copper, tin, and other ingredients of a blacksmith’s craft. Under the lodge’s watchful eye, tradesmen work raw metal into ingots, create vital alloys, and shape tools and armaments for their pekumi overlords’ use. Whether as assistants or laborers, employment by a lodge is the surest path to security in Randan, offering escape from life as a fisher, trader, or cutpurse. Merchants who deal in a lodge’s craft — or the raw materials thereof — answer to its pekumi. Those wishing to sell the lodge’s wares directly must fund their operations with money borrowed from the lodge itself, creating a financial debt to match the moral debt a merchant owes her artisans. These loans accrue little interest, but artisans consider it a provocation to repay them in full, as doing so would effectively end a merchant’s relationship with that craft-lodge.

Greater and Lesser Lodges

The Potters’, Weavers’, and Smiths’ Lodges stand above the rest. Their social clout derives in large part from

And as she finished the blade, she died. She’s given her soul to the sword.” And Alveua cursed, for she knew she’d lost. Since then, no demon has ruled in Randan. And the potter, weaver, and blacksmith were praised above all others, and their daughters were named chiefs of the village. This is why artisans now rule in Randan.

Their products’ importance throughout Randani society and in trade bolster their economic strength, allowing them to outbid or bribe their way into staying on top, and to get first bid on adopting heimin and foreign thaumaturges.

Several lesser lodges jockey for power and position. These include the Brewers’, Cooks’, Leatherworkers’, Masons’, and Shipwrights’ Lodges.

### Society and Culture

Randani homes are one-story affairs, their wooden outer walls decorated with white limestone. Sliding panels open to let the breeze flow throughout the house. Red pottery tiles typically cover their sloped roofs, though poorer heimin families make do with thatch. Builders form stonework structures by stacking stones without mortar; some feature elaborate geometric patterns that are beautiful to look at and maintain the structure’s integrity if a stone is damaged or removed. Arches are common features of bridges, covered walkways, and monuments.

Randani fashion features robes with long, flowing sleeves dyed with rich pigments. Pechin tend to wear silks, while heimin wear more affordable linen. Elaborate embroidery decorates Randani clothing for all but the poorest, and wide-brimmed felt hats are common accessories. Most grow their hair long, bringing it up in a bun and holding it in place with a hairpin. Blue hair is favored; people with other hair colors often dye it with indigo.

Vegetables and fruits comprise much of Randani cuisine, with dishes featuring purple sweet potatoes, taro root, and bitter melon. Fish such as mackerel and tilapia are common and versatile ingredients, whether they’re fried, pickled, grilled, or used in soups with flavorful seaweed broth suffusing sea lettuce, bird’s-nest fern, or squid ink. Pork is also prominent in Randani meals. Home cooks and chefs alike waste very little of the animal; beyond meals of perfectly cooked tenderloin and sumptuous pork belly, Randani eat marinated roasted hearts, crispy pig’s ears, black pudding, panhaas, and more. Pechin consume more meat, eggs, and spices than heimin; their dishes also include white rice, red fermented bean curd, and a wide variety of baked sweets.

### Governance

Randan’s queens trace their lineage back to the valiant women who freed the island from demonic overlords in an age of myth. The queen’s court technically includes all pekumi, but in practice, only the craft-lodges’ representatives, city administrators, admirals, and similar high-ranking officials join her advisory secretariat. When a queen dies, those same advisors choose

her successor from among the pekumi of the Lodges of Smiths, Potters, or Weavers, in recognition of those craft-lodges’ legendary preeminence as Randan’s saviors.

The queen holds limited authority; each craft-lodge oversees areas related to its purview. The craft-lodges’ ruling councils push their supporters in the Queen’s court to propose policy changes that redirect power to their lodges. For example, the Smiths’ Lodge now oversees all of the military’s outfitting and provisioning, forcing the queen to consult with them on new conquests. Meanwhile, the Weavers’ Lodge lobbies for control of trade outside its usual purview. The Potters’ Lodge treads carefully — Randan’s current queen, Dove White Sky, was elevated from their lodge, and while they’d like to secure power for a time when another craft-lodge holds the throne, overstepping now might cause the others to unite against them. While the three greater lodges’ cultural importance remains undisputed, the lesser lodges seek opportunities to achieve similar political power. More and more, they see the larger lodges broadening the definition of what’s under their control, arrogating power not only from the Queen, but also from the lesser lodges’ spheres of influence. To combat this, pekumi from lesser lodges often vote as a bloc, advise one another, or provide a united front backing the queen.

One concern ties the lodges together: that a queen might show her own craft-lodge favoritism or grant it permanent control of the throne. While the pekumi of the Potters’ Lodge would happily claim such power, they fear that the elderly Dove White Sky would die before cementing such authority, allowing a successor from another lodge to reap the benefits. The queen may convene her court at any time to propose an edict, including levying new taxes, changing a law, signing a treaty, or pressing a war. All attendees may submit their own petitions — such as funding for their cities, official censure of certain personages, or a ruling on other grievances — but only those on the queen’s secretariat may vote.

### Religion

Since time immemorial, the Randani have venerated two local spirit courts. Officers and soldiers alike praise the war-gods of the Glittering Spear Court; the craft-lodges make offerings to the artisan-gods of the Earthly Ministry of Western Crafts; and the pekumi

EX3

### THAUMATURGY IN RANDAN

The greatest Randani masterworks combine artistry and thaumaturgy, giving form to beauty and Essence alike. The wealthy array themselves and their retainers with singing stones, coldfire cloaks, and brocade armor, but there are too few thaumaturges for these enchanted treasures to pass into common use. Each represents a significant investment of time and resources from a master thaumaturgist and must be treated with reverence. These procedures require a basic or major craft project appropriate to the item’s scope, using at least one exotic ingredient that resonates with the ritual. Unless otherwise specified, these procedures are mutually exclusive; one object can’t possess multiple enchantments.

Seven-Sided Sheets (•)

In the Bookbinders’ Lodge, cunning paper-makers create this paper using a thick pulp of fiber and human tears. Each sheet can be turned over up to six times, each time revealing a unique side in addition to the first. This magic fails if the sheet is bound into a book or other compendium. Pekumi officers use these sheets for correspondence, hiding sensitive information from those unfamiliar with the process, typically by writing the first two pages in triplicate, and either hiding additional material on the seventh or encoding it in slight differences between the duplicate pages. Magic that deciphers hidden messages can detect and analyze this trick. Finding the Stone’s Soul (••)

Among the most striking procedures known to the Randani, this rite allows a sculptor to imbue their work with a faint echo of life. Moving with slow, dreamlike grace, these statues obey simple instructions and deliver messages through gestures and body language; they can’t perform complex or strenuous activities. Delicate engravings cover their bodies, damage to which ruins their magic.

Brocade Armor (••)

One of Randan’s best-known thaumaturgical arts allows Weavers’ Lodge thaumaturges to spin armor from silk ritually harvested by innocent children. Strong as iron and infinitely more comfortable, under casual inspection, brocade armor appears as nothing more than ostentatious clothing, although those familiar with the style recognize its unique embroidery. Similar two-dot rites exist to allow skilled artisans to use other unorthodox materials for their creations. Individual families sometimes maintain proprietary rituals not shared with the rest of the craft-lodge — for example, the Amarumi family know the secrets of folding paper into wickedly sharp knives, the Oka bake mighty shields of lacquered clay which can hold back a battering ram without shattering, and the Kon craft crystal flutes which can mimic the songs of a hundred different birds.

revere both. While the heimin venerate various divinities of weather, grain, sea, and fish, they too acknowledge the gods of these two courts as Randan’s divine champions, and worship them accordingly.

Worship-hungry gods have also spurred Randan’s colonial ambitions, blessing the ships and soldiers of pekumi willing to bring new islands under Randan’s banner. Conquered lands’ gods must submit to the Randani pantheon just as their people submit to the queen and

her pekumi, lest their temples be cast down and their

priesthoods stamped out.

EX3

The greatest pekumi — those whose excellence exceeds even their peers — sometimes wed Randani gods, though rarely more than as a matter of ceremony. It often takes decades for a pekumi to reach such preeminence, meaning this honor is usually bestowed upon older Randani. God-Blooded children born of these unions live as retainers to their godly parents, with no claim to a mortal caste or lodge. To the Randani, having the blood of immortals in one’s veins is so advantageous that such a child cedes the ability to prove their worth on their own terms.

Randani priesthood requires that its pechin leaders serve as mediators and diplomats. Though the Randani spirit courts maintain a begrudging peace, they’re still prone to petty squabbles. Centuries-old slights intermittently rear their heads, causing upset among worshipers and craft-lodges. Often, the quarrelling gods’ clergy arrange games and challenges to appease their deities and release tension between them, such as district-wide war games, sailing contests, crafting competitions, or grand hunts.

Noteworthy Gods of Randan

Foremost among the Randani war-gods is Qulu the Thunderer, a spirit of victory who blesses warriors to feel neither pain, fear, nor mercy. He sees in Randan’s long peace the beginnings of complacency and decline. Many Randani from conquered lands still tell stories of how Banner Ablaze took to the field like a comet to strike down their great-great-grandparents. Desiring fiery battlefield prayer over staid temple worship, she encourages priests and fellow war-gods to embroil Randan in armed conflict.

Each year, gods of a different craft hold ascendancy over the artisan-gods’ court. This year, the weaving-god Jesmera Silk-Spinner oversees her peers from her sanctum, its entrance a shrine gate in a sacred mulberry grove outside Ohdanu. Members of the Weaver’s Lodge sing songs praising her as they weave sails for Randan’s fleet.

Foremost patron of the Brewers’ Lodge, Joyous Ahina is beloved throughout Randan. Adherents crush dried hops in ritual offerings; wedding guests scatter barley before newlyweds to wish them luck and happiness. The war-herald Bloodheed, whose drums resound with the songs of the earth itself, counts both soldiers and members of the Musicians’ Lodge among his followers. His shamans beat cadences on sacred instruments for raiding warriors.

### Prominent Figures

Randan’s aging queen, Dove White Sky, is renowned as a shrewd peacemaker and diplomat. Though a merely competent artisan in the Potters’ Lodge, Dove distinguished herself as a brilliant thaumaturge, enchanting flasks to cleanse water, stopper fire, or bottle a seabreeze. As queen, she’s served as a mediator between the spirit courts. Despite her efforts, the patron deities of Randan hold fast to their bitter feuds. She fears her death will destabilize the precarious peace she’s created.

A leading voice among the pekumi, Joje u Sen WhoConquers-All oversees Kinele, the forested province that girds the city to its west and north. Lest other powers begin eyeing Randan’s ports, she advocates for a preemptive show of strength, punishing the nearby city-state of Okudo for encroaching on Randani trade routes. Dove White Sky has rejected her proposals, but Sen’s impassioned speeches and sharply worded correspondence sway increasingly more pekumi to her way of thinking. Sen has assembled a small private fleet of mercenaries and privateers, seeking to provoke a conflict that that justifies broader military action. Rui u Ekoyu of the Forge-Hymn is perhaps the greatest swordmaster his craft-lodge has known in three generations, and a talented thaumaturge to boot. He’d be on the lodge’s guiding council were he not the lowborn son of a pauper and a foreigner, a situation that makes him bitter and vindictive. He’s also a vociferous advocate for peace who’s unafraid to step outside his position to deride pekumi warmongers as irresponsible and foolish. Ekoyu’s activism has garnered many political enemies and more than one assassination attempt; he bears the scars with pride.

Lapdog Dejoku is both native and foreign — a Randani ship’s carpenter by birth, the Guild-backed Golden Anchor Company bought him as a slave from Lintha slavers who seized his ship in his youth. Over the last twenty years, he charmed his way from a life of shackles to the luxuries of an envoy for the Directorate. His current charge: to open Randan’s markets to Guild merchants, for which other Randani name him “Lapdog.” He wears the insult with good humor and patience, seeking every opportunity to insinuate himself into the city’s affairs and intrigues. He’s already amassed several important debtors, including pekumi who now serve as his puppets, advocating for the Guild and its interests. Beddu Scythe-swinger is sometimes called the Hermit Crab, for her coastal home resembles a wet

EX3

Xhe for raw silk harvested from the enormous moths who gorge themselves on the island’s mulberry forests. Pechin governors oversee these colonies; forever pursuing efficiency, they press islanders to meet strict quotas or face the lash. The islands see regular rebellions, especially Anem Arehima, whose priesthoods waylay unwitting Randani visitors with lesser spirits of water, rock, and vine.

### RANDANI TRIBUTARIES

Islands that accept Randan as suzerain pay regular tribute: lumber for shipbuilding and soldiers to stand on the front lines in raids and wars. They also agree to trade key raw materials exclusively with Randan, forcing its rivals to procure those goods from Randan at a steep markup or seek them elsewhere in the West.

The City That Sails is a federation of pirates and brigands, bound together by their loyalty to one another and to their newly chosen king, Imil Inkhand. They’ve found strength in numbers and coordination, harrying Randani ships and raiding vulnerable colonies. The Guild-affiliated Pelican Hull Company privately backs these operations, its merchant princes eager to break Randan’s stranglehold on the region.

In return, tributaries receive beneficial trade terms and such economic support as food during famine or tools to improve artisans’ production. Randan protects tributaries from outside raiders, though that protection is also a message: break with Randan and become a target — not only of enemies circling like sharks, but of Randan itself.

sandcastle adorned with a mosaic of shell fragments. Once a pekumi scion to the Weavers’ Lodge, Beddu was a rare sorcerous prodigy capable of enchantments beyond thaumaturgy. In her hubris, she sought greater knowledge and power, finally turning to diabolism. For this, Dove White Sky stripped Beddu of all rights and titles. Piqued, the sorcerer exiled herself to a meager spit of rock and scrubgrass off the coast, where she continues her practices in isolation. Those in need still seek her out, offering spiced wine and rare herbs to win her favor. But they come quietly, lest rumor of diabolism cling to them also.

### Neighbors

The nearby polity of Okudo was once a Randani tributary, providing timber, coal, rare herbs, and healing lore. But during the devastating storms of RY 654, its leaders found opportunity to rebel. Embittered by its long subordination, the nation now raids Randani shipping whenever possible, daring its former masters to test its expanding navy and coastal forts. Okudo recently seized the murex-producing Randani tributary of Eo-ah, erecting coastal forts from which to gather the mollusks and their dye. This provocation has led many pekumi to call for war, but while Okudo’s fleet isn’t Randan’s equal, it’s strong enough that a prolonged conflict might leave Randan and its colonies vulnerable to other powers of the West. Randani merchants travel a well-known circuit from one Western vassalage to the next: Anem Arehima for ivory, Jesim for perfume, Galagi for spices, and

## Manigal

Once, the great island of Manigal was ruled from the sea.

Long ago, the semiaquatic ancestor people rose from the waves to settle Manigal’s shores. Plumbing the island’s First Age ruins for lost lore, they built the marvelous library-city Tomil Teb as a repository for that knowledge and a seat for their princes. The ancestor people initially split their lives between the sea and the land, but a caste system developed that placed the land-bound farmers — who became today’s Manigalese — firmly at the bottom. Ruling from their library-palace, the ancestor nobility became tyrannous, backed by their scavenged magic and their control of the dreadful elemental sihl-kidi.

Then the hero Moqon came from across the sea. Rallying the Manigalese, he waged an insurgency from the forested hills. Searching the innumerable cays surrounding the island, their forces discovered and seized several of the hidden creche-atolls where the ancestor people made their progeny amphibious, demanding their enemies’ surrender lest the children perish. The Manigalese deposed and executed the ancestor people’s old dynasty, clearing the way for today’s ruling Ponolei dynasty.

The treaty between the ancestor people’s new Ponolei dynasty and the land-dwelling leadership stipulates that the Manigalese provide food and other surface goods to the ancestor people. In exchange, the ancestor people offer seafloor treasures; further, they may not

EX3

set foot on Manigal proper, enter Tomil Teb unless to offer tribute, or speak to any Manigalese but the sarawi caste of scholar-priests.

For centuries, they’ve maintained an uneasy peace. But the ancestor people — suffering from raids by the elemental sihl-kidi who once served them — have begun raiding the land once more to take what they can no longer easily bargain for. Meanwhile, foreigners who’ve gathered at Tomil Teb’s gate grow in number, and some among them agitate to seize what they will from the library-city rather than wait upon the sarawis’ pleasure. Manigal now finds itself pressed from two sides.

### The Islanders

Islanders live in small farming and fishing communities across the island’s ten districts. They tend orchards of breadfruit, moringa, carambola, coconut, orange banana, and candlenut in Mehlel District; harvest precious hardwoods and medicines from Ingale District’s upland forests; husband pigs and domestic fowl in Nubue District; and keep plots of taro, peppercorn, and sweet potato in Kinolu District. They hunt flying foxes — the only mammals native to the island — and various birds for meat. Some keep cats and terriers procured from foreigners to winnow the rats that arrived on trading ships; these are prepared much like flying foxes.

The Manigalese pride themselves on their egalitarianism, a trait that distinguishes them from the ancestor people in their eyes. Each district is governed by a wahnmark: a provincial leader elected from among the district’s heads of household. Each wahnmark is responsible for the families in her district, ensuring that they’re kept safe, their disputes are resolved, and their storehouses remain full. These storehouses feed both the sarawi and the ancestor people; without this surplus, the surface-dwellers lose their trading advantage over their aquatic neighbors, and librarians starve. Hospitality is essential among the Manigalese. Hosts greet guests with plates of nuts, roasted breadfruit, or taro fritters. During the course of the visit, they often tell stories over cups of kava grog.

Manigalese warriors patrol the seas in small, quick skiffs, particularly around Tomil Teb. From these, they defend against both raiders and any potential insurgence of the ancestor people from beneath the waves. They make armor from the scales of a local fish; the scales are hard enough to protect them from a weapon’s impact but buoyant enough not to drag them down

if they’re pulled into the water. Cleverly designed cords set them free with a swift tug should they begin to sink. The warriors are proficient with harpoons and polespears — the weapons’ long reach grants advantage over both human swimmers and aquatic predators.

### Tomil Teb

Since Moqon’s time, the scholar-priests of the sarawi caste have dwelt among the bones and scrolls of the sacred city Tomil Teb, spread across a tiny artificial archipelago off the coast of the island Manigal. Within its walls — outside of which they hold no formal power — they guard the border of the ancestor people’s undersea dominion, pray to Manigal’s gods, and bury the dead. No others may enter without their leave. The scratchings of sarawi pens whisper long into the tropical evenings as they recopy texts before their pages succumb to brine and damp. From across the West, from Brightwork, Onyx, and Randan, seekers come to study in Tomil Teb’s hundred libraries, or to bargain with the sarawi for treasures that the ancestor people once scavenged from the seafloor. More foreigners arrive every day; they grow restless waiting for their turn to enter the city.

Shape of the City

Tomil Teb is an archipelago of blocky artificial islets, platforms framed in stone and filled with crushed coral, set in a wide lagoon on Manigal’s west coast. A web of rope bridges connects the islets, and a seawall of columnar basalt girds them against approaches by water. Recently, carpenters erected a wooden palisade on the shore in response to increasingly frequent raids. Four are the city’s gates. Karakar Gate and Palikapi Gate stand on the beach, ancient edifices of patinaed bronze that open onto quays where ferrymen tie reed boats. Liliabi Gate and Kepenar Gate puncture the seawall, arches of black stone that allow ingress from both above and beneath the waves.

Sarawi and visitors alike don hardwood geta when traveling the islets’ streets, lest the razor-sharp coral fill slice their feet. Stalls selling or renting them set up every morning at the city’s gates. Even protected, locals walk Tomil Teb’s streets with a careful, deliberate gait.

The Sarawi

Ruling in a vast collegial squabble, the sarawi are a hereditary caste of academics and religious officials, numbering a few hundred. Mortuary-librarians comprise the College of Bones, which maintains the city’s

EX3

collection and perform burial rites. Diving-apostles from the College of Pearls are diplomats and merchants, arranging the customary exchanges between surface and deeps. Between them, the two Colleges manage the city’s prodigious wealth, accumulated through library access fees and taxes on foreign trade with the ancestor people. They disburse treasure to fund diplomatic missions and to acquire new texts. Tomil Teb’s libraries serve as both repositories of knowledge and as ossuaries. The city’s largest library, Refuge Stone, has three stories above ground and two beneath the surface. Other islet-libraries are single-story affairs aboveground, with ossuary-cellars carved out beneath. The Manigalese burn their dead on ghats cut into the shoreline; then, the mortuary-librarians integrate the decedents’ bones into new library stacks. Only Refuge Stone holds sarawi remains. On the rare occasion a ghost rises, sawari exorcists put them swiftly to rest.

The city’s collection spans vast ranges of scholarship. The mortuary-librarians carefully keep the organizational system a cipher, preventing foreigners from navigating it should they evade their sarawi chaperones.

A single mortuary-librarian oversees each islet with hand-picked staff; the Colleges assign them in annual council.

At a plaza just inside Kepenar Gate, sarawi diving-apostles receive the ancestor peoples’ tribute each month from below. It’s a formal process, full of ritual obeisance on the part of the ancestor people, after which the sarawi accept the offered treasure and hand over the produce that the sea-dwellers need to sustain themselves. At Tomil Teb’s center stands the market-platform called Earth Mound, where foreigners peruse treasures dredged up from the depths. Prospective buyers pay a fee to the Colleges to enter, then must bargain with individual apostles for offerings like gemstones that purify water, clockworks far in advance of current technology, rare corals, and troves of pearls. At sunset, a rush of black wings emerges from the libraries’ narrow stone doors. These bats are tame, kept as pets and as pest control to deal with Manigal’s incessant mosquitoes. Apprentice librarians regularly clean guano from the bat lofts; this the sarawi give to the Manigalese as fertilizer.

### The Ancestor Peoples

### PALIKAPI

Beneath the waves, Manigal’s true scope becomes evident. A massive seamount, its craggy slopes descend gently into the dark; the visible island was the peak of a much larger landmass until ancient catastrophe sent it crashing down. Profuse seagrass meadows and reef gardens grow across what were once verdant foothills.

So long is the wait to gain access to Tomil Teb that foreigners have formed a rude township — called Palikapi — on the shore outside Palikapi Gate. Recently, the population has boomed; for several years, there have been more foreigners than sarawi. The shacks and shanties spill up the beach, cookfires burning into the night, accompanied by the shouts of drunks and gamblers.

Among the brilliant coral seascapes hide patches of filmy, flickering light. An old magic originally meant to ward off floods, tidal waves, and driving rain, these gossamer shields mark entrances to the ancestor peoples’ settlements. They’re the original inhabitants of Manigal and the builders of Tomil Teb, descendants of those few who were able to seal themselves away when catastrophe struck.

Foreigners raise goats, cows, and other domesticated animals in Palikapi. Many maintain shops or carts hawking outlander goods such as oil, wine, glassware, textiles, and iron tools. An increasing share of the island’s food surplus goes to Palikapi; some worry that this won’t leave enough to meet Manigal’s treaty obligations to the ancestor people.

Prominent Figures

Iawasa Menseng Teb serves on the city’s treasure-disbursement council and is the mortuary-librarian for Refuge Stone. It’s said that nothing happens in the library without Iawasa hearing about it. Some whisper she has a network of spirit-spies, but she does much of the eavesdropping herself; she knows every hidden nook and alcove in Refuge Stone. People across the city venerate her for her long years of service, for leading the library’s defense against raiders, and unshakable calm in the face of foreigner and ancestor folk provocations. She nurses a decades-long grudge against the ancestor people for kidnapping her only child. Pehri Ketieu is the wahnmark from Mehlel District, within whose borders Palikapi lies. A controversial figure, she takes a hardline stance against Palikapi’s growth that borders on xenophobic. This conflicts with deeply-held Manigalese ideals of hospitality, but many cannot help but share her unease. She invites other wahnmarks to visit and see the changes foreigners have wrought in her district, seeking their support and hoping they’ll take it as a warning for what might befall their own districts.

Jeddei the Broker, a Randani merchant residing in Palikapi, has made several profitable tours through the libraries, coming away with trade secrets that have enriched her craft-lodge. She hasn’t failed to notice the increasing numbers — and armament — of her fellow foreigners in Palikapi. A clever woman, she’s covertly ingratiated herself with those planning a raid so she gets a share, while preparing to warn the sarawi in exchange for reward if a raid seems likely to fail.

The ancestor people stand taller than the Manigalese, though they share the same dark complexion and curly hair. They wear colorful woven lavalavas featuring stripes and geometric patterns, and jewelry made from coral and shell. They can hold their breath for hours, but still must breathe. A scavenger folk, they comb both the ruins of settlements destroyed when old Manigal sank, and seafloor ruins from lost benthic civilization. They trade scavenged treasures to other undersea peoples for rare coral from the voracious Reefeater League, jewels of nacre from the sessile spongefolk beneath the Utterstorm Gyre, and the like. They hand relics and jewels alike over to Tomil Teb’s diving-apostles in exchange for surface goods — weapons, tools, and foodstuffs and spices unavailable beneath the sea. They worship gods of coral and ocean brine to whom they build shrines on the reefs, guiding the coral into magnificent living temples. Many leave offerings of smaller fish for the spirits to ensure a bountiful catch of milkfish and blue trevally, or to gain their blessing against attacks from sharks and other predators.

They call their benthic city Karoun Kan-Neng. Hidden in the coral-crusted slopes, its tunnels wind deep into the seamount. Here, the ancestor people conceal laboratories and workshops where scavenger-captains can bring their finds to clean and tinker with, along with sleeping areas, kitchens, and other amenities. The same magic that seals their pocket homes generates a thin atmosphere for the ancestor people within, but the airflow is weak and sometimes unreliable. This restricts their ability to cook food to a handful of scavenged smokeless First Age cooking devices.

EX3

The waters around Karoun Kan-Neng are clear and bright. There, the ancestor people have built elaborate coral gardens in which they take their leisure, sunning themselves or hunting jewel-bright fish with nets and spears. Fresh fish is often served raw, cubed and tossed with oil and sea salt. Other popular dishes include milkfish steamed in taro leaves, mixed seafood ceviche, yam and banana salad, and thick sweet poi. They sleep and cook within their city, but otherwise spend their time in the water, communicating in a sophisticated sign language. The grandest of these gardens is the Reef of Heaven, where the ruling Ponolei dynasty holds court among a profusion of anemones and sea lilies.
