Unlike the Manigalese, the ancestor people are governed by an aristocracy, with the Ponolei set above a handful of backbiting noble broods. Most ancestor people are effectively indentured servants, beholden to one of the noble families, performing menial labor to earn their place in the city, or in the handful of smaller settlements sheltered by similar magic. Most such labor takes the form of scavenging; there are still troves of relics to be found among old Manigal’s ruins and beyond.

Prominent Ancestor People

Social mobility follows two avenues. Successful and wily scavengers can marry into a noble family to become scavenger-captains, or parents may secure their children’s futures by pledging them to the Surgeons’ Guild. The Surgeons are doctors and thaumaturges who maintain and oversee the creche-atolls where newborn ancestor people are reared. Children who fail out of the Surgeons’ rigorous practical examinations are shamed and returned to their families.

Desertion would be bad enough, but the sihl-kidi — embittered by a servitude they long ago came to resent — have actively turned on their former masters. Over the years, as the ancestor people’s infighting enervated their defenses, the elementals’ depredations grew more frequent. Where once they were threats to individuals straying from the safe waters around Karoun Kan-Neng, now the sihl-kidi hunt scavenging parties of ancestor people for sport, making such expeditions more dangerous than they’ve ever been.

Ponolei Kalanueh, prince of the ancestor people, displays the arrogance and self-absorption common to his dynasty. When not indulging in music, dance, or raids against other peoples of the deep, he plays favorites among the aristocracy, having affairs with others’ spouses or delivering outsized punishments for trivial slights. Huge, strong, and keenly alert, Kalanueh has survived two assassination attempts, feeding the would-be killers to his shark familiar Ango. Thus far, this has dissuaded further attempts, and many aristocrats still seek his fickle favor. But a sufficiently outrageous act on his part may yet turn the tide against him. Mahluki Kaselel, head of the Surgeons’ Guild, seeks an answer to the sihl-kidi’s increased aggression.

Sihl-Kidi

The sihl-kidi are elementals unique to Manigal, born when cold abyssal waters rise to meet the tropical waters of the island’s shelf. They resemble seals, though hazy and indistinct: ghosts of dark water that glide through the sea. When angered, they erupt in a fury of foam and bubbles, tripling in size and unsheathing vicious fangs of black ice. In this form, they resemble terrible mastiffs surrounded by a sharp aura of menace. Once, the sihl-kidi served as enforcers and pack beasts, dragging blocks of basalt from the seafloor to build Tomil Teb itself. In their hound forms, they rode down dissenters and fugitives from the ancestor peoples’ rule. But the ancient pact that bound them required the ancestor people to deliver them victims to maul. After the ancestor people surrendered to Moqon and the wahnmarks, however, they couldn’t deliver enough victims to the sihl-kidi, who broke the pact and abandoned their masters. As a result, the ancestor people have been

EX3

### CRECHE-ATOLLS

The ancestor people are not only born but made. Their enhanced lung capacity is the result of a thaumaturgic procedure performed by the Surgeons on children between six and twelve months of age. This procedure must be undertaken on land; the atmosphere is too poor in Karoun Kan-Neng. Before Moqon’s uprising, Tomil Teb contained the primary creches, but space considerations required the ancestor people to construct several external sites hidden among the hundreds of cays comprising the atolls surrounding Manigal.

Sawari records retain the locations of the crecheatolls, though this is a sensitive subject. There’s a long history of kidnapping on both sides of the sea, whether Manigalese “rescuing” infants from crecheatolls or ancestor people stealing Manigalese infants to supplement their diminishing numbers. One of the diving-apostles’ primary roles is keeping the peace when babies are either given, or denied, the transformation that makes them ancestor people.

Unwilling to ask others to take risks she wouldn’t take herself, she leads Surgeons out to the edge of the abyss surrounding Manigal, hoping to glean knowledge from sihl-kidi spawning grounds. If she finds a new way to bind them to her people’s will, so much the better. Kaselel speaks bluntly and makes no attempt to soften bad news; she respects those who do the same. The scavenger-captain Heale Ahmwek climbed to join the ancestor people’s nobility through marriage. Born to a servant family, he’s old, cunning, and well-liked among the indentured. He deeply resents the sarawi, considering them usurpers and do-nothings, leeching off the hard work of better people like himself. As scavenging becomes more difficult, he’s begun to speak openly, attempting to inflame sentiment against the land-dwellers.

### Neighbors

The Wi’ohu Clans steal unseen across the waves. They hail from a chain of mist-shrouded, long-dormant volcanic islands with fertile soil and two-faced stone heads keeping watch along the shore. The clans never speak the names of their homelands, which aren’t recorded on any map that can be found in sarawi records. The Wi’ohu would know — they were the ones who erased the references.

Wi’ohu thaumaturges can bring the gray mist that hides their homes along with them, concealing raiding parties and scouting expeditions. Properly conjured, the mists induce forgetfulness and pliability, allowing the Wi’ohu to enter where they will and leave without being detected. An insidious scourge on the waters, Fair Folk of the Pearl Knife Company pilot sleek caravels and hulking galleons crewed by goblin sailors. They arrive in port with holds full of impossible treasures that they exchange for slaves. But their contracts’ slippery terms twist in the mind; a slaver may find herself chained beside her former inventory without remembering how she arrived there. Only the sarawi seem to ever come out ahead in their dealings with the Company, whose merchant-nobles — as hungry for knowledge as for souls — pay princely sums to access Tomil Teb’s libraries.

They have no clear leader, but Captain Twelve-Night stands notorious among them as a merchant-trickster. His caravel, The Heart’s Desire, is a silvered shard of

dream that appears in the evening. He’s a graceful creature with fine white hair piled atop his head who decks himself in an outfit of velveteen spangled in bright brass buttons. He wines and dines potential business partners and delights in trapping them in webs of their own avarice.

## Makelo

At the heart of the sprawling Western island of Sinti, the Ukama people endured the Contagion and invading Fair Folk within the caverns beneath A’fi Mountain under the forge-goddess Ninegala’s protection. From her, they learned the arts of smithcraft, mastering them to a degree unmatched by their neighbors.

Emerging from the mountain after the plagues ended, the survivors founded the city of Makelo. Applying the skills that Ninegala taught them in new ways, they’ve made incredible advancements in agriculture, construction, engineering — and war. Over the centuries, they’ve conquered all of Sinti, subjugating rival peoples while driving out the fae. Today their gaze extends to lands beyond their shores.

### Social Structure

The empire of Makelo consists of over a dozen peoples. The dominant Ukama people descend from the empire’s founders, while the other peoples descend from Makeloan conquests. These include the mountain-dwelling Canta, who served as mercenaries in Sinti’s wars, and still indulge in raiding and banditry; the cosmopolitan Tolo and their many ports, who once ruled much of Sinti; and the dragon-worshiping Askuë, a fiercely independent people currently embroiled in internal strife.

The Ukama divide themselves into a score of clans. The emperor and the clan chiefs sit at the top of the social ladder along with their family members, followed by those in other positions of authority: priests, artisans, metallurgists, and war leaders. Together, these form the nobility. Commoners include farmers, fishermen, hunters, and manual laborers. Slaves — often prisoners of war from Makeloan conquests — comprise the lowest class. Each other Makeloan people has its own prince, subservient only to the emperor. Their social structures vary, though most share many similarities.

EX3

### Culture

milk, onions, and tomatoes. Dumplings and breadfruit drizzled with coconut syrup make for a sweet dessert.

Makeloan handiworks fetch handsome prices throughout the region. Artisans — particularly among the Ukama — are primarily known for metalwork; metallurgists coax iron from Sinti’s black sands and extract other metals from raw ore. Smiths turn out sturdy weapons, intricate ironwork, and precisely molded components for engineering projects. Woodworkers, sculptors, masons, and engineers from across the West seek Makeloan tools to create superior works.

Most Makeloan peoples have little interest in foreign trade. This allows the Toloan people to dominate maritime commerce. Many other Makeloans stereotype them as greedy, wealth-obsessed, materialistic, and vain. The Toloans, for their part, deem themselves cosmopolitan, hiring foreign artists, artisans, and scholars to beautify their city. They grow imported fruits and vegetables such as oranges, peaches, spinach, and onions, melding them with Western spices to form a vital new cuisine. Dishes include pork shoulder simmered in bitter orange juice with garlic and spices, cassowary stewed with coconut milk and tamarind, cardamom-spiced peaches sautéed in ghee and khoya, and sweet onions stuffed with breadcrumbs, cheese, and herbs.

The island’s mines not only yield copper but also tin — rare in the West — allowing Makelo to produce sought-after bronze. Most miners are slaves; they labor deep below the ground, their lives considered expendable should they be lost in a collapse. Fishing is also a major industry on Sinti. Fisherfolk of the coastal tribes venture out in long outrigger canoes to catch catfish, goby, and dragonet. Makeloan smiths craft fishhooks to the fishers’ exacting specifications, making different hooks for each species of fish. Some smiths add etchings and other decorations to these crafts to further showcase their skill. Traditional Makeloan clothing styles vary from one people to another, but most use either barkcloth or textiles woven from bast fiber or thin strips of screw palm leaf. They fashion the resulting supple fabrics into dresses, shawls, and skirts, the latter fastened with a braided rope belt. The mountain-dwelling Canta also tie a headcloth of such fabric to cover their hair. Toloan clothing uses various imported fabrics and distinctive styles, typically combining a skirt or tights with a gilet and a cape or shawl.

Makeloans gather breadfruit, bananas, and coconut from Sinti’s abundant groves. They dig taro and yams from the ground and extract starchy sago from palm trees. Hunting is a major element of Makeloan culture. Lessons begin early; young children make snares for smaller game and find turtles hiding amid greenery. Older children join the hunt as early as age twelve. Seasoned hunters stalk pigs, deer, boar, certain breeds of dog, quoll-lions, macaques, and large birds like cassowaries and moa. Most food is wrapped in leaves and baked; each type of leaf instills its own flavor. Makeloans cure quoll-lion meat by marinating it in salty brine with peppercorns and mustard seeds for several days; simmered until tender, it’s often baked in taro leaves with coconut

### Governance

Makelo has been ruled by a prince for generations; currently, Prince Gora Ormen holds the empire’s throne. A council of elders reports to him, advising him and helping him to determine and judge secular law. The other tribes’ princes retain their positions, if not the full extent of their former power. They report to the Makeloan prince, advocating for their people. Lesser nobles report to the princes, overseeing various estates; the specifics of their governance vary by tribe, with authority largely decentralized. Rust-resistant iron pillars line the way toward the Quoll House in Ordo Sevaï, where the prince and his councilors meet. Scribes etch the terms of new laws and treaties into their surfaces, so Makeloans and foreigners alike always know the prince’s intent and are reminded of their responsibilities.

High-ranking priests from throughout Sinti form the Ruby Lake Council. In accordance with Makeloan law, the Council — not the prince — judges matters of tradition. It meets every three months at the eponymous Ruby Lake, its waters dyed by runoff from Ninegala’s forge. There, councilors hear worshipers’ petitions, review the festival calendar, and negotiate matters important to the gods. The Council itself decides which priesthoods may send councilors; exact membership varies, but is typically several dozen. In their conquest of Sinti, Makelo’s leaders didn’t only depend on warfare. A series of strategic marriages tied otherwise independent kingdoms more

EX3

tightly to Makelo’s rule, eventually bringing them under Makeloan control. The last major independent kingdom, the Pahapi, only married into the Makeloan royal line a generation ago. Pahapi’s folk haven’t yet fully assimilated, leading to prejudice, social friction, and intermittent rebellions.

Any Makeloan can petition for their children to become priests. Families make substantial offerings to the temples to keep their child’s name at the forefront of priests’ minds. However, the priesthood first looks toward their own children when a position comes available, making the honor semihereditary.

### Religion and Spirituality

In addition to temple duties, warrior-priests accompany the empire’s military forces into battle. They’re strategists and evangelists, spreading Makelo’s influence throughout their corner of the West.

While the Makeloans hold Ninegala in special honor, they also worship a variety of other gods. The fickle wind goddess Ili-Pasu bestows gentle breezes one day, then shakes the leaves from the palms in a destructive gale the next. The boar-tusked forest god Tiama sits in the shade of the breadfruit trees braiding her silver hair. Those who give her gifts of moa feathers to adorn her plaits awaken the next morning to find an arduous task finished for them. The trickster spirit Insiku often runs afoul of the Ruby Lake Council; he expresses his displeasure with the Makeloans for conquering his favored people, the Sikele, by blessing rebels and insurrectionists — many of whom now seek his favor — and by throwing large stones at their temples to the gods. Several structures bear the pockmarks from his wrath.

Prominent Gods of Makelo

The forge-goddess Ninegala exiled herself to Creation millennia ago, establishing her smithy on the island of Sinti. Eventually, mortals came to her, offering service in exchange for the exquisite weapons she crafted. This practice continues to this day, with the goddess demanding exacting feats before she’ll fulfill her end of the bargain. She’s Sinti’s protector, acting as patron and mentor to Makeloan youths. When Fair Folk threaten the island, Ninegala dons her exquisite armor and rides them down in her flying chariot (Adversaries of the Righteous, p. 105).

EX3

God of the northern cassowary and of hunting on Sinti, Ritara-Kesu has parlayed centuries of veneration from Sintian hunters into an unofficial role as Makelo’s wargod. Craving mortal worship, he accompanies Makeloan troops in major engagements and offers blessings before battle, though he only involves himself directly to counter supernatural opposition. His creed lauds the hunter’s virtues of awareness, deliberation, and valor without cruelty. He resembles a tall, bronze-armored Western man, feathered and crested like a cassowary.

Njima

To be seen as a Makeloan noble, one must acquire a spirit-touched talisman called a njima. Common forms of njima include an amulet forged on Ninegala’s own anvil or a cassowary feather plucked from a wild living bird and blessed by Ritara-Kesu or Ili-Pasu. Priests are the final arbiters as to whether an object is truly njima; Makeloans often present such objects at the temple not only to confirm their authenticity, but also to boast that they’ve acquired one. Owning many njima grants a Makeloan great status. Having a surplus provides the opportunity to award njima to others to express esteem toward them or to earn their loyalty. Chieftains often gift them to favored warriors or to smiths who produce superb armor.

Njima can be taken in war to count coup. Warriors protect the njima they carry as fiercely as they do their weapons. Should one lose all the njima in her possession, she also loses her noble status until she can retrieve one or gain another. Presenting a counterfeit object as if it were an authentic njima insults the gods, as does stealing or knowingly destroying one. Priests punish such transgressions harshly, from stripping the guilty party of all their njima to arduous labor as penance. Peers who learn of this behavior often shun the perpetrator.

### Warfare

All Makeloan adults train at arms. Directed by the clan chief, they stand ready to defend their homes from invaders or to raid nearby islands for food, goods, and slaves. In times of war, Makeloan princes assemble armies from many such clan war bands. Most warriors look forward to riding in war bands; morale remains high as long as they don’t face overwhelming odds or supernatural forces.

With no major threats to their supremacy over Sinti, the Makeloans have sustained their warrior culture

### RULES FOR NJIMA

While njima can be supernatural talismans (Exalted, p. 580), the vast majority aren’t. Any authentic talisman qualifies as a njima by default. Spotting fakes is a matter of reading intentions rather than assessing occult qualities.

through martial tournaments, suppressing rebels and mountain-dwelling isolationists, and expanding seaborne raids on neighboring islands. But Makelo’s warriors seek opportunities for glory. Having conquered all of Sinti, they’ve set their sights on annexing other islands. They’ve claimed a few small islands in the past decades, starting even before the marital union with Pahapi that sealed Makeloan control over Sinti. Makeloan shipwrights work ceaselessly to construct new vessels and repair older craft. Engineers innovate new designs, such as armored turtle ships akin to Azure’s.

Ninegala takes no active part in their plans; this fight isn’t hers. She aids indirectly through the war materiel and training she provides. These advantages all but ensure Makeloan success. Despite her aloof demeanor, however, should some other power go to war with the Makeloans or put up a bloody resistance against them, they will no doubt draw the brunt of her attention.

### Noteworthy Holdings

The city Makelo stands in the shadow of Hahilo, Ninegala’s holy mountain. Streets sprawl along the banks of the Sweetwater River, lined with frondthatched homes, tile-roofed workshops, and copper and iron statuary. Makelo has grown into a city of culture and industry, from the District of Smiths to the raucous university that trains young engineers, architects, metallurgists, and theology. The temple of Ninegala dominates the city center; the priesthood holds much power here, challenging the Gora prince. A far-flung colony from the Auspice Islands’ long-ago thalassocracy, many-towered Tolo was Sinti’s greatest port for centuries. It grew cosmopolitan on foreign trade, brief subjugation by Randan, and its own former petty empire on Sinti. Tolo remains rich despite enduring centuries of foreign raiding and its new Makeloan overlords. Its proud people, resentful of foreign rule, mutter of rebellion; its elected council of merchant-magistrates bargain with overseas princes, seeking personal wealth as much as military support.

EX3

Several years ago, Makelo’s emperor settled his formerly itinerant court in the Toloan city of Ordo Sevaï, a sprawling port on the river Kimene. New construction rises throughout the city, including temples, schools, wharves, mills, shops, and housing. Fortunes are made and lost daily in the enormous Striped Coral Market, which deals in luxuries and bulk goods from throughout Sinti and from overseas. Warriors drill on the gleaming plaza before the emperor’s Cassowary Palace, readying themselves for the next war.

The rugged island of Chalk Cliff is Makelo’s most recent conquest. It’s been divided up among prominent nobles involved in the invasion. As settlers from Sinti move in, they drive the locals away from the best farmland and coves in a series of bloody and not entirely one-sided clashes. Chalk Cliff collaborators retain greater privileges than other locals. Folk who fled to the mountains inland maintain an armed resistance, hiding among the tombs of a lost people.

### Prominent Figures

Gora Ormen — Emperor of Makelo, Sovereign of the Seven Peoples of Sinti, Suzerain of the Islands of Bakari and Chalk Cliff — rules a burgeoning empire. He resides in the Cassowary Palace amid luxury and splendor, feasting on fresh game and honeyed fruits from gem-crusted platters. He believes that his wealth demonstrates his importance, and through him, Makeloan power and influence. He’s short and muscular, his skin dark from months of training in smithcraft with Ninegala; he favors garments dyed a rare purple imported from Randan, a fashion now spreading through his court.

Ormen takes pride in his martial talents. Though he inherited countless njima from his imperial mother, he prizes those he’s personally won in battle. He gives great latitude to the priests of Ritara-Kesu, revering him as Ninegala’s equal, and has built on his mother’s and grandmother’s efforts to expand the kingdom. New

Tiny green jade glyphs inlaid along its haft recount the covenant between Ninegala and the Makeloan people.
