warships being constructed in Sinti’s harbors will be ready to set sail next year.

Warrior, priest, and savant, Ileo Sataki stands at the emperor’s right hand. Born to a prominent Makeloan noble family, she studied engineering at the university, led a war band in the conquest of nearby Bakari, and joined both the priesthood and Ormen’s council. Today she’s Ordo Sevaï’s chief priest of Ritara-Kesu. Despite not being high priest, she’s a dominant figure in the Ruby Lake Council by dint of rhetorical skill, intimidating presence, numerous njima, and closeness to the emperor. Sataki’s loyalty is more to imperial expansion than to Ormen himself; the two agree firmly on principles but clash furiously on details. Faleti of Tolo grew immensely rich by selling Randani textiles, including their legendary enchanted brocades, to the Makeloan imperial family. Today she dominates the textile trade on Sinti, owns properties scattered across the island, and has even purchased a princely quantity of njima with which to command respect — an anomaly the Ruby Lake Council has yet to rule against. She advises the emperor on economic matters as she did his imperial mother. Her ambitions on behalf of her family and the Toloans are well-known; for now, her wealth, njima, and political connections shield her from rivals.

### Neighbors

Makelo trades briskly with Manigal (p. XX), although the Makeloans look down their noses at what they consider a weaker nation. Traditionally, both peoples consider Moqon to be from Makelo, a son last in line for the throne who struck out to make his own fortune. The Makeloans believe this puts the Manigalese in their debt and take offense at not receiving special trade considerations. Manigal’s wahnmarks listen warily for rumors that Makelo has set its sights on conquering Tomil Teb.

On the bordermarch-isle of Seseli, the tide wears holes in skerries and sea stacks, and stones with such holes can speak. Neighboring peoples seek oracles of these howling stones, albeit rarely, for they fear the island’s inhabitants.

Upon being routed by Makelo, the Umo people fled to Seseli with their gods. There they begged an alliance with the Clashing Spears Tribunal, a court of warrior Fair Folk who’d raided Sinti’s shores for centuries. The court agreed to shelter the Umo in exchange for eleven souls each Calibration. The Umo seize Sintians by

EX3

preference, but near year’s end they’ll raid anyone they can rather than sacrifice their own.

### OTHER WESTERN LOCALES

Only recently a notorious pirates’ den, the ruin of Sharktooth now shelters little more than ghosts. The Realm’s Vermilion Legion stormed the nameless islet’s harbor only months ago, burning the town and its crude fortress. Outside of a few sandy beaches, the isle is jagged and mountainous. Rumor says that hidden caves conceal vast treasure hoards stashed by the pirates over the years, though thus far scavengers have found nothing but wild beasts and truculent elementals.

## The Azurite Empire

On Morning Island, at the city of Azure’s stone-carved docks, countless tributary ships unload the plunder of empire. These ships bear a hundred different sigils and signs: the elegant feathered crests of Auspicene princelings, Ironguard’s chrysanthemum mon, and the iridescent scales of fae ships risen from the Nacre Whirlpool. Legions of stevedore-slaves carry the West’s immeasurable wealth up terraced streets to administrative palaces, where trusted custodians count and store it in the sea lords’ treasure houses. Magistrates drag thieves in chains through the streets to the Kraken’s Pool, their gruesome punishment to serve as both spectacle and threat to would-be lawbreakers. Every ship in Azure’s harbor abides by the law of the sea lords, masters of an empire upon the waves.

From their deliberative chamber in the city’s heart, the sea lords guide Azure to dominate the Coral Archipelago and territories beyond. Supported by assemblies of wealthy citizens and one of the West’s most fearsome navies, Azure is an ascendant power in the Great Western Ocean, feared and envied by many, yet poised to form a bulwark against the expanding Realm’s ambitions. Islands caught between the two must weigh the familiar demands of Azure against subjugation at the hands of House Peleps and the Realm.

### Government

After the Contagion, a foreign dynasty of DragonBlooded — refugees from a crumbling Shogunate successor state — conquered the nascent fortress-town of Azure and transformed it into Morning Island’s most influential city. But their final prince’s tyranny was so great that his admirals cast him down and took power for themselves. Azure would never again have a prince; instead, its wisest and most prosperous citizens would rule.

The First Sea Lord is the grand admiral of Azure’s navy, chief general of the city’s army, and chief magistrate of the civil government. Only Azure’s assemblies may appeal the First Sea Lord’s judgements. The Conclave of Sea Lords (p. XX) advises the First Sea Lord and may call for new elections every three years should the First Sea Lord displease them, but there are no term limits for one who performs well. When the First Sea Lord and the Conclave act in concert, which is typically in matters of war, few can withstand their might.

Born out of an undersea middlemarch beyond the great Western archipelagoes, the Deep Lotus Cities nestle in the mile-wide buds of a vast plant that flowers on the sea floor. At irregular intervals, a bud rises to the surface and blossoms, revealing a strange, wondrous city whose air-breathing mortal residents bear floral mutations. Visitors can win a fortune in one visit by trading surface goods for cargoes of Wyld treasures; gambling; or performing strange favors. But the flower closes suddenly and unpredictably, drawing the city back down to the seafloor — along with visitors unable to depart in time.

Electors and the Assemblies

Electorship — the right to vote — is a hereditary privilege afforded to few Azurites. Once, all electors were highborn descendants of Azure’s founding clans, but many prosperous persons from Azure and its protectorates have joined their ranks, purchasing electorship by making lavish tributes to the city. Broad policy decisions for Azure’s governance fall to three great assemblies that hold conventions, pass laws, and designate officials to oversee Azure’s affairs. Elections are held each year to fill vacancies. Membership is for life.

The largest assembly, the Convocation of Waves, consists of lowborn Azurites and people of annexed islands, and theoretically advocates for their interests. The Convocation sends representatives to address the Thousands Sails Assembly. It also appoints magistrates and naval officers; thus, earning its goodwill is critical for any Azurite aspiring toward a political career. Lastly, its most celebrated duty is electing other officials to serve as priests of Azure’s patron deities in addition to their temporal duties. Almost all officials of note also hold priestly office.

Naval and military veteran electors comprise the Thousand Sails Assembly. Together, they possess the

EX3

Judges: Judges investigate and apprehend criminals of all kinds to face harsh punishment by Azure’s laws, which focus on state security, public order, and traditional morality; well-contained vendettas and the like aren’t the magistrates’ concern. While judges must render swift and harsh punishments, many make their fortunes accepting gifts to slow their pursuit or turn a blind eye. They’re also called sword-magistrates for the ring-pommel swords that serve as their badge of office.

### DRAGON-BLOODED OF AZURE

Lest Azure return to the tyranny of princes, law and custom bar Dragon-Blooded from elected office, but Azurites nevertheless respect and fear their awesome power. The Azurite navy welcomes their Exalted might; roughly two dozen Dragon-Blooded currently serve as masters-at-arms, weather witches, and captains under the command of the admiralty and the First Sea Lord. An equal number of civilian Dragon-Blooded wield great influence as merchants, privateers, and mercenaries.

power to declare war, elect Azure’s high officials — such as the First Sea Lord or governors of tributaries — and serve as the highest court of appeal. Azure’s wealthiest highborn clans dominate the voting and cow their lessers into line, though other members often form coalitions to acquire more power in the Assembly. Tension between these blocs occasionally erupts into violence; magistrates stand ready to break up brawls whenever the Thousand Sails gather.

Membership in the Conclave of Sea Lords is exclusive to the most ancient Azurite clans, the wealthiest nouveau-riche, and the descendants of elected high officials. Its official power is limited to making recommendations to the other assemblies. In practice, its influence is so great that the other assemblies treat its recommendations as edicts; nearly all influential magistrates boast membership in the Conclave or have close kin there, and few willingly risk their ire by not complying with their advice. The debates and votes held on their deliberative floor direct Azure’s destiny.

The Magistracy

Magistrates, ranging in seniority from the juniormost First Echelon to the seniormost Sixth Echelon, oversee the day-to-day affairs of Azure’s government. Each has the personal power to arrest and punish citizens and to overrule or discipline lesser magistrates. Retinues of junior clerks, specialized slaves, and personal retainers support them in carrying out their duties. The Convocation of Waves elects magistrates from those who’ve cultivated connections and gained experience by serving in another magistrate’s retinue. The Convocation also votes to promote magistrates on a senior magistrate’s recommendation; this is normally a formality.

Examples of magisterial positions include:

Censors: Azure’s priest-magistrates maintain Azure’s harmony with the gods. Censors augur omens before each gathering of the assemblies and organize the city’s divine festivals. Their most sacred duty is to maintain the city temples, which also serve as Azure’s treasure houses. Service as a censor is a vital step on the path to high office.

Venators: Originally tasked with culling Morning Island’s tiger populations, these magistrates investigate and hunt powerful beasts, the hungry dead, and other monsters that threaten Azure and its allies. Ambitious highborn scions usually avoid the role, seeing it as a dead-end position with a high mortality rate. Venators are storied figures in Coralite folklore, tracking devils with the aid of the tame tigers they once hunted.

### Society and Culture

Centuries of conflict in the Coral Archipelago’s harsh conditions and mistreatment at the hand of its fallen tyrant-princes have shaped Azure’s culture. Families organize into lineage-based clans. The highborn clans, who claim great naval heroes as their forebears, maintain a tight grip on most high-ranking government offices. Lowborn clans, who encompass most of the populace, largely descend from subjugated peoples from Morning Island’s hinterlands and the lowborn of conquered city-states. They once comprised distinct ethnic groups who elected clan representatives to the Convocation of Waves; today they’re largely administrative divisions for taxation and conscription purposes.

Slavery props up Azure’s prosperity. Nearly a third of the population is enslaved, working as anything from field laborers and miners to domestic servants and personal tutors. To lack even a single household slave is deemed a deplorable mark of poverty. Azure obtains many slaves as war prisoners; others are purchased from foreign slavers, born to slave parents, or lose their freedom as collateral on a failed loan

EX3

Azurite families impress the importance of strength, courage, and ambition — tempered by loyalty and respect for authority — upon their youth from an early age. Young Azurites face great pressure to outdo their rivals in politics and on the battlefield. Those who fail to redirect their aggression toward the empire’s enemies must contend with Azure’s unforgiving laws. Since the time of the princes, criminals in Azure have received unforgiving, brutal punishments. Magistrates flog thieves bloody in public squares and tattoo repeat offenders across their faces to shame them. They may hold criminals’ family members guilty by association; if a magistrate deems it appropriate, the accused’s family faces the same punishments as the criminal herself. Magistrates punish severe crimes such as treason, kinslaying, and witchcraft with leg-bending, nose-cutting, and other forms of torture, followed by public executions in which criminals are thrown alive into the Kraken’s Pool to be devoured by the eponymous beast as a spectacle.

Azure penal codes include a ransom system that allows the wealthy to pay a fine in place of corporal punishments for all but the most severe crimes. A popular

movement among the assemblies currently lobbies for banishment of wealthy and well-connected criminals, restricting them to pursuing their interests beyond Azure’s sphere.

In contrast to these strict laws and harsh punishments, Azurites engage in lively, raucous entertainments. Highborn Azurites have revived the soldier’s pastime of pitch-pot as an aristocratic game, attend dance performances hosted in private courtyards, and visit one another at coastal countryside villas or on the resort-island of Serene. Wrestling, gambling, and dice games are popular among all classes, and hold religious significance in the worship of the gambling god Plentimon of the Dice.

In addition to fish and shellfish, traditional Azurite recipes may include cabbage, radish, sand leek, coastal hog fennel, fiddleheads, apples, melons, five-flavor berries, maesil plums, jujubes, pine nuts, and chestnuts. Condiments include black pepper, mustard, horseradish, fish sauce, and vinegar. Some chefs also incorporate foodstuffs originating outside the Coral Archipelago, such as chilis, maize, potatoes, squash, tomatoes, and walnuts. As rice and wheat are expensive, common folk

EX3

mix them with the more abundant barley and millet, and accompany them with beans, fish, seaweed, and a wide variety of spiced pickles.

Lunch is the largest meal for Azurite workers. The upper classes instead do business in the morning, have a light lunch, bathe, then settle in for an evening of lavish banquets. Traditional dishes include fish fritters, sweet and savory stewed black beans, fried bracken, and “Sea Lord Stew,” which is made with three kinds of fish, pepper, herbs, and dry bread, all simmered in rice wine. Fish in the stew vary, from cod, snapper, and mussels in lower-class recipes to pufferfish, oysters, and sole in richer versions. Fruit and shellfish are served for dessert, often chilled by snow stored in ice cellars.

Sexism in Azure

Highborn Azurite culture bars women from high office, naval service, and the electorate. They justify these sexist practices as a way to avoid the displeasure of misogynistic spirit patrons — primarily the Ocean Father, as well as the Three Storm Sisters, a trio of Storm Mothers whose spirit courts command the waters around the southern Coral Archipelago and the Auspice Isles. Over the centuries, evolving conditions in Azure have seen wealthy, powerful Azurite women and foreigners alike challenge these restrictions.

Azurite women traditionally manage the household, where they hold significant power over finances and share management of businesses. They also manage businesses while their husbands are traveling or at war, and own them outright as widows. Officials’ spouses influence their husbands’ political decisions as well, sometimes in organized blocs. And certain priestly roles, such as the high priestess of Howling Nyo (p, XX), are only open to women.

Foreign women aren’t held to Azurite expectations. Meanwhile, Dragon-Blooded Azurite women are no longer bound to mortal constraints. Joining a Tya guildhouse (p. XX) also frees Azurite women to work at sea. As Azure’s empire expands and the demand for disciplined sailors increases, tattooed Tya sailors have become a common sight aboard naval vessels, respected for their skills yet held at a distance for their insular traditions.

### Religion

Traditional Coralite shamans once acted as official intermediaries with gods and ancestor spirits for families and local communities, allowing spirits to possess them

to dictate prophecy and bestow the gods’ favor. But as Azure’s empire grew, the shamans were supplanted in their civic role by aristocratic priest-magistrates who call upon longstanding compacts to commune with the gods of Sea-and-Sky, Azure’s modern pantheon. Despite this, highborn and lowborn Azurites alike privately consult with still-practicing shamans regarding spiritual matters, particularly on less populated islands or in Morning Island’s interior, where itinerant shamans outnumber temples and priests. Azure attributes its success as an empire to harmonious accords with the Sea-and-Sky, thanks to the patronage of the city’s chief deity, the Ocean Father. In Azurite myth, the Ocean Father governs the Great Western Ocean, commands the West’s lesser deities, and rules a treasure-filled city beneath the sea. Azure’s assemblies sponsor archipelago-wide festivals to honor him. The First Sea Lord is both Azure’s chief magistrate and the Ocean Father’s high priest, required to seek his counsel on matters of state through omens and sacrifice. Coralite merchants revere the Ocean Father as a patron, and view maintaining their family’s prosperity as a sacrament.

The Sea-and-Sky encompasses numerous deities, with stone-carved pagodas housing idols littering the Coral Archipelago to honor them all. Alongside their patron, Azurites honor the red-haired ship-goddess Rudhira the Storm Rider; Bashixun, the Wise Crab, god of fisherfolk and the shore; Howling Nyo, the fierce, aloof dragon-goddess of Morning Island itself; and many more, ranging from high-ranking divinities to minor godlings of islets, rivers, and fields. Some clans worship accomplished ancestors, venerating them with feasts and games during religious festivals. Superstitious Azurites also propitiate more frightful deities, like the Three Storm Sisters who threaten their ships and spouses, and Zhuziao, lord of deep waters, a titanic octopoid god who claims all ships that sink into his sunless domain. Azurite law forbids worship of a few gods, most notably Siakal, Western goddess of battle and bloodshed. Siakal’s worship often involves bloody human sacrifice and prolonged violent conflict. In Azure’s early days, her then-powerful cult — the Maw of Siakal — nearly supplanted the Ocean Father’s as Azure’s dominant religion, but failed and was driven underground. The Maw persists in secret among highborn clans tied to Azure’s navy and more openly among the ranks of Azure’s privateers, who make bloody offerings to hungry siaka far from Azure’s prying eyes.

EX3

Azure expands its portfolio of divinities with each conquest, making worship of local gods contingent upon backing foreign rule, while retrieving idols from subjugated cities for worship in Azure’s temples. With the annexation of the island of Manta, the gambling god Plentimon of the Dice brought his worship to Azurite shores. The temple of Kireeki, the dolphin-souled huntress of the waves, was disassembled when the citystate of Skein burned, then rebuilt on Azure’s streets.

The Ocean Court

The Ocean Father and many other deities of the Seaand-Sky belong to the Ocean Court, an overarching spirit court encompassing numerous Western thalassic deities and their courts. The Ocean Father has used his traditional authority as ruler of the Ocean Court to recruit his divine subordinates as patrons to Azure, or at least to ensure that they don’t interfere when Azurite ships set sail.

Centuries ago, the Ocean Father was demoted from god of the Great Western Ocean to oversight of the Northwestern seas. But Heaven has yet to appoint a successor, leaving the Western spirit courts in disarray. He retains an informal leadership role, albeit one that his major rivals in the Ocean Court challenge; these include the bloodthirsty shark-goddess Siakal and the possessive Zhuziao, god of the depths.

While the Ocean Father takes pleasure in mortal worship, he’s more concerned with the leverage that commanding a pantheon gives him over other gods. As the empire’s foremost divine patron, he can sway the Azurites to worship gods of his court while rejecting divine rivals, or to invade peoples who worship rival gods. Azure isn’t the first civilization he’s championed; should he be convinced it will break, he may seek a new empire to spread his worship, as he did when the Auspice Isles faltered.

Over the centuries it’s become clear that the Ocean Father no longer commands the power he once did. Siakal tests his resolve most frequently, competing for his followers and slaughtering them when opportunity arises. Other spirits, sensing weakness behind the Ocean Father’s restraint, pursue their own interests, sometimes at the Ocean Court’s expense. As the West grows more violent and unstable, it may face a test that ancient bonds won’t survive.

of cold-resistant iron palms grown in the southern Coral Archipelago. Their armored turtle ships, which form the fleet’s vanguard, boast iron roofs to prevent enemies from boarding, and a dragon’s-head prow that spews flame toward enemy vessels ahead. Azurite sailors are hailed for their rigid discipline and advanced naval tactics. Sailors earn a share of all goods their ship plunders, and may retire after twenty years of loyal service with a substantial pension and much social clout. Foreign recruits are barred from captaincy, but may purchase citizenship upon retirement at a steep discount; many wealthy foreigners have been thus enfranchised.

Azure supplements its naval dominance with privateers. The First Sea Lord offers letters of marque to independent captains, who pay tribute to Azure from their spoils. These privateers viciously raid any vessels not belonging to Azure’s allies. Unconstrained by the Navy’s rigid standards, privateer captains are famously idiosyncratic, the subjects of romantic tales at home and fearful warnings abroad. For many captains and crews unsuited to the Navy’s discipline or engaged in practices forbidden by Azurite law — such as witchcraft or worship of forbidden gods — privateering is an alternative path to wealth and influence.

### The City Ascendant

The city of Azure sits resplendent at the heart of the Bay of Shrines, an elegant, terraced city carved from the harsh rock of Morning Island’s southern coast. Above the stone cliffs rising at the city’s rear, farmland radiates outward along the banks of the Horned River, struggling to feed the ever-increasing population of the Coral Archipelago’s most populous city. Only the wealthiest clans can afford to live in Old Azure, where elegant tile-roofed hanok and administrative palaces line orderly rows of streets and canals. Built in harmony with geomantic principles, the picturesque gardens and proximity to the assemblies’ meeting-halls make residence in Old Azure a key marker of prosperity.

### The Azure Navy

The largest fleet native to the West, Azure’s navy is famous for its finely crafted vessels, built from the wood

EX3

### THE AZURITE ARMY

Soldiers in Azure’s army don’t gain anywhere near the glory of their naval counterparts. Azurites respect their service, but many believe the army is less disciplined and more prone to looting, especially in garrison roles.

Most residents live beyond the old city’s walls in the urban sprawl of the Dry Reefs, in tall, cramped apartments of timber and mudbrick or in squat, straw-plaited hanok. Conditions range from pleasant to squalid, and cheap construction makes some apartments prone to fires. Those who live close to the ground use stone floor heating to stay warm during Morning Island’s bitter winter months. The modern city’s outermost walls now enclose the once-rural Blue-Sky Necropolis, which casts a shadow over the Dry Reef when the setting sun hangs low. Shamans and lowborn servants maintain this nest of tombs and shrines to Azure’s ancestors and princes. Each tomb overflows with grave goods and murals depicting daily life and the gods. The largest belongs to the Last Prince of Azure; a mighty sorcerer in life, many fear that his enraged spirit awaits an opportunity to exact vengeance upon his killers’ descendants. Magistrates execute unfortunates who attempt to trespass on his tomb in the Kraken’s Pool. The Shell Gardens’ vibrant markets welcome merchants from across the Coral Archipelago and beyond. Pale, bejeweled traders from Onyx deal in gemstones and metalwork; Mantanese street vendors sell skewered fishcakes, blood sausage, and savory pancakes to hungry sailors and market slaves. Always lively, the Shell Gardens overflow with brothels, theaters, and gambling dens that cater to sailors’ whims. On the Grand Shore, Azurites and their servants crowd together to see the Navy’s heroes return home after months at sea. Countless warehouses dot the Shore, storing tons of barley and wheat imported from the annexed isle of Serene. It’s the heart of Azurite commerce; there are few hours in the day when people aren’t working or walking down the cobbled streets. East of the Grand Shore stands the Storm’s Eye, Azure’s military port. Navy ships and active privateers dock in its walled-off outer harbor, while an inner cothon houses the naval shipyard. The cothon, its encircling walls capped with stone tiling like a sea beast’s scales, can hold dozens of ships. The Admiralty’s offices reside on Admiral Gan Island at the cothon’s center, giving their council seat a commanding view of all docked vessels. On the Grand Shore’s western banks, churning waters fill an enormous chasm. This is the Kraken’s Pool, where judges publicly execute traitors and other great criminals — and where citizens privately resolve lethal vendettas by night. Magistrates throw the guilty in alive to be devoured by a titanic, immortal beast with eight hooked tentacles and a whirlpool of sharp teeth. This

divine beast, tamed by a long-dead sorcerous prince, has come to define Azurite justice: swift, brutal, and gruesome. Architecture, art, and couture throughout Azure’s empire incorporates the kraken as an apotropaic symbol.

### Prominent Figures

High Sea Lord Gim Hanjul has held his position for nearly two decades. Elected for boldness and naval prowess, his first years as High Sea Lord were marked by bloody victories that filled Azure’s coffers. In recent years, his two sons’ deaths in battle have disillusioned him with Azurite politics, leaving him reluctant to draw Azure into further conflicts. Now the Thousand Sails murmurs about calling a new election. Fourth-Echelon Magistrate Sem Teong has spent years climbing the ranks, catching thieves and smugglers and bringing them to justice in the Kraken’s Pool. Aristocrats expect him to get the job done; Azure’s criminals afford him begrudging respect. Seeking to achieve Echelon Five, he’s investigating the Maw of Siakal. The cult proves elusive and its agents cunning and dangerous. He’s survived their ambushes, but wavers as cultists deliver threats to his family. Kang Narae is a Dragon-Blooded rear admiral in the Azurite Navy. Her grandfather’s execution for sedition — charges she believes were spurious — engenders suspicion from some peers and commanding officers, but she strives to prove her loyalty on the open sea. Narae’s recent military victories have drawn the eyes of those in power. Her family’s remaining political allies have approached her about backing their maneuvers, should the High Sea Lord’s recent weakness prove disastrous for Azure; their proposals intrigue her. Tya Tanari, housewarden of Azure’s most prominent Tya guildhouse, is an ambitious foreigner who helped spearhead the Tya’s integration into the Azure Navy. Now, she seeks to foster ties with sailors to forge a political bloc in Azure’s assemblies to bring greater prosperity to the Tya. The more she works to bring more of the Tya to Azure, the more she earns the disgust of highborn Azurites for her foreign birth and for her ambition.

### The Coral Archipelago

Azure’s empire spans the Coral Archipelago and beyond. The Western Isles — including Azure itself — are large, mountainous, and heavily populated. Annexed centuries ago, they’ve strongly integrated with Azurite

EX3

rule. The Eastern Isles trend smaller, with cold, harsh climates and fewer resources. They’re littered with crescent-shaped fortresses built to repel raiders from the mountains and the sea.

BRIGHTWORK’S SEXIST LEGACY

The Auspice Isles (Exalted, p. 104) exported their culture across the West centuries ago. Even before the hero-admiral Tetram of Brightwork conquered much of the West, Auspicene sailors sailed everywhere between the Coral Archipelago and Wavecrest, sharing stories, skills, and traditions. Their merchants offered tools, ceramics, and jewelry; their physicians exchanged herbs and remedies. Trading posts grew into cosmopolitan civilizations such as the Neck’s Moonglory and Tylo (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 246), mingling Auspicene and native populations’ customs.

The Eastern Isles’ peoples frequently raid one another and target western Coralite ships, courting harsh Azurite reprisals. Many reject Azure’s rule; the archipelago’s history is rife with uprisings. Others travel to Azure in search of opportunity, signing on with the navy or privateers.

Islands of the Archipelago

Few islands have fared as well as Manta under Azurite rule. Manta is the second-largest island in the archipelago after Morning Island, and for much of Azure’s history was its chief rival. Since Azure annexed it centuries ago, the Mantanese have become an integral part of Azure’s empire. Manta City’s port remains a major trade center; apprentice shipwrights from Morning Island spend time at its drydocks, honing their craft. The god Plentimon of the Dice spends much of the year overseeing his Diving Sea Snake Casino, where gamblers can wager anything from coins in their purses to years of their lives. Many in the archipelago believe Plentimon’s luck extends to his people and consider it fortunate to have a Mantanese sailor among one’s crew. Whether due to ancient sorceries or an unknown deity’s blessing, temperate Serene’s weather remains clement year-round. Known as the breadbasket of the Coral Archipelago, the island’s native serfs and slaves grow soybeans, wheat, and millet on massive plantations. Many of Azure’s most prominent clans have constructed fortress-villas along its southern coast to winter in. On the northern coast, the overbuilt city of Morningstar ships more slaves through its port than Azure, selling them throughout the West. The twin islands of Jushir and Kanir at the archipelago’s eastern tip chafe under the burden of Azurite taxes and rule. The snow-covered port of Dazri straddles the strait between them; it’s the gateway to trade with the far North, though business has suffered over the last century as shipping through Wu-Jian has shifted commerce away from the northern route. Long ago, Fajadi settlers built the mosques where the native Jahiri people practice the Abhari Creed (The Realm, p. 154), a foreign religion. The Azurite governor, Sea Lord Pae Nakil, continues the tradition of permitting the Jahiri to practice their faith in exchange for higher taxes, but he’s recently ordered purges of local assemblies based on rumors that Uluiran merchants seek to foment an uprising.

Not all of what the Auspicenes conveyed was beneficial. They forbade female sailors on their ships because of their Three Storm Sisters’ hatred of women; their stories were similar enough to other peoples’ experiences with storm mothers that the tradition took root. Meanwhile, women in Auspicene colonies suffered the same indignities as at home — restriction to domestic roles, subordination to male relatives, and limited education. In many places these prejudicial traditions never took hold, or suffragists suppressed them through heroic effort. In some they lingered, or transformed as native folk adapted them to their own cultures. Azure, in conquering the Auspice Isles and taking its people as slave tutors, has internalized them the most.

Ancient grottoes litter the Finreefs. a series of stormy, rocky islands north of Azure. Legend holds that mortals first honored Siakal with blood here. After centuries of conflict with local tribes, Azure seized control and enslaved the Finreefs’ people in their islands’ iron mines. Working conditions are poor, and God-Blooded children of local sea-spirits frequently lead uprisings against their keepers.

### Neighbors

Tributaries, independent islands, and as-yet unconquered principalities radiate outward from the Coral Archipelago.

Azure controls the nearby Auspice Isles. Bastions of art and education, the Isles’ artisans learn ancient techniques as they study their trades — architectural secrets, fine lacquer work, intricate tapestries — though the Sea Lord demands they put their talents to work on practical creations for the military. Still, the city-states remain relatively prosperous; the Azurite aristocracy has a rosy, admiring view of Auspicene culture, and

EX3

doesn’t meddle much beyond ensuring they provide reasonable tribute (including skilled slaves) for Azure. Here, scholars and philosophers stroll between volute-capped columns in covered colonnades. Citizens meet and shop in open air markets. Representatives debate laws and policy in assembly buildings; while the city-states are ostensibly republics, aristocratic families dominate most of their councils. Lookouts patrolling the northwestern waters watch for ships from the Skullstone Archipelago. Though trade agreements between the two powers keep overt conflicts to a minimum, past battles leave seasoned admirals wary. On outlying islands, the Silver Prince’s agents attempt to stir the Maw to action, encouraging them to overthrow the priest-magistrates.

## The Tya

Laborers, sailors, tradesfolk, merchants and mercenaries, the outcast Tya are subjects of a thousand rumors, each more scandalous than the last — they’re unlucky, they steal and kill, they kidnap and seduce youths. They bear these slanders unflinchingly; the joy of their truths isn’t for the outside world, but for each other.

### Lifestyle

The Tya are a cultural tradition and minority group with origins in women seeking escape from sexist Auspiscene restrictions (p. XX). Most reside in and around the Neck, but they can be found scattered along trade routes in ports as far-flung as Nai Lei and Fajad. The societal position of Tya varies greatly by location, but they’re always outsiders of a sort. In places influenced by Auspicene culture, Tya are largely ignored, spoken of derogatorily as witches who tempt daughters. In Randan, many regard Tya lodges as suspicious challengers to pechin hegemony over crafts. In Utahi, they’re thought to be lucky and hired as retainers or guards.

Dress varies by region, but Tya are known for dressing in simple clothes that defy gender legibility. In private — and more rarely in public — they dress ostentatiously: dyed silks, bright feathers, bead jewelry, and intricately patterned embroidered. Many embrace piercings and body modification. They engage in communal arts and crafts, sing (often bawdy) shanties, and maintain their own clipped cant that’s impenetrable to outsiders.

Tya culture prizes authenticity, freedom, and respect. What these things mean to each Tya are highly personal, but a Tya’s honor is tied intimately to being recognized as honest, respected, straightforward, and shrewd by their peers. Disrespecting fellow Tya by saying they lack these qualities or by refusing to recognize them has birthed a thousand grudges.

Tya become members of, and live in, communal lodges. Each lodge features a central common area adjoining a storeroom, and often encompasses multiple additional buildings renovated to connect with the original structure. As space is always at a premium, members sleep, eat, and live in close proximity. Looms, pottery wheels, forges, and similar equipment allows members to produce salable goods with which to fund the lodge’s expenses.

A small core of Tya live full-time at their lodge. Tya from other lodges may visit freely, while non-Tya guests require a member’s endorsement; either must leave if the lodge votes them out, although foreign Tya are expelled rarely to avoid conflict with other lodges. Non-Tya guests are typically refuge-seekers or a Tya’s traveling companions.

Resources are shared communally. Tya and guests receive food and lodging; in exchange, everyone contributes money, goods, or labor (including chores) to support the lodge as they are able. Non-members’ access to these resources beyond the basics — and to lodge business networks — is more limited. Most Tya return regularly to their lodge, as the longer one is away, the more support one is expected to bring back. Most Tya come and go as work takes them, moving between lodges alone or in small groups. Although Tya are entitled to a warm reception at foreign lodges, cultural clashes aren’t uncommon. Those who stay at other lodges for long periods are referred to as “adrift”; it’s not uncommon for such Tya to become members of multiple lodges for practicality’s sake, though this can become financially taxing to maintain. Rarely, Tya who’ve dramatically aided another lodge may receive honorary full membership without obligations. Lodges are ruled democratically, overseen by an esteemed older member referred to as the Eldest. The Eldest speaks for the lodge to the outside world and moderates group discussions, a duty that requires iron composure, indisputable authority, and strong lungs. It’s rare for a city to have more than one Tya lodge, but exceptions exist: for example, the feuds between the

EX3

Knotted Krait and Red Smoke lodges of Solid Shell are legendary, with members refusing to associate with one another.

A TYA’S LIFE

To the rest of the crew of the Thrice-Oriented, he’s just “Tya” — he’s the only one aboard, after all, so there’s no need for a name, especially when he barely talks. If they bother to ask him, for whatever reason, he’ll say his name is Bronze Thorn; or, if he’s feeling generous, Vehu. Captain Hyung-ae, though, saved his life in a nasty storm a few years back; for this, when they’re alone, she gets to call him Vehulanki, and she instead of he (Vehulanki doesn’t much care which). The captain isn’t Tya, but she’s earned it.

Lodges are prone to vicious infighting; often, the loudest voice dominates. Bullying or abuses can occur, with Tya prizing peace in the lodge over justice, or fearing to dissent from the majority. Tya who break heavily from custom grow used to arguing with their peers or being called traitors; it’s not uncommon for new lodges to splinter from old ones, resources and circumstance permitting.

### Religion

The gods of the Tya comprise a secret and motley pantheon. Each lodge has its own patron spirit called a compeer, a tutelary spirit with whom a covenant is struck upon founding. Tya venerate every lodge’s compeer where appropriate, but reserve special honor for their own. Compeers are welcomed as honored family, granted safety and prayer. In return, they offer magical protection and blessings; these usually manifest as wards against storms or misfortune on ships and buildings, subtle magical mutations, or minor wonders. Spirits approached to become compeers typically lack worshipers, owing to factors such as ill temper, circumscribed worship, or simple strangeness. Examples include the storm mother Shan-Anisi, the forbidden rot-god Last Sweetness, and the venomous snail-spirit Kogri of the Secret Trail.

Most compeers maintain a measure of distance towards their Tya — whether preferring solitude, having reason to keep a low profile, or being kept at a distance due to their inhospitable nature. For their part, the Tya worship as required, led by an elected priest and offering food at every meal. Priests are elected as much for piety as their ability to serve as intermediary between their siblings and ornery spirits.

### Gender Among the Tya

Gender among the Tya is complicated. They dress as men and outsiders treat them as such — more or less — but this isn’t the whole picture. Tya identity exists at an intersection of gender, class, and religious practices; it comprises its own gender in itself.

Tya expect to be referred to with masculine terms of address by outsiders, and are usually addressed as simply “Tya” — whether respectfully or otherwise. They use one name with outsiders, and another with loved

ones and fellow Tya; they deem the latter their true name. Tya often uses different pronouns in private than in public.

### Initiation

Most who join the Tya are oppressed, isolated or impoverished: criminals, outcastes, orphans, manual laborers, beastfolk and mutants, escaped slaves, escapees from repressive households or societal norms. Most — though not all — are dissatisfied with their assigned gender and sexual roles; they seek out the Tya for support and the freedom to be themselves. Tya are usually endogamous (though not monogamous), able to take outside lovers but rarely marrying them. Tya forswear having children, but lodges are known to take in foundlings who are raised collectively. It’s not uncommon for these to be unrecognized children of Tya; such things are an open secret. Foundlings may remain until they come of age, when they either leave or become initiates.

Prospective members are allowed to live in the lodge temporarily. After this observation period, the Eldest calls a majority vote to determine if they’re accepted. If yes, an induction ritual follows, requiring the attendance of every Tya present. Initiates take a new Tya name, and drink poison made from shellfish extract (of which there are sterilizing variants, if desired) to symbolically die and be reborn as Tya; it’s nonlethal, but wracks the body for days or even weeks. During convalescence, the initiate is nursed back to health in the lodge by their fellow Tya. Once recovered, they receive a mark of membership, such as tattoos, a facemask, or an intricately woven bracelet. Such marks, designed with help from fellow lodge members, name or evoke their lodge and compeer.

EX3

Banishment from the Tya is exceedingly rare, reserved for such deeds as murdering a peer, revealing ritual practices to outsiders, or betraying or bringing grievous harm to one’s lodge. Banishment requires a two-thirds majority vote, upon which the Tya is ritually scarred on the forehead so all may know they’re Tya no longer.

### Noteworthy Tya Lodges

The Three-Sided Coin Lodge of Port Monarch (Heirs to the Shogunate, p.246) was awarded an entire neighborhood years ago for service to the last governor of the Crescent Archipelago. This visibility is a mixed blessing: though they’re esteemed as bodyguards, they’re subject to heightened scrutiny, and wary of violence from increasingly agitated neighbors. Eldest Adanna, a scarred old battleax, has beseeched their compeer Rehaka the Aegis, former goddess of anchors, to instruct lodge members in defensive martial arts. Rehaka has answered yes, contingent on a dramatic increase in offerings to her — wealth the lodge currently lacks. Ilessa Who-Comes-On-Midnight-Tides lost his worshipers in the Contagion. For centuries, the half-shark god-goddess of moonless nights mourned alone, forgotten to all Creation — until she became patron of Brightwork’s Eventide Lodge. Among the oldest lodges, the Eventide Lodge has endured centuries of hardship, largely due to Ilessa’s ferocity. Ilessa cultivates a close relationship with their Tya, receiving atypically pious worship; overprotective and possessive, he participates in lodge votes overbearingly. The lodge’s priest Petrichor, lover to Ilessa, oversees sacrifices under the new moon, including enemies of the Tya chosen by the compeer. A local Azurite magistrate known to harass Tya has recently gone missing; suspicion falls on the lodge, though Ilessa maintains his innocence. Once, the Tya of the Burning Snow Lodge of Fajad (The Realm, p.153) grew wealthy sailing with Abhari merchants. But trade has dried up since the Wu-Jian route opened a century. Now they compete with Fajadi traders in Uluiru and Crocus, or find employment as advisors to nobles. Though they live in comfort and relative safety, they’re resented by other merchants — Yasmin Taraq and her consortium especially. As tribute demands squeeze the Realm, Yasmin has begun paying ruffians in ports from Fajad to Azure to harass local and visiting Tya alike. Eldest Ismil, an esteemed member of Prince Aalani’s court, seeks evidence to present to the Prince in hopes he might stop her; under the table, he’s put out a call for guards and investigators. Their compeer, the brooding wraith Candle-in-the-Cold, quietly urges Ismil to add assassins to the list.

### Prominent Tya

Sun-weathered and with a face marked by laugh lines and wrinkles, Eldest Haholi of Seahaven’s Shredded Palm Lodge is a living legend among Tya. In his youth he guarded princes, sailed with one of Cabochon’s god-admirals, and hawked wares across the West; for the last forty years, he’s led his lodge with an even hand and kindly aura. But underneath the warmth is a cold, pragmatic intelligencer and broker; Haholi leverages his extensive network of contacts to ensure the safety of his Tya through favor-trading, blackmail and extortion. He will do anything to keep the Tya safe, even if it means sacrificing one for many. Tya from across the Neck come to him seeking advice and arbitration. Haholi is known to mentor young Tya who catch his attention, whether for their potential or because they need guidance. Those under Haholi’s wing serve as his eyes and ears, and are often tasked with ensuring bargains he’s made for the Tya are upheld or making new ones.

Tall, handsome, and with a zest for life, Windflower is a charismatic and passionate soul who found a second life with the Tya after manumission from slavery. Captured by Western Trade Alliance slavers in his youth, he labored for many long years on Kerkeis until he’d saved up enough to buy his freedom. Now elderly, he spends his days sailing the Neck as a businessmen and weaver with seemingly inexhaustible energy, selling beautiful tapestries of sisal and ramie. He takes his earnings from business investments and puts them into funding companies that undercut the Western Trade Alliance and Realm merchants, sometimes co-operating with Guild companies seeking Western inroads. Alumai of Tylo was banished from the Frozen Lightning lodge after they traded its compeer’s occult secrets to the Lintha for aid defending the lodge against a lynch mob. Once a gentle blacksmith, Alumai grew bitter over the following years; they still bear the scars of robberies and assaults suffered while traveling alone, rejected by both the Tya and by outsiders. Finally seeking comradeship among the Lintha, she joined forces with the sorcerer Lintha Ujoki Hwei-Lam to found the heretical Great Mother’s Lodge in the Chelenarisi Islands, west of Sinti.

The Great Mother’s Lodge recruits Chelenarisin seeking refuge from cruel plutocratic rulers and ravenous fae, as well as orphaned youths from throughout the region. They work together uneasily with the exiled Ujoki sept; Alumai leads them in raiding ships from Makelo and Randan. They sacrifice captured elites and

EX3

warriors in the name of their demonic compeer Lovota, the Shores of Obedience — summoned and bound by Hwei-Lam — and to Kimbery. Alumai grows more audacious to ensure her continued supremacy, planning

bigger and bolder raids; regional Tya lodges regard them and theirs with a mix of revulsion, fear, and fascination.

EX3

The seas were dark gray today, the relentlessly churning waves of their last few days’ journey gone eerily still. The sky had turned that shade of brittle white that signals impending snow, and Ragara Kalis was contemplating shaving his beard to rid himself of the salty rime that kept freezing it stiff. Several members of his expedition stood at the rail with him, craning their necks for their first glimpse of Atmu’s shores. Dense, low-hanging fog concealed the island, dashing their hopes. Kalis checked his map and his compass once more, then touched the place where the old woman at the outpost had marked it. “As safe a harbor as you’re likely to get, there,” she’d muttered. “Safest if you sail back homeward and forget you were ever here.” It was the most anyone in that dreary cluster of fishing huts cared to say to anyone on the expedition. At first, the Fire Aspect suspected the taciturn inhabitants disliked Dynasts, but they took his crew’s coin just fine and raised no arms against them. Yet, when questioned about Atmu, they grew even stonier and made warding gestures in the island’s direction.

Next to him, Nellens Para muttered under her breath and stared at the coastline. When Kelis touched the cartographer’s arm to get her attention, she bit back a yelp. “It will do the crew good,” he said, pretending he hadn’t noticed her startlement, “to make land and build a fire.” She offered him a tight-lipped smile. “Perhaps.”

“I have casks of wine to bring to shore. Imagine, drinking summer wine chilled by Atmu’s snows!” He forced mirth into his voice in the hopes that he’d spark some in her. They were cousins; as a child, she used to trace the trade routes on the map at his family’s vineyards, imagining where the wine barrels were off to. Neither of them had imagined a bottle might travel this far. Instead of laughing, Para shuddered. “I’m not sure that’s wise,” she murmured. “I’m not sure that’s wise at all.”

These last few days at sea had been tense. The crew spoke of strange dreams full of shifting figures and eerie music. They’d doubled the watch at night after the lookouts complained the stars were too close, that the constellations shifted at the edge of their vision. Twice, they’d heard cries over the water and sounded the alarms, only to decide it was nothing but the wind’s frenzied howl. Kalis himself had dreamed poorly. He recalled little aside from a feeling of vast emptiness and a long, desolate walk between columns of massive stones that stretched to the horizon. Very little could make Kalis — whose Hearth had once fought a tyrant lizard — feel small. But these uncaring monoliths had done it. He’d woken in a cold sweat each time; lighting his lantern did little to banish the feeling of dread in his throat. He’d shared this with no one, not even Para. As head of the expedition, he had to be strong, even — especially — when the people he led started to fray. Surely this would all cease when they dropped anchor and rowed ashore. Being at sea for too long could do strange things to a person.

Someone cried out, and fingers pointed toward the shore. Ahead, the fog thinned and slunk away. The chatter on deck cut off abruptly as figures formed out of the parting gloom, great hulking stones rising above the beach. They weren’t natural rock formations; though worn with age, their shapes were too regular to be anything but deliberately crafted. Someone moaned softly. Kalis didn’t turn to see who it was. His own mouth had gone dry; he bit his cheek against a gasp of awe.

These were the same stones he’d stood beneath in his dream.

# Chapter Nine: The Northwest

Chapter Nine

The Northwest

Strangeness pervades the Northwest. The region’s history is thick with mysterious disasters, nightmarish monsters, and unknown magics. Even during the First Age, it was never as heavily populated as other parts of Creation, though it produced enough civilizations to litter the coast with picturesque ruins. Today, folk deem the region cursed, and it remains thinly populated. The Great Western Ocean’s currents — which grow tumultuous here, more so than anywhere else in Creation — moderate the coastal Northwest’s cool climate. Summers are short and rainy, winters long and snowy, and much of the year sees intermittent storms. Days are often overcast; high winds alternate with sluggish, blanketing fogs. Weird, unnatural weather phenomena — hailstorms of frozen animals, rains of fossils, choking ebon fogs, winds that whisper terrible secrets, things falling upward toward holes in the sky — occur every few years, often enough for folk to watch for and fear them.

## Uluiru

North of Fajad, a city-state nestles between low mountains, icy rivers, and the glossy black sea. Many-colored banners dance and snap in the bitter wind; pagodas tower over walled and terraced compounds. Palaces and shrines blaze in the sunlight, adorned in gold and precious gems. By night, wisps of rainbow fire illuminate both street and home. This is Uluiru, marvel of marvels, where mighty Sovereigns contend for the throne, ancient magic thrums beneath the earth, and Wyld monsters plot conquest and revenge.

### Queen and Sovereign

It isn’t easy to live at world’s edge, but the people who would one day settle Uluiru grew strong through centuries of ordeal, lifetimes of accumulated wisdom, and the dedication of their shamans, who dared to barter with creatures of the Wyld for passage and power. When their bargains finally offended, the people were driven from their original homeland by Fair

Folk predators: Huthugin Pierced-by-Arrows, Omo the Lightning-Eater, and the ravenous Storm of Fangs. The people followed their queen, Ulu, and her godly guide, Cantata-of-the-Depths, to an ancient barrow where an aurora-god once bled, laid low in the Divine Revolution. In that secret, sacred place, Cantata-of-theDepths drank deeply from the flame of the Exigence. His own Essence mingled with the fallen god’s kaleidoscopic ichor to ignite a pool of rainbow flame, thereafter called the Fount of Glories. Newly baptized as the first Sovereign, Exigent of lost Cantata, Ulu rode against her enemies on a steed of living fire, a rainbow sword in hand.

That is the story of Uluiru. It is known; it is shared; it is cherished. Given long life by Exaltation, Ulu was a legend made flesh for her people, who lavished her with song and saga. Her story dominated art, history, literature, and policy, and even the basest beggars took some small pride in their god-queen.

Knowing that her own life would one day end, Ulu anointed her great-granddaughter Nuwa as her heir, to the acclaim of the people and relatively minimal jealousy from other contenders. For a decade they ruled together, awaiting the day when Ulu would bow and offer her throne to Nuwa.

The day never came.

Nuwa died, cold and alone, in the frost-covered woods of her demesne. Her wounds had the putrid, sickly-sweet scent of Wyld-poison, and so Queen Ulu mounted her flaming steed and vented her wrath against the Fair Folk. For over a year, her grief waxed alongside her rage; she could sate neither, no matter how many raksha she slaughtered or Wyld-hives she put to the torch. When Ulu died, she died as Nuwa had before her: Feverish from her one-woman crusade, shot through with darts and arrows, scraped and scarred by a hundred swords and talons. Alone. For six months, the city has mourned, draped in purple. Now, as their mourning

EX3

ends, the eyes of Uluiru’s Sovereigns all turn towards an empty throne.

### To Rule by Merit

The Uluiruan people are enamored with the glamour of merit. They enshrine accomplishment over ability at every possible opportunity and organize their lives around elaborate games of counting coup. Childhood is especially rigorous for Uluiruan children. Those who seek high office must distinguish themselves in a ritualized series of examinations, competitions, and trials called the Forty-Four Distinctions. The schedule is grueling, and although families needn’t (and often don’t) submit all their children to each distinction, there’s a ruthless calculus among ambitious families, who spend time, energy, and money to train their prodigies with an eye toward return on investment. A failed trial is judged more harshly than one left unattempted, but many trials build to others — for instance, no child can enter the Seven Swords Tournament unless they compete first in the Blunted Blades Exhibition. Among the Forty-Four Distinctions, the most important concern warfare, statecraft, and literature. Young warriors often distinguish themselves in mock combat and archery tournaments, but Uluiruans expect would-be officers to further excel at strategy, history, and horsemanship. Those aspiring to civil service must instead prove themselves in philosophy, poetry, sculpture, and diplomacy. Once confirmed as a clerk or counselor, they may advance through the bureaucracy according to their other distinctions, all aiming for the rank of minister.

For those who share Ulu’s blood, however, the FortyFour Distinctions offer the opportunity for a far greater prize: the right to bathe in Cantata’s pool of prismatic fire and become a Sovereign. This doesn’t guarantee Exaltation — Cantata’s flame raises some up while burning others to ash. Even those who do Exalt face agonizing pain, as their mortal frames cannot entirely contain the blazing power within. They live with this pain for centuries as it grows and sharpens, sometimes debilitating them with fugues of agony or pressing them to feats of utter ruthlessness.

### The Empty Throne

In Ulu’s absence, her Sovereigns have slowly, quietly begun dividing her powers and responsibilities among themselves. Many such takeovers are relatively simple, with the highest-ranking Sovereign in a given field

assuming control over a ministry or province. Others have been more contentious, such as Seven-Sword Cilu appointing herself chief military officer; while many pressed their claim, no other held as many officers in their sway. To their credit, most Sovereigns recognize that such struggles are best fought outside the public eye; only the most covetous, brash, or desperate make their moves openly.

The queen’s day-to-day power has largely devolved to the ministries. Her chief ministers formed a hasty cabinet of equals, coordinating their affairs according to majority rule. This solution is imperfect: Uluiru’s ministries have never been equal in standing or scope. The largest ministries — Culture, Finance, Law, Mining, Public Works, and War — now grudgingly share power with far smaller departments such as the Ministry of Records, the Office of Distinctions, and the Invigilators Royal. And ministers must contend with Sovereigns who claim direct, legitimate authority over them or seek to undermine them through innuendo and slander.

### Among Gods and God-Kings

Shrines abound in Uluiru, consecrating streets, houses, and government buildings alike. The lion’s share are devoted to Cantata-of-the-Depths or Queen Ulu, who has long been worshiped as a living god by her people — the mother of a pantheon of Exalts. Those who seek a particular Sovereign’s favor often commission increasingly elaborate shrines in their honor; those who receive a Sovereign’s largesse sometimes devote a portion of their time as lay-priests, tending to shrines and conducting rituals. Ambitious social climbers with wealth to spare hire acolytes, occultists, and devotees to serve in their place. Sovereigns’ cults tend towards bombastic performances, passion plays, and public spectacle, extolling a patron’s virtues and mythologizing their accomplishments.

Worship of the city’s divine patrons is more subdued, but no less important. While nothing remains of Cantata-of-the-Depths except his legacy, he’s venerated in every Uluiruan household, invoked at evening meals with prayers comparing the stars themselves to the gems of the earth. Miners owe him special devotion as their profession’s patron; his most elaborate and well-kept shrines adorn mine entrances, and miners leave offerings of small cakes, incense, and quartz in his honor. The earth elementals who followed him when he led Queen Ulu through the wastelands honor his memory with acts of generosity — especially a silver coin left in the paths of the faithful and deserving.

Of Uluiru’s other gods, among the most powerful are the jewelry-goddess Slumbering Star and the stonegod known as Strider Upon Mountains. They’re minor figures in the city’s founding myth, although the vain, flighty Slumbering Star insists her role has been viciously minimized. They reign over a coterie of lesser godlings who squabble and preen, always eager to win followers with a small miracle here or there. Queen Ulu frowned on this as vulgar and unbecoming, but since her disappearance, several have returned to their old tricksome ways.

### Architecture

Bounded on two sides by mountains and on the others by river and sea, the city of Uluiru has no walls save for the Iron March, a swath of meter-long iron spikes that warn away most Fair Folk invaders. Uluiru proper rests atop a series of terraces and raised mounds that radiate from the queen’s palace. This harmonious design emerges from generations of careful planning, shaping the city to avoid impeding the region’s abundant geomantic energies.

The royal palace is a complex of soaring spires; the Ministry of Public Works erects a new tower in each Exalted Sovereign’s honor, to reside in as she pleases. Smaller gardens and memorials are dedicated to those who attempted the Fount and perished. Spruce-lined avenues radiate downward and out, covered in shops, homes, and clan-complexes of artisans, bureaucrats, and the other monied professions. These also host ministries, temples, shrines, and spacious parks. Farthest from the city’s center, farmers, fisherfolk, and merchants dwell on the riverbanks and coast, while shepherds and miners live in mountainside hamlets.

### Food and Clothing

Sorcerous workings keep the soil warm and fertile in a few fields, allowing for small crops of tomatoes, cucumbers, husk cherries, sweet peppers, and fresh herbs. Otherwise, agriculture tends toward hardier, cold-tolerant plants like potatoes, parsnips, beets, cabbage, sorrel, and various berries. Meat comes from wooly cattle, yak, and reindeer. Other staples include barley, oats, rye, spelt, beans, and imported spices and dried fruit.

EX3

are common fashions. To combat the cold, people add gloves and heavy blanket-like cloaks bearing bold geometric designs. Common folk wear plain wool; aristocrats prefer silks and accessorize their outfits with splendid jewelry.

### OTHER NORTHWESTERN LOCALES

A thousand years ago, a star fell on the city Whilom, tearing a burning gash through towers and plazas. Today, strange vegetation overgrows the ruins: twisted trees with oddly colored foliage that flutters without wind, soporific-scented lichens that drink blood with a touch, and more besides. Those who’d plunder Whilom’s Shogunate-era vaults must contend not only with these terror-plants, but with weird, malevolent astral spirits that rode the star to earth.

### Clans

Life and architecture both center around family. Clan compounds encompass numerous individual households, with shared outbuildings for cooking, storage, bathing, and other necessities of daily life. Wealthier clans establish larger, more luxurious compounds; the palace itself serves as the royal Ulu clan’s compound.

Ten miles of rubble and salted earth surrounds the First Age ruin known only as the Slab. An enormous square block of basalt, close to three hundred feet on a side and twenty feet high, dominates the site; a field of jagged, twisted spikes jut from the ground around it in all directions. Stone slabs ring the site, etched with worn, largely unreadable script in several prehuman tongues; a single damaged First Age obelisk provides only a cryptic warning of some buried danger. Near a deliberately collapsed tunnel dug under one edge of the slab stands a far more recent stone cairn, carved in Skytongue with prayers for the dead.

While historically patriarchal, clan membership is matrilineal, passing from mother to child. The entire clan shares child-rearing responsibilities. Servants and retainers are attached to their employers’ clans as “distant cousins”; loyal service grants each generation increasingly familiar terms until they’re cousins in truth, initiated into the clan through marriage. This is among the few avenues for lower-class Uluiruans to better, if not their own lives, then their grandchildren’s. Still, this depends on the clan patriarchs’ continued largesse; they may demote a retainer to “distant cousin” again for a single mistake.

The Gulf of Embers — a circular pit half a mile across where gravity turns sideways — contains a forest that grows horizontally from its walls towards its center. Motes of glowing dust drift among the pale trees, eerily illuminating the alien vista. Explorers have reported sightings of unique spirits and fauna, and have found evidence of lost, perhaps prehuman civilizations. These include fields of empty caskets of black stone embedded by the thousand in the pit’s walls, delicate glass tower-bridges that meet in the pit’s center like a cyclopean spiderweb, and sand labyrinths whose symmetries are marred only by careless explorers’ meddling. No two expeditions have reported the same journey; none, no matter how persistent, have glimpsed the bottom.

Clans have no official role in Uluiru’s governance, but wield considerable influence through support to promising upper-class scions. The elite often afford children who perform well at the Forty-Four Distinctions opportunities for socializing and training, and clans expect a successful child to repay them for their years of dedicated support when the child comes of age. The ministries are replete with counselors and clerks who, knowingly or not, guide policy to favor their clans above others.

Uluiruans favor hearty, filling meals, with dishes such as barley, fava bean, and red currant stew, rounded out with seasonally available meat; gemmifera sprouts roasted with salty cheese; oxtail braised with onion, anchovies, and butternuts; fried mackerel with spicy shrimp paste; curried fish on rye toast; and ceviche of chopped beef, seafood, or snail, mixed with spring onions and spices. Most dishes are accompanied by stiff oat-flour porridge.

Uluiruans clothing features bright colors and elaborate patterns. Ankle-length wrap skirts, loose trousers, and a long shawl worn draped over one shoulder

Although much of Uluiru’s wealth and population is centered in its eponymous capital, minor provinces and settlements extend along the coast and into mountainous hinterlands. Provincial serfs form an underclass outside the laws and customs set down by Ulu. So-called “provincials” belong to no clan (unless they become “distant cousins”), have limited rights, and are forbidden to carry weapons unless a clan’s militia conscripts them. Their children are technically allowed to compete in the Forty-Four Distinctions, but no allowance is made for travel to and from the city, shutting out all but the most dedicated and desperate.

EX3

### The Mines

### HEARTEATERS

While the Uluiruans rely on root vegetables, brassicas, livestock, fish, and wild game, they’d have perished long ago without trade — and the silver to support it. Uluiru’s mines extend in all directions deep underground, offering up bountiful mineral resources. They’re rich in gold — and where icy Essence condenses just right, precious blue jade — but also provide silver, marble, iron, and tin, as well as garnets, opals, diamonds, and even cherished adamant. These riches fill the city’s treasure-houses to bursting. Miners may claim the first piece of a newly uncovered deposit, called the “first chit,” with the remaining ore divided between the state and the miner’s clan. The chit’s exact size varies from clan to clan. Meant as a gesture of gratitude and an incentive for hard work, particularly lucky finds can change a family’s destiny forever. For example, the prosperous Uyun clan adopted the Eyu family when their youngest uncovered a vein of blue jade. The family received a nugget the size of the child’s head. The mines conceal bizarre wonders and dangers, so miners often work alongside savants and exorcists who investigate mysterious phenomena and quell strange spirits. The shafts closest to the Fount of Glories are especially bountiful, turning up not only rich veins of ore and gems, but also such marvels as crystallized fire and Essence-rich fungi. Administrators from multiple ministries oversee these shafts, carefully planning their exploitation and expansion to avoid encroaching on the Fount and its sacred energies.

### Neighbors

Azure and Fajad trade cloth, medicine, and food in exchange for a bounty of metals; they leverage the city’s needs — and their routes’ perils — to justify steep prices. Some of Fajad’s princes have made (thus far unsuccessful) overtures toward unmarried Sovereigns, while the Sea Lords extort tribute in exchange for access to their ports.

Closer to home, the cliff-girt islands of Spire-Bough trade with Uluiru only grudgingly. The insular Spirefolk guard the secrets of their gargantuan ironwood cedars, crafting wooden blades with fine-honed edges and ships fitted with ramming-bows, which they use for piracy. In Ulu’s absence, they’ve stepped up their raiding, seizing merchant vessels and plundering coastal towns. Agitators in Uluiru now clamor for war, hoping to turn the full might of the state’s fleet and the Sovereigns against the Spirefolk.

The Hearteaters, optional Exalted introduced in Exigents, make natural antagonists for the Sovereigns if you’re using them in your game. These monstrous Exalted hollow out victims, soul and all; they seek to claim the Fount of Glories — for their own ends. The precise motives and size of the Hearteater threat is up to the Storyteller, based on the themes, power level, and story of the chronicle. Even a lone Hearteater can be a formidable antagonist to a Circle of Sovereigns.

The graceful, aquiline Thousand Talon Family fly to war on snow-white wings and envenom their talons with a deadly mixture of nightmare-poetry and toxic sighs. Although these fae sometimes raid in force, swooping down on outlying settlements and leaving before Uluiru can muster a response, they prefer to goad would-be heroes into duels. They feed on enmity, carefully crafting decades-long vendettas to wring every drop of malice from their nemeses. In contrast, Fair Folk of the Labyrinth Domain are patient, subtle, generous, and mercurial. They inhabit a maze-palace of ice polished to a perfect sheen, and their eight lords keep entourages of reflections — alternate versions of themselves stolen from the mirror’s other side. These faceless raksha barter for mortals’ best features, collecting eyes, lips, hair, and voices to work into elaborate masks. They don these grotesque costumes alongside veils of glamour to disguise themselves as the people they’ve bargained with, walking among Uluiruans undetected to sate their appetites for intrigue, drama, betrayal, and romance.

### A Calamity of Princes

While the Sovereigns number hardly more than a score, their hubris and appetites match the Scarlet Dynasty’s, especially with neither queen nor heir to curtail their excesses.

No contender for Ulu’s throne is more qualified than Thousand-Hours Gwai, who’s devoted himself to the smooth functioning of the ministries. His ruthless clarity and dispassion — for which he’s sometimes called the city’s shadow-king — often tempered Ulu’s bold nature. As the eldest and most experienced politician among the Sovereigns, he would be a natural successor… if family and citizens alike didn’t despise him as a humorless taskmaster. His support could make or

fortnight; to this end, he manipulates Uluiru’s finances through aggressive trade and lending, aiming to entangle rivals in a web of debt and obligations.

### PLAINSFOLK LANGUAGES
