But in his earnest grief over the queen’s death, he lashes out; the city’s long mourning period made him bitter and quick to anger when any of his cousins fail to meet his standards of orderly and dignified conduct.

Khedaja Opal-Gauntlet came to Uluiru from afar, the daughter of a Sovereign exiled for an attempted coup. Stern but mild of temperament, Khedaja proved herself in every distinction, eventually joining the Sovereigns herself despite her mother’s treachery. Now she advocates for conquest and expansion, telling stories of her travels and the lands that would prosper under Uluiruan rule — starting with Fajad and its neighbors. To prove her mettle, she’s mustering a punitive expedition of mercenaries and patriots against the SpireBoughs to excite the city’s appetite for war. The people love Sword-Dancer Cilu for her heroics, especially her recent efforts in routing the Thousand Talon Family in two decisive raids. She’s positioned herself as a champion of the underclass. Her visits among them provoke awe and unrest — and may inadvertently stir them towards a violent uprising that would sweep her into power astride a wave of blood. To her credit, she’s earnest in wishing to improve their lives, but hopelessly naïve as to how to do so in any meaningful way. She respects only those who can contend with her in battle — a rare and precious few, thanks to her formidable skills and the uncanny reflexes drawn from her adamant daiklave, the Frozen Moment.

Behold him in his splendor: Luck-of-Seven Taiju! Warden of mine and tunnel, master of rock and gem, Sovereign of Uluiru!

Thus speak Taiju’s heralds, who announce him at every gathering more formal than his own dinner table. Even by Sovereign standards, Luck-of-Seven Taiju is dangerously smug, wearing etiquette like armor. His bravado isn’t without merit — he is a remarkably skilled administrator who keeps the city’s coffers flush with coin, and a seasoned duelist who’s triumphed against mortal champions, travelling God-Blooded, and the occasional Fair Folk bravo. He seeks the throne out of conviction that any of his relatives would beggar the city in a

Descended from a royal by-blow, then adopted into the royal clan after daring the Fount, Vigilant Faijul has always had something to prove to her Sovereign peers. Everything she has cost decades of bitter work. With little claim to the throne, she works more to disqualify her royal cousins than to win it for herself, leaking the family’s secrets in hope of revealing them as a band of hungry vipers. Still, she remains a dark horse candidate, idolized by commoners and provincials as a symbol of their aspirations. Other Sovereigns with lesser claims likewise seek the throne. Clever-Eyed Tanoh wields his superior sorcery, spying on rivals using a soulsteel mirror. Ohwa Blazing-Heart schemes with Fair Folk paramours, bewitching well-placed bureaucrats and carefully planning fae “raids” that she can publicly foil. Even Ahlu, among Uluiru’s youngest Sovereigns, presses his claim as heir apparent Nuwa’s son and an exemplar who achieved all Forty-Four Distinctions.

## The Silverswept Plains

Surrounded by darkness, the smell of wet soil, and the sound of worms boring through the earth, the dying ancient sleeps. While it waits to die, it dreams; its nightmares ooze toward the surface and poison the air. Decades pass between one heartbeat and the next. Far above, the world trembles at that single, slow pulse.

### People of the Plains

On the mainland northeast of Fajad, where a thousand skerries and rocky shoals line the coast, lies a prairie full of streams, most shallow enough for a child to cross without getting their knees wet. In winter the streams freeze, resembling miles of silver trails. Thickets and fruit bushes dot the vast, empty grassland, small homesteads occasionally breaking the monotonous view. These are the Silverswept Plains, home to a thousand shipwrecked sailors and their descendants. These seminomadic people travel the Plains in family groups called clans, ranging from 10 to 200 members. They harvest mollusks, raid seabirds’ nests, fish the lagoons and inlets from rafts or coracles, and forage. Common dishes include mussels steamed in seaweed, stinging nettle soup, and pickled kittiwake eggs.

EX3

Plainsfolk clothing incorporates a mishmash of styles, taken from those of shipwrecked ancestors and changed by time, distance, and available materials. Echoes of Azurite aquatic motifs appear in Uluiruan-style blanket cloaks, while short-sleeved, fur-lined Fajadi coats are embellished with the swirling patterns common to the Lost Isles of Aiun.

These punishments largely involve shaming, assigning unpleasant tasks, or corporal punishment. Exile is reserved for the worst crimes, like rape and murder; killing for any cause other than self-defense is prohibited, as death is the purview of fate and the gods. Clan heads negotiate crimes and disputes between clans; failing to come to an agreement can beget long, ugly vendettas.

Dozens of homesteads lie scattered across the Plains; each clan moves from one to the next every few months, giving vegetation and wildlife time to replenish. Built from local timber, fieldstone, wrecked ships, and thatch, the homesteads are durable if not elegant. Each resembles a small village, with herb gardens, houses, irrigation and sewage ditches, and a communal firepit. Particularly large homesteads might have a forge or workshop. Plainsfolk customarily leave the homestead tidy for the next family group.

The Plainsfolk treat all sails as potential raiders and slavers, and expertly vanish into groves, thickets, marshes, and ravines when ships approach. They’re accomplished swimmers, foragers, hunters, and netmakers; pursuers may well be drowned, shot, or caught in snares and booby traps.

Plainsfolk intermittently construct new homesteads to replace dilapidated or destroyed ones, or to accommodate population growth. Clans follow regular circuits between them, leaving them fallow for months between visits; smaller clans often travel together and share a homestead. Should outsiders use a fallow homestead, reactions to their presence varies between clans. However, tradition dictates that when outsiders visit homesteads in active use, Plainsfolk should welcome them for a night’s hospitality. A few small, permanent settlements exist in fertile valleys, where unassimilated foreigners — largely refugees from Azure, Uluiru, and Fajad — made their homes. Their settlers built these communities atop ruins of other, far older villages, though none living know anything more about the people who first worked the land. In other places, the wind whistles through towns abandoned for centuries. Nomadic Plainsfolk avoid these sites; farmers deem them cursed, forbidding their children from settling such land no matter how fertile it seems.

Plainsfolk Culture

A people of community and safety, the Plainsfolk value family above all. Clans settle differences with wrestling, boxing, and debate. They gather most often for marriages and for embarkations — celebrations when a new clan splits off from one that’s grown too large. If a Plainsfolk commits a serious crime, their clan brands and shuns them.

Clan heads have full discretion to punish their kinfolk as they like for matters that don’t affect other clans.

Plainsfolk worship gods of grove and stone who bless their marriages and hunts. New clans may maintain their parent clan’s worship, or adopt new gods that represent them in some fundamental way. Even the crudest homestead hosts a shrine where the current clan may place its idols and burn offerings. Omen-readers travel between homesteads, offering advice on the coming seasons: whether to prepare for a harsh winter or thin hunting season, or when to set out for the next homestead. Their predecessors passed down knowledge of strange signs that herald doom; modern augurs have never seen their like until recently. Now, though, birds flock in strange patterns, and plants grow pale and twisted. Beasts panic or lash out in anger. Many animals have fled the Plains entirely. A few Plainsfolk consider doing the same.

### Beneath

The Plainsfolk weren’t the first to live here. Under the Silverswept Plains’ soft sands and rough scrub, something stirs in uneasy slumber, its dying heart beating slowly and intermittently. Each days-long heartbeat comes decades apart, sending waves of panic, nightmares, and mental anguish across the surface. At each wave’s peak, people across the Plains collapse for a time, swept into the buried entity’s dying dreams. They rouse hours later, remembering only fragments of that impossible experience. The worst waves can kill, slaying Plainsfolk, animals, or even spirits by the dozens or hundreds.

The Plainsfolk sing half-remembered shanties and lullabies after every heartbeat. Older Plainsfolk say this soothes the thing beneath the plains for a time, ending the waves more quickly by easing its pain. In truth,

EX3

### The Visitor

### WOUNDED GODS

Drawn by omens, prophetic dreams, and ancient annals from a people long dead. the sorcerer Olma arrived on the Plains last year. Her presence causes intense debate among the clans. Some distrust her motives as an outsider; others — especially the omen-readers — welcome her and invite her counsel.

The Silverswept Plains’ spirits are all somewhat wild, having been repeatedly scarred over the centuries by fear and devastation. Few understand what horror lies beneath the plains, but many pretend to. Some offer protection in exchange for sacrifice, though it’s questionable whether any have such power or whether they’ll merely claim unearned credit for their wards’ survival.

none can say whether whatever lies beneath can even hear or understand their language, let alone take comfort from it. The elders and sages of the Plainsfolk, few as they are, recognize that there’s a very simple question they don’t have the answer to:

If these are just its heartbeats, what happens when it dies?

### Noteworthy Clans

Plainsfolk rely on the scouts, heralds, and hunters of Clan Brighteyes for news and meat. The clan matriarch, Senda, claims to know every Plainsfolk by name, and sometimes delivers news to other clans herself. Clan Brighteyes’s shamans and augurs often gather in a copse of strange trees at the center of the plains, where mossy fragments of glyph-carved smoky quartz jut up from the soil; they say that its elementals sing awful, moaning songs when a heartbeat is imminent. Shore-dwelling Clan Breakwater provides much of the fish and seaweed in the Plainsfolk diet. Mercurial and curious, they venture offshore in coracles to scavenge shipwrecks and scout for sails on the horizon. They’re quickest to deal with outsiders, offering to trade goods or act as guides. Some even leave the Plains behind, signing onto outsider ships or exploring inland. Clan Skywide claims descent from a Fajadi sorceress. These teachers and dabblers in the occult build their houses in accordance with arcane calculations. Many treat with the Plains’ mad gods, risking life and sanity to gain their blessings and earn their secrets. Other Plainsfolk distrust or even shun Skywide, deeming them weird and treacherous. But even their most ardent detractors turn to them when local spirits cause trouble.

Olma believes the creature’s next heartbeat may indeed be its last, a declaration that’s sent ripples of apprehension throughout the Plainsfolk and caused upheaval among the clans. After a recent sorcerous experiment left her head ringing and her sleep nightmare-plagued, she’s retreated to an abandoned homestead. Those who dare visit her report a valley rife with agitated elementals, and a sorcerer who’s descended into paranoia.

Prominent Figures

Lesek is Clan Breakwater’s matriarch. A stern, compassionate woman in her early 60s, she tries to maintain peace and calm within her family. She sends emissaries to other clans, hearing their concerns at their homesteads and visiting their permanent settlements. Far-traveled in her youth, she knows a great deal about the Northwest beyond the Plains. More than once, visitors to the Plains have borne letters of introduction to her from foreigners who knew her decades before. Upon hearing Olma’s prediction, Tioska grew fearful of the death and destruction that he believes the creature’s death throes will wreak over the Plains, and agitates for the clans to take action. He’s gathered a band of like-minded followers; they’ve come to believe that the dying being lies buried beneath Clan Brighteyes’ sacred grove, and intend on exhuming it before it can cause greater harm.

Shaman and omen-reader Yovak reads dire days ahead in cloud formations and subtle shifts in the tides. She maintains hope that her people can somehow placate the creature beneath the Plains and bring it a tranquil death. Even so, she also petitions clan leaders to plan for the worst: ration food, build sledges, and gather warm clothing for the long trek to other lands should they need to flee, though she knows doing so will cost many lives.

## The Lost Isles of Aiun

The Lost Isles are a wound upon the West, a twisted archipelago that curls in on itself. At the center, a vast whirlpool consumes anything caught in its currents,

EX3

devouring ships and even krakens whole. Fog enshrouds the Isles, making them all but impossible to find or to leave — at least intentionally. They’re more asylum than sanctuary: a covetous, secretive world unto itself that grinds down its unfortunate inhabitants.

### MORE NORTHWESTERN LOCALES

Pyrene stood as a mighty metropolis until the occult coterie called the Cardinal House sought apotheosis there. Today it’s an overgrown ruin that even wild beasts avoid. Vast, inhuman footprints as large as city blocks lie filled with cloudy amber fluid; those who plumb their depths report the thoughts and dreams of long-dead citizens seeping into their own psyches. Scavengers sometimes bring back relics of the Cardinal House, such as cultic images of a many-armed dancer, jeweled masks with seven eyes, and grimoires written in a variety of nigh-indecipherable codes and ciphers. Other scavengers never return, lost to the ruins’ perils.

When the sorceress Aiun shook Creation to raise up a continent in the Northwest, she held a single hope in mind: to create a home for her sealfolk clansmen and their allies, a place of refuge where they could forge their own destiny unmolested by the affairs of gods and non-beastfolk. Aiun reached out for power in desperation — and to her eternal doom, received it. Wielding the fabled Eye of Autocthon, she discovered, conjured, or created a numinous power called the Spiral, which twisted the world where she walked. With it, she brought forth a new land of bounty and wrapped it in a wall of mist to keep out those who’d hunted her people to the brink of extinction.

The Wyld forest of Siray boasts soft grasses and beds of sumptuous, sweet-smelling leaves. Those who lay their weary heads upon them enter a dreaming world of sun-dappled paths and drowsy, pleasant afternoons. They fall asleep in that place and dive ever deeper into dreams within dreams, from which little can wake them. Moss and vines grow over the sleepers — a gentle, verdant tomb for their bones.

But the Spiral knows no master. When Aiun passed, her palace crumbled into the sea. The land heaved. The great whirlpool quickened, and entire mountains fell into its greedy maw. For centuries, the Lost Isles’ people have held out, even as this vortex tears their homes asunder.

The ruins of Vernal Wing — a fallen First Age starspire — lie canted at an angle among the Yunura mountains. Strange and luminous beasts, drawn down from some otherworldly realm, haunt this sky-palace’s dead gardens and broken halls. When the moon is right, an archway in the manse’s courtyard glows a cold, harsh azure, showing beyond it an unfamiliar sky. The brave — or foolhardy — may then step through into a desert of blue rock in a world alien to Creation, peopled by creatures unfamiliar to even the most knowledgeable Exalted savants.

Slowly, inevitably, the Spiral will have its due. Its influence extends beyond simple destruction. Where the Spiral’s pull is strongest, it bends and distorts the land and its people: Tree branches curl back on themselves in great loops, standing stones arrange themselves into gyre-shaped patterns, and even living flesh begins to slant, bend, and curve, giving people unearthly figures and proportions and painfully bending their joints the wrong ways around.

### Aiun’s Children

The people of the Lost Isles call themselves Aiun’s Children, taking her name out of honor, spite, fear, and hope. Most are beastfolk, especially seal-, walrus-, and frogfolk. Some are Aiun’s progeny; others trace their lineage to allies, friends, and servants — those who accompanied her into self-imposed exile. The few non-beastfolk descend from Aiun’s slaves or are marooned sailors from the world beyond. Clothing on the Lost Isles features long tunics and ponchos with embroidered trim and geometric patterns. Necklaces with stone beads and shells drape from hammered metal brooches, and people carry small tools and belongings in leather satchels attached to a woven belt. Spiral motifs dominate the designs.

Boiling and roasting are common cooking methods on the Isles. Popular dishes include roasted auk with cabbage; smoked fish; and squash and bean stew; and potato cakes made with milk, honey, and mint. Fermented cereal grains make a mild alcoholic drink that’s used both at the table and in rituals.

Sealfolk and the Scythe

The largest of the Lost Isles is a sweeping curve called the Scythe. Its clay-rich fields yield grains, beans, and cabbage; its calm shoals and gentle rivers play host to fat fish and fowl. Here, tribes of Aiun’s Children live amongst one another and envoys from other isles gather to trade, talk, and scheme. The city of Osoro, its stone towers twisting toward the sky, serves as the Lost Isles’ capital. Here, the Vigilant Queen’s palace perches on a promontory overlooking

EX3

the waves. Onesse, the queen’s sister, trains her army on the rocky shores outside the fortress-city of Takil, to the north. Other settlements dot the Scythe’s shores, including Yril, which sits at the eye of an ever-churning storm; Utash with its hundred shrines; and Raft, where farmers sow crops in helical patterns. While sealfolk form a slim majority of the Scythe’s population, they have a death grip on the Vigil — a collection of petty lords, village heads, and war-leaders that administrates the Scythe under their Vigilant Queen’s watchful eye. When a queen passes, the Vigil elects her successor from among the half-dozen families who trace an unbroken lineage to Aiun. A strong queen can unite her Vigil in mutual interest, but the Vigil hasn’t chosen a strong queen in generations. The resulting fractious body cooperates little, except to maintain its members’ privileges. Communities that belong to the Vigil continue their long-standing vendettas, extracting wealth and tribute from lesser villages and islands at spearpoint. The Vigil itself ignores these, so long as they don’t balloon into greater concerns. By their own accounts, the sealfolk are the truest and most deserving of Aiun’s Children. For centuries, nonbeastfolk raiders hunted them for their precious pelts, which sorcerers especially favor for the lingering magic that first transformed their ancestors. The sealfolk are diplomats, architects, warriors, and scholars. Some sealfolk occultists see themselves as upholding Aiun’s legacy, though none have matched her wonders. Despite their position of power as hegemons of the Lost Isles, the sealfolk regard themselves as a persecuted people, nursing their ancient grudge against non-beastfolk to a fever pitch. The walrusfolk and frogfolk are their cousins — sometimes favored, sometimes not, but they all know what it was to be hunted. Sealfolk always trust them above non-beastfolk.

Walrusfolk

The walrusfolk have the next largest population. They make their living throughout the Lost Islands as traders, laborers, smiths, and sellswords — especially on the Scythe, where mercenary companies always seek walrusfolk warriors and captains. Those who stay on their ancestral islands of Weeping Moon, Brightclaw, and Nine Thunders treat these bare and icy lands as a challenge that they’re honor-bound to tame. Lowland farmers work the stubborn earth around the base of the mountains, while warrior-nobles maintain estates farther upslope. Life is long and difficult for the walrusfolk, who’ve adopted a grim outlook that

Frogfolk have three-dot Gills and Wall Walking (Exalted, pp. 166-167). enshrines suffering as the foremost virtue and teaches that all who live must serve.

Only the holiest walrusfolk dwell on the snow-girded mountaintops, huddled inside crumbling temples where they study Creation’s many mysteries, pass down ancient rites to apprentices, and watch for omens favorable to battle. When those omens appear, the walrusfolk make war upon one another, and upon the Lost Isles’ other peoples.

Walrusfolk conduct vicious raids stoked more by religious fervor than by need or greed. Only in conquest do the walrusfolk feel nearer to their lost gods, including their ancient Lunar progenitor Jaryn Thousand-Spears. For all their battle-frenzy, they don’t raze settlements or shatter tribes entirely. It’s poor husbandry to strip a herd down to nothing, and wiser to leave enough for them to rebuild and repopulate so their shepherds can cull them again.

Frogfolk

The frogfolk appear throughout the Lost Isles as travelers, tutors, merchants, and scholars, but they have only a single homeland: the cliff-ringed island of Gen’s Spindle. There they worship their queen, the Witch of the Fens, whose strange sorceries weave hand-stitched automata of leather, straw, wool, and bone. These gruesome poppets free the frogfolk to live lives of intellect, artistry, and leisure — at least by the Lost Isles’ standards. In their grim workshops, they collect flora and fauna samples from their travels abroad, dissect human and beast cadavers to investigate the mechanisms of life, and pursue the Spiral’s mysteries to the brink of madness.

Coddled from everyday life’s rigors, the frogfolk see themselves as separate from and superior to the Lost Isles’ other peoples, often bringing them into conflict with the sealfolk. Unlike the walrusfolk, this smug superiority leads them not toward conquest, but toward detachment; they welcome visitors to Gen’s Spindle only out of curiosity, and they travel the islands with a

EX3

certain scholarly distance, as if they’re merely spectators of a world unworthy of their intervention.

Other Inhabitants

Finally, the descendants of Aiun’s non-beastfolk slaves and of later arrivals marooned on the islands form an underclass, kept as pets, servants, and slaves — especially by the sealfolk. Some have broken off into their own villages and tribes, usually living far inland to deny any advantage to their amphibious foes. Of these settlements, the largest is the island-fortress of Shy Rook. Through decades of hard labor, its people have prepared this mean and meager land for a rebellion that may come in a year, a decade, or a century. Other non-beastfolk are held in thrall; they serve as chattel in the fields of the Scythe and beyond. The sealfolk are especially harsh taskmasters, treating slaves with cold contempt. Walrusfolk and frogfolk are less intractably hostile; Bright Claw’s walrusfolk permit a few trusted non-beastfolk warriors among their kind, and the frogfolk treat non-beastfolk refugees like abused pets.

Other things creep in the Lost Isles, unaccounted for in their fractured lore: a clan of narwhalfolk who claim

the Spiral’s power twists through their tusks; tribes who give themselves wholly to the Spiral, transforming them into mockeries of life; monstrous snails large enough to swallow mortals whole, which disgorge acid that dissolves flesh in an instant; a spinning black fog that congeals into an attenuated human figure, seizing lone victims and vanishing with them into thin air. These, and other horrors still, haunt dark places where others fear to tread — and they’re the Spiral’s children, not Aiun’s.

### Lesser Isles

Thousands of islands comprise the Lost Isles, from the vast Scythe to tiny outcroppings barely accommodating a single hut. Most near the Scythe lie under the Vigil’s rule; those farther away are often fiercely independent. The stronghold of Grayreef stands atop a cluster of enormous coral. The sealfolk and walrusfolk who call it home dive the reef to hunt titan-eels, which provide them food, oil, and fearsome sawtooth knives. Those who dwell here begin to have bloody dreams, hearing the death-rattle of some gargantuan beast whose name and nature are lost to the ages. These dreams

Broken Places

THE SPIRAL’S POWER

Many wonders were lost or corrupted in the cataclysm that shattered Aiun’s paradise.

### The Spiral

’s Essence touches those who commune with it. This sometimes imparts unique powers such as thaumaturgical procedures, mutations, and other Merits. Purposefully seeking such a transformation or power requires a character to open themselves to the Spiral entirely — a dangerous proposition that often changes them in unsavory ways. Characters exposed to the Spiral may purchase inherent Merits usually available only at character creation, but also gain a Flaw of the Storyteller’s choice (usually a Minor or Major Derangement) as the Spiral takes its due.

Below the sea lies ruined Algyen. There, glass-eyed ghosts of the drowned pantomime their former lives, but devour any interlopers who disturb their dark farce. Atop the stair-banded spire of Nul’s Dagger stands a house of healing; the Spiral has contorted its stones into impossible loops. Inside, bronze automata tend wounds and illnesses with supernatural skill, but refuse to let anyone leave.

Commanding the Spiral itself is a more significant endeavor for a sorcerer or Exalt, requiring one or more stories’ worth of occult research, investigating places of power, performing sorcerous workings, crafting artifacts, repairing or constructing manses, delving beneath the sea into the Spiral’s distorted realm, and similar projects. Its controller can perform mighty feats related to its warping power or its bond with the islands, at the Storyteller’s discretion; these might include twisting the wind into tornadoes and hurricanes, rearranging or reshaping the archipelago’s islands, or moving the entire archipelago across the Great Western Ocean. Any such powers hold similar perils to communing with the Spiral, and should be diminished or inaccessible outside of the Lost Isles.

Near the center of the Lost Isles, overlooking the maelstrom, stand the Fountains of Ninua. Once, they issued forth sweet wine to the people of Aiun’s capital. Now, assassins bottle their viscous ooze for poison.

sometimes cause eruptions of mass hysteria as phantasmagoric wounds appear on Grayreef’s inhabitants, dripping oily blood that’s not their own.

Savants may recognize the Spiral’s influence as loosely akin to, but distinct from, the Wyld. The Spiral is specific, intentional, and covetous — it’s dimly aware of the people it protects and, in its own crude way, wants them to use it. It frequently empowers mortals and animals with terrible strength and supernatural ability. The gruesome changes it imparts are never fatal, despite appearances: fingers curl back on themselves, joints bend the wrong way, and limbs grow until they should snap, yet the Spiral’s children survive. Sometimes, they even thrive.

The Spiral

What is the Spiral? Only Aiun knew, and even her understanding was imperfect. It’s a presence that permeates the Lost Isles, a source of magical power, and a storm of dark feelings and impulses. This grinding, twisting, changing force touches everything on the Isles from stone to stem: Trees grow in corkscrew turns, people are tall and bent and stretched, and even fires spin in its dance.

The Spire of Uolo is a relic of Aiun herself, one of many manses she erected when she governed the Lost Isles. Today, the half-sunken palace rises from the sea as an artificial islet. It’s a port of call for traders, wanderers, and pilgrims, ruled by the cult of Aiun called the DeathDrinkers. Supplicants bring them the brains of the recently dead, from which they distill powerful elixirs that allow communion with the deceased’s memories. The cult’s storehouses are fabled to contain a sample of Aiun’s own brain, preserved against the ravages of time — a sample that’s remained untouched because none are holy or blasphemous enough to consume it. There are hundreds of other islands: iron-rich Bloody Paw; the Screaming Island, where ancient stone sentinels cry out in ceaseless agony; Bone Arch, littered with cathedrals carved from leviathan skeletons. Despite a world of hardship where even the land begrudges them their existence, Aiun’s Children survive, creating fleeting beauty in their dark, twisted home.

For the Lost Isles’ people, the Spiral is both divinity and natural disaster, as terrible and sacred as a monsoon amid a drought. They don’t worship it so much as live within it, embracing its mysteries. On Four Sons, islanders carve spirals into the chalky hills, walking them in holy communion. On Gen’s Spindle, frogfolk tattoo themselves with a curling script understood by none but intuited by all. Weeping Moon’s raiders practice ritual contortions, using pain to better contemplate the Spiral and its ever-changing nature.

EX3

Spirits are especially vulnerable to the Spiral’s power. When Aiun’s continent was sundered, the Spiral twisted and tore the gods and elementals of that new land into half-conscious phantasms, if it did not devour them entirely. A few have found ways to protect their sanctums from the Spiral’s power; or dwell within protective reliquaries devised by sorcerers and thaumaturges. Such spirits provide wisdom and blessings to their chosen people in exchange for worship and protecting their dwellings. Ghosts fare no better: the Spiral beckons those who leave their shadowlands to throw themselves into its churning gyre.

Sorcerers who dare consider themselves Aiun’s equal have learned their folly when trying to control the Spiral. None since Aiun herself have successfully bound or compelled it for any significant length of time, although many a would-be sorcerer king has broken their power on the Lost Isles’ shores in their attempts.

### Beyond the Isles

Aiun’s Children rarely deal with the world beyond their shores, for the Isles are nigh impossible to find. The fog enshrouding them confuses all but the most powerful magical navigation, dashing the unwary against hidden rocks or dragging errant ships ashore. Flotsam is inevitable — every year, a handful of mortals wash ashore, their fates largely determined by where they arrive. Will they be slaves, servants, freemen, or prey? Powerful spirits, sorcerers, and Chosen occasionally visit the Lost Isles, either by accident or seeking Aiun’s fabled treasures. Most are disappointed to discover the grim lands, but savants from Skullstone, Randan, and a few other nations have investigated the Spiral with varying degrees of success and consequence. These visits are uncommon and costly; although a precious few routes can deliver travelers to or from the Lost Isles, they’re dangerous even for seasoned mariners.

Now, as tensions rise between members of her Vigil, their border skirmishes erupt into allout battles that she believes herself powerless to stop. Her sister Onesse is fearsome and strong-willed, a true descendant of Aiun blessed with the gift of sorcery. Sickly throughout her life, she’s rallied under the care of her personal physician, the Spiral-addled frogfolk thaumaturge Pirou, and now builds her power through alliance and conquest, aiming to seize the throne and usher in an era of bloody reform. For the nonce, she’s demurred at Pirou’s proposals to further fortify her body and mind with drugs, arcane tattoos, and whorled yantras — not for fear of the Spiral’s warping power, but because she wishes to achieve victory by her own strength. Sworn-to-the-Sea leads Weeping Moon’s walrusfolk. Built like a mountain of muscle, hide, and blubber, he tipped his spear with ivory from his own tusk as a reminder of the only battle he ever lost. Spiraling scars across his arms and shoulders imbue him with inhuman strength; his tusk-spear, etched with helical scrimshaw, can penetrate any armor while in his hands. In shamanic trances, he seeks out wisdom from Jaryn ThousandSpears; now, he senses his patron’s spirit stirring in the world, calling the walrusfolk to conquer the Isles and prepare them as his new holdfast.

The scavenger-savant Gimble is the envoy of Gen’s Spindle to the Lost Isles at large. He takes perverse, voyeuristic delight in observing others’ lives, peppering them with interminable questions. Few in the Isles can match his knowledge of natural and occult sciences; his satchels brim with alchemical powders, medicinal herbs, and coded journals full of theories about the Isles’ geomancy and the Spiral. Aes has taken him as a confidant and tutor, but he’s primarily concerned with accounts of an eldritch weapon hidden on the Scythe — the Ravenous Maw — that Aiun left bound to her descendants’ lineage.

### Prominent Figures

Elas the Wise, an Air Aspect outcaste from Crocus, was once a merchant prince famed for her fleet of treasure ships. Marooned on the Lost Isles, she’s risen to prominence among the non-beastfolk, helping arrange trade between the island of Shy Rook and its neighbors. In doing so, she’s disrupted vital sealfolk trade routes, positioning Shy Rook as a more convenient port for merchants willing to trade with non-beastfolk.

Aes Nightspear is the Vigilant Queen of the sealfolk — and thus queen of the Lost Isles, if only in name. She’s polite but withdrawn, and despite a lifetime of training at arms, she remains ill at ease with the political power she now wields to mete out life and death. The Vigil

Kega Sea-Lace contemplates the mists enshrouding the Lost Isles. A sorceress to rival Aiun — at least, Aiun before she acquired the Eye — Kega studies the magic that conceals and protects her homeland, and though she dare not seek to command the Spiral directly, her

For their part, Aiun’s Children hold the outside world in contempt, having spent generations building a mythology about the Creation that once hunted their ancestors. Dire as the Isles are, they’re still a refuge, and centuries of blood and labor have made their inhabitants strong.

### STILL MORE NORTHWESTERN LOCALES

## Atmu

lies in the farthest Northwest, a vast triangular island hundreds of miles from the mainland coast. Most of the year, a thick layer of ice covers the ground. Even during brief, mild summers, any earth exposed in the temporary thaw remains frozen solid. No trees grow on Atmu; the only vegetation consists of mosses and lichens. The island’s environment is hostile to life: harsh winds scour the terrain day and night. Blizzards cause whiteout conditions and bury landmarks. Snowdrifts and windstorms sculpt an ever-shifting landscape. What little wildlife survives on Atmu is exceptionally hardy, tenacious, and often ruthless.

The very stones of Atratus are black as midnight; the trees and grasses, rather than green, grow a lush, unsettling sable. Millennia ago, a clique of ambitious Solar sorcerers evoked a timeless, ill-omened shadow-entity from beyond the stars — one that, in the end, even they could not control. Their mountaintop manse, smashed like an eggshell by the forces they called upon, now stands empty to the sky, its inky remains home to weird shadow-beasts and corrupted spirits. Once one of the Lost Isles of Aiun, the Stray spun off from the Spiral and wanders the seas alone, shrouded in mist. Those who dock at its lone port are greeted by sealfolk who speak an archaic tongue. The stars above the Stray seem to move in a spiral against the sky, though navigators argue over whether that’s due to the island’s own endless turning or something stranger.

However, some historians suggest life once flourished on Atmu. They refer to ancient records — scattered, fragmented, and often contradictory — that paint a picture of a prehuman society that once settled the island. Explorers’ drawings depict ruins peeking from beneath the snow. Private collectors boast about items in their possession recovered from Atmu: idols with alien faces, relics sculpted into eye-twisting shapes, and curios molded from materials heavier than they appear. Their origins — and, occasionally, their authenticity — are topics of lively debate. The ancient manuscripts devolve into nonsense, and those studying the sketches and sculptures frequently comment on their disturbing nature.

The ancient city of Seruku lies in ruins around a perfectly circular lake where, legend says, centuries ago an airborne “wheel of light” pulled the city’s center up into the sky. The city’s domes and tenements, though thickly overgrown and cracked by roots and winter ice, remain largely intact, albeit choked with debris, moldering relics, and bones.

A small band of Yatani’s Children (Dragon-Blooded, p. 126) camp in Seruku. Their Exalted leaders, the arrogant mathematician-musician Tokei and the inquisitive occultist Praywind, theorize that whatever mechanism stole the city’s heart might also convey them to their lost homeland. Thus far they’ve found bas-reliefs littered with odd geometric designs, fragments of cryptic texts, and a twisted homunculus in a jar that whispers of secrets buried underground. occult workings draw upon its aspects. Her lighthouse-manse, Bellwether, is a beacon in the otherwise featureless mists. She’s among the few who know how to leave the Isles, but takes greater delight in luring ships into the mists, sending demonic servants to raid them for wealth and fresh subjects for her experiments.

Atmu

Wind wails over Atmu’s frozen expanse. Waves crash on its barren, rocky shores, the surf occasionally churning up strange, twisted relics from beneath the frigid sands. Dark clouds scud across the sky; their smudgy shadows pass over eldritch structures whose origins are unknown to modern scholars. Though audacious

Yet sailors whose routes take them past Atmu share stories that corroborate parts of the records. They describe harrowing encounters with entities they can’t name, whose features stirred terror in their hearts. Shipwreck survivors spin apocryphal tales of sheltering amidst uncanny ruins while awaiting rescue, and of the bizarre experiences they had therein. They speak of skies full of unfamiliar stars, figures performing moonlit rituals atop snowy plateaus, and the bone-chilling howls of alien beasts. Skullstone’s Silver Prince made the best-known effort to exploit Atmu decades ago. A small army of living colonists and zombie laborers, led by the ghostly necromancer Skua’s Echo, established a settlement at Atmu’s southwestern tip. Initially, the venture seemed promising; a Skullstone fleet visiting later that year brought back ore mined from Atmu’s rock, treasures from a sunken ship, and several curios found in abandoned structures inland. But the next visit found nothing — the settlement and all within had vanished utterly. Isolated and desolate, Atmu lies far enough from inhabited lands that explorers traversing its ice-bound terrain might imagine they’re the only living beings in Creation.

EX3

Even the most misanthropic souls find the remoteness daunting; soon enough, the weight of all that emptiness becomes unsettling. Are they truly on their own? What beings raised and lived amongst these ruins in eons long past, and what remains of them now? What vast temples might the ice conceal, and do their dead gods and restless ghosts stir at the sound of boots on the snows above? Do they sense the warm blood singing through trespassers’ veins? What eerie music skirls beneath the wind’s low moans and the crash of the waves?

### WHAT THE CHOSEN FEAR

Horror stories set in the Northwest’s strange locales can prove challenging for Storytellers. The extraordinary powers of the Exalted allow them to face terrifying foes and wield magics that shape Creation itself. How do you incorporate Charms like Inviolable Essence-Merging, God-King’s Shrike, and Immortal Soul Vigil without diminishing the story or bypassing interesting parts of the setting? Players put time and experience points into developing their characters’ abilities, and losing access to those to retain the Storyteller’s plot points can be frustrating.

### Unsafe Harbor

One outpost exists, on the islet of Emris off Atmu’s coast. There, a few whalers and fishers eke out their livings from the icy waters. Emris is little more than a collection of salt-weathered buildings huddled close together, offering temporary shelter to traders, though sea traffic is infrequent.

The islet’s residents never travel to Atmu. While they tolerate outsiders, they don’t pretend to like them. In fact, the islet’s occupants make it quite clear that visitors are unwelcome and should complete their business as quickly as possible, then be on their way. Some offer dire warnings to those who announce their intention to explore Atmu. Few are foolish enough to accept work as guides, no matter how much coin an expedition leader offers. Dark dreams haunt those who come this close to Atmu; Emris’s residents stave off the nightmare visions with potent herbal concoctions that send them into dreamless sleep. Many take shifts sitting by one another’s bedsides to wake the sleepers, should terrors seep in anyway. Wisa has fished the waters of Emris since she was young. She’s in her late fifties now, her dark hair shot through with gray and her skin leathery from wind and salt. She brews the dream-dulling potion for the islet’s residents, marking its price up sharply for foolish explorers whom she cannot deter from sailing on to Atmu. Lyeaz is a recent arrival to Emris, there for his first fishing season. He not-so-secretly yearns to explore Atmu himself, though his uncles forbid it. He has a catalogue of stories in his head that his family passed down, and — to the great dismay of Emris’s other residents — has been known to share them with outsiders.

### Expedition: Atmu

Despite its frightful reputation, rumors of massive treasures hidden beneath the snow and ice tempt explorers and fortune-seekers to Atmu’s shores. Many have

A key element of successful horror is taking the familiar — settings, people, abilities — and changing it subtly. This uncertainty fuels unease. We encourage Storytellers to let the setting’s eeriness affect Exalted abilities. Perhaps the region’s geomantic power twists its Essence, distorting spells and making Charms act unreliably. Or effects may go off as expected, but sizable expenditures of Essence act as a beacon to disturbing creatures or set long-dormant mechanisms into motion.

Expeditions that hew close to the coast spy deserted, ancient ruins in the distance, and bring curious relics aboard. Logs and journals from those who venture farther inland reflect their authors’ slow descent into delusion and paranoia... if they return at all. Some adventurers dream of unearthing caches of jade and precious gems or returning home with holds full of relics to make collectors part with their wealth. For others, riches pale in comparison to stories they’ve heard of esoteric machinery buried in forgotten tombs whose mechanisms still whirr and click away in the dark, or of lost hieroglyphs outlining sciences and sorceries unfamiliar even to the Exalted. They seek maps of strange realms, outlining continents unknown in Creation, the Underworld, or Yu-Shan. Their fingers ache to grasp the fine silver pipes ancient explorers sketched, rumored to make even an empress dance to their otherworldly tune.

Recently, the Guild-affiliated Garland Mast Company announced a major expedition into Atmu’s interior. It’s sponsored ships and supplies, and seeks Exalted aid — both to help unlock the island’s ancient mysteries, and to protect expedition personnel from any hostile entities who might object to their presence on Atmu.

# Appendix: The World We Know

Appendix

The World

We Know

Creation is a flat world built of the five elements, home to fantastical spirits and monsters. But it’s also a world that superficially resembles our own, with largely — though not entirely — familiar flora and fauna, celestial bodies, and natural laws. This appendix addresses broad topics about Creation, covering both similarities to and differences from historical Earth.

## The Natural World

Much of Creation’s natural world resembles our own, with a sun, moon, and stars in the sky. Familiar plants and animals populate its regions, and people keep track of time according to differing calendar systems.

### The Heavens

The sun’s golden barque sets sail across the sky each day, englobed in life-giving holy light, eventually setting below the horizon. It drifts south as noon approaches, then back north later in the day; this, along with the elemental poles’ influence, makes the North’s climate cool and the South’s warm.

The farther north one goes, the longer days grow in summer and the longer nights are in winter. Indeed, in the uttermost north, it’s said that the sun doesn’t set at all in summer, nor does it rise in winter. Modern savants have few means to uncover the causes of these

### FLY ME TO THE MOON

Visiting celestial bodies isn’t part of typical Exalted play. As such, we’ve left their specific nature — whether blazing chariots, looming skyships, barren orbs, or verdant worlds — up to your chronicle’s specific needs. To make them more accessible in your game, feel free to incorporate mystic gateways, Spirit Charms, First Age aetherships, or other mechanisms allowing player characters to more easily reach them.

phenomena, and First Age academic texts on the subject remain obscure and difficult to interpret. The ever-shifting moon follows the sun’s path through the night and the edges of the day, phases changing through the month. Savants predict solar eclipses produced by their rare intersections, and lunar eclipses produced when Luna hides the moon’s face. Sun and moon alike fly far above Creation, beyond reach of all but the mightiest fliers and powerful magics. Farther out, stars move in regimented patterns across the night sky. Many cultures recognize the twenty-five constellations whose occult power the Sidereal Exalted wield — the Peacock, Gauntlet, Treasure Trove, and so forth. Five planets move among them, following patterns obscure to all but the wisest astrologers. Only the North Star remains fixed on the horizon. Other celestial phenomena include the Great Celestial Waterfall, a shimmering band of distant light resembling our Milky Way; comets, whose appearances often portend great change; meteors that flare brilliantly through the sky and occasionally crash to earth; and auroras, appearing only in the farthest Northern and Southern skies.

Spirits of the Unconquered Sun, Luna, and the Maidens gather around sun, moon, and planets, pursuing celestial business of little interest to mortals. Stranger entities dwell in the outer dark, such as monstrous devil-stars; these rarely descend to Creation, where they can wreak terrible havoc.

The Calibration Sky

The moon vanishes during Calibration. Other celestial bodies remain visible, although clouds often hide the sun and planets move unpredictably. Even stars occasionally appear in the wrong places, although the constellations’ overall shapes remain familiar.

EX3

### Flora and Fauna

### CAN I DO SCIENCE?

Creation’s flora and fauna are stunningly diverse. Most of our world’s plants and animals thrive there alongside numerous extinct species. Unfamiliar nonmagical creatures in published Exalted books are typically such prehistoric creatures. For instance, raitons are Archaeopteryx, tyrant lizards are tyrannosaurids, and yeddim are inspired by Paraceratherium.

Inspired by mythology and sword-and-sorcery fiction, Creation superficially resembles the real world. This allows Storytellers and players to more easily establish a shared understanding of the setting, which already has enough esoteric details to keep track of. Major divergences are largely a matter of theme and tone — for instance, adding extinct animals supports a “lost world” vibe, while replacing firearms with firewands signposts a broader rejection of anachronistic modern technology.

Fantastical plants and animals also inhabit Creation. Some appear in published Exalted material. Storytellers and players can invent others, such as by introducing a fact (Exalted, p. 237).

However, the deeper underpinnings of the setting — its physics, chemistry, biology, etc. — are another matter. While your group is welcome to play out A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court or Lest Darkness Fall, with the Circle’s Twilight or No Moon wielding modern science to fashion setting-transforming technologies, this falls outside the thematic scope of normal Exalted play.

People have transplanted flora and fauna from their original native areas over millennia of travel and trade. As such, cultivated plants and domesticated animals are often distributed more widely than in our world’s ancient civilizations.

It’s the Storyteller’s responsibility to determine how things work if player characters start prying into nature’s underpinnings. We recommend a relaxed approach to Lore’s Introducing a Fact mechanic (Exalted, p. 237), allowing players to establish as little or as much detail as they like, while being ready to veto facts that undermine your chronicle’s intended tone and transform the nature of the setting.

### Climate and Weather

Creation’s climate — like Earth’s — varies by region, with long, cold winters in the North and long, hot summers in the South. Likewise, tropical regions largely have wet and dry seasons. Specifics appear in the previous chapters’ introductions. Local climates tend to follow real-world rules involving ocean currents, rain shadows, and the like. Divergences can be attributed to elemental Essence flows, spirit activity, and other supernatural causes, but these should be regarded as exceptions rather than the rule.

## The Mortal World

While this game’s title is “Exalted,” the Exalted exist in a world of mortals. Although the Chosen, gods, and other supernatural entities sway history’s tides with their power and personal drive, they are few where ordinary humans are many. Most princes, generals, merchants, and other noteworthy personages are mortal. As such, assume that characters named in this book and other Exalted material are mortal unless specified otherwise, either explicitly or implicitly (e.g., satraps are always Dragon-Blooded Dynasts, as per DragonBlooded and The Realm).

### Society and Customs

Social mores vary from culture to culture; these don’t always line up with modern morality. It’s not uncommon

to find societies that approve of social stratification, inflexible legalism, vendetta, bribery, or hedonism, just as one can find societies that laud their opposites. Players shouldn’t feel pressured to give their approval to moral codes they find reprehensible, both in and out of character.

Legal systems vary widely, but the larger the polity, the more inclined they are to prioritize rulers’ and merchants’ interests over commoners’ needs. Legal codes vary widely; some are lax and others draconian, while they may base themselves primarily on divine proclamations, royal edicts, legal precedent, or an individual magistrate’s whim. Enforcement typically falls to soldiers, hired muscle, or mob justice, and prioritizes maintaining civil order over individual needs. Punishments tend toward the quick and direct, e.g., fines, beatings, maiming, exile, or death. Other than slavery, long-term imprisonment is rare because it’s economically inviable.

Many cultures place great weight on hospitality, regarding it as a mutual obligation of generosity, courtesy,

EX3

conversation, and reciprocity. Harming one’s guest or host is usually a severe crime. Specifics vary from place to place; these may involve rules and customs such as a handshake, sharing salt, or even signing a contract. Individuals don’t typically revere one specific god. Rather, they worship various gods depending on current needs, such as praying to gods of rain and field during the harvest, then to the road god for safe travel to market, and finally to the market god for fair and profitable bargains. Likewise, while a god might have a dedicated priest or priesthood, many priests lead prayers to a variety of gods.

### States and Governance

Modern nationalism isn’t the default in Creation. People typically think of themselves more in terms of family, tribe, settlement, occupation, language, or culture than in terms of a nation-state. Social class is a notable bonding factor, in that princes of rival states may see themselves as having more in common with one another than with local commoners who they’ve never met. Similarly, local leaders in service to princes and governors may feel more loyal to the lords they’ve sworn service to and fought beside than with the peasantry they oversee. Personal relationships take precedence over other obligations for most figures in authority. Warlords place their companions in charge of local affairs. Hereditary princes regularly visit their vassals — or summon them to the prince’s court — in large part to maintain these relationships and the loyalty that accompanies them. Custom and princely edict are more prevalent than written codes of law. Autocracy and aristocracy dominate at the state level; republics tend toward oligarchy, plutocracy, or timocracy. In many bureaucracies, clientage and kickbacks are accepted or even lauded as a natural element of governance. But power is typically decentralized; sovereigns struggle to enforce their will at the state’s periphery. On the community level, policies and conflicts are typically addressed democratically or by community leaders chosen through acclamation or vote, whose voices hold greater sway than those of distant rulers. Democracies are more likely to resemble classical Athens than modern governments. Most princes need buy-in from local leaders, who likewise need the people’s support. Increasing demands on or taking powers away from those lower in the hierarchy is an invitation to revolt; as a result, archaic laws and traditions may persist long past the point of

meaninglessness. Law enforcement typically falls to soldiers, private guard forces, traveling magistrates, or a local posse. Professional enforcers prioritize maintaining order and supporting the interests of the wealthy and powerful.

### Languages

Creation’s great Directional languages — Low Realm, Riverspeak, Flametongue, and the like — are best described as language families consisting of countless related languages and dialects, with various degrees of mutual intelligibility. People often know multiple languages and dialects, both within their native language family and beyond it. Reasons for this include personal travel, dealings with foreign travelers and immigrants, exogamous relationships, or rule by foreign conquerors. Someone gifted with languages, such as a typical player character, can adapt quickly to another language in the same family. The Storyteller may call for Linguistics rolls upon first encountering a new language in a familiar language family, but should be generous in the name of sword-and-sorcery genre adherence and for ease of play.

### Demographics

Seven centuries ago, the Great Contagion killed ninetenths of the world’s human populace. Famine, mundane pestilence, war, and other misfortunes followed — and remain ongoing. Overall, Creation’s population rebounded across the centuries, especially in wealthy and militarily powerful polities like the Realm. But in some places, civilization is still rebuilding; others remain largely wilderness to this day or became so due to post-Contagion disasters.

Still, few places are truly uninhabited. Some places may seem unattractive to settlers due to extreme environment, poor soils, limited mineral wealth, and other factors. But given time, folk will spread out to take advantage of unclaimed resources — and to avoid wars, oppressive laws, crushing taxes, or the like. Populations lean heavily toward rural agriculture to support relatively small urban numbers. Even the most urbanized polities rarely have more than one-quarter of their people living in cities. Likewise, only locales with enormous resources — typically acquired through ongoing raiding or tribute — can maintain sizable cohorts of aristocrats, full-time soldiers, artisans, merchants, etc. High urban mortality, including from

EX3

illness, malnutrition, and violence, may require immigration to maintain population numbers. Most cities and towns are small by our standards. Towns generally contain only a few thousand people; cities typically range from 10,000 to 50,000 people. These numbers vary with climate, agricultural and sanitation technology, administrative sophistication, centralization of authority, supernatural boons, and so forth. Only wealthy, powerful polities support and maintain stable city populations approaching 100,000, let alone such rare 1,000,000+ metropolises as the Imperial City or Nexus.

Exalted rarely assigns concrete numbers to cities’ populations, instead providing rough estimates of how large or how crowded a place is. In part, this gives Storytellers the option of adjusting location details to fit their chronicles. Additionally, though much thought and research goes into making Creation feel as realistic as possible, its writers and developers are laypersons; declaring specific numbers risks introducing errors.

### Measuring Time

Various cultures use different tools for measuring time: sundials, water clocks, graduated candles, hourglasses, and even the Varang City-States’ famous mechanical clocks. Sophisticated devices are largely the province of the rich and powerful; common folk instead observe celestial bodies’ positions or recite sutras of an established length. While the Realm and much of the Threshold follows a traditional calendar year (Exalted, p. 73), different calendar systems find use elsewhere in Creation. Similarly, not everyone measures years from the Scarlet Empress’s accession. For example, Iscomay’s lunar calendar counts back to when the Book of the Bear was written, Zephyr employs regnal lists based on each Sky Prince’s accession, and the Seventh Legion’s system of five-year cycles, 25-year eras, and 125-year epochs counts back to the Dragon-Blooded Shogunate’s founding.

### Conveniences

Many societies possess systems for heating, cooling, refrigeration, or other conveniences. Hypocausts, kang bed-stoves, masonry heaters, ondols, and similar radiant heating methods warm rooms and floors. Windcatcher towers direct cool air through buildings without mechanical aid. A yakhchāl’s above-ground dome pours cooler air into subterranean chambers,

### ANACHRONISMS ARE OKAY

Technology in Creation ranges from the Bronze Age to the Age of Sail, and varies from place to place. This allows Storytellers and players flexibility in what tools to make available in play, and helps various locales emulate specific fantasy subgenres. We justify this by Creation’s post-post-apocalyptic nature allowing unexpected rediscoveries, and because technological development needn’t follow one specific track.

making and preserving ice in the desert. Some societies even possess flowing-water toilets that flush waste through sewer systems.

While various light sources — hearths, oil lamps, candles, rushlights, and so forth — find widespread use, few people can afford the the expense to produce sufficient light for reading or fine crafting after dark. A few cities arrange street lighting on key thoroughfares using candles or oil lamps; most nighttime travel requires bringing one’s own light or hiring a torchbearer, and remains difficult and risky.

### Warfare

The farming calendar heavily impacts warfare; fulltime soldiers are rare, available only to rich and powerful polities, so most soldiers are citizen volunteers or rural conscripts. Military leaders prefer to march in summer — it’s easier to raise an army while crops are growing. They raid and conquer while weather is warm, days are long, and nights are mild, then send conscripts home at harvesttime.

But campaigning doesn’t cease in autumn. Mercenaries fight whenever coin says so. Wandering or displaced soldiers offer services year-round, bolstering would-be conquerors’ reserves or besieging resource-rich towns. Some become bandits or river pirates, seizing harvests in fall and winter; nearby kingdoms must march in those seasons to fend them off. Lastly, empires like the Realm maintain professional soldiers in all seasons. Raids, border skirmishes, and small-scale ritual conflicts far outnumber full-scale wars. Reining in unsanctioned military actions by one’s own common folk and vassals — or disavowing while privately supporting such — may occupy much of a sovereign’s diplomatic and political efforts.

A state’s military may see more action against rioters, bandits, and rebels than against neighbors. Indeed, city

Navigation, Maps, and Borders

### THESE MAPS ARE YOURS

Compasses point to the Imperial Mountain at Creation’s center, simplifying travel to and from the Blessed Isle, but complicating other forms of navigation. Travelers rely on the rising and setting sun for direction; they may have access to other tools such as sextants, star charts, and charts of winds and currents.

Published Exalted maps aren’t intended to be comprehensive, and the Storyteller mustn’t feel restricted by them. Individual playgroups should feel free to add new cities, islands, territories, and even entire continents as the story demands. Likewise, playgroups can define blank areas as civilized or wilderness as needed. Lastly, feel free to rename, alter, and delete locales as you choose to better suit your chronicle’s needs — though you should mention that you’re doing so to your players before the chronicle begins so that they aren’t caught by surprise.

### Travel and Communication

Journeys in Creation suffer restrictions unfamiliar to modern urban readers. Foot travel is slow and arduous. Mounts require fodder, water, and rest, including days of recovery time after strenuous journeys. Vehicles demand maintenance and repair. Roads are few outside of settlements; smooth, intact roads are far fewer. Roads and trails alike usually bend and twist to follow elevation lines and avoid difficult terrain, except for rare, well-engineered roads built by the Realm and other wealthy civilizations, or leftovers from the Shogunate or the First Age.

Going off-road slows land travel considerably and increases risks from wild animals and bandits. Rivers, swamps, and lakes require boats to traverse if a bridge, ford, or causeway can’t be found.

Under ideal circumstances, maritime travel is far quicker, more efficient, and more comfortable than by land. But it’s dependent on infrastructure, winds, and currents, and bears risks of its own — storms, doldrums, and pirates.

For the most part, communication requires travel. A few societies possess faster methods — whether heliographs, semaphore, or sorcery — but typically even important messages must go by courier. Folk of lesser means must send letters that pass through the hands of whatever travelers are going that way, or else visit interlocutors personally. Most news travels slowly and capriciously via rumor and gossip.

Geographers in the Realm, Lookshy, and some other societies possess sophisticated mapmaking skills. However, as drawing and copying maps is time-consuming and requires specialized expertise, most travelers make do with a travel schematic (an itinerarium) or a list of landmarks (a periplus). Local maps are often crude at best — except for land ownership maps drawn by surveyors, which tend toward greater accuracy and sophistication.

Political borders are often vague and blurry. Borders typically follow natural boundaries such as rivers and forests, leading to strife when, for example, a river changes its course. Buffer zones can exist with no official claimant, while disputed territories may be claimed by two or more polities. Such borderlands attract nomadic peoples, outlaws, and others seeking to avoid control by sedentary civilizations.

Currency and Finance

While Guild dinars are widely accepted throughout the Threshold, they’re by no means the only — or, indeed, the primary — medium of exchange. Setting aside how most businesses, banks, and governments deal more in credit or corvée labor than in coin, the Guild’s “silver standard” isn’t a single universal denomination used everywhere. Rather, it’s a tool by which the Guild pressures local markets to transact with silver coinage using relatively standard weights and measures. Individual polities and business ventures produce their own coinage — not all of it is silver, and not all silver coinage in the Threshold neatly matches the Directorate dinar. In addition, most coinage comes in smaller denominations than the dinar, which is an immensely valuable coin despite being the Guild’s smallest official denomination. Most smaller coins use lesser metals like gold, copper, or bronze; this allows governments to spend most of their silver on imported grain, mercenaries’ pay, tribute, or the like without taking all of their coinage out of circulation. The specifics of hard currency (and other forms of money) — such as purity, wear, debasement, counterfeiting, and rates of exchange — could fill many books, but they’re of little concern to Exalted heroes, and are better left to a Dynast’s steward or the local money changer.

EX3

Realm banks, Guild factors, merchants, and wealthy speculators employ a variety of fiscal instruments, such as promissory notes and letters of credit to tradeable stocks, bonds, and options. There’s no universally accepted standard for such instruments; they may take distinct names and forms in different polities and cultures. As with currency, the specifics aren’t relevant to the freewheeling sword-and-sorcery adventure of the typical Exalted chronicle.

Ceremonies such as scripted greetings, initiatory oaths, and similar formalities carry elements of a fraternal organization or mystery cult, as does the secret cant these ceremonies demand. Membership grants a sense of belonging and importance, helping members to identify with the Guild and its tenets — financial stability, longterm profit, independence from supernatural forces, maintaining its reputation, and expanding its mercantile interests throughout Creation.

### The Guild

Most consider Guild dues — funneled first to the local hub city’s Guild council, then to the Nexus Directorate — fair compensation for membership benefits. While factors and Hierarchs do grow fat on this wealth, they also use it to support the Guild: investing in talented young Guildfolk’s careers and in risky but lucrative ventures, undermining non-Guild rivals, and quashing troublemaking by disenchanted Guild members.

Rather than a monolithic Creation-wide corporate entity, the Guild (Exalted, p. 77) is a loose syndicate and mutual aid society, composed of countless local businesses, regional trading companies, affiliated financiers, and the like. Membership offers such perks as a network of trade contacts wherever one travels; participation in Guild caravans and convoys; preferential treatment from fellow members; and increased trust from local buyers and sellers in areas with popular, well-run Guild infrastructure. Meanwhile, as the Guild secures dominance in a region, merchants who fail to join suffer from their lack of these benefits.

Still, membership presents downsides. Dues-paying merchants and businesses must abide by Guild practices, limiting their own freedom to operate. Some must sever ties with non-Guild business partners and suppliers, or charge them double or triple their old rates.

### HOW COMMON ARE SUPERNATURAL

### THINGS?

Guild operations are largely decentralized. Councils, factors, and merchant princes operate with limited oversight, imposing their own policies and approaches when expanding into new regions. Specific locales — from individual cities, to regions, to entire Directions — have distinct Guild cultures and traditions influenced by local laws and customs, and by the personalities and goals of members and factions. Intra-Guild competition and policy disagreements can escalate from heated arguments to trade wars.

### Spirits

’ prevalence should vary with your playgroup’s tastes and the chronicle’s needs. In one chronicle, most locations and noteworthy objects have gods, wildernesses throng with elementals, and shadowlands teem with ghosts. In another, what few gods still oversee their purviews remain concealed within their sanctums, while other spirits only appear in places of power

The same applies to manses and demesnes. Whether you can find manses in every city or only in a few scattered ruins, and whether demesnes lie strewn across the landscape or only in remote wildernesses, depends on story structure and personal taste.

Some areas have successfully limited Guild intrusion. This is often the work of countervailing mercantile institutions using similar methods to the Guild’s own. Examples include the Varang City-States’ counting-temples (p. XX), Randan’s craft-lodges (p. XX), and the Western Trade Alliance (Heirs to the Shogunate, p. 246). Beyond the Scavenger Lands, great distances, seas, and hostile terrain also diminish Guild penetration.

Guild Structure

The Guild has three main branches. Artisans range from apprentices to prestigious masters; these often assemble in lodges that oversee and control local production and sales. Merchants include street vendors, innkeepers, wholesalers, caravan masters, and sea-captains; the most successful are dubbed merchant-princes, while those rich enough to retire and become investors are called factors. Lastly, administrators — clerks, bookkeepers, aides, and the like — manage the Guild’s inner workings.

Most settlements with a sizable Guild presence have a Guild warden to enforce the Guild’s rules. This includes collecting dues, verifying weights and measures, and investigating reports of fraud, abuse, etc. In cities where the Guild maintains a good reputation, a dedicated warden is usually responsible. Cities of major economic and political importance to the Guild — often at a nexus of key trade routes — are termed hub cities. Each hub city has a nine-member Guild council, composed primarily of local factors, that oversees local trade policy, mediates disputes, and channels funds to the Directorate. The Directorate

The Directorate’s (p. XX) job in large part is to smooth over such disagreements, applying economic, political, and social pressure to quash local Guild practices that might cause significant backlash or undermine the organization’s unity and culture. It also attracts ambitious Guild members; many find the prospect of claiming a Hierarch’s seat more appealing than establishing a Guild splinter faction.

The Guild and the Supernatural

Supernatural beings — from gods and elementals to the Exalted themselves — find it challenging to rise to the top of the Guild’s hierarchy. This stems from a deep-rooted ideological prejudice against outsiders coming into an extant Guild culture and using its people as tools serving some private agenda, reinforced by exclusionary language embedded in its ceremonies, oaths, and scriptures. Out of character, it helps prevent “take charge of the Guild” from being an easy, one-sizefits-all solution for your Circle’s political and economic issues.

As a result, the Guild centers of the Scavenger Lands have a symbiotic relation with the Seventh Legion. Lookshy’s gentes offer opportunities for advancement to outcaste artisans, financiers, and merchants barred from the Guild’s upper echelons.

## The Supernatural World

While other Exalted books address supernatural setting elements in detail, it’s worth reviewing them through the lens of mortal experience and society.

Spirits

The Celestial Bureaucracy dispatches gods from Heaven to Creation to oversee all manner of things — cities, rivers, beasts, professions, events — whose

EX3

disposition matters to the planned course of destiny. Not everything has a god. Larger and more important things are more likely to have gods assigned to them; it’s rare (but not unheard-of ) for a god to oversee an individual tree, house, or flock.

RULES AREN’T PHYSICS

Exalted assumes that things in Creation largely work in familiar ways except where narratively appropriate. Game mechanics are meant as a tool to serve the narrative. This causes problems when mechanics imply that mundane people and things work differently than players expect. When not using game mechanics to resolve player characters’ success or failure, and when the supernatural isn’t involved, we strongly recommend that Storytellers prioritize how things work in the real world — or, where appropriate, follow the narrative language of action movies — over peculiar rules outputs. Creation’s people are like us; the game gains nothing and loses much by extrapolating alien qualities for them from rules interaction.

Gods typically remain concealed in their sanctums or travel the world invisible and immaterial, minimizing interaction with mortals as per divine law. Even gods who abuse their power, establishing cults or otherwise toying with mortals, often only interact directly with priests, lovers, or the like. As such, people rarely encounter them directly. A few gods move freely among mortals or openly stalk the wilderness, inciting rumors and legends.

It’s not always clear when environmental phenomena or strange coincidences are natural or divine in origin. Thus, gods don’t necessarily need to appear directly or produce unmistakable miracles to receive worship. Though elementals are rarely malicious, their peculiar drives and manifestation of elemental forces can make them dangerous for ordinary mortals. As such, human societies avoid regions where elementals dwell in numbers. Still, those who make a living in the wilderness — hunters, trappers, herbalists, scavengers, and the like — occasionally encounter them. And intelligent, gregarious elementals such as the South’s humanlike ifrits occasionally travel among mortals.

While most ghosts linger in the hidden Underworld, some aid their descendants at times, and folk often venerate ancestors through cult worship and offerings. But as with gods, ancestor cults needn’t witness blatant spiritual intervention to revere the dead. Meanwhile, hungry ghosts are among Creation’s most common and most feared spirits. In places where too many people died too quickly for proper burial, swarms of hungry ghosts can leave the region all but uninhabitable.

Hungry for human dreams and emotions, the Fair Folk often present active threats to human society, whether leading faerie armies or slipping into settlements to beset unwary sleepers. The bordermarches and middlemarches where they dwell likewise inspire fear, as mortal interlopers often find themselves tainted by the Wyld. But society doesn’t entirely shun the fae — a few find uneasy roles as artisans or guardians, while slavers sell people to their courts in exchange for faerie wonders and souleaten slaves.

### Magical People

All sorts of human folk wield supernatural powers. Exactly how others perceive them depends on local culture.

By and large, those who serve their society as intermediaries with the supernatural are well-regarded. Those in society’s highest strata, such as high priests and court astrologers, provide legitimacy to authorities by asserting a divine mandate for rule. Those of more ordinary standing — lesser priests, shamans, astrologers, tea leaf readers, dream interpreters, and so forth — may offer advice and guidance to ordinary folk on both life-changing and prosaic matters. Meanwhile, people who wield supernatural forces for personal gain — such as sorcerers, God-Blooded adventurers, and outcaste mercenaries — often find themselves feared by folk wary of their power and ambition.

### Places of Power

Dragon lines — invisible flows of elemental power that wend through earth, sea, and sky — converge to form demesnes that manifest weird supernatural phenomena and allow geomancers to construct magical manses. Demesnes and manses attract spirits and beasts that find their energies pleasing, as well as Exalted, sorcerers, and other powerful beings aiming to wield those energies. As such, mortals typically regard manses and demesnes as holy or cursed, and rarely visit them except to petition, bargain with, or serve a site’s masters.

EX3

While gods send reports to Heaven by numinous means, they also attend spirit courts where they meet with peers and immediate superiors among earthly divinities. Other local spirits, especially the more intelligent elementals, may attend as well. Spirit courts typically meet in isolated locales; rumors spread of unearthly manifestations, warning away ordinary folk.

All manner of other magical locales lie scattered throughout the Threshold. These range from First Age ruins to bordermarches, shadowlands, focal points of sorcerous workings, and stranger things. In places offering no obvious threat, such as benign sorceries or ruins cleared of threats by scavengers, people settle in and take advantage of their benefits. Ordinary folk largely avoid potentially dangerous sites, or develop taboos to discourage triggering their perils.

EX3

From frozen Northern tundra to vast Southern deserts, from dense Eastern forests to the West’s endless waters, Creation shelters myriad cultures and civilizations. Night horrors stalk the farmlands outside Whitewall, while residents and refugees within struggle with overpopulation and hunger. In the rebel satrapy of Fray, dragonlord Hanto Galina has named herself Empress and laid claim to the Scarlet Throne. Intelligent wolves rule in Wolf’s Paw, adopting human finery and demanding loyalty from human servants. By the Dreaming Sea, Tzakul relicts play their soul game, competing to seize opponents’ bodies. Varangian astrologers study citizens’ horoscopes, setting social status from the moment of birth. Alien structures loom over Decanthus, a Southwestern city recently returned from Hell. Smiths in the empire of Makelo produce fantastic works, their craft handed down from the forge-goddess Ninegala. An ominous heart beats beneath the Silverswept Plains, drawing the plains clans into the entity’s inhuman nightmares.

Across the Eight Directions provides details about locations throughout Creation, including their history, culture, government structure, religious practices, and more. It introduces new settings, and expands upon familiar locales. It also discusses prominent figures active in each location, and presents information on local neighbors such as allies, rival cities, or wilderness areas with intriguing mysteries for explorers to encounter.
